questions.question: On hospital day 3, he becomes unresponsive and is transferred to the intensive care unit. while reviewing the medical record, the ICU team discovers that the patient received 1o0 units of regular insulin intravenously instead of the intended 10 units. A bedside glucose after arrival in the intensive care unit is 18 mg/dL. He is stabilized with dextrose infusion and recovers fully. The hospital launches an investigation into the incident. which of the following actions would best represent a root cause analysis?

options.A: Issuing a formal reprimand to nurse who administered the insulin
options.B: Identifying hypothetical reasons insulin overdoses may occur
options.C: Interviewing all staff who interacted with the patient prior to receiving insulin
options.D: Increasing the frequency of blood glucose monitoring in all insulin-treated patients
options.E: Requiring staff education on insulin pharmacology

questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This man developed severe hypoglycemia due to a tenfold overdose of insulin, a serious and preventable medical error. A root cause analysis (RcA) is a structured process to investigate adverse events and identify system failures that allowed the error to occur. Interviewing all staff who were involved in the patient's care prior to the insulin administration is a key part of RCA. This process gathers firsthand accounts, uncovers safety issues, and helps the team understand how the error occurred in real time. The goal is to identify underlying causes of adverse events. analysis is not about assigning individual blame but about identifying system-level flaws. Blaming individuals undermines the culture needed to improve patient safety.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Identifying hypothetical reasons for insulin overdoses does not meet the standards of a root cause analysis. RCA requires an investigation of the specific event, not a speculative or theoretical discussion.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Increasing the frequency of glucose monitoring may reduce harm from future dosing errors, but it does not address why this specific error happened. This is a mitigation strategy rather than a root cause analysis.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Requiring staff education on insulin pharmacology may help improve knowledge, but does not explore system-based issues like drug labeling, workflow design, or lack of safety checks. RCA focuses on comprehensive systems improvement rather than education alone.

questions.question: A 74-year-old man is hospitalized for acute systolic heart failure. His son reports that the patient's home is poorly maintained and that his father often does not leave the house for days at a time. Which of the following may have prevented this man's readmission to the hospital?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): Ideally, when patients are discharged from a hospital their health status is improved and they are ready for a return to community living. Unfortunately, readmissions to the hospital after discharge Mc G are common and some are preventable. Readmissions to the hospital within 30 days of discharge are monitored as a quality-of-care metric. Among medical conditions tracked by the Us Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMs), heart failure has the highest rate of 30-day readmissions, followed by pneumonia and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (CopD). A number of strategies are used to prepare patients for hospital discharge and reduce the risk that a readmission will occur. These include pre-discharge education, close follow-up after discharge, nutrition education, physical therapy evaluation, and involvement of social workers. The patient in the question has cognitive impairment, lives alone, and has limited family support. These "social" issues are ideal for intervention by a social worker. Duties of a social worker include working with patients, families, and community resources to meet the needs of the patient after discharge. A social worker could have provided this patient with transportation resources, explored barriers to getting his prescriptions filled, suggested a pill box and counseled the patient's son about the importance of checking on his dad frequently with attention to medication use, salt intake and review of daily weights.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Discharge checklists are useful for ensuring nothing is missed at the time of discharge. This could include things like prescriptions and follow-up clinic appointments. There is no evidence in the question that something was forgotten at the time of discharge. Based on the description of his living situation, a social worker is what he needs more than anything else.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Education about disease is an important component of preparing for discharge. Heart failure teaching includes education about avoiding sodium, daily weight (because a weight increase may indicate fluid retention and early heart failure), and medication compliance. This man was provided many elements of standard heart failure education at discharge including instructions to avoid sodium and follow-up with his physician. It is unlikely that additional heart failure education would have prevented his readmission. A social work evaluation is what he needs most. they evaluate the ability of patients to transfer out of bed and ambulate. Special note: Physical therapists evaluate and treat mobility issues in hospitalized patients. Occupational therapists evaluate and treat issues related to daily living activities such as dressing and bathing.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Discharge time outs have been proposed as an intervention to reduce readmissions. These involve stopping the discharge process with all healthcare team members present to hold a "time out" and ensure the patient is completely ready for discharge. questions.question: A 35-year-old woman presents for a discussion of weight loss. She weighs 220 Ibs, with a body mass index (BMI) of 40 kg/m?. She wishes to lose weight. Her blood pressure is 155/92 mmHg. Which of the following should be recommended at this time?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): Obesity is defined as a body mass index greater than 30 kg/m². The initial management of patients with obesity is lifestyle modification. This includes a combination of diet, exercise, and behavior modification. Patients should receive nutritional and exercise counseling, with goals for weight loss. Other interventions for obesity like drug therapy and bariatric surgery are only indicated after a trial of lifestyle modification. Of note, this woman has elevated blood pressure and may have hypertension (she needs a second measurement before the diagnosis can be made). Weight loss often reduces blood pressure to the normal range among hypertensive patients without need for medication.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Bariatric surgery restricts the amount of food the stomach can hold, which leads to weight loss. It is indicated only after a trial of lifestyle modification.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Liraglutide is an analog of human glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) used in treatment of diabetes. GLP-1 is an incretin, a substance that increases insulin release from the pancreas, which can be beneficial in diabetes. An additional effect of liraglutide is suppression of appetite. For this reason, it has been studied for weight loss, but is only indicated after a trial of lifestyle modification.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Lorcaserin is a weight-loss drug that activates central nervous system serotonin receptors, leading to early satiety and decreased food intake. This is indicated only after a trial of lifestyle modification.

questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): Mechanical falls among geriatric patients are common, and often lead to a loss of independence. The cause of falls is usually multifactorial and involves many factors including postural control, vision impairment, and osteoarthritis. Drugs affecting the central nervous system are among the most common medications associated with falls. These include benzodiazepines like alprazolam, antipsychotics, and antidepressants. Geriatricians regularly review medications of elderly patients, looking for opportunities to "de- prescribe" any drug associated with increased fall risk. questions.explanation: Answer F (correct answer): The Tanner stages (also known as sexual maturity ratings) are a classification system for tracking development of secondary sexual characteristics during puberty. Due to natural variation, individuals progress through the sexual development at varying rates. Tanner stages provide a standard naming format for pubertal development of male genitalia, female breast development, and pubic hair development in males and female. Tanner stage 1 always represents the pre-pubertal state. For breast development, Tanner stage 2 is the onset of thelarche (breast development), which is indicated by formation of breast buds. Breast buds are swellings beneath the nipple, creating a small mound of tissue on the chest wall. In stage 2, the buds do not extend beyond the areolae. In Tanner stage 3, the breast buds grow in size and extend beyond the borders of the glands in stage 3. In Tanner stage 4, the areola elevates above the breast, forming a second mound of tissue and giving the entire breast a "double scoop" appearance. In Tanner stage 5, the areolar mound recedes into the breast. At this point, the breast has reached full adult size. The question describes Tanner 3 breast development. In stage 3, the hair becomes darker, courser, and curlier and extends laterally. Stage 4 pubic hair extends above the pubic bones but not to the thighs. In stage 5, pubic hair extends from thigh to thigh. The question describes Tanner stage 4 pubic hair. Puberty usually begins by age 10 in girls and age 12 in boys. Puberty is usually complete by age 14 in girls and age 16 in boys. About 20% of adult height is achieved due to a growth spurt associated with puberty. The limbs accelerate before the trunk, which can cause arms, legs, and feet that are bigger than the trunk, giving awkward proportioning to teenagers going through puberty. MSW

Up to 40% of high-school boys report having had sexual intercourse.

Answers A, B, C, D (incorrect answers): This boy's masturbation and fantasies are normal. Referral to a psychiatrist is not indicated. Evaluation of sex hormones or testicular anatomy by ultrasound is unnecessary.

questions.question: A 74-year-old man is evaluated for cough and lethargy. Five days ago, he developed a cough productive of yellow sputum. Vital signs include blood pressure 100/70 mmHg, pulse 120/min, respiratory rate 40/min, and room air oxygen saturation 89%. A chest X-ray shows a left lower lobe infiltrate. Serum pH is 7.3 (normal 7.4) and lactate is 5 mmol/L (normal <1). Shown below is the chemical structure of glycine. In this man, glycine is most likely to be found with what overall (net) charge?
questions.explanation: Answer B (correct answer): This man has lactic acidosis due to sepsis from pneumonia. His serum pH is 7.3 which is below the amine pKa of glycine (9.6) and above the carboxylic acid pKa (2.3) of glycine. At this pH, the amine group will have a +1 charge (NH3+) and the carboxylic acid group will have a -1 charge (COO-). Thus, glycine is most likely to be found in the uncharged (o) state. group with a pKa below plasma (e.g., less than 3). These amino acids will be neutral with no charge in plasma just like glycine. Only amino acids with a charged side chain assume a charge of +1 or -1 in plasma.

questions.question: A 6-month old boy is evaluated for irritability. The baby has been febrile and difficult to console for the past 24 hours. On exam, the skin is jaundiced and the fingers are swollen. Laboratory testing shows a hemoglobin of 6g/dL (normal 9.5 to 13) and LDH of 900 IU/L (normal <300). Hemoglobin electrophoresis shows the presence of hemoglobin S. which of the following features of hemoglobin S (compared to normal hemoglobin) is primarily responsible for this baby's presentation?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This baby has clinical features of sickle cell anemia including hemolytic anemia with jaundice, dactylitis (sausage digits), and presence of hemoglobin S. In this disorder, the amino acid valine is polar and hydrophilic. Thus, the valine portions in Hbs display increased hydrophobicity compared to normal hemoglobin. These portions bury themselves within nonpolar sections of the folded, globular hemoglobin protein to avoid exposure to water within cells. This changes the conformation of hemoglobin leading to the clinical features of sickle cell anemia. Normal hemoglobin contains the hydrophilic/polar amino acid glutamate. Because of its polarity, glutamate is located on the outside of the hemoglobin near water within cells.

Answers B,C,D,E(incorrectanswers):Valine is nonpolar and, therefore,demonstrates lesspolarity compared with the polar amino acid glutamate. Valine (C5H11NO2) has a smaller molecular weight of 117 g/mol than glutamate (C5H8NO4; 147g/mol). Valine has the same number of nitrogen molecules compared with glutamate. The two amino acids have the same number of carbons.

questions.question: Researchers are studying neuronal proteins among patients with Alzheimer's disease and normal controls. An amino acid substitution is identified in a cytoskeletal protein among cells from Alzheimer's disease patients. The substituted amino acid has the titration curve shown below. Which of the following most likely represents the amino acid under evaluation?
questions.explanation: Answer A (correct answer): The amino acid titration curve has three plateaus indicating an ionizable side chain chain with acid-base properties. Of the four answers, only arginine has an ionizable side chain. The other amino acid choices would have only two plateaus in a titration curve: one for the amine group and one for the carboxylic acid group. Glycine has no side chain so cannot have a third plateau. The side chain of alanine is a CH3 group that is nonpolar and cannot be protonated. The side chain of phenylalanine is a carbon ring also incapableofcarrying aproton.

questions.question: Researchers are studying a neuronal cell membrane protein associated with Alzheimer's disease. One portion of the protein contains a sequence of twenty identical amino acids. This sequence is embedded within the phospholipid bilayer of the cell membrane. Which of the following most likely represents the amino acid found in this part of the protein?
questions.explanation: Answer B (correct answer): Amino acids found within the cell membrane phospholipid bilayer are hydrophobic. To avoid water, they embed within the membrane, away from the water outside the cell and within the cytosol. All amino acids have an amine group (NH3) and a carboxylic acid group (COOH). What distinguishes one amino acid from another is the side chain. This is also what determines an amino acid's hydrophobic or hydrophilic properties. Of the answer choices, only leucine has a hydrophobic side chain made up entirely of carbons and hydrogens. Structures made of carbons and hydrogens (like lipids) tend to be nonpolar and hydrophobic. They willnotdissolveinwater. Arginine, aspartate, and glutamate have polar side chains which are hydrophilic. These side chains contain oxygen and nitrogen which are polar molecules. Water is polar and polarized structures are hydrophilic. Polarized amino acids are less likely to be found within the phospholipid bilayer of cell membranes. They are usually on the outside of the membrane exposed to water.

questions.question: A 42-year-old man is evaluated for paresthesias. He is a refugee from a war-ravaged village in Croatia. A month ago he arrived at a military camp where he was provided with three meals per day, clothing, and shelter. On arrival at the camp, he was diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis and started on anti-mycobacterial therapy. He now complains of numbness and and several ulcers on his oral mucosa. Deficiency of which of the following vitamins may explain this man's symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This manhas oral ulcers and glossitis (inflammationof the tongue).Maintenance of the oral mucosa is critical to prevent the entry of bacteria that can lead to inflammation. For this reason, stomatitis and glossitis are common to a number of conditions where cellular metabolism is impaired leading to mucosal breakdown. For example, chemotherapy patients commonly suffer from "mucositis" meaning oral inflammationandpain. Stomatitis, glossitis, and peripheral neuropathy (numbness/tingling) are seen in many vitamin deficiency syndromes. The key feature in this man's history is tuberculosis. He is likely being treated with isoniazid (INH). This drug is a classic inhibitor of vitamin B6 metabolism.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency is associated with dry beriberi, wet beriberi, and Wernicke-Korsakoffsyndrome. been provided meals for 4 weeks). When deficiency does occur, it often co-exists with other B vitamins deficiencies. Classic symptoms include cheilosis, scaling and cracks at the corners of the mouth.

Answer C (incorrect answer): By causing B6 deficiency, INH may also lead to B3 (niacin) deficiency since niacin synthesis requires B6. Niacin deficiency results in pellagra. The dominant clinical feature is dermatitis (red skin similar to sunburn) in sun-exposed areas. Stomatitis, glossitis, and peripheral neuropathy are not typical.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Vitamin B5 is required for the synthesis of acetyl-CoA. Deficiency is rare outside of severe malnutrition. When deficiency does occur, it often co-exists with other B vitamins deficiencies. Based on "burning feet syndrome" which involves burning pain of the extremities.

questions.question: Researchers are evaluating a new drug for the treatment of systolic heart failure. Phase I clinical trials are halted due to high acid. Which of the following adverse effects most likely occurred in patients on the drug?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): Vitamin B5 (pantothenic acid) is required for the synthesis of acetyl-CoA. Deficiency is rare as the vitamin is widely distributed in many foods. When deficiency does occur, it often co-exists with other B vitamins deficiencies. Based on animal models, vitamin B5 deficiency is known to cause adrenal failure. The vitamin is thought to be necessary for the maintenance of a normal adrenal structure. Another classic feature of B5 deficiency is the "burning feet syndrome" which involves burning pain of the extremities.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Megaloblastic anemia occurs in folate and vitamin B12 deficiency.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Cheilosis refers to scaling and cracks at the corners of the mouth. It is a classic feature of vitamin B2 (riboflavin) deficiency.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Seizures are seen in vitamin B6 deficiency as this vitamin is necessary for the synthesis of neurotransmitters.

Answer E (incorrect answer): High output heart failure occurs in vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 24-year-old male begins a new diet and exercise regimen. As part of this, he consumes ten B complex vitamin tablets four stocking-glove pattern. The substance most likely causing this man's symptoms is involved in the synthesis of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This man has evidence of peripheral neuropathy while consuming massive doses of B vitamins. While deficiency of many B vitamins may lead to neuropathy, the only major B vitamin that exhibits toxicity inhigh dosesis vitamin B6.Peripheral neuropathy as described in the question is typical of B6 toxicity. VitaminB6 is a cofactor in a number of metabolic processes including synthesis of neurotransmitters, cystathionine,andheme.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Thymidine is a nucleotide. Synthesis requires folate and vitamin B12.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Acetyl-CoA requires vitamin B5 (pantothenic acid).

Answer D (incorrect answer): Flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) requires vitamin B2 (riboflavin).

Answer E (incorrect answer): Tryptophan is an essential amino acid acquired through the diet.

questions.question: A 6-year-old girl is evaluated for muscle cramps. She is a refugee who fled her village in the African Sahara when local militia invaded. She has consumed fewer than 400 calories per day for the past month. She complains of pain in her hands and feet. Her legs are "cramped" and she has difficulty walking. On exam, she is emaciated. Ribs are visible through the skin of her chest. Lower extremities display distal sensory loss and weakness. Deficiency of which of the following vitamins is most likely responsible for this girl's findings?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This girl has dry beriberi caused by vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency. Features of dry beriberi include muscle cramps, sensory loss, burning pain, and paresthesias (numbness/tingling). In contrast, wet beriberi (also caused by thiamine deficiency) presents as high-output heart failure with dyspnea, peripheral edema,and lowerextremitypitting edema. Similar symptoms to dry beriberi may occur with deficiencies of vitamins B6 and B12. In addition, vitamin B5 may cause the burning feet syndrome. Deficiency of these four vitamins (B1, B5, B6, and B12) should come to mind when faced with nutritional deficiency questions involving peripheral neuropathy.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Vitamin B2 deficiency causes dermatitis, glossitis, and cheilitis. Neuropathy is unusual.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Vitamin B3 (niacin) deficiency causes pellagra which consists of dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia (the 3 Ds). Neuropsychiatric symptoms (confusion) may occur but neuropathy is not typical.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy which presents with bruising, skin findings, and bleedinggums. Mc Graw

questions.question: Researchers are investigating an enzyme inhibitor of unknown cellular kinase. When this inhibitor is administered to lab animals, symptoms of a vitamin deficiency develop. The activity of which of the following vitamins is most likely deficient in these lab animals?
questions.explanation: Answer C (correct answer): Kinases are enzymes that phosphorylate a substrate. Of the B vitamins listed, only vitamin B6 requires phosphorylation to its active form, pyridoxal phosphate. This reaction is catalyzed by the enzymepyridoxalkinase. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 54-year-old female presents for evaluation of joint pain and fevers. She has a history of systolic heart failure with a left wrists. She also reports subjective fevers. Review of systems is negative for headache, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. On physical exam, she has an erythematous rash on her cheeks. She was started on isosorbide dinitrate and hydralazine six months ago for treatment of heart failure. Antibodies to which of the following are most likely involved in the pathogenesis of this woman's condition?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This is the typical presentation of drug-induced lupus. Most patients present with signs of inflammation such as fever plus arthritis. The arthritis of lupus (drug-induced or otherwise) is usually polyarticular (more than 5 joints) and symmetrical. Drug-induced lupus is a milder form of lupus. Malar rash is less common. Renal failure, CNs involvement or bone marrow suppression are rare. Drug-induced lupus classically occurs months to years after a patient is exposed to a triggering medication. Medications most associated with drug-induced lupus can be remembered by the mnemonic SHIPPE (Sulfonamides, Hydralazine, Isoniazid, Phenytoin, Procainamide, Etanercept). Drug-induced lupus is an autoimmune reaction involving anti-histone antibodies. One component of histones targeted by the reaction is the H1 histone linker protein which binds to the nucleosome and stabilizes chromatin fibers. Anti-histone antibodies are rarely seen in typical (i.e., non-drug-induced) lupus.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Anti-U1 ribonucleoprotein antibodies are involved in Mixed Connective Tissue Disease (MCTD).

Answer C (incorrect answer): Anti-DNA topoisomerase I antibodies, also known as anti-Scl-70 antibodies, are seeninthediffuseformofscleroderma.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies are associated with celiac disease.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Anti-Smith antibodies are involved in systemic lupus erythematosus (non-drug- induced). In clinical practice, this patient would likely be evaluated for SLE in addition to drug-induced lupus. However, the time course of symptoms emerging after starting hydralazine (one of the SHIPPE medications) is more consistent with drug-induced lupus. Mc Graw 1IH

questions.question: NIH researchers are studying leptin gene expression in diabetic patients. Their data show that diabetic patients have lower levels of leptin compared to age-matched nondiabetic controls. Which of the following changes would explain the decrease in leptin gene expression in the diabetic patient group?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): Epigenetics is the study of changes in gene expression that do not involve changes in the underlying gene itself. A number of biochemical changes to genetic material lead to increased or decreased modifications. For the Step 1 exam, some principles of epigenetics worth knowing are summarized in the slide above. Methylation of DNA leads to decreased gene expression.The enzyme thatcarries out DNA methylationis DNA methyltransferase. Acetylation of histones leads to increased gene expression. The enzyme that carries out histone acetylation is DNA acetyltransferase. The enzyme histone deacetyltransferase removes acetyl groups from histones leading to decreased gene expression. The following mnemonic may be helpful: "Methylation Mutes the genes, Acetylation Activates the genes.

Answer C (incorrect answer): An increase in DNA methyltransferase activity results in methylation of "CG islands" within DNA. These DNA segments contain large amounts of the nucleotide base cytosine which can be methylated. When this occurs, DNA transcription is suppressed leading to less gene expression. Methylation has been described as a potential mechanism for decreased leptin levels in diabetics (see reference). A decrease in DNA methyltransferase activity would have the opposite effect on transcription and gene expression.

Answers A and B (incorrect answers): Histone deacetylase removes acetyl groups from chromatin which decreases transcription and gene expression. A decrease in histone deacetylase activity would increase transcription and expression of leptin. Histone acetyltransferase adds acetyl groups to chromatin. This unwinds chromatinleadingtoincreasedgeneexpression. Reference:https://www.nature.com/articles/srep05282 Mc Graw IH

questions.question: Researchers are studying glucose uptake in tissue culture. Cells are bathed in a glucose solution. The glucose concentration in solution is measured at baseline and after one hour. Shown below are data for this system with and without insulin present. No insulin Which of the following cell types is most likely being studied?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): The data demonstrate glucose uptake that is insulin-dependent. Note that glucose concentration falls significantly in the presence of insulin, but changes minimally when insulin is absent. This is typical of cells with GLuT-4 transporters such as adipose tissue and skeletal muscle. These tissue beds take up more glucose in the presence of insulin due to the insulin-dependent glucose transporter, GLUT-4.

Answers A and D (incorrect answers): Neurons and the placenta contain GLUT3 and GLUT1 transporters which are insulin-independent.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Red blood cells contain GLUT1 transporters which are insulin-independent.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Hepatocytes contain GLUT2 transporters which are insulin-independent. GLUT2 is also bidirectional and can move glucose into or out of cells. Mc Graw

questions.question: A compound is discovered that inhibits celular ATP-dependent membrane sodium pumps. In a laboratory study, the compound is administered to cells in culture. The data show that cells lose their ability to uptake glucose in the presence of the compound. The cells being studied are most likely which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): There are many glucose membrane transporters in the human body but only a few depend on sodium. Sodium-dependent glucose transport occurs in the gastrointestinal tract and the kidneys. In both of these locations, glucose is transported against a concentration gradient (i.e. from a low concentration to a high concentration).I Inordertomove ("co-transport") as shown in the image above. to sodium uptake

Answers A, C, D, and E (incorrect answers): Skeletal muscle myocytes, cells of the central nervous system like astrocytes, red blood cells, and hepatocytes take up glucose in a sodium-independent manner. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 22-year-old male medical student volunteers for a nutrition study. A baseline blood sample is obtained. The student is then given a large bowl of rice to consume over 30 minutes. After eating the rice, a second blood sample is drawn. which of the following substances will increase most significantly in the second blood sample compared to baseline?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): Rice contains large amounts of glucose polymers called starch. In the gut, starch is brokendownand absorbed as themonosaccharide,glucose.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Disaccharides include sucrose, lactose and maltose. These substances are not directly absorbed. They are broken down into glucose which is taken up by enterocytes.

Answers A and E (incorrect answers): Only a very small portion of rice consists of fats such as fatty acids and triglycerides.

Answers D and F (incorrect answers): The only sugars absorbed from the GI tract are the monosaccharides, glucose, fructose, and galactose. Other sugar structures like starch, lactose, glycogen, or sucrose are not absorbed into the bloodstream.These substances are metabolized to monosaccharides for absorption. Mc Graw Hmi

questions.question: A 40-year-old Caucasian woman is evaluated by her primary care doctor for GI distress. For the past few months, she has went out for ice cream with her children and developed abdominal pain and bloating for several hours afterward. A similar the following most likely explains this woman's symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This woman has typical symptoms of lactose intolerance. Lactose is a pizza). Patients with lactose intolerance cannot metabolize lactose into the monosaccharides glucose and galactose. Lactose remains in the GI tract and functions as an osmole that prevents water absorption. This leads to symptoms including abdominal pain, bloating, flatulence, and osmotic diarrhea. Lactose intolerance often develops in adulthood as the digestive enzyme, lactase, is lost ("lactase non-persistence"). This enzyme is important in babies for digestion of mother's milk but is commonly lost in adulthood. Up to 25% of Caucasians develop lactose intoleranceby adulthood.

Answers A, B, and C (incorrect answers): Isolated malabsorption syndromes of glucose, sucrose, and fructose are rare, and much less common than lactose intolerance. Sucrose is also a dissacharide like lactose, but its absorption is not affected inlactose intelerance.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Malabsorption of protein is uncommon but can occur due to bacterial overgrowth or protein-losing enteropathy.

Answer F (incorrect answer): Fat malabsorption may occur in biliary disorders (loss of bile salts for fat emulsification), pancreatitis (loss of digestive enzymes), or diseases of the small intestine (where fats are absorbed). Mc Graw

questions.question: A 2-month-old boy is evaluated for diarrhea. His mother reports that his stools are always loose and foul-smelling. The baby is at the 2oth percentile for height and weight. On exam, hypotonia is noted in all extremities. Serum testing reveals reduced hemoglobin and elevated bilirubin. Intestinal biopsy is shown below: Inability to form which of the following may explain this baby's diarrhea and lab findings?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This baby has abetalipoproteinemia, a rare,autosomal recessive disorder.Children with abetalipoproteinemia are unable to form beta-lipoproteins, structures that contain apoB48 or apoB100. These include VLDL and chylomicrons. In abetalipoproteinemia, a genetic mutation leads to abnormal microsomal triglyceride transfer protein, a protein required for secretion of beta-lipoproteins from the liver or intestines. In the gastrointestinal tract, the inability to form chylomicrons causes steatorrhea and malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins, the major cause of the clinical features at presentation. Additionally, the inability to synthesize VLDL in the liver leads to very low LDL levels and total cholesterol. Symptoms of vitamin E deficiency (a fat-soluble vitamin) are common at presentation including weakness or hemolysis as seen in this baby. Additional findings may occur due to malabsorption of other fat-soluble vitamins (e.g., A, D, K). The classic intestinal biopsy finding is the presence of fat accumulation in enterocytes (shown in image). On peripheral blood smear, up to 90% of red blood cells may be acanthocytes (RBC with spiked membrane). Later in life, signs and symptoms of neurologic dysfunction may develop including lack of muscle

Answers A, B, C (incorrect answers): Low levels of VLDL, IDL, and LDL occur in abetalipoproteinemia but are not the cause of the patient's diarrhea, weakness, and hemolysis.

Answer D (incorrect answer): HDL is not a beta-lipoprotein (does not contain apoB). It is not affected in this disorder.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman presents for an annual physical examination. She is a marathon runner and runs approximately 50 miles per week. She eats a vegan diet of fruits, vegetables, and beans but no dairy, meat, or fish. She has no history of chronic medical conditions. Her BMI is 20kg/m2 (normal <25). Blood pressure is 110/74 mmHg and pulse is 52/min. Serum fasting lipid profile shows total cholesterol of 1oomg/dL. The majority of her total cholesterol is most likely associated with which of the following?
questions.explanation: Answer C (correct answer): The majority of plasma cholesterol is usually lipoproteins (LDL) regardless of an individual's overall health status. For example, an optimal total cholesterol level is about 100mg/dL. In this setting, the LDL is usually about 50 mg/dL with the remainder of plasma cholesterol found in VLDL, IDL, and HDL. In contrast, the majority of triglycerides are found in VLDL or chylomicrons (after meals). Although exercise can raise HDL, it is very unusual for HDL to exceed LDL even in athletes. Key points: Most plasma cholesterol is found in LDL. Most triglycerides are found in VLDL or chylomicrons. present after meals but not when fasting. Chylomicronsarep Mc Graw

questions.question: A 58-year-old man presents for an annual physical. He lives a sedentary lifestyle and his diet consists of mostly high-fat foods. His BMI is 32kg/m2 (normal <25). On exam, he has a protuberant abdomen with significant abdominal fat. He is referred for fasting plasma lipid measurement but forgets to fast and eats his usual breakfast of pancakes, sausages, cheese, and bacon. Test results demonstrate an increased level of total cholesterol and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol. The majority of plasma cholesterol derives from which of the following sources in this man?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): The majority of plasma cholesterol is associated with low-density lipoproteins (LDL) regardless of overall health or fasting status. LDL particles (and their associated cholesterol) )aresynthesizedin the liver. The liver secretes very low density lipoprotein (VLDL) particles which are converted to intermediate density lipoproteins (IDL) and then LDL. The majority of plasma cholesterol (about 80%) is synthesized in the liver and secreted as VLDL which becomes LDL. The remaining cholesterol (about 20%) comes from our diet. This has clinical implications since some patients will have elevated plasma cholesterol even if they eat a low cholesteroldiet.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Most fat in our diet is in the form of triglycerides. Fasting is often recommended fasting is to avoid high triglyceride levels. These levels transiently increase after a meal which can interfere with laboratory estimation of LDL. Fasting does not change the distribution of cholesterol among lipoproteins. In this man, most cholesterol will be associated with LDL even though he did not fast.

Answers B, D, E (incorrect answers): Adipocytes, skeletal muscle, and the adrenal cortex are not significant sourcesofplasmacholesterol. Mc Graw

questions.question: lipoproteins are separated from plasma. The lipoproteins are further separated based on size into four groups. Each group is analyzed for content of apolipoprotein B. Sample 4 most likely contains large amounts of which lipoprotein?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): The lipoproteins in group 4 have little or no apoB. HDL is the only major lipoprotein that does not contain apoB. Group 4 must contain mostly HDL. The other groups have significant apoB content indicating gtheycontainnon-HDLparticles.

Answers A, B, C, E (incorrect answers): ApoB-1o0 is found on VLDL particles secreted by the liver. This apolipoprotein remains as VLDL transforms into IDL and LDL. These particles (VLDL, IDL, LDL) are sometimes referred to as the "apoB particles." Additionally, chylomicrons contain ApoB-48.

questions.question: this drug have on LDL and HDL cholesterol?
questions.explanation: Answer E (correct answer): Cholesteryl ester transfer protein (CETP) t transfers cholesterol (in the form of cholesteryl esters) from HDL to VLDL particles. Inhibition of CETP leads to accumulation of cholesterol in HDL and decreased cholesterol inVLDL.SinceVLDL goes on to form LDL, serum LDL also decreases with CETP inhibition. This is not purely theoretical: clinical trials results of CETP inhibitor drugs have shown signficant decreases in serum levels of LDL and signficiant increases in serum HDL. high HDL and low LDL are associated with less atherosclerotic plaque formation, pharmaceutical Because companies have long tried to bring a CETP-inhibiting drug to market. Unfortunately, clinical trials in humans have failed to show a significant reduction in rates of cardiovascular disease when CETP is inhibited. This occurs despite higher HDL and lower LDL levels among patients taking these drugs. Mc Graw

questions.question: shows the majority of HDL cholesterol is in the form of cholesteryl esters. Which of the following enzymes is most responsible for forming these structures?
questions.explanation:
r a o n s i o cholesterol attached to fatty acids. Esters can be densely packed in the core of lipid particles allowing for more cholesterol transport. For the Step 1 exam, it's high yield to know the enzymes that make these esters in the different lipid particles. In HDL, the majority of esters are formed by the enzyme lecithin-cholesterol acyl transferase (LCAT). HDL is a scavenger lipoprotein responsible for "reverse transport" of cholesterol back to the liver. This limits atherosclerosis since peripheral cholesterol taken up by HDL is returned to the liver and cannot form plaque. then be packed in the dense core of HDL to make room for more cholesterol uptake on the surface of the particle. Once LCAT makes esters in HDL, those esters can be transferred to other lipoproteins. Thus, LCAT supplies most esters to all plasma lipid particles.

Answers B, C (incorrect answers): Lipoprotein lipase and hepatic lipase are enzymes that breakdown triglycerides into fatty acids.

Answer D (incorrect answer): HMG-CoA reductase is the rate-limiting enzyme in hepatic cholesterol synthesis. It doesnotform cholesteryl esters.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Acyl-CoA cholesterol acyltransferase esterifies cholesterol into cholesteryl esters in not HDL (high-yield fact!).

questions.question: noted distortion of his facial bones. In addition, he does not crawl like the other children his age. Since birth, he has had six sinus infections. On exam, the boy has an enlarged skull, wide nasal bridge, and flattened midface. He lays flat on the floor and is unable to push up or get to a sitting position. Examination of the eyes reveals corneal clouding. On abdominal exam, the liver is palpable below the costal margin and there is splenomegaly. This boy's findings may be explained by abnormal accumulation of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This boy has typical features of the lysosomal storage disease, Hurler's syndrome. sulfate. These substances are glycosaminoglycans, a type of complex carbohydrate.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Hurler's and Hunter's syndromes are unique from other lysosomal storage diseases like Tay-Sachs and Fabry disease which involve the accumulation of lipids. Hunter's and Hurler's are examples of mucopolysaccharidoses, disorders involving the accumulation glycosaminoglycans. develop including an enlarged skull, wide nasal bridge, and flattened midface. Developmental delay occurs infections caused by soft tissue enlargement in the airways due to the accumulation of glycosaminoglycans. Other common features are corneal clouding and hepatosplenomegaly. A pattern of skeletal abnormalities can

Answers B and D (incorrect answers): Accumulation of proteins or nucleic acids is not seen in lysosomal storage diseases which are disorders of complex lipid or carbohydrate structures.

Answers E and F (incorrect answers): Sphingosine is a component of sphingolipids including ceramide. Ceramide accumulates in the sphingolipidosis disorder,Fabry disease. Mc Graw Hmi

questions.question: A 15-year-old boy is evaluated for paresthesias. For the past three months, he has woken with a burning and tingling day. When he runs during gym class, the symptoms also get worse. Vitals signs are within normal limits. The skin finding below is seen on the abdomen. This boy's condition may be explained by abnormal accumulation of which of the following substances?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This is a classic presentation of the lysosomal storage disorder, Fabry disease. This disorder is caused by a deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme alpha-galactosidase A leading to accumulation of ceramide trihexoside. Ceramides are complex lipids made of sphingosine and fatty acids. The classic phenotype of Fabry disease presents in adolescence or young adulthood. The first features to occur are usually acroparaesthesias (pain, burning, tingling, pinpricks) and angiokeratomas (skin finding shown in image). Lack of sweat (hypohidrosis) may also be present at diagnosis although this feature is not always obvious. Some patients will complain of heat intolerance due to lack of sweat. Later in life, as the disease progresses, other features develop including renal failure, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and TIA or stroke. These are unlikely to be described at the time of presentation. The diagnosis of Fabry disease is often missed for many years due to the vague presenting symptoms. Diagnosis can be made by measuring alpha-galactosidase A enzyme activity. Treatment is available with enzyme replacement therapy. In contrast to some lysosomal storage diseases like Tay-Sachs, patients with Fabry live into adulthood although lifespan is reduced due to heart failure, stroke, and kidney disease. which involve complex lipid or carbohydrate structures.

Answer A(incorrect answer): Polysaccharides accumulate in lysosomal storage disease of glycosaminoglycans like Hunter's and Hurler's syndromes.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Glycogen accumulates in glycogen storage diseases.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Ceramide trihexoside is a complexlipid structure. Like all lipids and fats, it is nonpolar and does not dissolve in water. In contrast, carbohydrates like glycogen or glycosaminoglycans are polar and dissolve in water.

questions.question: A 9-month old boy is evaluated for developmental delay. The mother reports that her son does not crawl like other children his age. In addition, she has noted distortion of his facial bones over the past few months. The baby has had five upper respiratory infections since birth. On exam, he has an enlarged skull, wide nasal bridge, and flattened midface. He is unable to sit up. Examination of the eyes reveals corneal clouding. Skeletal anomalies are identified by x-ray. Fibroblasts from the child reveal intracellular inclusions. The genetic analysis finds no mutations of genes encoding for lysosomal enzymes. The majority of lysosomal enzymes in this boy are likely to be found in which of the following locations?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This boy has I-cell disease, a rare lysosomal storage disorder. I-cell disease is caused by the deficiency of the enzyme UDp-N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase in the Golgi apparatus which adds mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) to lysosomal enzymes. This causes an error in intracellular trafficking. In the absence of M6P, enzymes are secreted into the extracellular space rather than directed to lysosomes. Enzymes In I-cell disease, complex molecules that are normally degraded in lysosomes accumulate within cells. These are visible as cellular "inclusions" under the microscope hence the name "inclusion cell" or I-cell disease. Whereas most lysosomal storage diseases involve deficient activity of a lysosomal enzyme, I-cell disease involves an enzyme in the Golgi apparatus. Deficient activity of this enzyme causes a secondary functional deficiency of multiple lysosomal enzymes which are trafficked to the extracellular space instead of lysosomes. the diagnosis can be made prenatally through detection of skeletal and bony abnormalities. Over the first year of life, coarse facial features develop including an enlarged skull, wide nasal bridge, and flattened midface. pattern of skeletal abnormalities can be identified on X-ray called dysostosis multiplex.

Answers A, B, C, and D (incorrect answers): The majority of lysosomal enzymes in I-cell disease are found in the extracellular space, not in the nucleus, cytoplasm, rough endoplasmic reticulum, or Golgi apparatus. Mc GraW

questions.question: A 10-year-old boy presents for follow-up of a wrist fracture. One week ago, he had a minor fall in gym class and fractured his left wrist. In the emergency room, an x-ray showed a left radial and ulnar fracture which was reduced and placed in a cast. d ( ) (- ) y s o n 100,0o0/ml (normal > 150,0o0). A biopsy is obtained and shows the finding below: Which of the following best describes the cell shown in the picture?
questions.explanation: of the enzyme glucocerebrosidase with the accumulation of glucocerebroside. The cell shown in the picture is a Gaucher cell, a macrophage that has accumulated excessive glucocerebroside. This is a classic finding on bone marrow biopsy of those with Gaucher's disease. The nucleus is pushed to the side. The cytoplasm has the The clinical features of Gaucher's disease are caused by infiltration of Gaucher cells into theliver, spleen, and bone marrow. The presentation may occur at any age but most cases are diagnosed before age 20. The majority of patients have splenomegaly on exam at presentation. Bone marrow suppression may cause anemia, thrombocytopenia, or leukopenia. Bone pain and fractures are common. Diagnosis is made by demonstrating reduced glucocerebrosidase activity in leukocytes. Prognosis is variable but many patients live into their 6Os or 70s. Treatment is available with recombinant glucocerebrosidase enzyme replacement therapy.

questions.question: A family pedigree is evaluated by a geneticist. A married couple emigrated to the United States in 1914 and had three suicide. The two girls had a total of six children including two boys who also had neuropathy as well as a skin rash. An abnormal gene is identified on genetic testing among members of the family. This gene is most likely involved in the metabolism of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): The question describes a genetic disorder with x-linked inheritance (only occurs in males). Most lysosomal disorders and glycogen storage diseases are autosomal recessive. One exception is Fabry's disease which is X-linked. Fabry's disease is caused by deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme the breaks down ceramide trihexoside. Symptoms include neuropathy and skin rash.

Answers A, B, C, and E (incorrect answers): Glycogen debranching is abnormal in glycogen storage disease type III. Sphingomyelin breakdown is abnormal in Niemann-Pick disease. Glucocerebroside breakdown is abnormal in Gaucher's disease. Ganglioside processing is abnormal in Tay-Sachs disease. All of these disorders are autosomal recessive. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 4-month-old boy is evaluated for developmental delay. According to his mother, the baby displays little movement of his head, arms, or legs. He lies on his back and does not roll over or sit up. He is unable to push up on his arms and does not follow objects with his eyes. Exam reveals a cherry-red spot on the macula. He is the only child of his mother and father. The boy's mother and father are healthy with no chronic medical conditions. Each has a cousin with a disorder similar to their son. If this couple has another child, what is the chance that child will have the same disorder as their son?
questions.explanation: Answer C (correct answer): This baby has Tay-Sachs disease, a lysosomal storage disease caused by the deficiency of the enzyme hexosaminidase A and accumulation of GM2 ganglioside. The disorder usually presents in the first six months of age. The dominant feature is neurodegeneration caused by the accumulation of GM spot on the macula is a classic finding. Classic histology findings are neurons with ballooned vacuoles in the cytoplasm. Electron microscopy may show lysosomes with whorling ("onion skinning"). There is no treatment, Like most lysosomal storage diseases, Tay-Sachs is autosomal recessive. Since this boy has the disease, both Mc Graw

questions.question: A 5-month-old boy is evaluated after a seizure. He was born by vaginal delivery after an uncomplicated pregnancy. He was healthy at birth with normal Apgar scores. Development had been normal up to this point. Earlier in the day, his mother was rocking him when he developed tonic-clonic activity. On exam, the baby's arms and wrists are stiff and flexed. Vitals include The pathogenesis of this baby's condition most resembles which of the following?
questions.explanation: Answer A (correct answer): This baby has Krabbe disease, a lysosomal storage disease caused by the deficiency of galactocerebrosidase and abnormal metabolism of galactocerebroside. With this enzyme deficiency, galactocerebroside is not catabolized normally and is shunted into a toxic substance, galactosylsphingosine. As a result, the brain shows a loss of myelin and oligodendrocytes. This is a similar pattern to other demyelinating diseases like multiple sclerosis. Demyelination in Krabbe is rapid and survival beyond 2 years is uncommon. Key point: Loss of myelin is a major mechanism of the pathology of Krabbe disease. The dominantclinical features of Krabbe disease are neurologicincluding seizures,stiffness,and weakness.Some of these features resemble Tay-Sachs disease, however, Tay-Sachs presents with muscle weakness with hypotonia and a cherry-red spot on the macula. The classic pathology finding in Krabbe disease is an engorged macrophage in the brain called a globoid cell (shown in image). disease, classic galactosemia, or hemochromatosis. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 22-year-old woman presents for evaluation of chest pain and dyspnea. She has a history of sickle cell anemia with three hospitalizations for acute pain crises. Earlier in the day, she developed fatigue and subjective fevers followed by chest pain and dyspnea. Her only medication is oral contraceptive pills which she stopped three months ago when her prescription ran out. Temperature is 101.2°F. Chest x-ray shows a right upper lobe infiltrate. Hemoglobin is 8.5 g/dL, ferritin is 150 ng/ml, and MCV is 94fl. Serum beta HCG is elevated. She is administered antibiotics, intravenous fluids, and morphine. Which of the following additional therapies is indicated in this woman?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This woman with sickle cell anemia has acute chest syndrome defined as a new density on X-ray, fever, and respiratory symptoms. The treatment for chest syndrome is antibiotics, intravenous fluids, and morphine. In some cases, blood transfusion is necessary. Her hemoglobin level is reduced due to chronic hemolysis. In addition to chest syndrome and sickle cell disease, this woman is pregnant (elevated serum HcG). All pregnant women should be administered folate for the prevention of neural tube defects. Pregnancy among women with sickle cell disease carries a higher risk of adverse outcomes, but most pregnancies will result in a live must be evaluated as this may alter management.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Iron is used to treat iron-deficiency anemia. This woman has a normal ferritin level and is unlikely to be iron deficient.

Answers B, C, and E (incorrect answers): Erythropoietin, vitamin B6, and vitamin B12 are not indicated for sickle cell anemia or chest syndrome. Erythropoietin is sometimes administered to patients with chronic kidney disease and anemia.

Answer F (incorrect answer): Hydroxyurea is a treatment for chronic sickle cell anemia. It is an antimetabolite that disrupts nucleotide synthesis. This drug is contraindicated in pregnancy due to fetal toxicity. Hmi

questions.question: A 32-year-old man presents for routine evaluation. He follows a strict vegan diet. His meals consist of breads, cereals, nuts, vegetables, and fruits. He eats no chicken, beef, fish, or dairy. which of the following vitamins should be supplemented in this man?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): Vitamin B12 is unique among vitamins in that it is only found in animal products deficient. Vitamin B12 is stored in the liver which makes the body resistant to deficiency states. In the absence of B12 intake, deficiency takes one to two years to develop. In contrast, poor dietary intake of most other B vitamins leads to a deficiency syndrome within a few weeks or months. (NoTE: Folate is also stored in the liver butstores last onlya fewmonths).

Answer A (incorrect answer): Vitamin B1 (thiamine) is a water-soluble B vitamin found in many foods including whole grains and legumes (peas, beans).

Answer B (incorrect answer): Vitamin B2 (riboflavin) is also a water-soluble B vitamin widely distributed in many foods. It can be found in meats, fish, eggs, milk, vegetables, and breads. strawberries,andspinach.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Vitamin D can come from the diet, but may also be synthesized in the skin. Assuming this man gets enough sun exposure, he will not require vitamin D supplementation.

questions.question: A 16-year-old girl is evaluated for abdominal pain. She has no chronic medical conditions and takes no regular medications. For the past month, she has had intermittent, sharp abdominal pain in the right lower quadrant. Last night, the pain became severe and woke her from sleep. Abdominal exam is significant for right lower quadrant tenderness. CT scan shows thickening and inflammation of the terminal ileum. Absorption of which of the following will most likely be impaired in this girl?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This girl has a classic presentation of Crohn's disease including right lower quadrant abdominal pain and imaging evidence of terminal ileitis. Vitamin B12 absorption occurs in the terminal ileum and will be impaired in this girl. Vitamin B12 absorption requires intrinsic factor, a glycoprotein secreted by parietal cells in the stomach. Intrinsic factor-B12 complex is absorbed by enterocytes in terminal ileum. Because Crohn's disease commonly involves the ileum, lab testing reveals evidence of B12 deficiency in about 20% of patients.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Folate is absorbed in the jejunum. AnswerC(incorrectanswer):Ironisabsorbedintheduodenum.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Vitamin C is absorbed in the jejunum.

Answer E (incorrect answer):Vitamin B1 is a water-soluble vitamin absorbed mostly in the duodenum. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman is evaluated for fatigue. For the past two months, she has felt exhausted. She owns a fishery on a wharf and has found it difficult to work past noon each day. questions.question: A 31-year-old woman is evaluated for hyperglycemia. She recently gave birth to her first child. During pregnancy, she had hyperglycemia identified through glucose tolerance testing. Laboratory testing six weeks after delivery showed persistent fasting hyperglycemia. She feels well and has no complaints. Vital signs and physical exam are within normal limits. Further patient with normal glucokinase function for fasting beta cell glucose-6-phosphate (G6P) concentration and insulin release?
questions.explanation: Answer D (correct answer): This woman has a mutation of the glucokinase gene causing hyperglycemia. The classic forms of diabetes (type I and type II) are polygenic meaning they result from abnormal function of multiple genes (many of which are incompletely understood). Glucokinase mutations represent a rare form of usually asymptomatic and is rarely associated with the vascular complications seen in type I and II diabetes. Diet alone is often sufficient therapy. Glucokinase deficiency is commonly detected in pregnancy when women undergo standard glucose tolerance sugar levels normally rise to a modest degree (to provide glucose for the fetus). Women with glucokinase deficiency can develop significant hyperglycemia due to the added effect of the genetic mutation. (G6P). In glucokinase deficiency, beta cells have persistently low levels of intracellular G6P. This is interpreted by the cellular machinery as a hypoglycemic state. Cells respond with decreased insulin secretion which causes hyperglycemia. Reference:https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4935018 Mc Graw Hi

questions.question: A 1-day-old male baby is evaluated in the newborn nursery for lethargy and pallor. The baby was delivered pre-term due to discoloration, and scleral icterus is present. The spleen is enlarged. Serum level of unconjugated bilirubin is elevated. Hemoglobin is 9 mg/dL (normal 14-24) and mean corpuscular volume is 90 fL (normal 80-96). Peripheral blood smear shows burr cells. An abnormality in which of the following best explains this baby's presentation?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This is a classic presentation of newborn hemolytic anemia due to pyruvate kinase (PK) deficiency. Babies born with deficient levels of pyruvate kinase cannot sufficiently generate ATP through the conversion of phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) to pyruvate. This has the greatest effect on red blood cells which lack mitochondria. This leads to hemolysis due to deficient ATP generation. The severity of hemolysis is variable. to an asymptomatic normocytic anemia. Peripheral blood smear classically shows burr cells (echinocytes). There are two cellular mechanisms for the generation of ATP. Oxidative phosphorylation produces ATP via the electron transport chain. Substrate level phosphorylation produces ATP via direct enzymatic phosphorylation of soh o o s pa s ' s

Answer A (incorrect answer): Abnormalities of red cell membrane proteins can lead to spherocytosis, another potential cause of newborn hemolysis. This baby, however, has normal mean corpuscular volume (McV) and spherocytosis is associated witha reduced Mcv.

Answers C, D, and E (incorrect answers): Inborn errors of metabolism involving the urea cycle, fatty acid metabolism, or glycogen breakdown do not present as isolated hemolytic anemia. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 56-year-old man is evaluated for weakness and fatigue. He has a history of type I diabetes and end-stage renal disease due to diabetic nephropathy. He requires dialysis three times per week but missed his last two sessions. Serum BUN is 100 mg/dL (normal 6-20) and creatinine is 6.2 mg/dL (normal 0.6-1.1). Serum potassium is 6.7 mg/dL (normal 4.0 to 5.1). He is administered intravenous insulin and glucose. After this intervention, serum potassium decreases to 5.4 mg/dL. which of the following enzymes will show increased activity in this man's liver at this time?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): Insulin is standard therapy for hyperkalemia. Insulin drives potassium into cells, lowering the serum potassium level. Insulin is always given together with glucose when treating hyperkalemia. If given alone, insulin can cause hypoglycemia, seizures, or death. Administration of insulin and glucose to this patient mimics the fed state where serum glucose and insulin levels are elevated. Glucokinase is activated in the fed state to bring more glucose into cells for glycolysis.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Hexokinase is found in muscle cells and adipose tissue but not in liver cells (the question asks for a liver enzyme). This enzyme increases activity when glucose levels are high.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Glycogen phosphorylase is an enzyme that breaks down glycogen in the fasting state. It is activated by glucagon and epinephrine.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Hormone-sensitive lipase breaks down fatty acids and is active in the fasting state. It is also activated by glucagon and epinephrine. s enzyme is not active in the fed state. Mc Graw

questions.question: Researchers are studying hepatocytes grown in culture. Answer D (correct answer): The data show a substance in liver cells that has a high concentration in the nucleus when glucose levels are low, and a high concentration in the cytosol when glucose levels are high. Answer E (incorrect answer): Isocitrate dehydrogenase is the rate-limiting enzyme of the TCA cycle. It is located in the mitochondria. questions.question: A 35-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital with acute pancreatitis. She is given IV fluids and morphine. She is allowed removed from the common bile duct. questions.question: A 58-year-old woman comes to the office for a follow-up visit. She suffered a myocardial infarction three years ago. Her amlodipine, aspirin, metoprolol, and simvastatin. She does not smoke, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. She does not exercise regularly, and her diet consists of frozen and fast foods. Her blood pressure is 118/76 mmHg and heart rate is 64/min. questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This patient has atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (AscVD) given her history of myocardial infarction (MI). Patients with AsCVD are at risk for additional cardiovascular events (MI, stroke) and can reduce their risk with statin therapy. Patients with AsCVD should be on high-intensity statin therapy (see chart above) which includes atorvastatin 40-80 mg or rosuvastatin 20-40 mg. This patient is on moderate intensity therapy with simvastatin. Thus, she should switch to a high intensity dose of atorvastatin or rosuvastatin. Note that this patient has good control of her LDL cholesterol on simvastatin, as her LDL cholesterol is less than 70 mg/dL. Despite this, guidelines recommend she should still switch to a high intensity therapy given her history ofAsCVD,regardlessofher LDLlevel.

Answer E (incorrect answer): This patient's hemoglobin A1C is in the prediabetic range (5.7-6.4%). Lifestyle modifications should be recommended to reduce her A1C. If lifestyle modifications fail, it would be reasonable contraindicated if creatinine is greater than 1.5 mg/dL. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 52-year-old man presents to the cardiology clinic. He has a history of familial hyperlipidemia and suffered a myocardial infarction eight years ago. He has been unable to tolerate multiple high-dose statin medications due to myalgias. Recently he began low-dose rosuvastatin every other day. He reports occasional mild myalgias on this regimen. Vital signs and management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This patient has atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (AscVD) and is at a high risk with a high-intensity statin, such as high-dose rosuvastatin or atorvastatin. The goal for patients with AsCVD is to drive LDL cholesterol below 70 mg/dL. important to find the maximum dose of statin that a patient can tolerate without side effects. For this man, the maximum tolerated regimen appears to be a low dose of rosuvastatin every other day. On this maximally tolerated dose, he has an LDL cholesterol above 70 mg/dL. Thus, the addition of further LDL-reducing therapy is indicated, either with ezetimibe or a PcsK-9 inhibitor. levels (greater than 5o0 mg/dL). only used if more effective medications, such as ezetimibe or a PcsK-9 inhibitor, have failed or are contraindicated.

Answer E (incorrect answer): This patient is at a very high risk for future cardiovascular events and requires lipid optimization to reduce this risk. Patients with AscVD should continue the highest dose of statin that they can tolerate.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man presents to the clinic for follow up. He has hyperlipidemia that was diagnosed five years ago. His most recent LDL cholesterol was 216 mg/dL. questions.question: A 4-year-old boy is seen in a pediatrics clinic. He has met normal childhood milestones and has received all routine preventative care. questions.question: A 42-year-old man is seen for a primary care visit. The patient has a history of reflux nephropathy and underwent a renal been complicated by diabetes mellitus, for which he is now taking insulin. His endocrinologist recommends high-intensity the following side effects of statin therapy?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This patient has diabetes that developed after a renal transplant. Patients on calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine and tacrolimus) are at an increased risk for developing metabolic syndrome and diabetes mellitus. These patients should be managed with standard medical therapy for diabetes. Part of standard diabetic medical therapy includes moderate or high-intensity statin therapy for patients over 40years old. Most statin medications including atorvastatin are metabolized by the liver's P450 system and interact with drugs that inhibit this system (see figure above). Cyclosporine is a potent inhibitor of the CYP3A4 system and increases the levels of circulating statins. If placed on high-dose statin therapy, this patient would be at risk for developing rhabdomyolysis. For transplant patients on cyclosporine who require statin therapy, low-dose statin drugs are used with careful monitoring of serum creatine kinase levels. Of note, the two statins pravastatin and rosuvastatin do not depend on the CYP450 pathway for metabolism.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Hepatotoxicity is a potential complication of statin therapy, and this patient is at an increased risk for hepatotoxicity because of the elevated statin levels caused by CYP inhibition from cyclosporine use. The most common presentation of liver toxicity associated with statin use is mildly increased liver function tests (transaminitis). Clinically significant acute liver failure is extremely rare with statin use,. occurring in about 0.o01% of patients.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Although there are anecdotal reports of cognitive dysfunction with statins, this has not been demonstrated in clinical trials.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Diarrhea is not a common side effect of statin therapy.

questions.question: An 11-year-old girl presents to the pediatric clinic for a physical prior to starting summer camp. As a newborn, she was found to have phenylketonuria with tetrahydrobiopterin deficiency. She has followed a controlled diet since that time. Which of the following should be recommended for this child when she attends camp?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): Phenylketonuria (PKU) is an inborn error of metabolism caused by the inability to metabolize the amino acid phenylalanine into tyrosine. Screening for PKU is mandated in the United States. In most cases, PKU is caused by a deficiency of the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH). A required cofactor for this enzyme is tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4). A small percentage of cases of PKU (about 2%) are caused by deficient metabolism of BH4. Although all forms of PKU (PAH deficiency and BH4 deficiency) may be managed with a phenylalanine-restricted diet and BH4 supplementation, BH4 deficiency requires additional interventions. BH4 is necessary for the synthesis of the neurotransmitters dopamine and serotonin. For this reason, treatment with the dopamine precursor levodopa and the serotonin precursor 5-hydroxytryptophan is required. These interventions are not necessary in PAH deficient cases of PKU as BH4 metabolism is intact.

Answer A(incorrect answer):Phenelzine is aninhibitor of monoamine oxidase used in the treatment of depression. It has no role in treating PKU with BH4 deficiency.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Selegiline is an inhibitor of monoamine oxidase B (MAO-b) used in the treatment of Parkinson's disease. It is not indicated for PKU. In addition, the oral tablets contain small amounts of phenylalanine.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Metyrosine is an inhibitor of tyrosine hydroxylase that will blunt the synthesis of L- DOPA. This is not helpful among patients with PKU with BH4 deficiency. untreated BH4 deficiency.Since treatment withdopamine precursors(carbidopa/L-dopa) restores dopamine function, prolactin administration is not required.
