questions.question: A 24-year-old woman presents with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. She has been unable to keep down liquids or solids for 12 hours. Urinalysis shows presence of ketones. which of the following is the major source of ketone bodies in this woman?

Answer D (correct answer): Triglycerides are liberated from adipose tissue and transported to the liver. In the liver, they are metabolized into fatty acids and then into acetyl-CoA via beta oxidation. This generates more acetyl-CoA than can be handled by the TCA cycle. As a result, acetyl-CoA accumulates and is diverted into synthesis of ketones. Key point: In the fasting state, fatty acid metabolism in the liver generates lots of acetyl-CoA (more than glucose can generate). The accumulation of acetyl-CoA leads to ketone synthesis.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Glucose is synthesized by the liver in the fasting state via gluconeogenesis. Glucose is not metabolized intoketones during a fast.

questions.question: A 24-year-old man is admitted to the hospital with acute pancreatitis. He is treated with IV fluids and opioids. He is allowed no oral intake for 24 hours. In this setting, fatty acids are metabolized in the liver into acetyl-coA via beta oxidation. This generates more acetyl-CoA than can be handled by the TCA cycle. As a result, acetyl-CoA accumulates in the liver and is diverted into synthesis of ketones.If the TCA cycle could metabolize more acetyl-CoA, less would be available for ketone synthesis. Isocitrate dehydrogenase is the rate-limiting enzyme of the TCA cycle. Increased activity of this enzyme would consume more acetyl-CoA in liver cells, leaving less available for ketone synthesis.

Answers B, C (incorrect answers): Carnitine palmitoyl transferase-1 (CPT1) and medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (McAD) are enzymes of fatty acid breakdown. Levels of ketones may become so high that a life-threatening acidosis occurs. The TCA cycle stalls in DKA because oxaloacetate (OAA) is depleted. OAA is diverted towards gluconeogenesis even though glucose levels are high. In addition, fatty acid metabolism generates NADH which favors conversion decreased amounts of NADH in the setting of DKA. questions.question: A 21-year-old is evaluated after a seizure. Earlier in the day, he completed his first marathon. He consumed alcoholic beverages while celebrating afterward with several friends. While standing, he fell to the ground and developed tonic-clonic this man's seizure?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): Glycogen is an important source of glucose during exercise and fasting. This man has completed a marathon which has depleted his liver glycogen stores. Following this, he likely consumed alcohol during g his celebration. Alcohol depletes NAD+ which shunts oxaloacetate into malate. This inhibits gluconeogenesis leading to hypoglycemia. Consuming alcohol when glycogen stores are low after strenuous exercise is a classic cause of hypoglycemia via this mechanism.

Answers A and B (incorrect answers): Consumption of alcohol leads to decreased NAD+ and increased NADH.

Answers D and E (incorrect answers): Ketone bodies and lactic acid may be synthesized with alcohol consumption but are not an important cause of this man's hypoglycemia and seizure. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 45-year-old man is evaluated for yellow skin discoloration. He recently lost his job and began consuming alcohol heavily. He has been waking with headaches for which he takes acetaminophen. On exam, the skin is jaundiced and scleral icterus is present. Serum levels of AsT and ALT are elevated. which of the following may have caused his presentation?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): Chronic ethanol consumption activates the microsomal ethanol-oxidizing system (MEos) in the liver. This is associated with a rise in cytochrome P-450 enzyme metabolism. The acetaminophen metabolite NAPQI (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine) is produced via p450 metabolism and is toxic to liver. NAPQI is produced in higher quantities among chronic ethanol users. Heavy alcohol users like this man are at risk for acetaminophen toxicity even when consuming standard dosages of the drug.

Answer A (incorrect answer): The ratio of NADH/NAD is increased with heavy alcohol consumption. This limits the supply of NAD+ for metabolism. B, C, and E (incorrect answers): Lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, and ketone bodies may occur among AnswersE heavy alcohol users but are not involved in the development of this man's liver failure. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 55-year-old woman presents for an annual physical. She has no chronic medical conditions and takes no prescribed medications. She drinks approximately four glasses of wine per night. On exam, the liver edge is palpable 4 cm below the normal liver, which of the following are expected in this woman's hepatocytes for levels of malonyl-CoA and glycerol-3- phosphate?
questions.explanation: Answer A (correct answer): This woman has alcoholic fatty liver disease. Metabolism of ethanol generates high levels of NADH. Recall that NADH is normally high when cells are replete with energy. Thus, high NADH triggers energy storage by the liver including synthesis of fatty acids. Fatty acids accumulate leading to alcoholic fatty liverdisease. Malonyl-CoA is produced by the rate-limiting enzyme of fatty acid synthesis, acetyl-CoA carboxylase. The activity of this enzyme is increased among chronic alcohol users, leading to increased levels of malonyl-CoA. Glycerol is normally metabolized into glycerol-3-phosphate in the liver for entry into glycolysis. In the setting of high NADH from alcohol consumption, glycerol metabolism is inhibited. Glycerol-3-phosphate levels increase, leading to the production of triglycerides which contribute to fatty acid buildup in the liver. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 52-year-old man presents for an evaluation of foot pain. He drinks 4 to 5 alcoholic beverages per day. He has been hospitalized for acute pancreatitis secondary to alcohol consumption in the past. Yesterday, he spent the day drinking alcohol while eating very little solid food. He woke in the morning with a throbbing sensation of his left foot. On exam, the great toe of his left foot displays warmth and redness at the base. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his presentation?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This man has acute gouty arthritis, an inflammatory joint disorder caused by deposition of uric acid crystals. Consumption of ethanol is a classic trigger for gout. Ethanol depletes cellular NAD+ and increases cellular NADH. This high ratio of NADH/NAD drives the synthesis of lactate from pyruvate leading to lactic acidosis, a common finding among heavy alcohol users. Uric acid and lactic acid utilize the transporter URAT1 (urate transporter-1) for excretion in the proximal tubule of the nephron. In the setting of lactic acidosis, this transporter excretes more lactic acid and reabsorbs more uric acid. For this reason, alcoholic Users may develop hyperuricemia from underexcretion of uric acid in the urine which can lead to a gout attack.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Metabolism of purines generates uric acid. Increased purine metabolism can lead to gout, but this is not the mechanism of gout among alcoholics.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Increased dietary uric acid can lead to gout but this man has eaten little for the pastday.

Answers D and E (incorrect answers): Increased muscle breakdown and cell lysis are potential causes of hyperuricemia and gout but are not the cause in this patient. Mc Graw

Fomepizole is an inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase which will halt the metabolism of ethanol. questions.question: An 18-year-old male high school student goes on a 48-hour fast as part of a charity fundraiser. At the completion of his fast, serum glucose concentration is 96 mg/dL (normal > 90). which of the following is being used to maintain serum glucose at this time?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): During fasting, dietary sugars are exhausted within about six hours. Glycogen in the liver can be broken down to maintain serum glucose until about 24 hours. After this, gluconeogenesis synthesizes glucose from several sources including lactic acid, alanine, glucogenic amino acids, odd-chain fatty acids, and without food.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Glycogen in the liver can be broken down to maintain serum glucose until about 24 hours into fasting.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Even chain fatty acids can be metabolized to acetyl-CoA for entry into the TCA cycle to generate ATp. They cannot, however, enter gluconeogenesis and contribute to a rise in serum glucose levels. Conversely, odd chain fatty acids can be metabolized to succinyl-CoA which can be used as a substrate for gluconeogenesis.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Leucine and lysine are the two ketogenic amino acids. They can generate acetyl- CoA to be used in the TCA cycle like even chain fatty acids. They cannot, however, be used by gluconeogenesis to synthesizeglucose. Mc Graw

questions.question: A six-year-old boy is evaluated in a remote village after a prolonged drought and famine. He is at the 1oth percentile for Which of the following is contributing to the lower extremity findings?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): Malnutrition in resource-limited countries occurs in two forms: kwashiorkor (or edematous malnutrition)and marasmus.The two forms are distinguished by the presence of edema which only occurs in kwashiorkor. Kwashiorkor is associated with severe protein malnutrition leading to hypoalbuminemia. Low serum albumin reduces capillary oncotic pressure allowing capillary fluid to leak into tissues. Accumulation of fluid is the cause of peripheral edema. Other factors in addition to hypoalbuminemia also play a role including renal sodium and water retention. In contrast, marasmus involves total calorie insufficiency involving all nutrients, not just protein. This leads to muscle and fat wasting in the absence of edema. themechanismofperipheral edema. country. In addition, excess water alone does not cause edema provided there is no disruption of capillary oncotic and hydrostatic pressures.

questions.question: A 32-year-old man gets lost in the Appalachian Mountains during a hike. He survives for one week consuming no food and drinking creek water. During this time, what changes are expected compared to normal (i.e., adequate food intake) for hepatocyte levels of fructose 2,6 bisphosphate, activity of pyruvate kinase, and activity of glucose-6-phosphatase?
questions.explanation: Answer C (correct answer): This man is in a state of prolonged fasting and starvation. questions.question: A 2-day-old baby girl is evaluated for somnolence. The baby has been breastfed. She sleeps most of the day and is difficult to arouse. Twice she has awoken and vomited. Respiratory rate is increased. Serum pH is 7.5 (normal 7.4). Serum ammonia is >1500 ug/dL (normal <150). which of the following dietary modifications would be most helpful to this baby?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This baby has findings of a urea cycle disorder. Key features include (1) presentation in the first 24-48 hours after birth, (2) severe hyperammonemia, and (3) absence of acidosis or other metabolic transcarbamylase. As a result, ammonia cannot be metabolized into urea. This leads to marked hyperammonemia. Ammonia accumulation causes cerebral edema which often leads to hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis. The absence of acidosis and other metabolic derangements helps distinguish urea cycle disorders from other inborn errors of metabolism. Urea cycle disorders develop in the first few days of life because breast milk contains proteins and amino acids. These cannot be metabolized and hyperammonemia occurs. Babies with urea cycle disorders should avoid breastfeeding and consume a very low protein diet. The diet is adjusted in these children to maintain normal serum levels of amino acids.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Frequent feedings are helpful in glycogen storage diseases and beta-oxidation disorders where fasting hypoglycemia may occur.

Answer B (incorrect answer): A low carbohydrate diet will not improve the hyperammonemia associated with a urea cycle disorder. Babies with urea cycle disorders can process carbohydrates, but not proteins.

questions.question: A 10-day-old male baby is evaluated for failure to thrive. The baby is lethargic and difficult to arouse. The liver is palpable below the costal margin. Serum glucose is 56 mg/dL (normal >90), AST is 500 U/l (normal <40) and ALT is 550 U/l (normal <56). Urinalysis shows the absence of ketones. Which of the following additional findings may be present?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This baby has hypoketotic hypoglycemia, the hallmark of a beta-oxidation disorder involving fatty acid metabolism. A number of enzyme deficiencies may cause beta-oxidation disorders including deficiency of medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD), long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (LCAD), and others. Liver dysfunction develops in these disorders due to the accumulation of fatty acids. Urinary dicarboxylic acids will be present in the urine. These acids are produced by omega oxidation of fatty acids which occurs when beta-oxidation cannot proceed normally. (HFI). questions.question: Researchers are studying serum glucose values among college students during exam time. A study of 1o0 subjects reports a mean serum glucose value of 108 mg/dL. The glucose values are normally distributed with a standard deviation of 4 mg/dL. Based on these findings, 95% of the glucose values among study subjects would be found within which of the following ranges?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): The standard deviation is a measure of dispersion of a set of values. For data that are normally distributed, 95% of samples will fall within two standard deviations of the mean. For the data in the question, the mean is 108 mg/dL. Therefore, 95% of samples should fall between 100 mg/dL (two standard deviations below the mean) and 116 mg/dL (two standard deviations above the mean).

Answer A (incorrect answer): The range from 96 to 120 mg/dL is 3 standard deviations above and below the mean. This range includes 99% not 95% of samples. B, C and E (incorrect answers): None of these ranges is +/- two standard deviations from the mean and, AnswersB therefore, will include more or less than 95%of samples. Mc Graw

questions.question: Researchers are studying serum levels of an epithelial cell protein among women at risk for breast cancer. Shown below are the distribution of measurements for this protein from a group of 1,ooo women. The mean, median and mode for the data set are determined and denoted with blue dots on the graph. Which of the following most likely describes points 1, 2 and 3?
questions.explanation: Answer B (correct answer): The question shows data with a negative skew / (i.e.,the tail of the dataset is to the left). In data with a negative skew, the mode is the x-axis value with the largest number of subjects (point3). The median is closer to the mode in negatively-skewed data than the mean. Therefore, point 2 is the median and point 1 is the mean. The mean is lower than the median due to many smaller numbers in the left tail.

questions.question: Researchers are studying mean serum glucose values among hospitalized patients at the time of admission in a rural area of the United States. The mean glucose level for this population is normally distributed with a mean value 120 mg/dL and a standard deviation of 10 mg/dL. A 50-year-old woman at an area hospital has a serum glucose value of 140 mg/dL at admission. Which of the following is this woman's Z score?
questions.explanation: Answer B (correct answer): The Z score describes the relationship of a single value to the mean of a group of values. For the woman in the question, it is equal to the difference between her serum glucose value and the population mean divided by the standard division. From the data given, her Z score is (140-120)/10 = 2.

questions.question: Fasting serum glucose measurements are obtained from 2o0 patients with well-controlled diabetes. The data follow a normal distribution. Statistical characteristics of the dataset include a mean of 100 mg/dL, standard deviation of 10 mg/dL, standard error of the mean of 0.71 mg/dL, and 95% confidence interval of the mean 100 +/- 1.39 dL. If the experiment were conducted with 400 volunteers instead of 2o0, which of the following changes would be expected in the standard error of the mean and 95% confidence intervals?
questions.explanation: Answer E (correct answer): The standard error of the mean (SEM) quantifies uncertainty in the estimate of the mean. Its main function is to construct confidence intervals (cIs). CIs represent the range of means, which encompass the actual (true) value. In the experiment with 200 samples, the mean is 100, standard deviation (o) is 0.71, and SEM is 0.71. This yields a 95% CI equal to 100 +/- 1.39 (see above). It should be intuitive that 400 samples will give a smaller confidence interval, since SEM = o /√ n. The table above shows the calculation for SEM and CIs for a data set with 2o0 samples and for a similar set with 400 samples and an identical mean and standard deviation. As shown, the SEM and CIs decrease with more samples. The SEM and CIs will also decrease ifthestandarddeviationdecreases.

questions.question: Twelve systolic blood pressure measurements are recorded from high school athletes (data shown below). The mean, median, and mode are determined. On further review, athlete 7 is believed to have an erroneous measurement due to a faulty blood pressure cuff. If this athlete's blood pressure is removed from the data set, which of the following will be most affected?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): Athlete number 7 is an outlier. This blood pressure measurement is significantly higher than the others. The greatest effect of an outlier is on the mean. The mean is determined by totaling all the values and dividing by the number of samples. If we remove the highest value for blood pressure, we significantly change the total value of the samples which changes the mean. In this example, the mean changes from 120.8 to 117.3 mmHg with the removal of the outlier athlete.

Answers B, C and D (incorrect answers): Outliers have the least effect on the mode. The mode in the data set is This is minimally affected by the removal of an outlier. In the original dataset, the number of samples (12) is even, so the median is halfway between 118 and 122 mmHg, which is 120 mmHg. With the removal of the outlier, the median becomes 118 mmHg. The mean for the original data set is 120.8 mmHg. It falls to 117.3 mmHg after removal of athlete 7. Original Data (mm Hg): 100 104 112 112 112 118 122 122 128 128 132 160 Mean 1450/12 = 120.8; median 120; Mode 112 Data after athlete 7 removed with BP 160 mm Hg: 100 104 112 112 112 118 122 122 128 128 132 Mean 1290/11 = 117.3; Median 118; Mode 112

questions.question: Six systolic blood pressure measurements are recorded from high school athletes (data shown below). which of the following is the median blood pressure for the athletes?
questions.explanation: Answer C (correct answer): The median is the value of the middle sample when all samples are placed in numerical order. When the number of samples is even, the median is midway between the middle two samples. For this dataset with six samples, the median value is midway between samples 3 and 4 which is 124 mmHg.

questions.question: A study is conducted to determine the blood pressure within a community where salt intake is high. One thousand patients have their blood pressure recorded. The mean systolic blood pressure is 165 mmHg with a normal distribution. The standard deviation is 5 mmHg. How many patients in the study have a systolic blood pressure greater than 175 mmHg?
questions.explanation: Answer D (correct answer): A systolic pressure of 175 mmHg is two standard deviations above the mean of 165 for the data described. In data sets with a normal distribution, 5% of samples lie more than two standard deviations away from the mean. Half of these (2.5%) are two standard deviations above the mean, and half (2.5%) are below. Thus, 2.5% of the 1,000 samples are above 175 mmHg which is 25 patients. ····.·.

questions.question: A local pharmacy institutes a program of texting customers to remind them to refill medications. A study is conducted to determine if this program is associated with improved medication adherence. Five hundred subjects are identified at the local pharmacy. A similar group of five hundred subjects is identified from a neighboring city pharmacy without a texting program. The total number of prescriptions filled over the past two years is determined from pharmacy databases. Which of the following best describes this study?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): The question describes a retrospective cohort study of an exposure (a pharmacy texting program) and an outcome (medication adherence). Presence or absence of the exposure is determined first as is typical for cohort studies. The research subjects are separated into two "cohorts": one that is exposed to the pharmacy texting program and one that is not. After exposure status is determined, the outcome (medication adherence) is assessed retrospectively.

Answer B (incorrect answer): In a case-control study, research subjects are identified by the presence or absence of the outcome (medication adherence).

Answer C (incorrect answer): In a cross-sectional study, subjects are chosen based on some factor other than the presence of exposure or disease, and outcome and exposure are assessed at the same time.

Answer D (incorrect answer): A case series is a descriptive study of patients with disease. These are often done when new diseases emerge. By collecting cases and describing patient characteristics, clues about risk factors and cause can be obtained. monitored prospectively for outcome (e.g., development of disease). This question is based on an actual study. Mc Graw

questions.question: A study is conducted to evaluate a potential association between oral health and cardiovascular disease. Adults from a local community are asked to participate in a baseline evaluation that includes a dental examination for evidence of periodontitis. Based on this evaluation, subjects are categorized as having periodontal disease or no periodontal disease. Study participants are reevaluated annually for 17 years. At study completion, the rate of coronary artery disease is 10.1% among patients with periodontitis and 8.1% among those without periodontitis. Which of the following best describes this study?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): The question describes a cohort study evaluating the association of an exposure (periodontitis) and an outcome (development of coronary artery disease). At study enrollment, subjects are identified by the presence or absence of the exposure. This is typical of cohort studies where exposure status is determined first. Subjects are followed over time for the development of coronary artery disease (the outcome) making this a prospective cohort study.

Answer B (incorrect answer): In a case-control study, research subjects are identified by the presence or absence of the outcome. For the scenario in the question, subjects would need to be chosen based on the presence or absence of coronary artery disease to conduct a case-control study.

Answer C (incorrect answer): In a cross-sectional study, exposure and outcome are assessed at the same time. For the study in the question, exposure is established first followed by outcome.

Answer D (incorrect answer): A case series is a descriptive study of patients with disease. These are often done when new diseases emerge. By collecting cases and describing patient characteristics, clues about risk factors and cause can be obtained.

Answer E (incorrect answer): In a clinical trial, patients are assigned to an exposure (e.g., a new therapy) and monitored prospectively for outcome (e.g., development of disease). This question describes an actual study. W

questions.question: A local community has a significant number of cases of a rare uveal infection. There is a concern that environmental the best study design to evaluate this hypothesis?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): A case-control study is the ideal design for the evaluation of rare diseases. In case- control studies, subjects with an outcome (e.g., uveal infection) are identified and compared to matched cases can be easily identified and quickly associated with exposure.

Answers A and B (incorrect answers): In cohort studies, subjects are identified by presence or absence of exposure (i.e., use of contact lens solution). This creates two "cohorts" for evaluation: one with exposure and one without exposure. Subjects are then evaluated for development of the outcome (i.e., uveal infection). Because the outcome of uveal infection is rare, few cases are likely to occur in either the exposed or unexposed cohort. This makes cohort studies a poor design for rare conditions. Because the outcome of uveal infection is rare, a cross-sectional study will identify a very small number of cases of disease. This will make it difficult to draw conclusions. A case-control study is a better design because it ability to draw conclusions about the differences between exposed subjects (cases) and unexposed subjects (controls).

Answer E (incorrect answer): In a clinical trial, patients are randomly assigned to an exposure (e.g., a new therapy) and monitored prospectively for the outcome (e.g., development of disease). Special note: A case series could also be used to evaluate the association of uveal infection with contact lens use. In a case series, cases of rare conditions are pooled to create summary data of patient and disease characteristics. Case series are purely descriptive. questions.question: A 42-year-old man with type I diabetes records his blood sugar on 100 consecutive mornings. The mean glucose concentration by glucometer is 110 mg/dL with a standard deviation of 4 mg/dL. If he had recorded blood glucose on only 10 mornings and obtained the same mean and standard deviation, what change would occur in the 95% confidence interval of the mean?
questions.explanation: Answer B (correct answer): This man is sampling his blood sugar to estimate his mean morning serum glucose. His experiment of 1o0 samples gave a mean value of 110 mg/dL. That value may be different from another experiment conducted with 100 samples. To quantify this uncertainty, a 95% confidence interval (c1) of the mean is determined. This gives a range in which 95% of repeated experimental means are expected to fall. The 95% confidence interval can be determined from the standard deviation (SD) and number of samples (n) in an experiment using the following equation: 95% Confidence Interval= Mean+/- 1.96 * SD/(Vn) In this case with a mean 110 mg/dL, standard deviation of 4 mg/dL and 100 samples the 95% confidence interval is +/- 1.96 (4 /V100) = 110 +/- 0.8. This indicates that a repeated experiment should yield a mean between 109.2 and 110.8 mg/dL 95% of the time. Based on the equation above, the 95% CI depends on the mean, standard deviation, and the number of samples. A repeat experiment with fewer samples will have a larger or "increased width" of the 95% CI. If 10 samples =() = that repeated experiments should yield a mean between 107.5 and 112.5 mg/dL 95% of the time. Think of this interval as a measure of our certainty in the experimental mean. With more samples (e.g., 1oo), we are more certain the mean is accurate, and the 95% CI width will be narrower (e.g., 110mg/dL with a 95% CI 109.2 and 110.8). With only 10 samples, we are less certain and the 95% confidence interval will be wider (e.g., 110mg/dL with a 95% CI of 107.5 and 112.5). Mc Graw

Answer C (correct answer): The study described is comparing categorical variables. Patients are categorized into high or low aerobic activity. Contrast this system with a quantitative variable for aerobic activity such as total exercise time per week.When categorical variables are studied, the chi squared test is used.

Answer A (incorrect answer): The two-sample t-test is used to compare two quantitative means.

Answer B (incorrect answer): The one sample t-test is used to compare a sample mean to a known true mean. For example, if we had a sample population with a mean age of 5o years, we could use a one sample t-test to compare this to the established mean age of a population. This can help in determining whether a sample is representative.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Analysis of variance is used to compare more than two quantitative means. This test is used in studies with three or more groups.

questions.question: A meta-analysis is performed that includes five case-control studies of the effects of smoking on the development of symptom flares among patients with ulcerative colitis. The table below shows the odds ratio and 95% confidence intervals for the five trials and the combined meta-analysis. Which of the following summarizes the findings of the meta-analysis? Smoking is associated with the

options.B: Smoking has no association with the development of ulcerative colitis flares
options.C: Smokers have a 6o% increase in rates of ulcerative colitis flares
options.D: Smokers have a 40% increase in rates of ulcerative colitis flares
options.E: development of fewer ulcerative colitis Smoking is associated with the symptoms

questions.explanation:
powerful conclusions. In the question, researchers are evaluating the odds ratio for development of ulcerative colitis flare among smokers compared with non-smokers. This is a confusing description (which, unfortunately, is common in the medical literature) and it's important to sort out its meaning. An odds ratio is a measure of association between an exposure (smoking) and an outcome (development of ulcerative colitis). the question: Was the 0.6 odds ratio significant? The CI for the combined meta-analysis is 0.4 to 0.8. This range does not include the number 1.0. This indicates a 95% chance that the true odds ratio is between 0.4 - 0.8, less than one. Thus, the finding of the study is statistically significant. This means that ulcerative colitis flares were less common among smokers compared with non-smokers. This finding is consistent with other data in the medical literature. There are a few disorders where smoking improves outcomes and ulcerative colitis is one of them. The mechanism is not clear. Note that many of the studies included in the meta-analysis (studies 1 through 5) have a confidence interval that includes 1.o, indicating the results were not significant. However, when all the studies are combined into one meta-analysis, the results are significant (i.e., the confidence interval does not include 1.o). This is the advantage of a meta-analysis. It can often draw conclusions where smaller studies could not. The downside to a meta-analysis is that it includes all the flaws in study design that may have been part of the smaller studies. lead to similarly flawed findings.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Smoking is associated with less development of ulcerative colitis symptoms, not more.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Smoking has a significant association with symptoms.

Answers C and D (incorrect answers): Smokers do not have an increase in flares of 60% or 40%. If there were a 60% increase in flares, the combined meta-analysis would be 1.6 and the CI would not include 1.0.

A confusing aspect of ROC curves is that the diagnostic test value (e.g., troponin level) is not shown on the graph. Instead, each troponin cutoff value generates a sensitivity and specificity and those are used to create the Roc curve. The y-axis on the ROC curve is the sensitivity which is proportional to the true positive rate. The x-axis is 1- specificity which is proportional to the false positive rate. Different cut-off points for troponin level yield different points on the RoC curve. The point closest to the top left corner is the cutoff point that maximizes true positives while minimizing false positives. Thus, the troponin cutoff that generated point B will diagnose the maximum number of patients with myocardial infarction (i.e., maximum true positives) with the least false positives.

questions.question: A new nasal steroid spray is evaluated for treatment of seasonal allergic rhinitis. A clinical study finds the spray effective for reducing symptoms. The major adverse effect is a statistically significant increase in the rate of bacterial sinusitis associated with treatment. In a subgroup analysis, there is an increased risk of sinusitis among smokers taking the spray compared to untreated smokers (RR=2.1; 95% confidence interval 1.6 - 2.5). When non-smokers are analyzed, the data show no increase in the risk of sinusitis associated with use of the spray (RR=1.01; 95% confidence interval 0.81 - 1.09). Which of the following is present in this study?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer):The question describes a study that found an increased risk of an outcome (bacterial sinusitis) associated with an exposure (nasal spray) among the overall study population. When the study population was broken down into smokers and non-smokers, the increased risk persisted among smokers but not non-smokers. This is consistent with effect modification due to smoking. Effect modification occurs when a third variable (e.g., smoking) modifies the effect of exposure on the outcome. This generates misleading results since exposure (e.g., nasal spray) appears to be associated with the outcome (e.g., sinusitis) among all subjects, but this is not the case.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Confounding occurs when a third variable distorts the association between exposure and outcome. If smoking were a confounder in this study, subgroup analysis of smokers and non- smokers would show no increase in rates of sinusitis when the groups were analyzed separately. In the question, subgroup analysis showed a persistent association of exposure and outcome but only among smokers. This finding is consistent with effect modification not confounding.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Selection bias is the selection of study subjects that do not represent the population intended to be analyzed. There is no reason based on the question that subjects in the study are not representative of allergic-rhinitis sufferers in general.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Observer bias occurs when observers know the status of subjects being studied. This form of bias is avoided by blinding so those who interpret data in a study do not know the status of study subjects.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Measurement bias occurs when study findings are not measured properly. If the use of nasal spray, smoking status, or development of sinusitis was improperly assessed, measurement bias could result. There is nothing in the question stem to suggest measurement bias. Mc

Researchers plan a randomized, controlled trial of aspirin versus placebo in this population to further evaluate this association. which of the following advantages will the randomized trial have over the other studies?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): Randomized trials are the strongest form of evidence for the effects of a therapy (e.g., daily aspirin) on an outcome (e.g.., colorectal cancer). The reason they are so powerful is that the randomization process should eliminate confounding. If done properly, randomly assigning subjects to aspirin or placebo should distribute any potential confounder equally among groups so the confounders cannot influence diabetes, smoking history or any other variable that might influence the development of colon cancer. Randomized trials also eliminate selection bias. The other benefit is that it not only equalizes factors we think might affect results but also factors we do not know might affect results. Case-control and cohort studies, no matter how rigorously conducted, are always vulnerable to confounding because subjects are not randomly assigned to one group or the other.

Answer A (incorrect answer): There is no reason for patient recruitment to be easier in a clinical trial compared to a case-control or cohort study. In fact, patients are sometimes reluctant to be randomly assigned to therapy making clinical trials more difficult to conduct.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Statistical power is the ability to detect a difference between groups if one exists. It is based on sample size and the frequency of the outcome under study (e.g., colorectal cancer). The question gives no information to indicate power will be increased in the clinical trial.

Answer A (correct answer): The abdominal aorta is the most common site of atherosclerotic plaque formation in the human body. Atherosclerosis tends to affect large elastic and muscular arteries, particularly at sites of branch points and vessel curvature, where flow patterns are disturbed. Although the flow in the abdominal aorta is not grossly turbulent, it is characterized by low shear stress (slow flow near the vessel wall) which allows build- endothelium more susceptible to inflammation and lipid accumulation. Additionally, the abdominal aorta has relatively fewer vasa vasorum compared to the thoracic aorta, limiting its ability to repair and maintain the vessel wall, which further promotes atherosclerosis.

Plaque rupture in this vascular structure results in brain ischemia and stroke, with neurologic deficits that correspond to the specific artery that is occluded. patients with elevated LDL, diabetes, or older age. However, epidemiologic studies show that the abdominal aorta is even more frequently affected.

Answer D (incorrect answer): The internal carotid artery is also a common site of atherosclerosis and stroke risk, especially at the carotid bifurcation. However, it ranks below the abdominal aorta and coronary arteries in terms of overall frequency of involvement. Atherosclerotic plaques in the internal carotid arteries may rupture and then embolize to the brain, resulting in either embolic stroke or transient ischemic attack.

Answer E (incorrect answer): The popliteal artery is often involved in peripheral artery disease (PAD), especially still not the most common site overall for initial plaque formation.

In 1o%of patients, the PDA is a branch of the left circumflex (LCX). Such patients are called left dominant. Since the occluded artery for this patient is the LCX, and her ECG shows an inferior infarction pattern, she must be left dominant. Inferior ST changes in an LCX occlusion suggest that the LCX supplies the inferior wall and that the patient is left dominant.

questions.question: supplemental oxygen. A loud systolic murmur is heard along the left sternal border. Chest x-ray shows increased pulmonary septal defect and supplying both the aorta and pulmonary arteries. This congenital anomaly is most likely due to abnormal development of which of the following embryologic structures?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This newborn has clinical features of persistent truncus arteriosus, a congenital heart defect in which a single arterial trunk arises from the heart and gives rise to the systemic, pulmonary, and coronary circulations. This condition results from failure of the truncus arteriosus to divide into the aorta and pulmonary artery during development. Normally, the truncus arteriosus is partitioned by the aorticopulmonary septum, which arises from neural crest cells. Abnormal development or migration of these cells leads to a persistent common arterial outflow tract. This defect is almost always associated with a ventricular septal defect, which allows mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood and contributes to cyanosis and increased pulmonarybloodflow.

Answer A (incorrect answer): The bulbus cordis contributes to the smooth outflow tracts of both ventricles (aortic vestibule and conus arteriosus) but does not give rise to the great vessels themselves.

Answer B (incorrect answer): The endocardial cushions form the atrioventricular valves and portions of the atrial and ventricular septa. while defects in these structures can cause septal abnormalities and AV canal defects, they are not responsible for division of the truncus arteriosus.

Answer C (incorrect answer): The septum primum is involved in atrial septation, not in the development of the arterial outflow tract. Its abnormal development leads to atrial septal defects, not persistent truncus arteriosus. coronary sinus. It plays no role in the development of the arterial outflow tract.

questions.question: A newborn is evaluated for a heart murmur detected during routine examination. The infant is well-appearing and feeding normally. On auscultation, a systolic ejection murmur is heard at the left upper sternal border along with a wide and fixed shunting of blood. The defect is located in the region of the fossa ovalis. This congenital abnormality is most likely due to abnormal development of which of the following structures?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This infant has clinical features of a secundum-type atrial septal defect (AsD), the most common form of AsD. It results from incomplete formation or excessive resorption of the septum secundum, which normally overlaps the septum primum to close the foramen ovale. Failure of this overlap leaves a persistent communication between the atria in the region of the fossa ovalis. This allows left-to-right shunting of blood during both systole and diastole, increasing flow through the right atrium, right ventricle, and pulmonary circulation. The increased flow through the pulmonary valve produces a systolic ejection murmur best heard at the left upper sternal border, which is due to increased pulmonary blood flow, not a structural abnormality of the valve itself. The wide, fixed splitting of the second heart sound (s2) occurs because the increased right heart volume These auscultatory findings are classic for a left-to-right shunt at the atrial level.

Answer A (incorrect answer): The bulbus cordis contributes to the smooth outflow tracts of the ventricles, not the interatrial septum.

Answer B (incorrect answer): The membranous septum forms part of the interventricular septum and is involved in ventricular, not atrial, septal development.

Answer C (incorrect answer): The muscular septum also forms part of the interventricular septum and is unrelated to atrial septal formation.

Answer D (incorrect answer): The primitive atria give rise to the trabeculated portions of the atria but do not form the interatrial septum. Septation involves the septum primum and septum secundum, not the primitive atrial walls themselves.

questions.question: A newborn is evaluated shortly after delivery for a cardiac murmur detected on routine examination. The infant is otherwise well-appearing with normal oxygen saturation and no signs of respiratory distress. Echocardiography is performed and reveals a cleft in the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve, resulting in mild mitral regurgitation. The remainder of the cardiac anatomy is normal. The affected valve structure in this patient is derived from which of the following embryologic components?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This newborn has a congenital cleft mitral valve, which is most commonly due to improper fusion of the endocardial cushions during cardiac development. The endocardial cushions are embryologic structures that form the atrioventricular (AV) valves (mitral and tricuspid), the membranous portion of the interventricular septum, and part of the atrial septum. Maldevelopment of these cushions can result in structural defects such as AV septal defects and clefts in the mitral or tricuspid valves.

Answer A (incorrect answer): The bulbus cordis contributes to the smooth outflow tracts of the ventricles, including the aortic vestibule and conus arteriosus. It does not give rise to the AV valves.

Answer C (incorrect answer): The posterior cardinal veins are involved in the development of parts of the systemic venous system, including segments of the inferior vena cava, but they do not contribute to valve or septalformation.

Answer D (incorrect answer): The right common cardinal vein contributes to the formation of the superior vena cava. It is not involved in the formation of the mitral valve.

Answer E (incorrect answer): The truncus arteriosus gives rise to the proximal portions of the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk. It is involved in outflow tract development, not AV valve formation. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 55-year-old man is referred for a transthoracic echocardiogram after an episode of exertional chest discomfort and shortness of breath. He has a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia but no prior cardiac events. Echocardiography reveals normal biventricular function and no valvular abnormalities. The coronary sinus is clearly visualized in the posterior portion of the atrioventricular groove. This structure derives from which of the following embryologic sources?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): The coronary sinus develops from the left horn of the sinus venosus during embryologic development. The sinus venosus initially has right and left horns that drain the common cardinal veins. As development progresses, the left horn diminishes in size and becomes the coronary sinus, which functions as the main venous drainage vessel of the heart. It empties into the right atrium near the septal leafletofthetricuspidvalve.

Answer A(incorrectanswer): The bulbus cordis contributes to the smooth outflow tracts of bothventricles. It does not contributeto the formation of the coronarysinus. not contribute to the formation of the coronary sinus, which develops from the sinus venosus. the right atrium and forms the smooth part of the right atrium known as the sinus venarum. It does not form the coronary sinus.

Answer E (incorrect answer): The truncus arteriosus gives rise to the proximal portions of the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk. It contributes to the arterial outflow tract, not the venous structures like the coronary sinus. Mc Graw Himi

questions.question: A newborn is delivered at term but develops profound cyanosis and respiratory distress shortly after birth. Despite opened, and a portion of its internal surface is noted to have a smooth surface. This portion of the left ventricle is most likely derived from which of the following embryologic structures?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This question describes the smooth-walled portion of the left ventricle, which corresponds to the aortic vestibule. This smooth region near the outflow tract is derived from the bulbus cordis, a component of the embryologic heart tube that contributes to the outflow tracts of both ventricles. In the left ventricle, the bulbus cordis forms the smooth-walled aortic vestibule that leads into the aortic valve and ascending aorta. In contrast, the trabeculated portion of the left ventricle, which makes up the majority of its muscular wall, is derived from the primitive ventricle. This region is characterized by irregular muscular ridges called trabeculae carneae, which develop early in cardiac morphogenesis. Key point: the internal surface of the left ventricle is composed of two distinct embryologic regions: a trabeculated region from the primitive ventricle and a smooth outflow region (near the aortic valve) from the bulbus cordis.

Answer B (incorrect answer): The primitive atria give rise to the rough, trabeculated portions of the right and left atria, not to the smooth portions of the ventricles.

Answer C (incorrect answer): The primitive ventricle forms the trabeculated portion of the left ventricle, not the smooth outflow tract region.

Answer D (incorrect answer): The sinus venosus contributes to the smooth part of the right atrium (sinus venarum), not to the left ventricle.

Answer E (incorrect answer): The truncus arteriosus gives rise to the proximal aorta and pulmonary trunk, not the internal smooth surfaces of the ventricles. Mc M

questions.question: A 40-year-old woman comes to the clinic for a routine health maintenance visit. She has no significant medical history and feels well. Her brother was recently diagnosed with a patent foramen ovale (PFO) after undergoing an echocardiogram for
questions.explanation: Answer C (correct answer): In utero, the foramen ovale allows fetal blood to pass from the right atrium to the left atrium. At birth, a rise in left atrial pressure and a fall in right atrial pressure closes the foramen ovale forming the fossa ovalis. In about 25% of patients, the foramen ovale does not close leading to the formation of a patent foramen ovale (PFo). In most cases, this has no clinical consequences, but rarely paradoxical embolism may occur leading to stroke. For a physician with 10o0 patients, approximately 250 would have a PFO.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman gives birth at 39 weeks gestation to a male child. In the delivery room, the baby has no physical abnormalities. Apgar scores are 8 at one minute and 9 at 5 minutes. Which changes occurred in systemic vascular resistance (SVR) and pulmonary vascular resistance (PvR) in this baby after delivery compared to in utero?
questions.explanation: Answer D (correct answer): In utero, pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) is high. The lungs are filled with amniotic fluid which increases flow resistance. Also, oxygen tension is low in the fetal lungs. This leads to hypoxic vasoconstriction further increasing PVR. Because of high PVR, fetal pulmonary blood flow is low and most blood bypasses the lungs via the foramen ovale or ductus arteriosus. At birth, when the lungs fill with air, PvR falls. The fetal vasculature is connected to the low-pressure placenta. This lowers systemic vascular resistance (svR) in utero. At birth, the placenta is removed from the fetal circulation raising SVR. ····.·.

questions.question: A 41-year-old woman presents at 38 weeks gestation with placental abruption. At C-section, her baby is stillborn and pronounced dead. An autopsy is performed. questions.question: A new drug is developed which slows conduction through the AV node. which of the intervals below would increase?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): Drugs that slow AV node conduction include beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers (these drugs also slow the rate of sA node firing and, therefore, reduce heart rate). Conduction through the AV node, HIs bundle, bundle branches, and Purkinje fibers occurs after atrial depolarization (i.e. the start of the P wave) and before ventricular depolarization (i.e. the start of the QRs complex). Prolonged conduction through any of these structures can increase the PR interval, the distance on ECG between A and B in the question.

Answer B (incorrect answer): The distance from B to C is the QRS interval. This interval may prolong from bundle branch blocks or drugs that slow ventricular depolarization (class I antiarrhythmics).

Answer C (incorrect answer): The distance from C to D is the Q-T interval. This interval may prolong with drugs that block ventricular repolarization (class III antiarrhythmics).

Answer D (incorrect answer): The distance from D to E is diastole.Drugs that slow SA node activity and, therefore, heart rate increase diastole. Mc Graw

questions.question: A new drug is developed which slows the rate of firing of the SA node. which of the intervals below would increase?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): The heart rate (i.e. the pulse) is determined by the "R-R interval" meaning the distance between QRS complexes. A decrease in the SA node firing rate will increase the R-R interval and slow the heart rate.On the EcG, the distance between QRS complexes will increase. There are two reasons for the increased R-R interval at slower heart rates. Ventricular repolarization takes longer at slower heart rates. Thus, the Q-T interval prolongs when the heart rate slows. Also, the length of time the heart spends in diastole increases. At slower heart rates, it takes longer for the SA node to generate a new P wave after each cardiac cycle. In the question, the time between points D and E represents diastole. This will increase with a fall in the sinus rate. Key point: At slower heart rates, the R-R interval, Q-T interval, and time of diastole will lengthen/increase.

Answers A and B (incorrectanswers): Conduction through the AV node,HIS bundle,bundle branches, and Purkinje fibers occurs after atrial depolarization(i.e. the start of the P wave) and before ventricular depolarization (i.e. the start of the QRs complex). Prolonged conduction through any of these structures can increase the PR interval which is the distance on the ECG between A and B in the question.

Answer C (incorrect answer): The distance from B to C is the QRs interval. This interval may prolong from bundle branch blocks or drugs that slow ventricular depolarization (class I antiarrhythmics). Mc Graw

questions.question: A patient's ECG shows a QRs interval of 160ms (normal <120ms). which of the following may be the cause?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): The QRs interval represents the time required for ventricular depolarization. In patients with right bundle branch block or left bundle branch block, this interval prolongs. When one bundle branch does not conduct electricity, the remaining bundle branch must depolarize both ventricles. This is a slower process because the remaining bundle branch cannot use the normal HIs-Purkinje system of the bundle branch that is lost. Conduction must occur from myocyte to myocyte which prolongs the time required for completedepolarization.

Answers A and E (incorrect answers): Slow AV node conduction or slow HIs bundle conduction prolongs the PR interval but does not change the QRs interval.

Answers B and C (incorrect answers): Bradycardia and tachycardia will change the Q-T interval, but not the QRS interval. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 17-year-old girl presents after a seizure. She collapsed while standing in the hallway at school and twitched briefly after falling to the ground. Patients with congenital long Q-T syndrome must avoid a number of Q-T prolonging medications including many antiarrhythmic drugs and macrolide antibiotics.

questions.question: A 75-year-old man presents with a complaint of muscle weakness and fatigue. He has a history of coronary artery disease and congestive heart failure with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 30%. Strength testing shows 3/5 strength bilaterally in the lower extremities. Answer B (correct answer): This patient has classic findings of hypokalemia, including muscle weakness and U waves on ECG. In patients with congestive heart failure, as in the question, this may occur due to excessive use of loop diuretics (i.e.furosemide) which increase potassium excretion.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Digoxin toxicity leads to visual disturbances, gastrointestinal symptoms, and confusion. ECG findings include premature atrial and ventricular contractions, AV block, and other abnormalities.

questions.question: Researchers are studying conduction speed through myocardial tissue. Cells from five different portions of the cardiac conduction system are grown in culture. Shown below is the time required for an impulse to travel through different tissue samples of the same size. Which tissue sample (A through E) represents the Purkinje fibers?
questions.explanation: Answer A (correct answer): Conduction velocities (as explained in the video) are fastest for Purkinje fibers and fibers compared with 0.o3 m/s in the AV node. The graph shows conduction time for five samples, meaning the time required for an impulse to move through a tissue sample. Since all samples are the same size as stated in the question, cells that rapidly conduct electrical impulses will have a short impulse conduction time. Cells that slowly conduct impulses will have a long conduction time. Purkinje fibers are the fastest conducting structures in the cardiac conduction system. Thus, they will have the shortest conduction time which is sample A. In other words, for these fibers the time to conduct an impulse will be shortest since impulses move so quickly through the sample. questions.question: A 70-year-old man presents to the emergency department with increasing shortness of breath, fatigue, and swelling in his jugular venous distension, an S3 gallop, and bilateral pitting edema. Chest auscultation reveals bibasilar crackles. Laboratory testing shows a brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) level of 2,100 pg/mL (normal <100 pg/mL). Which of the following is the most likely source of this hormone?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This patient has clinical features of decompensated heart failure, and his elevated brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) level reflects ventricular strain. BNP is primarily secreted by the right and left ventricular myocytes in response to volume expansion and pressure overload. In particular, the right ventricle is often a dominant source in conditions associated with right-sided pressure overload such as pulmonary used as a biomarker in the evaluation of heart failure severity.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Atrial myocytes secrete atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), not BNP. ANP is released in response to atrial stretch and also promotes natriuresis and vasodilation, but it is distinct from BNP in origin andregulation.

Answer B (incorrect answer): The hypothalamus is involved in regulating water balance via vasopressin (ADH) secretion but is not involved in BNP production.

Answer C(incorrectanswer):Maculadensacellsregulatesodiumconcentrationin the distal tubuleand influence reninreleasebutarenotasourceofBNP.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Neurons do not produce BNP.Although BNP was first isolated from brain tissue in pigs, its main source in humans is ventricular myocardium, not the nervous system. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 68-year-old man comes to the clinic due to progressive shortness of breath and leg swelling. He has a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and has been hospitalized twice in the past year for COPD exacerbations. He reports venous distension, bilateral lower extremity edema, and a palpable liver edge. Lung auscultation reveals faint expiratory wheezes without crackles. Cardiac auscultation reveals a normal S1 and S2. which of the following additional findings would be most consistent with left-sided heart failure in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This patient has clinical findings that suggest right-sided heart failure, possibly due to cor pulmonale from longstanding COPD. However, it is also possible that left-sided heart failure is the underlying cause of his right-sided symptoms, rather than isolated pulmonary disease. The presence of a third heartsound(S3)would support left-sidedventricular dysfunction.AnS3occursin earlydiastolewhenblood rapidly fills a volume-overloaded or noncompliant left ventricle. It is a specific marker of left-sided systolic heart failure and would help distinguish primary left ventricular dysfunction from isolated right-sided failure due to pulmonary hypertension.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Dyspnea on exertion is a nonspecific symptom that can occur with either right- or left-sided heart failure, as well as with COPD itself. It does not reliably distinguish between the two and is not specific for left-sided heart failure.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Elevated jugular venous pressure reflects increased right atrial pressure and is a classic finding of right-sided heart failure. It is commonly seen in cor pulmonale or right heart failure caused by left-sided failure.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Hepatomegaly results from passive congestion of the liver due to elevated central venous pressure in right-sided heart failure. It is not a feature specific to left-sided heart failure.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Lower extremity edema is a common manifestation of right-sided heart failure due to elevated hydrostatic pressures in the systemic venous system. It does not distinguish between left- and right-sided heart failure unless accompanied by other specific signs. MW

questions.question: A 72-year-old man is brought to the clinic by his daughter due to worsening fatigue, poor appetite, and confusion over the past few weeks. He has a history of ischemic cardiomyopathy with an ejection fraction of 15%. He reports unintentional weight loss and has had increasing difficulty performing daily activities. On physical examination, he appears cachectic with cool extremities and diminished peripheral pulses. There is jugular venous distension and bilateral pitting edema. Auscultation reveals a soft, distant heart sound. which of the following additional findings is most likely present in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This man has clinical features of end-stage systolic heart failure, including low cardiac output symptoms such as fatigue, confusion, and cool extremities. These findings reflect severely pressure is relatively preserved due to compensatory vasoconstriction, leading to a narrow pulse pressure (the difference between systolic and diastolic pressures). Narrow pulse pressure is a hallmark of low cardiac output states such as advanced heart failure.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Bradycardia is not a typical feature of end-stage systolic heart failure. In fact, sympathetic nervous system activation in response to decreased cardiac output usually leads to tachycardia.

He works as a truck driver and frequently eats fast food while working. The patient is trying to lose weight by cutting calories via intermittent fasting. Which of the following additional lifestyle modifications would be most effective in improving this patient's blood pressure?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): Lifestyle modifications are essential in the management of a patient with hypertension. Weight loss is typically the most effective intervention. Studies have demonstrated an average of 0.5 to 2 mmHg of blood pressure decrease per 1 kg of weight loss. The second most important intervention is the Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DAsH) diet. This diet is high in vegetables, fruits, fish, poultry, and plant-based fats. It eliminates red meat and foods with added sugar. Strictly following the DASH diet can result in a blood pressure decrease of over 10 mmHg. Exercising, reducing dietary sodium, and decreasing alcohol intake have also been shown to decrease blood pressure. However, the magnitude of this decrease for these interventions is not as large as that for weight loss and the DASH diet.

questions.question: A 70-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with acute-onset dyspnea, lightheadedness, and chest discomfort. He has a history of lung cancer with pericardial metastases. On examination, his blood pressure is 88/60 mmHg and heart rate is 118/min. Jugular venous distension and muffled heart sounds are noted, and pulsus paradoxus is present. An echocardiogram shows a large pericardial effusion with right atrial and right ventricular diastolic collapse. Emergent pericardiocentesis is performed with immediate hemodynamic improvement. which of the following best describes the following this procedure?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This man has cardiac tamponade, as evidenced by hypotension, jugular venous collapse. In tamponade, pericardial fluid restricts cardiac filling, leading to an underfilled left ventricle and decreased stroke volume. The resulting hypotension triggers a sympathetic compensatory response, which increases systemic vascular resistance (svR) to maintain perfusion. At the same time, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PcwP), a marker for left atrial pressure, becomes elevated due to external compression of the left atrium by pericardial fluid. Following pericardiocentesis, the removal of pericardial fluid relieves the external pressure on the heart and reverses these hemodynamic abnormalities. Diastolic filling improves, stroke volume rises, and cardiac output increases. As a result, svR decreases due to improved perfusion and withdrawal of compensatory vasoconstriction.Pcwpdecreases because the leftatriumis nolonger externally compressed.

Answer B, C, D and E (incorrect answers): As explained above, after pericardiocentesis, SVR falls and RVEDP decreases due to relief of pericardial pressure. Mc Graw

questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This is a typical presentation of peri-infarction pericarditis (fibrinous pericarditis). Myocardial inflammation after myocardial infarction (MI) sometimes involves the pericardium leading to It worsens with lying flat and improves with sitting upright. Answer C (incorrect answer): Systolic heart failure causes dyspnea, fatigue, and edema. Lungs will have rales. An S3 is often present. Jugular venous pressure is usually elevated.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman is evaluated for dyspnea. She was recently diagnosed with Hodgkin's lymphoma. For the past two days she has had fatigue and exertional dyspnea. Exam reveals fine bibasilar rales. Heart sounds are distant with no murmurs. Jugular venous pressure is 12 mmHg (normal <8). Blood pressure is 100/70 mmHg and falls during inspiration. Echocardiography reveals a large pericardial effusion. She is treated with pericardiocentesis and removal of 1 liter of fluid from the pericardial space. Following this intervention,
questions.explanation: Answer D (correct answer): Cardiac tamponade occurs in the setting of a pericardial effusion when pericardial pressure rises to the point that ventricular filling is impaired. Acute tamponade may occur after trauma and presents with Beck's triad: distended neck veins, distant heart sounds and hypotension. This patient has a subacute presentation that has developed over several days. This occurs when tamponade is caused by malignancy, uremia or following pericarditis. Under normal circumstances (i.e. in absence of tamponade) the right and left atrial pressures are determined by the volume of blood within the chamber. More blood leads to higher pressure and vice versa. In tamponade, however, a high-pressure fluid collection in the pericardial space surrounds the right and left atria. In this case, atrial pressure is determined by the pressure in the pericardial space that compresses the atrial walls. Consider that if pericardial pressure is 20 mmHg in a case of tamponade then right atrial pressure cannot fall to a normal value of 6mmHg. The right atrial pressure will be at least 20 mmHg, determined by the pressure of the pericardial fluid compressing the right atrium. The same is true for the left atrium (i.e. left atrial pressure will also be 20 mmHg). When right atrial pressure rises in tamponade, right ventricular end-diastolic pressure (RVEDP) rises. In diastole, right ventricular pressure rises until it reaches right atrial pressure and closes the tricuspid valve. Thus, high right atrial pressure leads to high RVEDP. Based onthesemechanisms,lowcardiacoutputand high RVEDPare expected in tamponade.Following treatment with pericardiocentesis, cardiac output will increase and RVEDP will decrease.Pericardiocentesis resolves the abnormal hemodynamics of tamponade by lowering pericardial pressure through fluid removal. Reference: http://circ.ahajournals.org/content/circulationaha/58/2/265.full.pdf Mc Graw 1IH

Answer E (correct answer): Left-sided heart failure is the most common cause of pulmonary arterial hypertension (i.e. high pressure in the pulmonary artery). When the left ventricle fails, left ventricular end- diastolic pressure (LVEDP) rises. This pressure is transmitted backwards to the left atrium, the pulmonary veins and ultimately the pulmonary arteries causing pulmonary arterial hypertension. Left heart failure causing pulmonary hypertension is referred to as pulmonary venous hypertension because the pressure is elevated in the pulmonary veins which connect to the left atrium. In contrast, isolated pulmonary arterial hypertension originates in the lungs and is associated with normal pulmonary venous pressure. The elevated pulmonary e (PcwP) in this patient indicates high left atrial and pulmonary venous pressures. capillarywedgepressure

Answers A, B, C (incorrect answers): In the setting of tension pneumothorax and obstructive shock (prior to chest tube insertion), the sympathetic nervous system is activated. This leads to vasoconstriction, increased heart rate, and increased cardiac contractility. These mechanisms are unable to prevent shock when intra- thoracic pressure is increased. This represents blood oxygen content after venous blood from the body has emptied into the right atrium and "mixed." The Mvo2 is used to calculate cardiac output with the Fick equation (shown above). questions.question: A 28-year-old male motorcyclist presents after a crash. Massive blood loss occurred at the scene of the accident due to severing of the brachial artery. Transfused blood adds volume to the leftventricle and raises cardiac output.The increase in cardiac output leads to a fall in SNS activity. As a result, SVR declines.
