questions.question: An 82-year-old woman presents to the rheumatologist for evaluation of joint pain. The pain is primarily in her hips, knees and lower back and it has been slowly progressive over several years. In the morning, her joints feel stiff for 20 minutes and then gain. She has no joint redness or warmth, rash, sun sensitivity, dysuria, hematuria, chest pain, shortness of breath or breast cancer and a carpal tunnel release. Her current medications include acetaminophen, amlodipine, losartan, hydralazine and levothyroxine. Vital signs include a temperature of 98.5°F, heart rate of 83 beats/minute and blood pressure of 123/67 mmHg. Her body mass index is 30.6 kg/m2. She is well appearing and in no acute distress. She has moist mucous membranes. A 2-cm ulcerated lesion is noted on her right buccal mucosa. Auscultation of the heart and lungs is normal. The abdomen is motion present in bilateral knees. Results of a comprehensive metabolic panel and complete blood count are normal. Other laboratory results and an x-ray of the knee are shownbelow. Otherresults Antinuclearantibodies positive,titer 1:80 negative Anti-Smithantibodies Anti-dsDNAantibodies negative negative Anti-histoneantibodies Antibodiesto negative citrullinatedpeptides negative Rheumatoidfactor Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This woman has osteoarthritis (oA) based on the insidious onset of joint pain, morning stiffness that lasts less than 30 minutes, restricted range of motion and evidence of joint space narrowing on x-ray (see red arrow above). Her arthritis is not typical of patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) who generally have a symmetric migratory polyarthritis that often affects the hands and knees. In contrast, she has slowly progressive pain in the hips, knees and back. Her examination shows crepitus, which is suggestive of OA but not SLE. The patient does have a positive anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) on laboratory testing; however, 5% of normal patients may have a positive result. Although this patient has arthritis, a positive ANA and an oral ulcer, she does not meet American College of Rheumatology criteria for SLE.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Avascular necrosis is associated with glucocorticoid use, lupus and sickle cell disease.It most commonly affects the femoral head and presents with acute severe hip or groin pain. This patient has chronic pain in multiple joints and joint space narrowing consistent with a diagnosis of osteoarthritis.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Patients with rheumatoid arthritis typically have the gradual onset of symmetric joint inflammation. They may present with morning stiffness lasting for greater than one hour as well as systemic symptoms such as fever, fatigue or weight loss. Laboratory results typically show a positive rheumatoid does not have systemic symptoms and has a negative RF making rheumatoid arthritis unlikely.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Patients with SLE typically have a symmetric migratory polyarthritis that often affects the hands and knees. They also have a variety of other systemic manifestations including rash, photosensitivity, cytopenias, renal disease and serositis. Patients with lupus typically have an ANA titer of greater than 1:160. They may also have other autoantibodies including anti-double stranded DNA or anti- Smith.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Patients may develop drug-induced lupus secondary to treatment with medications such isoniazid, hydralazine or procainamide. They may develop symptoms including rash, arthritis, anemia or thrombocytopenia. Typically, patients have positive anti-histone antibodies. Although this patient is on hydralazine, she is unlikely to have drug-induced lupus because her anti-histone antibodies are negative, and her symptoms and x-ray are suggestive of osteoarthritis. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 37-year-old woman presents to her physician for evaluation of pain in both knees and both hands. She reports feeling achy minutes and then improves. She also reports fatigue. She has no double vision, blurred vision, loss of visual acuity, oral ulcers, pressure of 133/67 mmHg. She is well-appearing and in no acute distress. Auscultation of the heart and lungs is normal. The abdomen is soft and nontender without hepatosplenomegaly. Skin examination reveals circular patches of erythematous scaly skin on bilateral forearms. There is mild swelling of bilateral knees without any redness or warmth. Initial laboratory results are shown below. Her physician plans to prescribe hydroxychloroquine. Which of the following additional interventions are recommended at this time?

options.A: Advise 60 minutes of sunlight per day
options.D: Recheck basic metabolic panel in one week

questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This patient has systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) based on her positive antinuclear antibodies, positive anti-Smith antibodies, discoid skin rash and arthritis. Hydroxychloroquine is an anti-malarial drug with immunosuppressant properties that is a common first-line therapy for SLE. This medication may rarely cause retinopathy, corneal deposits and vision loss; therefore, eye exams are required in patient taking hydroxychloroquine.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Patients with lupus should avoid excessive exposure to sunlight because lupus this patient's vitamin D level is low, and sunlight may increase vitamin D levels, pharmacologic supplementation with vitamin D is more appropriate than increased sun exposure in patients with lupus. rheumatoid arthritis should be screened for latent tuberculosis (TB). Therapy with these antibody-based treatments increases the risk of reactivating latent TB. Hydroxychloroquine is not typically associated with reactivation of TB, so TB screening is not necessary in patients taking hydroxychloroquine.

Answer D (incorrect answer): This patient's basic metabolic panel is within normal limits. Hydroxychloroquine does not typically affect any of the laboratory values reported in the basic metabolic panel and does not need tobe re-checked. Although these adverse effects are rare, routine eye exams are required for patients taking hydroxychloroquine. MSW Hmi

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) presents with left groin pain. It started a week ago, is worsening and is now so painful that she cannot bear weight on her left leg. Three weeks ago, the patient started taking daily oral prednisone for an acute flare of her SLE. She has no recent trauma, surgery, fever, chills or joint swelling. Her past medical history also includes obesity, osteoarthritis, gastroesophageal reflux disease, hyperlipidemia and osteopenia. She has of cigarettes per day and drinks four 12-ounce beers per day but does not use illicit drugs. On evaluation, vital signs show a temperature of 97.5°F, heart rate of 79 beats/minute and blood pressure of 142/76 mmHg. Her body mass index is 32.5 kg/m2. On musculoskeletal evaluation, there is no redness or tenderness of the joint appreciated. Strength and range of management?

options.E: Magnetic resonance imaging of the hip

questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This patient with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) has acute groin pain due to avascular necrosis (AvN) of the femoral head. Although the mechanism of this condition is poorly understood, it is thought to occur due to interruption of blood flow to the bone, resulting in thinning of the cortex and Mc subsequent collapse of the femoral head (see image above). Risk factors for AVN include glucocorticoid use, SLE, Graw sickle cell disease, chronic alcohol use and cigarette smoking. Often plain radiography of the hip is normal for weeks to months after the initial symptoms. In contrast, magnetic resonance imaging has a high sensitivity for the diagnosis of AVN and obtaining this study is the best next step in management. The treatment of AVN is typically surgical; surgical options may include bone grafting, osteotomy (making cuts into the existing bone to offload pressure caused by the necrosis) or joint replacement.

Answer A(incorrect answer): Hydroxychloroquine is an anti-malarial drug with immunosuppressive properties patients with SLE. Unlike other tests such as serum anti-double stranded DNA levels, the ANA level is not typically associated with SLE disease activity. It is primarily used as part of a diagnostic evaluation to assess a patient for SLE. This woman has a known diagnosis of SLE and checking ANA levels would not aid in her management.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Patients with SLE experiencing severe organ dysfunction due to a disease flare may be admitted to the hospital for high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone. Examples of indications for this caused by lupus disease activity and should not be treated with intravenous glucocorticoids. Glucocorticoid use is a risk factor for developing AVN and should be avoided in patients with this condition.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Patients with septic arthritis may be admitted to the hospital for intravenous antibiotics. This patient is afebrile and has AVN based on findings on magnetic resonance imaging. Antibiotics arenotgenerallyused in thetreatmentofisolatedAvN. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 26-year-old woman presents with fatigue and facial rash. These symptoms have been slowly progressive over the last four months. She has no heartburn, fever, arthralgias, focal weakness, joint pain or change in the color of her fingers. She has no known prior medical conditions. Her only medications are oral contraceptive pills and a multivitamin. She does not smoke, drink alcohol to excess, or use illicit drugs. On evaluation, vital signs show a temperature of 98.5°F, heart rate of 71 beats/minute and blood pressure of 152/77 mmHg. Skin examination reveals a red, scaly rash on the bilateral upper cheeks and bridge of the nose. There is no skin thickening or thinning of the lips. Evaluation of the oral mucosa shows a one- centimeter ulcer. Auscultation of the heart and lungs is normal. The abdomen is soft and nontender without hepatosplenomegaly. Neurologic evaluation shows strength 5/5 bilaterally in the upper and lower extremities. Sensation is intact to light touch bilaterally. Reflexes are 2+ bilaterally at the biceps and patella. Initial laboratory results are shown below. Which of the following additional positive laboratory results would you expect to find in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This woman has systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). She has five findings antinuclear antibodies (ANA). To be classified as having SLE, patients need to meet four of eleven criteria specified by the American College of Rheumatology. The classic SLE rash is a "butterfly" rash affecting sun exposed areas of the face. Anti-double stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA) is a confirmatory test that is specific for SLE; it is often positive in the setting of renal involvement. Anti-smith (anti-Sm) is another autoantibody that is specific for SLE. The extractable nuclear antigen panel is useful in patients suspected of having autoimmune disease to clarify the specific diagnosis.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Anti-histone antibodies are typically positive in the setting of drug-induced lupus. hydralazine, isoniazid or procainamide. Patients with drug-induced lupus typically do not develop renal or central nervous system abnormalities. This patient has not taken any medications associated with the development of drug-induced lupus.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Anti-Jo-1 antibodies are typically positive in the setting of polymyositis, which is an autoimmune myopathy that may cause muscle weakness. This woman does not have weakness. Patients with polymyositis do not typically have a malar rash, oral ulcers or kidney disease. autoimmune condition that causes skin thickening, thinning of the lips and fibrosis of the skin, often involving the hands. Patients may have Raynaud's syndrome and heartburn. This patient's clinical presentation does not suggestscleroderma. connective tissue disease. Patients with this condition may have features including arthritis, myalgias, pulmonary fibrosis, pulmonary hypertension or Raynaud's syndrome. They are less likely to have kidney disease. Patients with mixed connective tissue disease do not meet diagnostic criteria for other rheumatologic conditions such as SLE. This woman meets the American College of Rheumatology criteria for SLE. Mc

questions.question: A 23-year-old man comes to the clinic for evaluation of a new murmur detected during a routine physical examination. He reports no chest pain or dyspnea but notes occasional fatigue with exertion. He has a history of tetralogy of Fallot that was surgically repaired during infancy. Physical examination reveals normal vital signs and a murmur at the left upper sternal border. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This young adult has a history of surgically repaired tetralogy of Fallot and now presents with a diastolic murmur and right ventricular dilation, which are classic signs of pulmonic regurgitation. This is the most common long-term complication after repair of tetralogy of Fallot. Over time, chronic volume overload from pulmonary insufficiency can lead to right ventricular enlargement, arrhythmias, and right heart failure if not monitored and managed. In many patients, pulmonic valve replacement or repair becomes necessary in adolescence or early adulthood to prevent long-term deterioration in right ventricular function.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Mitral regurgitation typically causes a holosystolic murmur best heard at the cardiac apex and is not a typical late complication of tetralogy of Fallot repair.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Pulmonic stenosis is a component of the original tetralogy of Fallot but is usually relieved surgically during the initial repair. It is not a common late complication unless there is residual obstructionorre-stenosis.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Tricuspid regurgitation can occur secondary to right ventricular dilation but is less common and would produce a holosystolic murmur along the lower left sternal border,not a decrescendo diastolic murmur.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Tricuspid stenosis is rare and not associated with repaired tetralogy of Fallot. It typically causes a mid-diastolic murmur at the lower left sternal border and is often linked to rheumatic heart disease.

questions.question: A 2-month-old infant is brought to the pediatrician for evaluation of poor feeding and failure to thrive. The parents also report that the baby is unusually sociable and has an unusually wide mouth. Physical examination reveals a murmur. Blood pressure is elevated in the upper extremities. Facial features include a broad forehead, short nose, full cheeks, and a wide mouth with a prominent upper lip. Serum calcium is elevated. Genetic testing reveals a deletion on chromosome 7q11.23 consistent with williams syndrome. In this patient, blood flow is most likely to be obstructed at which of the following sites?
questions.explanation:
Answer B(correct answer):Thisinfant has Williams syndrome, a genetic disorder caused by deletion of the elastin gene on chromosome 7q11.23. A classic cardiovascular finding in williams syndrome is supravalvular aortic stenosis, which obstructs blood flow from the left ventricle to the aorta. This results in a systolic murmur best heard at the right upper sternal border, and left ventricular hypertrophy over time. Other features of the syndrome include hypercalcemia, hypertension, distinctive facial features, and an overly friendly personality.

Answer A(incorrectanswer):Obstructionof blood flowfrom theleftatrium to theleftventricleoccurs in conditions like mitral stenosis, which is not characteristic of williams syndrome. stenosis, which can be seen in other congenital syndromes (e.g., Noonan syndrome), but is not a vascular lesion the occurs in williams syndrome.

Answer D(incorrect answer):Obstructionfrom the rightatriumtothe rightventricle occursin tricuspid stenosis, a rare condition not associated with Wwilliams syndrome.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Pulmonary valve stenosis causes obstruction from the right ventricle to the Fallot, it is not associated with williams syndrome. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 62-year-old woman comes to the office due to worsening shortness of breath and leg swelling. She also reports episodes of facial flushing and diarrhea over the past several months. Physical examination reveals jugular venous distension, hepatomegaly, and bilateral lower extremity edema. A 24-hour urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) level is valvular lesions is most likely present in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This woman has carcinoid syndrome, characterized by diarrhea, flushing, and right- sided heart failure due to secretion of vasoactive substances (especially serotonin) by a neuroendocrine tumor with liver metastases. In the setting of liver metastases, these substances bypass hepatic metabolism and reach the right heart, where they cause endocardial fibrosis and valvular dysfunction-most commonly tricuspid regurgitation. Leads to a holosystolic murmur that increases with inspiration. Pulmonic valve involvement can also occur, but the left heart (aortic and mitral valves) is generally spared unless there is a right-to-left shunt or bronchial carcinoid tumor.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Aortic regurgitation is not typically associated with carcinoid syndrome. The aortic valve is part of the left heart and is generally spared because serotonin and other vasoactive substances are inactivated in the lungs before reaching the left heart. AnswerB(incorrectanswer):Aorticstenosisisunrelated tocarcinoidsyndromeandmorecommonlyresults from age-related calcification or congenital bicuspid aortic valve. The left heart valves are usually unaffected in carcinoid syndrome due to pulmonary metabolism of vasoactive substances.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Mitral regurgitation is a left-sided lesion not commonly caused by carcinoid syndrome. Serotonin and other substances secreted by carcinoid tumors are deactivated in the pulmonary circulation, preventing damage to left-sided valves.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Mitral stenosis, like other left-sided valve lesions, is not a typical feature of carcinoid syndrome, which preferentially affects the right side of the heart unless there is a right-to-left shunt or primary pulmonary carcinoid tumor. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the clinic by his parents due to fever and joint pain for the past 5 days. He was treated for a sore throat 3 weeks ago but did not complete the full course of antibiotics. His temperature is 101.9°F. Physical examination shows a new murmur. Swelling and tenderness are noted in the knees and ankles. There are no skin rashes or nodules. Laboratory results reveal elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and positive anti-streptolysin O titers. This child is at greatest risk for which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This child has clinical features of acute rheumatic fever, including fever, migratory diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever is based on the modified Jones criteria, which require evidence of a preceding pharyngitis) along with either two major criteria or one major and two minor criteria. Mitral regurgitation is the most common early valvular complication of rheumatic fever and is caused by inflammation and edema of the mitral valve leaflets and chordae tendineae, which impair proper coaptation and result in a holosystolic murmur best heard at the apex. Among patients with acute rheumatic fever, mitral valve involvement occurs in up to 70% of cases, followed by aortic valve involvement (20-25%), with right-sided valve disease being much less common. In rheumatic fever, early valve problems occur during the acute phase of the illness and are due to inflammation and edema of valve leaflets. This most often affects the mitral valve, leading to mitral regurgitation. Late valve problems develop months to years later as a result of chronic rheumatic heart disease. This phase is marked by fibrosis, scarring, and commissural fusion of affected valves, which can lead to stenotic lesions. The most classic late complication is mitral stenosis.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Aortic regurgitation can occur in rheumatic heart disease but is less common than mitral valve involvement. Rheumatic fever typically affects the left-sided valves, but the mitral valve is more frequently involved than the aortic valve in both acute and chronic phases.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Aortic stenosis due to rheumatic heart disease is uncommon in children and usually presents later in life as a result of chronic scarring and calcification of the valve. In the acute setting, stenotic lesionsarerare.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Pulmonic stenosis is not a typical manifestation of rheumatic fever. Right-sided valves are rarely involved, and pulmonic stenosis is more commonly a congenital defect rather than acquired.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Tricuspid regurgitation is rarely caused by rheumatic fever and is far less common than mitral valve involvement. when present, it is usually associated with very severe or longstanding disease that involves multiple valves.

questions.question: A 32-year-old female with a history of mitral valve prolapse presents for evaluation of fatigue. She is a runner and typically runs approximately 25 miles per week. For the past week, she has been unable to complete a one-mile run. She denies fever, cough or chest pain. Pulse is 60/min and blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg. Lungs are clear and jugular venous pressure is normal. A 3/6 holosystolic murmur is heard at the cardiac apex. ECG shows normal sinus rhythm with a normal axis and expected in this patient for stroke volume and contractility compared to a normal patient of similar size?
questions.explanation: Answer B (correct answer): This woman has mitral regurgitation (MR) caused by mitral valve prolapse (MVP). In MVP, the mitral valve leaflets are stretched and billow into the left atrium during systole. This may severe MR if tension from prolapse tears one or more chordae tendineae of the mitral valve. The abrupt onset of dyspnea with a new holosystolic murmur is a classic history for a torn chordae tendineae leading to mitral regurgitation in a patient with Mvp. This patient's stroke volume will be increased compared to a similar, normal patient. Her left ventricle must generate a normal forward cardiac output (about 5L/min) in addition to the blood volume lost through backward flow into the atrium. To do this, the amount of blood pumped with each contraction (i.e., the stroke volume) must increase. In order to increase stroke volume, contractility will increase. The left ventricle will receive increased blood from the left atrium due to regurgitation. This stretches left ventricle myocytes causing increased contractility via the Starling mechanism. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman is evaluated for the acute onset of shortness of breath. Earlier in the day, she noted the abrupt onset of dyspnea at rest. There is no chest pain, cough, fever or chills. She has a history of mitral valve prolapse. Physical exam reveals a new holosystolic murmur heard best at the cardiac apex. which of the following changes are expected in this woman
questions.explanation: Answer D (correct answer): This woman has a history and exam findings suggestive of acute mitral regurgitation (MR) from mitral valve prolapse (MvP). In MVP, the mitral valve leaflets prolapse into the left atrium. This produces a late systolic clicking sound heard after the carotid pulsation. In patients with MVP, rupture of mitral chordae tendineae (flail leaflet) may occur leading to the acute onset of MR. When this happens, patients may develop pulmonary edema and dyspnea. In addition, acute MR classically causes a holosystolic murmur at the cardiac apex as described in the question. In acute MR, blood leaks across the mitral valve in systole. This reduces the afterload on the left ventricle. Normally (i.e. in absence of MR), the left ventricle can only pump blood to the aorta. In MR, the left ventricle pumps blood both to the aorta and to the low-pressure left atrium. This makes it easier to push blood from the left ventricle (i.e. more places for the blood to go) and lowers afterload. In terms of preload, in MR left ventricular blood is pumped backwards into the left atrium. The extra volume of blood in the left atrium is pumped again to the left ventricle in diastole increasing preload. is normal due to compensatory changes in the left ventricle. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman is evaluated for dyspnea. Physical exam reveals an opening snap and a diastolic rumble heard best at the cardiac apex. Echocardiography confirms the diagnosis of valvular heart disease. Which of the following changes are expected in this woman compared to a normal patient for left atrial pressure (LAP) and left ventricular end diastolic pressure (LVEDP)?
questions.explanation: Answer D (correct answer): This woman has exam findings consistent with mitral stenosis most likely from rheumatic heart disease. In mitral stenosis, the mitral valve leaflets are thickened with reduced mobility. This causes an opening snap in diastole followed by a rumbling diastolic murmur. These are best heard at the mitral intercostal space at the midclavicular line. In mitral stenosis, blood flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle is limited by the stenotic mitral valve. Thisraisestheleftatrialpressure (LAP). Elevated LAP is the major causes of morbidity from mitral stenosis. High LAP is transmitted to the lungs causing g dyspnea and pulmonary edema. The left atrium may become massively dilated and compress nearby structures. Underfilling of the leftventricle also occurs inmitral stenosis.Indiastole,obstructed blood flow from theleft atrium limitsventricular filling.This leads to reduced leftventricular end diastolic pressure. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 42-year-old man is referred for evaluation of a heart murmur. He has a history of a bicuspid aortic valve. On exam, he has a systolic ejection click and a blowing diastolic murmur. which of the following changes are expected in this man compared to a normal patient for pulse pressure and left ventricular end diastolic volume (LVEDv)?
questions.explanation: Answer B (correct answer): This man has exam findings consistent with aortic regurgitation (AR) from a bicuspid aortic valve. A bicuspid aortic valve causes a systolic ejection click - a clicking sound in early systole before the carotid pulsation. Bicuspid aortic valves commonly develop aortic stenosis, but may also develop AR. This man has a blowing diastolic murmur consistent with AR. In AR, blood leaks across the aortic valve in diastole. The left ventricle fills normally from the left atrium but also receives addedfillingfrom theaorta.Thisincreases thevolumein theleftventricleat theendofdiastole (LVEDV). Higher LVEDV leads to increased contractility and stroke volume via the Starling mechanism. Higher stroke volume results in higher aortic systolic pressure. High stroke volume also causes "bounding" pulses. Diastolic pressure also falls in AR as blood leaks out of the aorta and back into the left ventricle (see picture above). The combination of rising systolic pressure and falling diastolic pressure will raise the pulse pressure. AR is a classic condition to cause high pulse pressure. In extreme cases, the diastolic pressure may get so low seen in chronic aortic regurgitation. These are largely historical from the era before heart surgery was available. diastolic pressure that occurs in chronic AR.

questions.question: The table below shows hemodynamic measurements from patients A through D. Which patient's readings are consistent with aortic stenosis? (all pressure values are mmHg)
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): In a normal patient with no aortic stenosis (As), the left ventricular systolic pressure should be nearly identical to the aortic systolic pressure. In patient A, the left ventricular pressure (140mmHg) is significantly higher than aortic systolic pressure (12ommHg). This is consistent with As. In As, the aortic valve leaflets are thickened with decreased mobility. The left ventricular pressure must rise higher than normal to push open thevalve.For patient A, the data show a pressure difference (a "gradient") from the left ventricle to the aorta of 2ommHg. This is consistent with significant As. Left atrial pressure is usually normal in patients with aortic stenosis until very late stages when the left ventricle begins to fail. In earlier stages of the disease, the left ventricle increases its workload (i.e., contractility) to open the aortic valve and empty the ventricle. So long as ventricular emptying occurs, the left atrial pressure will not rise.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Patient B has data consistent with mitral stenosis. The left atrial pressure is significantly higher than left ventricular diastolic pressure.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Patient C has data consistent with aortic regurgitation. The pulse pressure (difference between aortic systolic and diastolic pressure) is wide. The left ventricular diastolic pressure is elevated indicating a rise in preload. mitral valve has increased left atrial pressure. The left ventricular diastolic pressure is elevated indicating a rise in preload. In contrast to patient C with aortic regurgitation, the pulse pressure is normal for patient D. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 5-year-old girl is evaluated in a rural clinic in India for joint pain. The girl developed right knee pain one week ago. This resolved after two days but was followed by pain in the left knee, both elbows, and the right ankle. The girl's temperature is 101.2°F. A pink, non-pruritic rash is noted on the trunk. There is a 3/6 holosystolic murmur at the cardiac apex. Blood cultures show no evidence of bacteremia. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this child's heart murmur?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This child has a presentation consistent with acute rheumatic fever. The Jones criteria are used for the diagnosis of this condition. These criteria include migratory polyarthritis. Note that the girl has symptoms that fluctuate from one joint to another (migratory). Note also that she has involvement of five or more joints (polyarthritis). The most commonly involved joints in acute rheumatic fever are the knees, ankles, elbows, and wrists. This child also has evidence of valvular inflammation (valvulitis) leading to the heart disease. She also has a pink rash on her trunk consistent with erythema marginatum. Acute rheumatic fever is common in patients with limited access to antibiotic therapy for streptococcal heart and other tissues leading to the symptoms of the disorder. Rheumatic fever is an example of a type II autoimmune disorder. Episodes of acute rheumatic fever usually last less than 3 months but recurrence is possible. Later in life, this girl is at risk for valvular rheumatic heart disease including mitral stenosis.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Various congenital heart defects like cleft mitral valve or ventricular septal defect may cause a heart murmur but would not cause arthritis, fever and rash.

Answers B, C (incorrect answers): Bacterial endocarditis must be considered in the differential with acute rheumatic fever. Migratory polyarthritis and erythema marginatum are not typical features of endocarditis. The same is true for fungal endocarditis. In addition, blood cultures were sterile for this patient. but does not explain other features of this case.

questions.question: A 75-year-old man presents with exertional chest pain and an episode of syncope while walking. He has no history of cardiac disease. Cardiac auscultation reveals a harsh systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur. Which of the following additional clinical features is most likely present in this man's case?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This patient has a systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur. The two major causes of this finding are aortic stenosis and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM). Both cause a similar murmur and symptoms (chest pain, syncope) although the murmur behaves differently with maneuvers. In general, this murmur in a young person suggests the diagnosis of HCM. In an older person (>65 years), aortic stenosis is the most likelydiagnosis. Because of this man's older age, aortic stenosis is the most likely diagnosis. HcM is rare in general, and usually diagnosed in younger patients. Patients over 65 commonly develop "senile calcific aortic stenosis," which is a "wear and tear" phenomenon of the aortic valve. With aging, aortic valve collagen is destroyed and calcium deposits on the leaflets. Leaflet mobility becomes impaired and aortic stenosis occurs. The classic symptoms of severe aortic stenosis are exertional chest pain, heart failure and syncope. Symptoms are worse with exertion because the stenotic aortic valve blunts the rise in cardiac output needed for exercise. Because this man has exertional chest pain and syncope his aortic stenosis is severe. Milder forms do not cause Mc these symptoms. Clinical findings in severe aortic stenosis include delayed and weak carotid upstrokes. This refers toa weakpulse thatoccurslateinsystolewhenthecarotid arteryintheneckis palpated.Resistance to the force of the carotid pulse is weak. These findings can be appreciated by palpating the carotid pulse on physical exam.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Prior endocarditis most often leads to regurgitant lesions due to valve destruction from infection. Aortic stenosis from prior endocarditis is extremely rare.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Patients with rheumatic fever can develop rheumatic heart disease decades after common lesions are mitral regurgitation or stenosis. Rheumatic fever is a very rare cause of aortic stenosis and aortic valve disease typically only occurs in conjunction with mitral disease. For this older man with aortic stenosis, senile calcific disease is the far more likely cause.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Intravenous drug use commonly leads to tricuspid endocarditis and tricuspid regurgitation by introducing bacteria into the venous system through the use of contaminated needles.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Severe aortic stenosis is associated with a soft second heart sound, not a loud secondheartsound. Mc Graw

On exams and in practice, the first step is characterizing the murmur as systolic, diastolic or continuous. Just by doing this, the list of potential causes narrows significantly. The murmur in the question is a continuous murmur consistentwith a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). Continuous murmurs are rare. They occur due to flow throughout the cardiac cycle in systole and diastole. The classic cause is a PDA where blood flows from the aorta to the left pulmonary artery. Other causes include coarctation of the aorta, AV fistula or ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm.

questions.question: A 78-year-old woman presents for routine evaluation. She has not been to a doctor for many years. She has severe osteoarthritis. Her functional capacity is limited mostly to walking short distances in her home. She denies chest pain, dyspnea or syncope. On physical examination, a 3/6 systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur is detected. which of the following suggest severe valvular disease in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): A systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur in an elderly patient is strongly suggestive of aortic stenosis. "senile calcific aortic stenosis" is common among patients over 65 years of age. With aging, aortic valve collagen is destroyed, and calcium deposits on the leaflets. Leaflet mobility becomes impaired and aortic stenosis occurs. The classic symptoms of severe aortic stenosis are chest pain, heart failure, and syncope. Symptoms are worse with exertion because the stenotic aortic valve blunts the rise in cardiac output with exercise. Patients with limited mobility as described in the question may not have symptoms despite severe disease. In the modern era, echocardiography is used to establish the severity of aortic stenosis. Prior to the widespread severe disease included a quiet S2, a late peak of intensity of the murmur and weak carotid upstrokes (i.e.a weak carotid pulse on palpation of the neck). S2 is quiet in severe disease because valve leaflets produce little sound due to limited mobility. Blood flow across a severely thickened valve is slow which leads to a late peaking murmur and weak ("delayed") carotid upstrokes.

Answer A (incorrect answer): S1 is produced by mitral and tricuspid valve closure. It can be loud in mitral stenosis, although the major features of mitral stenosis are the rumbling, diastolic murmur. Mc MeJ5

questions.question: A 60-year-old woman with a history of nonischemic, dilated cardiomyopathy presents for evaluation. Auscultation of the heart at the cardiac apex is recorded below. which of the following correctly lists the direction of blood flow causing the murmur? =Play Audio -00:08
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): The question describes the holosystolic murmur of mitral regurgitation. The lesion is common in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy. When the left ventricle dilates, the mitral valve leaflets fail to come together normally and do not completely close. This allows blood to leak from the left ventricle into the left atrium during systole.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Blood leaks from the right ventricle to the right atrium in tricuspid regurgitation. This condition also causes a holosystolic murmur like mitral regurgitation. A tricuspid regurgitation murmur is usually loudest at the left sternal border. The murmur also increases with inspiration in contrast to mitral regurgitation which decreases during inspiration.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Blood flow from the pulmonary artery to the aorta is seen in patients with a patent ductus arteriosus. The murmur is continuous (systole and diastole) and "machine-like".

Answer C (incorrect answer): Blood flow from theleft atrium to the right atrium is seen in cases of patent foramen ovale (PFo) or atrial septal defects.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Blood flow from the left ventricle to the aorta occurs normally as the left ventricle ejects blood across the aortic valve. This blood flow is responsible for the murmur of aortic stenosis. Mc Graw

options.B: Increased left ventricular end diastolic pressure

questions.explanation:
Answer D(correctanswer):Themurmur describedinthe questionisconsistentwithmitralstenosis.Inmitral stenosis, the mitral valve leaflets become thickened and fused. This leads to obstruction of blood flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle in diastole. The classic auscultatory findings are an opening snap in diastole followed by a rumbling diastolic murmur. The opening snap is caused by abnormal leaflet motion due to thickening and fusion of the leaflet tips. The major hemodynamic consequence of mitral stenosis is increased left atrial pressure (LAP). As the valve becomes more stenotic, the LAP rises. This eventually causes symptoms like dyspnea. With higher left atrial pressure, more forces push on the valve leaflets and they move more quickly. Thus, higher pressure causes the opening snap to occur sooner in diastole. For this reason, the left atrial pressure determines the timing of the opening snap. In the modern era, echocardiography is used to determine the severity of mitral stenosis. Prior to the widespread availability of this test, the time from S2 to the opening snap was used as a marker of disease progression.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Increased left ventricular contractility is not a common feature of mitral stenosis and does not correlate with the timing of the opening snap.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Increased left ventricular end diastolic pressure is not seen in mitral stenosis. Obstruction to mitral inflow decreases filling of the left ventricle leading to a fall in left ventricular end diastolic pressure.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Mitral annular calcification is the deposition of calcium near the annulus of the mitral valve. This can be seen with aging and among patients with renal failure. Rarely, severe calcification can lead to obstruction of flow. This would not be expected in a young patient as described in the question. MSW

Answer D (correct answer): The question describes a patient with tricuspid stenosis (Ts). This valve lesion causes adiastolicrumbling murmur similar to mitral stenosis. (Ms). In contrast to Ms which is heard best at the cardiac apex, the murmur of Ts is heard best at the left lower sternal border. In addition, the murmur of TS increases with inspiration whereas Ms decreases with inspiration. This occurs because inspiration increases venous blood flow through the right heart, but decreases blood flow through the left heart. Exhalation has the opposite effect - less blood flow through right heart, more blood flow through left heart. Isolated Ts is a very rare murmur. Ts may result from rheumatic heart disease but when this happens the mitral valve is almost always involved as well. Patients with carcinoid syndrome may develop isolated tricuspid stenosis, but tricuspid regurgitation is more common. This patient has abdominal pain which may be from a carcinoid tumor in the GI tract. Abdominal pain may also occur in Ts from passive congestion of the liver due to high right atrial pressure.

Answer A(incorrect answer): Mitral stenosis causes a diastolic murmur similar toTs, however, mitral stenosis is usually heard best at the cardiac apex. In addition, the murmur of mitral stenosis decreases during inspiration.

Answer G (correct answer): Micturition (the act of urinating) is mediated by the parasympathetic and somatic (voluntary) nervous systems. Parasympathetic activation of M3 receptors, located on the detrusor muscle of the bladder, trigger contraction of the detrusor, forcing urine into the urethra. Activation of M3 receptors also causes relaxation of the internal urethral sphincter, allowing urine to flow. The external urethral sphincter is under voluntary (somatic) control and must relax for urination to occur. Alpha-1 receptors cause constriction of the internal sphincter during bladder filling. Beta-3 receptors cause relaxation of the detrusor during filling. This man has postoperative urinary retention secondary to receiving opioids. He is unable to activate M3 receptors, which is causing urinary retention. Volatile anesthetics interfere with the autonomic nervous system, causing bladder atony (lack of muscle tone or strength). Narcotic medications such as fentanyl cause urinary retention by inhibiting acetylcholine release from parasympathetic sacral neurons that innervate the detrusor Treatment for postoperative urinary retention includes catheterization. Administration of low-dose naloxone, an opioid antagonist, may reverse urinary retention induced by opioids.

Answer C (correct answer): Epinephrine is used for treatment of anaphylaxis. Through activation of beta-2 receptors in bronchioles, it causes rapid bronchodilation to improve respiratory distress. Administration of epinephrine also stimulates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, leading to an increase in serum glucose. Epinephrine also decreases insulin release via stimulation of pancreatic alpha-2 adrenergic receptors. For all of these reasons, a mild increase in serum glucose is often seen after administration of norepinephrine or epinephrine.

questions.explanation: Answer E (correct answer): This patient is in hypovolemic shock due to massive intrabdominal blood loss. As a result, the sympathetic nervous system is activated. Venous constriction is mediated by alpha-1 adrenergic receptor activation. This contracts venous smooth muscle, forcing blood volume into the heart to raise preloadand cardiac output. Answer B (correct answer): This man has clinical features of acute coronary syndrome and new poor R wave progression, which refers to the failure of the R wave amplitude to increase normally across the precordial leads V1 to V4. In a normal ECG, the R wave typically becomes progressively taller from V1 through V4 as the vector of depolarization moves anteriorly through the interventricular septum and left ventricle. When this progression is lost, particularly if new compared to a prior ECG, it strongly suggests acute anterior wall myocardial infarction,most commonly due to occlusion of the left anterior descending (LAD) artery. The LAD supplies the diminished Rwavedevelopment.

Although occlusion of the first diagonal can contribute to lateral ischemia, it does not typically result in poor R wave progression across the anterior precordial leads.

Answer E (incorrect answer): The right coronary artery (RCA) typically supplies the inferior wall of the left ventricle and the right ventricle. Despite being the furthest from the coronary vessels, it is less prone to ischemia than the subendocardium because the endocardium directly interfaces with blood in the left ventricle to meet its oxygen needs.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia presents to the emergency room with chest pain. For the past two weeks, he has noticed pressure-like discomfort in his chest. Symptoms first occurred when climbing stairs in his home. The past few days, symptoms developed when walking across his bedroom. This morning he noticed symptoms while sitting at the breakfast table, prompting him to call 911. ECG is within normal limits. Serial blood measurements of creatine kinase and troponin are normal. which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

Answer B (correct answer): This is a classic history for unstable angina.Unstable angina is angina in absence of elevated biomarkers that occurs either at rest or with "progressive" symptoms (i.e. more frequent, longer duration, occurring with less and less effort). Unstable angina is associated with rupture of the fibrous cap of an atherosclerotic plaque leading to thrombus formation (see picture). In unstable angina, coronary narrowing leads to ischemia and angina symptoms, however, enough blood flows past the coronary narrowing to supply the myocardium with oxygen. There is no tissue damage or elevation of cardiac biomarkers as seen in myocardial infarction. Unstable angina can be a challenging diagnosis to make since ECG and biomarkers are normal. The key is to identify classic features on history such as exertional chest pain with a progressive pattern. reproducibly at a certainlevel of exertion and resolve with rest. Stable angina is associated with an intact fibrous cap and absence of plaque rupture or thrombus. Treatment of the two types of angina is also different.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Non-ST-Elevation myocardial infarction is anginal symptoms with elevated cardiac biomarkers (creatinine kinase, troponin).

Answer D (incorrect answer): ST-Elevation myocardial infarction is anginal symptoms with ST-segment elevations onECG.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Coronary vasospasm is episodic anginal symptoms at rest caused by coronary vasoconstriction. Mc

questions.question: A 58-year-old male presents to the clinic with progressively worsening chest pain on exertion over the past few months, described as a pressure-like sensation in the middle of his chest radiating to his left arm, typically lasting a few minutes and relieved by rest. He has a medical history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and peripheral artery disease. He is a former smoker with a 20-pack-year history, having quit 2 years ago. His father died of a heart attack at the age of 48. The patient has become more sedentary over the past year and states that he sometimes misses doses of his antihypertensive and lipid- lowering medications. Physical examination reveals a blood pressure of 145/90 mmHg, BMI of 32, and diminished peripheral pulses in bilateral lower extremities. Recent diagnostic studies show elevated LDL and reduced HDL cholesterol levels, and an ECG reveals nonspecific changes without acute ischemic findings. Which of the following carries the highest risk for developing the cardiac condition that this patient most likely suffers from?
questions.explanation:
PAD is considered one of the major risk factors for CAD. Alongside PAD, other coronary risk equivalents include diabetes and chronic kidney disease, all of which indicate the presence of significantly increased risk of coronary artery disease.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Hypertension is a significant risk factor for coronary artery disease, but in this patient, the presence of PAD immediaterisk. the presence of peripheral artery disease in this patient suggests a more advanced state of atherosclerosis and a higher overall risk.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Obesity is a well-known risk factor for coronary artery disease (CAD), and it is associated with other comorbidities such as hypertension and hyperlipidemia, all of which contribute to the development of atherosclerosis. However, in this predictorofcoronaryevents.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Smoking is a well-established risk factor for coronary artery disease, particularly in those with a significant pack-year history. Although the patient's history of smoking is notable, his diagnosis of peripheral artery disease is a more direct and severe indicatorofhiscurrentriskforcoronaryevents.

questions.question: A 65-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a chief complaint of severe chest pain that began 30 minutes prior to presentation, while he was watching Tv. The pain is described as a crushing sensation radiating to his left performed, showing changes consistent with an acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). In what order would this patient's ECG changes appear over the course of several hours to days?

options.A: elevation, pathological Q wave, T wave inversion
options.B: elevation, T wave inversion, Hyperacute T wave, ST segment pathological Q wave
options.C: wave, pathological Q wave, T wave ST segment elevation, Hyperacute T inversion
options.D: wave, T wave inversion, pathological Q ST segment elevation, Hyperacute T wave
options.E: wave, Hyperacute T wave, T wave ST segment elevation, pathological Q inversion

questions.explanation:
Answer A(correct answer): In the typical progression of an acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMl), the earliest ECG change that can be detected is a hyperacute T wave, which reflects early ischemia. This is soon followed by sT segment elevation.As the infarction progresses, a pathological Q wave develops.Finally,T wave inversion occurs.This sequence-hyperacuteT wave,ST segment elevation, pathological Q wave, and T wave inversion—is the most common order in the evolution of ECG changes during STEMl.

Answer B (incorrect answer): This sequence places T wave inversion before the development of a pathological Q wave, which is not typical in the ECG progression during STEMl. Typically, the Q wave develops before the T wave inversion as the infarction progresses. myocardium. wave is an early sign of ischemia and typically precedes ST segment elevation during the early phase of myocardial infarction.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Similar to option C, this sequence incorrectly places the hyperacute T wave after ST segment elevation. The hyperacute T wave typically precedes ST segment elevation in the early phase of myocardial infarction, followed by pathological Q wave formationandthenTwaveinversion. which is not the typical progression seen in STEMl. The hyperacute T wave is an early sign of myocardial ischemia and usually appears first, followed by ST segment elevation. A pathological Q wave usually develops later as the infarction progresses followed by T wave inversion. Mc Graw
