questions.question: A critically-ill patient is administered a drug which increases heart rate and contractility. Which of the following changes is expected?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): Dobutamine, a beta-1 receptor agonist, is used in critically ill patients with heart failure and low cardiac output. Beta-1 activation increases left ventricular contractility and heart rate. The in the left ventricular chamber at the end of systole (i.e. at the end of contraction). Thus, left ventricular end Heart rate also increases in patients on dobutamine from beta-1 receptor activation. This decreases diastolic filling time which will slightly lower the left ventricular end diastolic volume (EDv) as well (i.e., the preload). This change is usually small compared to the change in EsV caused by dobutamine. Strokevolume is equal to the EDV minus the EsV.Both of these volumes can fall in patients on dobutamine as explained above, however, the fall in EsV caused by dobutamine is larger than the slight fall in EDV. As a result, the stroke volume (EDV - EsV)increases. Thus,dobutamine increases stroke volume and cardiac output which is beneficial in patients with heart failure.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Left ventricular EDV will decrease with dobutamine as a result of increased heart rate (less filling time) as explained above. EDv is a marker of preload. This will increase when preload increases, as occurs when saline or blood is infused into the venous system, or when the heart rate slows to allow more filling.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Dobutamine will increase stroke volume as explained above. Stroke volume falls when negative inotropic drugs are administered (e.g., beta blockers), or in the setting of myocardial disease like ischemia, infarction or cardiomyopathy.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Ventricular filling time will decrease with dobutamine due to faster heart rate. It will notincrease. IIH

questions.question: An 80-year-old man presents with dyspnea. He has a history of ischemic cardiomyopathy with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 15%. His medications include metoprolol and lisinopril. He recently celebrated his birthday with dinner at a restaurant. On exam, he has rales 1/3 up in both lungs fields. Jugular venous pressure is elevated. There is 2+ lower extremity edema. A drug which causes venous dilation is administered and his dyspnea improves. Which of the following changes occurred after the administration of nitroglycerine for preload and cardiac output?
questions.explanation: Answer A (correct answer): The question describes the effects of the drug nitroglycerine whose major mechanism in heart failure is dilation of venous structures (see the video on acute heart failure). This leads to pooling of blood volume in the venous system. Thus, less blood is delivered to the left ventricle and preload falls. The fall in preload is beneficial for the patient's symptom of dyspnea. Less blood volume in the left ventricle others are heart rate, contractility, and afterload). Less preload means less cardiac output. Indeed, one of the side effects of nitroglycerin is hypotension - a result of the fall in preload. For patients with heart failure, it may seem counterintuitive to use drugs that lower the cardiac output but this is done commonly in clinical practice. The reason is that dangerous symptoms like dyspnea must be treated regardless of the physiologic effects of therapy. Most heart failure patients can tolerate the decline in preload after nitroglycerin and they appreciate the benefit of being able to breathe easier. Special note: The fall in cardiac output that occurs immediately after nitroglycerine administration activates the sympathetic nervous system which triggers a rise in heart rate (a "reflex tachycardia"). This blunts some of the fall in cardiac output caused by the drug. For patients like this man on a beta blocker (metoprolol), the reflex tachycardia will be blunted (i.e., the rise in heart rate will be minimal).

questions.question: A 27-year-old male motorcyclist presents after a crash. Internal bleeding is detected with large amounts of blood in the peritoneal and thoracic cavities. Blood pressure is 80/40 mmHg and pulse is 120/min. What changes are expected for this patient in left ventricular preload and contractility compared to his normal state?
questions.explanation: Answer C (correct answer):Thispatient is suffering fromvolume loss due to hemorrhage.The loss of volume will reduce the preload to the left ventricle. Volume depletion will activate the sympathetic nervous system (SNS). In turn, the SNS will increase cardiac contractility. Ofnote,activation oftheSNsleads toconstriction ofvenousstructureswhichwill sendvenous blood totheleft ventricle in an attempt to maintain preload and cardiac output. In this patient, however, venous constriction is insufficient to maintain preload. He has low blood pressure - a sign of low cardiac output from decreased preload. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 25-year-old medical student presents with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Blood pressure is 100/70 mmHg and pulse is 110/min. One liter of normal saline is infused intravenously. which of the following effects will the infusion have on left ventricular preload and total peripheral resistance (TPR)?
questions.explanation: Answer D (correct answer): Infusion of normal saline will increase preload to the left ventricle. This intervention adds volume to the venous system which returns to the left ventricle during filling (diastole). The left ventricular volume at the end of diastole (LVEDV), a marker of preload, will rise. When this patient presents, she is volume depleted which activates the sympathetic nervous system (SNs). In turn, the SNS causes vasoconstriction which increases total peripheral resistance (TPR). Thus, at presentation, she has a high TPR. Infusion of normal saline will add volume and bring her volume status closer to normal. This will decrease SNS activity. Less SNS activity means less vasoconstriction and, therefore, TPR will decrease.

questions.question: A hypertensive patient is administered a drug which causes arteriolar vasodilation. Which of the following changes are expected in afterload, cardiac output, and work of the heart?
questions.explanation: Answer D (correct answer): The question describes the effects of the hypertensive drug, hydralazine, which is a direct vasodilator. Vasodilation will decrease afterload. Afterload is one of the four determinants of cardiac output (the others are heart rate, contractility, and preload). When afterload falls, stroke volume and cardiac output increase. With less afterload working against the left ventricle, work of the heart will decrease. To put it another way, with afterload reduction, fewer forces resist the flow of blood out of the left ventricle so less work is required to fill the vascular system. ··.···

questions.question: A 32-year-old female presents with a sore throat, cough, fevers, and chills for two days. which of the following are expected in this patient for heart rate and end systolic volume compared to the normal state?
questions.explanation: Answer D (correct answer): This patient has symptoms of a respiratory infection. In the setting of an immune rate and contractility. The ventricle will "squeeze" harder and push more blood into the vascular system. In doing so, less blood will remain in the left ventricular chamber at the end of systole (i.e. at the end of contraction). Thus, left ventricular end systolic volume will fall. This change occurs any time contractility increases (high yield fact!). ··.···.

questions.question: A 65-year-old man with a history of myocardial infarction and ischemic cardiomyopathy passes out while sitting in a chair. When emergency medical personnel arrive at his home, heart rate is 300/min. The ECG strip below is obtained. What is the cause of this patient's syncope?
questions.explanation:
Answer C(correct answer): This man's EcG strip shows ventricular tachycardia(VT) at a rate of nearly 300bpm. Note that the QRS complexes are wide as seen in VT. Note also that approximately 1 big box separates each QRs complex indicating a heart rate close to 3oobpm. At this rapid heart rate, the left ventricle does not have enough time to fill. Thus, preload (i.e. filling in diastole) falls and this leads to a low stroke volume. If stroke volume is low enough, insufficient blood flow to can occur in the acute setting during a myocardial infarction. It can also occur years later as scar tissue in the leftventricle alters electrical conduction.UnstableVT (i.e.VT leading to low blood pressure and syncope) is a medical emergency and requires immediate cardioversion. Left untreated, it can degenerate into ventricular fibrillationwhichcanbefatal. (alpha blockers,hydralazine).Markedlyreduced peripheral resistance canlead tolowblood pressure and syncope.

Answer B (incorrect answer):Venous dilation is caused by nitrates. These drugs can cause syncope in some cases by dilating veins which then pool blood volume and reduce preload to the left ventricle.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Decreased contractility can be caused by myocardial infarction or drugs including beta blockers and calcium-channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem).

Answer E (incorrect answer): Stroke is a potential cause of syncope. In addition to syncope, stroke usually presents with neurological deficits such as weakness or vision loss. Mc Graw H

questions.question: An 82-year-old man presents to the emergency department with palpitations and dyspnea. An ECG reveals new-onset atrial fibrillation at an average rate of 140 bpm. A beta receptor antagonist is administered and the heart rate falls to 90 bpm. Which of the following changes occurred after metoprolol administration in contractility and left ventricular end diastolic volume (LVEDv)?
questions.explanation: Answer C (correct answer): Metoprolol is a beta-1 selective beta receptor antagonist. This will block the sympathetic stimulation of the heart and slow the heart rate. For patients in rapid atrial fibrillation, this often improves symptoms (i.e. even though the arrhythmia persists, the patient feels better). Palpitations often subside at lower heart rates. In addition, a slower heart rate allows more time for left ventricular filling in diastole. This improves cardiac output and can resolve pulmonary edema (a cause of dyspnea in atrial fibrillation). Through the blockade of beta-1 activity, metoprolol will decrease contractility. By slowing the heart rate and allowing for more filling time, the LVEDV will increase. ··.·····.

questions.question: In the ECG tracing below, blood volume in the left ventricle at which point represents preload?
questions.explanation: Answer B (correct answer): Preload is the volume in the left ventricle at the end of diastole (left ventricular end-diastolic volume or LVEDV). On the surface ECG, the QRS complex represents ventricular myocyte contraction. Thus, point B is the beginning of systole (or the end of diastole), the point where blood volume represents preload. In actual practice, the surface ECG is used to identify the timing of systole and diastole for measurement of heart volumes and pressures. Left ventricular systole ends at point D when the left ventricular myocytes are nearly all repolarized. Thus, point A (the start of the p wave) is mid-diastole. Point C is mid-systole. Systole Diastole

questions.question: A 27-year-old male motorcyclist presents after a crash. Internal bleeding is detected with a large amount of blood in the peritoneal and thoracic cavities. He is hypotensive and tachycardic. What changes are expected for this patient for end- systolic volume (Esv) and pulse pressure compared to prior to his accident?
questions.explanation: Answer A (correct answer): This patient is suffering g fromvolume loss due tohemorrhage.Volumedepletionwill activate the sympathetic nervous system (sNs). Sympathetic stimulation of the heart leads to increased contractility. This will decrease the end systolic volume as more vigorous contraction leaves less blood volume in the leftventricle at the end of systole. Pulse pressure is the difference between systolic and diastolic pressure. This patient has hemorrhagic shock with hypotension in the setting of blood loss. Cardiac output will be low. Cardiac output is the major determinant of systolic blood pressure so systolic pressure will be reduced and pulse pressure will fall. In most cases, high cardiac output states (i.e. exercise, inotropic drugs) lead to increased pulse pressure and low cardiac output states (volume depletion, hemorrhage, heart failure) lead to reduced pulse pressure. The low pulse pressure is the cause of "weak" pulses in patients with various causes of low cardiac output. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 64-year-old man with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy comes to the emergency department with worsening shortness of breath, fatigue, and orthopnea. He has no history of arrhythmia. Physical examination reveals an irregularly irregular pulse. There is jugular venous distention and bibasilar crackles on auscultation. ECG shows atrial fibrillation, which was not present Which of the following best explains the absence of the S4 in this patient?

options.A: Early rapid filling of the left ventricle
options.C: Late passive filling of the left ventricle

questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This man has hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HcM) complicated by new-onset atrial fibrillation, which has led to acute decompensated heart failure. In HcM, the left ventricle is hypertrophied and stiff, leading to impaired diastolic filling. As a result, atrial contraction becomes important for maintaining left ventricular preload and cardiac output. A fourth heart sound (S4) is commonly heard in patients with HCM. It is generated during late diastole when the left atrium contracts to force blood volume against a stiff, noncompliant ventricle. With the onset of atrial fibrillation, coordinated atrial contraction is lost, eliminating the mechanical event that produces the S4. In addition, the loss of atrial contribution to ventricular filling can cause a sudden drop in disappearance of the S4 and the patient's clinical decompensation into acute heart failure.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Early rapid filling of the left ventricle occurs during early diastole and may generate an S3 in volume-overloaded states, not an S4. It is unrelated to atrial contraction and does not explain the disappearance of the S4.

Answer B (incorrect answer): High left atrial pressure is common in heart failure and can contribute to pulmonary congestion, but it does not explain the loss of the S4. Elevated atrial pressure can cause an S3, but not an S4.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Late passive filling of the left ventricle is not a distinct physiologic phase that generates a discrete heart sound. The term may refer to residual flow in diastole, but it is not associated with the S4, which specifically requires active atrial contraction.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Left ventricular wall stiffness is the underlying reason an S4 is generated in the first place, as it causes the atrium to contract forcefully to fill a noncompliant ventricle. It does not explain the disappearance of the S4. Its loss in this patient is due to the loss of atrial contraction from atrial fibrillation. MSW

questions.question: A 67-year-old man with a history of hypertension and coronary artery disease presents with progressive shortness of breath examination, his blood pressure is 142/86 mmHg, heart rate is 92/min, and respiratory rate is 20/min. Jugular venous distention and bilateral lower extremity edema are present. On cardiac auscultation, the physician hears an extra heart sound suspected to be an S3. Which of the following findings related to this heart sound is most consistent with an S3?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This man has signs and symptoms of decompensated heart failure, including orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and volume overload. An S3 gallop is a low-frequency sound the apex of the heart with the bell of the stethoscope when the patient is in the left lateral decubitus position. Presence of an S3 is a sign of acute heart failure that resolves when patients are no longer congested. The diaphragm is used for high-frequency sounds such as murmurs of aortic regurgitation or mitral regurgitation.

Answer B (incorrect answer): An S3 is a low-pitched (low-frequency) sound. High-pitched sounds include valve opening snaps and certain murmurs and are not characteristic of s3. ventriculardiastole.It does not occur in early systole.

Answer E (incorrect answer): A heart sound in late systole suggests mitral valve prolapse with a mid-to-late systolic click. S3, in contrast, occurs in early diastole. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 55-year-old man comes to the office for evaluation of exertional fatigue. He has a history of hypertension but is otherwise healthy. Vital signs are within normal limits. On cardiac auscultation, the second heart sound is audibly split into two components during both inspiration and expiration. The splitting becomes slightly wider during inspiration. The first heart sound is normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's heart sound findings?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This man has persistent (wide) splitting of the second heart sound (S2), in which the aortic and pulmonic valve closures are audibly separated during both inspiration and expiration, with a wider gap during inspiration. Right bundle branch block delays right ventricular depolarization and contraction, leading to prolonged right ventricular systole and delayed closure of the pulmonic valve. This causes the persistent splitting of S2. Other causes of persistent splitting include conditions that delay right ventricular ventricular systole delays closure of the pulmonic valve, leading to a widened S2 split that is present during both phases of respiration but increases with inspiration.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Atrial septal defect causes fixed splitting of S2, meaning the A2-P2 interval does not change with respiration. This results from chronic left-to-right shunting that increases right heart volume continuously, delaying P2 during both inspiration and expiration without variation. dynamic left ventricular outflow obstruction that prolongs aortic valve closure. In paradoxical splitting, the split is heard during expiration and disappears during inspiration-the opposite pattern of persistent splitting. This is not consistent with the patient's findings.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Left bundle branch block delays left ventricular contraction and aortic valve closure. This can result in paradoxica/ splitting, in which the split is heard during expiration and disappears during inspiration-the opposite of physiologic splitting. It does not cause persistent splitting as seen in this patient.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Left ventricular systolic dysfunction can also lead to paradoxical splitting due to delayed aortic valve closure from prolonged LV systole. However, paradoxical splitting is heard during expiration and disappears with inspiration, which does not match this patient's persistent S2 splitting. Mc MeiS

questions.question: A 39-year-old man comes to the clinic for a routine physical examination. He has no chronic medical conditions and feels well. His vital signs are within normal limits. On cardiac auscultation, the second heart sound is single during expiration but audibly splits into two components during inspiration. There are no murmurs, rubs, or gallops. which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's heart sound findings?

options.B: Delayed closure of the aortic valve
options.C: Early closure of the pulmonic valve

questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This man has a normal physiologic splitting of the second heart sound (S2), in which the aortic valve closes before the pulmonic valve during inspiration. Inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure and increases venous return to the right heart, leading to increased right ventricular filling and stroke volume. As a result, right ventricular ejection time is prolonged, which delays closure of the pulmonic valve. This causes an audible splitting of S2 during inspiration that resolves during expiration.

Answer A(incorrectanswer):Decreased rightventricularstrokevolumewould shortenrightventricular systole, potentially causing earlier pulmonic valve closure. This would narrow or eliminate the inspiratory split, which is inconsistent with the finding of physiologic splitting.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Delayed closure of the aortic valve can be seen in aortic stenosis or left bundle branch block. It would narrow or reverse the normal S2 split and is not consistent with the normal finding described in this patient. interval between A2 and P2, making a split less likely to be heard. It does not explain splitting that occurs during inspiration.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Increased intrathoracic pressure, such as during expiration or with Valsalva, reduces venous return to the right heart and would shorten right ventricular systole. This would tend to narrow or eliminate the S2 split rather than produce it.

questions.question: A 42-year-old man presents for routine evaluation. He has no history of cardiovascular disease. On physical exam, the first heart sound is single. The second heart sound is single with exhalation and splits during inspiration. ECG is within normal limits. Which of the following explains the splitting of the second heart sound?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): The question describes the normal physiologic splitting of the second heart sound. The second heart sound has two components from the closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves. With blood into the pulmonary artery (more blood = more time to push blood out). This delays closure of the pulmonic valve and splits the second heart sound.

Answer A (Increased pulmonary artery pressure): Pulmonary hypertension results in wide or fixed splitting of S2 (not physiologic). It does not cause splitting only with inspiration.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Atrial septal defect causes fixed splitting of the second heart sound (i.e. splitting with exhalation and inhalation).

Answer C (incorrect answer): Aortic stenosis causes paradoxical splitting of the second heart sound and a systolic ejection murmur.

Answer E (incorrect answer):Increasedleft atrial pressure causes an S3. Of note (and unrelated to heart sounds): with normal inspiration, the left atrial pressure falls slightly because the capacity of the lungs to hold blood volume goes up. There is slightly less flow in the left heart during inspiration. For this reason, left side murmurs become quieter with inspiration.

questions.question: A 24-year-old female presents with the acute onset of tearing chest pain that radiates to her back. ECG is within normal limits. On exam, blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg in the left arm and 90/75 mmHg in the right arm. Cardiac auscultation reveals an early systolic ejection click. Chest x-ray shows a widened mediastinum. Which of the following is the cause of this patient's presentation?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): The question describes a classic presentation of aortic dissection. This condition is caused by a tear in the intimal layer of the aorta which allows blood to enter the space between the intima and the media. When this occurs, blood can "dissect" (i.e. separate) the two layers and disrupt blood flow through the aorta and into large arteries. Classic clinical findings are chest pain radiating to the back, widened mediastinum on imaging, and blood pressure differential between the left and right arms. significantly increased risk of thoracic aortic aneurysms and aortic dissection. Unfortunately, some patients are unaware their valve is bicuspid until the development of an aortic dissection.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Coronary ischemia may cause chest pain that can mimic aortic dissection but this is unlikely in a 24-year-old patient with a normal ECG.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Marfan syndrome is a connective tissue disorder that can lead to aortic dissection. Patients with Marfan syndrome commonly have mitral valve prolapse (MvP) which may cause a systolic click. However, MvP causes a "non-ejection" click that occurs late in systole after the carotid pulse. In clinical practice, clicks are difficult to hear and even harder to distinguish in terms of early versus late. However, in none of the typical features of Marfan syndrome including a wide wingspan and tall stature. more often causes valvular regurgitation and does not typically lead to ejection clicks.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Patients with the autoimmune disorder lupus may develop nonbacterial endocarditis (Marantic endocarditis). This does not typically lead to ejection clicks.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman presents for routine evaluation during pregnancy. She is at 32 weeks gestation. Cardiac exam reveals a systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border. The second heart sound is single with expiration and becomes split with inspiration. Her physical exam is otherwise normal for her stage of pregnancy. Which of the following is best explains her cardiac findings?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This woman has normal findings for pregnancy. The systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border is consistent with a flow murmur across the pulmonic valve. This is a common finding in normal pregnancy due to increased blood volume and blood flow. The question also describes normal findings for S2. During exhalation, S2 has two components: one from aortic valve closure (A2) and one from pulmonic valve closure (P2). Many times, these sounds are so close together splitting of A2 and P2 is increased during inspiration from increased venous return. A "split S2" is usually easy to hear during inhalation. An S3 may also be heard in women during normal pregnancy.

Answers A and C (incorrect answers): Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and left bundle branch block cause paradoxical splitting of the 2nd heart sound.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Right bundle branch block and pulmonary hypertension cause persistent splitting of the 2nd heart sound.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Atrial septal defect causes a fixed splitting of S2 (no change with inspiration). Mc Graw

questions.question: A 42-year-old man presents for routine evaluation. He has no history of cardiovascular disease. On physical exam, the first heart sound is single. The second heart sound is single with exhalation and splits during inspiration. ECG is within normal limits. Which of the following explains the splitting of the second heart sound?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): The question describes the normal physiologic splitting of the second heart sound. The second heart sound has two components from the closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves. With inspiration, venous return to the right ventricle increases. As a result, the right ventricle takes longer to eject blood into the pulmonary artery (more blood = more time to push blood out). This delays closure of the pulmonicvalveandsplitsthesecondheartsound. with exhalation and inhalation).

Answer C (incorrect answer):Aorticstenosis causesparadoxical splitting of the second heart sound and a systolicejectionmurmur.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Increased left atrial pressure causes an S3. Of note (and unrelated to heart sounds): with normal inspiration, the left atrial pressure falls slightly because the capacity of the lungs to hold blood volume goes up. There is slightly less flow in the left heart during inspiration. For this reason, left side murmurs become quieter with inspiration.

questions.question: A 78-year-old woman presents for routine evaluation. Her ECG is shown below. Which of the following is expected on cardiac exam?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): The ECG shows sinus rhythm with a right bundle branch block (RBBB). The QRS is prolonged at approximately 160ms (normal <120ms or 3 small boxes). Compare the QRs in the question to the the typical R-S-R' ("R-S-R prime") pattern of an RBBB. The second heart sound has two components from the closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves. In right bundle branch block, closure of the pulmonic component (P2) is delayed. This causes a persistent split of S2. During exhalation, S2 is usually single but in RBBB it is split because of delayed closure of the pulmonic valve related to the RBBB. With inspiration, the normal physiologic delay in closure of S2 occurs and further splits the second heart sound. Thus, S2 is "persistently" split during both inspiration and exhalation.

Answer A (incorrect answer): In physiologic splitting of S2, the second heart sound is single during exhalation and splits with inspiration.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Fixed splitting of S2 is seen with atrial septal defects. In fixed splitting, the timing between A2 and P2 is fixed. In persistent splitting, the timing is not fixed and increases with inspiration.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Paradoxical splitting of S2 occurs with left bundle branch blocks. Mc Graw

questions.question: Shown below is a phonocardiogram for a patient during inspiration. Which of the following conditions explains the phonocardiogram findings?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): The phonocardiogram shows a fixed split of s2. Note that there is no change in the splitting of S2 as the patient inspires. Although the entire respiratory cycle is not shown, there should be a dsa (sy o be xa a o so d a s s under normal conditions. The absence of any change in S2 during inspiration indicates a fixed split of the second heartsound. A fixed split of s2 is seen in atrial septal defects. The second heart sound has two components from closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves. This causes a fixed split of S2, meaning the splitting of the 2nd heart sound is the same during exhalation and inspiration, and does not change withrespiration. the 2nd heart sound. questions.question: A 62-year-old man presents with dyspnea, fatigue, and lower extremity swelling. questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): Patients with cardiomyopathy and left bundle branch block (LBBB) have "paradoxical" splitting of the second heart sound. The second heart sound has two components from closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves. In cardiomyopathy or LBBB, the aortic component (A2) is delayed due to slow emptying of the left ventricle. As a result, during exhalation, the second heart sound is split whereas normally it is single. With inspiration, the pulmonic component of the second heart sound (P2) is delayed due to the normal physiologic increase in venous return. This causes a single second heart sound with inspiration. Thus, the second heart sound is split with exhalation and single with inhalation - the opposite of what is normally heard.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Fixed splitting of the 2nd heart sound occurs in cases of atrial septal defect.

Answer C (incorrect answer): S3 is heard with high left atrial pressure. This can occur in patients with cardiomyopathy, however, the patient in the question has been treated. At the time of discharge, his symptoms of heart failure have resolved and an S3 should not be present. Atrial flutter is a type of supraventricular tachycardia caused by a reentrant circuit within the right atrium, most commonly traveling in a counterclockwise direction around the tricuspid annulus. This creates rapid, regular atrial depolarizations, typically at a rate of about 3o0 beats per minute. These are seen on ECG as sawtooth flutter waves, especially visible in the inferior leads (II, III, aVF), although the image here is from a single lead. In atrial flutter, not all atrial impulses conduct through the AV node, so the ventricular response depends on the degree of AV block. This ECG shows a conduction pattern of 3:1, meaning every third flutter wave is conducted to the ventricles, resulting in a ventricular rate of approximately 1oo beats per minute (half of the atrial rate). Note that the ECG shows two clearly visible flutter waves before each QRS complex.The QRS complex occurs at the same time as the third flutter wave creating a ratio of 3:1 conduction. To estimate the ventricular rate, count the number of large boxes between successive QRs complexes. In this ECG, there are slightly less than 3 large boxes between QRs complexes, which gives a rate of approximately 100 to 120 beats per minute (300 ÷ 3 = 100).The QRS complexes occur at regular intervals, confirming that the rhythm (and, therefore, the patient's pulse) is regular. Thus, this patient has a regular pulse with a heart rate in the range of 1o0-120 beats per minute, consistent with atrial flutter with3:1AVconduction.

questions.question: A 2-month-old boy is evaluated for failure to thrive. His parents state the child used to breastfeed regularly but has fed only intermittently for the past week. On exam, a murmur is heard best at the left upper chest. There is a loud S2. Peripheral pulses are bounding. Pulse pressure is widened. which of the following conditions is most likely in this child?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This child has clinical features consistent with a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). A PDA allows shunting of blood from the aorta to the pulmonary artery. If a PDA is not detected at birth and goes untreated, pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure may occur. This baby has a loud S2 - a UsMLE buzzword for pulmonary hypertension. He also has a wide pulse pressure. Widening of the pulse pressure occurs when the stroke volume rises (increasing systolic pressure) or when peripheral resistance falls (lowering diastolic pressure). In a baby with a PDA, stroke volume is high which raises systolic pressure (explanation below). In addition, in a child with PDA, blood leaks out of the vascular system in diastole. This lowers the diastolic pressure and widens the pulse pressure. These same mechanisms lead to a widened pulse pressure in aortic regurgitation and AV fistulas. This baby also has "bounding" peripheral pulses. This is a USMLE code word for high stroke volume. The classic cause of bounding pulses is chronic aortic regurgitation but this can also be seen in PDA. In this baby with PDA, the left ventricular stroke volume will rise to maintain blood pressure. The left ventricle must pump the normal blood volume required to fill the vascular system but also additional volume to replace blood lost through the be seen during exercise and high catecholamine states (i.e. sepsis, trauma). The question gives only a vague description of the murmur but based on the loud s2, pulse pressure and bounding pulses PDA is the only diagnosis that fits. None of the other answer choices will cause a widened pulse pressure or bounding pulses.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Tetralogy of Fallot causes a systolic ejection murmur and single S2.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Aortic coarctation causes a continuous murmur near the scapula in the back.

Answer C (incorrect answer): An atrial septal defect causes a fixed split S2, systolic ejection murmur and, in some cases, a diastolic murmur.

Answer D (incorrect answer): A ventricular septal defect causes a holosystolic murmur.

questions.question: A 2-year-old girl presents for routine evaluation. Weight and height are normal for her age. On exam, she has a 2/6 systolic ejection murmur heard best at the left upper sternal border. There is also a 1/4 diastolic murmur at the left lower sternal
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This child has cardiac findings consistent with an atrial septal defect (AsD).An ASD allows communication between the left and right atria. Because left atrial pressure (~10 mmHg) is normally higher than right atrial pressure (~6 mmHg) flow across an ASD is left to right under normal conditions. This increases blood flow through the right atrium, right ventricle and pulmonary arteries. Increased blood flow across the pulmonic valve causes a systolic ejection murmur in the 2nd left intercostal space. A diastolic murmur may also occur due to increased flow across the tricuspid valve. A "fixed split" s2 is heard because of delayed closure of the pulmonic valve.

Answer A(incorrect answer): Tetralogy of Fallot causes a systolic ejection murmur and singleS2.

Answer B (incorrect answer): A ventricular septal defect causes a holosystolic murmur.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Pulmonic stenosis causes a systolic ejection murmur similar to the systolic murmur in AsD. It does not, however, cause a diastolic murmur or fixed split S2.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man comes to the emergency department with 1 hour of substernal chest pain that radiates to his left arm. questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): The patient's ECG shows ST-segment elevations in leads V2-V5, which localize the infarction to the anterior wall of the leftventricle.ST elevations are characteristic of transmural ischemia, where the full thickness of the myocardial wall is affected. The associated myocardial necrosis causes release of troponins, so increased serum troponin is expected in this setting.

Normal serum troponin levels can occur in unstable or stable angina, but this man has ST elevations on ECG.

questions.question: Hospital X has an average door-to-balloon time for treatment of myocardial infarction with angioplasty of 45 minutes. questions.question: A 60-year-old man presents for follow-up one month after being diagnosed with new-onset heart failure. At the time of diagnosis, echocardiography showed a severely reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF 25%) and electrocardiogram reported smoking one pack of cigarettes daily. He was started on guideline-directed medical therapy, including a loop diuretic, an ACE inhibitor, a beta blocker, and an SGLT2 inhibitor. Over the past month, he has quit smoking, begun a regular improvement. His heart rate is 60/minute and regular and his blood pressure is 118/72 mmHg. Lungs are clear to auscultation and cardiac exam shows a normal S1 and S2 with no murmurs, rubs or gallops. Repeat echocardiography shows a normal LVEF of 60%. which of the following is most likely responsible for the improvement in his ejection fraction?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This patient's marked improvement in left ventricular systolic function over a short period is characteristic of tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy, which occurs due to sustained high heart rates commonly from atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. This form of cardiomyopathy can be rapidly reverse by a reduction in heart rate, either through rate control of atrial fibrillation or restoration of sinus rhythm.A lower heart rate allows for improved ventricular filling and reversal of myocardial dysfunction. The rapid normalization of ejection fraction within one month in this man strongly supports this diagnosis. and can improve ventricular remodeling, they do not typically lead to rapid recovery of ejection fraction within weeks, especially not to complete normalization. Recovery of left ventricular function on guideline directed therapies like ACE inhibitors generally takes months to years.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Improved diabetes control is beneficial for cardiovascular outcomes but is not expected to restore ejection fraction so quickly, particularly in cases of longstanding disease.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Exercise improves overall cardiovascular health and functional capacity but would not be the primary cause of rapid LVEF improvement in a patient with recent onset of severe systolic dysfunction.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Smoking cessation reduces long-term cardiovascular risk but is not known to cause rapid reversal of left ventricular dysfunction. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 58-year-old man presents with worsening shortness of breath and lower extremity swelling over the past 3 weeks. He has a history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and often forgets to take his medications. He also has chronic tobacco use of 1 pack per day for 30 years. He reports drinking 2-4 beers nightly and consuming fast food most days of the week. He does not exercise regularly. Physical examination reveals an S3 gallop, bibasilar crackles, and bilateral pitting edema. Echocardiography shows global hypokinesis of the left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 25%. which of the following interventions is most likely to lead to improvement in this patient's left ventricular function?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This patient has new-onset systolic heart failure and a history of chronic alcohol consumption. Alcoholic cardiomyopathy is a well-recognized cause of dilated cardiomyopathy and reduced ejection fraction. Continued alcohol use exerts direct toxic effects on cardiac myocytes, leading to progressive ventricular dysfunction. Discontinuation of alcohol can lead to significant improvement or even normalization of left ventricular function, especially if implemented early in the course of the disease. In patients with new onset cardiomyopathy of unclear cause, cessation of alcohol is recommended. This can result in complete resolution of thecardiomyopathy.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Improved glycemic control is beneficial for long-term cardiovascular health and may slow the progression of heart failure, but it does not typically reverse established systolic dysfunction.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Reduced sodium intake can help improve heart failure symptoms by reducing fluid retention, but it does not address the underlying myocardial dysfunction or directly improve left ventricular contractility.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Smoking cessation improves overall cardiovascular risk and long-term mortality but is not known to directly improve left ventricular ejection fraction in the short term.

Answer E (incorrect answer): A structured exercise program is appropriate for stable patients with chronic heart failure, particularly with cardiac rehabilitation. However, it is not an initial intervention for acutely decompensated systolic heart failure and does not reverse myocardial dysfunction caused by alcohol toxicity.

questions.question: A 61-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with acute-onset chest pain and shortness of breath that Electrocardiogram shows ST-segment elevations in the anterior precordial leads, and troponin is mildly elevated. Emergent coronary angiography shows no evidence of obstructive coronary artery disease. A diagnosis of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is considered. If this diagnosis is correct, which of the following findings is most likely to be seen on echocardiography?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This woman has clinical features of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (also known as stress-induced or"broken heart" cardiomyopathy), a condition often triggered by intense emotional or physical stress. It presents similarly to acute coronary syndrome (chest pain, ST elevations, elevated biomarkers) but without significant coronary obstruction. The hallmark echocardiographic finding is left ventricular apical akinesis with preserved basal segments, producing a balloon-like appearance of the apex during systole. This is "apical ballooning" meaning akinesis or hypokinesis of the apex of the left ventricle.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Inferior wall hypokinesis is usually associated with right coronary artery occlusion in myocardial infarction and is not a characteristic finding in Takotsubo cardiomyopathy.

Answer C(incorrectanswer):A normal leftventricular ejectionfraction would notbe expected during theacute phase of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, which typically involves reduced systolic function due to apical akinesis.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Right ventricular dilation is not a defining feature of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy. The condition primarily affects the left ventricle, especially the apex.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Severe mitral regurgitation is not a typical finding in Takotsubo cardiomyopathy. echocardiographic abnormality. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 66-year-old woman presents with new onset exertional dyspnea and lower extremity swelling. She has a history of long- heart sound, elevated jugular venous pressure, and mild pitting edema in both legs. Chest auscultation reveals bibasilar crackles. Echocardiography shows a normal left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF). Which of the following additional findings is most likely on echocardiography?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This woman has clinical features of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), also referred to as diastolic heart failure. HFpEF is commonly seen in older adults with a history of echocardiography, a hallmark finding is increased left ventricular wall thickness, reflecting pressure overload pressures and signs of congestion.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Increased left ventricular cavity size is typical of systolic heart failure (HFrEF), in which the ventricle dilates due to volume overload and weakened contractility. It is not expected in HFpEF.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Increased right ventricular cavity size occurs in chronic right-sided pressure or volume overload, such as in pulmonary hypertension or congenital heart disease. It is not a primary feature of HFpEF.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Increased right ventricular wall thickness is seen in chronic pulmonary

Answer E (incorrect answer): Thickened aortic valve leaflets may suggest calcific aortic stenosis, which could contribute to heart failure symptoms, but this is not likely in a patient with no murmurs on exam.

questions.question: A 5-year-old girl is brought for evaluation to a medical mission tent in rural China. The child lives on a remote farm and eats a diet consisting only of rice. The girl's mother states the child has been lethargic for several weeks. In addition, her ankles have become swollen. The girl feels like sleeping all the time. She becomes easily breathless with exertion. On exam, jugular venous pressure is 12cmH20 (normal <8). Bilateral rales are present. There is 2+ pitting edema. Laboratory studies show a reduced thiamine level. which of the following is expected for cardiac output and left atrial pressure in this child compared to a healthy child?
questions.explanation: Answer B(correct answer):This child's historyis consistent with high-output heart failure from thiamine deficiency. Thiamine (vitamin B1) is a co-factor for several enzymes in cellular metabolism. Deficiency can lead to neurologic symptoms including neuritis and muscle weakness (called dry beriberi). Deficiency may also lead to high-output heart failure or wet beriberi.Deficiency is common in Asia where some diets consist of polished rice which is deficient in thiamine. The exact mechanisms leading to high-output heart failure are not well understood. From a hemodynamic perspective,cardiac output rises and systemicvascular resistance is low.This is the opposite of what is seen in typical systolic or diastolic heart failure where cardiac output is reduced and vascular resistance is high due to sympathetic activation. Despite the high-output,left atrial pressure rises leading to typical heart failure findings including pulmonary edema and right heart failure. Thus, an increased cardiac output and high left atrialpressure are expected findings. High-output heart failure may also be seen in patients with severe anemia and AV fistulas. These patients will have similar hemodynamics (high cardiac output, high left atrial pressure, low vascular resistance) to those with wet beriberi.

questions.question: A patient with dyspnea has an end-diastolic volume of 200cc and an end-systolic volume of 150cc. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's dyspnea?
questions.explanation: Answer A (correct answer): Stroke volume is end-diastolic volume minus end-systolic volume. For this patient, the stroke volume is 200-150=50cc. Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) is equal to stroke volume divided by end diastolic volume. For this patient, the LVEF is 50/200 = 25%. This patient has a reduced LVEF (normal >55%) consistent with systolic heart failure. B, C, and D (incorrect answers): In diastolic heart failure, restrictive cardiomyopathy, and cardiac Answers tamponade the LVEF is normal. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 72-year-old man with diabetes presents with dyspnea. He has no history of cardiac disease. He has been extremely tired for the past week. He gets easily short of breath with walking. On exam, he has bilateral rales. Jugular venous pressure is 14cmH20 (normal <8). There is 1+ pitting edema. Blood pressure is 142/90 mmHg. Echocardiography shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 30% (normal >55%) with anterior wall hypokinesis. Which of the following is the primary cause of this man's condition?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This patient has signs and symptoms of acute heart failure including fatigue, dyspnea, pitting edema, pulmonary edema, and elevated jugular venous pressure. His echocardiogram shows a reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) consistent with systolic heart failure. In patients with systolic heart failure, the primary problem is a decrease in left ventricular contractility. wall. He most likely suffered a silent myocardial infarction involving the anterior wall. This led to decreased left ventricular function and symptoms of heart failure. Many patients with silent infarctions first present for medical attention after the infarction when they develop heart failure.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Increased afterload is seen in patients with hypertension. This can lead to hypertensive heart disease. Initially, the heart develops concentric hypertrophy, and diastolic heart failure may occur. If hypertension becomes long-standing and untreated, eventually systolic heart failure and a low LVEF may occur (a "blown out" ventricle). In the late stage hypertensive heart disease, global hypokinesis is typically seen involving all left ventricular walls.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Decreased compliance is the primary cause of diastolic heart failure. In diastolic heart failure, the LVEF is normal.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Decreased preload is seen in volume depletion or hemorrhage. Mc Graw HimI

questions.question: An 82-year-old woman with diabetes and hypertension presents with dyspnea. She has no history of cardiac disease. She has been extremely tired for the past week. She gets easily short of breath with walking. On exam, she has bilateral rales. Jugular venous pressure is 14cmH20 (normal <8). There is 1+ pitting edema. Blood pressure is 160/90 mmHg. Echocardiography shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60% (normal >55%) with increased left ventricular wall thickness. The left atrium is dilated. Which of the following is the most likely primary cause of this woman's condition?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This patient has signs and symptoms of acute heart failure including fatigue, failure, the primary problem is a decrease in left ventricular compliance. This patient also has increased wall thickness in the left ventricle indicating concentric hypertrophy likely from hypertension. This finding is commonly associated with diastolic heart failure. In addition, she has a dilated left atrium. This is seen in patients with all forms of heart failure (systolic and diastolic) due to elevated left atrial pressure.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Decreased afterload is seen in patients with vasodilation and low blood pressure.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Decreased contractility is the primary cause of systolic heart failure. In systolic heart failure, the LVEF is reduced.

questions.question: A 78-year-old man presents with dyspnea. He has been short of breath and fatigued for the past three days. It is difficult for him to breathe when lying flat so he has been sleeping in a recliner. He has also noticed swelling of his ankles. On physical pitting edema. The primary cause of this man's condition is an abnormal function of which structure in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This patient has heart failure caused by abnormal function of the left ventricle (structure A). He has evidence of left heart failure including rales, dyspnea, and orthopnea. The left ventricle is identificable on imaging because it has a thicker myocardial wall compared with the right ventricle (structure B). The right ventricle is also more anterior (toward top of picture) than the left ventricle. Of note, the question does not provide enough information to definitively determine if this man has systolic or diastolic heart failure. Both of these conditions, however, are due to abnormal function of the left ventricle. In systolic heart failure, the left ventricle cannot contract normally. In diastolic heart failure, the left ventricle does not fill normally.

Answers B, C, and D (incorrect answers): There is also evidence of failure of the right ventricle (structure B), including elevated jugular venous pressure and pitting edema. However, the right ventricle is not the primary cause of his condition as he also has left heart failure symptoms. The most common cause of right heart failure is left heart failure. Other structures in the image are the left atrium (structure C) and the aorta (structure D). Mc Graw

questions.question: A 63-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia presents to his primary care eluting stent placement in his left anterior descending artery six years prior. Medications include aspirin, lisinopril, metoprolol, and rosuvastatin. He works as a mechanical engineer. Temperature is 97.8 °F, pulse is 68/min, and blood pressure is 140/82 mmHg. Cardiac examination reveals regular rate and rhythm. S1 is auscultated, and S2 is split with expiration. S2 split disappears with inspiration. No murmurs are auscultated. Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. What is the most likely underlying cause of his split-second heart sound?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This patient is presenting with a paradoxical split s2. The S2 sound occurs due to simultaneous closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves. This sound can be physiologically "split" during In this question stem, the patient has a split S2 during exhalation, which improves with inspiration. This describes a paradoxical split S2. A paradoxical split S2 occurs due to delayed closure of the aortic valve. On expiration, the split is audible. With inspiration, and increased venous return to the right heart, pulmonic valve closure is delayed. Because valve closures are delayed, the split disappears. Etiologies of delayed closure of the aortic valve include left bundle branch block, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. or aortic stenosis. This patient, with a history of myocardial ischemia, is at risk for development of a left bundle branchblock.

Answer A (incorrect answer): An Atrial Septal Defect (AsD) is a common cause of a fixed split S2. This is a split S2, which is present on expiration and does not change on inspiration. This occurs due to increased flow of blood across the AsD, resulting in constant increased right sided volume and delayed valve closure.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Physiologic splitting of S2 occurs during inspiration only. This is due to increased disappears with inspiration.

Answers D, E (incorrect answers): Pulmonary hypertension and right bundle branch blocks can result in persistent (or wide) S2 splitting. This split is present on inspiration and expiration due to delayed closure of the pulmonic valve and is further split with the increased venous return on inspiration.

questions.question: He also notes worsening dyspnea during this time and can no longer sleep while lying flat. He suffered from an anterior myocardial infarction last year. His medical history also includes hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Medications include mmHg, respiratory rate is 20/min, and oxygen saturation is 94% on room air. Which of the following features would be most helpful to confirm the diagnosis of heart failure in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This patient is presenting with progressive lower extremity edema, dyspnea, and orthopnea, consistent with heart failure. Heart failure is a clinical syndrome that is diagnosed based on the history and physical examination. This patient's history of progressive edema and dyspnea after a myocardial infarction is suggestive of heart failure. Physical examination features of heart failure include elevated jugular venous pressure, lower extremity edema, crackles, and S3 gallop. The S3 gallop represents rapid early filling of LV and occurs when left atrial pressure is elevated in acute heart failure. failure (99%). Given the high specificity, an S3 can confirm the diagnosis of heart failure in this patient. An S3 also has a low sensitivity, so lack of an S3 is not helpful in ruling out heart failure. The table above lists the specificity of various examination findings for heart failure (from Mant et al. in 2009).

Answer A (incorrect answer):Estimation of jugular venous pressure (JVP) is helpful in evaluating right sided filling pressures in the heart, but elevated JVP is not specific for heart failure. JVP can be elevated in patients with tricuspid regurgitation in the absence of heart failure. such as venous insufficiency, cirrhosis, and renal failure.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Orthopnea is moderately specific for heart failure (89%); however, this finding can also be caused by bronchial asthma, pericardial disease, ascites, or anxiety. Orthopnea is not as specific for heart failure as a S3 gallop.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Crackles only have moderate specificity for heart failure (81%) and are associated with a variety of other pulmonary processes, such as infections and interstitial lung disease. Mc Graw

The remainder of her physical examination is within normal limits. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? =Play Audio +0:00-

Answer D (correct answer): This patient is presenting with a systolic click and murmur heard at the apex which is consistent with mitral valve prolapse (MvP). Note that the audio file contains an extra heart sound in addition to S1 and S2. This sound is the click of mitral valve prolapse. In patients with MVP, cardiac auscultation reveals a non-ejection (late systolic) click followed by a murmur from mitral regurgitation. The click is caused by snapping of the mitral valve chordae when the valve prolapses (i.e., bulges) into the atrium during systole. The murmur increases in intensity with the Valsalva maneuver. MvP is usually asymptomatic.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Aortic stenosis causes a systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur. This condition is rare before age 40. Rarely, an early systolic click may occur in cases of aortic stenosis assocaited with a bicuspid aorticvalve.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Aortic regurgitation causes a blowing diastolic murmur. An early systolic click may occur in cases of aortic regurgitation assocaited with a bicuspid aortic valve. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 64-year-old man with chronic systolic heart failure due to ischemic cardiomyopathy is started on guideline-directed medical therapy, including metoprolol succinate. questions.question: A 42-year-old man presents for an evaluation of sexual dysfunction. For the past two months, he reports an inability to maintain an erection. He has also noted a watery discharge from his nipples on several occasions. He has a history of hypertension and was started on a new drug several weeks ago. Blood pressure and pulse are within normal limits. Physical presentation?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This man's presentation is concerning for hyperprolactinemia. Elevated prolactin leads to hypogonadism and galactorrhea. In men, common presenting symptoms are sexual dysfunction and nipple discharge. Next steps in this patient's management should include a MRI to evaluate for a pituitary adenoma. Drug-induced hyperprolactinemia is considered once pituitary adenoma is ruled out by MRI. Many classes of drugs are associated with hyperprolactinemia. Most of these drugs block dopamine such as the antipsychotics risperidone and haloperidol. Of the choices listed in the question, verapamil is a rare cause of elevated serum prolactin. The mechanism of this effect is not well understood.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Metoprolol is a beta-1 selective beta blocker. This drug is associated with sexual dysfunctionbutnotgalactorrhea.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Amlodipine is a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker. A common adverse effect islowerextremityedema.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Lisinopril is an ACE inhibitor. The major side effect is cough due to elevated bradykininlevels.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Hydralazine is a direct vasodilator.Adverse effects include reflex tachycardia and drug-induced lupus. Mc Graw

questions.question: Two patients are administered pindolol. Heart rate changes are shown in the table below. Which of the following is most likely different between patients A and B?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correctanswer):Pindolol is a partial agonist tobeta receptors.The drug can increase or decrease When the SNS is active, the drug occupies receptor sites and blocks the effects of the SNs. Although the drug exerts modest activity at the receptor site as a partial agonist, that activity is less than the SNs.As a result, an overall decrease in SNS activity occurs. When SNS activity is low (i.e. when beta receptors are likely to be found increase in SNs activity. Patient A has a high heart rate at baseline reflecting high sympathetic tone. After pindolol, there is a fall in heart rate. Patient B has a low heart rate at baseline reflecting low sympathetic tone. This patient has a rise in heart rate with pindolol. These different responses relate to the baseline sympathetic tone. This is a classic property of pindolol and acebutolol, beta blockers with "intrinsic sympathomimetic activity." These drugs are rarely used in the modern era. Their advantage is less bradycardia at rest when SNs activity is low, but intact heart rate suppression with exercise when SNs activity is high. A disadvantage is that, in theory, these drugs can cause angina through beta-1 stimulation although studies have shown these drugs effective at reducing angina frequency.

Answer E (incorrect answer): A difference in pindolol dose cannot explain the two responses. The maximum stimulatory effect of pindolol occurs at low doses.Both patients should have achieved maximum pindolol effect with any differences due only to sympathetic activity.

Answers A, B, D (incorrect answers): Pindolol is metabolized by the liver and excreted by the kidneys. Differences in absorption, liver metabolism, or renal excretion could alter the effective dose of the drug. As above, however, the dose cannot explain the two patient responses. questions.question: A 72-year-old woman is found unresponsive at home. Pulse is 30/min and blood pressure is 70/30 mmHg. ECG demonstrates sinus bradycardia. Answer D (correct answer): This patient has signs and symptoms of beta blocker overdose including altered mental status, bradycardia, and low blood pressure. Glucagon is the first line therapy in this setting. Glucagon the heart as beta stimulation but its action is not impaired by beta blockers. Answer E (incorrect answer): Hemodialysis (answer E)has only a small role in beta-blocker overdose.It is not a first line intervention. It is effective only for the removal of some beta blockers like atenolol and nadolol. Hemodialysis does not remove metoprolol and propranolol. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 56-year-old man presents for an evaluation of somnolence. He reports daytime sleepiness for the past one month that interferes with his ability to work. In the periphery, this causes a fall in adrenergic tone which lowers blood pressure. In the central nervous system, the fall in adrenergic tone leads to somnolence. Excessive sleepiness is a common complaint of patients taking this drug. In fact, clonidine is

questions.question: He is prescribed amlodipine. At follow-up one month later, his blood pressure is 138/78 mmHg. He feels well with no complaints. Lungs are clear. Jugular venous pressure and cardiac exam are normal. There is 1+ pitting lower extremity edema. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his edema?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer):Edemais a common adverse effect of dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers like amlodipine. These drugs block calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle leading to a fall in blood pressure. Their effects are largely on pre-capillary arterioles. By reducing tone in these vessels, blood floods systemic capillaries. This raises capillary hydrostatic pressure, causing edema. this is only true in the capillaries. Calcium channel blockers dilate pre-capillary arterioles. Mean blood pressure within the arterial system falls due to this effect. In the capillaries, however, hydrostatic pressure rises as the dilated arterioles allow more fluid into the capillary system.

Answers A, B, C, and E (incorrect answers): Heart failure, hypoalbuminemia, renal failure, and increased vascular permeability may all cause pitting edema. None of these is likely in this patient with a normal physical exam and no complaints other than edema. Mc Graw

questions.question: An 82-year-old woman with dementia accidentally takes multiple doses of her anti-hypertensive medication. She is evaluated in the emergency room and the EKG below is obtained. Which of the following drugs did she most likely take?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This woman's EKG shows complete AV (3rd degree) heart block. Note that the p waves and QRs complexes are independent of one another. Note also that the QRs complexes occur at regular intervals indicating they are "escape" beats from a pacemaker below the AV node. Verapamil is a calcium channel blocker with AV nodal slowing effects. By slowing conduction through the AV node, it may prolong the PR interval and, if taken in excess, cause complete AV block. This adverse effect may also occur with beta-blockers which also slow conduction through the AV node.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Hydralazine is a direct vasodilator. Overdose may cause hypotension but not AV block.

questions.question: An 83-year-old woman presents with sudden onset left sided weakness. On exam, she has dense hemiparesis on the left side of her body. Neuroimaging shows a large middle cerebral artery territory stroke. Carotid ultrasound shows no significant plaque. An ECG is performed as shown below. The patient has no history of cardiac disease. Which of the following is the most likely source of embolism for this patient's stroke?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This patient has a stroke involving a large territory supplied by the middle cerebral artery in the setting of atrial flutter. Strokes involving large territories of the central nervous system are often embolic. An embolism from a distant site can"shower" multiple branches of a cerebral artery with clot causing extensive ischemia. In contrast, small vessel atherosclerosis within the CNs tends to cause more focal areas of infarction. An embolic stroke in the setting of new-onset atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter is most likely caused by thrombus patients are unaware of the arrhythmia until they have a stroke. Strokes in these disorders originate most commonly from the left atrial appendage. This outpouching of the left atrium has relatively slow blood flow of thrombus. To lower the risk of thrombus formation, patients with known atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter are often treated with anticoagulants.

Answer B (incorrect answer): In atrial fibrillation or flutter, an embolism can originate from the left atrium but this is less common than the atrial appendage and usually occurs only when clot extends out of the left atrial appendage.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Thrombus can form in the left ventricle in the setting of left ventricular aneurysms

Answer D (incorrect answer): Atrial fibrillation rarely leads to thrombus in the right atrium. Thrombus in this location may cause a pulmonary embolism.
