Answer D (incorrect answer): Balloon valvuloplasty is a treatment for valvular stenosis (e.g., aortic or pulmonary stenosis), not coarctation of the aorta. Balloon angioplasty may be used for coarctation in select older patients, but is not the first step in neonatal management.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Atrial septal defects are not typically associated with coarctation of the aorta and would not explain the ductal-dependent physiology in this case. Surgical repair of an AsD is not indicated or beneficial here. Mc Graw IH

questions.question: A 2-day-old baby develops sudden-onset respiratory distress. Exam reveals labored breathing and bilateral rales. Despite resuscitative measures, the baby dies. Autopsy reveals a dilated left ventricle. The descending aorta is narrowed distal to the subclavian artery. Which of the following is the primary cause of this baby's death?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): The autopsy findings demonstrate aortic coarctation, a congenital narrowing of the descending aorta usually located just beyond the subclavian artery. The narrowing obstructs blood flow to the lower half of the body. If the narrowing is severe, it can lead to heart failure in the newborn period due to severely increased afterload on the left ventricle. If the narrowing is not severe, it may go undetected until hypertension develops in the adult. At birth, many babies have a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). This delivers blood from the aorta to the pulmonary artery. In cases of severe coarctation, this conduit can be life-sustaining. Because of the PDA, the entire cardiac output of the left ventricle does not need to flow past the coarctation. Some of the blood is diverted into the PDA. This reduces afterload. When the PDA fully closes a few days after birth, the hemodynamics change. At this point, all blood from the left ventricle must pass the coarctation. If the narrowing is severe, afterload on the left ventricle becomes massive. This can lead to acute dilation of the left ventricle and left heart failure as described in the question.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Decreased contractility was present in this baby prior to death. The left ventricle is dilated at autopsy. Very high pressure inside the chamber led to reduced myocardial blood flow and ischemia. This is not, however, the primary cause of death for the baby. The fall in contractility occurred secondarily to the massive rise in afterload caused by the coarctation.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Right to left shunting is seen in Tetralogy of Fallot and other forms of cyanotic congenitalheartdisease.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Left to right shunting is seen in atrial septal defects and ventricular septal defects.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Turner syndrome is associated with coarctation of the aorta. Nothing in the question suggests Turner syndrome is present.

questions.question: A 24-year-old man presents for routine evaluation. He is physically active and has no complaints. Blood pressure is 178/92 mmHg. He is noted to have delayed femoral pulses compared with the radial pulse. Physical exam is otherwise normal. He is following is true of blood flow in this man?

options.A: Lower extremity flow resistance is high
options.B: Upper extremity blood pressure is low
options.C: Upper extremity flow resistance is high
options.D: Lower extremity blood pressure is high

questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): Aortic coarctation is a congenital narrowing of the descending aorta usually located just beyond the subclavian artery. The narrowing obstructs blood flow to the lower half of the body. If the narrowing is severe, it can lead to heart failure in the newborn period due to severely increased afterload on the left ventricle. If the narrowing is not severe, it may go undetected until hypertension develops in the adult. Classic findings are delayed femoral pulses and low blood pressure in the lower extremities. Aortic coarctation can lead to high blood pressure in the upper extremities (proximal to the coarctation) and lowblood pressure in the lower extremities (distal to the coarctation). When this occurs, local autoregulation will maintain regional blood flow. Tissue beds, especially muscles, in the upper and lower extremitiesarecapableofautoregulationwhichmeansarteriolescanconstrictordilatetocontrolblood flow (seevideoonRegulationofBloodPressure). In the upper extremities, this patient has high pressure due to coarctation. This could lead to high blood flow (high pressure driving more flow) but does not because autoregulatory vasoconstriction of arterioles will reduce blood flow toward normal levels. In the lower extremities, this man has low blood pressure due to coarctation. This could lead to low blood flow but does not because autoregulatory vasodilation will increase blood flow toward normal levels. In this man's upper extremities flow resistance is high due to vasoconstriction. This keeps blood flow closer to normal despite high pressure. The opposite is true of his lower extremities. For this reason, he has a normal physical exam. There is no evidence of increased blood flow (i.e. hyperemia) in the upper extremities and no evidence of cyanosis in the lower extremities.

Answer A(incorrect answer): Lower extremity flowresistance is low as explained above.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Upper extremity blood pressure (proximal to the coarctation) will be high in this man.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Lower extremity blood pressure (distal to the coarctation) will be low in this man. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 54-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a 1-hour history of palpitations and anxiety. questions.question: A 56-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a 2-hour episode of palpitations, lightheadedness, and mild shortness of breath. Answer D(correct answer):Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia(PsVT) refers to a group of arrhythmias that originate above the ventricles and have a sudden onset and termination. The most common form is Av nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT), in which a reentrant circuit within or near the AV node causes rapid and regular ventricular activation. Patients with PsVT typically present with sudden palpitations, often associated with narrow QRS complexes.Among the most specific features is regular R-R intervals (consistent distance, without variation, on EKG between R waves of the QRS complexes), reflecting the consistent activation of the ventricles by the reentrant circuit. questions.question: A 30-year-old woman presents with the abrupt onset of palpitations. ECG shows a supraventricular tachycardia at a rate of 200bpm. Further work-up leads to a diagnosis of AV nodal reentrant tachycardia. Which of the following is required for development of this arrhythmia?

Answer C (correct answer): AV nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT) is a common form of paroxysmal short episodes of rapid heart rate (i.e. different from the gradual increase in heart rate seen with exercise). system (i.e. not a ventricular tachycardia). The term PsVT is used to refer to disorders that cause the sudden onset of regular tachycardia with a narrow QRs complex (i.e. normal QRs duration of less than 120ms). Other than AVNRT, other disorders that lead to PsVT are atrial tachycardia, AV nodal tachycardia, and junctional tachycardia. Of these, AVNRT is the most common. Patients with AVNRT experience sudden episodes of palpitations caused by rapid heart rate. questions.question: A 47-year-old woman is diagnosed with pheochromocytoma and administered phenoxybenzamine. Which of the following describes the physiologic changes that will occur in this woman after receiving this drug?
questions.explanation: Answer C (correct answer): Pheochromocytoma is an adrenal tumor that secretes epinephrine and norepinephrine. Definitive treatment is through surgical removal of the tumor, but before this can be done, blood pressure must be controlled pharmacologically. Part of the treatment of hypertension due to excessive adrenergic effects. Phenoxybenzamine, an irreversible alpha antagonist, and propranolol, a nonspecific beta blocker, are used for this purpose. Blockade of alpha-1 receptors by phenoxybenzamine decreases peripheral resistance and therefore lowers blood pressure. Heart rate increases reflexively through sympathetic activation in response to the fall in blood pressure. Cardiac output increases from sympathetic activation as well as the fall in afterload associated with peripheral vasodilation. After alpha blockade is achieved in patients with pheochromocytoma, propranolol is administered to antagonize beta receptors. Importantly, beta blockade is never done first. Peripheral beta-2 receptors cause vasodilation in the setting of high catecholamine levels. This offsets some of the rise in peripheral resistance caused by excessive alpha activity. If a beta blocker is given before alpha blockade, alpha activity will be "unopposed" and blood pressure can become dangerously high. Mc Graw

questions.question: Researchers are studying the hemodynamic effects of autonomic drugs in healthy volunteers. When given before epinephrine, it prevents alpha-mediated vasoconstriction, allowing only beta-2-mediated vasodilation and beta-1-mediated tachycardia to remain. The result is a drop in MAP and a rise in HR, which is the classic epinephrine reversal effect. It is called epinephrine reversal because phenoxybenzamines reverses the effect of epinephrine on blood pressure cause a fall instead of a rise in MAP.

questions.question: A 75-year-old woman is evaluated for confusion and agitation. Earlier in the day, she underwent a lipoma excision under general anesthesia. A scopolamine patch was placed preoperatively because she has a history of postoperative nausea and
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): Scopolamine is an anticholinergic drug that blocks M1 muscarinic receptors. Histamine and acetylcholine are the principle neurotransmitters involved in nausea and vomiting. Through blockade of central nervous system muscarinic receptors, scopolamine is effective at controlling postoperative nausea and vomiting, as well as motion sickness. Because scopolamine crosses the blood-brain barrier (BBB), it can lead to central nervous system side effects including confusion. Elderly patients in particular may develop this side effect of anticholinergic drugs. Other side effects of scopolamine include dry mouth, constipation, and urinaryretention. To counteract central nervous system effects of anticholinergic drugs, a centrally-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor is required. Physostigmine, a tertiary amine, is the only acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that crosses the BBB.

questions.question: An 85-year-old man presents to the ophthalmologist with decreased visual acuity in his right eye. He is diagnosed with acute angle closure glaucoma. Pilocarpine is instilled in the eye. which of the following describes the mechanism by which pilocarpine reduces intraocular pressure? Beta-2 receptor antagonism >>

questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): Glaucoma is a condition of increased pressure in the anterior chamber of the eye. Left untreated, it can lead to vision loss. The anterior chamber contains the transparent liquid, aqueous humor. Mc Graw Excess aqueous humor, either from overproduction or impaired drainage, can lead to glaucoma. Modulation of aqueous humor volume by drugs is the mainstay of treatment for glaucoma. Aqueous humor is produced by the ciliary epithelium of the ciliary body. Aqueous humor first flows from the ( ( s image above). The aqueous humor then drains through the trabecular network, an area of tissue near the base of the cornea. The trabecular network is a spongy tissue that leads to Schlemm's canal, which then allows the aqueous humor to flow back into the bloodstream. For distance vision, the ciliary muscle changes the shape of the lens in a process called accommodation. Ciliary muscle changes also alter the flow of aqueous humor. Contraction of the ciliary muscle increases the size of the pores in the trabecular meshwork, leading to increased aqueous humor drainage. Relaxation of the ciliary muscle decreases trabecular meshwork pore size, reducing aqueous humor outflow. muscle contraction. This in turn opens the trabecular network, leading to more drainage of aqueous humor, which lowers intraocular pressure. Answer E (incorrect answer): Activation of the M3 receptor by pilocarpine causes ciliary muscle contraction, not relaxation. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 77-year old woman with a history of memory loss is diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease. Her primary care physician prescribes galantamine. Which of the following is a potential side effect of this medication?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): Alzheimer's disease is a chronic neurodegenerative disease that usually occurs in the elderly (most cases have onset after age 65). Symptoms include disorientation, memory loss, mood swings, difficulty with self-care, and behavioral problems. Early studies of Alzheimer's disease identified central nervous system deficits in choline acetyltransferase, the enzyme that synthesizes acetylcholine. This led to the "cholinergic hypothesis" of Alzheimer's disease, which posits that the disorder results from decreased acetylcholine synthesis. As a result, drugs that increase acetylcholine activity have been used to treat Alzheimer's disease. Galantamine is a reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that crosses the blood-brain barrier (it is a tertiary amine). It is used to treat Alzheimer's disease and other types of dementia by increasing acetylcholine levels in the synaptic cleft. In addition to this effect, galantamine has also been shown to bind nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, inducing a conformational change that makes the receptors more sensitive to acetylcholine. The most common side effects of galantamine are nausea and vomiting. In very rare cases, the increased acetylcholine concentration and increased sensitivity of the receptors can cause seizures by stimulating central acetylcholine receptors. Although rare, of the answer choices, seizures is the only choice that could occur with a cholinesterase-inhibiting medication.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Increased acetylcholine secondary to galantamine can cause diarrhea, not constipation.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Galantamine may cause lacrimation, not eye dryness.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Higher concentrations of acetylcholine can stimulate muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in the heart, leading to bradycardia, not tachycardia.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Increased acetylcholine can lead to stimulation of the detrusor muscle of the bladder via M3 muscarinic receptors. This can cause urinary incontinence, not urinary retention. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 70-year-old man with chronic systolic heart failure (LVEF 35%) comes to the clinic for follow-up. He is clinically stable on guideline-directed medical therapy, including a beta blocker and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist. His physician adds empagliflozin to further reduce his risk of hospitalization and disease progression. which of the following is most likely to occur as a result of this patient's new medication?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This man with chronic systolic heart failure (LVEF 35%) is now starting empagliflozin, an sGLT2 inhibitor. Originally developed as a glucose-lowering medication for diabetes, empagliflozin is now also used in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), regardless of diabetes status, due to its ability to reduce hospitalizations and slow disease progression. Empagliflozin blocks sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) in the proximal renal tubule, reducing glucose and sodium reabsorption. This causes an osmotic diuresis, leading to polyuria (increased urine output). This mild diuretic effect contributes to reduced preload and improved hemodynamics in heart failure. Polyuria is a common and expected effect of SGLT2 inhibitors. eplerenone), but SGLT2 inhibitors do not typically cause hyperkalemia and may actually have a mild potassium- loweringeffect. natriuresis, but the sodium loss is usually modest and not enough to induce clinically significant hyponatremia.

These drugs may slightly increase urinary calcium or phosphate, but the risk of stone formation is not significantly elevated.

questions.question: A 62-year-old woman with chronic systolic heart failure (LVEF 35%) comes to the clinic for follow-up. She recently started guideline-directed medical therapy including a beta blocker and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist. Her physician recommends adding dapagliflozin to her heart failure regimen, and she asks about potential side effects of this drug. Which of the following should this woman's physician discuss?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This woman is being recommended dapagliflozin, an SGLT2 inhibitor. This class of medications was originally developed for type 2 diabetes and is now used in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) to reduce hospitalizations and mortality. SGLT2 inhibitors act in the proximal renal tubule to block glucose reabsorption, resulting in glucosuria, which can predispose patients to genital mycotic infections (i.e., Candida or yeast infections). In women, this often presents as vaginal discharge, itching, or irritation caused by Candida species.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Angioedema is associated with medications that raise bradykinin levels, such as ACE inhibitors and neprilysin inhibitors (e.g., sacubitril). SGLT2 inhibitors do not affect bradykinin metabolism.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Dry cough is a well-known adverse effect of ACE inhibitors, not SGLT2 inhibitors. It results from bradykinin accumulation in the respiratory tract.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Gynecomastia is most commonly associated with spironolactone, a non-selective mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist with antiandrogenic effects. It is not a side effect of sGLT2 inhibitors.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Hyperkalemia is a potential adverse effect of RAAS inhibitors such as ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists. SGLT2 inhibitors are not typically associated with elevated potassium levels. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 65-year-old man with chronic systolic heart failure (LVEF 30%) comes to the emergency department with acute facial swelling. He reports that his lips and tongue began swelling earlier today, making it difficult to speak. He has no rash, itching, wheezing, or difficulty breathing. He has no known drug or food allergies. questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This patient has bradykinin-mediated angioedema, likely triggered by sacubitril, a neprilysin inhibitor. Neprilysin degrades bradykinin. When it is inhibited by sacubitril, bradykinin accumulates and can increase vascular permeability, leading to non-pruritic, non-urticarial angioedema-induced reactions. Sacubitril is used in combination with valsartan (ARNI) as part of guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Angioedema may also occur due to AcE inhibitors which inhibit bradykinin degradation similarly to sacubitril. Because both drug classes increase bradykinin, they are never given together, due to the heightened risk of angioedema.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Dapagliflozin is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor that improves heart failure outcomes but is not associated with angioedema. Its common side effects include urinary tract infections and genital mycotic infections.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Ivabradine lowers heart rate by inhibiting the funny current (If) in the SA node but has no known association with angioedema. Side effects include visual phenomena (phosphenes) and bradycardia.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Metoprolol is a beta-1 selective blocker used in heart failure and hypertension.

questions.question: A patient with systolic heart failure is administered ivabradine. Which of the following ECG changes is most likely?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): Ivabradine reduces heart rate through inhibition of the funny current (If) in SA nodal cells. This is a mechanism unique from beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers which may also be used to lower heart rate. The funny current is an inward Na flux that occurs in SA nodal cells in diastole (phase 4 of the pacemaker action potential). This slowly raises the membrane potential until a threshold is reached and depolarization occurs. The funny current is responsible for the automatic depolarization of the SA node ("automaticity"). By inhibiting this current, ivabradine slows the heart rate. This drug has been shown to lower the rate of hospitalization and mortality among chronic heart failure patients when used together with beta- blockers. By slowing the heart rate, ivabradine will increase the R-R interval. The R-R interval is the time between QRS complexes on the ECG. This interval varies with the heart rate (longer at slow heart rates, shorter at high heart rates).

Answer B (incorrect answer): The QRs interval is not affected by ivabradine.

Answer C (incorrect answer): PR depressions are seen in pericarditis.

Answer D (incorrect answer): U waves may be seen in hypokalemia

Answer E (incorrect answer): T wave inversions may be seen in subendocardial ischemia.

questions.question: A 23-year-old medical student goes on a hike on a hot August day. She gets lost in the woods and has no water. After two hours, she finds her way home. She asks her roommate to check her blood pressure so she can compare it to prior to her hike. Her weight is down three pounds compared to before her hike. Which of the following is most responsible for maintaining her blood pressure?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This medical student is volume depleted from sweating while hiking in the heat without water (this is why her weight is down). Volume loss should lead to a fall in blood pressure but has not because her body has responded physiologically. Loss in blood pressure from volume depletion is sensed by the aortic arch and carotid sinus. Baroreceptors in both locations will decrease their firing to the brain in the setting of low pressure, although the carotid sinus is much more effective at signaling the brain when blood pressure is low. The brain will respond to decreased firing of baroreceptors by activating the sympathetic nervous system and limiting the parasympathetic system. As a result, blood pressure will be maintained via increased

This may contribute to the maintenance of blood pressure by generating more angiotensin II, however, activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) takes time. The major mechanism of maintaining blood pressure in the acute setting is via baroreceptors and the sympathetic nervous system.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Aortic arch baroreceptor firing decreases, not increases, with volume depletion.

Answers D, E (incorrect answers): In volume depletion, parasympathetic activity decreases and sympathetic activityincreases.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department after experiencing several episodes of syncope, which often occur while buttoning a tight-collared shirt. He reports that the episodes started a few weeks ago, and during the most recent one, he felt lightheaded and briefly lost consciousness. He denies chest pain, palpitations, or shortness of breath. He has no significant medical history and recalls feeling normal after each episode. The patient denies any associated dizziness, 125/80 mmHg, heart rate is 75 beats per minute. When his neck is gently massaged during the examination, he experiences lightheadedness. Which of the following hemodynamic changes most likely explains this event?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This patient likely has carotid sinus hypersensitivity, a condition where pressure on the carotid sinus (as occurs when buttoning a tight-collared shirt or shaving) triggers an exaggerated baroreceptor reflex. Normally, when blood pressure is elevated, the carotid sinus sends afferent signals through the glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX) to the nucleus solitarius in the medulla. The brain interprets this sympathetic nervous system is suppressed. This results in arteriolar vasodilation, venous dilation, and a decrease in heart rate. This reflex causes a significant drop in blood pressure. In this case, the carotid sinus hypersensitivity tricks the body into thinking blood pressure is higher than it actually is, leading to increased parasympathetic stimulation and decreased sympathetic activity. This results in reduced heart rate, vasodilation, and decreased blood pressure, ultimately causing the patient's fainting episodes.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Increased contractility results from sympathetic activation. In carotid sinus hypersensitivity, parasympathetic activity increases and sympathetic activity decreases leading to a decrease in contractility.

Answer C (incorrect answer): An increase in heart rate is driven by sympathetic activation. In this case, parasympathetic tone is elevated, causing a decrease in heart rate.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Increased peripheral resistance would be caused by sympathetic activation. Here, the parasympathetic activity is dominant and the sympathetic activity is decreased, leading to vasodilation and a reduction in peripheral resistance. s hypersensitivity, the parasympathetic activity is dominant and the sympathetic activity is decreased, leading to venous dilation and reduced venous return.

questions.question: A 68-year-old male presents to the clinic reporting worsening bilateral leg swelling over the past two weeks. He notes fever. Answer B (correct answer): In heart failure, the heart's reduced ability to pump blood effectively leads to increased venous pressure, resulting in increased capillary hydrostatic pressure. Also, the decrease in cardiac output activates the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS), which results in fluid retention, volume causes fluid to move from the capillaries into the interstitial space, leading to the formation of edema. In heart failure, increased capillary hydrostatic pressure is the predominant factor causing edema.

questions.question: A 59-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 2 hours of central chest pain described as pressure-like and radiating to his left shoulder. He has a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. On examination, he is diaphoretic and mildly tachycardic. His ECG shows no ST-segment elevations but reveals T wave inversions in leads V4-V6. The clinical team suspects a non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NsTEMI) and begins further evaluation. Which of the following laboratory values can be measured to help determine whether this patient is experiencing myocardial injury consistent with NSTEMI?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): Aspartate aminotransferase (AsT) is a mitochondrial enzyme found in liver, skeletal muscle, and cardiac muscle. Although no longer used as a primary cardiac biomarker, AsT levels can rise during used to detect myocardial injury before more specific markers like troponin and CK-MB became standard. A rise in AST is consistent with cellular injury, including that caused by NSTEMI.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Creatine is a molecule involved in muscle energy metabolism, but it is not used to diagnose myocardial infarction. You may be thinking of creatine kinase (CK) or CK-MB, which are cardiac biomarkers, but creatine itself is not clinically relevant in this context.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Hemoglobin is measured to assess anemia or oxygen-carrying capacity but is not a marker of cardiac muscle injury. It provides no diagnostic value in determining whether a patient is having an NSTEMI.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Potassium is important in cardiac electrophysiology and is often monitored during acute coronary syndromes for arrhythmia risk, but it does not indicate whether myocardial infarction has occurred. It is not a diagnostic biomarker for NSTEMI. utilization but is not specific to cardiac injury and cannot confirm or rule out NSTEMI. Hm

ECG demonstrates ST-segment depressions and T wave inversions inbothconditions.

questions.question: A 61-year-old man with hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidemia presents to the emergency department with chest pain. He describes a constant, intense pressure in the center of his chest. Symptoms began 2 hours ago and have progressively worsened. Vital signs include a temperature of 989F, heart rate of 104/min, respiratory rate of 14/min, blood pressure of 142/99 mmHg, and pulse oximetry of 93% on room air. Physical exam reveals diaphoresis and mild respiratory distress. Electrocardiogram (ECG) reveals ST-segment depressions in leads V2-4. Serum troponin is 0.07 ng/mL. Creatine kinase (CK) levels are obtained. Which of the following laboratory findings is most likely in this patient?

options.A: Elevated CK levels, no predominant CK type

questions.explanation:
presenting as progressive, ischemic chest pain with ST-segment depressions on ECG and a mildly elevated serum troponin level (normal range is less than or equal to 0.04 ng/mL). NSTEMI is caused by coronary artery plaque rupture and thrombus formation, leading to subtotal vessel occlusion and subsequent subendocardial infarction. Creatine kinase-MB (CK-MB) is a more cardiac-specific subtype of creatine kinase that rises 4-6 hours after myocardial infarction. In contrast, serum troponin levels rise within 2-4 hours after myocardial infarction. This CK-MBtorise.

Answers A, B, C and D (incorrect answer): CK-MB is a cardiac-specific subtype of CK that rises 4-6 hours after myocardial infarction. Other CK subtypes include CK-BB (more concentrated in brain tissue) and CK-MM (more concentrated in skeletal muscle). Since most tissues contain varying amounts of all 3 subtypes, CK-MB can be elevated in disorders outside the heart. However, it is the predominant subtype in myocardial infarction. Given this patient's symptoms began 2 hours ago, CK-MB levels are likely to be in the normal range.

questions.question: An elderly man develops the sudden onset of chest pain and collapses to the floor. His wife calls 911 and when the EMTs arrive the man has regained consciousness but complains of ongoing chest pressure. An ECG performed at the scene shows ST elevations in leads II, III, and aVF. Aspirin and nitroglycerin are administered and the patient is taken to a nearby hospital 10 minutes away. On arrival at the hospital, IV access is established and blood is sent to the laboratory. Total time since the onset of the man's symptoms is 45 minutes. Which of the following lab abnormalities for creatine kinase (CK), creatine kinase MB fraction (CK-MB) and troponin are expected?
questions.explanation: Answer C (correct answer): This patient is presenting very early after the onset of cardiac ischemia due to ST- remain normal until at least 2 hours into an ischemic syndrome. Patients who present very early like the man in the question often have normal biomarkers on initial testing. CK and CK-MB are elevated in the plasma about 4 to 6 hours after infarction and remain elevated for 24 to 48 hours. Troponin levels are elevated 2 to 4 hours after infarction and remain elevated for up to 2 weeks. "High sensitivity troponin" tests are in development which may allow even earlier detection of myocardial damage fromischemia. For the patient in the question, the diagnosis of acute MI was obvious based on the ECG. However, in many patients with chest pain, the ECG is non-diagnostic. Because it can take several hours for cardiac biomarker levels to rise in the plasma, these patients are often observed in a chest pain unit (sometimes called a "rule out MI" protocol) where serial biomarker testing is performed. The idea behind these units is that initial biomarker levels may be normal but subsequent testing several hours after symptom onset may be abnormal. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 62-year-old man with a history of diabetes and hypertension presents to the emergency room complaining of chest pain. The pain is dull, substernal, and has been present on and off for the past six hours. ECG shows ST-segment depressions in leads V2, V3, V4, and V5. Blood work reveals creatinine kinase of 500 U/L (normal <150) and troponin I of 1.1 ng/ml (normal <0.01). Which of the following is the most likely finding at coronary angiography?

options.D: 95% occlusion by ruptured plaque with thrombus

questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): The question describes a patient with non-ST-segment myocardial infarction (NSTEMI). The clinical syndrome of NSTEMI includes chest pain, ECG changes including ST depressions and T wave inversions, and elevated cardiac biomarkers. ST-segment myocardial infarction (STEMI), NSTEMI, and unstable angina (UA) are all considered "acute coronary syndromes" because of their association with acute plaque rupture and thrombus formation. The major pathologic distinction is that blood vessel occlusion is subtotal (i.e. not 1oo%) in UA/NsTEMI. For this reason, some blood flow reaches the myocardium beyond the obstruction.

Answer A (incorrect answer): In contrast, STEMI is caused by complete (1oo%) occlusion of a coronary artery due to plaque rupture and thrombus. AnswerB(incorrectanswer):Patientswithstablecoronaryatheroscleroticplaque(i.e.withoutrupture or thrombus) that obstructs 75% or more of a coronary artery lumen will develop stable angina. Blood flow is adequate at rest and symptoms are absent. with exertion, blood flow cannot increase to meet oxygen demand andischemiaoccurs.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Stable coronary plaques that obstruct less than 75% of a vessel lumen do not cause symptoms even with exertion. The coronary vessels can generally tolerate narrowing until about 75% of the flow area is lost.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Coronary vasospasm may lead to a clinical picture similar to NsTEMI. However, vasospasm is much less common than NsTEMI particularly in a patient with diabetes and hypertension as describedinthequestion.

Answer F (incorrect answer): Normal coronary arteries would not be expected in this patient with NSTEMI.

questions.question: A 72-year-old man presents to the emergency room with chest pain of seven hours duration. ECG shows ST-segment depressions in leads II, III, and aVF. Creatinine kinase is 350 U/L (normal <150) and troponin I is 2.1 ng/ml (normal <0.01). During evaluation in the emergency room, the patient develops ventricular fibrillation and dies. questions.explanation:
Limiteddistalflow Non-ST-elevationMyocardialInfarction Unstable angina Ulcerated Plaque-Thrombus Subtotalocclusion Limiteddistalbloodflow (NSTEMI). The clinical syndrome of NSTEMI includes chest pain, ECG changes including ST depressions and T wave inversions, and elevated cardiac biomarkers. ST-segment myocardial infarction (STEMI) and NSTEMI are considered "acute coronary syndromes" because of their association with acute plaque rupture and thrombus formation. In both conditions, myocyte necrosis leads to elevation of serum cardiac biomarkers. The major pathologic distinction is that blood vessel occlusion is not 100% in NsTEMI. The coronary lesions of NSTEMI are subtotal and some blood flow reaches the myocardium oxygen and does not undergo necrosis. In contrast, the subendocardial myocardium is furthest from the coronary arteries and will develop necrosis. For these reasons, subendocardial necrosis is the expected finding in NSTEMI.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Transmural necrosis is the expected finding in STEMI.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Because elevated cardiac biomarkers indicate necrosis of cardiac myocytes, normal myocardium is not expected in cases of myocardial infarction (STEMI or NSTEMI).

questions.question: A 49-year-old man comes to the clinic for management of recurrent symptomatic atrial fibrillation. He has a history of type 1 diabetes mellitus complicated by peripheral neuropathy, a seizure disorder well controlled with medication, and coronary fraction of 60% with mild apical hypokinesis. His sister has been successfully treated with flecainide for paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, and he asks if he could try the same medication. Which of the following represents a contraindication to flecainide use in this patient?
questions.explanation:
effective for rhythm control in atrial fibrillation. It is contraindicated in patients with structural heart disease especially those with prior myocardial infarction or known coronary artery disease, due to the increased risk of ventricular proarrhythmia and sudden cardiac death. This patient's history of MI and mild apical hypokinesis on exercisetolerance.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Diabetes mellitus is not a direct contraindication to flecainide use. While diabetes contributes to cardiovascular risk, the contraindication specifically relates to existing structural or ischemic heart disease,not diabetes alone.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Diabetic peripheral neuropathy does not affect the safety or efficacy of flecainide and is not a contraindication to its use.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Frequent endurance exercise is not a contraindication to flecainide. However, exercise can promote toxicity due to use-dependent sodium channel blockade, especially at high heart rates. For this reason, patients started on flecainide are often monitored with exercise stress testing to assess for QRS widening or new arrhythmias during exertion. If this does not occur, flecainide can be safely used even in patientswhoexerciseoften.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Seizure disorder is not a contraindication to flecainide. Although the drug can cause mild CNs side effects like dizziness or visual disturbances, it is not known to lower the seizure threshold or interact with common antiepileptic medications.

questions.question: Researchers are studying the electrophysiologic effects of antiarrhythmic drugs on cardiac sodium channels. In their experiments, they expose isolated ventricular myocytes to a train of rapid depolarizing pulses that repeatedly open sodium channels. They then measure how much drug is bound to sodium channels during the stimulation period. Which of the following drugs is most likely to show the greatest sodium channel binding with stimulation?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): Propafenone is a class IC antiarrhythmic that exhibits strong use-dependence, meaning it binds more avidly to open or inactivated sodium channels during periods of frequent depolarization, such as during tachycardia. This makes it highly effective at slowing conduction in rapidly firing tissues, such as cardiac myocytes in the setting of atrial fibrillation or AV reentrant tachycardias. The strong binding affinity and slow dissociation from sodium channels explain its enhanced effect at higher stimulation frequencies. This sameuse-dependentbehavioralsoincreases theriskof toxicityat highheartrates,as excessive sodium channel blockade can lead to QRs widening and proarrhythmic effects, particularly in patients with structural heart disease. Of the class I antiarrhythmic drugs, class IC agents (flecainide, propafenone) demonstrate the strongest use dependence.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Disopyramide is a class IA antiarrhythmic with intermediate sodium channel binding and moderate use-dependence. It also blocks potassium channels, prolonging the action potential duration. Its use-dependence is weaker than that of class IC drugs like propafenone.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Lidocaine is a class IB antiarrhythmic that has weak use-dependence and preferentially binds sodium channels in ischemic or depolarized tissue. It dissociates rapidly from sodium channels and is more effective at lower heart rates or in damaged myocardium, not during high-frequency stimulation in healthy tissue.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Mexiletine is the oral analog of lidocaine and, as a class IB antiarrhythmic, shares its weak use-dependence and rapid unbinding from sodium channels. Like lidocaine, it is more effective in ischemic tissue than in rapidly firing normal myocardium.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Procainamide is a class IA antiarrhythmic that exhibits moderate sodium channel blockade and some use-dependence, but not to the extent of class IC drugs. It also prolongs the action potential by blocking potassium channels. Its sodium channel binding increases slightly with frequency, but not asstronglyaswithpropafenone. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 55-year-old man comes to the clinic due to fatigue, joint pain, and low-grade fever that began several weeks ago. It is associated with the presence of positive ANA and anti-histone antibodies, with negative anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith antibodies, distinguishing it from idiopathic systemic lupuserythematosus. questions.question: A 68-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after collapsing at home. He reports feeling lightheaded and briefly losing consciousness while walking to the kitchen. Answer D (correct answer): Lidocaine is a class Ib antiarrhythmic that blocks cardiac sodium channels. Lidocaine preferentially binds ischemic cardiac tissue. In the setting of ischemia, the resting membrane potential in cardiac cells rises from the usual value of -85mEv to higher values closer to -60mEv. In this more depolarized state, lidocaine binds more readily and exerts more effect.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Lidocaine also binds more readily when sodium channels are in use and out of the resting state. Thus, it binds more at fast heart rates when sodium channels are more active. It binds less in the setting of bradycardia.

questions.question: A 31-year-old G1p0 woman is brought to the emergency department at 32-weeks' gestation due to a severe occipital headache. Answer E (correct answer): This pregnant patient with severe hypertension, proteinuria, elevated creatinine and seizure has eclampsia. Answer B (correct answer): This newborn has asymmetric septal hypertrophy, a finding commonly seen in infants of mothers with poorly controlled diabetes or gestational hyperglycemia. This form of cardiomyopathy typically resolves spontaneously over time as insulin levels normalize after birth.

questions.question: A 31-year-old woman presents to the office for evaluation of intermittent chest pain for 2 months. She reports daily episodes exertion and slowly resolve on their own. She smokes 1 pack of cigarettes daily. Vital signs include a temperature of 97°F, heart rate of 72/min, respiratory rate of 16/min, blood pressure of 119/77 mmHg, and pulse oximetry of 98% on room air. angiography is performed. The two images below show sequential views of the left anterior descending artery obtained 30 seconds apart. No coronary intervention is performed. A medication with which of the following mechanisms is most appropriate for treatment of this patient's condition?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This patient has vasospastic angina, as suggested by her young age, intermittent chest pain in the mornings, normal resting ECG, and normal serum troponin levels. Her coronary angiography n s ( ) r ss (outlined by blue dots). This finding is due to vasoconstriction, which temporarily blocks the flow of contrast dye down the coronary artery. Vasospastic angina is characterized by transient coronary artery vasospasm causing narrowing of the coronary arteries and resulting in ischemia. Calcium channel blockers like nifedipine cause coronary artery vasodilation, alleviating coronary artery vasospasms and reducing the frequency of anginal episodes. Similarly, nitrates also induce coronary artery vasodilation. Both are used to treat vasospastic angina.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Aspirin is an antiplatelet drug that irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase (COX) enzymes like COX-1 and COX-2. This decreases platelet activation. Aspirin is used to treat acute coronary syndromes secondary to atherosclerotic plaque rupture and thrombus. This patient's young age, normal resting ECG and troponin values, and coronary artery vasospasm during angiography are consistent with vasospastic angina, which is not mediated by thrombus formation. Therefore, aspirin would not be effective in treating this patient'sunderlyingdisease.

Answer C (incorrect answer): This patient's normal ECG, normal serum troponin, and reversible coronary artery spasm observed during coronary angiography are consistent with vasospastic angina. Non-selective beta blockers like propranolol block both beta 1 and beta 2 receptors, leading to unopposed alpha receptor angina.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Fibrinolytics like alteplase activate plasmin and promote clot degradation. They rupture, leading to subsequent thrombus formation and total coronary artery occlusion. This patient's normal ECG, normal troponin values, and transient coronary artery narrowing during angiography are more suggestive of vasospastic angina than STEMI. Vasospastic angina is not caused by a coronary artery thrombus and is not treated with fibrinolytics.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Heparin is an anticoagulant that inhibits thrombin and other clotting factors and prevents clot propagation. It is used to treat ACs. This patient's normal EcG, normal serum troponin, and transient coronary artery vasospasm seen during angiography are indicative of vasospastic angina rather than ACs. Since vasospastic angina is not precipitated by a thrombus, anticoagulation with heparin is not indicated. Mc Graw

questions.question: The pain is dull, located in the center of his chest, and consistently occurs while climbing stairs or walking briskly. He has no pain at rest. Vital signs include a temperature of 98°F, heart rate of 42/min, respiratory rate of 14/min, blood pressure of 118/84 mmHg, and pulse oximetry of 98% on room air. ejection fraction of 37%. The patient undergoes treadmill exercise testing. At a heart rate of 135/min, ECG demonstrates transient ST-segment depressions in leads V3-V5. He also develops chest pain on the treadmill that resolves when he stops exercising. Which of the following is a contraindication to nitrate therapy in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This patient has stable angina, evidenced by exertional chest pain that resolves with rest and exercise-induced ST-segment depressions on ECG. Stable angina is caused by atherosclerotic plaque occluding > 75% of the coronary artery lumen, leading to a mismatch of coronary blood flow and demand during exertion. Nitrates are used in stable angina to reduce myocardial oxygen demand, primarily by causing venous dilation and subsequently reducing cardiac preload and ventricular wall stress. Nitrates also cause arterial vasodilation and a reduction in blood pressure. Phosphodiesterase 5 (PDE5) inhibitors like sildenafil are used to treat erectile dysfunction and enhance the effect of nitric oxide. When combined with nitrates, PDE5 inhibitors can lead to severe hypotension. As a result, sildenafil use is a contraindication to nitrate therapy.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Nitrates reduce cardiac preload and afterload, which can lead to reduced blood pressure. Baseline hypotension is therefore a contraindication to nitrate therapy. This patient's baseline blood pressure of 118/84 mmHg is normal.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as diltiazem are negative inotropes that reduce cardiac contractility and heart rate. They are contraindicated in patients with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (< 40%) due to the risk of worsening heart failure. This patient's reduced ejection fraction of 37% is not a contraindication to nitrate therapy.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Beta blockers (e.g., metoprolol) inhibit beta receptors, reducing heart rate and cardiac contractility. They are contraindicated in patients with low resting heart rates due to the risk of hypotension and severe bradycardia. This patient's low heart rate of 42/min is not a contraindication to nitrate therapy.

Answer E (incorrect answer): This patient has transient ST-segment depressions on ECG during exercise, which are consistent with stable angina. These ECG findings are not a contraindication to nitrate therapy. Hmi

questions.question: An 80-year-old man develops exertional chest pain. He is unable to walk on a treadmill due to osteoarthritis of the hip and knee. He is referred for a chemical nuclear stress test. Regadenoson is administered and radiotracer is injected. Nuclear images demonstrate decreased blood flow to the anterior wall of the left ventricle after regadenoson infusion. A subsequent coronary angiogram demonstrates an 80% narrowing of the left anterior descending artery with no significant flow obstruction in other coronary vessels. Which of the following effects of regadenoson explains the nuclear stress test findings?

options.E: Increased right coronary artery blood flow

questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): In nuclear chemical stress testing, coronary vasodilators (regadenoson dipyridamole, adenosine) are administered to induce coronary steal for the diagnosis of coronary artery disease. The patient described in the question has a stress test showing anterior wall ischemia from a left anterior descending (LAD) artery stenosis. At rest, this patient's LAD arterioles (located beyond the atherosclerotic narrowing) are maximally dilated to maintain normal blood flow through the LAD despite the narrowed vessel (i.e. the LAD has a narrowing but the small arterioles beyond the narrowing are dilated to increase flow). When the vasodilator regadenoson is administered, LAD arterioles are unable to respond since they are already maximally dilated. Arterioles in the other vessels, however, can vasodilate in response to the drug. Therefore, right coronary artery (RCA) and left circumflex (LCX) blood flow will increase significantly. This will "steal" blood from the diseased LAD artery. Nuclear tracers indicate areas of high and low blood flow. In the case described, they demonstrate a fall in perfusion to the anterior wall as a result of coronary steal in the settingof LADstenosis.

Answer A (incorrect answer): This patient's stress test indicates a narrowing of the LAD artery. However, that is not the effect of regadenoson that explains the stress test findings.

Answers B and c (incorrect answers): Increased contractility and heart rate occur when exercise stress testing is performed. These effects also occur when dobutamine (beta 1 agonist) is used as a chemical stress test agent. Dobutamine is much more cumbersome to administer than vasodilators like Regadenoson. For this reason, it is less commonly used in chemical stress tests.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Increased afterload does not occur with regadenoson infusion. The drug is a vasodilator and often produces a modest fall in blood pressure.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man with a history of hypertension and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation is started on diltiazem to control his performed showing sinus rhythm. Answer C (correct answer): This man is receiving diltiazem, a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that inhibits L-type calcium channels, particularly affecting the AV node. By slowing conduction through the AV node, diltiazem prolongs the PR interval on the ECG. This effect is dose-dependent and is a known pharmacodynamic property of the drug. Prolongation of the PR interval reflects delayed conduction from the atria to the ventricles, which is the intended therapeutic effect in controlling ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation. Studies have demonstrated that diltiazem administrationleads toa measurableincrease inPR intervalduration.If Av conduction becomes markedly delayed, various forms of Av block and associated bradycardia may occur.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Premature ventricular complexes (PvCs) are early depolarizations originating in conduction through the atrioventricular (AV) node.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Prolongation of the QRs interval indicates delayed intraventricular conduction, often due to bundle branch blocks or ventricular conduction system disease. Diltiazem primarily affects the AV node and does not significantly impact intraventricular conduction; therefore, it does not typically cause QRS prolongation.

Answer E (incorrect answer):Prolongation of the QT interval is associated with delayed ventricular repolarization and can predispose to torsades de pointes. Diltiazem does not significantly affect ventricular repolarization and is not commonly associated with QT interval prolongation.

questions.question: An autopsy is performed on a patient who died from metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma complicated by streptococcal pneumonia and acute renal failure. On the mitral valve, several one-centimeter tan masses are attached to both sides of the leaflets. Analysis shows the masses contain only fibrin and platelets. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the mitral valve findings?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): Patients with advanced malignancy like pancreatic cancer are at risk for nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE), also called marantic endocarditis or Libman Sacks endocarditis). In NBTE, vegetations develop on cardiac valves consisting mostly of platelets and fibrin. As the name implies, these do not contain bacteria and are not infectious. The most common locations for NBTE are the mitral and aortic valves. In contrast to bacterial vegetations which usually form on one side of heart valves, the vegetations of NBTE may form on both sides of the valve. Other than malignancy, patients with systemic lupus erythematosusarealsoatriskforNBTE. NBTE is often asymptomatic and identified at autopsy. when symptoms occur from NBTE, they are most often due to embolism. Because the vegetations lack bacteria and inflammatory cells, they adhere poorly to heart valves. NBTE easily dislodges leading to embolicphenomena. Many sites ofembolization have been reported including the CNs, splenic infarction and ischemic limbs.

Answers A, B, C, D (incorrect answers): The vegetations of NBTE are non-infectious, and not caused by bacteria likeStaphylococcus Aureus,Viridans Streptococcus, Streptococcus Bovis, or Coxiella Burnetii.

questions.question: A 62-year-old female with a history of mitral valve prolapse develops fevers and joint pains over a 3 week period. One month ago she had a tooth extraction. Subacute endocarditis has a slower onset (weeks) and is less severe than acute endocarditis which causes a rapid (days), intense illness. More often, affected heart valves are already damaged in some way such as the prolapse in this patient. Viridans strep are normal mouth flora. Dental procedures are a classic predisposing condition to endocarditis from these bacteria. Boards&Bevond In contrast, acute bacterial endocarditis occurs rapidly over days and is associated with more severe symptoms endocarditis and is capable of infecting normal heart valves. In clinical practice, the presentation of endocarditis is not reliable for the determination of the microbial cause. Patientsaretreatedbroadlywithantibiotics until bloodculture results areavailable.However, thedistinction between subacute and acute endocarditis is often tested on exams. Also, you should be aware that staph aureus is a highly virulent bug that may cause severe illness.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Staphylococcus aureus causes acute not subacute bacterial endocarditis. It is often seen on the tricuspid valve of intravenous drug users.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Pseudomonas aeruginosa also causes acute illness and is a very uncommon cause of endocarditis.

questions.question: A 76-year-old man with chronic systolic heart failure and atrial fibrillation is hospitalized for worsening dyspnea. His medications include furosemide, carvedilol, lisinopril, and digoxin. On hospital day 2, his ventricular response slows and his symptoms begin to improve. A cardiology fellow explains that digoxin enhances cardiac contractility by altering ion transport and calcium handling within ventricular myocytes. Which of the following best explains digoxin's inotropic effect? Inhibition of the sodium-potassium ATPase, leading to increased calcium (A) 12.97% extrusion via the sodium-calcium exchanger

options.B: ATPase, reducing the sodium gradient and decreasing calcium efflux
options.C: ATPase, increasing intracellular calcium Stimulation of the sodium-potassium via sodium accumulation
options.D: ATPase, directly increasing calcium Inhibition of the sodium-potassium influx through L-type calcium channels
options.E: Inhibition of the sodium-potassium ATPase, leading to activation of ryanodine receptors on the sarcoplasmic reticulum

questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): Digoxin inhibits the Na+/K+ ATPase, increasing intracellular sodium. This reduces the gradient driving the sodium-calcium exchanger, which normally brings sodium in and extrudes calcium. With a diminished sodium gradient, less calcium is removed from the cell, causing intracellular calcium to rise. This extra calcium is stored in the sarcoplasmic reticulum and released with each action potential, leading to enhanced contractility (positive inotropy).

Answer A (incorrect answer): Inhibiting the sodium-potassium ATPase reduces, not increases, calcium extrusion. If calcium extrusionwere increased,contractilitywould decrease.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Digoxin inhibits, not stimulates, the Na+/K+ ATPase. Additionally, stimulation of the ATPase would increase the sodium gradient, promoting calcium removal-not retention-and reduce contractility.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Digoxin does not directly increase calcium influx through L-type calcium channels. Its effects on calcium handling are mediated indirectly through sodium accumulation and reduced calcium extrusion via the sodium-calcium exchanger.

Answer E (incorrectanswer):Ryanodine receptors mediate calciumrelease fromthesarcoplasmic reticulum,but digoxin does not directly activate them. Their increased activity is a secondary effect of elevated sarcoplasmic calcium content resulting from altered exchanger dynamics.

Answer A (correct answer): The patient has paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PsVT), likely due to AV nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT). The drug used to treat this arrhythmia was adenosine, which has a very short half-life and acts on A1 adenosine receptors in the AV node. It activates potassium channels, leading to potassium efflux and hyperpolarization of AV nodal cells. It also inhibits calcium influx, thereby suppressing AV nodal conduction. This transient AV nodal block is often sufficient to terminate reentrant tachycardias dependent on the AV node.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Atropine is a muscarinic antagonist that increases heart rate by inhibiting parasympathetic tone. It is used to treat bradycardia, not tachycardia, and does not act by modulating potassium or calcium channels.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Digoxin increases vagal tone and slows AV nodal conduction, which can be helpful in rate control for atrial fibrillation. It does not acutely terminate PsVT and does not directly activate potassium channels or block calcium influx in the same manner as adenosine.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Magnesium is typically used for arrhythmias like torsades de pointes or for treating digoxin-induced arrhythmias. It does not act by activating potassium channels or blocking calcium influx in nodal tissue.

Answer A (correct answer): The administration of intravenous magnesium sulfate is the treatment of choice for Torsade de Pointes, a form of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia often associated with a prolonged QT patients to developing Torsade de Pointes. questions.question: bpm. Examination of the jugular venous pulsation shows cannon a waves. Which of the following is required to produce this clinical finding?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): Cannon a waves are caused by contraction of the right atrium when the tricuspid valve is closed. Normally, atrial contraction occurs when the tricuspid valve is open, but if it occurs with the valve closed a cannon a wave will occur. When this happens, blood cannot pass through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. As a result, atrial contraction forces blood backwards into the jugular vein of the neck producing a cannon a wave which can be easily seen on physical exam as shown in this video. Cannon a waves occur in the setting of heart block and AV dissociation which can cause the tricuspid valve to close prior to atrial contraction. Normally, right atrial contraction occurs when the tricuspid valve is open, before right ventricular contraction. This timing is coordinated by the electrical conduction system in the heart. If electrical conduction through the AV node fails, sinus impulses cannot reach the ventricle to cause contraction. A "lower pacemaker" will take over the role of ventricular depolarization meaning some structure below the AV node (HIS bundle, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers) will assume the role of pacemaker for the ventricles. In this situation, the atria and ventricles are depolarized by separate pacemakers. If the right ventricle contracts and closes the tricuspid valve at the same time the right atrium contracts, a cannon a wave will be generated as atrial contraction pushes blood backward into the jugular vein instead of forward into the right ventricle.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Cannon a waves require ventricular contraction (not relaxation) simultaneous with atrialcontraction.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Cannon a waves occur when the right atrium contracts, not during right atrial relaxation. Mc Graw

PvCs are a common, benign finding in patients with healthy hearts, especially during times of increased sympathetic stimulation of the heart (illness, exercise). questions.question: A 20-month-old girl presents for routine evaluation. On eye examination, there is a white reflection from the left retina. retinoblastoma. Two other children in the mother's family died from retinoblastoma. Which of the following findings is expected in cells from the tumor?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This child has an inherited form of retinoblastoma, a rare childhood tumor accounting for 13% of tumors in children under 1 year of age. The classic presentation is a child less than 3 years of age with leukocoria (loss of the red reflex). Normally, a reddish-orange reflection occurs when light is shone into the back of the eye. An abnormal white reflection is called leukocoria. This can be seen in retinoblastoma, as well as other rare childhood disorders including cataracts and vitreous hemorrhage. Retinoblastomas are caused by mutations in the retinoblastoma (Rb) gene. This gene encodes the retinoblastoma protein, a tumor-suppressor protein that normally limits cell growth. Decreased synthesis or function of the retinoblastoma protein leads to uncontrolled cell growth and malignancy. Because this girl has a family history of retinoblastoma, she inherited one abnormal (mutated) copy of the Rb gene and one normal copy. Thus at birth, her retinal cells were heterozygous_for the Rb gene with one mutated and one normal copy. If a cell loses the normal copy of the Rb gene, that cell becomes homozygous for the Rb gene mutation. With only mutated Rb genes, cancer will develop. This process of oncogenesis is called loss of genes. A heterozygous cell with one normal copy of a tumor-suppressor gene will not develop cancer. If that normal copy is lost (loss of heterozygosity), the cell will have absence of tumor-suppressor activity, leading to uncontrolledcell growth. There are many mechanisms by which a heterozygous cell can lose one copy of a gene, leading to loss of cellular acquisition of the "second hit" in Knudsen's two-hit hypothesis of cancer arising from tumor-suppressor gene inactivation. Of note, loss of heterozygosity is a "non-mutational event", meaning it leads to cancer through loss of genetic material, not through mutation.

Answers A and B (incorrect answers): Oncogenes are genes with products that cause uncontrolled growth. mutation occurs. while oncogenes and proto-oncogenes cause some cancers, retinoblastoma is caused by a mutation in the Rb gene, a tumor-suppressor gene.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Retinoblastoma is caused by inactivation of the Rb tumor-suppressor gene.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Ionizing radiation is radiation with enough energy to displace electrons. Major sources of ionizing radiation include gamma rays and X-rays. In contrast, Uv light, infrared, microwaves, and radiation is not the cause of retinoblastomas.

Answer B (incorrect answer): The retinoblastoma protein is a tumor-suppressor protein that prevents cell growth. Abnormal activity of this protein is associated with some cancers, including retinoblastoma. Mutations involving the retinoblastoma gene are not common in anaplastic thyroid carcinomas. s associated with anaplastic thyroid carcinoma.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman is referred for colposcopy after an abnormal PAP smear. Application of acetic acid to the cervix identifies a region of acetowhite epithelium with sharp borders. Biopsy identifies evidence of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia. Pathologic inhibition of which of the following directly contributed to this finding?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This woman has cervical dysplasia, an abnormal growth of cervical epithelial cells that may lead to cervical cancer. Infection with human papilloma virus (Hpv), a sexually-transmitted resolves; in others, chronic infection occurs, which can lead to cervical dysplasia and cancer. HPV subtypes 16 and 18 cause approximately 70% of cervical cancers. Subtypes 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58 cause an additional 20%. HPV vaccines are available that protect against many of these subtypes. Expression of the HpV oncogene E6 leads to synthesis of the E6 protein. This protein binds the p53 protein, the cellular protein ubiquitin. This targets them for degradation in proteasomes. Normally, p53 prevents cell growth. When degraded by the action of E6, unchecked cell growth occurs (sometimes referred to as an "anti- apoptotic" effect). This can lead to cervical dysplasia and cancer. the cell cycle to grow (hence the name cyclin for their cyclical up-and-down levels). Answer E (incorrect answer): The Rb protein binds the E2F transcription factor to limit cell growth. The E7 protein of HPV causes the Rb protein to release E2F. This leads to increased, not inhibited, E2F activity.

questions.question: A 24-year-old man presents to establish care with a new primary care physician. He has a family history of Li-Fraumeni syndrome. He had a rhabdomyosarcoma treated surgically at age 11. His mother has breast cancer. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of cancer in this man and his family?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): The Li-Fraumeni syndrome is an inherited, autosomal dominant disorder of multiple malignancies. It is sometimes called the Sarcoma, Breast, Leukemia, and Adrenal gland (SBLA) cancer syndrome. The cause of Li-Fraumeni is a mutation in the p53 tumor-suppressor gene. The p53 protein blocks progression through the cell cycle in the setting of damaged DNA. This allows time for either DNA repair or leading to malignancy. The ultimate result is a failure of apoptosis that allows malignant cells to divide indefinitely. Special note: Many malignancies are associated with a failure of apoptosis leading to uncontrolled cell growth. oncogene. Tumor-suppressor genes lead to malignancy when inactive, in contrast to oncogenes which must be activatedtocausecancer.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Defective DNA repair enzymes can lead to cancer in a number of disorders, including xeroderma pigmentosa, Lynch syndrome, and ataxia telangiectasia. The p53 protein is a tumor- suppressor protein, not a DNA repair protein. Although failure of the p53 gene in Li-Fraumeni allows cells to grow despite DNA damage, there is no defect in the function of DNA repair enzymes. associatedwithdefectivedouble-strandedDNA repair. to growth arrest, not malignancy. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 60-year-old man is evaluated for urinary frequency. He urinates approximately ten times per day and wakes several times per night to urinate. He has difficulty starting a urinary stream, and flow during urination is slow. Digital rectal exam identifies an enlarged, firm, and nontender prostate. An increase in which of the following has contributed to this man's condition?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This man has benign prostatic hyperplasia, a common condition among men over age 50. When glandular prostate cells grow in number (hyperplasia), the prostate gland enlarges. This can impede passage of urine. Urinary frequency (needing to urinate many times) and nocturia (waking to urinate) may occur due to incomplete bladder emptying. Difficulty initiating urination (hesitancy) and slow urinary flow may alsodevelop. Tissues with hyperplasia, like this man's prostate, have an increase in the frequency of cell division such that cell growth.
