Examples of disorders caused by type III hypersensitivity reactions include systemic lupus erythematosus, serum sickness, and poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. EM is due to a cell-mediated type IV hypersensitivity reaction. Mc

questions.question: A 42-year-old woman presents for evaluation of a pigmented lesion on her upper back. She first noticed the lesion several months ago while working as a lifeguard during the summer. Since that time, the lesion has increased in size and changed in irregular borders. It is not painful or pruritic. Physical examination shows a 1.2-cm asymmetric pigmented lesion with irregular borders and multiple shades of brown. A biopsy confirms melanoma. Which of the following is most predictive of risk of metastasis for this type of lesion?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This patient is presenting with an evolving pigmented lesion with irregular borders and variable coloring concerning for melanoma. In melanoma, the most predictive factor for metastasis is depth of invasion, also known as Breslow thickness. Melanomas initially grow along the epidermis in a radial growth phase, but eventually begin to invade vertically into the dermis. The deeper the tumor penetrates into the dermis, the greater the likelihood of lymphatic or hematogenous spread.

questions.question: A 72-year-old man presents to his dermatologist with a new lesion on his left cheek. He reports that it has slowly enlarged over the past several months. His brother was recently diagnosed with melanoma, which prompted him to seek evaluation. Physical examination reveals a translucent, pearly papule with rolled borders and visible surface blood vessels. A biopsy is performed and identifies the findings shown below: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This man has basal cell carcinoma, a common skin cancer arising from basal keratinocytes of the epidermis. Histology shows nests of basaloid cells in the dermis with peripheral palisading and retraction artifact between the tumor nests and surrounding stroma. Clinically, these lesions appear as pearly papules or nodules with rolled borders and surface telangiectasias. Basal cell carcinoma is locally invasive but rarely metastasizes and is treated with surgical excision.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Actinic keratosis is a premalignant lesion caused by chronic sun exposure and is characterized by dysplastic keratinocytes confined to the epidermis. Histology shows hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis, and atypical cells limited to the lower portions of the epidermis. It does not form nests of basaloid cells extending into the dermis.

Answer C (incorrect answer):Keratoacanthoma is a rapidly growing squamous neoplasm that presents as a dome-shaped nodule with a central keratin-filled crater. Histology shows well-differentiated squamous epithelium with central keratinization. It does not demonstrate basaloid nests with peripheral palisading.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Melanoma is a malignant tumor of melanocytes and often shows atypical melanocytes proliferating at the dermal-epidermal junction with invasion into the dermis. Cells may contain melanin pigment and demonstrate significant cytologic atypia. The basaloid cell nests described here are not consistent with melanoma.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Squamous cell carcinoma arises from keratinocytes and demonstrates invasive nests of atypical squamous cells with keratin pearl formation on histology. It lacks the basaloid appearance and peripheral palisading seen in basal cell carcinoma. Mc MeS

Answer D (correct answer): This woman has melanoma and is receiving adjuvant immunotherapy following complete surgical resection. Pembrolizumab is a monoclonal antibody that inhibits programmed cell death protein 1, also known as PD-1, on T lymphocytes. PD-1 is an inhibitory receptor that downregulates T-cell Mc activation when engaged by its ligand on tumor cells. Answer C (incorrect answer): Inhibition of mutant EGFR is most commonly used in certain non-small cell lung cancers that harbor activating EGFR mutations. Answer E (incorrect answer): Parakeratosis, retained nuclei in the stratum corneum, is not seen in BcC. Parakeratosis is often associated with hyperkeratosis in other skin disorders like psoriasis and actinic keratosis. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the clinic for evaluation of a new light-colored patch on his back. His parents noticed the lesion several days ago. He has a history of seizures since infancy and underwent surgical resection of a cardiac rhabdomyoma shortly after birth. Physical examination reveals multiple erythematous papules over the nose and cheeks and a hypopigmented macule on the back as shown below: Which of the following embryologic germ layers gives rise to the primary tissues affected in this patient's condition?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This child has clinical features of tuberous sclerosis including seizures, facial angiofibromas, hypopigmented ash leaf macules, and a history of cardiac rhabdomyoma. Tuberous sclerosis is a organs. Neurocutaneous syndromes primarily affect tissues derived from the ectoderm, including the central nervous system and epidermis. Because the most prominent manifestations of this disorder involve the brain and skin, both of which arise from ectoderm, the embryologic origin is ectoderm.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Embryogenic stem cells form the inner cell mass of the blastocyst and are differentiation into ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm, so this is not the best answer. primarily involve the skin and nervous system rather than endoderm-derived structures.

Answer D (incorrect answer): The mesoderm gives rise to connective tissue, muscle, bone, blood vessels, and portions of the genitourinary system. Although cardiac rhabdomyomas involve mesoderm-derived cardiac muscle, the defining features of this neurocutaneous disorder primarily involve ectoderm-derived tissues.

Answer E (incorrect answer): The trophectoderm forms the outer layer of the blastocyst and contributes to the placenta. It is present before gastrulation and does not represent one of the three primary germ layers responsible for the tissues affected in this condition.

questions.question: A 28-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after losing his balance while walking. A friend prevented him from falling and he did not sustain head trauma. Over the past several months, he has experienced progressively worsening imbalance and intermittent headaches. He has no personal medical history. His father has a hereditary cancer syndrome and underwent nephrectomy for a renal tumor last year. Brain MRI reveals a well-circumscribed mass in the cerebellum. The tumor is surgically resected. Genetic testing demonstrates a mutation in the VHL tumor suppressor gene. Which of the following tumors is most likely to be identified on histopathology?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This man has clinical features suggestive of von Hippel Lindau (VHL) disease, given his family history of renal cell carcinoma and the presence of a cerebellar tumor with a confirmed VHL mutation. VHL can present in young adulthood (20s-30s) when tumors lead to clinical features such as in this case. Von Mc Hippel Lindau disease is an autosomal dominant cancer syndrome caused by loss of function of the VHL tumor individuals are predisposed to renal cell carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, pancreatic cysts, and hemangioblastomas. Hemangioblastomas are highly vascular, well-circumscribed tumors that most commonly arise in the cerebellum, spinal cord, or retina and are the most likely pathology in this patient.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Astrocytomas arise from astrocytes and may occur in various regions of the central nervous system. Certain subtypes are associated with Tuberous sclerosis complex, which presents with seizures, facial angiofibromas, hypopigmented macules, and renal angiomyolipomas. Astrocytomas are not the tumor most strongly associated with VHL mutations.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Ependymomas arise from ependymal cells lining the ventricles and central canal of with VHL mutations.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Glioblastoma is a high-grade astrocytic tumor that usually arises in the cerebral hemispheres of older adults. It is characterized by necrosis and microvascular proliferation and is not a hallmark tumorofVHL-associateddisease.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Optic gliomas are low-grade astrocytic tumors associated with Neurofibromatosis type 1. Patients with that condition often have café au lait macules, axillary freckling, Lisch nodules, and cutaneous neurofibromas. Optic gliomas are not associated with VHL mutations.

questions.question: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department after her parents witnessed a seizure. She was in her usual state of minutes. She has no history of seizures. Since birth, she has had a dark red discoloration over the right side of her face involving the forehead and upper eyelid. which of the following is most likely to be seen on brain imaging to explain this patient's seizure?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This child has clinical features of Sturge Weber syndrome, including a facial port wine stain in the trigeminal nerve distribution and new onset focal seizures. Sturge Weber syndrome is caused by a somatic activating mutation in the GNAQ gene leading to abnormal vascular development. Affected patients develop leptomeningeal angiomas over the cerebral cortex, usually ipsilateral to the facial port wine stain. often occur in early childhood and may involve the contralateral side of the body.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Acoustic neuroma, also known as vestibular schwannoma, is associated with balance difficulties. It is not associated with facial port wine stains or early childhood seizures.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Astrocytomas, including subependymal giant cell astrocytomas, are commonly seen in Tuberous sclerosis complex. That disorder presents with seizures, intellectual disability, facial angiofibromas, hypopigmented ash leaf spots, and shagreen patches rather than a facial port wine stain.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Hemangioblastomas are vascular tumors associated with von Hippel Lindau disease. Patients may develop cerebellar or spinal cord tumors along with renal cell carcinoma, pancreatic cysts, and pheochromocytoma. A facial capillary malformation and early onset focal seizures are not characteristic of this condition.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Optic gliomas are associated with Neurofibromatosis type 1 and may present with vision changes in children who also have café au lait macules, axillary freckling, and Lisch nodules. They are not linked to facial port wine stains or leptomeningeal vascular malformations.

questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This adolescent has clinical features of tuberous sclerosis including seizures, formation of hamartomas in multiple organs. Renal angiomyolipomas are common in these patients and are composed of abnormal blood vessels, smooth muscle, and adipose tissue. These lesions are prone to spontaneous hemorrhage due to their dysmorphic vasculature, which explains this patient's acute flank pain and imaging findings of a hemorrhagic renal mass.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Clear-cell renal carcinoma is the most common subtype of renal cell carcinoma in adults and is associated with mutations in the VHL gene. Although renal cell carcinoma can occur in patients with tuberous sclerosis, it is less common than angiomyolipoma and usually presents later in adulthood rather thanadolescence.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Metastases to the kidney are uncommon compared with primary renal tumors. In a patient with stigmata of tuberous sclerosis and a hemorrhagic renal mass, a primary lesion related to the underlying genetic disorder is much more likely than metastatic disease.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Papillary renal cell carcinoma is another subtype of renal cell carcinoma that usually presents in older adults and is associated with MET proto-oncogene alterations. It is not strongly associated with tuberous sclerosis and would be less likely in a teenager with characteristic cutaneous findings.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Simple renal cysts are common and usually contain clear fluid. Although cysts can rarely hemorrhage, they do not account for a heterogeneous renal mass in a patient with tuberous sclerosis. Angiomyolipoma is the more likely diagnosis given this clinical context. Mc

questions.question: A 4-year-old girl is brought to the pediatrician due to progressively increasing dark spots on her skin. Her parents first noticed several light brown patches on her abdomen during infancy, but additional lesions have recently appeared on her demarcated, light brown macules greater than 1.5 cm in diameter on the trunk and extremities. There is freckling in the axillary and inguinal regions. Ophthalmologic examination reveals multiple pigmented iris hamartomas. Which of the following best describes the pattern of inheritance of this patient's condition?

options.C: Autosomal dominant with complete penetrance and variable expressivity

questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This child has clinical features of Neurofibromatosis type 1, including multiple café au lait macules, axillary and inguinal freckling, and Lisch nodules of the iris, along with a family history in her father. Neurofibromatosis type 1 is caused by a mutation in the NF1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 17, which encodes neurofibromin, a negative regulator of the RAS signaling pathway. The disorder is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with complete penetrance, meaning individuals who inherit the mutation will express the disease phenotype. However, there is variable expressivity, so affected individuals can have different degrees of clinical severity. Patients are at increased risk for learning disabilities, cutaneous neurofibromas, skeletal abnormalities, optic pathway gliomas, and hypertension due to renal artery stenosis or pheochromocytoma.

Answers A, B, D, E (incorrect answers): Neurofibromatosis 1 is not inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, an X-linked pattern or with incomplete penetrance which would mean that not all who inherit the condition expressit.

questions.question: An 8-year-old girl is brought to the office for seizures. Since she was an infant, she has had frequent seizures despite taking antiepileptic medications. She had a cardiac rhabdomyoma that was diagnosed by prenatal ultrasound and removed surgically after she was born. On physical examination, she has six oval, hypopigmented macules on her trunk and arms. A picture of her face is shown below: She undergoes a brain MRI. Which of the following is the most likely tumor to be found on imaging?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This girl has tuberous sclerosis (Ts), a neurocutaneous disorder that causes tumors in many organ systems, including the brain, skin, eyes, heart, and kidneys. Brain tumors associated with Ts include subependymal giant cell astrocytomas, subependymal nodules, and cortical tubers. Subependymal tumors and nodules occur beneath the ependyma, which is the lining of the ventricles. Cortical tubers, which are benign growths (hamartomas) of the cortex, and cortical dysplasia are especially common in Ts, leading to seizures from an early age, as occurred in this girl. Subependymal tumors can sometimes obstruct the ventricles, causing hydrocephalus and increased intracranial pressure. In addition, intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorder are common in people with Ts. This girl has cutaneous findings associated with Ts: facial angiofibromas (skin bumps as shown in image) and oval hypopigmented (lighter-colored) macules called ash-leaf spots. Other cutaneous findings include periungual fibromas (fibromas near the nailbeds, called Koenen tumors) and Shagreen patches, which are thick connective This girl also had a cardiac rhabdomyoma, which occurs in 9o% of patients with Ts, usually before the age of 2. They can sometimes be diagnosed by prenatal ultrasound, as occurred in this girl. Renal angiomyolipoma is another common tumor in Ts, seen in 60 to 80% of patients.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Hemangioblastomas are seen in von Hippel-Lindau disease, not TS.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Leptomeningeal angiomas (capillary-venous malformations of the innermost meningeal membranes) are seen in Sturge-Weber syndrome, along with glaucoma and port-wine stains on the face.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Optic nerve gliomas are associated with neurofibromatosis type 1, not TS.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are tumors that arise from the myelin sheath of the eighth cranial nerve. These tumors are commonly seen in neurofibromatosis type 2, not Ts. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman presents with difficulty walking. She has had headaches and increasing difficulty keeping her balance when she walks for the past several months. Brain imaging reveals a cerebellar tumor that is surgically removed and found to preventing which cellular process?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This woman has von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease, a genetic disorder that causes pheochromocytomas, and renal-cell carcinomas. In VHL, a genetic mutation in the VHL gene promotes the transcription of hypoxia inducible genes, leading to excessive cellular growth (see figure above). In absence of a mutation, a normal pVHL (von Hippel-Lindau protein, the product of the VHL gene) binds to the protein HIF1a and adds ubiquitin, marking HIF1a for destruction by proteasomes. During periods of hypoxia, pVHL does not bind to HIF1a, promoting the transcription of hypoxia inducible genes. In VHL disease, a mutation in the VHL gene creates an abnormal pVHL that is unable add ubiquitin to HIF1a. Although VHL disease is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, it may not be expressed until later in life. One normal copy of the VHL gene is sufficient to prevent tumor formation, but 9o% of people with one mutated VHL gene will eventually also develop a sporadic mutation in their second normal VHL gene, causing tumor formation. This woman's VHL gene mutation caused her cerebellar hemangioblastoma, which led to her headaches and ataxia (difficulty coordinating voluntary movements like walking). In VHL disease, hemangioblastomas are most common in the cerebellum, spine, and retina.

Answers A, B, and C (incorrect answers): Acetylation, methylation, and phosphorylation are epigenetic phenomena, meaning modifications that alter DNA transcription without changing the DNA base sequence. These processes are not disrupted in VHL disease.

Answer E (incorrect answer): In females, one copy of the X chromosome is inactivated in each cell. X- inactivation is not disrupted in VHL disease. Mc

questions.question: A 22-year-old woman presents with hearing loss. Her hearing has become progressively worse over the past year. Her father was recently diagnosed with neurofibromatosis type 2. Her hearing loss is most likely caused by the excess proliferation of which type of cell?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This woman has neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2), a genetic disorder associated with bilateral vestibular schwannomas. Schwannomas are tumors comprised of Schwann cells, a type of glial cell. Glial cells are cells that surround and support neurons. In addition to Schwann cells, other types of glial cells include oligodendrocytes, astrocytes, and ependymal cells. NF2 is also associated with other tumors, including neurofibromas, which are peripheral nerve sheath tumors derived from precursors to Schwann cells, and meningiomas, which are derived from meningeal cells. Schwannomas can also occur in other parts of the nervous system, but the most common schwannoma in NF2 is thevestibularschwannoma. NF2 has an autosomal dominant inheritancepattern.Since this woman's father was diagnosed withNF2, shehas a 50% chance of inheriting the disease-causing gene. Her hearing loss at a young age suggests that she has inherited the NF2 gene and developed bilateral vestibular schwannomas. These tumors usually develop in adolescence or early adulthood before the age of 30. Vestibular schwannomas damage the eighth cranial nerve (the vestibulocochlear nerve) responsible for hearing and balance. Vestibular schwannomas can cause hearing loss, tinnitus (ringing in the ears), and ataxia. should not be confused with dendrites, which form the part of the neuron that receives signals from other neurons.NF2 does notcausetumors indendritic cells nor dendrites.

Answer B (incorrect answer): NF2 may cause cataracts due to dysplastic lens epithelial cells, but the tumors that most commonly cause hearing loss in NF2 are schwannomas.

Answer D (incorrect answer): NF2 is associated with meningiomas, which are tumors of meningeal cells, but the most common type of tumor in NF2 that causes hearing loss is a vestibular schwannoma.

Answer E (incorrect answer): NF2 does not cause proliferation of nerve cells (neurons). The vestibular schwannomas seen in NF2 surround the eighth cranial nerve, and are comprised of Schwann cells, not sensory nerve cells. Mc

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with fatigue, nausea, and generalized weakness. She reports unintentional weight loss and salt cravings. She also notes darkening of the skin in the creases of her palms and around her mouth. She has no significant past medical history and takes no medications. On physical examination, her skin shows diffuse hyperpigmentation. Laboratory testing reveals low serum sodium, elevated potassium, low cortisol, and elevated plasma ACTH. which of the following additional clinical findings is most likely present in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This woman has primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), which is caused by destruction or dysfunction of the adrenal cortex, most commonly due to autoimmune adrenalitis. This results in deficiency of both cortisol and aldosterone. Cortisol deficiency contributes to symptoms such as fatigue, potassium retention. Hyperpigmentation of the skin also occurs due to elevated adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) levels from the pituitary gland. pressure at baseline that becomes more pronounced in the upright position due to impaired vascular tone and from a seated position. Hypotension can be an early finding in Addison disease prior to the development of other clinical features.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Cortisol raises blood glucose through gluconeogenesis and inhibition of insulin-

Answer B (incorrect answer): Hyperlipidemia is not associated with adrenal insufficiency. In fact, chronic cortisol deficiency may lead to weight loss and reduced lipid stores.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Immunosuppression is characteristic of cortisol excess, such as in Cushing syndrome or during exogenous steroid therapy. In adrenal insufficiency, there is no suppression of immune function. Patients may even exhibit systemic signs of autoimmune disease (e.g., fever) associated with autoimmune adrenalitis.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Cortisol promotes insulin resistance by increasing hepatic glucose output and opposing insulin's action. In cortisol deficiency, insulin sensitivity is enhanced, not decreased.

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman is evaluated for progressive weight gain, facial rounding, proximal muscle weakness, and new-onset hypertension. Physical examination reveals central obesity, a dorsocervical fat pad, and purple abdominal striae. Laboratory testing shows elevated serum cortisol and elevated plasma ACTH. MRI reveals a pituitary mass consistent with Cushing disease. The ACTH in this woman directly increases activity of which of the following enzymes in the adrenal gland?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This patient has Cushing disease, a form of hypercortisolism caused by a pituitary adenoma that secretes excessive amounts of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). The elevated ACTH stimulates the adrenal cortex to produce excess cortisol, leading to characteristic clinical features such as central obesity, moon facies, dorsocervical fat pad ("buffalo hump"), thin skin, easy bruising, abdominal striae, and proximal muscle weakness. ACTH stimulates the zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortexby binding to ACTH receptors (alsoknown as melanocortin 2 receptors). This activation increases transcription of enzymes involved in steroidogenesis. The primary enzymatic target of ACTH is cholesterol desmolase (also called CYP11A1), which catalyzes the conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone, the rate-limiting step in steroid hormone synthesis. This upregulation leads to increased production of cortisol and, to a lesser extent, adrenal androgens. directly upregulated by ACTH binding. It is indirectly affected via increased expression of upstream enzymes and substrate availability.

Answer B (incorrect answer): 17-α hydroxylase (CYP17A1) is involved in the synthesis of both cortisol and androgens, but it is not a primary target of ACTH.

Answer C (incorrect answer): 21-a hydroxylase (CYP21A2) is required for the synthesis of cortisol and aldosterone, but it is not the enzyme directly activated by ACTH.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2) is located in the zona glomerulosa and is primarily regulated by the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), not by ACTH.

questions.question: A 46-year-old woman with a 10-year history of rheumatoid arthritis comes to the clinic for management of worsening joint but both were discontinued due to inadequate symptom control and side effects. The decision is made to initiate long-term therapy with daily oral prednisone to manage her disease activity. At a follow-up visit three months later, she reports significant improvement in pain and function. Which of the following adverse effects is most likely if she continues prednisone indefinitely?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This woman is being treated with prednisone, a synthetic glucocorticoid. Chronic glucocorticoid therapy is associated with multiple systemic side effects, including osteopenia and osteoporosis. Glucocorticoids reduce bone formation by inhibiting osteoblast activity and increase bone resorption by excretion, both of which contribute to bone mineral loss. Patients on long-term glucocorticoids are at increased treatment with calcium, vitamin D, or bisphosphonate drugs. contributes to skin thinning, poor wound healing, and easy bruising. They do not cause excess collagen deposition.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Fat malabsorption results from conditions that impair bile salt availability or pancreatic enzyme secretion, such as chronic pancreatitis or celiac disease. Glucocorticoids do not impair fat absorption.

Answer C (incorrect answer):Hyperkeratosis refers to thickening of the outer layer of the skin and is seen in conditions such as psoriasis or actinic keratosis. Glucocorticoids are more likely to cause skin thinning and atrophy, not thickening.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Glucocorticoids decrease insulin sensitivity and increase hepatic gluconeogenesis, resulting in hyperglycemia and an increased risk of steroid-induced diabetes. They do not enhance insulin action. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman with a history of systemic lupus erythematosus comes to the clinic due to worsening joint pain, fatigue, symptoms have significantly improved. which of the following effects of the drug contributed to the improvement in this patient's symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This woman has a flare of systemic lupus erythematosus, an autoimmune disease characterized by widespread inflammation driven by abnormal immune activation, especially involving T and B lymphocytes. Glucocorticoid drugs like prednisone are anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive agents. One of their mechanisms is inhibition of interleukin-2 (IL-2) production, a cytokine critical for T cell proliferation and survival. By decreasing IL-2 production, glucocorticoids impair T cell activation and reduce autoimmune-driven inflammation, leading to clinical improvement. allergic and inflammatory responses. They do not accentuate (increase) mast cell histamine release.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Glucocorticoids reduce lymphocyte access to inflamed tissues by impairing expression of adhesion molecules and chemokines. They do not increase lymphocyte trafficking to sites of inflammation. neutrophilapoptosis.

Answer B (correct answer): This woman has Cushing disease, which is a form of hypercortisolism caused by a pituitary adenoma that secretes excessive amounts of adrenocorticotropic hormone (AcTH).The elevated ACTH stimulates the adrenal cortex to produce excess cortisol, leading to characteristic clinical features such as and proximal muscle weakness. cortisol binds toitsintracellularreceptor located inthecytoplasm.The cortisol-receptor complexthen translocates to the nucleus, where it modulates gene transcription. Answer E (incorrect answer): Although the cortisol-receptor complex acts within the nucleus to regulate transcription, the initial receptor binding occurs in the cytoplasm, not the nucleus. Mc W

questions.question: A 67-year-old man is evaluated for left-sided flank pain, weight loss, and hematuria. Computerized tomography scan of the kidney and adrenal gland is planned. During resection, the surgeon identifies and dissects the left adrenal vein as it leaves the inferior portion of the adrenal gland. To resect the adrenal gland, the surgeon must sever the connection of this vein to which of the following?

Answer D (correct answer): This man has renal cell carcinoma, the most common kidney malignancy, comprising approximately 80% of kidney cancer cases. Patients usually present with visible blood in the urine (gross hematuria), flank pain, weight loss, and a palpable abdominal mass. The preliminary diagnosis is usually made on CT scan. questions.question: A 54-year-old man presents for blood pressure evaluation. His home blood pressure diary shows an average value of 160/95 mmHg. Physical examination reveals a blood pressure of 155/92 mmHg and a body mass index of 34. Treatment for the following regions of the adrenal gland will be inhibited due to this medication?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This patient has hypertension, which is commonly treated with angiotensin- converting enzymes (AcE) inhibitors. ACE inhibitors block the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II. Decreased levels of angiotensin II results in peripheral vasodilation, sodium and water excretion, potassium retention, and blunting of aldosterone and vasopressin secretion. Angiotensin II simulates aldosterone release from the adrenal glands. For this reason, ACE inhibitors also inhibit the zona glomerulosa in the adrenal cortex from secreting aldosterone.Aldosterone causes sodium and water retention and promotes potassium and hydrogen excretion. Because aldosterone secretion is decreased in patients taking ACE inhibitors, less potassium is excreted in the urine, which can lead to hyperkalemia.

Answer B (incorrect answer): The zona fasciculata in the adrenal cortex secretes corticosteroid hormone such as cortisol.

Answer E (incorrect answer): The macula densa are a specialized group of cells in the kidney in the distal tubule. They secrete prostaglandins, which trigger the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). HlI

questions.question: A 44-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis develops sudden onset of joint pain and swelling. She is unable to walk more than a few steps without experiencing pain. On examination, she has bilateral knee and ankle swelling, left elbow swelling, and right hand swelling. She is treated with oral glucocorticoids. Which of the following changes in adrenal cortisol secretion, pituitary adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) secretion, and hypothalamic corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) would be expected in this patient?
questions.explanation: Answer A(correct answer): This patient has rheumatoid arthritis, a systemic autoimmune disease affecting synovial joints. Patients with rheumatoid arthritis have multiple affected joints; often fingers and hands will be affected. Usually patients complain of pain and morning stiffness. Rheumatoid arthritis can be treated with glucocorticoids for their immunosuppressant effects. Glucocorticoids alleviate clinical signs and symptoms of inflammation, and sometimes delay disease progression. Long-term therapy with glucocorticoids results in chronic suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis. If glucocorticoids are stopped abruptly, clinical features of low cortisol (i.e., adrenal insufficiency) may develop, since the HPA axis cannot immediately return to a functional state. questions.question: A 47-year-old woman is evaluated for persistent hypertension. Her blood pressure is 166/100 mm Hg despite treatment with a calcium channel blocker and thiazide diuretic. Imaging identifies increased size of the adrenal glands bilaterally. A drug with which of the following mechanisms is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?

options.C: Loop diuretic action in the thick ascending limb
options.E: Sodium-chloride symporter inhibition in the distal tubule

questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This patient has primary aldosteronism (PA), a condition characterized by regulation. The most common causes are bilateral adrenal hyperplasia and aldosterone-producing adenomas. Excess aldosterone promotes sodium retention, potassium loss, and hydrogen ion excretion, leading to hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis. The most appropriate treatment is a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist such as spironolactone or eplerenone, which blocks aldosterone's action at the distal nephron. This corrects volume overload and electrolyte abnormalities and reduces blood pressure.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Angiotensin-converting enzyme (AcE) inhibitors reduce aldosterone levels indirectly by inhibiting angiotensin II formation. However, in primary aldosteronism, aldosterone secretion is autonomous and not responsive to renin-angiotensin system blockade.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) block angiotensin II receptors and can lower aldosterone indirectly, but are ineffective as monotherapy in primary aldosteronism where aldosterone is secreted independently of angiotensin II.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Loop diuretics inhibit sodium reabsorption in the thick ascending limb and promote potassium loss. They may lower blood pressure but worsen hypokalemia, making them inappropriate as primary therapy for aldosterone excess.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Thiazide diuretics inhibit sodium-chloride reabsorption in the distal tubule and are useful in general hypertension. However, they exacerbate potassium loss and are not the preferred treatment for primary aldosteronism. Mc

questions.question: A 62-year-old man with a long-standing history of alcoholic cirrhosis presents with progressive fatigue and generalized pruritus. Physical examination reveals scleral icterus, splenomegaly, gynecomastia, and a distended abdomen suggestive of ascites. Laboratory evaluations show a total bilirubin of 4.2 mg/dL, a prothrombin time (PT) of 21 seconds, and an INR of 2.2 (normal ~1.0). Which of the following changes in sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG), total testosterone, and estradiol are expected in this man?

Clinical features of cirrhosis include anorexia, weight loss, and fatigue. Advanced cirrhosis is associated with failure of liver functions leading to hyperbilirubinemia and jaundice, prolonged prothrombin time, and hypoalbuminemia. Portal hypertension from cirrhosis leads to abdominal distension, ascites, splenomegaly, varices, and upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Gynecomastia is a common complication in males with cirrhosis due to increased estrogen activity. This occurs estrogen. Second, alcoholic cirrhosis is associated with a 9o% decrease in serum testosterone levels primarily due to decreased pituitary luteinizing hormone (LH) production but also because chronic ethanol use damages Leydig cells in the testicles (recall that cirrhosis is a cause of male hypogonadism with associated testicular atrophy and infertility). A final reason for increased estrogen activity is related to sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG). Like all steroid hormones, which are not water-soluble, estrogens are carried by a carrier protein in the blood stream. SHBG binds estrogens and testosterone, but binds testosterone to a greater degree. Higher circulating estrogen levels in cirrhosis stimulate Sertoli cell release of SHBG, raising the serum content of SHBG. Since SHBG binds androgens more than estrogens, increased SHBG leads to a higher ratio of free estrogens to free androgens (i.e., more androgens become bound and therefore unable to exert cellular effects). This amplifies the effects of estrogens. Cirrhosis is thus associated withincreased SHBG,decreased total testosterone,and increased estradiol levels. This combination of effects leads to gynecomastia. Mc Graw

Patients with Graves' disease present with classic features of excess thyroid hormone including tachycardia, weight loss, increased appetite, heat intolerance, goiter and increasing number of loose stools. Answer B (correct answer): This man has a right-sided varicocele secondary to renal cell carcinoma. Varicoceles are collections of dilated veins in the scrotum caused by dilation of the pampiniform plexus of the spermatic veins (plexus = network). Patients with varicoceles present with testicular pain and a large, soft scrotal mass that is classically described as a "bag of worms." Venous blood flow changes with the Valsalva maneuver and lying flat, so these maneuvers change the size of the varicocele, an important diagnostic clue. The pain and swelling are most noticeable when standing and frequently disappear when recumbent. Varicoceles usually develop on the left side_based on the anatomy of testicular venous drainage. The left spermatic vein drains into the left renal vein which travels between the aorta and superior mesenteric artery. This vein can become compressed between these two vessels, creating flow obstruction termed the "nutcracker effect." On the right side, the spermatic vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava (IVC), making it much less pathologic obstruction of the Ivc. The combination of a right-sided varicocele and red blood cells in the urine are strongly suggestive of renal cell carcinoma (RCC) with an IVC thrombus. For this reason, this man needs an abdominal CT scan to rule out RCC or other causes of venous obstruction. questions.question: A 46-year-old man presents with joint pain, fatigue, and decreased appetite. He has lost 15 Ibs in the last eight months, which he attributes to nausea and abdominal pain. He is also voiding more than usual. Vital signs are blood pressure 96/58 Examination reveals dark patches of skin over his nose, cheeks, and in the palmar creases of both hands. Morning cortisol (Na), serum potassium (K), and serum adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) would be expected?
questions.explanation: Answer B (correct answer): This man has primary adrenal insufficiency, or Addison's disease, a condition most commonly caused by an autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex. This results in low glucocorticoid (cortisol) and mineralocorticoid (aldosterone) levels.Initially, patients experience nonspecific symptoms, such as fatigue, weight loss, nausea, abdominal pain, muscle aches, and joint pains. As the disease progresses, patients develop skin hyperpigmentation (due to increased ACTH levels), hypotension (due to low cortisol and low aldosterone),and salt cravings (due to increased sodium excretion). Because initial symptoms develop slowly and are nonspecific, the diagnosis is often missed until the clinical manifestations become more obvious, as in the case of this patient. In Addison's disease, low cortisol production triggers the anterior pituitary to release ACTH to stimulate cortisol secretion, leading to high AcTH levels. Because the adrenal cortex is destroyed in the autoimmune process, mineralocorticoid deficiency also occurs. One of the main functions of aldosterone is to increase urinary potassium excretion, so aldosterone deficiency causes hyperkalemia (high potassium levels). Low sodium (hyponatremia) levels occur because of several mechanisms. Low aldosterone levels result in urinary sodium loss, causing a "salt-wasting" effect. Volume loss accompanies sodium loss, and volume depletion triggers pituitary release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH). This causes retention of free water, which can lead to hyponatremia. In hormone (ADH) levels, which causes an additional increase in water resorption. Adrenal insufficiency is a classic cause of hyponatremia, which occurs in 70% to 80% of cases. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 28-year-old man presents to the emergency room with confusion, headache, abdominal pain, and a rash. On examination rate 129 beats/min, a respiration rate of 28 breaths/min, temperature 103°F (39.4°C), and pulse oximetry 81%. Blood cultures following laboratory results will most likely be found in this man for baseline cortisol and cortisol after cosyntropin administration?
questions.explanation: Answer A (correct answer): This man has acute adrenal insufficiency due to disseminated meningococcal disease, or Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (WFS). In Waterhouse-Friderichson syndrome, patients have a systemic infection (sepsis) from Neissieria meningitides, which causes bilateral adrenal hemorrhage. Patients with acute adrenal insufficiency (adrenal crisis) typically present in shock, which involves altered mental status, hypotension, and tachycardia. Patients in shock can have cool, mottled-appearing extremities due to poor circulation. This patient has shock, fever, and a petechial rash, all key features of disseminated meningococcal infection. A cosyntropin stimulation test (stim test) is used to evaluate adrenal cortisol production. Cosyntropin is a synthetic form of adrenocorticotropin hormone (ACTH). The stim test involves measuring baseline serum cortisol levels prior to injection of cosyntropin, then 30 or 60 minutes after the injection. In a healthy person, cortisol levels should be within normal range (10 to 20 μg/dL) at baseline and then increase to more than 18 μg/dL at 60 minutes after the injection. In patients with adrenal insufficiency, baseline serum cortisol levels will be low. In forms of primary adrenal insufficiency like WFS, cortisol levels fail to rise significantly after cosyntropin injection because the adrenal glands are dysfunctional. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 47-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis controlled by prednisone develops a fever, vomiting, and diarrhea. Family members living with her have had similar symptoms. She complains of abdominal pain, and her family reports that she has been disoriented. Vital signs are blood pressure 86/52 mmHg, heart rate 125 beats/min, respiration rate 24 breaths/min,
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This woman is experiencing acute adrenal crisis due to tertiary adrenal insufficiency. She has rheumatoid arthritis (RA), an autoimmune disorder involving the joints, skin, and other systems. RA is treated with glucocorticoid medications such as prednisone. Patients taking chronic glucocorticoid medications like prednisone are at risk for adrenal crisis, an acute disorder of cortisol deficiency. During an acute illness such as infection, surgery, or trauma, the adrenal gland responds with increased cortisol. This counteracts vasodilatory actions of inflammatory mediators, and therefore maintains blood pressure and tissue perfusion. In patients on chronic steroid therapy, adrenal cortisol production is chronically suppressed by the oral, exogenous intake of cortisol-like drugs. This leads to a diminished capacity of the adrenal gland for cortisol production. When an acute illness occurs, the adrenal gland cannot respond with increased cortisol. This causes adrenal crisis, a condition of acute adrenal insufficiency and shock. Shock (hypotension) is the hallmark feature of adrenal crisis, along with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and confusion. Fever usually occurs in the case ofinfection, but low cortisol levels can exacerbate fever. Nearly 60% of adrenal crisis patients have a precipitating viral or bacterial gastrointestinal illness similar to this case.

Answers A and B (incorrect answers): Low- and high-dose dexamethasone suppression tests are used in diagnosis of Cushing's syndrome, a state of cortisol excess. This patient's presentation is consistent with cortisol deficiency,not cortisol excess.

Answers C and E (incorrect answers): Intravenous antibiotics and antiviral medications may be required for this patient's care, but the first step is to treat her shock with intravenous fluids and glucocorticoids. Mc

questions.question: A 62-year-old woman is evaluated for a four-week history of palpitations, weakness and dizziness. Her medical history includes hypertension and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. She has no history of thyroid disease. Physical examination reveals an irregularly irregular pulse of 120/min. EKG findings are consistent with atrial fibrillation. She is treated with amiodarone. After 2 weeks on this drug she feels well with no new complaints. Her EKG now shows normal sinus rhythm. Which of the following changes in triodothyronine (T3) and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TsH) are expected 2 weeks after starting amiodarone therapy for this woman?
questions.explanation: with atrial fibrillation. Amiodarone inhibits the 5'-deiodinase enzyme, which converts thyroxine (T4) into triiodothyronine (T3). Blocking conversion of T4 to T3 in peripheral tissues decreases serum T3 and increases the secretion from the pituitary gland, resulting in increased TsH levels. While symptomatic hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism can occur in patients on amiodarone, these problems are uncommon. Most patients with normal underlying thyroid function develop mild thyroid hormone level changes without symptomatic thyroid dysfunction. In patients with normal thyroid function who start amiodarone treatment, serum T4 can increase up to 40% above pre-treatment levels within the first few months of treatment. T3 levels can decrease up to 30% of pre-treatment levels. In some cases, TsH levels increase but rarely beyond the upper limit of normal. After three to six months of treatment, most patients who were previously euthyroid will have normalized values. When prescribing amiodarone, it is important to monitor months after initiating treatment to ensure normalization of thyroid function. Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed?term=27129624

questions.question: A 52-year-old male undergoes emergency surgery for acute cholecystitis. Postoperatively he develops fever, racing heart, vomiting, and confusion. He was diagnosed with thyroid nodules one month ago but has not begun treatment. His vital signs are heart rate 143 beats/minute, temperature 1049F (40°C), blood pressure 195/102 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths/min, generalized abdominal pain, and delirium. The thyroid is enlarged, with palpable nodules. Which of the following laboratory abnormalities for serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TsH), serum glucose, and serum calcium (Ca) would be expected in this man?
questions.explanation: Answer E (correct answer): This man has "thyroid storm,” a severe, life-threatening form of hyperthyroidism. He had untreated multinodular goiter prior to his surgery. Thyroid storm often occurs in patients with underlying hyperthyroidism. It is typically precipitated by an acute event such as illness, surgery, or trauma. The key clinical features are the abrupt onset of fever, tachycardia, and hypertension in a patient with preexisting failure. Cardiac arrhythmias are also possible. Other clinical features include diarrhea, abdominal pain, jaundice (from hepatobiliary dysfunction), hand tremors, and altered mental status (agitation, delirium, or even coma). Mortality rates from this condition are as high as 30%. Thyroid hormonelevels are elevated in thyroid storm due toincreased production by the thyroid gland. In response,pituitary release of TsH is decreased.In addition to elevated thyroid hormonelevels, thyroid storm is associated with a surge of catecholamines. This contributes to many clinical features of thyroid storm including tachycardia and arrhythmias. Catecholamines inhibit insulin release and increase glycogen breakdown causing hyperglycemia (elevated serum glucose is part of the fight or flight response). High thyroid hormone levels also cause increased bone resorption, leading to hypercalcemia in thyroid storm.

AHO is an autosomal dominant disorder associated with a loss of function mutation in GNAS1, a G protein that is part of the parathyroid hormone (PTH) receptor. This mutation prevents cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) activation and signal transduction when PTH binds to its receptor. The result is a PTH receptor that does not respond appropriately to PTH, and behaves as if there is an insufficent serum PTH level.This"PTH resistance"leads toelevated PTH levels(as the parathyroid gland releases morePTH to overcome the receptor defect), hyperphosphatemia, and hypocalcemia. Patients present with signs and symptoms of hypoparathyroidism including hypocalcemia, including muscle spasms (tetany), seizures, and tingling of the fingers and toes. A classic sign of tetany is Chvostek's sign: contraction of the ipsilateral facial muscle by tapping the facial nerve just anterior to the ear. Up to 50% of patients with Mullerian dysgenesis have urologic abnormalities including renal agenesis (like this patient). The diagnosis can be made with a combination of normal gonadotropin levels, ultrasound demonstrating absent uterus and testes, and normal-appearing ovaries. Treatment options include vaginal dilators and surgical creation of a vagina. Although women with Mullerian dysgenesis cannot carry a pregnancy, their eggs can be harvested.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Patients with complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (CAIs) have mutations in the androgen receptor that lead to an absence of androgen effects. Like patients with Mullerian dysgenesis, CAIS patients develop breasts during puberty. However, CAIS patients have no response to androgens and do not develop pubic or axillary hair because this requires androgen effects. Key point: Development of pubic and axillary hair requires androgen effects.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Patients with hypothalamic amenorrhea present with secondary amenorrhea (have a history of previously normal menstrual cycles). Patients can also develop decreased bone mineral density, mood disorders, and infertility (secondary to lack of ovulation). In addition, patients with hypothalamic amenorrhea have low luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) levels.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Patients with constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP) have delayed puberty and a delayed bone age. Bone age (or skeletal age) is determined from an X-ray of the left hand and lack of uterus and significant delay of menarche rules out CDGP in this girl.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Patients with Turner syndrome, a genetic disorder characterized by loss of part or all of the X chromosome, present with short stature, widely-spaced nipples, a short or webbed neck and cubitus valgus (forearm angled away from body - also known as "wide carrying angle"). This leads to significant fluid loss, contributing to symptoms of fatigue, tachypnea, and other signs of dehydration. T1DM is an autoimmune disorder characterized by T-cell-mediated destruction of glycosuria and an osmotic diuresis causing volume depletion. Patients present with polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia (increased hunger), nocturia or nocturnal enuresis, and weight loss. The net effects are decreased oxaloacetate levels, increased acetyl-CoA, and increased ketone bodies including β-hydroxybutyrate.

questions.question: A 23-year-old woman comes to the urgent care clinic requesting emergency contraception. She had unprotected intercourse acetate. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of the drug prescribed?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): Ulipristal acetate is a selective progesterone receptor modulator (SPRM). It acts as a progesterone receptor antagonist in the hypothalamus and pituitary, delaying or inhibiting the LH surge and preventing ovulation. It is effective for emergency contraception up to 120 hours (5 days) after unprotected intercourse and may also interfere with endometrial receptivity. Because it modulates (rather than purely blocks or activates) the receptor depending on tissue context, its mechanism is best classified as SPRM.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Ulipristal does not act on estrogen receptors. Estrogen receptor antagonists like clomiphene are used in fertility treatments to induce ovulation.

Answer B (incorrect answer): GnRH agonists initially stimulate and then suppress gonadotropin secretion but are not used for emergency contraception. They are used in conditions like prostate cancer and endometriosis.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Inhibitors of prostaglandin synthesis (e.g., NsAIDs) may influence menstruation but are not effective or approved for emergency contraception.

Answer D (incorrect answer): A progesterone secretagogue is a drug that stimulates the secretion of progesterone from the ovaries, either by acting on the corpus luteum or indirectly through stimulation of luteinizing hormone (LH) release. This is not how ulipristal acetate works. It binds to progesterone receptors and blocks their activity.

questions.question: A 3-week-old boy is brought to the clinic for evaluation due to excessive drowsiness and poor feeding. The baby was distended abdomen. On examination, the infant has coarse facial features, an enlarged anterior fontanelle, an umbilical hernia, and cool, dry skin. Laboratory testing show low T4 and elevated thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) levels. If this baby's condition is left untreated, which of the following is most likely to occur?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (Correct answer): This infant's findings are consistent with congenital hypothyroidism, a condition commonly caused by thyroid dysgenesis or dyshormonogenesis. He has laboratory evidence of poor thyroid hormone synthesis including low T4 and elevated thyroid stimulating hormone (TsH). Thyroid hormones are critical for brain development and skeletal growth, especially during the first few years of life. Without timely treatment, infants with congenital hypothyroidism are at high risk for permanent intellectual disability, motor delays, and stunted growth. Early treatment with levothyroxine is essential to prevent these complications and ensure normal development.

This delay is often evident on radiographs as delayed epiphyseal development. stature rather than increased height in adulthood. Thyroid hormone replacement restores normal growth patterns if initiated early.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman presents to the clinic with complaints of palpitations and weight loss over the past 2 weeks. She reports eyes are normal on inspection. Laboratory testing reveals suppressed TsH and elevated free T4 levels. Thyroid autoantibodies are negative. Her erythrocyte sedimentation rate (EsR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) levels are elevated. Thyroid biopsy is performed. which of the following findings is most likely on histopathology?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (Correct answer): This patient's presentation of hyperthyroid symptoms, a tender thyroid, and a history of recent viral infection is characteristic of subacute thyroiditis (de Quervain thyroiditis). Subacute thyroiditis is often preceded by a viral upper respiratory infection and is associated with granulomatous inflammation of the thyroid gland. On histopathology, granulomas are composed of macrophages and multinucleated giant cells. These changes are driven by an immune response to viral antigens. Subacute thyroiditis typically causes transient hyperthyroidism due to the release of preformed thyroid hormones, followed by an euthyroid and hypothyroid phases as hormone stores deplete. This leads to symptoms of hyperthyroidism such as seen in this case including palpitations and weight loss.

Answer A (Incorrect answer): Fibrous tissue deposition is characteristic of Riedel's thyroiditis, a condition associated with extensive fibrosis of the thyroid gland and surrounding neck structures. It presents with a hard, fixed thyroid mass, but tenderness and systemic hyperthyroid symptoms are uncommon.

Answer B (Incorrect answer): Germinal centers in the thyroid are typically seen in Hashimoto thyroiditis, an autoimmune condition leading to hypothyroidism. Hashimoto thyroiditis presents with a firm, non-tender goiter and elevated thyroid autoantibodies, features absent in this patient.

Answer D (Incorrect answer): IgG4 plasma cells are a hallmark of IgG4-related thyroiditis, which overlaps with Riedel thyroiditis. This condition is part of the IgG4-related disease spectrum, characterized by fibrotic and inflammatory lesions in the thyroid and other organs. It presents with a hard, painless thyroid gland and fibrosis rather than the acute pain and inflammation. Hashimoto thyroiditis. Lymphocytic thyroiditis is typically painless and presents with transient hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism. Hmi

questions.question: A 46-year-old woman presents with a one-month history of lethargy, loss of appetite, shortness of breath with exertion, and constipation. She also notes hair loss and feeling cold. She has gained 20 Ibs over the last nine months. Her vital signs include heart rate of 52/min, respiratory rate of 15/min, temperature of 98.1°F (36.7°C), and blood pressure of 112/65 mmHg. Physical examination reveals periorbital and facial swelling, and diminished deep tendon reflexes. Which of the following laboratory tests is most likely to be abnormal?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This patient has clinical findings of hypothyroidism including bradycardia, myxedema (non-pitting edema), and hyporeflexia. In hypothyroidism, decreased cardiac output (from bradycardia and intravascular fluid loss due to myxedema) leads to release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH), causing reduced free water clearance. Excess water retention often leads to hyponatremia, a common lab finding in patients with significant hypothyroidism.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Serum ferritin reflects iron stores. In iron deficiency, serum ferritin is low. This patient does not have clinical findings of iron deficiency, and iron deficiency is not a known complication of hypothyroidism. Ferritin is also an acute phase reactant that may rise in the setting of inflammation.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Thyroid disorders do not affect the regulation of serum potassium.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Bone marrow function and blood cell counts typically remain normal in hypothyroidstates.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman presents to the clinic with complaints of amenorrhea for the past year. questions.explanation: Answer E (Correct answer): This patient has Asherman syndrome, a condition characterized by intrauterine adhesions that develop after endometrial trauma, commonly following dilation and curettage (D&C), uterine surgery, or infection. questions.question: A 16-year-old girl is evaluated for amenorrhea. She had menarche at 12 and her last menstrual cycle was five months ago. She is also concerned about increasing facial hair. Her temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), heart rate is 75/min, and blood pressure is 135/82 mmHg. Her height is at the 50th percentile for age and her weight and body mass index (BMI) are at the 99th percentile for age. Physical exam reveals cystic acne on her face, chest, and back and excess hair on her upper lip and chin. Laboratory evaluation reveals a negative urine pregnancy test. which of the following changes in serum insulin, estrone, and progesterone are most likely in this girl?
questions.explanation: Answer F (correct answer): This girl has secondary amenorrhea caused by polycystic ovarian syndrome (Pcos). The classic PcOs presentation is signs of hyperandrogenism (acne, facial hair), and oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea plus ultrasound demonstrating polycystic ovaries. Patients present with acne, hirsutism, irregular likely related to a combination of genetic and environmental factors, including diet. Common laboratory findings in PCOs include a luteinizing hormone (LH) to follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) ratio above 3:1 and elevated androgens (androstenedione and testosterone). Ruling out other rare causes of hyperandrogenism is also important because Pcos is a diagnosis of exclusion. Other causes include rare androgen-secreting adrenal tumors (these demonstrate high DHEA sulfate, an androgen produced largely in the adrenal glands) and congenital adrenal hyperplasia (the most common form has high 17-OH progesterone). Females with Pcos are also prone to hyperinsulinism, insulin resistance, and type 2 diabetes. Because these resistance to insulin effects. In addition, PcOs patients have elevated serum estrone levels because of increasing conversion of androstenedione to estrone in adipose tissue. Finally, girls with PcOs have low FsH and serum progesterone levels, leading to anovulatory cycles. Diagnostic criteria for Pcos include: 1. Evidence of hyperandrogenism: facial hair growth, high testosterone 2.Abnormal menses: amenorrhea or oligomenorrhea 3.Polycystic ovaries on ultrasound In summary, this girl has hyperinsulinism, low progesterone levels, and elevated serum estrone levels.

questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This girl has acanthosis nigricans: velvety, hyperpigmented skin plaques that are usually associated with insulin resistance. These plaques are usually located on intertriginous sites, including the Patients with insulin resistance have elevated serum insulin levels (hyperinsulinemia) as the pancreas releases more insulin to overcome the resistance to insulin effects. Patients with acanthosis nigricans are at increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes and should be evaluated with fasting blood sugar or glycosylated hemoglobin (hemoglobin A1C). Answer A (incorrect answer): Patients with Cushing's syndrome present with fat deposition in the cheeks (moon cheeks) and neck (buffalo hump), supraclavicular fat pads, striae, weight gain, menstrual irregularities, hypertension, bruising, and hyperglycemia. Screening tests for Cushing's syndrome include a 24-hour urinary free cortisol or midnight salivary cortisol levels. Although Cushing's syndrome can rarely cause acanthosis nigricans, Cushing syndrome is rare. Insulin resistance is a far more common cause of acanthosis nigricans.

Diabetes accelerates atherosclerosis through mechanisms involving chronic hyperglycemia, endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and dyslipidemia. As a result, patients with diabetes have a significantly increased risk of developing and dying from CAD compared to the general population.

questions.question: A 34-year-old man comes to the clinic for evaluation of episodic headaches, palpitations, and profuse sweating. questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This man has a pheochromocytoma, a catecholamine-producing tumor that arises from chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla. Pheochromocytoma is a rare tumor, but when it is identified clinicians should consider the possibility of an underlying genetic disorder. Approximately 30-40% of pheochromocytomas are hereditary. Genetic syndromes associated with pheochromocytoma include Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2A and 2B), and von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease. NF1 is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the NF1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 17. It is characterized by café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, Lisch nodules of the iris, neurofibromas, and an increased risk of pheochromocytoma and optic pathway gliomas. when pheochromocytoma is diagnosed, especially in a young patient or one with features of NF1, genetic counseling and testing are recommended to assess for syndromic causes.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man with type 1 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department by his wife due to confusion and unusual behavior. Answer C (correct answer): This man has severe hypoglycemia due to insulin overdose and missed food intake. His glucose is 39 mg/dL, and he is disoriented and unable to follow commands, which indicates neuroglycopenic symptoms (i.e., CNs dysfunction from hypoglycemia). Because he cannot safely take oral glucose and there is no indication that intravenous access is yet available, the most appropriate next step is administration of intramuscular glucagon. Glucagon rapidly increases blood glucose by stimulating hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. It is used in out-of-hospital or non-IV-access settings for severe hypoglycemia.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus presents to the emergency department with complaints of fatigue, increased urination, and excessive thirst over the past 12 hours. It can be given subcutaneously or intravenously, depending on severity of hyperglycemia. A rapid-acting insulin like lispro or aspart may also be used in this situation. questions.question: A 10-year-old boy with type 1 diabetes mellitus is admitted to the intensive care unit with vomiting and fever. Answer C (correct answer): This boy has diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), a life-threatening illness that occurs in 6- 8% of patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) each year. Patients present with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, deep respirations (known as Kussmaul breathing), and fruity odor to their breath (secondary to exhaled acetone). In addition to the hyperglycemia and ketosis, patients with DKA are usually volume-depleted with significant deficits in potassium and phosphate. The osmotic diuresis that occurs in DKA leads to renal loss of these electrolytes. Insulin drives potassium into cells by activating the sodium-potassium ATPases. For this reason, hypokalemia can be life-threatening. typically normalizes as water moves out of blood vessels with failing serum glucose. Failure of the sodium to rise is a risk factor for the development of cerebral edema.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Patients with DKA have total body depletion of phosphate due to decreased intake, metabolic acidosis, and renal losses. Because starting insulin drives movement of phosphate from the extracellular space back into cells, IV fluid should also be supplemented with phosphate to prevent hypophosphatemia.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Patients with DKA occasionally present with hypocalcemia secondary to renal losses and decreased intake. In addition, hypocalcemia can also develop if IV fluids are supplemented with too much phosphate.

questions.question: A 26-year-old woman is admitted to the intensive care unit following a prolonged seizure. She has a history of major (normal 70-140). She is given glucagon and dextrose-containing intravenous (IV) fluids. Which of the following best describes the duration of action for the medication that caused this woman's symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This woman overdosed on a rapid-acting insulin (Lispro, Aspart, Glulisine) that begins working in 15 minutes, peaks in 1 hour, and lasts for 2-4 hours. The active form of insulin is a monomer consisting of a single insulin protein structure, but insulin can form hexamers (six molecules) which have a slow rate of absorption. Rapid-acting insulins are modified to limit hexamer formation which increases the rate of absorption. For example, lispro has two amino acids that are modified, allowing rapid dissolution of the insulin from a hexamer to a monomer that is absorbed soon after subcutaneous injection. Hypoglycemia is the most common complication of excess insulin. Clinical features include a mix of autonomic (tremors, palpitations, sweating, and hunger) and neurologic symptoms (dizziness, drowsiness, confusion, and seizures). Treatment includes the administration of glucagon (promotes hepatic gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis) and intravenous glucose infusion.

Answers A, C, D and E (incorrect answers): Glargine begins working in 1-1.5 hours, lasts for 11-24 hours, and does not have a classic peak. Regular insulin begins working in 30 minutes, peaks in 2-3 hours, and lasts for 4-6 hours. Neutral protamine Hagedorn (NPH) insulin peaks in 4-8 hours and lasts for 12-16 hours. Detemir insulin lasts for more than 12 hours and does not have a classic peak. There are no insulin formulations that last for 1-2 hours. Mc Graw

In rare cases, symptoms of hoarseness and difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) may occur, as well as cervical lymph node enlargement. Calcitonin inhibits osteoclast function (bone resorption), so high levels of calcitonin can lead to hypocalcemia, although this is rarely seen in clinical practice. FNA results will show neuroendocrine tumor cells with eccentric nuclei and amyloid deposits. Thyroid function studies including serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) are normal in these patients, as the tumor does not disrupt overall thyroid function.

questions.question: An 82-year-old woman presents with a two-week history of difficulty swallowing, hoarseness, and fatigue. She also notes shortness of breath with exercise and has lost 5 pounds in the last two weeks. Physical examination reveals an enlarged, hard, non-tender thyroid gland with the right lobe larger than the left lobe. She also has bilateral anterior cervical lymphadenopathy. which of the following findings on thyroid biopsy is most likely?
questions.explanation: Answer D (correct answer): This woman has anaplastic thyroid cancer. Anaplastic cancer (also called undifferentiated cancer) accounts for less than 3% of thyroid cancers. The typical presentation is an elderly patient with a rapidly enlarging neck mass. This can lead to difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) due to tumor expansion into the esophagus, hoarseness due to tumor compression of the recurrent laryngeal nerve or larynx, and shortness of breath (dyspnea) because of expansion into the trachea. Lung metastases are common, occurring in up to 50% of cases. The thyroid gland in anaplastic carcinoma is diffusely enlarged, fixed, and firm. Often the enlargement is asymmetrical. The histology involves undifferentiated cells or a mixed morphology (versus other differentiated thyroid cancers such as papillary or follicular). Unlike other thyroid cancers, anaplastic thyroid cancer is highly aggressive, with mortality rates over 90%. patients (typically age 30 to 50). presents with symptoms of hypothyroidism, although transient hyperthyroidism may occur early in the inflammatoryprocess. cancer, which is the most common thyroid cancer.Papillary carcinoma presents as a painless, slow-growing thyroid nodule, not as a diffusely enlarged, hard thyroid gland.

questions.question: A newborn is evaluated shortly after birth due to ambiguous genitalia. Physical examination reveals clitoromegaly and consistent with 11β-hydroxylase deficiency. Excess adrenal androgens cause virilization of 46,XX infants, leading to ambiguous genitalia at birth as seen in this case.

questions.question: A newborn is evaluated shortly after birth due to poor feeding, vomiting, and lethargy. Physical examination reveals hypotension and dehydration. questions.question: A 22-year-old woman comes to the clinic due to irregular menstrual periods and increased facial hair over the past year. questions.question: A 30-year-old woman at 41 weeks gestation is admitted to the hospital for induction of labor. questions.question: A 36-year-old man is evaluated for chest pain. The pain occurs 2 to 3 hours after eating and wakes him up at night. questions.question: A 50-year-old man is evaluated for fatigue and difficulty breathing. His appetite has decreased and he has lost 10 pounds in the last three months. He gets tired walking from his house to the mailbox. Heart rate is 65/min and blood pressure is 85/50 mmHg. Physical exam reveals pitting edema of the feet and ankles and bilateral rales. Activation of which of the following is occurring due to this hormone?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This man has heart failure (HF) with associated production of B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP). Patients with HF present with dyspnea, fatigue, exercise intolerance, and unintentional weight loss. Advanced HF is frequently characterized by an inability to perform activities of daily living or walk short distances without significant fatigue. Patients also develop volume overload, as evidenced by abnormal lung findings (pulmonary edema with pleural effusion) and peripheral edema. Laboratory abnormalities in HF include elevated BNP levels. BNP is released from cardiac myocytes in response to high ventricular filling pressures. The physiologic role of BNP is to promote sodium and water excretion by the Mc kidneys (natriuresis) as a counterbalance to the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAs). Unfortunately, at physiologic levels, BNP is unable to overcome the deleterious effects of RAAS activation such as sodium and water retention. The major clinical role of BNP is as a diagnostic marker for HF when trying to distinguish HF from other causes of dyspnea. (Elevated BNP means the diagnosis is more likely to be HF.) At a cellular level, BNP activates guanylate cyclase and increases cyclic GMP production in natriuretic peptide receptors, promotingvasodilationand diuresis.
