questions.question: A 34-year-old G2P1 woman delivers a male baby at 39 weeks gestation. Physical examination of the baby shows a tachycardic and tachypneic male with pale blue skin. His abdomen appears caved-in, and the left side of his chest seems obtained and is shown below. A defect in which of the following structures may explain this baby's condition?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This baby has congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH), a medical condition in which the abdominal contents pass into the thoracic cavity through a hole in the diaphragm. This results in the "scaphoid-shaped"(curved inward) abdomen that is often seen at birth because abdominal contents are in the chest. The liver provides relative protection of the diaphragm on the right side of the body, so the herniation occurs more often on the left. When intestinal structures herniate into the chest cavity, they take up space that the lungs require for normal development. This can lead to pulmonary hypoplasia. CDH is believed to be caused by the defective formation of the pleuroperitoneal membranes, structures of embryonic mesenchyme (i.e., connective tissue) that separate the thoracic and peritoneal cavities. In the modern era, CDH is often diagnosed by ultrasound during pregnancy. If the diagnosis is not made until birth, findings similar to the newborn in this question will be seen. Chest x-ray shows air- or fluid-filled structures the abdominal organs back into the abdominal cavity and seal the diaphragm. Prognosis varies widely and depends on the degree of organ hypoplasia, especially pulmonary hypoplasia.

questions.question: A 76-year-old woman is evaluated for pain in the right groin. Her symptoms started one day prior and have progressed since that time. This occurs when the femoral ring widens and weakens over time from aging, following injury, or from frequent exposure to high intra-abdominal pressure (e.g., from bearing down due to constipation). questions.question: A 6-year-old boy comes to the emergency department because of sudden, severe abdominal pain. He also reports bloody diarrhea and nausea. The boy appears ill and in distress. In indirect hernias in males, the processus vaginalis fails to close, allowing a loop of bowel to enter the scrotum via the inguinal canal. The processus vaginalis is an embryonic outpouching of the parietal peritoneum. In males, the testes drag this structure downward into the scrotum. The processus vaginalis then closes so that no connection to the abdomen remains. Some tissue from the processus vaginalis remains, between the abdomen and the scrotum. Herniation of intestines through this opening causes indirect inguinal hernias. Indirect hernias pass laterally to the inferior epigastric vessels and through both the deep and superficial inguinal rings. Complications of groin hernias include trapping of herniated intestine, bowel obstruction, and immediate surgery. Special Note: The pathogenesis of an indirect inguinal hernia in children is the same as that of a hydrocele, in which fluid enters the incompletely closed processus vaginalis.

questions.question: A 43-year-old man is evaluated for peptic ulcers. questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This man has a gastrinoma, a gastrin-secreting tumor usually found in the pancreas or duodenum. Gastrin stimulates the release of gastric acid from parietal cells of the stomach. This leads to abdominal pain from peptic ulcers, diarrhea due to high-volume gastric secretions, as well as inactivation of fatty (from steatorrhea). Gastrinoma should be suspected in patients with multiple peptic ulcers and in those refractory to therapy, like this man. The first step in evaluation for gastrinoma is the measurement of a serum gastrin level, which should be high. Normal serum gastrin level is 0 to 1o0 pg/mL. Answer C (incorrect answer): Orlistat is an alternative treatment in patients with Crigler-Najar syndrome type however, it is rarely used clinically due to its modest effect on serum bilirubin levels. Side effects are considerable, and include headache, abdominal pain, steatorrhea, flatulence and frequent bowel movements.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Albumin infusion is also used along with phototherapy, intravenous hydration and plasmapheresis in patients with Crigler-Najar syndrome type II who present with acute hyperbilirubinemic crisis (total bilirubin greater than 20 mg/dL). Albumin decreases the amount of unbound (free) plasma bilirubin with a goal bilirubin/albumin ratio of greater than 0.7.

questions.question: A 31-year-old female presents to the emergency department with jaundice and dark-colored urine. She also complains of abdominal pain and increasing fatigue. She was seen in the emergency department three days ago for a urinary tract infection and given a five-day course of nitrofurantoin. She has a history of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency but is otherwise healthy. She is afebrile with a heart rate of 90 beats/min and a blood pressure of 121/71 mmHg. Physical peripheral blood smear. which of the following laboratory abnormalities is most likely to accompany this patient's current symptoms?
questions.explanation: Answer D (correct answer): This patient has hemolytic anemia caused by nitrofurantoin intake in the setting of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. Patients with G6PD deficiency have red cells vulnerable to oxidative stress. These patients develop episodic hemolysis when exposed to substances that cause oxidative damage to red cells, including antibiotics such as nitrofurantoin. Other causes of acute hemolytic episodes in G6PD deficiency include acute illness, fava bean consumption and certain medications (e.g., sulfonylureas, fluoroquinolones and primaquine). Patients with acute hemolytic episodes due to G6PD deficiency present with pallor, dark-colored urine and jaundice. These patients may have Heinz bodies on peripheral smear during hemolytic episodes, which are red cells with aggregates of denatured hemoglobin. Initial laboratory abnormalities in patients with hemolytic anemia of any cause include predominantly associated with excess heme breakdown and results in the overproduction of bilirubin. Hemolysis can lead to a bilirubin level increases primarily because of extrahepatic production, meaning bilirubin enters the bloodstream directly. Unconjugated bilirubin is not water soluble and does not cross the glomerulus, so in hemolysis urinary bilirubinwillbenegative. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 17-year-old male is evaluated for dark-colored urine. He also reports bilateral pain and cramping in his thighs and lower Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's current symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This patient has rhabdomyolysis associated with marked physical exertion. Rhabdomyolysis is a potentially life-threatening condition caused by muscle breakdown. As myocytes degrade, they release myoglobin into the blood which spills into the urine, turning it brown. Risk factors for rhabdomyolysis include excessive exercise, exertion in hot or humid conditions, impaired sweating (such aswearing heavy football equipment) and sickle cell trait.The characteristic triad of rhabdomyolysis is muscle pain, weakness and dark colored urine. Laboratory findings include elevated creatinine kinase (CK) which peaks 24 to 72 hours after the inciting event along with myoglobinuria, hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia and hyperuricemia. Treatment includes aggressive fluid resuscitation with normal saline, along with correction of any metabolic abnormalities.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Intermittent hemolysis causes anemia and elevated lactate dehydrogenase, which are both absent in this case. In addition, although this patient has sickle cell trait, this rarely leads to hemolysis.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Impaired bilirubin conjugation may be caused by decreased or absent UDp- glucuronosyltransferase activity in the setting of Gilbert syndrome or Crigler-Najar syndrome. Patients with these disorders present with jaundice along with total and unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (more severe in Crigler-Najar syndrome). unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Patients also present with a hepatocellular pattern of liver function tests, with more significant elevation in ALT and AST compared to alkaline phosphatase.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Cholelithiasis, with resulting cholestasis, is associated with jaundice, clay-colored stools and conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Patients also present with a cholestatic pattern of liver function tests, with more significant elevation in alkaline phosphatase compared to AsT and ALT. Mc Me5

questions.question: A 30-year-old man is evaluated for right upper quadrant pain that is worse after eating fatty meals. He has had episodes like tenderness but no guarding or rebound. There is no evidence of jaundice. Abdominal ultrasound reveals gallstones in the gallbladder. This man's symptoms developed due to a substance that flows through which structure in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This patient's symptoms and ultrasound are consistent with gallstones. The image depicts liver lobules including the portal triad. Point C corresponds to the bile duct, which carries bile from the liver to the hepatic ducts. In the portal triad, bile ducts are smaller than portal veins, and usually larger than hepatic arterial branches. Ultimately, bile collects in the gallbladder, where gallstones may form. Gallstones produce right upper quadrant pain, typically after fatty meals, which stimulate gallbladder contraction.

Answers A, B, D, and E (incorrect answers): These arrows point to other structures of the liver lobules as labeled intheimageabove.

Answer E (incorrect answer): The yolk sac normally disappears before birth but may persist as an anomaly called Meckel's diverticulum. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 3-week-old boy is evaluated for non-bilious vomiting. He has gained only 8 ounces since birth. His parents report he is a surrounding the second portion of the duodenum. Which of the following developmental mechanisms best describes the etiology of this condition?

options.A: Failure of pancreatic ventral bud rotation
options.B: Fibrotic obstruction of the pancreatic duct
options.C: Hypertrophy of gastric outlet smooth muscle
options.D: Failed fusion of pancreatic ventral and dorsal ducts

questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This baby's nonbilious vomiting and poor weight gain, combined with his abdominal prevalence estimated at 5 to 15 per 1oo,ooo. The pancreas forms from two outpouchings of the duodenum called the ventral and dorsal buds. The dorsal bud becomes the tail and body of the pancreas, while the ventral bud becomes the head and uncinate process. The ventral bud normally passes behind the duodenum during gut rotation to fuse with the dorsal bud. If the two buds instead surround the duodenum, this leads to a ring of pancreatic tissue surrounding the duodenum. Two-thirds of patients with annular pancreas are asymptomatic. Clinical manifestations relate to impaired flow through the duodenum due to constriction by pancreatic tissue.

Answer B (incorrect answer): The pancreatic duct joins the pancreas to the common bile duct. In patients with annular pancreas, obstruction of the pancreatic duct may occur due to fibrosis. This can lead to pancreatitis. This does not describe the embryological cause of the condition.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Hypertrophy of gastric outlet smooth muscle causes pyloric stenosis. This presents in infants with non-bilious projectile vomiting in the first two months of life. Imaging abnormalities of the duodenum are not consistent with this diagnosis.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Pancreas divisum is due to the failed fusion of the ventral and dorsal duct systems. This leads to two pancreatic ducts instead of a single duct. Imaging abnormalities of the duodenum are not consistent with this diagnosis.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Intestinal protrusion through the umbilicus leads to an umbilical hernia. Imaging abnormalities of the duodenum are not consistent with this diagnosis.

questions.question: A 30-year-old man is evaluated after a recent diagnosis of epilepsy. His doctor prescribes phenytoin and tells the patient to avoid drinking any alcohol while taking this medication. In which area of the image below does the major metabolism of phenytoin occur?
questions.explanation:
Liver Lobules Liver Zones ·Zone I (periportal) - Affected by viral hepatitis first · ZonesII (centrilobular) Furthest from blood supply Most vulnerable to ischemia Fat accumulationbeginshere in alcoholic liver disease High concentration P450 enzymes in hepatocytes

Answer D (correct answer): This corresponds to Zone 3, or the centrilobular zone. Drug metabolism occurs in this zone, including the metabolism of cytochrome p-450 drugs such as phenytoin, macrolides, rifampin, warfarin, and others. Oxygen content is lower compared to Zones 1 and 2 because this zone is farthest from the hepatic artery.

Answer A (incorrect answer): This corresponds to the portal triad, which consists of five structures: the proper hepatic artery, the hepatic portal vein, the bile ductules, the lymphatic vessels, and a branch of the vagus nerve.

Answer B (incorrect answer): This corresponds to zone 1, or the periportal zone. Oxygen content is highest here due to its proximity to the portal triad. This area is the first to be impacted by viral hepatitis.

Answer C (incorrect answer): This corresponds to zone 2, or the mid-zone.

Answer E (incorrect answer): This corresponds to the central vein.

questions.question: A 20-year-old woman is evaluated for difficulty speaking. She has difficulty finding the right words, which has never been a problem in the past. In addition, she reports trouble with walking. She has fallen twice over the last two weeks. Her exam is this woman for serum ceruloplasmin concentration, total serum copper, total body copper, and 24-hour urinary copper excretion?
questions.explanation: Answer E (correct answer): This woman has wilson's disease, an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism. Wilson's is characterized by impaired copper transport and excretion in the bile. It is caused by mutation of the ATP7B gene on chromosome 13. ATP7B is a copper transport protein that incorporates copper into the serum transport protein, ceruloplasmin, and also transports copper into bile for excretion. Impaired function of this protein causes copper to accumulate in the liver and other organs, leading to free radical production and tissue damage. The finding on this woman's slit-lamp examination is known as a Kayser-Fleischer ring. This represents corneal copper deposits along Descemet's membrane at the limbus (corneoscleral junction) neurologic impairment from copper accumulation in the brain, with symptoms such as ataxia (leading to falls) anddifficultyspeaking. Since patients with wilson's disease have impaired copper excretion, total body copper is increased compared to normal. However, the majority of the copper is trapped in organs such as the liver, brain, eye, and kidneys. Liver copper is paradoxically decreased compared to normal. In addition, ceruloplasmin, the copper transport protein serum copper is decreased in proportion to the decrease in ceruloplasmin. Urinary copper excretion over 24 hours is increased in wilson's disease. Because ceruloplasmin levels are low, there is more free copper in the serum among Wilson's disease patients. The free copper is filtered at the glomerulus and excreted, leading to elevated 24-hour copper excretion. Although urinary excretion is increased, the increase is not enough to reverse the total body accumulation of copper in tissues.

questions.question: A 19-year-old female is evaluated for difficulty walking. She has fallen six times over the past year. Two of her falls occurred exam of the right upper quadrants. Copper deposition in the brain leads to neurologic impairment with symptoms such as ataxia (leading to falls), and difficulty speaking. Oral chelation therapy with penicillamine aids in excretion of copper via the kidneys. questions.question: A 65-year-old man is evaluated for dyspnea. He has hemochromatosis treated with interval phlebotomy. He also has diabetes mellitus type II, for which he takes metformin. Over the last six months he has felt short of breath walking distances he is usually able to walk with ease. He has also noted a 5 Ib weight gain. Examination reveals dark skin. Bilateral pitting edema is noted in the ankles. The abdomen is soft and non-tender. Lungs have fine rales at the bases, and an extra heart sound is heard on cardiac auscultation. Which of the following radiologic findings is most likely to be seen in this patient?

options.A: Dilated common bile duct on right upper quadrant ultrasound
options.B: Bilateral honeycombing of lungs on chest X-ray
options.C: Enlarged cardiac silhouette on anterior- posterior (AP) chest X-ray
options.D: Dilated small and large bowel on abdominal plain film
options.E: Atrophic changes in the basal ganglia on head CT scan

questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): Hemochromatosis is a condition characterized by excess total body iron.The Mc disease can be hereditary due to a mutation involving the C282Y gene that codes for the HFE protein. Hemochromatosis may also develop in absence of a gene mutation from excessive blood transfusions for treatment of disorders like sickle cell anemia, beta thalassemia major, and myelodysplastic syndromes. All of these conditions require frequent blood transfusions, which eventually cause iron overload. Hemochromatosis can affect multiple organ systems. The skin may develop a dark bronze discoloration from iron deposition. In the pancreas, iron deposition may lead to diabetes ("bronze diabetes"). In the heart, the most common manifestation is dilated cardiomyopathy. This man's new complaint of dyspnea on exertion as leads to an enlarged cardiac silhouette due to the increased size of the left ventricle.

Answer A(incorrect answer):A dilated commonbile duct can be seen in obstructive disease of theliver and bile ducts, including choledocholithiasis, cholangitis, cholangiocarcinoma, and hepatocellular carcinoma.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Bilateral honeycombing of lungs on chest X-ray is a feature of interstitial lung disease.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Dilated small and large bowel on abdominal X-ray is characteristic of an ileus (lack of intestinal movement). Symptoms include abdominal bloating, nausea, vomiting, and obstipation.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Atrophic changes in the basal ganglia on head CT scan can be seen in wilson's diseaseduetocoppertoxicity. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 50-year-old man presents for routine evaluation. He has not seen a physician in several years and is concerned about a number of changes in his body. For the last several months, he has been thirsty and gets up multiple times per night to urinate. He also reports difficulty sustaining an erection. There is pain in his left elbow and both knees without recent trauma. He also notes his skin is getting darker. On examination, his skin has a bronze discoloration. Hepatomegaly is present. No testosterone?
questions.explanation: Answer H (correct answer): This patient has hemochromatosis, a condition of iron overload with iron deposition in multiple organs. Iron studies in hemochromatosis will show an elevated serum iron and ferritin, as well as an elevated transferrin saturation. Transferrin levels may be decreased or normal. Cardiac manifestations of iron deposition in the myocardium include dilated cardiopathy or, more rarely, restrictive cardiomyopathy. The skin may turn bronze from iron interaction with melanin. In the pancreas, iron deposition can lead to diabetes mellitus, sometimes called "bronze diabetes" in hemochromatosis because it occurs in conjunction with bronze skin. This patient's complaints of polyuria and polydipsia are consistent with hyperglycemia. His fasting blood sugar and hemoglobin A1C are likely to be elevated from pancreatic iron accumulation, leading to diabetes. risk of hepatocellular carcinoma. Iron deposition in the joints can lead to arthralgias, as this patient is experiencing. This patient's complaints of erectile dysfunction as well as small testes on physical exam are consistent with testicular atrophy. This will lead to decreased serum testosterone. Thus, compared with a normal patient, this patient is likely to have an increase in ferritin and hemoglobin A1C, andadecreaseinserumtestosterone. Mc Graw HimI

questions.question: A 40-year-old woman is referred to a gastroenterologist after receiving a diagnosis of hemochromatosis. Her avoid alcohol and vitamin C. Which of the following will occur if this woman consumes vitamin C?

options.D: Conversion of Fe2+ to Fe3+ in the gut lumen

questions.explanation:
Answer E(correctanswer):Patientswithhemochromatosis are counseled toavoid alcohol andvitamin C. Alcohol avoidance is recommended to protect the liver. Vitamin C avoidance is advised because of effects on consumption of red meat and is easily absorbed into duodenal epithelial cells. Non-heme iron (also called free iron) is absorbed into the duodenal epithelial cells predominately as Fe2+. Vitamin C enhances absorption of non-heme iron via conversion of the Fe3+ form to Fe2+. In patients with hemochromatosis, vitamin C should be avoided to limit absorption of iron from the diet.

Answers A and B (incorrect answers): Vitamin C plays no role in binding of iron to hemosiderin or the production of ferritin.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Vitamin C also plays no role in absorption of heme-iron.

Answer D (incorrect answer):Vitamin C favors conversion of Fe3+ to Fe2+,not Fe2+ to Fe3+. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 40-year-old woman is involved in a motor vehicle collision resulting in head trauma and multiple orthopedic injuries. Prior to the accident she was generally healthy and taking no medications. After initial resuscitation and surgery, she is admitted to the intensive care unit. On hospital day 4, she develops fever and tachycardia. Tenderness is elicited on palpation of the right upper quadrant. Blood work reveals a white blood cell count of 16,000 cells/mm3 (normal 4,000 to 11,000 cells/mm3) aspartate aminotransferase (AST) of 156 U/L (normal 8 to 48 U/L), and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) of 232 U/L (normal 7 of the gallbladder and bile ducts in this woman would most likely reveal which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This woman has acalculous cholecystitis, a type of acute cholecystitis not caused by gallstones. This is often seen when critical illness leads to gallbladder ischemia and bile stasis. This allows formation of thickened bile, commonly referred to as biliary sludge. Treatment generally involves drainage via a percutaneous cholecystostomy as the patient is usually too unstable to undergo cholecystectomy.

Answers A and B (incorrect answers): Black stones are pigmented stones composed of unconjugated bilirubin. These are caused by increased bilirubin secretion (hemolysis) or decreased bilirubin excretion (cirrhosis). Brown stones are found in conditions of infected bile,often in the setting of infection or sepsis.

Answer C (incorrect answer): The most common gallstone is a cholesterol stone. Risk factors include female gender, pregnancy or history of multiple pregnancies, obesity, and rapid weight loss. Additional risk factors and among patients taking fibrate medications. The onset of this patient's gall bladder findings on hospital day 4 in the setting of critical illness makes gall bladder sludge (acalculous cholecystitis) the more likely explanation for her clinical findings.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Bile duct strictures occur due to neoplasia (cholangiocarcinoma and pancreatic adenocarcinoma) as well as autoimmune conditions (e.g., primary biliary cholangitis and sclerosing cholangitis). Mc GraW

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman is evaluated for abdominal pain, fevers, chills, nausea, and vomiting. She has a history of hypothyroidism for which she takes levothyroxine. She had sushi for the first time two weeks ago. Vital signs include heart rate of 110/min, systolic blood pressure of 90 mmHg, and temperature of 101.39F. On exam, she is jaundiced with tenderness in her right upper quadrant. Right upper quadrant ultrasound reveals dilation of her common bile duct. No gallbladder wall cholangiopancreatography (ERCP). Blood work is shown in the table below. (AST = aspartate aminotransferase; ALT = alanine aminotransferase; WBC = white blood cell count) Antimicrobials in this patient should target which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This woman has ascending cholangitis, a life-threatening condition that can lead to septic shock and death. Treatment involves fluid resuscitation, antibiotics, and biliary drainage (usually via treatment should also be directed toward anaerobes, as obstruction and ischemia create a hypoxic ciprofloxacin) and an agent active against anaerobes (usually metronidazole) or a single broad-spectrum agent.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Gram-positive cocci like Staphylococcus aureus generally do not cause intra- abdominal infections except in the setting of abdominal surgery. These bacteria are often found on the skin and can enter the abdomen during surgery.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Gram-positive rods generally do not cause intra-abdominal infections. From a surgical perspective, certain species such as Streptococcus pyogenes and Clostridium perfringens are important pathogens in the setting of soft-tissue infections, notably necrotizing fascitis or gangrene.

Answer D (incorrect answer): A rare cause of ascending cholangitis is Clonorchis sinensis (Chinese liver fluke), a helminth found in infected fish. Blood work in these cases will show eosinophilia. Praziquantel is the drug of bacterial infection, not helminth infection.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Chronic infection of the biliary tree with a virus can be seen in the setting of AIDS s m a s s s sa o antiretroviral therapy.

questions.question: An 80-year-old man is evaluated for abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, fevers and chills. He has no significant medical history. questions.question: A 40-year-old woman is evaluated for yellow skin. For the past week, she has noticed yellowing of her skin and dark urine. She also reports intermittent abdominal cramping and poor appetite. Physical examination demonstrates an obese woman with scleral icterus and jaundice. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender. Ultrasound reveals a gallbladder with several gallstones, normal gallbladder wall thickness without pericholecystic fluid, a dilated common bile duct, and a normal-appearing pancreas. Compared to a healthy person, which of the following changes are expected in this woman for serum alkaline phosphatase, serum lipase, and international normalized ratio (INR).
questions.explanation:
Answer D(correctanswer):This womanhascholedocholithiasis,a gallstoneinthecommonbileduct(CBD) that obstructs passage of bile into the duodenum. Obstruction of bile flow leads to elevated serum bilirubin (hyperbilirubinemia). Presence of bile in the bloodstream causes yellowing of the skin (jaundice), yellowing of the sclera (scleral icterus), and dark urine. Obstruction of bile flow also causes elevation of serum alkaline phosphatase as this enzyme is released from bile duct epithelial cells. Choledocholithiasis generally does not cause advanced liver failure with elevation of the serum INR. Elevation of INR in this woman with new onset symptoms would represent acute liver failure which has a limited differential diagnosis and generally does not occur due to choledocholithiasis. Although choledocholithiasis can cause elevations of AsT and ALT, severe liver failure with elevation of INR is unusual due to a common duct stone. The major causes of acute liver failure with elevated INR in adults are acetaminophen toxicity and ischemic hepatitis. The normal abdominal exam and normal pancreas on ultrasound indicate an absence of pancreatic inflammation. Ultrasound in acute pancreatitis will show an enlarged pancreas with heterogeneous tissue due to edema. Thus, for this woman, serum lipase should be normal. Special note: Choledocholithiasis can lead to ascending cholangitis, in which bacteria ascend into the bile duct. This classically presents with Charcot's triad of jaundice, right upper quadrant abdominal pain, and fever. It can quickly evolve into overwhelming sepsis and Reynolds pentad: Charcot's triad + hypotension and altered mental status. This carries a high rate of mortality.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Stones that cause obstruction distal to where pancreatic duct joins the CBD can lead to gallstone pancreatitis, which would also lead to elevation in serum lipase. Gallstones are the most common cause of pancreatitis. Pancreatitis classically presents with abdominal pain, epigastric tenderness to palpation on physical exam, nausea, and vomiting. Hmi

questions.question: A 50-year-old woman is evaluated for nausea, vomiting, and increased abdominal fullness. She has a history of fibromyalgia is obtained (image below). Which additional finding is likely present in this woman?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): The radiologic finding in the image above is pneumobilia, or air in the biliary tree (red arrow). There are many causes of pneumobilia. This finding, combined with evidence of intestinal obstruction (nausea, vomiting, abdominal fullness, lack of bowel movements), is consistent with gallstone ileus. "Ileus" means a lack of movement of the intestines. In gallstone ileus, a large gallstone erodes into the bowel, causing intestinal obstruction. In addition, the gallstone forms a fistula between the bowel and bile ducts, allowing air into the biliary tree. Gallstone ileus generally occurs in the setting of chronic cholecystitis, in which prolonged inflammation of the gallbladder causes a fistula to form between the gallbladder and small intestine. When this happens, one or more gallstones can pass directly into the small intestine from the gallbladder. The ileum is the narrowest section of the intestines. If a stone is too large to pass through the ileum and ileocecal valve, it leads to gallstone ileus. Air behind the obstruction fills the biliary tree. The clinical presentation is that of a small-bowel obstruction (abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, obstipation) with air in the biliary tree. This woman's history of recurrent abdominal pain was likely caused by untreated gallstone disease that has now lead to gallstone ileus. Special note: Gallstone ileus is rare. In actual practice, pneumobilia is more commonly seen when the biliary tree cases, the finding represents a normal consequence of the procedure, and resolves on its own. Other causes include mesenteric ischemia, gastric ulcers, diverticulitis, or post bowel surgery.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Peripancreatic fat stranding is a radiologic finding observed in acute pancreatitis and represents inflammation surrounding the pancreas. diseaseaswell asmesentericischemia.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Diffuse Ilarge- and small-bowel dilation is seen in ileus due to a systemic cause such as excessive opioid use or electrolyte abnormalities (notably hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia).

Answer E (incorrect answer): Hydronephrosis is a common finding in obstructive urolithiasis (kidney stones). GraW

questions.question: A 43-year-old woman is evaluated for dry mouth and dry eyes for four months. She also notes fatigue over the same period of time. Examination of the mouth shows multiple dental caries. Her physician prescribes pilocarpine to treat her symptoms. Which of the following side effects is most likely?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This woman has Sjogren's syndrome (ss), a disease in which saliva production is diminished, causing dry mouth (xerostomia) as well as dry eyes (xerophthalmia). Lack of saliva frequently leads to dental caries (cavities). Pilocarpine stimulates muscarinic receptors (M1, M2, and M3), which results in increased oral and ophthalmic secretions in patients with Sjogren's. Unfortunately, the drug is intolerable for many patients due to its nonselective action on muscarinic receptors,which leads to cholinergic side effects (i.e.,effects related to increased acetylcholine activity). These include sweating, urinary frequency, diarrhea, bradycardia, nausea, weakness, flushing, and hypotension. Pilocarpine also causes miosis (pupillary constriction).

Answers A, B, D, and E (incorrect answers): These side effects are the opposite of what is expected with a cholinergic drug-like pilocarpine. They are caused by drugs with anticholinergic effects. Anticholinergic drugs include atropine and scopolamine. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 67-year-old man presents to his physician with a painless, firm, mobile mass in his right cheek. He has no significant medical history and takes no medications. He grew up in Kazakhstan and did not receive childhood vaccinations. Physical Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): Pleomorphic adenomas are the most common salivary gland tumors and are frequently located in the superficial lobes of the parotid glands. Pleomorphic adenomas are usually benign. However, they can undergo a malignant transformation and invade the facial nerve. Histologically, pleomorphic adenomas are called "biphasic," because they contain glandular epithelial cells surrounded by stroma (supportive tissue) of cartilage, hyaline, or bone. The tumor is sometimes described as "chondromyxoid," because it contains cartilage (chondroid tissue) and mucous cells (myxoid tissue). Surgery to remove pleomorphic adenomas is frequently associated with local recurrence.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Type I branchial cleft cysts are cavities that form near the parotid gland caused by incomplete regression of ectodermal structures in the embryo. This vignette is not consistent with a branchial cleft cyst.

questions.question: A 44-year-old male is evaluated for decreased libido and erectile dysfunction. He was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes three months ago. questions.explanation: Answer B (correct answer): This patient has hereditary hemochromatosis (HH), an autosomal recessive disorder associated with increased intestinal iron absorption. Answer C (correct answer): This patient has hereditary hemochromatosis (HH), an autosomal recessive disorder associated with increased intestinal iron absorption. HH is most commonly caused by a homozygous C282Y mutation (cysteine-to-tyrosine substitution at amino acid 282) on the HFE gene on chromosome 6. Male patients typically present after age 40 with signs and symptoms of iron overload, including generalized rarely, skin hyperpigmentation. Females often present in their 5os (later than males because of menstrual blood loss) after their total body iron accumulation reaches 20 grams. Laboratory abnormalities include elevated serum ferritin (can be over 1oo0 mcg/L in some patients), abnormal Mc Graw liver function tests and elevated transferrin saturation (greater than 45%). Definitive diagnosis is made with genetic testing, which often demonstrates an HFE gene mutation. Liver biopsy is recommended to stage the degree of liver disease. Patients should also have chest and abdominal MRI to estimate iron stores in the liver and heart. Treatment is designed to decrease total body iron stores (serum ferritin) and begins with phlebotomy in most patients. Phlebotomy is appropriate in patients with serum ferritin at or above 5o0 mcg/L, evidence of tissue injury (e.g., increased LFTs or reduced cardiac ejection fraction) or increased tissue iron by MRI or tissue biopsy. It is usually continued, as tolerated, until the ferritin level is less than 100.

MODY are clinically heterogeneous disorders characterized by noninsulin-dependent diabetes diagnosed at a young age (younger than 25 years) with autosomal dominant transmission and lack of autoantibodies. questions.question: A 30-year-old man presents to the emergency room with abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting following a night of heavy alcohol consumption. Answer C (correct answer): This man has a pancreatic pseudocyst as a complication of his recent episode of acute pancreatitis. A pancreatic pseudocyst is a collection of fluid with a well-defined inflammatory wall usually outsidethepancreas. Diagnosis is confirmed by CT or MRI imaging of the abdomen. As opposed to true cysts, pseudocysts contain no epithelium or endothelium. A pancreatic pseudocyst is composed of pancreatic fluid surrounded by a thin fibrous Mc layer. Suspicion for pancreatic pseudocyst should be raised in patients with pancreatitis that does not resolve Graw with conventional therapy, such as when amylase or lipase fail to normalize, or when abdominal pain persists or returns. Pseudocysts generally resolve without intervention. Occasionally they require drainage, which must be done cautiously, as it can lead to infection or rupture with resulting peritonitis.

Serum lipase and amylase may also be normal or low, since the fibrotic pancreas produces small amounts of these enzymes. pancreatitis. If this man had poorly controlled hypertension or were volume depleted, serum creatinine could rise. Given his normal blood pressure and moist mucous membranes, abnormal kidney function is unlikely.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Alkaline phosphatase is secreted by bile duct epithelium. Elevated levels occur in cholestasis (bile duct obstruction, inflammation, or tumor). There is no evidence of cholestasis or biliary disease in this man.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Although nutritional deficiencies are common in patients with alcohol use disorders, vitamin B12 deficiency takes years to form due to the large stores of the body. Common causes of B12 deficiency are atrophic gastritis (loss of intrinsic factor), ileal disease (e.g., Crohn's disease), and strict vegan diets, since B12 is found in meats. Patients with chronic pancreatitis are more likely to develop deficiencies of fat-soluble vitamins, including A, D, E, and K. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 54-year-old man is evaluated for abdominal pain and distention. His medical history is significant for coronary artery disease, hypertension, and an appendectomy at age 48. He reports progressive symptoms for the past 3 days. There has been no flatus during this time. His physical exam is significant for abdominal distension with diffuse tenderness to palpation. are the most likely cause of this man's presentation?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This man's presentation is consistent with small bowel obstruction most likely from abdominal adhesions (fibrous scar tissue) that developed following his appendectomy. Symptoms of small bowel obstruction include abdominal pain and distension, and failure to pass stools or flatus. In adults, adhesions are the most common cause of mechanical small bowel obstruction. Treatment involves bowel rest and intestinal adhesions is indicated.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Hernias are the second most common cause of mechanical small bowel the site of the hernia.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Intestinal malignancy is a rare cause of small bowel obstruction. Treatment involves removing the affected area of intestine.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Intussusception is a rare cause of small bowel obstruction in adults but a more common cause in children. Intussusception is characterized by "telescoping" of the intestine where the intestinal walls fold into the lumen. This leads to abdominal pain and obstruction, ischemia, and bleeding (classically "currant jelly stool"). The most common site is the ileocecal junction. Often there is an underlying lesion that adenovirus gastroenteritis). In adults, intestinal tumors can lead to intussusception.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Volvulus is the twisting of the intestines around themselves. This is a rare cause of large bowel obstruction. Volvulus commonly occurs at the sigmoid colon or cecum. In sigmoid volvulus, classic imaging findings include a dilated sigmoid and airless rectum. Volvulus is most commonly seen in the elderly population (mean age 7o). when it occurs in children, it can be associated with Meckel's diverticulum.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man is evaluated for bloating, nausea, and vomiting. His medical history is significant for obesity, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and osteoarthritis. His surgical history is significant for tonsillectomy at age 12. He was treatment with ibuprofen and oxycodone. Vital signs are within normal limits. Abdominal exam shows distension without tenderness on palpation. Abdominal X-ray is shown below. which of the following is the most likely cause of the man's symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): The patient in this vignette has an ileus (lack of movement of the intestines). Imaging demonstrates diffuse dilation of small bowel with air fluid levels as seen above. The most common etiology is recent abdominal surgery or medications. Abdominal surgery, especially if the bowel is manipulated, can cause a temporary ileus. This patient likely has ileus secondary to opioid medication for treatment of his back pain from his recent accident. In fact, when patients are prescribed opioid pain medications, they often alsoreceive stool softeners to limit constipation and ileus. disease (i.e., Crohn's disease), appendicitis, and diverticulitis. Inflammation impairs normal functioning of the muscular tissue of the intestine. In these cases, the ileus is often isolated to the affected segment of bowel. This man has no fever (normal vital signs), making inflammation less likely.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Small bowel tumors are a rare cause of ileus and obstruction.Given his recent treatment for a back injury, medications are the more likely cause.

Answer D(incorrect answer): Intussusception, where the wall of the intestine folds into thelumen, is rare in adults but can lead to ileus involving the affected segment of bowel.

Answer E(incorrect answer):Adhesions are the most commoncause of mechanical small bowel obstructionin adult patients. This man has no history of abdominal surgery or inflammatory bowel disease, so adhesions are unlikelytobepresent. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 2-day-old girl is evaluated for bilious emesis. She has had several episodes of vomiting in the last three hours. She has not passed meconium. Abdominal exam reveals a distended, non-tender abdomen. No stool is palpable in the rectal vault. Abdominal radiograph shows multiple dilated bowel loops and a lack of air in the region of the rectum. Findings of a contrast enema study are shown below. Which of the following tests will confirm the patient's most likely diagnosis?

options.B: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis

questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This girl has Hirschsprung's disease, a congenital disorder characterized by abnormal colonic peristalsis. Hirschsprung's is caused by absence of ganglion (nerve) cells in the colon. These cells derive from neural crest cells. In Hirschsprung's, failure of neural crest cells to migrate to the colon leads to an absence of nerve cells in Meissner's plexus (submucosa) and Auerbach's plexus (muscular layer). Absence of nerve cells emesis. The classic physical exam finding is absence of stool on digital rectal examination. Barium imaging in Hirschsprung's reveals a "transition zone" that is cone-shaped. (See image.) Bowel proximal Mc to the transition zone is dilated, and bowel distal to the transition zone is narrow and compressed.Definitive diagnosis is achieved via "rectal suction biopsy," which demonstrates absence of ganglion cells. Suction biopsy allows reliable sampling of the submucosa, as the mucosa itself is not affected. Treatment involves resection of the affected colon and rectum.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Abdominal ultrasound is an important diagnostic tool for abdominal disease in diagnosis appendicitis, intussusception, and disorders of the gallbladder and biliary tract. It is generally not usefulinsuspectedHirschsprung's disease.

Answer B (incorrect answer): CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis is an important diagnostic tool for abdominal

Answer C (incorrect answer): Upper endoscopy would not be useful in diagnosing Hirschsprung's disease, as it affects the colon andrectum.

Answer D (incorrect answer): A technetium-99m scan is useful for diagnosing Meckel's diverticulum. This disease is characterized by ectopic gastric and sometimes pancreatic tissue in the small intestine, which can be detectedviauptakeoftechnetium-99m. Mc

questions.question: A 62-year-old woman is evaluated for dysuria. Her medical history is significant several episodes of diverticulitis requiring antibiotics. Her last episode was one month ago. For the past 2 days she has had pain with urination. She has also noticed air interrupting her urine stream, with small bubbles in her urine. Physical exam is significant for suprapubic tenderness. Urinalysis is positive for nitrites and leukocyte esterase. which of the following may explain this woman's presentation?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This woman's presentation is consistent with cystitis with pneumaturia (air in the urine). The most likely etiology is a colovesical fistula following multiple episodes of acute diverticulitis. Inflammation from diverticulitis leads to adhesion of the diverticulum to the posterior wall of the bladder. Necrosis can lead to formation of an opening that allows passage of air and stool into the bladder. This will affected area of colon and repair the posterior wall of the bladder. presentation is that of acute diverticulitis with symptoms that do not resolve despite antibiotic treatment.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Perforation is a more severe complication of acute diverticulitis. Clinical features hemodynamic instability. Perforation is a surgical emergency.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Diverticular inflammation can impair peristalsis of the affected portion of large bowel. This can lead to obstruction, with symptoms of nausea, vomiting, abdominal distension, and obstipation. This patient does not have evidence of obstruction.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Lower gastrointestinal bleeding is a common complication of diverticular disease. Significant bleeding generally occurs in the absence of diverticulitis. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 56-year-old woman is evaluated for confusion and a new skin rash. Her symptoms began six months ago. Initially she had episodes of feeling hot with heart palpitations. Her symptoms progressed to include abdominal pain with watery diarrhea. For the last month her friends have noticed that she is more forgetful. she has developed a slowly progressive rash on her hands and feet. On exam, the patient appears flushed. She is unable to serially subtract 7 from 100 more than two times. Skin exam shows a scaly, erythematous rash on the dorsa of her hands and forearms. A deficiency in which of the following vitamins may explain this woman's skin rash?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This woman has niacin deficiency in the setting of carcinoid syndrome. Symptoms of flushing, palpitations, abdominal pain, and diarrhea are consistent with elevated serotonin levels in carcinoid syndrome. Tryptophan is a precursor molecule to serotonin. Normally only 1% of tryptophan is utilized for production of serotonin. In the setting of carcinoid syndrome and elevated serotonin production, up to 7o% of tryptophan is used for serotonin synthesis. This can lead to tryptophan deficiency. Tryptophan, in turn, leads to Mc ME niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency, since tryptophan is used for niacin production. Symptomatic niacin deficiency is termed "pellagra" and is characterized by the three D's-diarrhea, dermatitis, and dementia. If left untreated, it can lead to a 4th D: death. This woman has diarrhea from both carcinoid syndrome and pellagra. The rash of pellagra is similar to a sunburn and appears in sun-exposed areas like the armsandhands,asseeninthiscase.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Deficiency in vitamin B6, pyridoxine, is occurs in patients taking isoniazid therapy for tuberculosis. Signs and symptoms include microcytic anemia, EEG abnormalities, dermatitis, cheilosis (scaling and cracks on the corners of the lips and mouth), and glossitis. swollen gums, mucosal bleeding, poor wound healing, and petechiae.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin) deficiency occurs with atrophic gastritis, strict vegetarian diets, and short gut syndrome, among other situations. It is characterized by a macrocytic anemia (pernicious anemia) as well as subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord (ScD), which involves demyelination of the spinocerebellar tracts, dorsal columns, and corticospinal tracts. Symptoms include ataxia, paresthesia, impaired vibration sense, and proprioception.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Thiamine deficiency is seen among patients with alcohol use disorder. It can lead to Wernicke's encephalopathy by causing atrophy of the mammillary bodies. Wernicke's encephalopathy is characterized by ataxia, ophthalmoplegia, and confusion, although only 10% actually experience all three features. Graw

questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This man's signs and symptoms are consistent with carcinoid syndrome. Diarrhea, flushing, palpitations, and tachycardia occur in carcinoid syndrome from elevated serum serotonin levels. Urine levels of 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA), a serotonin breakdown product, are elevated. Patients with carcinoid syndrome can develop carcinoid heart disease. This is caused by fibrous deposits on the tricuspid and sided valvular lesions are rare. The mechanism by which serotonin causes valvular damage is unclear but likely relates to serotonin effects on fibroblasts and smooth muscle cells. Of the answer choices, only tricuspid regurgitation is consistent with a right-sided valvular lesion involving the tricuspid or pulmonic valves.

Answers A, B, C and D (incorrect answers): Lesions of the mitral and aortic valve generally do not occur in carcinoid syndrome because serotonin is inactivated by the lung. Ventricular septal defects are not associated withcarcinoidsyndrome.

questions.question: An 8-year-old boy with Down syndrome is evaluated for lethargy. According to his mother, he has been difficult to arouse and napping often during the day. Temperature is 101.2°F. Scattered bruises are present on the thighs, upper arm, and abdomen. The liver edge is palpable 4 cm below the costal margin. There is splenomegaly. Laboratory testing shows hemoglobin 6 mg/dL and platelets 24,0o0/mL. which of the following is most likely to be found on bone marrow biopsy?

options.B: Presence of the BCR-ABL fusion gene

Answer C (correct answer): This boy has acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). The risk of developing this are often nonspecific including fatigue, malaise, or fever. Hepatosplenomegaly is often present. Infiltration of the bone marrow by malignant cells can lead to anemia and thrombocytopenia. Low platelet counts can

questions.question: A 42-year-old G1P0 woman presents for first-trimester evaluation at 12 weeks gestation. She is concerned about having a child with Down syndrome because of her advanced maternal age. In order to make a definitive diagnosis of Down syndrome in this woman's fetus, which of the following is the most appropriate test?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): There are many screening tests for Down syndrome including maternal blood tests and fetal ultrasound. These tests are for screening, meaning a positive test result does not definitively diagnose Down syndrome, it merely indicates Down syndrome is more likely than if the test were normal. To make a definitive diagnosis of Down syndrome, fetal chromosomes must be obtained to rule in or out the presence of trisomy 21. This woman is in the first trimester where the confirmatory test of choice for Down syndrome is chorionic villus makeup as the fetus. A karyotype of chorionic villi cells will show trisomy 21 in most cases of Down syndrome. In the second trimester, amniocentesis can be used to obtain fetal chromosomes for the diagnosis of Down syndrome.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Fetal ultrasound may identify increased nuchal translucency which raises the likelihood of a fetus with Down syndrome. But this is a screening test not a diagnostic test. Fetal ultrasound cannot make adefinitivediagnosis of Down syndrome.

Answers C, D, and E (incorrect answers): Serum pregnancy-associated plasma protein-A, total human chorionic gonadotropin, and alpha-fetoprotein are screening tests for Down syndrome similar to fetal ultrasound. They do not provide genetic material from the fetus, and are not used to definitively diagnose Down syndrome. Mc

questions.question: A 1-day-old boy is evaluated for bilious vomiting. He has a flat nasal bridge and low set ears. Small white circular lesions are present on the irises. The abdomen is distended and tympanic to percussion. Which of the following is most likely present in this child?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This boy has features consistent with Down syndrome including a flat nasal bridge, low set ears, and Brushfield spots on the irises. He also has bilious vomiting and abdominal distention consistent with a bowel obstruction. In a newborn baby with Down syndrome, the most likely causes of bowel obstruction are duodenal atresia or stenosis. Congenital anomalies of the GI tract like this occur in 5% of newborns with Down syndrome. Duodenal atresia and stenosis are the most common. Special note: Vomiting can broadly be divided into bilious and non-bilious causes. Non-bilious vomit is slightly yellow and contains only a small amount of bile. This type of vomiting is often seen in viral gastroenteritis (you have probably had this yourself). Bilious vomiting is green from large amounts of bile. This implies a lack of bile flow due to obstruction of the intestines (i.e., obstruction beyond the ampulla of Vater in the duodenum where bile enters the gut).

Answer A (incorrect answer): Pyloric stenosis classically presents in infants about 3 to 6 weeks old with projectile, non-bilious vomiting after feeding.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Gastroesophageal reflux may cause irritability in newborns, but does not lead to abdominal obstruction. Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is sometimes suspected in newborns or infants who are difficult to console. The abdominal exam is usually normal.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Malrotation with volvulus is also a congenital anomaly seen in newborns that causes intestinal obstruction and bilious vomiting. In malrotation, the cecum is positioned in the right mid to upper quadrant instead of the right lower quadrant. This often leads to volvulus, a twisting of the intestines around the mesentery. When this happens, intestinal obstruction occurs. Although this baby's presentation could be explained by malrotation with volvulus, duodenal atresia is the more common GI congenital malformation in Down syndrome.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Intussusception is a telescoping of the intestine into itself causing abdominal pain Down syndrome, this is an unlikely cause of obstruction. Mc Graw

Answer C (correct answer):This girl hasfeatures consistent with Down syndrome including a short neck protruding tongue, flat facial profile, and brachycephaly (flattened skull). She also has upslanting palpebral fissures (opening between eyelids). an atrioventricular septal defectalsocalledan atrioventricularcanal defect.These defectsinvolve the structures between the atria and the ventricles including the atrial septum, ventricular septum and the AV valves (i.e., the tricuspid and mitral valves). All of these structures derive embryologically from the endocardial cushions, hence the lesions are sometimes called endocardial cushion defects. Since the terminology varies by source, it is important to know all three potential names for the defect: AV canal defect, AV septal defect, and endocardial cushion defect. valve. If abnormalities in all of these structures are present, the lesion is called a complete AV septal defect. The holosystolic murmur in this girl is most likely due to either a ventricular septal defect or mitral regurgitation. Echocardiography is the test of choice to define the anatomy.

questions.question: A 1-day-old boy is evaluated in the newborn nursery. He has a flat nasal bridge and low set ears. Small white circular lesions are present on the irises. A blood sample is sent to the cytogenetics lab where 20 white blood cells are used for karyotyping. Fourteen cells contain 47 chromosomes and the remainder contain 46. which of the following may have led to this boy's condition?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This boy has features consistent with Down syndrome including a flat nasal bridge, low set ears, and Brushfield spots on the irises. The chromosomal analysis shows some euploid cells with a normal number of chromosomes (46). Other cells have an extra chromosome (47) indicating the presence of trisomy 21. Thisis consistentwithsomatic mosaicism. In somatic mosaicism, a mitotic error occurs in early embryo development. This leads to a mixture of cell types (i.e., a mosaic). Some have trisomy 21, others do not. This form of Down syndrome is unrelated to advanced syndrome may have milder features since some cells do not have trisomy.

Answers A and B (incorrect answers): Meiosis I nondisjunction is the most common cause of trisomy 21. Meiosis II nondisjunction is less common. Both lead to a uniform population of cells in the baby, all containing an extra chromosome21.

Answer C (incorrect answer): A Robertsonian translocation occurs when the long arms of two chromosomes are All cells in the offspring would have the same genetic content.

questions.question: A 46-year-old man presents for evaluation of a longstanding cough. For the past six years, he has had a recurrent cough productive of yellow-colored mucous. He has been hospitalized six times in the past two years for pneumonia. He has never smoked. There is wheezing in all lung fields on physical exam. Serum alpha antitrypsin level is 9mg/dL (normal 100-300). Genetic testing identifies a homozygous mutation in the AAT gene on chromosome 14. The patient's sister undergoes genetic testing and is found to be heterozygous for the same mutation. The sister has no respiratory symptoms. which of the following is true regarding this man's sister?

options.A: The disease-causing gene is not expressed

questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This man has many classic features of alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) deficiency.AAT is excessive. This leads to the destruction of alveoli similar to the pathology of emphysema and COPD. The classic presentation of AAT deficiency is a non-smoker with symptoms of chronic lung disease including cough, sputum production, and wheezing. Many patients are presumed to have asthma until the diagnosis of AAT deficiency is made. AAT deficiency is an example of a genetic disorder with codominant inheritance. Both copies of the AAT gene are expressed in affected individuals.The severity of the disease depends on both alleles because each contributes to the total amount of available AAT enzyme. This patient's sister is heterozygous for the same AAT sufficient AAT enzyme such that lung disease does not occur. AnswerA(incorrectanswer):Thedisease-causinggeneisexpressedinthesisterbutdoesnotlead todisease because of the presence of one normal copy of the AAT gene.

Answers B, C, and D (incorrect answers): The disease-causing gene for AAT deficiency is codominant, not recessive, dominant, or X-linked.

questions.question: A 28-year-old G1P0 gives birth to a boy. The mother's blood type is A positive. The father's blood type is B negative. Genetic testing shows the baby has genes for the A and B antigens. Which of the following is correct?

options.A: The child has type A blood

Answers A and B (incorrect answers): The baby will have type AB blood due to codominance of the A and B genes, not type A or type B. Neither the A gene nor the B gene is dominant over the other.

Answers C and D (incorrect answers): The A and B genes are codominant, not recessive. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman is evaluated for skin abnormalities. On her back and chest, she has numerous flat, hyperpigmented oval lesions that are nontender. Freckles are noted in the skin folds of her axilla and antecubital fossa. She also has clusters of soft, fleshy masses on her anterior thighs (image below). Genetic testing reveals a mutation on chromosome 17. The woman's four siblings are also tested. One carries the same mutation but has only freckles and no other skin abnormalities. Which of the following explains the findings in this woman's sister?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This woman has neurofibromatosis type 1 (NFT1), a neurocutaneous syndrome. Neurocutaneous disorders involve structures derived from the ectoderm including the skin, nervous system, and eyes. NFT1 is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the NF1 gene on chromosome 17. A classic feature is the presence of café-au-lait spots which are flat, oval-shaped, brown skin lesions. Freckles are also common, usually in folds of skin like the axilla, groin, or elbow. The image demonstrates neurofibromas, the lesions for which the disorder is named. These tumors often develop in cutaneous nerves leading to soft, fleshy, pedunculated growths on the skin. Although benign, these tumors are the most disfiguring element of NFT1. NFT1 is famous for variable expressivity. The mutation is autosomal dominant with 1oo% penetrance meaning all individuals with the disease gene develop the disease. Variable expressivity means disease severity varies among affected individuals as seen in this woman's sister. The sister carries the same mutation but has a milder phenotype due to variable expressivity.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Penetrance is different from expressivity. Penetrance refers to the proportion of affected individuals who will show evidence of disease. NFT has 1oo% penetrance, not incomplete penetrance. All carriershaveevidenceofdiseasetosomedegree. same individual. This does not occur in NFT, but does occur in genes related to Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes.

Answer D (incorrectanswer):Somatic mosaicismoccurs when mutations arise duringearlydevelopmentin utero after some normal cells without the mutation have formed. This leads to a mosaic (i.e., mixture) of somatic cells, some with the disease gene (derived from the original cell with the mutation) and others without the disease gene (derived from normal cells that formed in utero prior to the mutation). Somatic mosaicism occurs among new mutations that develop in the embryo. Inherited mutations that run in families cannot lead to somatic mosaicism as the gene mutation is inherited and therefore present in all cells.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Germline mosaicism refers to a mutation present in some but not all germline cells (i.e., eggs and sperm) of an affected individual. This does not explain the varying symptoms among this woman and her sister. Mc

questions.question: A 27-year-old woman presents for genetic counseling. She has a 9-year-old son with osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) due to a mutation in the gene for alpha-1 collagen. Genetic testing at the time of the son's diagnosis showed the absence of the mutation in the woman and her husband. She was told the mutation in her son was spontaneous. One week ago, she gave birth to a second boy who also has OI due to the same mutation. Which of the following most likely explains the two children with OI?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): Germline mosaicism refers to a mutation present in some but not all germline cells (i.e., eggs and sperm) of an affected individual. In the case described, one parent is a germline mosaic for an osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) mutation. That parent will test negative for the mutation using standard techniques that sample DNA from somatic cells (often the oral mucosa) because the mutation is only present in all germline cells. Two genetic disorders famous for germline mosaicism are OI and Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Both can occur mutation is the germline mosaicism revealed.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Identical serial spontaneous mutations in the same gene are highly unlikely. (i.e., different loci) may cause the disorder.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Variable expressivity means disease severity varies among affected individuals is given.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Penetrance refers to the proportion of affected individuals who show evidence of disease. In disorders with incomplete penetrance, some individuals with the disease gene may not develop with disease, but both parents tested negative for OI the mutation.

questions.question: A 5-year-old boy is evaluated in a remote village of Pakistan by physicians from Doctors Without Borders. The child has had no prior medical care. He is unable to walk. when he stands, he falls to his left side after a few seconds. He has blond hair, pale skin, and a musty body odor. He speaks one- or two-word phrases only. An extensive battery of tests is done. Elevated the boy's liver shows no abnormalities. which of the following explains the normal liver findings in this boy?

options.A: Absence of genetic mutation in hepatocytes

questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This child has phenylketonuria (PkU), a rare enzyme deficiency syndrome. Children with this disorder lack activity of the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH), and cannot metabolize phenylalanine into tyrosine. Phenylalanine accumulates, and its metabolites cause a musty body odor and have blond hair and pale skin. Due to widespread newborn screening, PKU is rarely seen in the developed world. Although all cells in this boy's body carry the PAH gene mutation, the effects of the mutation vary among different systems. This is an example of pleiotropy, the production of multiple effects caused by a single mutation. Hepatocytes in children with PKU carry the mutation and lack PAH activity (like all cells in the body of affected individuals), but unlike the skin and nervous system, liver dysfunction is not a prominent feature of PKU. A number of single-gene disorders lead to pleiotropic effects, meaning different effects in different organs. Other examples include Marfan syndrome, cystic fibrosis, and osteogenesis imperfecta. Liver transplantation has been shown to correct PkU since the donor organ can produce the PAH enzyme. children withPKU.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Germline mosaicism occurs when mutations develop in germ cells (i.e., oocytes and spermatozoa). A carrier of the mutation will have no evidence of disease as the mutation is only present in germ cells. This does not explain the normal liver findings in this boy.

questions.question: Geneticists are evaluating the frequency of two HLA-DR alleles associated with autoimmune disorders: DRB1*0301 and DRB1*1501. In a particular population, the frequency of DRB1*0301 is found to be 0.2. The frequency of DRB1*1501 is found to be 0.4. The frequency of the combined haplotype DRB1*0301/DRB1*1501 is 0.3. Which of the following explains these findings?

options.A: The two HLA-DR alleles display linkage disequilibrium
options.B: The two HLA-DR alleles sort independently
options.C: The frequency of the combined haplotype is lower than expected
options.D: The two HLA-DR alleles are not associated with autoimmune disease

questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): Human leukocyte antigens (HLAs) are proteins involved with the major histocompatibility complexes (MHCs) of the human immune system. The naming system for the large number of HLAs is complex. HLAs that correspond to MHC class I include HLD-A, HLA-B, and HLD-C. HLAs corresponding to MHC class II include HLD-DP, HLA-DM, HLD-DO, HLA-DQ, and HLA-DR. The HLA-DR group is eSpecially distinguished by denoting the specific allele found in a particular patient with an asterisk (*) such as HLA- DRB1*0301. Since the human genome is diploid, each individual has two genes for each HLA subtype including HLA-DRB1 as described in the question. Since HLAs are associated with autoimmune disease, geneticists frequently characterize the specific HLA alleles within various populations. Certain pairings of HLA genes have been associated with autoimmune disease. For example, the haplotype DRB1*0301/DRB1*1501 described in the question has been associated with Sjogren syndrome. HLA genes often display linkage disequilibrium. Linkage disequilibrium refers to genes found together at a frequency different than expected by independent assortment. In the question, the frequency of DRB1*0301 is 0.2 and that of DRB1*1501 is 0.4. If these two genes sorted independently, the combined frequency should be 0.2 x 0.4 = 0.o8. Instead, the combined frequency is higher at 0.3. This is evidence of linkage disequilibrium.

Answer B (incorrect answer): The two HLA-DR alleles do not sort independently because they display linkage disequilibrium.

Answer D (incorrect answer): The question does not give data to determine whether the two HLA-DR alleles are associated with autoimmune disease. Hmi

questions.question: A 40-year-old woman presents for genetic counseling. She recently gave birth to a girl with Down syndrome. Prior to this, she had three pregnancies that ended in spontaneous abortions. Her husband is 65-years-old and has three healthy children from a prior marriage. Which of the following may have led to Down syndrome in this woman's daughter?
questions.explanation:
RobertsonianTranslocation RobertsonianTranslocation ·Fusion of long arms of two chromosomes Mother Father i1i Occurs in acrocentric chromosomes 。Chromosomes with centromere near end (13, 14, 21, 22) 1421 14;21 Zygotes Trisomy 21Monosomy Normal Carrier (Down) 14 21 14

Answer D (correct answer): Down syndrome occurs in children born with three copies of chromosome 21 instead of the usual two (trisomy 21). Most commonly, this occurs due to spontaneous maternal nondisjunction in meiosis I. More than 90% of cases of Down syndrome result from this type of genetic error. When this happens, the risk of a second child with Down syndrome is relatively low (about 1%) although higher than for women without a prior Down syndrome child. In about 3% of cases of Down syndrome, a Robertsonian translocation in one parent leads to trisomy 21. In a Robertsonian translocation, the long arms of two chromosomes are fused. The carrier of a Robertsonian chromosomes. If the fused chromosome is passed to an offspring, the child may develop trisomy. Chromosomes 14 and 21 commonly fuse in a Robertsonian translocation due to their acrocentric size. In these chromosomes, the centromere is close to the end making a large long arm and very small short arm. If a parent passes the fused 21;14 chromosome and a normal chromosome 21 to an offspring, Down syndrome will occur. In addition to Down syndrome, fused chromosomes commonly lead to nonviable embryos and spontaneous abortions. A couple with multiple spontaneous abortions and a child with trisomy is a classic scenario when one parent is a carrier of a Robertsonian translocation.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Advanced paternal age may lead to infertility, and has a weak association with some birth defects and possibly autism. It is not associated with Down syndrome.

Answer B (incorrect answer): In uniparental disomy, a child receives two copies of a chromosome from one parent due to a meiotic error. A gamete (oocyte or spermatozoa) develops with two chromosomes instead of one. If this gamete fuses with a gamete having zero copies of a chromosome (On), the result is an offspring with uniparental disomy. Importantly, in uniparental disomy, the child is euploid (normal number of chromosomes) and will not develop aneuploidy disorders like trisomy 21. the developing embryo during mitotic divisions of fetal development. Although this could explain the child with Down syndrome in the question, this does not explain the recurrent miscarriages which are a classic historical feature when one parent is a carrier of a Robertsonian translocation. chromosomes. The carrier of a balanced translocation is genetically normal, carrying the normal amount of genetic material but in a different arrangement of genes among chromosomes. A carrier of a balanced translocation may pass translocated genes to offspring which can lead to recurrent spontaneous abortions, but not trisomy. In contrast, Robertsonian translocations are unbalanced or non-reciprocal. They can lead to aneuploidy among carriers and can cause trisomy in offspring.

questions.question: A 42-year-old woman is referred for in vitro fertilization after inability to conceive for one year. She is administered an injection of follicle-stimulating hormone (FsH) to prepare her ovaries for oocyte retrieval. Prior to exposure to FSH, ovarian follicles in this woman will contain oocytes in which of the following phases?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): Oocytes form in utero and enter meiosis I. Meiosis progresses from prophase to metaphase to anaphase and finally telophase. This process arrests in prophase of meiosis I where oocytes remain until puberty. At puberty, a few oocytes progress through meiosis I and enter meiosis II during each menstrual cycle when stimulated by follicle-stimulating hormone (FsH). In each ovarian cycle, about 20 follicles are activated, however, only one usually matures. At this point, a meiotic arrest occurs in metaphase of meiosis II where oocytes remain until fertilization. At the time this woman begins in vitro fertilization, her ovaries will contain many oocytes arrested in meiosis I. Stimulation with FSH will drive oocytes to complete meiosis I and begin meiosis II.

Answers B and C (incorrect answers): Metaphase of meiosis I and prophase of meiosis II occur after puberty prior to arrest in metaphase of meiosisII.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Oocytes arrest in metaphase of meiosis II at the time of ovulation, after stimulation by FSH. They remain in this phase until fertilization occurs.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Interphase is the preparation phase prior to entering meiosis where chromosomal replication occurs. Mc Graw Himi

questions.question: Epidemiologists are studying a remote population in Sub-Saharan Africa. Among this population, 14% have sickle cell anemia. Researchers wish to analyze this population using the Hardy Weinberg Law. Which of the following would make the HardyWeinberg Law invalid?

options.C: Stable sickle cell genetic pattern over generations
options.E: Protection against malaria among sickle cell gene carriers

questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): For a population to be in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium for a particular gene, the gene must not be evolving, and allele frequencies must be stable over generations. When this is the case, Hardy- Weinberg equations may be used to estimate frequencies of allele combinations.There are five basic assumptions that must be valid for Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium to exist. Among these is an absence of natural pressure which could violate a Hardy-Weinberg assumption. A protective carrier state would increase survival of carriers of the disease allele. Those who were not carriers would be more likely to die from malaria. Over time, this would lead to more carriers and fewer non-carriers which could prevent Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium from occurring.

Answers A, B, and C (incorrect answers): Random mating, a lack of migration, and a stable disease allele without mutations are all among thebasicHardy-Weinbergassumptions.

Answer D (incorrect answer): An average lifespan of 50 years would not violate Hardy Weinberg assumptions.

questions.question: For a rare, autosomal recessive disease, the frequency of the disease allele in the general population is determined to be 1/100. If a male carrier of the disease allele marries an unaffected female from a large family with no history of the disease, what is the likelihood of a child with the disease?
questions.explanation: Answer C (correct answer): The question gives the frequency of a disease allele in the general population as 1/100 or 1%. This is a description of the Hardy-Weinberg variable, q. Once q is known, p must be determined to use the Hardy-Weinberg Law for genotype frequencies. As shown above, p + q =1. For rare diseases like the one in the question, p can be assumed to be 1 (it is actually 0.99 in this case which is essentially 1). From the Hardy- Weinberg Law, the carrier frequency is 2pq which is 2 * 0.01 * 1 = 0.02 or 2/100 or 1/50. This represents the likelihoodoftheunaffectedmotherbeingacarrier. The father is a known carrier. His chance of passing the disease allele to a child is 1/2 (he may pass either his normal allele or his disease allele to his child). The chance of the mother passing a disease allele to a child is 1/2 * 1/50 = 1/1oo. Thus, the chance for the child to inherit a disease allele from both parents (i.e., to have the disease)is 1/2 *1/100 =1/200.

questions.question: A 10-year-old boy is evaluated for recurrent falls. He has a history of kyphoscoliosis. Exam demonstrates decreased position and vibration sense in the lower extremities.
