questions.question: A 43-year-old woman develops a painless breast lump. Excisional biopsy shows invasive ductal adenocarcinoma that is hormone receptor-positive and Her2/neu positive. Metastases are identified by CT scan in the pelvis. She is treated with trastuzumab as part of a multi-drug regimen. She has no history of heart disease and echocardiography is normal at the time of diagnosis. After her first infusion of trastuzumab, echocardiography demonstrates a left ventricular ejection fraction of 40% (normal >55). Which of the following is the most likely finding on cardiac biopsy at this time?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): Trastuzumabis a monoclonal antibody to HER-2,a surface receptor expressed on 25 Trastuzumab cardiotoxicityoccurs in up to27%of patients exposed to the drug although the exact incidence has not been firmly established. Cardiotoxicity usually presents as an asymptomatic fall in left ventricular function identified by an imaging modality like echocardiography. Clinical symptoms of heart failure are rare. The mechanism of trastuzumab cardiotoxicity is not well understood. In contrast to the cardiotoxicity of anthracyclines like doxorubicin, trastuzumab does not cause necrosis and inflammation. Myocytes appear Because myocytes do not die, the cardiotoxicity is usually reversible when the drug is stopped. This also contrasts with anthracyclines where cardiotoxicity is often irreversible.

Answers A, B, and C (incorrect answers): Fibrosis, acute inflammation, and necrosis may be seen in anthracycline cardiotoxicity where myocyte death occurs.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Chronic inflammation occurs in coronary artery disease but is not associated with trastuzumab. Mc Graw

questions.question: considered with anastrozole to reduce the risk of breast cancer. which of the following is a contraindication to this drug?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): Anastrozole is an inhibitor of aromatase, the enzyme that synthesizes estrogens from androstenedione and testosterone. Women taking this medication can reduce circulating estrogen levels significantly. This leads to decreased stimulation of breast tissue which can lower the risk of breast cancer. Aromatase inhibitors are not used in premenopausal women. These women have high circulating levels of androstenedione and testosterone which decreases the efficacy of aromatase inhibition. Furthermore, when estrogen levels fall after aromatase inhibition, the pituitary gland releases more FSH and LH as part of the normal hypothalamic-pituitary axis. In premenopausal women, these hormones stimulate the ovaries to synthesize more aromatase enzyme which further reduces the efficacy of drugs like anastrozole.Once menopause occurs, the ovaries produce about 5o% less estrogen and a higher proportion of estrogen comes from adipose tissue and other sources. In this setting, aromatase inhibitors are highly effective in reducing estrogen levels.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Venous thrombosis is associated with tamoxifen. In women with a prior pulmonary embolism, this drug is used with caution. ahighriskofvenousthrombosis.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Cardiomyopathy is associated with anthracycline drugs like doxorubicin. Women with known cardiomyopathy usually avoid these drugs unless a compelling indication exists.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Latent tuberculosis is a contraindication to some immunosuppressants particularly TNF-alpha blockers like infliximab and etanercept.

questions.question: A 28-year-old G1p0 woman and her partner present to the clinic at 14 weeks gestation to review the results of prenatal testing. The woman was discovered to have a cis variant of alpha thalassemia trait during routine prenatal screening. Her partner was subsequently screened and was also found to have a cis variant. The physician explains that the combination of
questions.explanation: Answer C (correct answer): Both parents of this couple carry cis deletions of alpha thalassemia, meaning each chromosome (--/aa). When both parents have cis deletions, there is a 25% chance that the fetus will inherit both abnormal chromosomes (--/--), resulting in deletion of all four α-globin genes. This genotype produces hemoglobin Barts (v4), which cannot deliver oxygen effectively and causes hydrops fetalis. If one or both parents had a trans deletion (-a/-a), it would be impossible (o% chance) for the baby to develop hemoglobin Barts because the fetus would always inherit at least one functional a-globin gene. This explains why a cis variant in a parent carries greater risk to the baby. alpha globin genes. This leads to a 25% chance (1 out of 4) that the baby will inherit both abnormal genes and lack alpha globin production.

questions.question: A 32-year-old man comes to the clinic for routine follow-up. He has HbH disease and has required several prior blood transfusions for anemia. He reports feeling well today and has no new complaints. His temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 82/min, blood pressure is 124/72 mm Hg, and respirations are 14/min. Physical examination shows mild splenomegaly without tenderness. There is no jaundice or peripheral edema. Laboratory studies show the following: Test Result 9.5 g/dL Hemoglobin 28% Hematocrit 72 fL Meancorpuscularvolume Red blood cell count 3.1 million/mm 6% Reticulocyte count 1025 ng/mL Ferritin 12 mg/dL Blood urea nitrogen Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment at this time?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This man has HbH disease, a form of alpha thalassemia with three gene deletions that results in chronic hemolysis and microcytic anemia. Patients with HbH disease often require transfusions, accumulation. The most appropriate treatment is iron chelation therapy with deferoxamine to reduce excess M iron stores and prevent long-term complications such as hepatic cirrhosis, restrictive cardiomyopathy, and endocrinopathies. Deferoxamine, deferasirox, and deferiprone are FDA-approved chelators used for treatment ofironoverload. Chelation therapy is indicated in patients with transfusion-dependent when serum ferritin exceeds 1oo0 ng/mL. Monitoring of iron status using serum ferritin and MRI assessment of liver and cardiac iron are recommended in patients receiving multiple transfusions for thalassemia.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Blood transfusion is sometimes required in HbH disease during episodes of severe anemia or physiologic stress. However, this patient's anemia is mild and he is clinically stable. There is no clear indication for transfusion at this time. His markedly elevated ferritin is the more immediate concern.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Iron supplementation is contraindicated in patients with HbH disease who have received transfusions and have elevated ferritin levels, because the underlying problem is iron overload rather than deficiency. Giving more iron would worsen organ damage.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Pneumococcal vaccination is indicated in patients who are asplenic or who have functional hyposplenism. This man has mild splenomegaly and preserved splenic function, and his main problem is iron overload.Vaccination does not address the present issue.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Splenectomy may be considered in HbH disease for patients with hypersplenism or massive splenomegaly causing worsening anemia or discomfort. This patient's splenomegaly is mild and asymptomatic, and his primary issue at this time is iron overload, not splenic destruction of red cells. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman of Mediterranean heritage presents at 10 weeks of gestation for her first prenatal visit. She feels well overall. Laboratory studies reveal hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL, hematocrit 32%, and mean corpuscular volume 71 fL. Iron studies and hemoglobin electrophoresis are normal. She has a known history of alpha thalassemia trait, confirmed by DNA analysis showing cis deletion of two a-globin genes within the α-globin cluster on chromosome 16. which of the following is associated with the highest risk of having an affected offspring in this woman?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This woman has α-thalassemia trait, meaning she carries deletions of two α-globin genes out of the normal four. In the cis configuration (--/aa), both deletions are located on the same copy of chromosome from the mother and normal globin genes from the father, the result is a-thalassemia trait like the as HbH disease or hydrops fetalis. For this reason, cis deletions carry the highest reproductive risk. In contrast, trans deletions (-a/-a) distribute one deletion to each chromosome 16, so every gamete still contains at least one functional a-globin gene. This configuration makes it impossible for the mother to transmit two deletions together to her offspring.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Hematocrit less than 34% indicates anemia but does not predict the inheritance pattern or severity of thalassemia in offspring. It reflects the mother's blood counts, not the genetic risk to the fetus.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Hemoglobin < 11 g/dL is a common finding in pregnancy and can occur with many conditions, including iron deficiency. By itself, it does not determine the genetic risk to offspring.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Mediterranean heritage is associated with β-thalassemia and trans a-thalassemia deletions, but heritage itself does not confer higher risk than the specific cis arrangement.

Answer E (incorrect answer): An McV < 70 fL supports microcytosis but does not predict reproductive risk. The key factor is the genetic configuration of the deletions, not the degree of microcytosis. Mc

questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This woman has microcytic anemia in early pregnancy. The test most likely to yield a diagnosis is iron studies, including a serum iron level. Iron deficiency is the most common cause of microcytosis worldwide and is especially frequent in pregnancy because of increased maternal iron usage. Although her family history raises suspicion for thalassemia trait, iron deficiency remains the most likely cause ofherpresentation. Special note: Guidelines recommend universal screening of pregnant women for hemoglobinopathies, with this woman could be tested for iron deficiency and thalassemia in parallel. Nevertheless, iron deficiency is the most likely explanation for her microcytic anemia. after 15 weeks gestation. Answer C (incorrect answer): Chorionic villus sampling is a prenatal diagnostic procedure that may be considered once both parental carrier statuses are defined and there is a clear fetal risk. Maternal evaluation mustcomefirst.

questions.question: A 27-year-old woman presents for routine prenatal care at 12 weeks of gestation. questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): A fetus with a single a-globin gene deletion (-a/aa) has silent carrier status, a condition known as alpha thalassemia minima.These individuals produce adequate a-globin chains because three functional a-globin genes remain. questions.question: A 23-year-old G1P0 woman presents to the emergency department at 28 weeks of pregnancy. For the last few days, she has felt minimal to no fetal movements. She received no prenatal care until this point and is a recent immigrant from China. An ultrasound confirms intrauterine fetal demise. After delivery of the fetus, post mortem analysis is performed. The fetus appears diffusely edematous. Fetal hemoglobin is 2.5 g/dL (normal >15). The predominant hemoglobin composition is a tetramer of gamma chains. which of the following is the most likely cause of fetal demise?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This case of intrauterine fetal demise is consistent with hydrops fetalis, a condition of diffuse soft tissue edema and serosal effusions due tohigh-output cardiacfailure.Severe anemia maycause hydrops fetalis as occurred in this case. As a result, gamma chains accumulate and form gamma-4 tetramers which have a high affinity for oxygen and cannot properly release oxygen to tissues. Lack of oxygen delivery leads to acidosis, hypoxia, high-output heart failure, and eventual hydrops fetalis. Other causes of severe intrauterine anemia may also lead to hydrops fetalis. Answer D (incorrect answer): Parvovirus B19 infection may cause hydrops fetalis but would not result in abnormal hemoglobin production.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Placental abruption causes massive maternal hemorrhage and fetal demise. Major uterine bleeding would be noted and fetal hemoglobin would be normal. Mc Graw

questions.question: An 8-year-old boy is evaluated in the hematology clinic. He has a history of beta-thalassemia major. He often requires blood transfusions to treat fatigue associated with anemia. questions.explanation: Answer D (correct answer): This patient has beta-thalassemia major also known as Cooley's anemia. questions.question: A 62-year-old male is evaluated for increasing fatigue for the last month. He has lost 5 Ibs in one month without trying. In primary amyloidosis, amyloid proteins are composed of immunoglobulin light chains. Patients present with fatigue, unintentional weight loss and the other symptoms that vary based on which organs are affected, including proteinuria, cardiomyopathy, peripheral neuropathy, macroglossia (enlarged tongue) and purpura of the face andneck. Laboratory abnormalities may include elevated alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase, proteinuria and increased serum creatinine. The purpura and bleeding symptoms that accompany primary amyloidosis are not caused by increased prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time, instead they are related to amyloid infiltration of blood vessels. Definitive diagnosis is made by identifying amyloid fibrils on histologic evaluation of a tissue sample; the abdominal fat pad is a common biopsy site. Amyloid fibrils are pink on standard microscopy but demonstrate apple-green birefringence when stained with Congo red and examined specifically identify the light chains that are characteristic of primary amyloidosis. because of the risk of bleeding. questions.question: A 19-year-old male presents to the emergency department with fever, abdominal pain and a painful red rash on his leg that started two days ago. He has no headache, shortness of breath, vomiting, diarrhea or blood in his stool. He has been seen in months ago that was normal. His family moved to the United States ten years ago from Turkey and his father and paternal uncle have a history of recurrent fevers. His temperature is 103.3°F, heart rate is 131 beats/min, respiratory rate is 22 guarding. He also has a tender, raised, erythematous rash on his right lower leg. Laboratory evaluation reveals: Computed tomography scan of the abdomen demonstrates peritoneal inflammation but is otherwise normal. which of the
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This patient has a clinical presentation suggestive of familial Mediterranean fever (FMF),arareautosomalrecessiveinflammatorydisordercharacterizedbyrecurrentepisodesoffeverand serosal inflammation. It occurs most commonly in patients from Turkey, Armenia and North Africa and it presents before age 20 in most patients. The clinical presentation includes fever, often as high as 104°F, severe abdominal or chest pain, joint pain and an erysipelas-like skin rash (red, tender, raised patches on the lower leg or foot). The episodes resolve spontaneously and are accompanied by leukocytosis, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and elevated C-reactive protein (CRP). repeated imaging and surgical exploration prior to diagnosis. Colchicine is prescribed for initial treatment of FMF; it is effective in treating acute exacerbations and preventing the development of amyloidosis, which is the most severe complication of FMF. Colchicine should be continued indefinitely, and patients should have complete blood count, liver function tests, creatinine, ESR, CRP and serum amyloid levels checked every 6 to 12 months to monitor for treatment efficacy and adverse events. Progression to secondary amyloidosis, including nephrotic syndrome or chronic renal failure, is the most serious complication of FMF.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Anakinra is an interleukin 1 inhibitor that is used in patients with FMF who do not respond to colchicine or who have treatment-related side effects. The best next step in this patient is colchicine. of amyloid cardiomyopathy, which is caused by the deposit of transthyretin in the myocardium. Unlike FMF, patients with amyloid cardiomyopathy do not have fever or abdominal pain and present with jugular venous distension, edema and shortness of breath.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Exploratory laparotomy is not indicated in this patient. Although he has peritonitis, characterized by rebound tenderness and guarding, the family history of recurrent fevers and personal history of a previous exploratory laparotomy make surgical exploration unnecessary in this patient.

Answer D (incorrect answer): The antibiotic ceftriaxone is not indicated in patients with FMF. The patient does have recurrent episodes of fever and abdominal pain; however, FMF is an inflammatory process that is not related to an infection. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 65-year-old female is evaluated for increasing shortness of breath over the last two weeks. She also reports bilateral foot and ankle swelling and intermittent chest pain. It is used in the management of familial Mediterranean fever, a hereditary inflammatory disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of fever and serosal inflammation. This patient does not have recurrent fever or abdominal pain, making FMF unlikely.

questions.question: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the physician due to recurrent nosebleeds and easy bruising. His parents report prolonged bleeding after minor cuts. questions.question: A 58-year-old man is admitted to the hospital for altered mental status. He lives alone and his family found him in his apartment after not going to work for two days. The man does not regularly see doctors and is not treated for any medical conditions. He has a history of alcohol abuse but it is unknown exactly how much he drinks per day. On physical exam, mild scleral icterus is noted. He has a protuberant abdomen with a positive fluid wave and hepatosplenomegaly. He has small hemorrhagic skin lesions as shown below. Ethanol level is 0 mg/dL. Platelet count is 40,000 /mm3 (normal 150,000-450,000) and INR is 2.0 (normal 1.0). Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's thrombocytopenia?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This man with an alcohol use history has physical exam findings consistent with cirrhosis. These include abdominal ascites, hepatosplenomegaly, scleral icterus, and spider angiomas (seen in this image). His altered mental status is likely due to hepatic encephalopathy caused by poor clearance of nitrogen products from the blood. Elevated prothrombin time and INR are caused by decreased coagulation factor production from the liver. Patients with cirrhosis develop thrombocytopenia for multiple reasons but most significantly due to splenic sequestration.Portal hypertension results in the backup of blood into the splenic circulation which results in the buildup of platelets in the spleen. Patients with alcohol abuse may also develop bone marrow suppression that can cause thrombocytopenia. Poor liver function can also decrease thrombopoietin production contributing to thrombocytopenia.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura can cause isolated thrombocytopenia but this is less likely than sequestration of platelets in a patient with cirrhosis and portal hypertension. (i.e., increased PT/PTT). These patients typically have bleeding and hemolytic anemia. time. Platelet counts are typically normal. prolongation. Mc Graw

questions.question: diagnosed in infancy and has required regular blood transfusions since early childhood. His parents report he becomes studies show reduced hemoglobin and increased lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). This patient is at greatest risk of developing which of the following complications?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This boy has beta-thalassemia major, a condition characterized by chronic hemolysis. Ongoing hemolysis increases bilirubin production, which is conjugated in the liver and excreted into bile. When the bilirubin content of bile increases, excess bilirubin can precipitate, forming pigmented gallstones. These gallstones are primarily calcium bilirubinate and are different from the more common cholesterol hemolytic states such as thalassemia, hereditary spherocytosis, and sickle cell disease. They may cause a range of gallstone-related conditions, including biliary colic, acute cholecystitis, or cholangitis.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Encephalopathy is not a common complication of beta-thalassemia major. It can occur in severe liver failure or metabolic disordersbutis not directlyrelated to chronic hemolysis.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Hyposplenism may occur after repeated splenic infarctions or splenectomy, but the major risk in beta-thalassemia major with splenomegaly is from gallstone formation due to hemolysis.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Pancreatic insufficiency is seen in disorders such as cystic fibrosis or chronic pancreatitis, not in beta-thalassemia major.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Splenic infarction is more strongly associated with sickle cell disease, where vaso- characteristic complication. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 10-year-old girl is brought to the clinic for follow-up. She has a history of beta-thalassemia major diagnosed in infancy and Physical examination shows short stature and frontal bossing. Laboratory studies reveal a hemoglobin of 9.2 g/dL. The physician is concerned about complications from repeated transfusions. Which of the following laboratory measurements is the most sensitive for assessing this patient for transfusion-related complications?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This girl has beta-thalassemia major, a chronic hemolytic anemia that requires lifelong transfusion therapy. Repeated transfusions lead to iron overload, which can deposit in the heart, liver, and endocrine organs. The most sensitive laboratory test for assessing body iron stores is serum ferritin. Ferritin reflects total body iron and rises early in states of iron excess, making it the best test to monitor for transfusion- related iron overload. In transfusion-dependent thalassemia, chelation therapy for iron overload is usually initiated when serum ferritin levels exceed 1ooo ng/mL, since sustained elevations above this threshold are associatedwithorgantoxicity.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Reticulocyte count reflects the bone marrow response to anemia. In beta- thalassemia major, ineffective erythropoiesis can lead to a low reticulocyte count, but this does not provide informationabouttotalbodyironstores. This value is subject to wide daily variation and dietary influences, so it is not a reliable indicator of iron overload. transferrin. TIBC is usually increased in iron deficiency and decreased in anemia of chronic disease. It does not accurately measure total body iron in patients with chronic transfusions.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Transferrin saturation, calculated as the ratio of serum iron to TIBC, can be elevated in states of iron overload. However, it is not as sensitive or reliable as ferritin for monitoring total body iron content. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 58-year-old man comes to the cardiology clinic for follow-up 2 weeks after hospitalization for acute substernal chest pain. During that admission, he was found to have an ST-elevation myocardial infarction and underwent percutaneous coronary metoprolol, atorvastatin, and clopidogrel. questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This man is taking clopidogrel, a antiplatelet agent that irreversibly blocks the platelet adenosine diphosphate (ADP) receptor P2Y12. P2Y12 is coupled to Gi proteins, and its activation reducing the risk of stent thrombosis. This drug is commonly co-administered with aspirin ("dual antiplatelet therapy") in patients receiving coronary stents to prevent stent thrombosis.

Answer B (incorrect answer): P2Y12 receptor activation decreases cAMP. Clopidogrel blocks this receptor, leading to increased, not decreased, cAMP.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Decreased thromboxane A2 production is the mechanism of aspirin, which irreversibly inhibits COX-1 in platelets.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Clopidogrel blocks P2Y12 activity. Increased P2Y12 activity would have the opposite effect and promote platelet aggregation.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Clopidogrel inhibits ADP binding to P2Y12 receptors. Increased ADP binding would lead to greater platelet activation and aggregation, not inhibition. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 58-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of an episode of hematemesis. He has a history of osteoarthritis and coronary artery disease. His medications include metoprolol, aspirin, and atorvastatin. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy reveals a bleeding gastric ulcer. Which of the following aspirin effects may have contributed to formation of this patient's ulcer?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This man has a bleeding gastric ulcer in the setting of aspirin use. Aspirin irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase (Cox)-1 in gastric mucosa, leading to decreased prostaglandin synthesis. Gastric prostaglandins stimulate mucus and bicarbonate secretion and enhance mucosal blood flow. Loss of these protective effects due to aspirin weakens the gastric mucosal barrier, allowing acid-mediated injury to occur and predisposing to ulcer formation and bleeding. vasodilation and inhibition of platelet aggregation. Its loss has little effect on gastric mucosal protection compared to prostaglandin deficiency.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Aspirin decreases thromboxane A2 synthesis by irreversibly inhibiting COX-1 in platelets. This impairs platelet aggregation and prolongs bleeding time, which can worsen blood loss once an ulcer is present but does not cause the ulcer itself.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Aspirin decreases, not increases, arachidonic acid metabolism. It inhibits cyclooxygenase activity, thereby reducing the conversion of arachidonic acid to prostaglandins and thromboxanes.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Aspirin irreversibly inhibits both COX-1 and COX-2. Its inhibition of COX-1 is responsible for gastric mucosal injury. COX-2 inhibition plays a minimal role in gastrointestinal toxicity. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 64-year-old man comes to the clinic for a follow-up visit after a recent hospitalization for substernal chest pain. During the admission, he was diagnosed with a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction. He was treated with placement of a drug- eluting stent to his left anterior descending artery, and started on aspirin, a beta blocker, and a statin. He reports ongoing osteoarthritis pain in his knees and asks if he can take celecoxib for relief. which of the following best explains why this medication should be avoided in this patient?

options.A: Inhibition of prostacyclin formation without inhibition of thromboxane A2
options.B: Inhibition of platelet aggregation leading to increased bleeding risk
options.C: Selective inhibition of COX-1 by celecoxib increases thrombosis risk
options.D: Decreased metabolism of arachidonic acid in platelets
options.E: Increased prostacyclin production in gastric mucosa cells

questions.explanation:
Answer C (incorrect answer): Celecoxib selectively inhibits COX-2, not COX-1. COX-1 inhibition would reduce thromboxane A2 production and decrease platelet aggregation, which would lower thrombosis risk rather than increase it.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Celecoxib does not alter arachidonic acid metabolism in platelets. Thromboxane A2 production by platelets remains intact, which is part of the reason for the prothrombotic effect.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Celecoxib decreases prostacyclin production by inhibiting COX-2 in endothelial cells. Increased prostacyclin production would promote vasodilation and inhibit platelet aggregation, which would not increase thrombosis risk. MW HimI

questions.question: A 45-year-old man comes to the clinic because of progressive fatigue and pallor. He has no significant past medical history and takes no medications. This condition also produces pancytopenia with hypocellular marrow, but it occurs in older patients without congenital anomalies such as absent thumbs or café-au-lait spots.

questions.question: A 23-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with progressive fatigue and frequent nosebleeds. She has no significant past medical history and takes no medications. She reports no recent infections, toxin exposures, or travel. Temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg, pulse is 94/min, and respirations are 14/min. Examination shows pallor, scattered ecchymoses, and gingival bleeding. There is no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 6.9 g/dL, hematocrit 20%, mean corpuscular volume 90 fL, white blood cell count 2,200/mm, and platelet count 18,000/mm?. Reticulocyte count is 1.5%. A bone marrow biopsy reveals hypocellularity with fatty infiltration and no malignant cells. Which of the following most likely explains this patient's condition?

options.A: Bone marrow infiltration by malignant cells
options.B: Defective DNA synthesis due to toxin exposure

questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This woman has aplastic anemia, characterized by pancytopenia, a low reticulocyte count, and a hypocellular bone marrow with fatty infiltration. There are many causes of aplastic anemia including viral infections (Epstein-Barr virus, HIV, hepatitis viruses), drugs and radiation. This woman has no obvious cause making her case idiopathic. In idiopathic cases, the underlying mechanism is usually immune- mediated destruction of hematopoietic stem cells by cytotoxic T lymphocytes. These activated T cells release cytokines such as interferon-y and tumor necrosis factor-a, which suppress hematopoiesis and induce apoptosis of stem cells. Clinically, this leads to anemia (fatigue, pallor), thrombocytopenia (bruising, mucosal bleeding), and leukopenia (infections).

Answer A (incorrect answer): Bone marrow infiltration by malignant cells is seen in conditions such as acute leukemia, lymphoma, or metastatic cancer. Infiltration produces a hypercellular marrow with abnormal cells, not hypocellularity with fatty replacement as seen here.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Defective DNA synthesis due to toxin exposure (eg, chemotherapy, radiation, consistent with aplastic anemia. She also reports no toxin exposure.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Impaired heme synthesis is the mechanism of sideroblastic anemia, which may be due to lead poisoning, alcohol, or vitamin B6 deficiency. It presents with microcytic anemia and ring sideroblasts on bone marrow biopsy, not hypocellularity with fatty infiltration.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Familial hyperlipidemia is a genetic disorder of lipid metabolism that increases cardiovascular risk. It has no relationship to pancytopenia or hypocellular marrow. Mc IH

questions.question: A 58-year-old man comes to the clinic because of progressive fatigue and shortness of breath on exertion. He has a history of hypertension, mild chronic kidney disease, and long-standing alcohol use. He was recently treated for syphilis with penicillin. His medications include amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide. He has no history of bleeding. Temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), examination is benign without hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, hematocrit 27%, mean
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): The man has a symptomatic normocytic anemia of unknown cause. The best next test in the evaluation of unexplained normocytic anemia is the reticulocyte count. This test distinguishes Mc between decreased red blood cell production and increased red blood cell destruction or loss. A low reticulocyte count suggests impaired production, which may result from bone marrow suppression, nutritional deficiency, alcohol use, or chronic kidney disease due to low erythropoietin. A high reticulocyte count indicates increased red blood cell turnover due to hemolysis or blood loss. Because this patient has normocytic anemia and multiple possible contributing factors (alcohol use, chronic kidney disease), the reticulocyte count is the key first step to guide further workup. microcytic anemias, iron studies are usually the first test. For macrocytic anemias, vitamin B12 and folate levels are usually thebest first test.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Bone marrow biopsy is performed when there is suspicion for intrinsic bone marrow disease such as myelodysplastic syndrome, aplastic anemia, or hematologic malignancy. It is invasive and should not be done until after a reticulocyte count indicates bone marrow failure.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Erythropoietin levels may be low in patients with chronic kidney disease, but this is not the first step in evaluating anemia. First a reticulocyte count should be done to determine if the anemia is due to underproduction of red cells or increased destruction/loss of red cells. or thrombocytopenia. Testing may be appropriate but only after establishing that this man's anemia is due to underproduction of red cells by the bone marrow. morphology, such as spherocytes in hereditary spherocytosis or schistocytes in microangiopathic hemolysis. However, it is most useful after the reticulocyte count indicates whether the anemia is due to increased destruction or decreasedproduction. Mc Graw

questions.question: An 82-year-old man is hospitalized for altered mental status. The patient has had progressive neurocognitive impairment confusion and disorientation. Answer D (incorrect answer): An increased peripheral reticulocyte count is characteristic of conditions with increased red cell destruction or blood loss, such as hemolytic anemia. In vitamin B12 deficiency, reticulocyte production is decreased because the marrow is unable to effectively synthesize DNA for new red cells. Mc Graw

Her medical history includes obesity, diabetes mellitus type 2, chronic kidney disease, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia. Prior to discharge from the hospital, she was informed that her hemoglobin was 9 g/dL and that she should discuss this with her primary care physician. questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This woman has a normocytic anemia with normal ferritin in the setting of chronic renal disease.Patients with chronic renal disease develop normocytic anemia due to decreased erythropoietin (EPO) release from peritubular capillaries. The anemia is characteristically normocytic and iron stores are adequate (i.e., are not decreased). This patient would likely qualify to receive EPO shots to correct her anemia. This woman has a normal ferritin level. In anemia of chronic disease, ferritin levels are elevated. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 4-year-old boy is seen for an annual examination by his pediatrician. He has several congenital abnormalities including hypoplastic thumbs and hypopigmented skin patches. questions.question: A 34-year-old woman is evaluated as part of routine preoperative testing prior to excision of a breast mass. questions.question: A 24-year-old woman is evaluated in the obstetrics clinic after a positive home pregnancy test. She is a recent immigrant to the United States. She had two successful vaginal births at full-term while living outside the Us. Serum HCG testing indicates she is 7 to 8 weeks pregnant. Laboratory testing shows she is not immune to rubella or hepatitis B. In addition, her blood type is Rh-negative. When her serum is mixed with Rh-positive red blood cells, agglutination occurs. Which of the following is the best interpretation of these test results?

options.E: Coombs testing result cannot be determined

questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This woman has a new pregnancy and is Rh-negative with evidence of antibodies against Rh(D) antigen in her serum. The fact that her serum causes agglutination when mixed with D+ red blood cells means she has circulating anti-D IgG antibodies. This is detected by the indirect Coombs test, which identifies antibodies present in a patient's serum by mixing the serum with reagent red blood cells of known antigenicity. A positive indirect Coombs test indicates alloimmunization, meaning antibodies to the Rh(D) red cell antigen. In pregnancy this can cause hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn if the fetus inherits the Rh(D) antigen from the father. AnswerA(incorrectanswer):ThedirectCoombstestidentifiesantibodiesorcomplementbounddirectlytothe surface of a patient's red blood cells. This test is used in conditions such as autoimmune hemolytic anemia. In this case the woman's own red blood cells are not coated with antibody, so the direct Coombs test would not be positive.

Answer B (incorrect answer): A negative direct Coombs test means that no antibodies or complement are bound to the patient's red blood cells. The question describes agglutination when the woman's serum is mixed with Rh(D) positive cells, which is the indirect Coombs test.

Answer D (incorrect answer): A negative indirect Coombs test means there are no antibodies in the serum that cells, the indirect Coombs test is positive rather than negative.

Answer E (incorrect answer): The test result can be determined because agglutination occurred when the serum was mixed with Rh(D) positive cells. This result corresponds to a positive indirect Coombs test, so it is incorrect to state that the result cannot be determined.

questions.question: A 42-year-old man brought to the emergency room after a high-speed car crash. He is awake and complaining of abdominal 99.0°F and oxygen saturation of 92% on 4L nasal cannula. questions.question: A 32-year-old G1P1 woman is admitted to the labor and delivery service. One hour ago, she delivered a healthy baby boy at 40 weeks gestation. Answer E (incorrect answer): Prednisone is used for autoimmune or inflammatory conditions and does not affect porphyrin accumulation or the underlying enzyme deficiency in porphyria cutanea tarda. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 31-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of severe abdominal pain that began earlier in the day. condition. Vital signs show blood pressure 164/96 mm Hg and pulse 122/min. Abdominal examination reveals a soft abdomen without rebound or guarding. She is treated with a glucose infusion which leads to improvement in her abdominal pain. The therapeutic effect of glucose in this patient occurs primarily through inhibition of which of the following enzymes?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This woman has a flare of acute intermittent porphyria (AIP), a disorder in which deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase leads to accumulation of neurotoxic precursors. Flares of AIP are often precipitated by fasting or alcohol intake. Acute symptoms improve with infusion of hemin or glucose. Both of these inhibit the hepatic enzyme aminolevulinic acid synthase, the rate limiting enzyme of heme synthesis. Decreasing aminolevulinic acid synthase activity lowers production of aminolevulinic acid and porphobilinogen and reduces thesymptomsof an acute attack.

Answer A(incorrectanswer):Aminolevulinic acid dehydratase converts aminolevulinic acid toporphobilinogen. It is not the target of glucose therapy and is not inhibited during treatment of acute intermittent porphyria.

Answer C (incorrectanswer):Ferrochelatase catalyzesthefinal stepof heme synthesis byinserting iron into protoporphyrin IX. This enzyme is inhibited by lead exposure and contributes to the anemia seen in lead poisoning, but is not involved in glucose treatment for acute intermittent porphyria. porphyria. Glucose does not inhibit this enzyme. disorder marked by photosensitive blistering. It is not involved in the mechanism by which glucose treats acute intermittent porphyria. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of severe abdominal pain that began earlier today. She describes the pain as diffuse, crampy, and not relieved by bowel movements. She has nausea, vomiting, and increasing anxiety. Her family reports she has been restless and had episodes of confusion over the past 24 hours. She recently started an intense fasting-based diet program. Vital signs show blood pressure 158/92 mm Hg and pulse 118/min. Abdominal examination reveals a soft abdomen with no rebound or guarding. Neurologic examination shows mild proximal muscle weakness. Urine collected during triage is light in color but becomes dark red after standing for several hours. Laboratory studies show normal amylase, lipase, and liver function tests. Which of the following best describes the mode of transmission of this patient's likely underlying disorder?
questions.explanation:
Answer B(incorrectanswer):Autosomalrecessiveinheritance is notassociated withacuteintermittent porphyria. Some other rarer porphyrias, including congenital erythropoietic porphyria, follow this pattern.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Mitochondrial inheritance involves disorders passed exclusively through maternal lineage and does not describe the inheritance pattern seen in acute intermittent porphyria.

Answer D (incorrect answer): X-linked dominant inheritance is not associated with acute intermittent porphyria. Disorders with this pattern affect both males and females but do not match the genetics of this condition. chromosome that primarily affect males. Acute intermittent porphyria is not inherited in this manner. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 55-year-old man presents with several months of painless blistering on the backs of his hands. He reports that the blisters form after sun exposure and rupture easily, leaving erosions and areas of darkened skin. He also notes increased hair growth on his face. His medical history includes chronic hepatitis C and long-term alcohol use. Physical examination shows multiple crusted lesions and areas of skin fragility on the dorsal hands. Urine collected during the visit fluoresces a reddish-pink color under a Wood lamp. This patient has a deficiency in a metabolic pathway that begins with which of the following molecules?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (incorrect answer): Delta aminolevulinic acid is produced in the first enzymatic reaction of heme synthesis rather than initiating the pathway. It is not the starting molecule in the overall sequence.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Heme is the final product of the pathway, formed when iron is inserted into protoporphyrin IX. It is not the molecule that begins the pathway.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Porphobilinogen is produced after delta aminolevulinic acid is converted by ALA

Answer D (incorrect answer): Protoporphyrin IX is a late intermediate in heme synthesis, just before heme is formed by ferrochelatase. It is not the molecule that initiates the pathway. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman presents with severe abdominal pain that began 12 hours ago. She describes the pain as diffuse and crampy. Over the past two days she has experienced nausea, vomiting, and episodes of anxiety and insomnia. Her family reports she has been confused at times. She has no fever or diarrhea. She has no significant medical history but recently started a new dieting program and has been fasting intermittently. Physical examination shows mild tachycardia and hypertension. Abdominal exam reveals no rebound or guarding. Neurologic exam shows mild weakness in the proximal lower extremities. Laboratory testing shows normal amylase, lipase, and liver function tests. Urine collected during the episode darkens on standing. which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This woman has acute intermittent porphyria, a disorder caused by decreased porphobilinogen deaminase activity leading to accumulation of ALA and porphobilinogen. Patients usually present with severe abdominal pain, autonomic dysfunction with tachycardia and hypertension, psychiatric symptoms, neuropathy, and darkening of urine during attacks. Fasting increases ALA synthase activity and can precipitate episodes, which explains her recent symptom onset after starting a dieting program. The most and decreases production of neurotoxic porphyrin precursors.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Insulin has no role in treating acute intermittent porphyria. It does not correct the fundamental overproduction of ALA and porphobilinogen. porphyria cutanea tarda, but it does not decrease ALA or porphobilinogen accumulation and has no role in the treatment of acute intermittent porphyria. benefit in acute intermittent porphyria where the defect is related to heme precursor overproduction rather than iron overload.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Prednisone is used for many inflammatory and autoimmune disorders but does not reduce porphyrin precursor synthesis and has no therapeutic role in acute intermittent porphyria. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 48-year-old man comes to the clinic because of several months of painless blistering on the backs of his hands. He states that the blisters rupture easily and leave areas of scarring and discoloration. He has also noticed increased hair growth on his cheeks and temples. He works outdoors as a landscaper and spends many hours in direct sunlight. His medical history includes back of the hands. Urinalysis shows a reddish-brown color under fluorescent light. which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This man has porphyria cutanea tarda, a disorder caused by deficiency of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase. Patients usually present with blistering skin lesions, skin fragility on sun- common triggers. The deficiency of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase leads to accumulation of uroporphyrinogen in the liver and increased porphyrins in the urine. This can cause discoloration of the urine as described in the question.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Aminolevulinic acid synthase is the rate limiting enzyme in heme synthesis. Increased activity can precipitate acute attacks in acute intermittent porphyria, but this patient has cutaneous findings without neurovisceral symptoms (abdominal pain, tachycardia), which argues against that disorder.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Ferrochelatase deficiency causes erythropoietic protoporphyria, a very rare as seen in porphyria cutanea tarda.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency causes acute intermittent porphyria, which produces neurovisceral symptoms such as severe abdominal pain, neuropathy, and psychiatric changes rather than blistering photosensitivity.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Protoporphyrinogen oxidase deficiency results in variegate porphyria, a very rare condition that has both neurovisceral symptoms and photosensitivity. This patient lacks the acute abdominal or neurologic symptoms expected in that condition. MSW

questions.question: A 33-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of sudden onset of agitation and severe abdominal discomfort. She reports that the pain began earlier that morning and has worsened throughout the day. She describes the pain as a deep, aching sensation without radiation. Over the past week she has experienced constipation, difficulty sleeping, project and has been drinking more wine than usual while also skipping meals to lose weight. Vital signs show blood pressure 162/94 mm Hg and pulse 112/min. Physical examination reveals no abdominal tenderness. Neurologic exam shows reduced Which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This woman has clinical features of acute intermittent porphyria, a disorder caused by deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase. This deficiency results in accumulation of aminolevulinic acid and porphobilinogen, which produce attacks characterized by severe abdominal pain, autonomic instability such as hypertension and tachycardia, neuropathy, psychiatric symptoms, and darkening of urine. Increased alcohol intake and decreased caloric intake can activate hepatic ALA synthase and precipitate attacks.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Aminolevulinic acid synthase is upregulated during attacks of acute intermittent porphyria, often due to fasting, certain medications, or alcohol use, but it is not deficient in this disorder. marked by painful photosensitivity rather than acute neurovisceral symptoms like abdominal pain.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Protoporphyrinogen oxidase deficiency leads to variegate porphyria, which presents with both neurovisceral symptoms and photosensitivity. This patient does not have cutaneous manifestations.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency results in porphyria cutanea tarda, which presents with blistering photosensitivity and chronic liver involvement rather than acute abdominal pain and neuropathy. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman is evaluated for skin blisters. She has a history of chronic hepatitis C but is otherwise healthy and takes no medications. For the past six weeks she has noted itchy skin blisters on the backs of her hands and forearms. Several blisters have burst leaking yellow fluid but no pus. She has been in the sun recently but has not had any sunburns. She also reports a deep red color to her urine. Skin exam reveals scattered blisters and bullae bilaterally on the backs of the hands and forearms. Erosions are present in areas of bullae rupture. Serum testing shows increased levels of AST and ALT. This woman's presentation may be explained by abnormal metabolism in which of the following locations?
questions.explanation: Answers A, B, C (incorrect answers): Although skin abnormalities develop in PCT due to porphyrin deposition in skin, basal skin cells, keratinocytes, and dermal endothelial cells are not the underlying cause of the disorder. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman is evaluated for recurrent abdominal pain. For the past six months she has had episodes of severe pain in her abdomen that occur every few days to weeks. Her primary care doctor ordered an abdominal CT scan with normal results. Today she noted abdominal pain that began while she was at work. She describes the pain as severe and sharp. The pain is diffuse and present in all abdominal quadrants. Her urine was red-colored this morning and she recalls the same discoloration during past episodes of pain. Her only medication is oral contraceptives which she began one year ago. On physical exam, the abdomen is soft with no rebound tenderness. Weakness and delayed patellar reflexes are present bilaterally in the legs. She is afebrile. Serum testing shows normal white blood cell count. which of the following is most likely to be found in her urine?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This woman has classic features of acute intermittent porphyria (AIP). The typical presentation is recurrent bouts of abdominal pain associated with neuropathy (weakness, paresthesias), and urine discoloration ("port wine-colored urine"). The pain in AIP is neuropathic so rebound tenderness, fever, and leukocytosis should be absent. AIP is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by decreased activity of the liver enzyme porphobilinogen deaminase. With enzyme deficiency, porphobilinogen accumulates and can be found in the urine. This gives urine a classic port wine color. Abdominal pain and neuropathy are due to nerve irritation. Many medications can trigger attacks in AIP including estrogens found in oral contraceptives. AIP is very rare and the diagnosis is often missed for many years due to the non-specific signs and symptoms.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Bilirubin is found in the urine in many forms of liver and biliary disease. It causes a brown discoloration ofurine.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Uroporphyrin is found in the urine of patients with porphyria cutanea tarda, a form of porphyria with skin blistering. tyrosine metabolism. The major clinical manifestation of this disorder is joint pain.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Glucose is found in the urine among patients with hyperglycemia or Fanconi syndrome. W Himi

questions.question: A 45-year-old man with a history of systemic lupus erythematous is evaluated for groin pain. For the past ten years he has required glucocorticoid therapy for lupus. For the past two months, he has found it difficult to bear weight on his left side due to constant, throbbing groin pain. On examination, pain is elicited with any motion of the left hip. MRI shows diffuse left femoral head edema with degenerative changes. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Answer C(correct answer):Thismanhas avascular necrosis(alsocalled aseptic necrosis orosteonecrosis)of the femoral head, a common problem in patients with lupus, especially those who take steroids. Vascular damage to the bone blood supply leads to necrosis of bone marrow elements and, ultimately, mechanical failure of the hip joint. The process is progressive with joint failure usually occurring within a few years, necessitating hip replacement surgery. The mechanism of the association between glucocorticoids and avascular necrosis is unclear. It may involve increases in bone marrow adipocyte size, which blocks venous outflow. The term osteonecrosis is a general term for necrosis of bone. Some cases have an obvious cause of ischemic damage (e.g., femoral neck fracture). In most cases, however, the exact cause is unknown. Many of these cases are associated with lupus or glucocorticoid therapy via a poorly understood mechanism.

Answers A, B, D (incorrect answers): Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and gout are problems of the joints ("arthritis") and not the bone. MRI findings of bone edema and degeneration do not occur unless a secondary boneprocessisinvolved.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Trochanteric bursitis isinflammation of the trochantericbursa located near the hips. Bursa are fluid-filled sacs that provide cushioning between bone and soft tissue. Trochanteric bursitis is a common cause of hip pain, but is not associated with femoral head abnormalities on MRI. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 60-year-old woman is evaluated for dyspnea and edema. She has type II diabetes and systolic heart failure (left ventricular ) ' s s is a ( = o o <1.1). Her medications include lisinopril, carvedilol, spironolactone, atorvastatin, and aspirin. Two weeks ago, she developed an upper respiratory infection and was treated with amoxicillin. Over the past three days, she has noted increasing shortness of breath and lower extremity edema. Her weight has increased by five pounds. On examination, she has crackles and 2+ lower extremity edema. A maculopapular rash is noted on her trunk and abdomen. blood cell casts. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This woman has interstitial nephritis, a hypersensitivity (i.e., allergic) disorder of the kidneys. Inflammation in this woman's kidneys has led to acute renal failure which in turn has caused fluid overload (dyspnea, edema, rales). White blood cell (wBC) casts indicate inflammation of the nephron as seen in interstitial nephritis. Urinary WBCs without bacteria are called "sterile pyuria," a classic finding in interstitial nephritis. This woman also has a rash consistent with hives. Interstitial nephritis triggered by antibiotics is often seen as in the case described.

Answer A(incorrect answer): The classic cause of WBC casts is pyelonephritis, but nothing in the case suggests this diagnosis. Pyelonephritis develops from an ascending bladder infection. Patients have dysuria and urinary frequency that indicate bladder involvement.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Diabetic nephropathy can lead to abnormal kidney function; however, it develops slowly over years. In addition, WBC casts are not usually seen.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Glomerulonephritis usually leads tothe nephritic syndrome.The major finding is glomerular bleeding with dysmorphic red blood cells and red blood cell casts.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Acute heart failure can cause rales and edema as seen in this patient. Indeed, heart failure is a very common cause of the clinical presentation described. However, the WBC casts in the urine and maculopapular rash cannot be explained by heart failure. Mc MeJ5

questions.question: An 82-year-old woman is referred for a chest X-ray to evaluate a cough. She has a history of rheumatoid arthritis for which she has taken glucocorticoids for many years. She also has chronic back pain. Lung findings on chest X-ray are normal, but an incidental finding is made of vertebral fractures in the lower thoracic spine. She is referred for dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) testing. Her T-score is -2.8. Which of the following most likely contributed to this woman's T-score?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This woman has glucocorticoid-associated osteoporosis. Osteoporosis is a condition of decreased bone density which increases the risk of fractures. Osteoporosis is generally asymptomatic until a fracture occurs. Vertebral fractures are most common, often identified incidentally by X-ray as in this case. The diagnosis of osteoporosis can be made by dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) testing. A T-score is a comparison of bone density in the patient to that of a healthy 30-year-old. A score of -2.5 indicates the patient is greater than 2.5 standard deviations below the bone density of a 30-year-old adult. T-scores less than -2.5 are consistent with osteoporosis. Glucocorticoids increase bone resorption by osteoclasts and decrease bone formation by osteoblasts. Like most Mc steroid hormones, glucocorticoids alter gene expression in cells. In bone, glucocorticoid nuclear receptors are Graw found in osteoblasts. With long-term use, glucocorticoids inhibit osteoblast proliferation, leading to decreased bone formation. Key point: Steroid hormones are lipid-soluble and cross cell membranes to exert effects intracellularly. In questions about the effects of steroid hormones (cortisol, estrogens, aldosterone), look for an answer that involves alterations in DNA transcription. This may include changes to cell growth and differentiation, or synthesis of proteins. synthesis of calcium channels. This leads to a fall in calcium, which increases parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels. The rise in PTH levels exacerbates the decline in bone density.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Glucocorticoids are associated with low vitamin-D activity and vitamin-D deficiency. The mechanism of this effect is unclear.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Glucocorticoids decrease renal calcium reabsorption, which increases calcium excretion. This further stimulates PTH release, which exacerbates the fall in bone density. Key Point: Glucocorticoids have many negative effects on bone density. A common theme is that all glucocorticoid-associated bone effects decrease serum calcium (less GI absorption, more renal excretion), raise PTH levels, decrease vitamin-D activity, and inhibit osteoblasts. Basically, most physiologic functions beneficial to bone density are inhibited by glucocorticoids. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 62-year-old man is evaluated for malaise and fatigue. He has a history of ischemic cardiomyopathy with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 15%. His medications include metoprolol, lisinopril, spironolactone, and furosemide. For the past week he has been taking ibuprofen several times per day for lower back pain. Serum creatinine is 4.6 mg/dL (normal <1.1) compared to 1.omg/dL one week ago. Which of the following effects of ibuprofen is responsible for this man's change in renal function?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This man has acute kidney injury caused by the non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) ibuprofen. NSAIDs inhibit the synthesis of prostaglandins by the enzyme cyclooxygenase. Prostaglandins are lipid molecules synthesized by many cell types. In the kidneys, they function as vasodilators. Under conditions of poor renal perfusion, prostaglandins are synthesized to dilate the afferent arteriole and maintain renal perfusion. This man has poor renal perfusion due to heart failure and treatment with diuretics (spironolactone and furosemide). His kidneys require prostaglandins to maintain renal perfusion. The inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis by ibuprofen has led to afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction and acute kidney injury (rising serum creatinine).

Answer B (incorrect answer): Prostaglandins in the kidneys are predominantly vasodilators. By inhibitng their effects, NsAIDs lead to vasoconstriction, not vasodilation.

Answers C, D (incorrect answers): The major renal effects of NsAIDs are on the afferent arteriole, not the efferent arteriole. hyperplasia. There is no reason for this man to develop urinary obstruction after one week of ibuprofen therapy. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 72-year-old man presents to the emergency department with chest pain. EKG shows anterior ST-segment elevations. He is administered aspirin. Aspirin is beneficial in this man due to inhibition of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This man is having an ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), an acute coronary syndrome cause by plaque rupture and occlusion of a coronary artery. Aspirin irreversibly inhibits prostaglandins. Inhibition of cyclooxygenase in acute coronary syndromes is beneficial because this reduces the level of thromboxanes in platelets.ThromboxaneA2is apotentactivator ofplatelets.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Phospholipase A2 uses lipids from cell walls to synthesize arachidonic acid, the substrate for cyclooxygenase. This enzyme is not affected by aspirin.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Lipoxygenase converts arachidonic acid into leukotrienes, which are signaling molecules. This enzyme is not affected by aspirin.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Thromboxane A2 synthase functions downstream of cyclooxygenase and converts PGH into thromboxane A2. This enzyme is not affected by aspirin.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Prostacyclin synthase also functions downstream of cyclooxygenase in the eicosanoid pathway. It converts PGH into prostacyclins. This enzyme is not affected by aspirin. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 15-year-old girl with moderate, persistent asthma is administered inhaled glucocorticoids. This therapy will improve her asthma via which of the following mechanisms?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): Glucocorticoids have a number of anti-inflammatory effects that are beneficial in They exert their effects by modifying gene transcription in the nucleus. When glucocorticoids enter cells, they bind to a cytoplasmic receptor which translocates to the nucleus where glucocorticoids inactivate pro- inflammatory transcription factors like nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-kB). NF-kB is the classic example of a pro- inflammatory gene transcription factor. It can increase expression of genes for inflammatory cytokines including interleukin 1 (IL-1) and tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-a). Through inactivation of NF-kB, glucocorticoids suppress inflammation.In addition to this anti-inflammatory effect, in T-cells, glucocorticoids have been shown to increase IL-10 synthesis. IL-10 is an anti-inflammatory cytokine that inhibits production of

Answer A (incorrect answer): Beta-2 receptors are found in bronchiolar smooth muscle. Activation of these receptors leads to bronchodilation. Inhaled beta 2 agonists like albuterol are used in the treatment of asthma, but this is not the mechanism of action of glucocorticoids.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Leukotrienes are lipid-signaling molecules derived from arachidonic acid with pro- inflammatory effects. Leukotriene receptor antagonists like montelukast are used in the treatment of asthma, but this is not the mechanism of action of glucocorticoids.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Muscarinic receptors in the lungs promote bronchoconstriction. Muscarinic receptor of action of glucocorticoids.

Answer E (incorrect answer): The enzyme 5-lipoxygenase inhibition synthesizes leukotrienes from arachidonic acid. Inhibitors of 5-lipoxygenase like zileuton are used in the treatment of asthma, but this is not the mechanism of action of glucocorticoids. Mc Graw Hmi

questions.question: An 87-year-old woman presents to her physician with redness and swelling of her right knee, which started suddenly yesterday. She has no recent trauma. She reports that she has chronic pain in her knees, but her current pain is much worse than normal. She has no fevers, chills, rash or recent trauma. Her medical history includes osteoarthritis, hypertension and hypothyroidism. Her current medications include acetaminophen, hydrochlorothiazide and levothyroxine. She drinks two glasses of wine daily. Vital signs include a temperature of 98.7°F, blood pressure of 152/67 mmHg and heart rate of 69 beats/minute. Evaluation of his right knee reveals swelling, redness, tenderness and warmth. Results of laboratory testing are shown below. An x-ray of the affected knee is also shown. Arthrocentesis is performed which shows 21o0 white blood cells/μL management?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (incorrect answer): This patient has a clincial presentation consistent with pseudogout, which is a arthritis, presence of risk factors (e.g., older age, hypercalcemia and underlying osteoarthritis) and xray findings of chrondrocalcinosis. Chondrocalcinosis is calcification of the cartilage (see red arrows in image above) that occurs due to calcium pyrophosphate deposition in the joints. The diagnosis of pseudogout should be confirmed with arthrocentesis, which typically shows rhomboid crystals that are positively birefringent, as well as a slightly elevated white blood cell count (greater than 2,ooo per microliter) with a negative Gram stain. Arthrocentesis in septic joints will have a markedly higher white blood cell count, generally over 25,oo0 cells per microliter. Treament for an acute pseudogout attack may include intraarticular glucocorticoid injection, non- steroidal anti-inflammatory agents (NsAIDs) or colchicine. Administering a intraarticular glucocorticoid injection is often a preferred initial treatment when only one joint is involved. NsAIDs are not an ideal choice in this patient given her impaired renal function.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Pegloticase is a recombinant form of uricase that promotes the breakdown of urate. It is given for prevention of acute gout attacks in patients who have severe, refractory gout. It is not used for acute attacks of either pseudogout or gout.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Probenecid is a uricosuric drug that promotes the excretion of urate. It is used to prevent gout attacks. It is not used in the treatment of acute attacks of either pseudogout or gout.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Naproxen is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agent that could be used to treat acute flares of gout or pseudogout. It should be avoided in patients with underlying kidney disease, such as this patient, because of the risk of acute kidney injury. e d and strength; however, it will not treat an acute pseudogout flare. Hmi

questions.question: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his mother due to knee pain. He has no known recent trauma. The boy is chronically nonverbal and appears uncomfortable when bearing weight on his right leg. Vital signs include a temperature of 98.5°F, blood pressure of 101/63 mmHg and heart rate of 72 beats/minute. The patient is sitting in a chair and repetitively banging his head against the wall. Intermittently he makes a writhing movement of his right then left arm. There is scabbing present on the lips and bilateral nail beds. Auscultation of the heart and lung is normal. The abdomen is soft, non-tender and non-distended; there is no hepatosplenomegaly. Neurologic evaluation reveals decreased tone in the muscles of the arms and legs. Evaluation of his right knee shows redness, tenderness and warmth. The other joints are normal. The skin is warm and dry with normal skin turgor and no rash. Arthrocentesis of the knee is performed which shows needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Answer A (incorrect answer): Hemochromatosis is a genetic disorder which causes increased intestinal iron skin, dilated cardiomyopathy and diabetes mellitus. It may be associated with cognitive impairment, but does not cause self-mutilating behavior, chorea or hypotonia. Patients with hemochromatosis are at increased risk fordevelopingpseudogout. associated with self-mutilating behavior, chorea or hypotonia.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Von Gierke's disease is a glycogen storage disease caused by glucose-6- phosphatase deficiency. It typically presents in infancy as severe hypoglycemia that occurs between meals. The hypoglycemia may lead to seizures. Patients with this condition are at increased risk for gout. This condition is not associated with self-mutilating behavior, chorea or hypotonia.

He states that in the hospital he had acute redness and tenderness of the ball of his foot; an aspiration was performed, and he was diagnosed with acute gout. He is interested in preventing future gout attacks. His other medical history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease and depression. His current medications include lisinopril, metformin, insulin and fluoxetine. He does not drink alcohol. He has been trying to lose weight, exercise and eat a vegetarian diet since he was discharged from the hospital. On evaluation, his BMI is 32 kg/m2 and vital signs are within normal limits. Musculoskeletal evaluation does not show any redness or swelling of the joints, but a non-tender nodule is palpated on his right elbow. The skin overlying the nodule has no erythema or rash. A non-tender nodule is also palpated at the first metatarsophalangeal joint on the left. Results of this patient to prevent future episodes of gout?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This patient had a recent gout attack and his current laboratory results reveal hyperuricemia and evidence of renal insufficiency (creatinine clearance of less than 60 mL/minute). On examination, he also has evidence of tophi, which are accumulations of urate in connective tissue. He should be started on pharmacologic urate-lowering therapy due to his renal insufficiency, which limits the body's abilities to remove urate through the urine, and evidence of tophi. The primary indications for urate-lowering therapy are frequent or disabling attacks of gout, tophi, joint damage and renal insufficiency. Urate-lowering therapy may helpprevent further tophi development and progressivejoint destruction.Allopurinol is a xanthine oxidase is to decrease the serum urate level to less than 6 mg/dL. Allopurinol is considered safe to use in patients with renal dysfunction, although it is typically started at a low dose (less than 1o0 mg/day) and titrated up as thrombocytopenia or diarrhea. Often patients are given colchicine in conjunction with a xanthine oxidase inhibitor for the first few months of treatment to prevent a gout flare. The patient should be encouraged to continue weight loss, exercise, avoidance of alcohol and reduction in consumptions of animal and seafood protein; lifestyle modifications may decrease the risk of gout flares; however, given his renal dysfunction and evidence of tophi, lifestyle modifications alone may be insufficient to prevent acute gout attacks or prevent joint damage from urate deposition.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Prednisone is a glucocorticoid that may be used to treat acute gout. It is not used chronically to prevent gout attacks.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Rasburicase is a recombinant form of uricase thatpromotes the breakdown of syndrome. It is not typically used to prevent gout attacks.

questions.explanation: Answer F (correct answer): This girl has tumor lysis syndrome associated with induction chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). Tumor lysis is an oncologic emergency that results from the release of potassium, phosphate, and nucleic acids into the systemic circulation. Nucleic acids are catabolized into uric acid, leading to hyperuricemia and acute kidney injury. The clinical symptoms of tumor lysis syndrome are related to the electrolyte abnormalities and include nausea, vomiting, lethargy, seizures, muscle cramps, cardiac dysrhythmias, andtetany. The phosphorus concentration in malignant cells is four times that of normal cells. For this reason, tumor lysis leads to hyperphosphatemia. Phosphate binds calcium and pulls it from the serum. Due to this effect, elevated serum phosphate concentrations lead to hypocalcemia and the precipitation of calcium phosphate crystals in the kidneys. Malignant cells also contain high levels of potassium, so tumor lysis leads to hyperkalemia.

Because the bladder is irritated in HC, patients may also develop "lower urinary tract symptoms" meaning symptoms related to the bladder (the kidneys and ureters are the upper urinary tract). These include burning with urination, urinary frequency, and a sensation of incomplete emptying. HC is caused by acrolein,a metabolite of cyclophosphamide that is toxic to the bladder. Mesna, a substance that binds acrolein, can be used to reduce the risk of HC. HC can occur in up to 4o% of patients receiving cyclophosphamide. questions.question: A 70-year-old woman with a history of rheumatoid arthritis is seen for her annual wellness exam. She has morning stiffness that improves throughout the day. questions.explanation:

The mechanism of Felty syndrome is unknown, and it usually occurs in patients with longstanding, severe RA. The chronic neutropenia of Felty syndrome is associated with recurrent bacterial infections, most commonly respiratory tract and skin infections. Treatment is with disease-modifying, anti-rheumatic drugs like methotrexate. Other long-term complications from RA include osteoporosis, which occurs secondary to disease progression and chronic steroid use. This is associated with an increased risk of hip fractures. questions.question: A 45-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis develops neutropenia and splenomegaly. She undergoes splenectomy. A subsequent peripheral blood smear has the finding shown below. This finding is due to loss of which of the following in the spleen?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This woman has Felty's syndrome, a rare complication of severe rheumatoid arthritis. Through a poorly understood mechanism, some patients with long-standing, severe rheumatoid arthritis develop neutropenia and splenomegaly, leaving them prone to infections. The triad of rheumatoid arthritis, neutropenia, and splenomegaly is called Felty's syndrome. Neutropenia in Felty's syndrome often improves after splenectomy. This woman also has target cells (also called codocytes) in her peripheral blood. Target cells are red blood cells cells occur when the ratio of cell volume to cell membrane decreases. This can be due to shrinking of red cells (decreased cell volume), as occurs in microcytic anemias due to iron deficiency or thalassemia. This can also happen in patients with liver disease. The liver enzyme lecithin-cholesterol acyl transferase (LCAT) influences the ratio of cholesterol to phospholipids in red-cell membranes. With decreased LCAT activity in liver disease, red- cell membranes increase in size. This reduces the ratio of cell volume to cell membrane, leading to target cells. As in liver disease, target cells are seen following splenectomy due to increased cell membrane size. The sinusoids in the red pulp of the spleen normally remove excess membrane from red cells in a process called "splenic conditioning." With splenectomy, red cells have generally larger cell membranes and a lower ratio of cell volume to cell membrane. This leads to target cells. The red pulp of the spleen contains the Cords of Billroth. Among their major roles are the conditioning of red cells and the removal of aging red cells.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Germinal centers are found in lymph nodes and the spleen. These are sites of B-cell growth, maturation, and conversion to antibody-secreting plasma cells.

Answer C (incorrect answer): The marginal zone is the portion of the spleen between the red pulp and the white pulp. Its major role is the removal of antigens (i.e., debris) from the blood, and exposure of antigens to antigen- presenting cells like macrophages and dendritic cells.

Answers D, E (incorrect answers): The follicles and periarteriolar lymphoid sheaths are part of the white pulp of the white pulp is the exposure of blood to B-cells and T-cells. Mc Graw Him

Answer C (correct answer): This woman has meningitis due to Streptococcus pneumoniae. Patients without a spleen (e.g., following splenectomy) are at increased risk for infection from encapsulated bacteria including S.pneumoniae. Encapsulated bacteria have a polysaccharide capsule that resists phagocytosis. The spleen is critical for defense against these pathogens because one of its major functions is removal of bacteria from the blood. When encapsulated bacteria become coated with small amounts of IgG and complement proteins, splenic macrophages recognize these opsonins(antibodies and complement)and clear the infection.Splenectomized patients are markedly deficient in the ability to remove IgG-coated bacteria from the blood. E. coli may cause meningitis in newborns exposed to the bacteria during vaginal delivery, but E. coli meningitis in adults is extremely rare. Mc Graw

Answer C (correct answer): This man has primary myelofibrosis, a myeloproliferative disorder in which bone marrow is replaced by fibrous tissue. questions.question: A 33-year-old G1p0 pregnant woman is evaluated for increasing fatigue. She also reports photophobia and itchy eyes that are worse at night and a dry mouth. She is otherwise healthy and is not taking any medications. Her vital signs are normal. Physical examination reveals dry, scaly skin on the lower extremities, halitosis and bilateral punctate conjunctival antibodies.
