This drug is not used in Mycobacteria avium complex prophylaxis. decreases the formation of tetrahydrofolate.Folate is required for bacterial thymidine and DNA synthesis. not MAC infections. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman presents to clinic with a cough. Ten days ago, she developed fever, congestion, and rhinitis. Over the last five days, she has had a hacking cough, which is productive of green sputum. The cough is keeping her up at night and she is fatigued from lack of sleep. Her past medical history is significant for hypertension, diabetes mellitus type II, and depression. Medications include lisinopril, metformin, and sertraline. She denies tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drug use. Temperature is 99.5°F, pulse is 85/min, blood pressure is 114/70 mmHg, respiratory rate is 16/min, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. Heart sounds are regular with normal S1 and S2. Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally with trace rhonchi. Percussion is resonant throughout. Chest x-ray is displayed below. which of the following is the most appropriate
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This patient is presenting with symptoms and chest x-ray findings consistent with acute bronchitis. The majority of cases of bronchitis occur after viral upper respiratory tract infection (URTI). The clinical presentation usually starts with viral URTI symptoms (low-grade fever, sore throat, congestion) with later development of productive cough. Patients can have rhonchi on examination that typically clear with likely in pneumonia. Management of acute bronchitis focuses on supportive care. The majority of cases are caused by viruses, so antibiotics are not indicated. Symptomatic treatment can include antitussives (benzonatate, dextromethorphan), non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and bronchodilators.

Answers A and D (incorrect answers): Azithromycin and levofloxacin are antibiotics for the treatment of dyspnea, hypoxemia, or a pulmonary infiltrate. Over 95% of cases of acute bronchitis are caused by viruses, so antibiotics are not prescribed.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Although ACE inhibitors can cause chronic dry cough through the elevation of bradykinin levels, this patient's productive cough with rhonchi is more likely due to bronchitis given the recent viral URTI.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Oral corticosteroids should not be used for acute bronchitis in adults because they do not reduce symptom duration or severity. An exception to this is in patients with asthma, who may develop asthma exacerbations in the setting of respiratory infections. Mc Graw IH

questions.question: A 62-year-old man presents to the emergency department due to fevers, dyspnea, and cough. His symptoms started 48 hours for left lower lobe pneumonia, which improved each time with broad spectrum antibiotics. Medications include amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide. He has smoked one-half pack per day of cigarettes for the last 40 years. He drinks four beers nightly. Temperature is 101.5°F, pulse is 105/min, blood pressure is 114/70 mmHg, respiratory rate is 22/min, and oxygen saturation is 87% on room air. Rales are present in the left lung base. A chest x-ray is obtained that shows left lower lobe pneumonia. Which of the following is the most likely cause of recurrent pneumonia in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This patient is presenting with recurrent pneumonia in the left lower lobe. Given that his pneumonia episodes in the past have responded to antibiotics, this current infection is most likely bacterial. Patients with recurrent pneumonia in the same location often have partial obstruction of a bronchus supplying that lobe. The most likely cause of bronchial obstruction in this patient is lung cancer, given his smoking history and older age. Endobronchial lung cancers compress the airway and prevent clearance of secretions, resulting in elevated risk of pneumonia in lung areas distal to the obstruction.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Aspiration is another cause of recurrent pneumonia. Aspiration pneumonias typically occur in the right middle or lower lobes, not the left lower lobe.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Patients with immunodeficiencies can develop recurrent pneumonia, but the pneumonia occurs in different locations or is multifocal.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Tuberculosis presents insidiously with chronic cough, weight loss, and night sweats. Mc Graw Hm

questions.question: A 55-year-old man presents to primary care clinic for fever, chills, and cough for the last 12 hours. He has also had dyspnea on exertion. He denies congestion, sore throat, abdominal pain, or increased urinary frequency. His past medical history includes obesity and type II diabetes mellitus. He does not use tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs. Temperature is 100.5°F, pulse is 85/min, blood pressure is 134/80 mmHg, respiratory rate is 16/min, and oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. Oropharynx is moist with normal mucosa. Heart sounds are regular with normal S1 and S2. Pulmonary auscultation reveals rales in the right lung base. Lower extremities have trace pitting edema. A chest x-ray is obtained and displayed below. which of the following is the most appropriate step in management?

options.B: Recommend repeat chest x-ray in one week
options.E: Start doxycycline and follow up in three days

questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This patient is presenting with clinical features consistent with the diagnosis of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP). CAP presents with fever, productive cough, and dyspnea, but can also cause sepsis and acute hypoxemic respiratory failure if severe. The diagnosis of CAP requires the demonstration of a pulmonary infiltrate on chest imaging along with a clinically compatible syndrome. This patient has a clear lobar infiltrate inthe right middle lobe. Patients with CAP can be hospitalized or managed as an outpatient. One commonly utilized scoring system for determining the need for hospitalization is the CURB-65 criteria (see above). If the patient meets two or more criteria, they are at higher risk for severe disease, and hospitalization is recommended. In this patient, the oral antimicrobial options include macrolides (azithromycin) or doxycycline. It is reasonable to follow-up with the patient in a few days because ongoing fever or persistent respiratory symptoms may warrant an escalation of therapy.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Acetaminophen and dextromethorphan are supportive therapies used for symptom startingantibiotictherapytakesprecedence. high-risk patients to confirm resolution of pneumonia and rule out underlying malignancy.

Answer C (incorrect answer): If this patient had a higher CURB-65 score, referral to the emergency department or direct hospital admission would be appropriate.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Sputum and blood cultures are typically obtained in patients with severe CAP that are admitted to the medical wards or intensive care unit. They are not usually obtained for outpatient CAP cases. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 55-year-old homeless man is admitted to the intensive care unit for altered mental status. He was found unconscious in a local park and was intubated upon arrival to the emergency department. Urine and serum toxicology screens were positive for alcohol, benzodiazepines, and opiates. After 60 hours in the ICU, he remains intubated for altered mental status and agitation. Over the last six hours, the FiO2 has been increased from 50% to 80% to maintain oxygen saturation over 94%. Past medical history is significant for uncontrolled type II diabetes mellitus and polysubstance use. He was last admitted to the hospital three months ago for osteomyelitis, for which he received intravenous antibiotics and right hallux amputation. are coarse bilaterally. A chest x-ray shows a left lingular infiltrate that was not present on admission. Endotracheal aspirate

options.D: Start intravenous fluids, vancomycin, and ceftazidime

questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This patient has developed fever, hypoxemia, and new pulmonary infiltrate, which is consistent with ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP). In addition, his VAP appears to be causing sepsis, as suggested by fever, tachycardia, and hypotension. VAP is a type of hospital-acquired pneumonia that develops Mc Graw hypoxemia, leukocytosis, and new pulmonary infiltrate on chest imaging. Initial management of VAP should focus on obtaining appropriate cultures to guide antibiotic treatment, including sputum and blood. After obtaining cultures, broad spectrum antibiotics should be initiated. This patienthas twokeyindicationsforbroad coverage of multidrugresistant organismslike methicillinresistant Staphylococcus aureus orPseudomonas.First,hereceived a course of intravenous antibioticswithin thelast three months. Secondly, he has developed sepsis. Therefore, MRsA coverage (with vancomycin) and Pseudomonas coverage (ceftazidime, cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, or meropenem) should be administered. In addition to these therapies, this patient should be administered intravenous fluids as part of the management of sepsis.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Obtaining a chest CT angiogram would be indicated if there was concern for acute pulmonary embolism. This patient's fever and chest infiltrate make VAP a more likely cause of his hypoxemic respiratory failure.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Bronchoscopy and bronchoalveolar lavage is typically used to obtain microbial data for cases of severe pneumonia that are not improving. This patient needs immediate medical therapy to managesepsis.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Ceftriaxone and azithromycin are appropriate for community acquired pneumonia, but do not cover organisms like MRsA or Pseudomonas.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Treatment of sepsis focuses on obtaining cultures, followed by broad spectrum antibiotics and intravenous fluids. If this patient's hypotension does not improve after appropriate fluid resuscitation, then vasopressor agents such as norepinephrine are indicated. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 62-year-old man presents to the emergency department due to cough. Over the last three weeks he has developed a cough that is productive of foul-smelling sputum. He has also had low-grade fever and night sweats. His past medical history includes hypertension, schizoaffective disorder, and alcohol use disorder. Medications include lisinopril and quetiapine. He smokes 1 pack per day of cigarettes. He drinks a pint of whiskey every two days. Temperature is 99.9°F, pulse is 95/min, blood dentition. He has rhonchi heard in the right mid and upper lung fields. A chest x-ray is displayed below. which of the
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This patient is presenting with clinical features consistent with a lung abscess. A lung abscess is a necrotic area of pulmonary tissue that is most commonly a complication of aspiration of anaerobic organisms, such as Bacteroides, Peptostreptococcus, and Prevotella. In rare cases, other respiratory tract flora can cause abscesses, such as Streptococcus species, Staphylococcus aureus, and Klebsiella. Risk factors for abscess development include alcohol use disorder and dysphagia. Patients present with indolent symptoms, such as productive cough, fever, and night sweats. The diagnosis is made with chest imaging that demonstrates a pulmonary infiltrate with a central cavity (white arrows in image above), indicating necrosis of tissue in this area. Treatment is with empiric antibiotic regimens with strong anaerobic coverage, such as ampicillin- sulbactam or piperacillin-tazobactam.

Answers B and D (incorrect answers): Ceftriaxone/azithromycin and levofloxacin are appropriate inpatient antibiotic regimens in patients with community-acquired pneumonia. Neither regimen covers anaerobic organisms.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside antibiotic with broad gram-negative coverage, including pseudomonas. It does not cover anaerobic organisms. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman who is sixteen weeks pregnant is evaluated for fever, headache, fatigue, and a rash on her arm. She recently returned from vacation in New Hampshire, where she spent a week hiking in the woods with friends. Her axilla. Which of the following antibiotics is the best choice for this woman?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This woman has erythema migrans, the classic "bull's-eye" rash associated with Lyme disease. She needs an antibiotic that covers Borrelia burgdorferi and is safe in pregnancy. This woman contracted Lyme disease in the woods of New Hampshire when she was bitten by a deer tick (Ixodes scapularis) that remained attached for 48 hours. Patients initially present with expanding erythema migrans and flu-like symptoms one to two weeks after the tick bite. Several weeks to months later, patients present with neurologic several years later with arthritis, peripheral neuropathy, and mild cognitive dysfunction (tertiary Lyme disease). considered first-line therapy in patients with Lyme disease, it is contraindicated in pregnancy because it crosses the placenta and can accumulate in fetal bones and teeth. For this reason, ceftriaxone is the best choice for this woman among the options presented.

Answers A and E (incorrect answers): Streptomycin and gentamicin are aminoglycoside antibiotics that are not effective in treating Lyme disease. In addition, these drugs are avoided in pregnancy (category D) due to risk of renal malformation and ototoxicity in the fetus. risk to developing cartilage in several animal studies. In addition, ciprofloxacin is not effective in treating Lyme disease.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, a sulfonamide antibiotic, is contraindicated in the first and last trimester because it disrupts folate metabolism (leading to neural tube defects) and displaces bilirubin from albumin (leading to kernicterus). In addition, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole is not effective in treating Lyme disease. Mc

questions.question: A 28-year-old man presents to the emergency room with a rash, headache and muscle soreness. Earlier in the day, he was evaluated for a non-pruritic, maculopapular rash involving the trunk and extremities, including the palms and soles. A single dose of penicillin was administered, and he was discharged to follow up with his primary care doctor. Twelve hours later after swimming outside, his rash expanded to involve his chest without pruritius. He also developed facial flushing, a headache and diffuse muscle soreness. He has a history of nausea after receiving amoxicillin in the past for sinusitis. His temperature is 100.5° F. Heart rate is 92/min and blood pressure is 110/75 mmHg. Physical exam reveals a diffuse maculopapular rash on the chest, trunk and extremeties including the palms and soles. Lung exam is normal. which of the following is the most likely cause of this man's current symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This man has theJarisch-Herxheimer (JH) reaction which occurs within 24 hours of penicillin administration in up to 35% of patients with spirochete infections. Classic features include fever, Mc Graw secondary to bacterial cell death and the resulting release in inflammatory cytokines and immune complexes. It is self-limited and usually resolves within 24 hours.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Photosensitivity occurs among paitents in response to certain drugs. Photosensitivity reactions are like sunburns and present with a diffuse red rash in sun-exposed areas. This man

Answer C (incorrect answer): Type I hypersensitivity reactions to drugs like penicillin typically occur within one hour of drug administration and are caused by immunogobulin E (IgE)-mediated histamine release. Clinical features include urticaria (raised red plaques), bronchospasm (wheezing), and anaphylaxis (diffuse vasodilation leading to hypotension). Patients may also present with angioedema (swelling of the face, tongue, and larynx), nausea, vomiting, and dry cough. A key distinction between hypersensitivity reactions and the JH reaction is that the JH reaction is a worsening of hoursofdrugexposure.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Resistance to penicillin among strains of T. pallidum is very rare. This man's presentation is classic for the JH reaction which is the more likely explanation for his presentation.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Disulfiram inhibits acetaldehyde dehydrogenase, resulting in acetaldehyde accumulation in patients who consume alcohol. Other drugs that have a similar effect are said to cause a flushing, tachycardia, nausea, and vomiting. This clinical scenario is not consistent with a disulfiram reaction. Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK557820/ Mc

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman is evaluated for fever, headache, red eyes, and myalgias. Ten days ago she returned from a triathlon in conjunctival erythema with subconjunctival hemorrhages and scleral icterus. Peripheral blood smear shows no red cell inclusions. Laboratory results include: Hemoglobin: 12.5 g/dL (normal 12 to 15 g/dL) Platelet count: 90 × 109/L (normal 150 to 400 × 109/L) Potassium: 2.9 mmol/L (normal 3.6 to 5.2 mmol/L) Creatinine 1.4 mg/dL (normal 0.5 to 1 mg/dL) Aspartate aminotransferase: 148 U/L (normal 10 to 40 U/L) Alanine aminotransferase: 115 U/L (normal 7 to 56 U/L) Serum bilirubin: 3.8 mg/dL (normal 0.3 to 1 mg/dL) Direct bilirubin: 2.2 mg/dL (normal 0 to 0.4 mg/dL) Which of the following is most likely indicated at this time?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (incorrect answer): Patients with severe disease from leptospirosis can be treated with the cephalosporins, ceftriaxone or cefotaxime, but not cefazolin. Cefazolin is a first generation cephalosporin used to cover grampositive skin flora.

Answer C (incorrect answers): Typhoid fever, caused by Salmonella typhi, is also in the differential diagnosis for diarrhea. Classic findings include rose spots on the trunk and abdomen, and pulse-temperature disassociation (bradycardia with fever). questions.question: A 32-year-old man presents to emergency department with fever and chills. He has been evaluated twice in the last month first fever. There is no history of weight loss or seizures. He feels well between febrile episodes. His temperature is 103.6°F (39.8°C), pulse is 131/minute, and blood pressure is 150/90 mmHg. Physical exam reveals hepatomegaly. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this man's current symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This man has a relapsing fever caused by Borrelia hermsii. Patients present with recurrent fevers (usually above 102.2°F [39°c]) that last 1 to 3 days, followed by an interval without fever of 4 to United States, relapsing fever is a rare tick-borne illness limited to the mountainous West or Southwest. It can be epidemic in developing countries, where it is spread from person to person by the body louse. Mc Graw Diagnosis of relapsing fever is similar to malaria, where thick and thin blood smears are used to visualize the spirochete. The recurrent fevers are caused by the spirochete's ability to produce several distinct surface antigens, a process know as antigenic variation. Treatment options include penicillin, doxycycline, and ceftriaxone.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Although this clinical scenario has some overlap with malaria, a parasitic infection relapsing fever, patients with malaria have traveled to endemic areas and present with anemia, splenomegaly, and fevers at irregular intervals each day.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Patients with dengue fever, a viral infection transmitted by a mosquito vector, present with high fevers but also develop signs of plasma leakage, including rash and hemorrhagic manifestations (epistaxis, petechiae, or purpura). In addition, patients have a history of travel to endemic areas (Southeast Asia, South America, and Africa).

Answer C (incorrect answer): Necrotizing fasciitis and Shigella gastroenteritis are conditions associated with toxin-producing bacteria. They are not associated with relapsing fever syndromes or tick-borne infections, and this clinical scenario is not consistent with a toxin-mediated illness.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Patients with Henoch-Schonlein purpura, or immunoglobulin A (IgA) vasculitis, present with arthritis, abdominal pain, and palpable purpura. This clinical scenario is not consistent with IgA vasculitis.

questions.question: A 4-month-old boy is seen for a well-child visit. His mother is concerned because his nose runs frequently and he has had a persistent rash since three weeks of age. Physical exam reveals white nasal discharge and a maculopapular rash on his back, his buttocks, and the soles of his feet. He also has epitrochlear and axillary lymphadenopathy, as well as hepatomegaly. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this infant's current symptoms?
questions.explanation: Answer E (incorrect answer): Infants with herpes infections can acquire the virus perinatally (during vaginal delivery) or as a congenital (intrauterine) infection during pregnancy. Perinatal infections present with fever, common than perinatal infections and present with the triad of skin vesicles, eye damage. and CNS abnormalities (microcephaly). Mc Graw

questions.question: An 8-year-old boy is evaluated for a fever and sore throat. Physical examination reveals exudative pharyngitis. Throat a glass slide. Which of the results below is expected?
questions.explanation: Answer F (correct answer): This boy has streptococcal pharyngitis ("strep throat") caused by Streptococcus pyogenes (group A streptococci). Clinical features include fever, sore throat, and exudative pharyngitis. S. Pyogenes are gram-positive cocci that form pairs and chains. S. pyogenes are beta-hemolytic, meaning they display complete hemolysis of blood agar. Beta-hemolytic bacteria turn blood agar white (answers A and F). These bacteria secrete an exotoxin called streptolysin which lyses red blood cells, producing the white color. Alpha-hemolytic bacteria turn the growth plate green (answers B hemolytic bacteria do not modify blood agar, so the growth media remains unchanged (answers C and D). All streptococci are catalase-negative (i.e., they lack the catalase enzyme), and this feature distinguishes streptococci from staphylococci which are catalase-positive. The catalase test is performed by placing bacteria be broken down into water and oxygen which makes bubbles (answers A, D, and E). Bacteria that lack catalase make no bubbles (answers B, C, and F).

questions.question: A 2-day old girl is brought for evaluation by her mother. For the past 24 hours, she has been fussy and unwilling to breastfeed. She vomited several times. Temperature is 103.2°F. questions.explanation:

MacConkey's agar contains lactose, which is metabolized by lactose-fermenting into acidic metabolites. A pH grow as pink colonies, and non-lactose fermenting bacteria grow as colorless colonies.

Answer B (incorrect answer): The catalase test is used to differentiate staphylococci (catalase-positive) from streptococci (catalase-negative). Some gram-negative bacteria are catalase-positive, including Pseudomonas, andE.coli.

Answer C (incorrect answer): The oxidase tests identifies bacteria that express cytochrome oxidase. E. coli are oxidase-negativebacteria.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman presents with fever, chills, and malaise for one day. She injects heroin daily. Temperature is 101.2°F. Physical examination identifies a 2/6 holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border. Echocardiography identifies a mass on the tricuspid valve. questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This woman has endocarditis caused by Staphylococcus aureus. Intravenous drug users are at risk for this condition. Bacteria may be introduced into the venous system by contaminated needles, of tricuspid regurgitation is a holosystolic murmur heard best at the left lower sternal border. Staphylococcal Mc Raardco.Ravnnd endocarditis oftenhas anindolent(mild)courseevolving overa week or more. S. aureus are gram-positive cocci that grow in clumps. Like all staphylococci they are catalase-positive, meaning they producebubbles whenplaced in hydrogen peroxide.

Answer C (incorrect answer): MacConkey's agar is a selective media used for identification of gram-negative bacteria. Gram-positive bacteria like S. Aureus will not grow on this media.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Novobiocin is an antibiotic used for characterization of coagulase-negative staphylococci like S. epidermis and S. saprophyticus. Coagulase-positive staphylococci like S. Aureus are not typically tested for novobiocin sensitivity. Most strains of staphylococci, including S. Aureus, are sensitive to novobiocin and therefore do not grow around novobiocin discs placed in culture. The exception is S. saprophyticus. Aureus, producing a yellow color. Growth on this media with a yellow color indicates S. Aureus.

questions.question: A blood culture is sent to the lab and grows gram-positive bacteria. Further testing indicates that these bacteria are catalase-positive and coagulase-negative. Bacteria are grown with a novobiocin disc present. Results are shown below: This blood culture most likely came from a patient with which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): The question describes gram-positive bacteria that are catalase-positive, meaning they are staphylococci. All staphylococci are catalase-positive, whereas streptococci are catalase-negative. The bacteria described in the question are also coagulase-negative, indicating they are not S. aureus (which are coagulase-positive). The two clinically relevant species of coagulase-negative staphylococci are S. saprophyticus and S. epidermidis. These bacteria can be differentiated using novobiocin. S. saprophyticus is resistant to novobiocin and will grow next to a novobiocin disc placed in culture (see image). In contrast, S. epidermidis is novobiocin sensitive and will not grow near a novobiocin disc. Most staphylococci other than S. saprophyticus are sensitive to novobiocin. Resistance to novobiocin strongly implies presence of S. saprophyticus. The bacteria in the question are novobiocin sensitive, indicating S. epidermidis. These bacteria are normal skin flora that rarely cause disease. The exception is among patients with prosthetic implants like joints or heart valves.S. epidermidis attaches to prosthetic material and forms biofilms.Biofilms allows the infection to evade immunity and also limit the effectiveness of antibiotics. Prosthetic materials infected with S. epidermidis often must be surgically removed.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Cellulitis is commonly caused by S. aureus, not S. epidermidis. These infections do not occur due to S. epidermidis.

Answer D (incorrect answer): S. saprophyticus is a common cause of urinary tract infection, but not S. epidermidis.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman is brought to the emergency room following a tonic-clonic seizure. She was seen by her primary care physician a day earlier for fever and headache, and diagnosed with a flulike illness. She has no history of a seizure disorder, diabetes, or hypertension. She went camping with her husband two weeks ago to celebrate their third wedding anniversary. Her temperature is 101.6°F, pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg. Physical exam shows a maculopapular rash on her chest, arms legs, and palms. She also has scattered petechiae on her chest and legs. Laboratory results include: Hemoglobin: 12.5 g/dL Platelet count: 80 × 109/L Sodium: 131 mmol/L Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL AST: 148 U/L ALT: 115 U/L PT: 16 seconds PTT: 40 seconds Which of the following antibiotics is most appropriate for this woman?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (incorrect answer): Rifampin is a tuberculosis drug not used in the treatment of Rickettsia rickettsii. For zoonotic infections, it can be used in the treatment of Brucella.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Streptomycin, an aminoglycoside antibiotic, is not effective in treating RMSF.For zoonotic infections, it may be used in treatment of Brucella, tularemia and Yersinia.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Amoxicillin-clavulanate is a broad-spectrum antibiotic. It is not used in treatment of RMSF. It can be used for treatment of zoonotic infections caused by Pasteurella. be used for treatment of zoonotic infections caused by leptospirosis and Bartonella henselae. Mc Graw

questions.question: An 8-year-old girl is evaluated for a painful lump in her left axillae. She denies fever, night sweats, or weight loss. Two weeks ago her mother noticed a small pustule on her left hand that resolved without intervention. The girl got a kitten for her left axillae. Which of the following is the most likely etiology of her current symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This girl has cat-scratch disease, caused by Bartonella henselae. Cats may harbor fleas that contain B. henselae. These bacteria can be transmitted to humans after a cat bite or scratch, Cat-scratch disease initially presents with a vesicle, pustule, or papular lesion at the site of a cat bite or scratch. The skin lesion usually lasts for 1 to 2 weeks and is followed by an enlarged, tender, and erythematous lymph scratch. Treatment options include azithromycin, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, and rifampin.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Pasteurella multocida lives in the mouths of cats and dogs and is associated with cellulitis or osteomyelitis following animal bites. Pasteurella infections are not associated with painful lymphadenopathy.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Yersinia pestis is transmitted to humans by rat flea bites. Patients present with flulike symptoms and exquisitely tender lymph nodes with swelling and erythema (known as buboes). Unlike cat- scratch disease, Yersinia infections present with multiple enlarged lymph nodes and usually affect the inguinal region.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Patients with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) present with fever, bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly. EBV is not associated with zoonotic vectors or painful unilateral lymphadenopathy. toxoplasmosis is transmitted by cat feces, only patients with cat-scratch disease have unilateral painful lymphadenopathy. questions.question: A 34-year-old man presents to the emergency department with fever and night sweats. He also complains of increasing fatigue. He has lost 5 pounds in the last two weeks. The fevers have occurred daily for the last week at irregular intervals and visited several farms. His temperature is 102.6°F (39.2°C), pulse is 117/minute, and blood pressure is 130/70 mmHg. Physical exam reveals cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this man's current symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This man has brucellosis, caused by Brucella melitensis. Patients present with undulant fevers (irregular daily fever spikes that can last for several weeks), profuse sweating that often has a strong odor, and weight loss. Physical exam findings are generally nonspecific but can include splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, and lymphadenopathy. Risk factors for brucellosis include contact with fluid from infected cattle and pigs (for workers in meatpacking plants) and consumption of unpasteurized milk and cheese (for travelers to Mc Graw Mexico who consume fresh goat or sheep cheese). Treatment includes doxycycline and streptomycin or gentamicin for six weeks. Vaccination of domestic livestock and instituting protective measures in slaughterhouses has significantly decreased the incidence of brucellosis in theUnitedStates.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Although the presentation described in this clinical scenario has some overlap with tuberculosis, the absence of cough and the relatively short incubation period between travel to Mexico and onset of symptoms would make tuberculosis less likely. recurrent fevers (usually above 102.2°F [39°c]) that last 1 to 3 days, followed by an interval without fever of 4 to brucellosis do not have fever-free intervals. Unlike brucellosis, relapsing fever is a tick-borne illness.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Patients with parrot fever, caused by Chlamydia psittaci, present with fever, headache, and a dry cough. This diagnosis should be considered in patients with symptoms of atypical pneumonia who work in pet stores or who have pet birds.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Patients with Q fever, caused by Coxiella burnetii, present with flulike symptoms vector to brucellosis (cattle and sheep), the clinical presentation is very different. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 28-year-old HIV-positive male is evaluated for a skin rash. He denies pain or itching. He reports poor compliance with his medications and has missed his last two follow-up appointments. His vital signs are normal. Physical exam reveals multiple pink, red, and purple papular lesions on face, chest, and legs. Biopsy of the lesion reveals lymphocytes. which of the following is the most likely cause of this man's current symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This man has Kaposi's sarcoma (Ks), a vascular tumor that occurs in patients with advanced HIV and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDs). KS is associated with human herpesvirus 8 infection. Patients present with red, purple, and pink papular lesions on the face, chest, and legs. Risk factors for KS include recent steroid use, low CD4 counts, and recent initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART). KS can be distinguished from bacillary angiomatosis, caused by Bartonella henselae, by skin biopsy. Biopsy in KS reveals lymphocytes (T cells against the infecting virus), whereas bacillary angiomatosis is associated with a vessels, a process known as angioproliferation. erythrogenic toxin produced by Streptococcus pyogenes. Erythrogenic toxin damages capillaries in the dermis, different clinical presentation from Ks. occurs 1 to3weeksafter medication exposure.It isassociated withfever and malaisefollowed bytender cutaneous and mucous membrane (eye, mouth, GU) lesions. Skin detachment with application of mechanical pressure (Nikolsky's sign) is classically associated with Sjs.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Bacillary angiomatosis, caused by Bartonella henselae, is often confused with Kaposi's sarcoma. Both present with flat red and purple skin lesions, and both occur in HIV-positive patients

Answer E (incorrect answer): Patients with cutaneous anthrax, caused by Bacillus anthracis, present with pruritic papules that erode to become painless necrotic ulcers on the face, neck, and arms. Unlike Kaposi's sarcoma, anthrax is not associated with HIV infection. Bacillus anthracis produces two toxins: edema toxin (which increases adenylate cyclase-mediated cAMP production) and lethal toxin (which causes cellular apoptosis). Mc Graw

questions.question: A 33-year-old woman is evaluated for fever, headache, and rash. Two weeks ago she traveled with her family to a cabin in Rhode Island, where she went hiking. Her temperature is 100.4°F. Physical exam reveals an 8 cm circular rash with central clearing on her upper arm near the axillae. Infection from which of the following may also be present in this woman?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (incorrect answer): Unlike babesiosis and Lyme disease, which are transmitted by Ixodes scapularis, the vector for Ehrlichia chaffeensis is the Lone Star tick. Patients with ehrlichiosis present with flulike illness and may also develop leukopenia and thrombocytopenia.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMsF) is the most common tick-borne illness in the United States and is caused by Rickettsia rickettsii. Patients present with headache and fever and develop a intravascular coagulation (DIC). This patient's "bull's eye" rash is not classic for RMSF.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Yersinia pestis, which causes bubonic plague, is transmitted to humans by rat flea bites. Patients present with flulike symptoms and exquisitely tender lymph nodes with swelling and erythema, knownasbuboes. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 32-year old woman is evaluated for fever and myalgias. She also complains of cough, sore throat, and nasal congestion. Her temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), her pulse is 105/min, and her blood pressure is 130/80 mmHg. Physical examination is significant for oropharyngeal erythema and anterior cervical lymphadenopathy. Laboratory evaluation demonstrates a rapid antigen test that is positive for influenza type A. Oseltamivir is prescribed. which of the following is the most important factor for determining if this therapy will improve outcomes for this woman?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (incorrect answer): Viral genotype is not a factor in determining whether patients benefit from antiviral therapy. Decisions about antiviral therapy should not wait for laboratory confirmation of influenza since delays in treatment decrease the effectiveness of therapy.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Tobacco use is not a risk factor that requires prompt initiation of antiviral therapy. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 26-year-old woman is evaluated for a skin lesion on her lower lip. She reports the onset of pain, tingling, and itching of her lower lip before the lesion appeared. She takes daily acyclovir for recurrent skin lesions. Physical examination reveals a painful vesicle crossing the vermillion border of her lower lip. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of acyclovir resistance in this woman?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This women has herpes labialis, caused by herpes simplex virus, type 1 (HsV-1). Patients with primary HsV-1 infections present with pharyngitis, including fever, sore throat, tonsillar exudate, border. These vesicles are frequently preceded by prodromal symptoms, including pain, pruritis, and tingling. Diagnosis of HsV-1 can be made from viral culture or polymerase chain reaction (PcR) of skin lesions. Acyclovir is the treatment of choice for HsV-1 in most patients. Acyclovir inhibits herpes virus DNA polymerase H following phosphorylation by thymidine kinase. This mimics guanosine in infected cells, leading to DNA chain termination and defective viral replication. This woman has developed herpes labialis despite daily acyclovir for viral suppression. This indicates viral resistance to acyclovir. One of the primary mechanisms of resistance to acyclovir is absent, decreased, or altered thymidine kinase."TK negative" HsV strains are encountered clinically, and can be challenging to treat.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Oseltamivir, a neuraminidase inhibitor, is indicated for patients with influenza in the first 48 hours of developing symptoms. Oseltamivir interferes with the sialic-acid-mediated release of influenza virus from infected cells, preventing new cells from becoming infected

Answer B (incorrect answer): Herpes simplex virus, type 1 (HsV-1) is a large, enveloped, double-stranded DNA virus with an icosahedral core. RNA polymerase mutations have no impact on acyclovir, which inhibits DNA polymerase.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Ganciclovir, a first-line drug in patients with cytomegalovirus (CMV) infections, chain termination and defective viral replication. Mutations in CMV phosphotransferase, a viral enzyme that phosphorylates ganciclovir, prevent the formation of ganciclovir triphosphate, which is essential in disrupting DNA polymerase activity and DNA synthesis. disrupts post-translational processing and replication of HCV. Protease mutations reduce HcV susceptibility to drugs like simeprevir, but can frequently be overcome by combination therapy. Simeprevir is not effective in patients with herpes virus infections. Mc Graw

questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This boy has leprosy, caused by Mycobacteria leprae. Leprosy is a very rare condition in the Us, and this boy likely contracted the disease in Bangladesh before being adopted.Patients present with thickened, hypopigmented skin patches with decreased sensation and tender peripheral nerves (pain in ulnar or radial nerves). questions.question: A 28-year-old HIV-positive male is evaluated for fever, abdominal pain, and diarrhea. He has lost 5 pounds in the last month. He recently stopped taking his antiretroviral therapy medications. His temperature is 102.2°F (39°C), heart rate is 110/min, and blood pressure is 100/60 mmHg. Physical exam reveals a pale, cachectic male with hepatosplenomegaly. Chest X-ray is normal. Laboratory results include: CD4 count: 45 cells/mm3 (normal 500 to 1,500 cells/mm3) Hemoglobin: 7.8 g/dL (normal 12 to 15 g/dL) Platelet count: 170 x 109/L (normal 150 to 400 x 109/L) AST: 32 U/L (normal 10 to 40 U/L) ALT: 45 U/L (normal 7 to 56 U/L) Alkaline phosphatase: 332 U/L (normal 40 to129 U/L) Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH): 415 U/L (normal 122 to 222 U/L) Which of the following antibiotics is the best choice for this man?
questions.explanation:

Answer C (incorrect answer): Clindamycin can be used in HIV-positive patients with toxoplasmosis infections. Patients with toxoplasmosis usually have CD4 counts of less than 100 cells/mm3 and present with fever, infections.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Paromomycin is an aminoglycoside antibiotic used in HIV positive patients with Cryptosporidium infections. Patients present with severe diarrhea and weight loss due to malabsorption. Unlike MAC infections, patients with cryptosporidiosis do not present with elevated LDH and alkaline phosphatase levels. questions.question: A 45-year-old man infected with the human immunodeficiency virus presents with confusion, weakness, and double vision. His symptoms started four weeks ago and have progressively worsened. Laboratory results show a CD4 count of 40/mm? (normal 500-15oo). Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain shows bilateral non-enhancing lesions in the periventricular white matter. Polymerase chain reaction of the cerebrospinal fluid is positive for the JC virus. This man's neurologic findings are due to viral replication in which of the following cell types?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This man has progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) due to reactivation of the JC virus within the central nervous system. Clinical features of PML include confusion, motor deficits, incoordination, and seizures. These symptoms develop over weeks, and often lead to death within a few months. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in PML shows multiple non-enhancing white-matter lesions in the brain, which correspond to areas of demyelination caused by reactivation of the JC virus. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of cerebrospinal fluid can identify presence of the JC virus to confirm the diagnosis of PML. Oligodendrocytes are glial cells (non-neuronal support cells) of the central nervous system. The JC virus infects oligodendrocytes, causing demyelination, which leads to the clinical features of PML.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Neurons are not known to play a role in the development of PML.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Schwann cells are glial cells of the peripheral nervous system. They are analogous to the oligodendrocytes of the central nervous system because they also surround axons and synthesize myelin. PMLdoesnotaffectSchwanncells.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Ependymal cells secrete cerebrospinal fluid.These cells line the ventricles and the central canal of the spinal cord. In addition to secretion of cerebrospinal fluid, ependymal cells help to circulate this fluid through movement of cilia.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Microglia are the resident macrophages of the central nervous system. Like other infection. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 65-year-old woman who lives in New York City presents with headache, fever, and neck stiffness. She recently underwent lung transplantation and now takes several immunosuppressant medications. Recent interferon-gamma release assay testing for latent tuberculosis was negative. A computed tomography scan of the head is normal. A lumbar puncture shows a white blood cell count of 45/mm3 (normal 0-5/mm3) with a mononuclear predominance, a glucose of 30 mg/dL (normal 40-70 mg/dL), and a protein level of 60 mg/dL (normal <40 mg/dL). Analysis of cerebrospinal fluid identifies a capsular organism on India Ink staining that grows on Sabouraud's agar. This woman's infection was most likely acquired through which of the following modes of transmission?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This woman has meningitis caused by Cryptococcus neoformans, an opportunistic headache, neck pain, and symptoms of increased intracranial pressure, such as nausea and vomiting. Cerebrospinal fluid (CsF) typically shows an increased white blood cell count with a mononuclear predominance, increased total protein, and reduced glucose. Cryptococcus is identified by India ink staining, which will show circular organisms surrounded by a capsule. Cryptococcus may also be cultured on Sabouraud dextrose agar. Cryptococcus is found widely in nature, especially in soil containing bird (especially pigeon) droppings. Infection in humans occurs due to inhalation of the yeast which disseminates into the central nervous system.

Answer A and B (incorrect answers): Cryptococcus infection is transmitted through inhalation, not through the skin or contaminated drinking water.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Exposure to cat feces may lead to toxoplasmosis but is not associated with cryptococcal infection.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Cryptococcus does not enter a latent phase that can reactivate causing disease. Latent infection and reactivation are important elements of the pathogenesis of toxoplasmosis and progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) caused by the JC virus. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman with human immunodeficiency virus infection presents with headache, confusion, fever, and seizures. On examination she has a white coating on her tongue and posterior pharynx. Neurologic examination shows disorientation and weakness of the left arm. Magnetic resonance imaging shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions. Labs show a CD4 count of 65 cells/mm3 (normal 500-1500 cells/mm3). Serum is positive for anti-toxoplasma IgG antibodies. This woman's current condition most likely developed through which of the following mechanisms?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This woman has encephalitis due to infection with Toxoplasma gondii. She has thrush on examination, an oropharyngeal infection caused by Candida that occurs in immunocompromised patients. She also has a low CD4 count consistent with chronic human immunodeficiency (HIV) infection. Toxoplasma encephalitis affects patients with HIV infection and a CD4 count of <100 cells/mm3 (normal 500- 1500 cells/mm?). Clinical features include headache, confusion, fever, and seizures. Imaging usually shows multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions, which often have surrounding cerebral edema. Toxoplasma gondii is an intracellular protozoan parasite. Primary infection of humans typically occurs through ingestion of T. gondii oocytes, which are present in the feces of infected cats. Initial infection is asymptomatic in the majority of patients. Following exposure, organisms penetrate the intestinal epithelium, disseminate throughout the body, and form cysts within cells. In healthy patients, cysts can lie dormant indefinitely without leading to clinical disease. Studies have shown latent infection rates that vary by population from 11 to 80%. In the setting of immunocompromise like HIV infection, reactivation can occur. Clinical disease from Toxoplasma gondii in patients with HIV is almost exclusively caused by reactivation of latent infection.

Answers A, B, D, and E (incorrect answers): An initial infection with Toxoplasma gondii occurs due to ingestion of oocytes. However, encephalitis in immunosuppressed patients occurs due to reactivation of latent infection. The other answer choices do not describe the transmission of Toxoplasma gondii. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 37-year-old man with a history of human immunodeficiency virus infection presents with fever, headache, and nausea for the past week. Laboratory testing shows a CD4 count of 75 cells/mm3 (normal 500-1500 cells/mm3). Computed tomography scan of his brain is normal. Lumbar puncture shows an opening pressure of 30 cm H20 (normal 10-18 cm H20). India ink stain of cerebrospinal fluid shows spherical cells surrounded by clear halos. A medication is started for treatment of his condition. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of action of this medication?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This man has Cryptococcus neoformans meningitis, an opportunistic fungal infection that causes meningoencephalitis in immunosuppressed patients. Symptoms of cryptococcal meningitis include headache, neck pain, and signs of increased intracranial pressure, such as nausea and vomiting. These symptoms develop slowly over one to two weeks. Imaging may be normal or may show "soap bubble lesions" in the periventricular space that develop due to accumulation of the organism. Lumbar puncture often shows an increased opening pressure, increased white blood cell count with a mononuclear predominance, and increased Mc protein level. Cryptococcus cannot be easily grown in the laboratory. It is identified by India ink staining, which will show circular organisms surrounded by a capsule. Antigen testing may also be used. Amphotericin B is used to treat Cryptococcus neoformans meningitis. This drug binds to ergosterol in fungal cell walls, leading to cell death. It often is administered together with flucytosine, an antimetabolite antifungal agent, to treat cryptococcal menignitis.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Penicillin and the beta-lactam antibiotics inhibit the synthesis of peptidoglycan, an important component of bacterial cell walls. These antibiotics are not effective against Cryptococcus neoformans meningitis because fungal cell walls do not contain peptidoglycan. bacterial DNA gyrase. Fluoqinolones are not effective in the treatment of Cryptococcus neoformans meningitis because C. neoformans is a yeast and does not contain bacterial DNA gyrase.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Macrolide antibiotics such as erythromycin, clarithromycin, and azithromycin bind to the 5os subunit of the bacterial ribosome. By inhibiting translocation, these drugs reduce bacterial protein synthesis. Although this mechanism is effective against a number of bacteria, marcolides are not effective against Cryptococcus neoformans, since yeasts have a different ribosomal structure than bacteria.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) inhibits two sequential steps in the synthesis of tetrahydrofolic acid. This leads to reduced availability of tetrahydrofolic acid, a folate compound required for bacterial deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) replication. TMP-sMX is not effective against Cryptococcus neoformans. Mc

questions.question: A 21-year-old woman with human immunodeficiency virus infection presents with blurred vision and "floaters." She denies any other neurologic symptoms. Neurologic examination is normal except for decreased visual acuity. Labs show a CD4 count of 65 cells/mm3 (normal 500-1500 cells/mm3). Retinal infection with cytomegalovirus is suspected. questions.explanation:

Risk factors for macular degeneration include older age and family history of the condition. Symptoms include loss of central vision, distorted vision, and decreased visual acuity. Macular degeneration is unlikely in this woman given her young age.

Answer D (incorrect answer): This image represents a retinoblastoma. The tumor is noted superior to the

questions.question: A 64-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis presents to his rheumatologist reporting continued pain in bilateral fingers despite regular use of methotrexate. His blood pressure is 109/55 mmHg, heart rate is 56 beats/minute, respiratory rate is 12 breaths/minute and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Physical examination reveals swollen proximal interphalangeal joints bilaterally on the third, fourth, and fifth digits. The rheumatologist changes the patient's medication to infliximab.
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): Before starting treatment with biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) such as infliximab, patients must be screened for latent tuberculosis (TB), as well as hepatitis B and hepatitis C. In patients with latent TB, the immune suppression caused by these drugs may precipitate progression of latent TB to active TB. If a patient is diagnosed with a TB infection, TB treatment should be initiated prior to starting infliximab.Complete blood count and renal function should also be assessed before and during treatment with infliximab and the other biologic DMARDs to assess for neutropenia, anemia and renal dysfunction. If renal insufficiency is identified dosing of infliximab may need to be reduced.

Answer A (incorrect answers): Testing for hepatitis A is not needed prior to starting therapy with biologic DMARDS.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Testing for human immunodeficiency virus is not required prior to starting treatment with biologic DMARDs.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Eye examination is not required prior to starting treatment with infliximab or because it can cause retinal damage. such as tocilizumab, tofacitinib and sarilumab can cause hyperlipidemia. W

questions.question: A 38-year-old woman presents for evaluation of joint pain in both hands for the past eight weeks. Her medical history is significant for hypertension and Sjogren's syndrome. She reports that her hands are stiff for about an hour and a half after joints and proximal interphalangeal joints of the second, third, fourth and fifth digits. Her rheumatoid factor is 22 IU/mL (normal is less than 14 IU/mL), anti-citrullinated protein antibody level is 65 EU/mL (normal is less than 20 EU/mL), C- management of her symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This patient has swelling of the metacarpophalangeal joints and proximal interphalangeal joints of both hands associated with prolonged morning stiffness (greater than one hour) that the disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) methotrexate. Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), which decreases purine nucleotide synthesis resulting in decreased DNA and RNA synthesis. This results in T cell and B cell suppression, which helps reduce joint inflammation. Methotrexate may cause bone marrow suppression, so it is essential to monitor blood counts during treatment. Folic acid is co-administered with methotrexate to partially mediate adverse effects of DHFR suppression. Other potential side effects of Mc Boards&Bevond Graw methotrexate include hepatotoxicity and stomatitis. of therapy to see clinical improvement. Bridging therapy for pain control may be needed until the DMARD takes effect; non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NsAIDs) are the drugs of choice. Corticosteroids may be used if NSAIDs do not provide adequate pain control, but they should not be used long term.

Answers A and B (incorrect answers): Etanercept and infliximab are biologic (antibody-based) DMARDs that are second-line agents for rheumatoid arthritis used when methotrexate is ineffective. Both etanercept and infliximab block tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-alpha), which is a pro-inflammatory cytokine that is elevated in rheumatoid arthritis. It may also be elevated in other inflammatory conditions such as psoriasis and latent tuberculosis,hepatitis B and hepatitis C.

Answers D and E (incorrect answers): Rituximab and tofacitinib are second-line DMARDs used to treat rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory conditions. These biologic medications do not target TNF-alpha. Rituximab is a monoclonal antibody that targets B cells, and tofacitinib is a janus kinase inhibitor, which reduces production of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin (IL)-7, IL-15, interferon-alpha and hepatitis C prior to initiating therapy. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 74-year-old man presents for evaluation of bilateral knee pain that has been worsening for several months. X-rays of bilateral knees show joint space narrowing and osteophytes. Which of

Answer A (correct answer): This patient has bilateral knee pain with morning stiffness lasting less than 30 minutes, joint space narrowing, and osteophytes which are findings indicative of osteoarthritis. Other signs of osteoarthritis noted in this patient's history include pain exacerbated by activity and relieved with rest. Initial treatment of osteoarthritis consists of oral or topical non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NsAIDs) such as meloxicam. questions.question: A 74-year-old woman presents to the outpatient clinic with chronic pelvic and lower back pain that has progressively worsened over the past eight months. She also notes a gradual enlargement of her skull and difficulty hearing in both ears over the significant for well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus, and she takes metformin. She does not smoke or consume alcohol. On physical examination, there is bilateral conductive hearing loss. There is tenderness over the pelvic bones and mild anterior bowing of the femur. Laboratory studies reveal serum alkaline phosphatase at 850 U/L with serum calcium at 9.4 mg/dL, phosphate at 3.6 mg/dL, and parathyroid hormone at 38 pg/mL. Radiographs demonstrate cortical thickening of the right femur and mixed lytic and sclerotic lesions of the pelvis. Which of the following is the most appropriate first line therapy for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (Incorrect answer): Calcium supplementation is important for general bone health and is usually given when someone has low calcium levels or osteoporosis. However, in Paget disease of bone, calcium levels are usually normal, like in this patient. The problem is not a lack of calcium but abnormal bone remodeling.

Answer C (Incorrect answer): Calcitonin can inhibit osteoclastic activity and was used historically for Paget like zoledronate. It is generally / reserved for patients who cannot tolerate bisphosphonates.

Answer D (Incorrect answer): Vitamin D supplementation is important in patients with vitamin D deficiency, but it is not a treatment for Paget disease itself. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 72-year-old man presents to the emergency department with left thigh pain and difficulty walking after experiencing a low-impact fall at home. He reports progressive bone pain in his lower extremities over the past several months. Additionally. he mentions that his winter gloves no longer fit, and he has noticed a change in the shape of his skull. His medical history is significant for hypertension and hyperlipidemia, and he takes amlodipine and atorvastatin. He does not use tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs. On physical examination, the patient has an antalgic gait. The left thigh is tender to palpation. Serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP) levels are 60o U/L. X-ray of the femur is shown in the image below. questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This patient presents with progressive bone pain, increasing hat size, and a pathologic fracture after minimal trauma. Imaging reveals a chalkstick fracture of the femur-an abrupt, transverse fracture through an area of abnormal bone remodeling. Additionally, the serum alkaline phosphatase Paget disease is a disorder of excessive and disorganized bone remodeling, where increased osteoclastic bone deformities, and at risk for fractures such as the chalkstick fracture seen in this case. Despite high bone turnover, serum calcium, serum vitamin D, and parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels typically remain normal in isolated Paget disease.Calcium homeostasis is maintained unless complications such as immobilization-induced hypercalcemia occur, which is not described here. Therefore, the serum calcium, vitamin D and PTH should be normal. The elevated alkaline phosphatase reflects increased osteoblastic activity but does not necessarily correlate with systemic calcium or vitamin D abnormalities. Thus, Answer D is correct.

Answer A,B,C, E,F,G,H (Incorrect Answers): Choices that indicate increases or decreases in serum calcium, vitamin D, or PTH are incorrect. In Paget disease of bone, calcium and vitamin D metabolism generally remain deficiency, PTH remains normal. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 22-month-old boy is evaluated for difficulty walking. On physical examination, he appears emaciated with swollen joints. He has bowing of the lower extremities and visible beading along the costochondral junction of the chest (see image below). Which of the following changes are expected in this boy for serum calcium, serum phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, and parathyroid hormone in comparison to a healthy child?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This boy has rickets, a bone disorder caused by calcium deficiency due to insufficient intake or metabolism of 25 OH vitamin D. In rickets, deficient mineralization of bone leads to abnormal bone development. Physical examination findings in severe rickets include genu varum (bowed legs) and rachitic rosary (costochondral beading), as seen in the photograph. Rickets has three stages with increasing severity. In stage one, deficiency of 25 OH vitamin D causes impaired calcium absorption from the intestines resulting in hypocalcemia. In stage 2, parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels rise, leading to hypophosphatemia from increased excretion of phosphate by the kidneys. Serum calcium can be normal in stage two because of increased renal calcium resorption due to elevated PTH. In stage 3, calcium becomes low again when hyperparathyroidism is no longer able to compensate for the severe decrease in available calcium. By stage 3, the clinical and radiological findings of rickets are severe, as seen in this case. Alkaline phosphatase levels are high in rickets due to high bone turnover. with increased PTH. PTH stimulates increases calcium reabsorption from bones and increased renal tubule reabsorption of calcium at the expense of phosphate loss.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Elevated PTH, calcium, and alkaline phosphatase with decreased phosphate is the pattern of laboratory abnormalities found in a patient with primary hyperparathyroidism.

Answer D (incorrect answer): This pattern of laboratory abnormalities is seen with secondary hyperparathyroidism. This occurs in patients with renal failure, where chronic calcium loss in the urine stimulates activity of the parathyroid gland. AnswerE(incorrectanswer):Normal laboratoryvaluesoccurinosteoporosis,a conditionofdecreasedbone mineral density that usually develops in adults. The bony abnormalities in this case are not seen in osteoporosis. Hmi

questions.question: A 25-year-old man comes to the clinic after injuring his right knee while pivoting during a basketball game. He heard a "pop" at the time of injury and was unable to continue playing. He now reports swelling and a feeling of instability when walking. On physical examination, the Lachman test is positive, and anterior drawer testing shows increased anterior displacement of the tibia relative to the femur. The damaged structure in this patient is attached to which of the following anatomic locations?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This man has clinical findings consistent with an anterior cruciate ligament (AcL) tear. A classic ACL injury involves a non-contact twisting motion, often accompanied by an audible "pop" and immediate swelling. The positive Lachman test-performed by flexing the knee to about 30 degrees and for ACL injury. The ACL originates from the anterior tibia and inserts onto the the lateral femoral condyle.

Answer A (incorrect answer): The head of the fibula is the insertion point for the biceps femoris tendon and the origin of the lateral collateral ligament (LCL). It is not involved in ACL anatomy.

Answer C (incorrect answer): The lateral femoral epicondyle is the origin of the lateral collateral ligament, not the insertion point for the ACL.

Answer D (incorrect answer): The medial femoral condyle is the site where the posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) inserts, not the ACL.

Answer E (incorrect answer): The medial tibial condyle provides attachment for the medial meniscus and medial collateral ligament. The ACL originates from the anterior intercondylar area of the tibial plateau, not from the condyleitself. Mc Graw

The valgus stress test is performed by flexing the knee to test is indicated by increased medial joint space opening, suggesting laxity or rupture of the MCL.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Anterior stress is assessed using the anterior drawer test or Lachman test. In the anterior drawer test, the patient lies supine with the knee flexed to 90 degrees, and the examiner pulls the tibia forward. Excess anterior translation indicates injury to the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL), not the MCL.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Posterior stress is tested using the posterior drawer test. The patient's knee is flexed to 90 degrees, and the examiner pushes the tibia backward. Increased posterior displacement of the tibia suggests injury to the posterior cruciate ligament (PCL). MCL injury does not affect this test.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Rotational stress is evaluated using maneuvers such as the pivot shift test or McMurray test. These assess for ACL instability and meniscal injuries. They do not specifically test the MCL, and would typically be normal in isolated MCL tears. ligament (LCL). An abnormal result suggests LCL injury, not MCL injury. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 66-year-old woman with a 10-year history of rheumatoid arthritis presents to the clinic with the sudden onset of pain and swelling in the posterior aspect of her left knee and upper calf. She says the area became swollen and tender over the past into the calf. Passive dorsiflexion of the foot elicits calf pain. Ultrasound reveals a fluid collection consistent with a cyst. This patient's condition is caused by a structure located adjacent to which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This patient has a ruptured Baker's cyst (popliteal cyst), which results from fluid distention of the gastrocnemio-semimembranosus bursa. This bursa lies between the medial head of the gastrocnemius and the semimembranosus muscle, near the posterior aspect of the knee. In patients with inflammatory arthritis like rheumatoid arthritis, chronic joint effusion can lead to increased synovial fluid pressure and cyst formation, which may rupture and track down the calf, mimicking a deep vein thrombosis. There can be tenderness in the popliteal fossa behind the knee. Calf pain on dorsiflexion may also occur.

questions.question: A 61-year-old man undergoes general anesthesia for elective hernia repair. Thirty minutes into the procedure, his temperature rises to 102.1°F. He becomes tachycardic and hypertensive. The anesthesiologist notes muscle rigidity and following functions?

options.C: Releases calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum

questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This man has clinical features of malignant hyperthermia (MH), including hyperthermia, muscle rigidity, and a rapid increase in end-tidal CO2. The rise in end-tidal CO2 is an early and sensitive indicator of MH in patients intubated under anesthesia. It reflects increased carbon dioxide production from sustained skeletal muscle contraction and hypermetabolism. MH is caused by defective calcium regulation in skeletal muscle, most commonly due to mutations in the RYR1 gene encoding the ryanodine receptor. This receptor normally releases calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the cytosol in response to depolarization. In MH, defective ryanodine receptors become abnormally activated by certain anesthetic agents (e.g., succinylcholine, volatile anesthetics), resulting in uncontrolled calcium release and cytosolic calcium overload. To restore calcium homeostasis, the SERCA (sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+-ATPase) pump works excessively to remove calcium from the cytosol and return it to the sarcoplasmic reticulum.This generates significant heat as a byproduct, contributing to the hyperthermia. The continuous cycle of calcium release and reuptake leads to sustained muscle contraction, acidosis, and eventual rhabdomyolysis if not treated promptly. defective protein in malignant hyperthermia. ATP hydrolysis occurs during muscle contraction, but the underlying defect here involves calcium regulation, not nucleotide hydrolysis.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Increased sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release is the abnormal process ryanodine receptor (RYR1) cause excessive calcium efflux from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the cytosol, leading to sustained muscle contraction and hypermetabolism.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Removing calcium from the cytosol is the function of the SERCA pump, not the excessive calciumrelease,it is notthe defective mechanism in the condition.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Sarcolemma depolarization is the initial step in muscle contraction, mediated by voltage-gated sodium channels. Although this process is necessary to activate the ryanodine receptor, it is not directly disrupted in malignant hyperthermia. The defect lies in calcium handling, not membrane excitability. Mc Graw

questions.question: Researchers are studying microscopic changes that occur during skeletal muscle contraction. Answer D (incorrect answer): Region D is another I band. Like Region B, it shortens during contraction due to overlap between actin and myosin increasing.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Region E is the H band, the central part of the A band where there is no actin- myosin overlap. This region narrows during contraction as actin filaments are pulled inward toward the M line. Mc Graw

questions.question: potential. Researchers measure the time course and ionic currents of the depolarization and repolarization phases. Which of the following most accurately describes the ionic movement responsible for the repolarization phase of the skeletal muscle action potential?

options.B: Potassium uptake by the sarcoplasmic reticulum

questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This experiment examines the ionic events during a skeletal muscle action potential. After the membrane is depolarized by sodium influx, repolarization occurs primarily due to the efflux of potassium through voltage-gated potassium channels. This outward movement of positively charged potassium ions restores the negative membrane potential, completing the action potential cycle. This mechanism is nearly identical to the repolarization process in neurons.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Calcium influx through L-type channels, also called dihydropyridine receptors, occurs during excitation-contraction coupling but not during the repolarization of the action potential. L-type channels facilitate calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum in response to membrane depolarization, but do not contribute to restoring membrane potential.

Answer B (incorrect answer): The sarcoplasmic reticulum actively takes up calcium during muscle relaxation, not potassium. Potassium is handled by ion channels in the plasma membrane and does not enter the sarcoplasmic reticulum as part of excitation-contraction coupling or repolarization.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Potassium influx would depolarize the membrane (increase the voltage) rather than repolarize it. During repolarization, potassium moves out of the cell to restore the negative resting membrane potential. Sodium efflux does occur slowly during the repolarization phase via the sodium-potassium

Answer E (incorrect answer): Sodium influx (i.e., into the cell) through voltage-gated channels is responsible for the depolarization phase of the action potential, not repolarization. This influx initiates the upstroke of the action potential by making the inside of the membrane more positive. Repolarization requires the opposite ionic movement, primarily potassium efflux. Mc Graw IIH

questions.question: Researchers are studying structural changes in sarcomeres during active contraction of skeletal muscle fibers. Answer A (correct answer): This experiment examines sarcomere behavior during active skeletal muscle contraction, which occurs via the sliding f filament mechanism. During contraction, thin filaments (actin) slide s (myosin), pulling Z lines closer together and shortening over thickfilaments the sarcomere. The H band, which represents the central region of the A band containing only thick filaments, decreases in width as actin filaments move inward. The I band, which contains only thin filaments, also shortens because more of the actin overlaps with thick filaments. In contrast, the A band, which represents the full length of the thick filaments, remains unchanged because thick filaments do not change in length. This combination of changes-decrease in the H and I bands with no change in the A band-is the classic signature of normal muscle fiber contraction.

questions.question: A 66-year-old man is referred for hemicolectomy for adenocarcinoma of the colon. During the operation, he becomes tachycardic and hypertensive. His temperature rises to 102.1°F. In malignant hyperthermia, excessive calcium in the cytosol already leads to persistent calcium-troponin C binding and sustained contraction. The drug used to treat this condition reduces intracellular calcium and therefore decreases, not increases, troponin activation.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Inhibition of the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+-ATPase (SERCA) pump would reduce reuptake of calcium into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, prolonging elevated cytosolic calcium levels and worsening muscle rigidity. Dantrolene, the treatment for malignant hyperthermia, does not inhibit SERCA but instead blocks further calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Decreased sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) calcium occurs in malignant hyperthermia due to sustained overactivation of ryanodine receptors, which release excessive calcium from the SR into the cytosol. This leads to depletion of SR calcium stores and a hypermetabolic state. The drug used to treat this condition, dantrolene, reverses this process by inhibiting the ryanodine receptor. This reduces calcium efflux from the SR, allowing calcium stores to be replenished and cytosolic calcium to fall. Therefore, dantrolene treatment results in increased, not decreased, SR calcium.

questions.question: Researchers are studying muscle function in endurance athletes. Compared to non-athletes, which of the following differences are expected in endurance athletes for skeletal muscle mitochondrial density and slow muscle fiber density in the quadriceps?
questions.explanation: Answer A (correct answer): Mitochondria generate ATP for skeletal muscle cells via oxidative phosphorylation. Endurance exercise (e.g., long distance running) increases the number of mitochondria in cells (i.e., mitochondrial density) as an adaption to training. Long-distance runners have more numerous and larger mitochondria in skeletal muscle cells. In contrast, resistance training (e.g., weight lifting) is not associated with significant changes in mitochondrial density. The predominant adaption to weight training is muscle hypertrophy, due to increased quantities of actinand myosin.This allows for generation of increased force. Slow-twitch fibers are also called red fibers because they have a deep red color and large quantities of myoglobin and mitochondria. Because depolarization occurs slowly in these fibers, they contract slowly, hence the name slow twitch. These fibers contain lots of mitochondria and myoglobin (which holds oxygen for energy generation), therefore they can generate large amounts of ATP and sustain contractions for long periods of time. These fibers are also slow to fatigue because of the large amounts of energy available, and because they store energy as triglycerides for use in long, sustained activity. The paraspinal muscles of the back are famous In contrast, fast twitch fibers are pale and have few mitochondria and little myoglobin. These fibers fatigue quickly and cannot generate sustained contractions, but can generate powerful contractions. Fast-twitch fibers are used for short, non-sustained contractions such as eye or hand movements. They are important for sprinting as opposed to slow-twitch fibers, which are important for long-distance running. Resistance training has been associated with increased quantities of fast-twitch fibers. Human muscles are a mix of slow- and fast-twitch fibers which is influenced by genetics. Many studies have shown that endurance athletes have more slow-twitch fibers compared with non-athletes. How exercise changes the mixture of slow- and fast-twitch fibers is incompletely understood. The treatment of osteoporosis consists of lifestyle modification and pharmacologic therapy. Lifestyle measures include adequate dietary calcium and vitamin D intake, weight-bearing exercise, smoking cessation and avoidance of heavy alcohol use.Weight-bearing exercise requires the person to work against gravity and puts repetitive stress on bones, which increases bone mineral density (BMD) and decreases the risk of fragility fractures. Examples of weight-bearing exercise include walking, jogging, climbing stairs, playing tennis and dancing.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Swimming is an excellent exercise for older adults because it reduces stress on the joints, increases strength and improves cardiovascular health. However, because it is not a weight bearing exercise, swimming is less likely to improve bone mineral density than dancing.

Answers C and D (incorrect answers): Recumbent and upright biking are forms of low-impact, lower body exercise.
