questions.question: A 37-year-old man is brought to the clinic by his wife due to unusual episodes that have occurred over the past few months. verbal stimuli and appears confused for several minutes afterward. Before the episode begins, he often reports an intense feeling of fear and sometimes smells a foul odor that no one else notices. Neurologic examination between episodes is normal. Damage to which of the following brain regions is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This man has temporal lobe epilepsy, a form of focal epilepsy that arises from the mesial (medial or inner region) structures of the temporal lobe. Seizures involving this region can affect the olfactory cortex (foul odor smells) and the amygdala, a limbic system structure important for emotional processing (causing intense fear). Other common features are lip smacking, blank staring, and post-ictal (post- seizure) confusion. These seizures are commonly associated with mesial temporal sclerosis, a condition of neuronal loss and gliosis of the hippocampus, which can be identified on MRI. posturing, and are typically brief with minimal post-ictal confusion. They may involve speech arrest but are less likely to cause auras of fear or olfactory hallucinations.

Answer B (incorrect answer): The occipital lobe processes visual information. Seizures originating here usually cause visual disturbances, such as flashes of light or visual hallucinations.

Answer C (incorrect answer): The olfactory bulb plays a role in the detection of odors. Damage to the olfactory bulb results in anosmia (complete loss of smell), not olfactory hallucinations or seizure behaviors. In this patient, seen in temporal lobe epilepsy, especially when the seizure focus involves the primary olfactory cortex in the medial temporal lobe.

Answer D (incorrect answer): The parietal lobe processes sensory input, such as touch and proprioception. Seizures here may involve paresthesias or spatial disorientation, but not emotional auras or olfactory hallucinations Mc Graw

questions.question: A 55-year-old man presents to the clinic with changes in his sense of smell. Over the past several months, he has had increasing difficulty detecting odors. His wife reports mild personality changes, including apathy and difficulty with which of the following anatomic regions is the most likely explanation for this patient's presentation?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This man has symptoms of anosmia (loss of smell), phantosmia (olfactory hallucinations), and mild personality changes, which are classic for an olfactory groove meningioma - a tumor arising along the anterior cranial fossa near the cribriform plate. These tumors compress the olfactory bulbs and tracts, which rest on the orbital surface of the frontal lobe. As the tumor grows, it can also compress adjacent frontal lobe structures, leading to executive dysfunction, apathy, or personality changes. MRI often shows a midline extra-axial mass (i.e., mass outside the cortex) near the cribriform plate (portion of the ethmoid bone nearnose).

Answer A (incorrect answer): The amygdala, located in the medial temporal lobe, is part of the limbic system and involved in emotion and behavior. Lesions of the amygdala are classically associated with Kluver-Bucy syndrome (hyperphagia, hyperorality, inappropriate sexual behavior), not olfactory symptoms.

Answer C (incorrect answer): The occipital lobe is responsible for visual processing. Lesions here may cause cortical blindness or visual field deficits butwould not result in olfactory disturbances.

Answer D (incorrect answer): The parietal lobe processes somatosensory information and spatial orientation. Damage here can cause sensory neglect or agnosia, but not anosmia or olfactory hallucinations.

Answer E (incorrect answer): The thalamus is a major sensory relay center, but olfaction is unique among the senses in that it bypasses the thalamus in its initial pathway. Lesions in the thalamus would not explain isolated olfactorysymptoms. Hm

questions.question: A 60-year-old man comes to the emergency department with the sudden onset of weakness on the right side of his body and difficulty moving his eyes. On neurologic exam, both eyes are deviated to the left. He is alert but unable to voluntarily move his gaze to the right. Which of the following brain regions is most likely affected?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This patient has damage to the frontal eye fields (FEF),which are located in theleft frontal lobe. The key clinical clue is the deviation of both eyes toward the side of the lesion (the left) combined with inability to voluntarily gaze to the right. The frontal eye fields control voluntary, conjugate eye movements to the opposite side, so a lesion in the left FEF prevents the eyes from moving rightward. As a result, the unopposed activity of the right FEF causes the eyes to deviate left. The presence of right-sided weakness further supports a lesion in the left hemisphere, consistent with involvement of the left frontal lobe. This combination of conjugate gaze deviation and contralateral motor deficits is characteristic of an acute lesion affecting the frontal eyefields.

Answer B (incorrect answer):The left occipital lobe is responsible for visual processing.Lesions here can cause

Answer C (incorrect answer): The left parietal lobe is involved in spatial processing and sensory integration. Lesions may cause neglect or agnosia but do not typically result in conjugate gaze deviation.

Answer D (incorrect answer): A lesion in the right frontal lobe would cause deviation of the eyes toward the right, not the left as seen in this patient. auditory processing. Lesions here do not explain the gaze deviation or right-sided weakness. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 68-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife due to sudden difficulty speaking. She reports that he seems frustrated because he knows what he wants to say but cannot get the words out. His speech is slow and halting, often consisting of short phrases with frequent pauses. He is able to follow commands without difficulty. which of the following brain regions is most likely affected?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This patient has Broca's aphasia, a non-fluent aphasia caused by damage to the left frontal lobe, specifically Broca's area. The diagnosis is supported by his effortful, broken speech, preserved

Answer B (incorrect answer): The left temporal lobe contains Wernicke's area, which is responsible for language comprehension. Lesions here cause fluent but meaningless speech and impaired comprehension, not the effortful, non-fluent speech seen in this patient.

Answer C (incorrect answer): The occipital lobes are responsible for visual processing. Lesions may result in cortical blindness or visual field deficits, not language disturbances.

Answer D (incorrect answer): The prefrontal cortex is involved in executive functions like judgment and planning. Lesions can cause disinhibition and poor decision-making but do not result in expressive aphasia.

Answer E (incorrect answer): The right parietal lobe is associated with spatial attention. Lesions often cause left-sided spatial neglect but are not involved in language production. Mc Graw

questions.question: An 82-year-old woman presents for evaluation one week after a stroke. She has no visual complaints. When asked to draw a clock and a flower she produces the drawing below: Damage to which of the following areas of the brain is most likely in this woman?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (incorrect answer): Lesions of the left parietal lobe cause right-sided spatial neglect. Right-sided spatial neglect is rare, probably due to redundant processing of right-sided information by the left brain.

Answers E and F (incorrect answers): The temporal lobe contains many structures including the auditory cortex, Wernicke's speech area (left temporal lobe), and the amygdala. Temporal lobe lesions can produce deafness, Wernicke's aphasia, or Kluver-Bucy syndrome.

Answers G and H (incorrect answers): The occipital lobe contains the visual cortex. Lesions in this region produce cortical blindness. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 24-year-old man is evaluated for abnormal behavior. Two weeks ago, he suffered head trauma from a motor vehicle remote controls. He is constantly hungry and has gained ten pounds in the past week. He has been masturbating frequently and often rubs his genitals against objects like chairs or tables. Damage to which of the following areas of the brain is most likely in this man?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (incorrect answer): The frontal lobe is important for many functions, including motor activity, emotions, and planning. Lesions of the motor cortex of the frontal lobe lead to motor loss. Lesions of the decisions), or personality changes. Broca's speech area may also be damaged by frontal lobe lesions.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Lesions of the right parietal lobe cause left-sided hemispatial neglect, characterized by reduced awareness of the left-side of space, despite normal sensory function.

Answer D (incorrect answer): The occipital lobe contains the visual cortex. Lesions in this region produce cortical blindness.

Answer E (incorrect answer): The midbrain is the uppermost portion of the brainstem. It contains the nuclei of cranial nerves III and IV as well as connections from the cortex, cerebellum, and peripheral nerves. Midbrain lesions do not produce Kluver-Bucy syndrome. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 68-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after suddenly collapsing at home. His wife reports that he was walking across the kitchen when he suddenly fell and was unable to move the right side of his body. She states there is no recent trauma or preceding symptoms. His medical history includes long-standing hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. He also has chronic atrial fibrillation and takes apixaban. On arrival, he is drowsy but arousable. Neurologic examination reveals paralysis of the right face, arm, and leg with intact sensation. There is no aphasia, neglect, or visual field loss. CT scan of the head shows a small region of hemorrhage. which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This man has pure motor hemiparesis due to a small hemorrhage in the internal capsule caused by rupture of a Charcot-Bouchard aneurysm. These microaneurysms occur in small penetrating arteries (such as the lenticulostriate arteries from the middle cerebral artery) and are associated with chronic hypertension. When they rupture, they produce small intraparenchymal hemorrhages, most commonly in the basal ganglia, thalamus, internal capsule, or pons. Depending on the location, the resulting hemorrhage can mimic a lacunar stroke. In this case, damage to the posterior limb of the internal capsule produces contralateral weakness of the face, arm, and leg without sensory loss or cortical signs.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Anterior cerebral artery (AcA) stroke causes contralateral leg weakness greater than arm involvement, along with behavioral changes or urinary incontinence due to frontal lobe involvement. This patient's presentation involves dense hemiparesis affecting the face, arm, and leg equally.

Answer B (incorrect answer): A lacunar infarct is a small ischemic stroke affecting the deep structures of the therefore the cause is rupture of a Charcot-Bouchard aneurysm, not vessel occlusion. weakness more than leg, along with possible aphasia (dominant hemisphere) or neglect (nondominant small hemorrhage, not a cortical infarct.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Posterior cerebral artery (PcA) strokes typically affect the occipital lobe and cause visual field deficits, such as contralateral homonymous hemianopia. This patient's motor-only symptoms without visual disturbance make a PCA stroke unlikely. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 66-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife due to sudden onset of involuntary movements. Earlier that morning, she noticed that his left arm and leg were flinging wildly and unpredictably. He cannot control the movements, which are continuous and interfere with walking and using his hands. He is alert and oriented and has no weakness, sensory loss, or speech difficulty. His medical history includes poorly controlled hypertension. Neurologic examination reveals large-amplitude, flinging movements of the left upper and lower extremities. MRI of the brain reveals a small area of hyperintensity. Which of the following brain regions is most likely affected in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This man has hemiballismus, a hyperkinetic movement disorder characterized by sudden, involuntary, large-amplitude, flinging movements of the limbs on one side of the body. It is most commonly caused by a lesion in the contralateral subthalamic nucleus, typically due to lacunar infarction from small vessel disease associated with hypertension. The subthalamic nucleus plays a role in the indirect pathway of the basal ganglia, which inhibits movement. Damage to this nucleus leads to reduced inhibition of the thalamus and excessive motor output, resulting in uncontrolled movements.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Cortical lesions can cause weakness, sensory loss, or cortical signs such as aphasia or neglect, but they do not result in isolated hemiballismus. The cortex is not the primary site involved in the

Answer B (incorrect answer): The globus pallidus is involved in both the direct and indirect pathways of the basal ganglia and plays a role in regulating movement, but lesions here typically produce other types of movement disorders such as rigidity or dystonia, not hemiballismus.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Lesions of the internal capsule affect descending motor fibers and typically result in contralateral hemiparesis or hemiplegia, not involuntary flinging movements. This patient has no weakness.

Answer D (incorrect answer): The putamen is involved in the initiation of voluntary movement and is associated with disorders such as Huntington disease when degenerated. Isolated putaminal lesions do not cause hemiballismus.

Answer F (incorrect answer): Thalamic lesions usually cause sensory deficits (as seen in pure sensory strokes) or can lead to thalamic pain syndromes. Hemiballismus is not a typical result of thalamic infarction.

He also reports numbness over the right side of his face. He has no difficulty understanding speech, speaking, or maintaining balance. His medical history includes hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Neurologic examination reveals reduced strength and diminished sensation to light touch and pinprick over the right face, arm, and leg. MRI of the brain reveals a small area of restricted diffusion. This pattern most commonly results from a small infarct in the thalamocapsular region, where both the posterior limb of the internal capsule (containing strokes are caused by occlusion of deep penetrating arteries and are strongly associated with chronic hypertension and diabetes mellitus. Unlike cortical strokes, sensorimotor lacunar infarcts do not produce aphasia, neglect, or visual field deficits, and symptoms are typically isolated to the face, arm, and leg on one D=unD.= Mc side.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Ataxic hemiparesis is another lacunar stroke subtype that involves weakness and incoordination on the same side of the body,usually due to infarction inthe basis pontis orinternal capsule. Sensory loss as described in this case is not a typical feature.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Cortical strokes result in symptoms such as aphasia, visual field deficits, gaze deviation, or neglect depending on the vascular territory involved. This patient lacks cortical signs and instead shows combined motor and sensory deficits in a pattern typical of a subcortical (lacunar) stroke. sensory deficits and no speech involvement, ruling out this subtype.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Pure motor strokes are lacunar strokes that involve weakness without sensory deficits and are usually due to infarction of the posterior limb of the internal capsule. This patient has both motor and sensory loss, making pure motor stroke an incorrect choice.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Pure sensory strokes are also lacunar strokes. They are caused by thalamic infarcts motor deficits as well, making pure sensory stroke unlikely. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 74-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after developing sudden difficulty speaking and using his right hand. He was eating lunch when his daughter noticed his speech had become slurred and difficult to understand. He also numbness, vision changes, or leg symptoms. His medical history includes hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. On neurologic examination, his speech is slow and slurred but fluent, and he follows commands appropriately. There is mild right lower facial weakness and impaired coordination of the right hand with difficulty performing rapid alternating movements. Strength in the right upper limb is slightly reduced. Lower extremities are unaffected. CT scan of the brain shows no bleeding. patient?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (incorrect answer):Infarction of the posteriorlimb of the internal capsule produces a pure motor stroke with contralateral hemiparesis affecting the face, arm, and leg equally. This patient's symptoms are limited to the face and hand and involve coordination and articulation more than strength, which is not consistent with internal capsule infarction.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Lesions in the motor cortex produce weakness of the face and hand, but cortical infarcts are usually associated with additional features such as aphasia (see above), gaze deviation, or seizures depending on the vascular territory involved. The absence of cortical signs and the presence of a small infarct on imaging make a cortical lesion unlikely.

Answer D (incorrect answer): A lesion in the sensory cortex would produce contralateral numbness or and articulation, not sensation.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Thalamic infarcts typically cause pure sensory strokes, with contralateral sensory affecting speech and fine hand movements, which are not characteristic of a thalamic lesion. Mc Graw

questions.question: that morning, she noticed tingling and decreased sensation on the left side of her face, arm, and leg. She denies weakness, vision changes, or difficulty speaking. Her past medical history includes hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Neurologic examination reveals diminished pinprick and light touch sensation over the left face, upper limb, and lower limb. Motor strength, reflexes, and gait are normal. MRI of the brain reveals a small area of restricted diffusion. Which of the following structures is most likely affected in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (incorrect answer): Lacunar infarcts involving the basal pons result in ataxic hemiparesis or symptoms without weakness or ataxia are not characteristic of pontine lesions.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Infarcts of the internal capsule result in a pure motor stroke, affecting descending corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers in the posterior limb. This patient has no motor deficits, making internal capsule involvement unlikely.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Lesions of the motor cortex would produce contralateral weakness, often with additional cortical signs such as aphasia, gaze deviation, or seizures. This patient has no weakness or cortical features, and her symptoms are restricted to sensory loss. may cause contralateral sensory deficits, but cortical strokes are usually accompanied by other signs of cortical involvement like neglect, aphasia, or visual field deficits. Additionally, cortical strokes often produce symptoms greater in the legs than the arms or vice versa. This woman has sensory loss affecting the face and all limbs equally. MM

questions.question: A 67-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife due to sudden-onset weakness. Earlier in the day, he was having breakfast when he suddenly dropped his fork and was unable to move his right arm and leg. He has no difficulty speaking or understanding language. His medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension. Neurologic examination shows 0/5 strength in the right upper and lower extremities, with intact sensation and no visual field deficits. Which of the following structures is most likely affected in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This man has a pure motor stroke, a common subtype of lacunar infarction. Lacunar strokes are small (<15 mm), subcortical infarcts that result from occlusion of deep penetrating arteries, such as standing hypertension or diabetes mellitus, which cause lipohyalinosis or microatheroma formation in small vessels. The resulting ischemia affects deep brain structures, such as the internal capsule, thalamus, basal ganglia, or pons. On MRI diffusion weighted imaging (DwI) sequences, restricted diffusion is the hallmark of acuteischemicstroke. Pure motor stroke is the most frequent lacunar stroke syndrome and is caused by a lesion in the posterior limb of the internal capsule. This region contains descending corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts, and its involvement produces contralateral weakness of the face, arm, and leg without accompanying sensory loss, visual field deficits, or cortical signs (such as aphasia or neglect). Lacunar strokes typically have an abrupt onset and are not associated with impaired consciousness or higher cortical dysfunction, making them distinct from cortical infarcts.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Lesions of the basal pons can be caused the ataxic hemiparesis subtype of lacunar hemiparesis, they usually also cause ataxia which is not described in this case.

Answer C (incorrect answer): A lesion in the motor cortex could cause contralateral weakness, but it is often accompanied by additional cortical signs (e.g., aphasia if in the dominant hemisphere or gaze deviation). The sudden onset of symptoms and absence of cortical findings suggest a subcortical rather than cortical lesion. In addition, cortical strokes often produce weakness greater in the legs than the arms or vice versa. This man has "dense" hemiparesis which equally affects the face and all limbs.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Involvement of the sensory cortex (located in the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe) would result in sensory deficits like numbness and paresthesias, but not motor weakness. This patient has no sensory loss. Damage to the ventral posterior nucleus of the thalamus results in contralateral sensory loss affecting the face, arm, and leg. This patient has preserved sensation. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 68-year-old man with atrial fibrillation presents with weakness. Physical examination shows decreased strength in the left foot and decreased sensation to light touch and pin prick of the left calf and foot. This man's symptoms are most likely caused by disrupted blood flow in which of the following vessels?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (incorrect answer): Strokes caused by occlusion of the middle cerebral artery result in decreased blood flow to part of the frontal lobe, the lateral temporal lobe, the parietal lobe, and the posterior limb of the lower extremity weakness and numbness, as occurred in this man, is an unlikely presentation of a middle cerebral artery territory infarct.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Strokes caused by occlusion of the posterior cerebral artery cause decreased blood flow to the posterior portion of the brain, affecting structures such as the occipital lobe, the thalamus, and the midbrain. Different clinical syndromes can develop depending on the part of the artery that is ischemic. One presentation of posterior cerebral artery stroke is homonymous hemianopsia in which the contralateral half of the visual field is blind. Other visual symptoms could include visual hallucinations or the inability to recognize objects (visual agnosia). Posterior cerebral artery stroke that affects the thalamus can cause contralateral sensory loss.

Answer A (incorrect answer): The posterior inferior cerebellar artery supplies blood to the brainstem and cerebellum. A stroke involving this vessel causes the lateral medullary syndrome. Symptoms include ipsilateral ataxia, nausea, vomiting, slurred speech, difficulty swallowing, and vertigo. Often there is a loss of sensation to the ipsilateral face and contralateral limbs.

Answer D (incorrect answer): The anterior inferior cerebellar artery supplies blood to the brainstem and cerebellum. A stroke involving this vessel can cause ipsilateral facial weakness, deafness, vertigo, and uncoordinatedeyemovement. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 69-year-old man with hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and smoking presents with numbness in the left face, arm, and leg. A non-contrast computed tomography (CT) scan of the head is normal. He undergoes magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain, and he is told that he had a stroke. Which area of the brain was most likely affected?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This man had a lacunar stroke affecting the thalamus. Letter E points to the thalamus. Lacunar strokes are small strokes associated with vascular changes caused by hypertension. They occur due to obstruction of a small artery of the brain. They most often affect the deep matter of the brain, a portion of which is depicted in the magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and drawing above. Lack of blood flow to the thalamus can cause a pure sensory stroke, resulting in numbness or sensory loss to the contralateral side of the body.

Answer D (incorrect answer): This arrow points to the internal capsule. A lack of blood flow to the internal capsule can cause a pure motor stroke, resulting in weakness of the contralateral side of the body. The internal capsuleis another common locationfor lacunar strokes.

Answer A (incorrect answer): This arrow points to the caudate nucleus. Along with the putamen (answer choice the motor activity of the body. Strokes affecting the caudate can cause weakness and increased deep tendon reflexes, typically in the face and upper extremities.

Answer B (incorrect answer): This arrow points to the putamen, another component of the basal ganglia. Although an uncommon location for a lacunar stroke, a stroke affecting the putamen can cause a movement disorder. A rare manifestation of a stroke to the putamen is hemiballismus, which causes wild, flinging movements of extremities. strokes to the globus pallidus would cause primarily motor symptoms such as weakness or abnormal movements. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 54-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy presents with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. His initial potassium measured in the emergency room is 2.4 mEq/L (normal 3.5-5.0 mEq/L). He develops ventricular tachycardia, and on physical exam his pulses cannot be palpated. The advanced life support protocol is activated, and he regains a pulse after nine minutes of cardiopulmonary resuscitation. After three days in the hospital he is improving. Vital signs are within normal limits; however, he has bilateral weakness of his shoulders and arms. He does not have any deficits in his mental status, vision, sensation, or balance. He denies having other symptoms. what mechanism of action most likely explains his neurologic findings?

options.B: Cerebral ischemia due to a cardioembolic stroke
options.E: Hypoperfusion to a watershed area of the brain

questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This man had a watershed infarct due to cerebral hypoperfusion from his cardiac arrest.He developed cardiac arrest due to electrolyte abnormalities caused by vomiting and diarrhea in the setting of known cardiac disease. When blood flow to the brain is inadequate, certain areas of the brain are more vulnerable to damage. Areas perfused by distal branches of major arteries are at particular risk. This can occur at the borders between areas of brain tissue supplied by major vessels. The watershed area between the anterior and middle cerebral arteries is depicted in the image above.A lack of blood flow to this area causes weakness of the shoulders and arms, with sparing of the face and feet. This syndrome is sometimes called "man- in-a-barrel" syndrome. If the watershed area between the middle and posterior cerebral arteries were affected, symptoms could includeblindness. Mc Graw

Answer D (incorrect answer): If a cardiac arrest resulting in cerebral hypoperfusion causes diffuse brain ischemia and damage, cerebral edema may occur. Symptoms of cerebral edema range in severity. Mild symptoms include nausea, vomiting, headache, and confusion. Severe symptoms include seizures and coma. His limited motor weakness and lack of other symptoms are not consistent with diffuse cerebral edema.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis occurs when a blood clot develops in the brain's cerebral venous sinus thrombosis is headache. Varying patterns of weakness can also occur, and seizures are common. Venous sinus thrombosis is unlikely in this man, given his lack of headache, hypercoagulable state, or seizures.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Emboli originating in the heart can cause ischemic stroke. This man is at risk for cardioembolic stroke due to his ischemic cardiomyopathy (left ventricular thrombus can form in severe cardiomyopathy). Symptoms of cardioembolic stroke vary based on which cerebral vessels are affected. Sometimes only one vessel is occluded, but in other cases, multiple cerebral vessels are affected. It would be unlikely for cardiac emboli to cause bilateral weakness of the shoulders and arms as seen in this man. Emboli would have to affect both sides of the brain in a similar vascular pattern. are some triggers of this condition. Symptoms include headache in addition to neurologic deficits based on the arteryinvolved.Sincetypicallyonlyonebloodvesselisaffected,anintracranialarterialdissectionwouldcause unilateral, and not bilateral, weakness. Mc

questions.question: A 76-year-old right-handed woman with diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and smoking is brought to the hospital because her family notices that she is weak. On examination, she has drooping of the lower-left face and weakness of the left arm. She produces the image below when asked to draw a clock. This woman's symptoms are most likely caused by disrupted blood flow in which of the following vessels?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This woman's symptoms suggest a right middle cerebral artery stroke. This blood vessel supplies part of the frontal lobe, the lateral temporal lobe, part of the parietal lobe, and the posterior limb of the internal capsule.When these parts of the brain lose blood flow,weaknessof the contralateral (opposite) face, arm, and sometimes leg occur. Patients can also develop hemineglect, in which they ignore sensory stimuli from the left side of the body. Hemineglect is illustrated in the drawing where this woman does not draw the left side of the clock. It is also notable that her family brought her to the hospital after noticing she was weak. This suggests she could have anosognosia, a term describing patients that are unaware they have neurologic deficits. Anosognosia is commonly seen with right middle cerebral artery strokes.

Answer B (incorrect answer): A stroke to the anterior cerebral artery causes decreased blood flow to the frontal lobe, the anterior corpus callosum, and the anterior limb of the internal capsule. This can cause weakness and decreased sensation to the opposite side of the body, but typically affects the contralateral leg and not the arm and face.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Strokes caused by occlusion of the posterior cerebral artery lead to decreased blood flow to the posterior portion of the brain, affecting structures such as the occipital lobe, the thalamus, and the midbrain. Different clinical syndromes can develop depending on the part of the artery obstructed. One presentation of posterior cerebral artery stroke is homonymous hemianopsia, in which the contralateral half of the visual field is lost (partial blindness). Other visual symptoms could include visual hallucinations or the inability to recognize objects (visual agnosia). If the posterior cerebral artery stroke affects the thalamus, it can cause contralateral sensory losses. AnswerC(incorrectanswer):Strokesaffecting thebasilar arterycausereduced bloodflowtothepons and midbrain. Symptoms include a decreased level of consciousness, facial weakness, and weakness in one half of the body. Often these patients have uncoordinated limb movement.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Superior cerebellar artery strokes affect the supply of blood to the cerebellum. Typical symptoms include dizziness, vomiting, slurred speech, and limb incoordination. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 69-year-old woman presents with a loss of vision in the pattern depicted below (black = no vision): No other neurologic deficits are found on physical examination. Obstruction of which of the following blood vessels in the Circle of willis is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This is the posterior cerebral artery. This woman most likely has a stroke affecting this vessel given the changes noted in her visual field. The image depicts homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. Lack of blood flow to the temporal and occipital lobes causes loss of the contralateral (opposite) side of the visual field (refer to diagram). Often vision persists in the central part of the visual field, because both the posterior cerebral artery and middle cerebral artery supply the region of the brain that processes input from the macula.

Answer A (incorrect answer): This is the anterior cerebral artery. Strokes affecting the anterior cerebral artery cause contralateral (opposite) weakness of the leg. Motor weakness is often accompanied by decreased sensation. Visual symptoms are not present.

Answer B (incorrect answer): This is the middle cerebral artery. Strokes affecting this vessel cause contralateral motor and sensory symptoms primarily affecting the arm and face. A complete occlusion of the middle cerebral artery may cause homonymous hemianopia, but affected patients would also have weakness and sensory losses.

Answer D (incorrect answer): This is the basilar artery. Strokes affecting the basilar artery cause reduced blood flow to the pons and midbrain. Symptoms include a decreased level of consciousness, facial weakness, and weakness in one half of the body. Often these patients have uncoordinated limb movement. Patients can have gaze palsy, but they do not typically have visual field losses.

Answer E (incorrect answer): This is the vertebral artery. Strokes affecting this artery can cause different syndromes depending on which part of the vessel is occluded. The cerebellum and brainstem could be affected. Symptoms can include dizziness, unsteadiness, weakness, and decreased sensation. Patients can have blurred vision or double vision, but they typically do not have homonymous hemianopia. Mc

questions.question: A 6-day-old newborn is brought to the emergency department due to fever, irritability, and poor feeding. Examination reveals a bulging anterior fontanelle and nuchal rigidity. Blood cultures are drawn, and a lumbar puncture is performed. Cerebrospinal fluid shows an elevated white blood cell count with a predominance of neutrophils, elevated protein, and low glucose. The clinical team suspects bacterial meningitis. Due to a global shortage of antibiotics, the only antimicrobials available are ceftriaxone and gentamicin. Administration of ceftriaxone in this baby increases the risk of which of the following complications?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): Kernicterus is a serious neurologic condition caused by deposition of unconjugated bilirubin in brain tissue, especially the basal ganglia. In neonates, ceftriaxone is avoided because it is highly protein-bound and can displace bilirubin from albumin, leading to increased free bilirubin levels. Neonates have an immature blood-brain barrier, making them more susceptible to bilirubin neurotoxicity. Use of ceftriaxone in neonates is therefore contraindicated due to this risk, particularly in jaundiced infants or those with elevated bilirubinlevels. Because of the risk of kernicterus, newborn meningitis is usually treated empirically (i.e., prior to culture results showing the causative organism and its specific sensitivities) with the combination of ampicillin and gentamycin.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Hearing loss is a complication of neonatal meningitis itself, and also a potential adverse effect of aminoglycosides like gentamicin due to ototoxicity. However, the question specifically asks about ceftriaxone, and kernicterus is the most specific and serious risk of using ceftriaxone in neonates.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Hydrocephalus can result from complications of meningitis, especially if there's obstruction of CsF flow due to inflammation or scarring. However, this is not directly linked to the use of ceftriaxone.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Seizures may occur in meningitis but are not a recognized adverse effect of the ototoxicity or nephrotoxicity.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Skin rash may occur as an allergic reaction to antibiotics, but it is not the primary concern when giving ceftriaxone to a neonate. The most dangerous and specific adverse effect is kernicterus.

questions.question: A 3-year-old boy is hospitalized with fever, vomiting, lethargy, and nuchal rigidity. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis reveals an days. At a follow-up visit one month later, he is doing well, but his parents are concerned about long-term complications. Which of the following is most likely to develop in this boy as a long-term complication of his condition?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (incorrect answer): Visual field loss is not a typical long-term complication of bacterial meningitis. It may occur in conditions affecting the optic chiasm or visual cortex, neither of which are commonly involved in uncomplicated meningitis.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Cerebral aneurysm formation is not a known complication of bacterial meningitis. inflammation. Mc ME

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman undergoes a lumbar puncture for evaluation of possible multiple sclerosis. The procedure is performed with the patient in the lateral decubitus position. As the spinal needle is advanced, it passes sequentially through several needle penetrates, from superficial to deep? Skin-> supraspinous ligament->

options.A: interspinous ligament-> ligamentum flavum-> dura mater-> arachnoid mater
options.B: supraspinous ligament-> ligamentum Skin-> interspinous ligament-> flavum-> arachnoid mater-> dura mater
options.C: ligament-> supraspinous ligament-> Skin-> ligamentum flavum-> interspinous dura mater-> arachnoid mater
options.D: Skin-> supraspinous ligament-> interspinous ligament-> arachnoid mater-> dura mater-> ligamentum flavum
options.E: Skin-> interspinous ligament-> ligamentum flavum-> supraspinous ligament-> dura mater-> arachnoid mater

questions.question: A 75-year-old man presents with 2 days of fever, headache, and neck stiffness. A lumbar puncture is performed and shows an added to target which of the following pathogens?

Answer C (correct answer): Listeria monocytogenes is a facultative intracellular gram-positive rod that can cause meningitis in older adults, neonates, and immunocompromised patients. It is transmitted through contaminated food such as unpasteurized dairy and deli meats. Empiric therapy in elderly patients with suspected bacterial meningitis should include ampicillin to cover Listeria, in addition to vancomycin and a third-generation cephalosporin (e.g., ceftriaxone). The mechanism of action of ampicillin is inhibition of peptidoglycan synthesis, leading to bacterial cell wall lysis.

Answer A (incorrect):Escherichia coliis a cause of meningitis in neonatesbut is not a commonpathogen in older adults. It is a gram-negative bacillus acquired via vertical transmission in newborns or from urinary tract sources in adults, but it would not be specifically targeted with a third antibiotic in this man's clinical context.

Answer B (incorrect): Group B Streptococcus(e.g., Streptococcus agalactiae) is a leading cause of neonatal in settings like college dorms and military barracks. It is already covered by ceftriaxone and does not require an additional agent in empiric therapy.

Answer E (incorrect): Streptococcus pneumoniae is a leading cause of meningitis in adults and the elderly. It is covered by both vancomycin and ceftriaxone, so an additional antibiotic specifically for this organism is not necessary. W Him

Answer C (correct answer): This woman has bacterial meningitis, an infection of the meninges, the membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord. Clinical features include fever, headaches, and sensitivity to light (photophobia) that develop rapidly, often in less than one day. On examination, neck stiffness (also called nuchal rigidity) is often present. Bacterial meningitis often leads to a markedly elevated serum white blood count,as seenin this case. Other symptoms of tuberculous meningitis may include confusion and cranial nerve deficits. Typically, symptoms do not develop rapidly over 1 day, as occurred in this case. Certain types of fungal meningitis may also have CSF findings similar to those of tuberculosis.

Answer B (incorrect answer): These CSF results suggest viral meningitis. The CsF in viral meningitis shows a normal glucose level, a protein level that is normal or high, and pleocytosis with a lymphocytic predominance. This woman is unlikely to have viral meningitis, given the short duration of her symptoms and marked serum leukocytosis, both findings that are rarely seen in viral meningitis.

Answer D (incorrect answer): These CsF results are normal other than an elevated glucose. Normally the CSF glucose value is approximately two-thirds of the serum glucose value. An elevated serum glucose may therefore cause an elevated CsF glucose. It is important to understand this relationship, because the CsF glucose may be normal in bacterial meningitis (rather than low) in the setting of an elevated serum glucose.

Answer E (incorrect answer): These CsF results have some characteristics suggestive of bacterial meningitis, including pleocytosis with a polymorphonuclear predominance and an elevated protein. However, the CsF in bacterial meningitis typically has a reduced glucose level due to bacterial metabolism of glucose.

Answer D (correct answer): This woman has eclampsia, which is the occurrence of generalized seizures in a patient with preeclampsia (hypertension and proteinuria after 20 weeks gestation). Because her seizure activity has continued without recovery of consciousness, she meets criteria for status epilepticus in the setting of eclampsia. The drug of choice for seizure control in eclampsia is magnesium sulfate, which acts as a CNS depressant by blocking NMDA receptors and inhibiting presynaptic glutamate release. It reduces neuronal excitability and prevents recurrent seizures more effectively than traditional anticonvulsants in this setting. It is both first-line treatment and prophylaxis in eclampsia.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Carbamazepine is a sodium channel blocker used for focal seizures. It has no role channels in thalamic neurons. It is ineffective in treating generalized tonic-clonic seizures or status epilepticus, and has norole in eclampsia. sulfate is superior for both controlling and preventing seizures, and it is safer for both mother and fetus.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Phenytoin blocks sodium channels and is used in many seizure types, including second-line for status epilepticus. However, it is not effective in eclampsia and poses additional risks during pregnancy, such as teratogenicity and maternal side effects.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman is brought to the clinic by her family due to episodes of abnormal behavior. During these episodes, she becomes unresponsive and repeatedly smacks her lips. The episodes last for 1 to 2 minutes. Afterward, she is confused for about five minutes before becoming oriented again. Further evaluation confirms evidence of a seizure disorder. Which of the following best describes this woman's seizures?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This woman has clinical features of a focal impaired awareness seizure. These seizures originate in one cerebral hemisphere and are characterized by impaired consciousness. They often involve automatisms, which are involuntary, coordinated, repetitive movements or behaviors such as lip- smacking, chewing, or hand movements. These seizures are usually followed by a brief postictal period of confusion. These features, especially the unresponsiveness and postictal disorientation, are consistent with focal impaired awareness seizures, previously known as complex partial seizures.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Focal aware seizures are seizures that arise from a localized area of the brain but do not impair consciousness. Patients remain aware of their surroundings and can often describe the episode. This patient's unresponsiveness and confusion afterward rule out focal aware seizures.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Atonic seizures involve a sudden loss of muscle tone, which can cause the patient to fall abruptly. These seizures are brief and are not associated with automatisms or prolonged postictal confusion. They are most commonly seen in pediatric generalized epilepsy syndromes. confusion and are not consistent with the patient's described behavior.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Generalized tonic-clonic seizures involve a tonic phase of stiffening followed by clonic rhythmic jerking of the limbs. These seizures are associated with a complete loss of consciousness and a longer postictal period. The absence of full-body convulsions and the presence of automatisms suggest a focal seizurerather thana generalized one. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 67-year-old man presents with a 2-day history of confusion, fever, weakness, and slurred speech. A lumbar puncture is performed, and analysis of the cerebrospinal fluid shows an elevated white blood cell count with a lymphocytic predominance and an elevated protein level. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain is shown below. which of the following is the most likely cause of his illness?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This man has encephalitis due to herpes simplex virus (HsV). Encephalitis is inflammation of the brain. It often occurs together with meningitis, a condition called meningoencephalitis. Symptoms of encephalitis include confusion, decreased level of consciousness, weakness, unsteady gait, slurred speech, and seizures. The cerebrospinal fluid (CsF) typically shows an elevated white blood cell count with a lymphocytic predominance similar to cases of viral meningitis. CsF also may show red blood cells. Typically the CSF protein level is elevated. Temporal lobe abnormalities by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are common in HsV encephalitis. The MRI study shows enhancement (bright white color) of the temporal lobes when infected by HsV. A diagnosis can be confirmed through CSF polymerase chain reaction testing for identification of HsV genetic material. HsV encephalitis is treated with intravenous acyclovir.

Answer A (incorrect answer): West Nile virus, a virus carried by a mosquito vector, may also cause encephalitis. Symptoms include headache, fever, neck stiffness, and confusion. CsF findings may be similar to those seen in this man. Infection with West Nile virus does not typically cause abnormalities in the temporal lobes, as seen on this man's MRI. Imaging in West Nile virus infection may be normal or show changes in the meninges, brain stem, or basal ganglia.

questions.question: A 53-year-old man presents with shaking of his hands. He notices that his symptoms are more pronounced when he writes with a pen, drinks from a glass, or tries to eat soup. The tremor improves when he drinks alcohol. On examination, a high- frequency tremor is present in both hands when he holds out his arms. Which term best describes his tremor?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This man has essential tremor, a condition previously known as "benign essential holding a sustainedposture.Essential tremor is common and estimated toaffect 5percentof adults over the age of 50. Essential tremor has a genetic predisposition, and patients with a family history of the condition are more likely to develop the disease. Alcohol often alleviates the tremor. Propranolol and primidone may be used to treat the condition.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Healthy patients may have a physiologic tremor, which is often more pronounced in the setting of strong emotion, tiredness, hyperthyroidism, fever, or low blood sugar. This may be observed by asking a person to hold a piece of paper in an outstretched hand.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Resting tremors cause repetitive movements of the hands or other parts of the body that improve with activity and are worse at rest. When they affect the hands, they are often called "pill- rolling" tremors. Resting tremors are common in Parkinson's disease.

Answer C (incorrect answer): An intention tremor causes a broad, zigzag tremor that occurs near the end of a purposeful movement. This tremor may be elicited on finger-to-nose testing during physical exam. Cerebellar dysfunction causes intention tremor.

Answer D (incorrect answer):A wing-beating tremor is a coarse, irregular tremor that is most obvious when the arms are held outstretched. The appearance of this tremor mimics a bird flapping its wings. Wing-beating tremor is classically associated with wilson's disease, which is a genetic disorder of copper metabolism.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman presents with depression and forgetfulness. She also has random, purposeless, and uncontrollable movements of her arms. She is afraid because her mother developed similar symptoms in her late 30s and died at age 45 due to complications from dementia. Damage to which of the following brain structures is the most likely cause of this woman's presentation?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This woman has symptoms of Huntington's disease (HD). She has depression, memory loss (which may be an early finding of dementia), and chorea (random, purposeless, and uncontrollable movements of her arms). Huntington's disease is an autosomal dominant disease that appears at an earlier age with more severe symptoms in successive generations, a phenomenon called "anticipation." The genetic mutation associated with Huntington's results in an excess release of glutamine within the central nervous system (CNs), which causes damage to neurons in the caudate and putamen.

Answers B, C, D, and E (incorrect answers): Huntington's disease is not associated with damage to the globus pallidus, internal capsule, or thalamus. Damage to the globus pallidus may occur in wilson's disease, which is a disorder of copper metabolism that may also cause movement disorders. Damage to the thalamus may occur due to an ischemic stroke and may cause sensory deficits or motor weakness. Damage to the internal capsule may also occur due to an ischemic stroke and causes motor weakness on the contralateral side of the body. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 43-year-old man presents with depression, dementia, and aggression. On examination he has random, jerky, and purposeless movements of his hands and feet. His neurologist prescribes a medication to control his abnormal movements. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of action of this medication?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This man has Huntington's disease (HD). Depression, dementia, and aggression are common findings in this condition. He has chorea, which is a movement disorder of random, jerky, purposeless movements of the hands and feet. Tetrabenazine and deutetrabenazine inhibit the vesicular monoamine transporter (VMAT). This protein is located in the membrane ofsynapticvesiclesand used totransportmonoamineneurotransmitterssuchas dopamine. Inhibition of VMAT results in decreased release of dopamine within the central nervous system. This improves chorea, which is thought to be caused by increased dopamine activity. Valbenazine, another VMAT Mc Graw inhibitor, is approved for the treatment of tardive dyskinesia but has not been studied in the treatment of Huntington's disease.

Answer A(incorrect answer): Inhibition of catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) reduces the breakdown of dopamine. Entacapone and tolcapone are COMT inhibitors used for the treatment of Parkinson's disease. Often these medications are used in combination with L-dopa therapy. These medications are not used for the treatment of Huntington's disease. are used to treat Alzheimer's disease. These medications inhibit the breakdown of acetylcholine in the central nervous system (CNs). Alzheimer's disease is associated with a deficiency of acetylcholine in the cerebral cortex. depression, anxiety, or agitation) in patients with this disease. They are not used for the treatment of Huntington's disease.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Inhibition of monoamine oxidase type B (MAO-B) within the central nervous system reduces the degradation of dopamine, thus increasing its availability. Selegeline and rasagiline are MAO- B inhibitors used for the treatment of Parkinson's disease. Often these medications are used in combination with L-dopa therapy. They are not used for the treatment of Huntington's disease.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Multiple drugs work by inhibiting phosphodiesterase. Medications such as sildenafil and vardenafil inhibit phospodisterase-5. questions.question: A 62-year-old woman comes to the clinic due to frequent involuntary blinking and forced eye closure that has been worsening over the past several months. She says the episodes occur throughout the day and are especially troublesome when she is in bright light or under stress. At times, the spasms are so severe that she has difficulty keeping her eyes open, which interferes with reading and driving. On examination, there are intermittent, sustained contractions of the orbicularis oculi muscles causing involuntary eyelid closure. Her neurological exam is otherwise normal. which of the following best describes this patient's movement disorder?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This woman has blepharospasm, a form of focal dystonia involving the orbicularis oculi muscles. Dystonia is characterized by sustained or intermittent involuntary muscle contractions that result or sustained closure of the eyelids. Symptoms are often worsened by stress or sensory stimuli such as bright light and may interfere with vision and daily activities. Other examples of dystonia include cervical dystonia (spasmodic torticollis), which causes involuntary turning or tilting of the head; writer's cramp, a specific hand dystonia triggered by writing or fine motor tasks; spasmodic dysphonia, which affects the muscles of the larynx and alters speech; and oromandibular dystonia, involving repetitive contractions of the jaw or tongue. These conditions share the common feature of involuntary, prolonged muscle contraction that may be sustained or intermittently repetitive, often interfering with voluntary movement and daily activities.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Athetosis refers to slow, writhing, continuous movements, often of the hands or fingers. It is not associated with focal or sustained muscle contractions around the eyes. between muscle groups. The movements in this patient are more sustained and localized, not consistent with chorea.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Myoclonus involves sudden, brief, shock-like muscle jerks that may occur spontaneously or be triggered by movement or sensory stimuli. These movements are transient, non-rhythmic, and not sustained. In contrast, dystonia, as seen in this patient, involves sustained or intermittent muscle contractions that lead to abnormal postures or repetitive movements. The spasms in blepharospasm last longer than those seen in myoclonus and occur in patterned bursts. The key difference is that dystonia produces sustained contractions, whereas myoclonus causes brief, shock-like jerks.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Tremor is a rhythmic, oscillatory movement that is regular in frequency and amplitude. It does not involve sustained muscle contractions or abnormal posturing. In contrast, the patient's symptoms are intermittent, prolonged contractions of the eyelid muscles causing forced eye closure. This is typical for dystonia.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Myoclonus involves sudden, brief, shock-like muscle jerks. It is not flowing or unpredictable like chorea and is more characteristic of metabolic encephalopathy or seizure disorders.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Tics are sudden, stereotyped motor or vocal movements that are often suppressible and associated with conditions like Tourette syndrome. The movements in this case are not stereotyped or suppressible.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man with a history of cirrhosis due to chronic hepatitis B is brought to the emergency department because of increasing confusion and lethargy over the past 24 hours. His family reports that he has been disoriented and has had sudden, involuntary jerks of his arms while resting. Answer E (correct answer): This man has hepatic encephalopathy, a complication of advanced liver disease associated with the accumulation of neurotoxins such as ammonia. His brief, sudden, shock-like jerking movements are characteristic of myoclonus, which refers to rapid, involuntary muscle contractions that can occur in healthy individuals (e.g., hiccups, sleep starts) or in pathologic states such as metabolic and unpredictable and may be worsened by tactile or auditory stimuli.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Athetosis consists of slow, writhing, continuous movements usually affecting the fingers and hands. It is most often associated with basal ganglia dysfunction and is not characterized by sudden,jerkingmotions.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Chorea is characterized by rapid, irregular, purposeless movements that flow unpredictably between muscle groups. It is commonly seen in conditions such as rheumatic fever and Huntington disease, not metabolic encephalopathy.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Choreoathetosis is a combination of chorea and athetosis, involving both rapid and slow writhing movements. This movement pattern does not match the abrupt, shock-like jerks described in this case.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Dystonia involves sustained or intermittent muscle contractions that cause abnormal, often repetitive movements or postures. It is slower and more sustained than the brief, irregular jerks described here. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 19-year-old man is brought to the clinic by his parents due to several months of worsening hand tremors and clumsiness. They report that he has become more irritable and withdrawn, and his school performance has declined. On examination, he has a low-frequency, high-amplitude tremor of the upper limbs that worsens when he holds his arms outstretched with elbows flexed. He also demonstrates mild dysarthria and rigidity. Slit-lamp examination reveals brownish rings at the corneal margins. Laboratory studies show low serum ceruloplasmin and elevated urinary copper excretion. which of the following brain regions is most likely to be damaged in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This man has wilson disease, an autosomal recessive disorder caused impaired hepatic copper transport and excretion into bile. As a result, copper accumulates in various tissues, especially the liver, brain, and eyes. The classic features include neuropsychiatric symptoms (irritability, cognitive decline), movement abnormalities (wing-beating tremor, dysarthria, rigidity), and the presence of Kayser-Fleischer rings, which are copper deposits in the cornea visible on slit-lamp examination. Laboratory findings such as low serum ceruloplasmin and elevated urinary copper excretion support the diagnosis. ganglia. Copper deposition in these regions contributes to the movement abnormalities seen in this patient, including tremor, dystonia, and rigidity.

Answer A (incorrect answer): The caudate nucleus is prominently affected in Huntington disease. It may also be affected in wilson disease, but the putamen is more commonly and severely damaged and more directly responsible for the motor symptoms described.

Answer D (incorrect answer): The substantia nigra is involved in Parkinson disease due to dopaminergic neuron degeneration. Although copper can accumulate here in wilson disease, the substantia nigra is not the site responsible for the symptoms in this case.

Answer E (incorrect answer): The thalamus plays an important role in sensory relay and motor coordination but is not a primary target of copper deposition in Wilson disease. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 62-year-old man presents with slurred speech and difficulty chewing. On neurologic exam, his jaw deviates to the left when he opens his mouth. He also has decreased muscle tone and atrophy near the masseter muscle on the left side of his jaw. The corneal reflex is intact bilaterally. Answer B (correct answer): The presence of jaw muscle atrophy, decreased tone, and deviation of the jaw toward the localize the lesion to the left mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal nerve, which carries LMN fibers to the muscles of mastication. weak, the unopposed action of the contralateral pterygoid causes the jaw to deviate toward the weak (affected) side, in this case, the left. Importantly, LMNs do not decussate (i.e., cross to the opposite side of the body). The motor fibers in V3 exit the brainstem and project directly to the ipsilateral (same side) muscles. Therefore, a lesion of the left V3 causes left-sided weakness and atrophy. Of note, the lesion in this case involves in V3 (mandibular division) which is motor only and controls the muscles of mastication, like the masseter and pterygoids. It does not affect the ophthalmic division (V1), which is responsible for the sensory limb of the corneal reflex. This is the reason for the intact corneal reflex.

questions.question: A 68-year-old woman presents with difficulty speaking and swallowing. On neurologic exam, her tongue appears small and spastic without any signs of atrophy. When she attempts to speak, her speech is strained and effortful. The jaw jerk reflex is brisk. These findings are most consistent with damage to which of the following structures?

options.C: Lower motor neurons in the spinal cord

questions.explanation:
Answer A (incorrect answer): Damage to the cranial nerves in the brainstem leads to bulbar palsy, which is characterized by lower motor neuron (LMN) signs-such as flaccid, wasted tongue and absent jaw/gag reflex. This patient has spasticity and a brisk reflex, indicating upper motor neuron involvement instead.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Lesions of lower motor neurons in the spinal cord affect limbs and trunk, not bulbar muscles. LMN damage in the spinal cord results in flaccid paralysis, fasciculations, and muscle wasting-features absent in this patient. The symptoms involve cranial rather than spinal motor control.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Disorders like myasthenia gravis involve the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) and can impair bulbar function but do not cause spasticity or brisk reflexes. questions.question: A 24-year-old man presents to the clinic several weeks after sustaining a crush injury to his upper arm. He reports progressive return of some motor function but still experiences mild weakness. Histological analysis of the affected nerve shows intact endoneurium and perineurium, with signs of Wallerian degeneration distal to the lesion and central chromatolysis in the neuronal cell body. which of the following best describes the type of nerve injury in this patient?

options.B: Complete transection with no regenerative potential

questions.explanation:
Answer B (incorrect answer): Complete transection with no regenerative potential describes a total severing of the nerve, in which the structural framework is lost, making regeneration extremely unlikely. The presence of intact perineurium and endoneurium in this patient makes this answer incorrect.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Focal demyelination without axonal damage is a hallmark of neurapraxia, the mildest form of nerve injury. It involves only localized myelin disruption without any axonal injury, Wallerian degeneration, or

Answer D (incorrect answer): Neurapraxia is characterized by a temporary conduction block due to focal demyelination, with no axonal or connective tissue damage. Recovery is usually rapid and complete. The patient's histologic findings, including axonal degeneration and chromatolysis, rule out neurapraxia.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Neurotmesis is the most severe type of peripheral nerve injury. It involves complete disruption of the axon and supporting connective tissue layers. There is no continuity across the lesion, and meaningful regeneration is unlikely. The preserved endoneurium and perineurium in this case are inconsistent with neurotmesis. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 42-year-old man sustains a deep laceration to his forearm, completely transecting the radial nerve. questions.question: A 44-year-old man is seen in evaluation after he fell through a glass door and sustained a severe laceration to the right wrist. Specialized gene activation and protein translation occur that allow Schwann cells to facilitate nerve regeneration. The success or failure of this process determines whether nerve function to skeletal muscles will ultimately be restored.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Oligodendrocytes are cells of the central nervous system that myelinate central (not peripheral) nerves. These cells are not a component of the peripheral nervous system.

Answer B (correct answer): This man has magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings indicating spinal cord damage to the left side near the 1oth thoracic vertebra. This results in Brown-Sequard syndrome, a neurologic or multiple sclerosis. Brown-Sequard syndrome is associated with hemiplegia on the side of the lesion and contralateral sensory loss to pain and temperature. It also causes ipsilateral loss of vibration and loss of proprioception and right-sided loss of pain and temperature sensation. Patients also have a loss of all sensation at the level of the lesion(for example, this patient would have loss of sensation in the dermatome innervated by the 1oth thoracic vertebra). questions.question: A 46-year-old man presents for a routine physical examination. As part of his neurologic examination, a high-frequency vibrating tuning fork is placed on his left knee. These fibers synapse in the nucleus gracilis in the medulla, which specifically receives input from the lower body. questions.question: A 52-year-old man is evaluated for progressive weakness and muscle atrophy in his arms and legs over several months. He reports frequent muscle cramps and twitching. Answer A (correct answer): This man has clinical features of a lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion, including muscle weakness, hypotonia, hyporeflexia, and fasciculations, with preserved sensation. The anterior horn of the spinal cord contains the cell bodies of lower motor neurons, which project out of the spinal cord to innervate skeletal muscle. Damage to this region produces LMN signs like those seen in this case. Other possible locations for LMN lesions include the spinal roots (radiculopathies) and peripheral nerves (neuropathies). This man's presentation is suggestive of some form of anterior horn cell disease, such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). ALS can selectively affect anterior horn cells, causing pure motor deficits, especially in early stages.

Answer B (incorrect answer): The corticospinal tract carries upper motor neuron (UMN) signals from the cerebral cortex to the spinal cord. Lesions in this tract cause UMN clinical findings like spasticity, hyperreflexia, and Babinski sign. UMN lesions may occur in the motor cortex, internal capsule, brainstem, or spinal cord. Unlike LMN lesions, they do not produce fasciculations or muscle atrophy.

Answer C (incorrect answer): The fasciculus gracilis is part of the posterior column-medial lemniscus pathway and transmits vibration and proprioception from the lower body. A lesion here would lead to sensory deficits, particularly in the legs, but would not affect muscle strength or cause fasciculations or atrophy.

Answer D (incorrect answer): The lateral horn contains autonomic neurons including preganglionic sympathetic fibers between T1 and L2. Damage here leads to autonomic dysfunction (e.g., Horner syndrome, bladder dysregulation) but not to the motor deficits observed in this patient.

Answer E (incorrect answer): The posterior horn is where sensory afferents synapse after entering the spinal would not produce the motor symptoms seen in this patient.

Answer A (correct answer): The question describes testing of proprioception, the sensation of the position of toe, or limb in space. Proprioceptive information is transmitted to the brain by the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway (DcML). The image depicts the spinal cord at thoracic level. Only at the thoracic level is the lateral horn seen. Sensory information about proprioception, vibration, and fine touch is transmitted from sensory structures in the periphery via nerves that travel in the dorsal column of the spinal cord (area A in the image). This pathway is located toward the back (dorsal area) of the spinal cord. These fibers synapse in the medulla at the gracile nucleus (lower body nerves) or the cuneate nucleus (upper body nerves).

questions.question: A 70-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being found wandering and confused in a parking lot. He is alert and oriented to person but not to time or place. He is unable to see anything to his left and bumps into objects on that side. Neurologic examination shows a visual field defects on the left half of both eyes. Pupillary reflexes are intact, and eye movements are full. Strength and sensation are normal in all four extremities. Which of the following arteries is most likely occluded in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This man has clinical features of a right posterior cerebral artery (PcA) stroke. The PCA supplies the occipital lobe, which contains the primary visual cortex. Infarction of the right occipital lobe results in a left homonymous hemianopia meaning loss of the left visual field in both eyes. Because the lesion is cortical, the pupillary light reflex remains intact and eye movements are preserved. There are no motor or

Answer A (incorrect answer): The anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) supplies the lateral inferior pons and inner ear. Occlusion causes lateral pontine syndrome, including ipsilateral facial paralysis, hearing loss, vertigo, and ataxia.It does not cause cortical visual field deficits.
