questions.question: A 62-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after developing sudden-onset dizziness, unsteady gait, and double vision. He reports nausea and vomiting. On examination, he has dysmetria on finger-nose testing with the right hand and a tendency to veer to the right while walking. Horizontal nystagmus is observed. He is alert and oriented, with normal strength and intact sensation in all extremities. Which of the following arteries is most likely occluded in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This man has clinical features of a stroke involving the superior cerebellar artery (ScA). The SCA supplies the superior cerebellum and parts of the rostral (upper) pons and lateral midbrain. Infarction in this region causes ipsilateral limb ataxia, dysmetria, and gait instability. Other features of cerebellar dysfunction may be present including vertigo, nausea, and nystagmus. Unlike AICA or PICA strokes which can also affect the cerebellum, hearing loss and hoarseness are typically absent. The midbrain involvement explains the patient's diplopia due to trochlear nerve dysfunction or impaired gaze control. Preservation of motor and sensory function helps differentiate this from more extensive brainstem syndromes.

Answer A (incorrect answer): The anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) supplies the lateral inferior pons, ipsilateral facial paralysis, hearing loss, vertigo, and ataxia. This patient's lesion is localized to the superior cerebellum and midbrain, not the lateral pons.

Answer B (incorrect answer): The anterior spinal artery supplies the medial medulla. Infarction here causes medial medullary syndrome, with contralateral hemiparesis, contralateral loss of proprioception, and ipsilateral tongue weakness. These signs are not present in this patient, and the lesion is in the cerebellum and midbrain rather than the medulla.

Answer C (incorrect answer): The basilar artery gives rise to several branches, including the superior cerebellar artery, but occlusion of the basilar artery itself typically produces much more extensive deficits, such as locked- in syndrome or bilateral pontine infarcts. This patient's symptoms are localized and consistent with a branch vesselocclusion. inferior cerebellum. Occlusion causes lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome, which includes hoarseness, involvement. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 66-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after he was found unresponsive at home. On arrival, he is awake but cannot speak or move his limbs. He has intact vertical eye movements and blinking in response to commands. MRI of the brain shows ischemic changes in the bilateral thalami, midbrain, and occipital lobes. Which of the following arteries is most likely occluded in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This man has clinical features of a stroke involving the distal basilar artery. Because the basilar artery is a midline vessel that gives off branches to left- and right-sided structures, the clinicall features are bilateral. The affected structures include the bilateral thalami, midbrain, occipital lobes, and sometimes the medial temporal lobes. Damage to the occipital lobes bilaterally can cause "cortical blindness," meaning loss of vision despite normal function of the eyes and optic nerves. Other possible features include altered consciousness, vertical gaze palsy, and visual hallucinations. Quadriplegia with preserved consciousness and vertical eye movements, sometimes referred to as a "locked-in" state, can occur when midbrain structures are involved.

Answer A (incorrect answer): The anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) supplies the lateral inferior pons, middle cerebellar peduncle, and portions of the inner ear. Occlusion can cause lateral pontine syndrome, which includes ipsilateral facial paralysis, hearing loss, vertigo, and ataxia, but not the bilateral thalamic and occipital infarcts seen in this patient.

Answer B (incorrect answer): The anterior spinal artery supplies the medial medulla, including the pyramids (corticospinal tracts), medial lemniscus, and hypoglossal nucleus. Occlusion leads to medial medullary syndrome, which presents with contralateral hemiparesis, contralateral loss of proprioception, and ipsilateral tongue weakness. It does not cause the occipital lobe or thalamic involvement seen here.

Answer D (incorrect answer): The posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) supplies the lateral medulla and the inferior cerebellum. Occlusion causes lateral medullary (wallenberg) syndrome, presenting with symptoms such as vertigo, dysphagia, hoarseness, and ipsilateral loss of facial pain and temperature. It does not involve the thalamus, midbrain, or occipital cortex.

Answer E (incorrect answer): The superior cerebellar artery supplies the superior cerebellum and parts of the occlusion would not explain bilateral thalamic infarction and cortical blindness as seen in this patient. Himi

questions.question: A 72-year-old woman presents with dizziness, nausea, vomiting, hoarseness, and numbness. On exam she is unable to feel pinpricks on the right side of her face or her left arm. The right posterior pharynx does not elevate when she vocalizes. Motor strength is otherwise intact. Obstruction of which of the following blood vessels in the vertebrobasilar circulation of the brain is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This woman has a stroke involving the posterior inferior cerebellar artery. Her constellation of symptoms is called the lateral medullary syndrome, also known as Wallenberg's syndrome. It occurs due to ischemia of the lateral medulla. Dizziness, nausea, and vomiting develop from ischemia of the sensation. The ipsilateral (same-sided) loss of facial sensation occurs due to involvement of the spinal trigeminal nucleus (and thus cranial nerve V). Hoarseness and lack of palatal elevation develop from damage to the nucleus ambiguus, which controls the vagus and glossopharyngeal nerves (cranial nerves IX and X). cerebellum. Symptoms including nausea, vomiting, and dizziness. Patients typically have ataxia or a lack of coordination of the ipsilateral side.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Lesions affecting the basilar artery impair blood flow to the pons and midbrain. Symptoms vary based on the portion of the artery affected. "Locked-in" syndrome may occur, causing bilateral weakness of the upper and lower extremities with retained cognition and ability to blink. If the lesion is limited to the upper artery, "top of the basilar" syndrome (TOBs) may occur. This results in a decreased level of consciousness, visual symptoms such as blindness or hallucinations, and gaze palsy.

Answer C (incorrect answer): A stroke affecting the anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) causes ischemia of the lateral medulla and pons. This may lead to lateral pontine syndrome. Like the lateral medullary syndrome, patients with this syndrome develop dizziness, nausea, vomiting, contralateral loss of pain sensation, and ipsilateral loss of pain sensation in the face. Unlike the lateral medullary syndrome, AICA lesions may cause weakness of the ipsilateral face due to involvement of the facial nucleus. Unilateral deafness and tinnitus may occur from impairment of the cochlear nucleus.

Answer D (incorrect answer): A stroke affecting the anterior spinal artery results in decreased blood flow to the medial medulla or the anterior spine. Impaired blood flow to the anterior spine leads to loss of all motor and sensory function except for vibration and proprioception below the level of the occlusion.Lack of blood flow to the medial medulla causes loss of strength, proprioception, and vibration on the contralateral side of the body. Weakness of the tongue may alsooccur. Mc

questions.question: An 82-year-old man is referred for colon resection. While under anesthesia, his blood pressure decreases to 60/40 mmHg. On norepinephrine stimulation, Gq receptors activate phospholipase C (PLC), which hydrolyzes phosphatidylinositol in the cell membrane. This produces inositol triphosphate (Ip3), which acts as a second messenger to release intracellular calcium, causing smooth muscle contraction.

Answers A and B (incorrect answers): Changes in cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) are associated with the Gs and Gi subtypes of G-protein receptors. systems, such as those associated with nitric oxide. Cyclic GMP levels are not affected by norepinephrine.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Norepinephrine causes increased, not decreased, levels of Ip3 in smooth muscle cells. Mc Graw

questions.question: Researchers are studying the effects of circulating hormones on the central nervous system. Laboratory animals receive an intravenous infusion of angiotensin II. Shortly afterward, the animals exhibit an increase in thirst and blood pressure. Which of the following brain regions is most likely responsible for this response to infusion?

options.C: Organum vasculosum of the lamina terminalis (OVLT)

questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): The subfornical organ (SFo) is a circumventricular organ (CvO) located on the anterior wall of the third ventricle. It lacks a blood-brain barrier, allowing it to detect circulating substances like angiotensin II. Activation of the SFO stimulates thirst and sympathetic outflow,contributing to fluid intake and blood pressure elevation.It also projects to other brain areas involved in fluid and cardiovascular regulation.The SFO has been studied in animal models for its role in responding to circulating angiotensin II, especially in the context of thirst, blood pressure regulation,and sympathetic nervous system activation. AnswerA(incorrectanswer):The areapostrema islocatedatthecaudal end ofthefourthventricleandfunctionsas a chemoreceptor trigger zone, involved in vomiting in response to circulating toxins. It is not involved in fluid balance or angiotensin sensing.

Answer B (incorrect answer): The median eminence of the hypothalamus is part of the hypothalamus-pituitary axis, located near the pituitary stalk. It allows hypothalamic hormones to enter the portal circulation but does not directly senseangiotensinII.

Answer C (incorrect answer): The OvLT is located on the anterior wall of the third ventricle and plays a role in siteforangiotensinIIsensing.

questions.question: A 70-year-old man presents with worsening headaches and confusion over the past 2 weeks. He has a history of lung cancer diagnosed 6 months ago. On neurologic examination, he is disoriented to time and has difficulty naming objects. Brain MRI shows a ring-enhancing lesion in the right parietal lobe with surrounding hyperintensity consistent with edema. Which of the following best explains the brain swelling seen in this patient?

options.A: Activation of astrocytes with intracellular fluid accumulation
options.B: Autoimmune destruction of oligodendrocytes in periventricular areas
options.C: Cytotoxic injury due to mitochondrial dysfunction and energy depletion
options.D: Disruption of the blood-brain barrier leading to extracellular fluid buildup
options.E: Mechanical shearing of axons due to rotational brain trauma

questions.explanation:
Answer A (incorrect answer): Activation of astrocytes with intracellular fluid accumulation suggests cytotoxic edema where swelling occurs inside cells due to loss of function of Na-ATPase pumps. This occurs early in ischemic stroke, not in the setting of a brain tumor withBBB disruption. sclerosis, where demyelination occurs in periventricular white matter. Although inflammation in Ms can cause vasogenic edema, the imaging and clinical context here point to a tumor, not Ms.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Cytotoxic injury due to mitochondrial dysfunction and energy depletion describes cytotoxic edema, typically seen in early ischemic stroke where cells swell due to ATP depletion.This generally does not occurintumor-related edema.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Mechanical shearing of axons due to rotational brain trauma describes diffuse axonal injury, a type of traumatic brain injury. It is not related to vasogenic edema from tumors. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 63-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after collapsing at home. He was last seen in his normal state of health about 45 minutes ago. On arrival, his blood pressure is 168/92 mm Hg. Neurologic exam shows weakness on the left side of his body and drooping of the left side of his face. A CT scan of the head shows no bleeding. An MRI is performed and shows bright signal in the right frontal lobe on diffusion-weighted imaging consistent with edema. Which of the following best explains the brain swelling seen in this patient?

options.A: Breakdown of the blood-brain barrier allowing fluid to leak out
options.B: Damage to axons following trauma to the head
options.C: Inflammatory damage caused by neutrophils and cytokines
options.D: Leakage of proteins from blood vessels into brain tissue
options.E: Swelling of brain cells due to failure of energy-dependent ion pumps

questions.explanation:
Answer E(correct answer): This patientis showing signs ofan earlyischemicstroke including the suddenonset of weakness and facial droop, with abnormal MRI findings indicating edema. In the first hours after a stroke, brain cells run out of oxygen and glucose, leading to failure of ATP-powered ion pumps. This causes sodium and water to build up inside the cells, making them swell in a process called cytotoxic edema. The blood-brain barrier remains intact at this point.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Breakdown of the blood-brain barrier allowing fluid to leak out describes vasogenic edema, which involves leakage of fluid into the space between cells due to a damaged blood-brain barrier. This is more common in later stages of stroke, usually beyond 24 hours, not in the early phase.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Damage to axons following trauma to the head refers to diffuse axonal injury, which can occur in traumatic brain injury. It does not explain the sudden symptoms or imaging findings seen here.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Inflammation can occur later after brain injury or with infections, but does not cause the early swelling seen in ischemic stroke.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Leakage of proteins from blood vessels into brain tissue is also a feature of vasogenic edema, not cytotoxic edema. Protein leakage into the brain occurs when the blood-brain barrier is disrupted, typically in tumors, abscesses or late stroke.

questions.question: A 56-year-old woman with a glioblastoma is enrolled in a clinical trial evaluating enhanced delivery of chemotherapy to the brain. Prior to administering the chemotherapeutic agent, she receives an intravenous infusion of mannitol. which of the following best explains how mannitol improves delivery of chemotherapy in this patient? 3.48% sdwnd

options.B: Displaces tight junction proteins via chemotactic signaling
options.C: Increases aquaporin expression in capillary endothelial cells
options.D: Induces endothelial cell shrinkage via osmotic gradient
options.E: Triggers inflammatory cytokine release from astrocytes

questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): Mannitol is a hyperosmolar agent that creates an osmotic gradient across the blood-brain barrier. This causes endothelial cells lining the brain capillaries to lose water and shrink, which leads to a temporary opening of tight junctions. As a result, larger molecules such as chemotherapeutic agents can cross into the brain parenchyma. The disruption is transient, typically lasting 20-30 minutes.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Activation of Na* /k+ pumps may play a role in cellular ion balance but is not the mechanism by which mannitol disrupts the BBB.

Answer B (incorrect answer): There is no evidence that mannitol disrupts the BBB through chemotactic signaling or displacement of tight junction proteins via chemical mediators. Its mechanism is purely osmotic. Thewater movement associated with mannitolis drivenby anosmotic gradient,not channelupregulation.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Mannitol does not act by triggering inflammatory cytokine release. Cytokines may cause vasogenic edema, not therapeutic BBB opening. Mc Graw

questions.question: Researchers are studying a novel compound that inhibits carrier-mediated transport across the blood-brain barrier. In a rodent model, the compound is found to impair cognitive function and reduce neurotransmitter synthesis. The effect is most likely related to decreased transport of which of the following substances?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): Alanine is a small, neutral amino acid that cannot freely diffuse across the blood-brain barrier (BBB).Instead,it relies on carrier-mediated transport to enter the central nervous system (CNS). Inhibiting these transporters would limit alanine uptake into the brain, potentially disrupting protein and neurotransmitter synthesis. Glucose and amino acids are substances the require carrier-mediated transport for CNS uptake across the BBB. AnswerB (incorrect answer): Carbon dioxide readily diffuses across theblood-brainbarrier due toits small size and high lipid solubility. It does not require carrier-mediated transport.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Ethanol is lipid-soluble and diffuses freely across the blood-brain barrier. It does not rely on active or facilitated transport and would not be affected by an inhibitor of carrier-mediated transport.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Oxygen, like carbon dioxide, is a small gas molecule that diffuses passively across the BBB. Its transport does not involve carriers.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Water crosses the BBB primarily via osmosis and aquaporin channels, not carrier- carrier-mediated transport used by amino acids and glucose. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 48-year-old man presents with confusion and generalized weakness. Laboratory tests reveal serum sodium of 122 mEq/L and serum osmolality of 260 mOsm/kg. This man's laboratory findings may be explained by dysregulation of a structure at which of the following locations?

options.A: Anterior wall of the third ventricle near the lamina terminalis
options.B: Caudal end of the fourth ventricle in the medulla
options.C: Inferior hypothalamus adjacent to the pituitary stalk
options.D: Lateral wall of the third ventricle near the anterior commissure
options.E: Roof of the third ventricle near the pineal gland

questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): The anterior wall of the third ventricle near the lamina terminalis corresponds to the lacks a blood-brain barrier and contains osmosensory neurons that detect changes in blood osmolality. When plasma signaling pathways that influence antidiuretic hormone (ADH) release. Dysregulation of this structure can lead to inappropriate water retention and hyponatremia as described in this patient.

Answer B(incorrectanswer):The caudal end of thefourthventricle in the medulla describes the area postrema,a involved in initiating vomiting. It plays no role in osmoregulation or sodium balance.

Answer C (incorrect answer): The inferior hypothalamus adjacent to the pituitary stalk describes the median eminence of the hypothalamus. It allows hypothalamic hormones to enter the hypophyseal portal system to reach the anterior

Answer D (incorrect answer):Thelateral wall of the third ventricle near the anterior commissure is not a recognized relevancetoosmoregulation.

Answer E (incorrect answer): The roof of the third ventricle near the pineal gland refers to the pineal gland, another structure outside the blood-brain barrier. It secretes melatonin in response to light cues and helpsregulate circadian rhythms, not fluid or electrolyte balance. Hmi

Answer C (correct answer): Histamine blockade in the central nervous system (CNs) commonly leads to sedation a side effect of many drugs with antihistamine properties. Non-sedating antihistamines (e.g., cetirizine) are barrier (BBB). This limits their sedating effects. questions.question: A 44-year-old woman with adenocarcinoma of the left breast is treated with doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, and paclitaxel. She develops intractable nausea and vomiting. This effect is due to a drug interaction at which of the following locations in the brain?
questions.explanation: Answer A(correctanswer):Theblood brainbarrier(BBB)is formed around capillariesfromtightjunctions between endothelial cells and foot processes of astrocytes. This barrier limits CNs penetration of many substances, including most chemotherapy agents. Chemotherapy drugs can, however, cause nausea and vomiting through interactions with the brain at the area postrema. The area postrema is a circumventricular organ, a brain structure that has highly-permeable capillaries that lack the BBB. These structures are located near the 3rd and 4thventricles(hence the name circumventricular). The area postrema detects toxins in the blood and can trigger vomiting. It is responsible for the nausea and vomiting associated with many chemotherapy agents. The area postrema is located in the brainstem near the base of the fourth ventricle, just below the level of the cerebellum. The fourth ventricle has a diamond shape and is found near the upper medulla of the brainstem. It spans from the obex (an area of the medulla) to the cerebral aqueduct near the upper brainstem. or the cerebral cortex (D,E). Mc Graw

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman is hospitalized with sudden-onset severe headache, nausea, and photophobia. CT scan reveals undergoes successful surgical clipping with no evidence of rebleeding or vasospasm. Which of the following is a potential long- term complication in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct): This woman has had successful treatment for subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). Enlargement Scarring in the subarachnoid space can impair reabsorption of cerebrospinal fluid at the arachnoid granulations, leading to ventricular enlargement and symptoms such as gait instability, cognitive decline, and urinary incontinence. Imaging typically shows ventriculomegaly without obstruction, consistent with communicating hydrocephalus.

Answer A (incorrect): Bacterial meningitis is not a typical long-term complication of subarachnoid hemorrhage. meningitis is not a common delayed consequence of successfully treated sAH.

Answer B (incorrect): Cortical atrophy occurs in neurodegenerative diseases or with chronic alcohol use, not as a specific consequence of subarachnoid hemorrhage. This finding would be unusual in a patient recovering from SAH unless another pathology is present.

Answer D (incorrect): Intraparenchymal bleeding is not a typical long-term complication of subarachnoid hemorrhage unless the patient has underlying hypertension or coagulopathy.

Answer E (incorrect): Non-communicating hydrocephalus results from obstruction within the ventricular system (e.g., aqueductal stenosis or tumor) and is not the form of hydrocephalus that occurs following SAH. Post-SAH hydrocephalus is usually communicating, due to impaired CsF absorption rather than obstruction.

questions.question: A 69-year-old man with a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus presents to the clinic with complaints of double vision and difficulty moving his left eye. On examination, his left eye is deviated down and out, and he is unable to elevate or adduct it. His left eyelid is ptotic. Visual fields are intact. Pupils are equal and reactive to light bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct): This man has a cranial nerve III palsy characterized by ptosis (eyelid dropping) and impaired extraocular movements, but without pupillary involvement. This presentation is classic for microvascular ischemia of the oculomotor nerve, often due to chronic diabetes or hypertension. The somatic injury.

Answer A (incorrect): Anterior communicating artery aneurysms cause subarachnoid hemorrhage when ruptured, and do not usually compress cranial nerves. They are more associated with visual field defects due to compression of the optic chiasm, not isolated oculomotor palsy.

Answer B (incorrect): Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms affect small deep perforating vessels and are associated with hypertensive intraparenchymal hemorrhages, especially in the basal ganglia, thalamus, or internal capsule. They do not typically affect cranial nerves.

Answer C (incorrect): Middle cerebral artery aneurysms are not closely associated with cranial nerve III and are more likely to cause cortical symptoms or intraparenchymal hemorrhage if ruptured. compressive CN III palsy and classically present with "blown" (dilated) pupil due to involvement of the superficial parasympathetic fibers. questions.question: A 60-year-old woman is hospitalized following sudden-onset severe headache and loss of consciousness. Initial CT of the lethargic and develops new right-sided weakness. Repeat imaging shows no rebleeding. A drug with which of the following mechanisms may have prevented this complication?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct): This womanhas a subarachnoid hemorrhage complicated by delayed cerebral vasospasm, which typically occurs between days 3 and 14 after the initial bleed. Vasospasm can lead to cerebral ischemia and new neurologic deficits, as seen in this patient. Nimodipine, a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, is routinely administered to patients with SAH to reduce the risk of ischemic complications from vasospasm. Although its precise mechanism is not completely understood, it is thought to inhibit calcium influx into vascular smooth muscle, thereby promoting vasodilation and protecting against ischemic injury.

Answer A (incorrect): Adrenergic receptor antagonists such as beta-blockers are used for hypertension and arrhythmias, but they do not prevent or treat cerebral vasospasm.

Answer B (incorrect):Alpha receptor agonists cause vasoconstriction and are sometimes used to increase blood pressure, but they would worsen cerebral vasospasm, not prevent it.

Answer D (incorrect): Drugs that promote smooth muscle contraction would worsen vasospasm by causing furthernarrowing of cerebral vessels.

Answer E (incorrect): Vitamin K antagonists such as warfarin inhibit clotting factors and increase bleeding risk. They have no role in preventing vasospasm and would be contraindicated in the setting of recent hemorrhage. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 55-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after suddenly collapsing at work. She had complained of a severe headache moments before losing consciousness. On arrival, she is lethargic and has nuchal rigidity. Non-contrast CT of which of the following locations?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This woman has a subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), most likely due to rupture of a saccular (berry) aneurysm, which is the most common cause of spontaneous SAH in adults. In SAH, arterial blood escapes into the subarachnoid space, which lies between the arachnoid and pia mater and contains cerebrospinal fluid (csF). As a result, blood mixes with CsF and can be detected on lumbar puncture, where it appears grossly bloody or xanthochromic (yellow-tinged due to hemoglobin breakdown). CT imaging often shows hyperdensity in the basal cisterns or sulci early on, and lumbar puncture is used for confirmation when CT is negative but suspicion remains high.

Answer A (incorrect answer): The basal ganglia are common sites of hypertensive intraparenchymal hemorrhage from rupture of Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms. They are not a site for blood accumulation in subarachnoid hemorrhage.

Answer B (incorrect answer): The potential space between the dura and arachnoid mater is the site of subdural hematoma caused by rupture of bridging veins. This is not the location of blood in a subarachnoid hemorrhage.

Answer C (incorrect answer): The space between the dura and the skull is the epidural space. Epidural hematomas occur here due to trauma and rupture of the middle meningeal artery. This is not the location of blood in subarachnoid hemorrhage. it is not where blood collects in subarachnoid hemorrhage. W

questions.question: A 70-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being found unresponsive at home. He has a history of blood pressure is 230/125 mm Hg. Answer A (incorrect answer): Anterior communicating artery aneurysms are located in the circle of willis and are a common cause of subarachnoid hemorrhage, which presents with sudden-onset headache and meningeal signs rather than focal motor deficits. Answer B (incorrect answer): Internal carotid artery aneurysms can cause subarachnoid hemorrhage or cranial nerve palsies due to mass effect. questions.question: A 67-year-old man with a history of poorly controlled hypertension is brought to the emergency department after being found unconscious at home. Answer B (correct answer): This man has a hemorrhagic stroke in the setting of poorly controlled hypertension. small penetrating arteries, most commonly the lenticulostriate arteries that supply the basal ganglia and internal capsule. The internal capsule contains tightly packed descending motor fibers and ascending sensory fibers, and hemorrhage here commonly causes contralateral hemiparesis and hemisensory loss, as seen in this patient.

questions.question: weakness of which part of the normal artery pictured below may have led to this finding?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This woman has a saccular intracranial aneurysm or "berry" aneurysm. These aneurysms typically form at branch points of the intracranial arteries. It is thought that weakness of the tunica media ("tunica" = layer of tissue) layer of the arterial wall contributes to the initial development of the aneurysm. When this layer weakens, holes appear in the tunica media. An outpouching forms as the tunica intima protrudes through the defect, leading to development of an aneurysm. They are called berry aneurysms due their appearance. There is a "neck" where the aneurysm originates from the weakened portion of the arterial wall. The narrow neck leads into a balloon-shaped dome where blood pools.

Answer B (incorrect answer): This is the tunica intima layer of the artery wall. It is made of an endothelial layer be the structure responsible for aneurysm formation.

Answer C (incorrect answer): This is the lumen of the artery. Normally, blood flows freely in this space. Obstruction of the lumen of a cerebral artery can lead to ischemic stroke.

Answer D (incorrect answer): This is the tunica externa layer of the artery wall. It contains elastic fibers, nervi vasorum (nerves that support the function of the artery), and vasa vasorum (blood vessels that supply blood to thearteryitself).

Answer E (incorrect answer): This arrow points to a vasa vasorum within the tunica externa layer of the artery wall. Abnormalities in the vasa vasorum are not implicated in the development of saccular aneurysms. may lead to aneurysm formation. questions.question: A 37-year-old man presents with the sudden onset of a severe diffuse headache that he describes as "the worst headache of the neck. There are no motor or sensory deficits on neurological exam. The appearance of the skin of the hands is represented below. A lumbar puncture is performed, and the cerebrospinal fluid appears yellow. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this man's presentation?

options.E: Abnormal activation of the trigeminal nucleus

questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This man with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDs) presents with subarachnoid hemorrhage from a ruptured intracranial aneurysm. EDs syndrome is a connective tissue disorder caused by abnormal synthesis and processing of collagen. Classic findings of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome include skin hyperextensibility, joint hypermobility, and tissue fragility. The skin of this man's hands displays classic features of skin hyperextensibility. Patients with EDs are at increased risk for intracranial aneurysms. This man presents with a severe headache, vomiting, and nuchal rigidity, which are common symptoms of a ruptured intracranial aneurysm. He also has xanthochromia, which is a yellowish discoloration of the cerebrospinal fluid (CsF). The CsF appears yellow due to the breakdown of red blood cells. Normally red cells and their breakdown products are not present in the CsF.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RcVs), also known as Call-Fleming syndrome, may also cause severe headache. Patients with this syndrome have recurrent headaches that last for minutes to hours and recur multiple times over a period of days to weeks. Some patients have transient neurologic deficits such as blurred vision, visual field losses, and weakness of one-half of the body. Patients with this syndrome do not have xanthochromia in the CSF.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Thromboembolism to the brain leads to an embolic stroke. Strokes do not cause headache and nuchal rigidity. Strokes usually lead to motor or sensory deficits on neurological examination.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis occurs when a blood clot develops in the brain's venous system. The most common symptom of cerebral venous sinus thrombosis is headache. Varying patterns of weakness may also occur, and seizures are common. Venous sinus thrombosis does not cause xanthochromia. in the pathogenesis of migraine headaches. Classically, patients with this type of headache first develop an "aura," which can include visual, sensory, or auditory symptoms. Following the aura, headache develops, which is often described as unilateral and throbbing. Migraines would not cause xanthochromia. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 68-year-old woman presents with a two-month history of headache and decreased vision. On examination, she has drooping of the left eyelid. The left pupil is dilated and unresponsive to light. When asked to look straight ahead, her left eye is directed inferolaterally. She undergoes an imaging procedure and is diagnosed with an intracranial aneurysm. In the depiction below of the cerebral circulation, what is the most likely location of her aneurysm?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This woman has an aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery (Pcom). Aneurysms are thin-walled protrusions from intracranial vessels. PCom aneurysms cause compression of the oculomotor nerve. This results in ipsilateral (same-sided) pupillary dilation, drooping of the eyelid (ptosis), and gaze that is directed "down and out." she also has a headache, which is a nonspecific but common symptom of an intracranial aneurysm.

Answer A (incorrect answer): The most common location for intracranial aneurysm development is the anterior communicating artery (ACom). ACom aneurysms may cause compression of the optic chiasm, resulting in a loss of vision of the lateral halves of the visual fields (bitemporal hemianopsia).

Answer B (incorrect answer): Aneurysms may develop at the first bifurcation of the middle cerebral artery (MCA). Aneurysms at this location do not typically cause neurologic deficits (e.g., weakened vision or vision loss). McA aneurysms may cause unilateral pain that radiates to the back of the eye.

Answers D and E (incorrect answers): Aneurysms may develop at the origin of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery or the posterior inferior cerebellar artery. Aneurysms at these locations do not cause neurologic deficits but may cause unilateral pain in the occipital region (back of the head) or cervical region (upper posterior neck). Mc Graw

questions.question: intracranial aneurysm. which of the following is the most likely location of the aneurysm?

options.C: First bifurcation of the middle cerebral artery
options.E: Origin of anterior inferior cerebellar artery

questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This man has an aneurysm of the anterior communicating artery that is causing vision loss due to compression of the optic chiasm. This results in a loss of the lateral or temporal part of the visual field in both eyes. (See diagram.) He also complains of headache, which is a common but nonspecific symptom of an intracranial aneurysm. oculomotor nerve. This results in ipsilateral (same-sided) pupillary dilation, drooping of the eyelid (ptosis), and gaze that is directed "down and out."

Answer C (incorrect answer): An aneurysm of the first bifurcation of the middle cerebral artery does not cause changes in vision. It may cause unilateral pain that radiates to the eye.

Answer D (incorrect answer): An aneurysm that develops where the ophthalmic artery branches from the internal carotid artery can compress the ophthalmic artery and cause ipsilateral (same-sided) visual loss. This would affect thevisual field of only one eye.

Answer E (incorrect answer): An aneurysm located at the origin of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) would not cause changes in vision. It may cause severe pain in the back of the head or the back of the neck. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 44-year-old man presents with a headache. Cerebral angiogram shows the findings seen in the image below. Which of the following conditions is most likely present in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (incorrect answer): Alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) deficiency is an inherited condition that affects the lungs and liver. AAT deficiency commonly leads to pulmonary emphysema and liver cirhosis. Patients with this condition are at increased risk for cerebral and cervical artery dissection. On angiogram, a dissecting artery may have a "flame" shape due to an accumulation of blood in the vessel wall followed by a tapering of blood flow. Other syndromes associated with an increased risk for cerebral or cervical artery dissection include EDs, Marfan's syndrome, osteogenesis imperfecta (OI), fibromuscular dysplasia, and homocystinuria.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT) is a vascular disease associated with telangiectasias (small dilated blood vessels beneath the skin) and arteriovenous malformations (AVMs).AVMs commonly form in the pulmonary vasculature but may also form within the central nervous system (CNs). On angiography, AvMs appear as entangled masses of blood vessels.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) is a vascular disorder associated with non- atherosclerotic narrowing of arteries. It classically causes abnormalities of the renal arteries leading to hypertension. It may also affect the internal carotid, vertebral, and cerebral arteries. The affected arteries have segmental areas of narrowing, which gives them a beaded or "string-of-pearls" appearance on angiography. Arterial narrowing increases the risk for ischemic stroke due to the development of thromboembolisms. The arteries in patients with FMD may also develop spontaneous dissection, causing intracranial ischemia.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Moyamoya disease is a rare cerebrovascular condition associated with bilateral stenosis or occlusion of major arteries, such as the internal carotid arteries or vessels of the circle of willis. appearance of these collateral bloodvessels.

questions.question: A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being struck in the right side of the head during a baseball game. He briefly lost consciousness, then regained awareness and was speaking normally. Thirty minutes later, he becomes scan of the head shows a biconvex, hyperdense collection over the right cerebral hemisphere. The man's condition was most likely caused by which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This man has an epidural hematoma, which is classically caused by trauma to the pterion, the thinnest region of the lateral skull where the frontal, parietal, temporal, and sphenoid bones converge. The middle meningeal artery runs just beneath the pterion and can be ruptured by a fracture at this site. This leads to arterial bleeding between the skull and dura mater, forming a biconvex (lentiform)hyperdense collection on CT. The presentation often includes a lucid interval followed by rapid neurologic deterioration and signs of uncal herniation such as a dilated, non-reactive pupil.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Berry aneurysms arise at arterial branch points in the circle of willis and rupture into the subarachnoid space, causing subarachnoid hemorrhage, not epidural hematoma. These present with a sudden, severe headache ("worst headache of my life").

Answer B (incorrect answer): Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms are microaneurysms of small penetrating arteries, usually in the setting of chronic hypertension. Their rupture causes intraparenchymal hemorrhage in deep structures like the basal ganglia, not epidural hematoma.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Lenticulostriate vessels are small branches of the middle cerebral artery that axial bleeding seen in epidural hematoma. hemorrhage, not a localized, biconvex epidural hematoma. The McA is a large artery within the sylvian fissure and is not typically damaged by trauma at the skull surface.

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after suddenly collapsing at work. Moments before losing blood pressure is 170/98 mmHg. A non-contrast CT scan of the head reveals hyperdensity within the basal cisterns and cerebral sulci. Rupture of which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This woman has clinical features of a subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), (e.g., nuchal rigidity). The classic CT finding is hyperdense blood within the basal cisterns and cerebral fissures. The most common cause of non-traumatic SAH is rupture of a saccular (berry) aneurysm, which arises at branch points in the circle of willis. Although berry aneurysm rupture is most common, an arteriovenous malformation (AVM) is the most likely cause among the answer choices listed. AVMs are congenital tangles of arteries and veins that lack a normal capillary bed, making them prone to rupture. They can present with spontaneous SAH, especially in younger patients without known aneurysms. head trauma, especially in elderly individuals or infants. Their rupture results in a subdural hematoma, not a subarachnoid hemorrhage.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms are microaneurysms of small penetrating vessels, commonly associated with chronic hypertension. Their rupture causes intraparenchymal hemorrhage, particularly in the basal ganglia, thalamus, or pons-not in the subarachnoid space.

Answer D (incorrect answer): The lenticulostriate arteries are small, deep branches of the middle cerebral artery intraparenchymal hemorrhage, not SAH.

Answer E (incorrect answer): The middle meningeal artery lies between the skull and dura mater and is typically hemorrhage. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 54-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance after experiencing a sudden, severe headache. She vomits en route and becomes progressively drowsy. On arival, her blood pressure is 180/100 mmHg, and she is somnolent but arousable. questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This woman has a subarachnoid hemorrhage, which most commonly develops due to rupture of a saccular (berry) aneurysm. The hallmark clinical presentation is a sudden, severe headache followed by loss of consciousness or altered mental status. The CT scan shows hyperdensity (brightness) in the basal cisterns and sulci, consistent with blood in the subarachnoid space. The subarachnoid space is located between the arachnoid mater and the pia mater and normally contains cerebrospinal fluid. Blood entering this space irritates the meninges, often causing meningeal signs such as neck stiffness, photophobia, and vomiting.

Answer A (incorrect answer): The basal ganglia are deep brain structures and are commonly involved in intraparenchymal hemorrhage in the setting of chronic hypertension. Blood in a subarachnoid hemorrhage is extracerebral and located within the meningeal layers, not within the basal ganglia.

Answer C (incorrect answer): The space between the dura mater and the arachnoid mater is the subdural space. Bleeding into this space results in a subdural hematoma, usually due to tearing of bridging veins. Subdural hematomas have a crescent shape on CT and do not fill the basal cisterns or sulci.

Answer D(incorrectanswer):The spacebetweenthe skull and dura materis thelocationof an epidural hematoma, usually caused by trauma and rupture of the middle meningeal artery. These appear as biconvex (lens-shaped) collections on CT and are not associated with diffuse subarachnoid blood. subarachnoid blood can overlie the cortex in the sulci, it is not within the cortexitself. Intraparenchymal hemorrhage into the cortex is a separate condition and presents differently on imaging.

Answer D (incorrect answer): The space between the skull and the dura mater is the site of epidural hematoma, which results from rupture of the middle meningeal artery after trauma. These appear as biconvex (lentiform) hematomas on CT and are distinct from the crescent shape of subdural hematomas.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man with a history of poorly controlled hypertension is brought to the emergency department after suddenly collapsing at home. On arrival, he is unconscious and requires intubation. Neurologic examination reveals right-sided hemiplegia and a left gaze preference. A non-contrast CT scan of the head shows a hyperdense lesion in the left basal branch of which of the following vessels?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (incorrect answer): The basilar artery supplies the brainstem and posterior circulation. Hemorrhage due to basilar artery pathology occurs in the pons or cerebellum, not the basal ganglia. The basilar artery is not the typical source of deep intraparenchymal hemorrhage in hypertension.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Bridging veins are responsible for draining blood from the cerebral cortex into the dural venous sinuses. Their rupture results in subdural hematoma, not intraparenchymal hemorrhage. This typically occurs after trauma and does not involve the basal ganglia.

Answer C (incorrect answer): The internal carotid artery is a large extracerebral artery that gives rise to multiple intracranial branches, including the anterior and middle cerebral arteries. It does not directly supply the deep structures affected in hypertensive hemorrhages and is not the usual site of vessel rupture in this setting. Mc Graw

questions.question: A premature newborn is evaluated in the neonatal intensive care unit on the first day of life. The infant was born at 28 weeks gestation and required positive pressure ventilation shortly after delivery. On physical examination, the baby is lethargic and has a bulging anterior fontanelle. Cranial ultrasound reveals an acute hemorrhage. Which of the following locations is the most likely site of blood accumulation in this infant?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This infant has clinical features of an intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH), a complication that commonly affects premature neonates due to fragility of the germinal matrix. The germinal matrix is a highly vascularized region located adjacent to the lateral ventricles, and it is especially vulnerable to rupture, blood accumulates within the lateral ventricles. IVH can lead to increased intracranial pressure, hydrocephalus, and long-term neurologic damage.

Answer A (incorrect answer): The space above the arachnoid mater corresponds to the subdural or epidural space, not the ventricular system. Intraventricular hemorrhage involves bleeding into the cerebral ventricles, not into the meningeal layers. trauma.

Answer C (incorrect answer): The basal ganglia are deep brain structures involved in motor control. premature infants, where the germinal matrix near the lateral ventricles is the most common source.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Blood below the dura mater refers to a subdural hematoma, usually from rupture of bridging veins. Subdural hemorrhages are rare in premature neonates and are not the typical location of bleeding from germinal matrix fragility.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being found unconscious following a fall from a ladder. On arrival, his right pupil is dilated and non-reactive. Epidural hematomas develop from tearing of the middle meningeal artery, which causes blood to accumulate between the skull and the dura mater.The dura mater is a connective tissue covering beneath the skull.Beneath the dura mater is the arachnoid mater and the pia matter, which tightly covers brain tissue. One characteristic clinical feature of this conditionis a "lucid interval."Althoughpatients may lose consciousness initially after the trauma, they awaken and are able to communicate until the hematoma enlarges and compresses intracranial structures, when they again lose consciousness. The development of the hematoma is often rapid, because the source of the bleeding is arterial. An epidural hematoma is considered a neurosurgical emergency. The blood must be promptly removed to prevent compression of the medulla, which can cause cardiorespiratory failure.

questions.question: A 92-year-old man with a history of hemorrhagic strokes presents with decreased vision. On exam, he has difficulty seeing objects on the right. He has no abnormalities of strength or sensation. A non-contrast computed tomography scan of the head shows an intracerebral hemorrhage in the occipital lobe. questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This man has a hemorrhagic stroke caused by cerebral amyloid angiopathy. In this condition, beta-amyloid protein deposits accumulate in the walls of small vessels within the brain. Amyloid accumulation weakens blood vessels and may lead to bleeding into the brain. The syndrome often affects the cerebral cortex. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy typically causes recurrent hemorrhagic stroke in older people. Mc

questions.question: A 42-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after suddenly collapsing while climbing stairs. He reports severe mid-back pain that was followed by immediate weakness in both legs. He has been unable to walk since the episode and also reports urinary retention. He notes that pinprick sensations feel "blunted" below his waist, but he can still tell where his legs are and feels vibration normally. On examination, there is flaccid paralysis of both lower extremities with absent deep tendon reflexes. Sensation to pinprick and temperature is decreased below the umbilicus, but proprioception and vibration sense are preserved. He is concerned because his brother was diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis one year ago. He has a remote history of a stab wound to the mid-back and was recently treated for gonorrhea. The corticospinal tracts and spinothalamic tracts are affected, leading to motor paralysis and loss of pain and temperature sensation below the level of the lesion. The dorsal columns, which carry proprioception and vibration sense, are spared because they are supplied by the posterior spinal arteries. Clinical features of AsA occlusion include the acute onset of severe mid-back pain, bilateral leg weakness, urinary retention, and a sensory level for pain and temperature with preserved proprioception. questions.question: A 54-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to worsening lower back pain for the past week. He now reports numbness in the perineal region and difficulty initiating urination. He also notes bilateral leg weakness that is worse on the right side. Physical examination shows decreased strength in the lower extremities and impaired sensation in the saddle distribution. Rectal tone is reduced. MRI of the lumbosacral spine reveals a large central disc herniation at the L4-L5 level compressing the cauda equina. Which of the following additional findings is most likely?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This man has clinical features of cauda equina syndrome, a condition resulting from compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots below the conus medullaris. The cauda equina is a bundle of spinal nerve roots that descend through the spinal canal after the end of the spinal cord, supplying motor and sensory innervation to the lower limbs, pelvic floor, and bladder. Symptoms of cauda equina syndrome include saddle anesthesia, urinary retention, reduced lower limb strength, and decreased rectal tone, all of which are present in this case. Because the cauda equina contains lower motor neurons, damage produces lower motor neuron signs such as decreased reflexes. An expected finding is an absent ankle jerk reflex, which depends on intact S1-S2 nerve roots. Compression of these roots disrupts the reflex arc, leading to loss of the reflex. such as in the corticospinal tract. Answer D (incorrect answer): The ano-cutaneous (anal wink) reflex is mediated by the S2-S4 nerve roots. This reflex is often diminished or absent in cauda equina syndrome due to involvement of those roots. A normal reflex would not be expected in this context.

Answer E (correct answer): This baby has clinical features of Werdnig-Hoffmann disease, also known as spinal muscular atrophy type 1. This disorder is caused by degeneration of anterior horn cells in the spinal cord, which leads to lower motor neuron signs such as muscle weakness and atrophy. It presents in the newborn period with poor head control, a weak cry, tongue fasciculations, feeding difficulties, and absent deep tendon reflexes. Wernig-Hoffman disease is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the SMN1 (survival motor neuron 1) gene. The SMN1 protein is involved in assembly of small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs), which are involved in pre-mRNA splicing. Defective snRNP assembly leads to degeneration of anterior horn cells in the

Answer B (incorrect answer): DNA processing defects are implicated in disorders such as ataxia-telangiectasia and xeroderma pigmentosum, which involve problems with DNA repair or replication. questions.question: A 64-year-old man comes to the clinic due to progressive difficulty walking over the past three months. This condition affects the lateral corticospinal tracts leading to increased rather than decreased reflexes. which is spared in subacute combined degeneration. This patient's sensory deficits involve proprioception and vibration sense, which are carried by the dorsal columns.

questions.question: A 23-year-old man presents to the emergency room with a stab wound to his back. He is unable to move his right leg. Strength testing is normal in the left leg. MRI of the spine reveals transection of the right spinal hemicord at the T11-12 level. Which of the following sensory deficits is most likely in this man's left leg?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This man has Brown-Séquard syndrome (Bss), a condition caused by damage to half of the spinal cord that leads to ipsilateral hemiplegia, ipsilateral loss of proprioception and vibration sensation, andcontralateral lossofpainand temperaturesensation. Motor deficits in BsS are caused by traumatic damage to upper motor neuron (UMN) fibers in the spinal cord. These nerve fibers decussate (cross over) in the medulla and descend through the corticospinal tract. UMNs synapse with lower motor neurons (LMNs) at spinal nerve roots on the same side of the body. Because descending fibers control muscles on the same side of the body, damage to the right side of this man's spinal cord leads to motor loss on the right side. Sensory deficits in Bss are caused by damage to posterior column and spinothalamic tract fibers. The posterior column carries proprioception and vibration information from the ipsilateral side of the body. In contrast, spinothalamic tract fibers carrypainand temperatureinformationfrom the contralateral side,because these fibers decussate within the spinal cord shortly after entering from the periphery. The right-sided lesion in this man will cause ipsilateral (right-sided) loss of proprioception and vibration with contralateral (left-sided) loss of pain and temperature. Key point: Motor and sensory loss in Bss is confined to the side of the injury, except for pain and temperature. In Bss, findings are also different at the level of the injury compared with below the level of the injury. At the level of injury, damage to LMNs of that level causes ipsilateral flaccid paralysis of skeletal muscles. Below the level of the injury, UMN signs of motor weakness are present, such as spastic paralysis and hyperreflexia. At the level of the injury, fibers of the lateral spinothalamic tract are damaged before decussation. This leads to loss of pain and temperature limited to the level of injury. Below the level of injury, pain and temperature loss willbecontralateral,asdescribedabove.

Answers A, B, D and E (incorrect answers): Motor and sensory loss in Bss is confined to the same side as the injury except for pain and temperature. Pain and temperature loss will occur on the contralateral side below the level of the injury. Mc

questions.question: A 42-year-old woman with Crohn's disease presents with difficulty walking. Over the past six months, she has felt increasingly unsteady on her feet. Answer B (correct answer): This woman has subacute combined degeneration (SCD), a condition of demyelination of the posterior and lateral columns of the spinal cord caused by vitamin B12 deficiency. Damage to the posterior column leads to impaired proprioception and vibration sense. Impaired proprioception leads to problems with gait and balance, and a positive Romberg's sign (losing balance when standing with feet together and eyes closed). Degeneration often begins in the posterior column and spreads laterally. If demyelination involves motor neurons of the lateral corticospinal tracts, this can lead to weakness, hyperreflexia, spasticity, and a positive Babinski's sign. questions.question: A 42-year-old woman presents with progressive difficulty walking over the past five months. She also describes recurrent shooting pains down both legs. On physical examination, she has a wide-based gait. Muscle strength is normal. She has diminished proprioception and vibration sense in her legs. Sensation of pain and temperature is intact. Patellar reflexes are absent. Romberg's sign is positive. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this woman's presentation?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This woman has tabes dorsalis, a spinal cord syndrome caused by Treponema pallidum infection. In tabes dorsalis, degeneration of the posterior column of the spinal cord occurs along with usually occurs 5 to 20 years after the initial infection. In tabes dorsalis, loss of dorsal root neurons leads to impaired sensation, causing absent deep tendon reflexes. Demyelination of the posterior columns leads to diminished proprioception and vibration sense, causing an unsteady, wide-based gait. Romberg's sign is positive (losing balance when standing with feet together and eyes closed), indicating a lack of proprioception. Mc Graw Muscle strength is often normal initially, but muscle atrophy and weakness may eventually develop in advanced cases of tabes dorsalis. Tabes dorsalis is also classically associated with recurrent shooting pains. Most patients also have small pupils that do not constrict with light, a condition known as Argyll Robertson pupils. Tabes dorsalis is largely historical from the pre-antibiotic era, and rare in the modern practice. Tabes dorsalis is treated with intravenous penicillin, which can limit progression of symptoms, but does not reverse nerve damage. Key point: Diminished proprioception and vibration, loss of knee and ankle reflexes, shooting pains and abnormal pupils are suggestive of tabes dorsalis.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Occlusion of the anterior spinal artery (AsA) damages the anterior two-thirds of sense are normal in AsA syndrome because the posterior spinal artery continues to supply blood to the posterior column of the spinal cord. questions.question: A 72-year-old right-handed man is brought to the emergency department after being found confused and unable to speak. On examination, he is awake but has difficulty following commands and is unable to produce coherent speech. Neurologic also appears unaware of his deficits and repeatedly reaches toward the left side of the room when asked to pick up an object. His eyes are deviated to the left. which of the following is the most likely location of this patient's lesion?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This man has clinical features of a left middle cerebral artery (McA) stroke involving the frontal lobe and adjacent cortical areas. His aphasia (difficulty producing speech), gaze deviation, and right face and arm weakness are cortical signs indicating that the stroke involves the cortex(frontal and parietal lobes). In addition, his unawareness of deficits (anosognosia) and reaching toward the wrong side suggest hemispatial neglect, another cortical sign commonly seen with parietal lobe involvement. These findings distinguish his condition from subcortical or brainstem strokes, which do not typically present with language dysfunction or neglect. The presence of cortical signs confirms that the lesion is located in the cortex, specifically the frontal lobe, where the motor cortex and Broca's area reside.

Answer B (incorrect answer): The lateral medulla is affected in Wallenberg syndrome (PICA infarct), which Mc Graw Cortical signs such as aphasia or hemispatial neglect are not associated with medullary strokes.

Answer C (incorrect answer): A lateral pontine infarct (often due to AICA occlusion) typically results in ipsilateral facial paralysis, hearing loss, vertigo, and contralateral pain and temperature loss in the body. This condition lacks cortical signs like aphasia or gaze deviation.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Medial medullary syndrome results from anterior spinal artery occlusion and causes contralateral hemiparesis, contralateral proprioceptive loss, and ipsilateral tongue weakness. Brainstem strokes like those in the medulla cause hemiparesis that affects the arms and legs equally. In contract, cortical strokes have effects that vary from arms to legs (McA strokes face/arms > legs; ACA strokes legs > arms/face). Also, medullary infarcts do not cause language deficits, hemispatial neglect, or eye deviation.

Answer E (incorrect answer):A medial pontine lesion would affect corticospinal fibers and possibly the abducens nerve, resulting in contralateral hemiparesis and ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy. Cortical features such as aphasia and neglectarenotassociatedwithpontinestrokes. nerve palsy and contralateral motor deficits, but they do not produce aphasia, neglect, or cortical weakness patterns such as face/arm-predominant hemiparesis.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man comes to the emergency department after suddenly developing dizziness, nausea, hoarseness, and difficulty swallowing. It does not produce hoarseness or dysphagia from nucleus ambiguus involvement, which is characteristic of lateral medullary syndrome.

questions.question: A 64-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of sudden weakness on the right side of his body. On neurologic examination, he has complete paralysis of the right arm and leg. He also has right lower facial droop with preserved forehead movement. His left eye is deviated down and out, and the left pupil is dilated and unreactive to light. He is alert but has dysarthric speech. Which of the following is the most likely location of this patient's stroke?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This man has clinical features of Weber syndrome, caused by infarction of the ventral (anterior) midbrain. Involvement of the cerebral peduncle results in contralateral hemiparesis (due to corticospinal tract damage) and contralateral lower facial weakness (due to corticobulbar tract damage). The lower face receives contralateral corticobulbar tract input only, but the upper face (forehead) receives bilateral input. As a result, a unilateral corticobulbar lesion causes weakness of the contralateral lower face only, with sparing of the forehead. In addition, Weber syndrome has involvement of the oculomotor nerve fibers causing ipsilateral CN III palsy, producing a "down and out" eye, ptosis, and mydriasis.

Answer A (incorrect answer): The dorsal midbrain includes structures such as the superior colliculi and the pretectal area. Lesions here cause vertical gaze palsies (inability to look up) and Parinaud syndrome. This patient has an oculomotor nerve palsy, hemiparesis, and contralateral lower facial weakness which is not consistent with a dorsal midbrain lesion.

Answer B (incorrect answer): A lateral medullary infarct causes ipsilateral facial sensory loss, contralateral body sensory loss, hoarseness, vertigo, and ataxia. It does not affect CN III or cause hemiparesis or facial motor weakness.

Answer C (incorrect answer): A lateral pontine syndrome causes ipsilateral facial paralysis (LMN), hearing loss, and vertigo, often due to AICA infarction. This patient's oculomotor findings and pattern of contralateral hemiparesis and lower facial droop point to a lesion above the pons.

Answer D (incorrect answer): A medial pontine lesion can cause contralateral hemiparesis and ipsilateral III involvement localizes the lesion higher, to the midbrain. Mc Graw IIH

questions.question: A 61-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being found unresponsive at home. On examination, he is awake but has difficulty moving the right side of his body. Key features include ipsilateral oculomotor nerve palsy, contralateral cerebellar signs such as tremor and ataxia (due to involvement of the red nucleus and superior cerebellar peduncle), and contralateral loss of vibration and proprioception from medial lemniscus involvement. questions.question: A 4-month-old infant is brought to the pediatrician for a routine check-up. Persistence of this reflex beyond the normal developmental window suggests a failure of cerebral cortex maturation, usually involving the frontal lobe. The frontal lobe plays a critical role in suppressing primitive reflexes as the brain Persistence of the Moro reflex beyond 1 year of age is a red flag for underlying CNs pathology such as cerebral palsy, global developmental delay, or structural/metabolic brain disease. questions.question: A 10-year-old boy is evaluated for abdominal pain and vomiting. He describes dull pain around the umbilicus that does not localize. CT scan of the abdomen identifies findings consistent with appendicitis. This boy's abdominal pain is transmitted through afferent fibers of which of the following spinal roots?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): Appendicitis is caused by obstruction of the lumen of the appendix near the cecum of the large intestine. Obstruction commonly occurs due to fecal matter or hyperplasia of lymphoid tissue. When this happens, ongoing mucous production by the mucosa of the appendix causes the appendix to become distended. The appendix lacks somatic sensory innervation but is innervated by the autonomic nervous system ("visceral innervation") similar to other portions of the bowel. These nerves, which sense only stretch and distension, carry sensory information via afferent fibers that enter the spinal cord at Tio, the level corresponding to the umbilicus. This is called "referred pain" because the appendix is located in the right lower quadrant but pain is felt near the umbilicus. Thus, in early appendicitis, the pain is periumbilical and poorly localized, as described in the question. As the inflammation of appendicitis progresses, the parietal peritoneum becomes involved. The parietal peritoneum contains somatic sensory fibers that will localize pain to the right lower quadrant. Thus, appendicitis classically begins as dull periumbilical pain that later "migrates" to the right lower quadrant.

Answers A, B, D, and E (incorrect answers): Referred pain of early appendicitis is via afferent fibers at the T10 level,not L1,L2,T12,or S1. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 58-year-old man undergoes MRI of the head to evaluate persistent headaches. V3 is the only division of the trigeminal nerve that carries motor fibers. It innervates the muscles of mastication, including the masseter, temporalis, and the medial and lateral pterygoids. Compression of this nerve can impair the ability to chew, leading to jaw weakness, fatigue during mastication, or deviation of the jaw toward the affected side.

The upward drift of the eye when attempting to look down is characteristic of superior oblique weakness.

It presents with facial droop meaning drooping of the forehead, eyelid, and mouth on the affected side. In this case, the likely cause is Lyme disease, which can involve the facial nerve, especially during the early disseminated phase of infection. The facial nerve innervates the stapedius muscle in the middle ear, which dampens the vibrations of the stapes bone to protect the cochlea from loud sounds. When the facial nerve is damaged in Bell's palsy, the stapedius becomes paralyzed, resulting in hyperacusis, or sensitivity to sound, on the affected side.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Diplopia, or double vision, results from dysfunction of cranial nerves III, IV, or VI, which control extraocular muscles. Bell's palsy, a peripheral facial nerve palsy, does not affect eye movements anddoesnotcausediplopia.

questions.question: A 56-year-old man is evaluated for double vision. The double vision disappears when he closes his left eye and worsens when he looks to his left. He denies eye trauma or pain. He has a history of hypertension and type II diabetes. Physical examination reveals left-sided esotropia and impaired left eye abduction. A lesion involving a cranial nerve that supplies which of the following is the most likely cause of this man's current symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This man has abducens (cranial nerve VI) nerve palsy (also called lateral rectus palsy) caused by ischemia. Microvascular ischemia leading to abducens nerve palsy often occurs in association with poorly-controlled diabetes or hypertension. Raised intracranial pressure can also compress the abducens nerves, leading to unilateral or bilateral abducens nerve palsy. The abducens nerve innervates the lateral rectus muscle, which abducts the eye. Patients with abducens nerve lesions present with horizontal diplopia that improves with closing the affected eye. They also develop an inability to move the affected eye laterally (look outward). This will cause diplopia when the patient looks toward the side with the lesion. An inward deviation of the affected eye may also occur (esotropia).

Answer A (incorrect answer): The trochlear nerve (cranial nerve IV) innervates a single ocular muscle: the superior oblique. This muscle turns the eye down and in. Patients with trochlear nerve palsy present with diplopia (double vision) and an outward tilt to affected eyes. These patients classically have problems reading or walking down the stairs because these activities require turning the eyes down and in.

Answers B, C, and E (incorrect answers): The oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve III) innervates the levator rectus, and inferior oblique muscles. These muscles adduct, depress, and elevate the eye. Patients with oculomotor neuropathy present with ptosis and eyes that are abducted and depressed ("down and out"). Mc GraW

Optic neuritis is an immune-mediated condition that develops in response to an unknown trigger. T-cell activation and release of inflammatory cytokines leads to inflammation and demyelination of the optic nerve. Optic neuritis is usually monocular (involving one eye) and associated with vision loss and painful eye movements. Inflammation involves the optic nerve (cranial nerve II) as well as autonomic nerve fibers that travel together with the optic nerve. An afferent pupillary defect (ApD) occurs if the other eye is normal. An Mc Graw APD (also called a Marcus Gunn pupil) can be demonstrated by the swinging flashlight test. Light shone into the unaffected eye will cause bilateral pupillary constriction because the optic nerve is normal on the unaffected side. When the flashlight swings to the affected eye, the pupils dilate because light is poorly transmitted via the diseased optic nerve. oblique, and sphincter papillae muscle. questions.question: A 55-year-old woman is brought for evaluation by her family due to memory loss and abnormal behavior. She has kissed behaviors are uncharacteristic for her. questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This woman has frontotemporal dementia (FTD), formerly known as Pick's disease. Clinical features include cognitive impairment with personality and behavioral changes. FTD is a common cause of early-onset dementia, most commonly occuring in patients under 65years ofage.In contrast, Alzheimer's disease commonly occurs in patients age 65 years and older. The development of FTD is associated with an abnormal accumulation of the tau protein within neurons. Other neurodegenerative disorders including Alzheimer's disease and corticobasal degeneration are also associated with abnormal accumulation of the tau protein, and are sometimes called "tauopathies." The tau protein plays an important role in stabilizing microtubules, which are essential components of the cell cytoskeleton.

These disorders are sometimes called the "synucleinopathies", since they are all associated with abnormalities in the alpha-synuclein protein. Answer B (correctanswer): This womanhas Lewy body dementia,which is the second most common type of dementia after Alzheimer's disease. Clinical features include memory loss, visual hallucinations, and Mc Graw IH Parkinsonian symptoms, including rigidity and bradykinesia (slowness initiating movements). The cognitive symptoms begin before the motor symptoms, a feature that helps to differentiate Lewy body dementia from Parkinson's disease, in which the cognitive manifestations occur late in the disease. In Lewy body dementia, Lewy bodies develop in the cerebral cortex. Lewy bodies are round, intra-cytoplasmic inclusions found within neurons. These inclusions are made of the protein alpha-synuclein.

Answer B (incorrect): The fourth ventricle itself develops but becomes cystically dilated and displaced due to the malformation. It is not the primary structure that fails to develop.

Answer C (incorrect): The medulla typically forms normally in Dandy-Walker malformation and is not the site of primary developmental failure.

Answer D (incorrect): The midbrain is not involved in the structural defect of Dandy-Walker malformation. Although elevated intracranial pressure may compress midbrain structures, the midbrain develops normally.
