The image shows blood filling half of the anterior chamber of this man's eye. This condition may occur after trauma to the eye and can lead to permanent vision loss. Clear aqueous humor normally fills the Oriris.

Answer A (incorrect answer): A hypopyon is a condition where white blood cells are found in the anterior chamber. This occurs due to bacterial infection and can be seen as a complication of cataract surgery. The accumulated fluid in a hypopyon appears white, not red-brown as shown in the image.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Cataracts are an opacification of the lens of the eye that obscures vision. Patients with cataracts develop cloudy vision. Cataracts develop slowly and are most common in older adults.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Scleritis is the inflammation of the sclera, the white portion of the eye. The sclera is a fibrous, protective layer made of collagen and elastic fibers. Clinical features of scleritis include redness and severe pain that worsens with eye movement (the extraocular muscles insert into the sclera). Scleritis is often associated with an underlying inflammatory condition such as rheumatoid arthritis or vasculitis.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Anterior uveitis is inflammation of the iris and choroid body. Clinical features include eye pain, blurry vision, and photophobia. Anterior uveitis can be caused by infection or autoimmunity. Up to 40% of patients with uveitis have a systemic autoimmune condition. Spondyloarthritis disorders, such as ankylosing spondylitis, are the most common systemic immune disorders associated with anterior uveitis.

questions.question: A 25-year-old man is evaluated for left eye pain and blurry vision. He has a history of ankylosing spondylitis. Bright lights are irritating to his left eye. On examination, there is perilimbal redness of the left eye and left-sided miosis. Leukocytes are seen in the anterior chamber of the left eye on slit lamp examination. Examinations of the vitreous humor, retina, and posterior chamber are normal. Inflammation of which structure is most likely occurring in this man?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This man has anterior uveitis. The uvea is the vascular layer of the eye. Anteriorly, it consists of the iris and ciliary body. Posteriorly, it consists of the ciliary body and choroid. Anterior uveitis is inflammation involving the anterior uvea, meaning the iris or ciliary body. This condition is sometimes called blurry vision, photophobia, and constriction of the pupil (miosis). Anterior uveitis classically produces redness near the limbus ("perilimbal"), as described in the question. The limbus is the border between the transparent cornea and the white sclera. When examining the eye, the limbus is located where the white sclera meets the Mc colored iris. Redness limited to this area is a distinguishing feature of anterior uveitis. Anterior uveitis can be caused by infection or autoimmunity. Up to 4o% of patients with uveitis have a systemic autoimmune condition. Spondyloarthritis disorders associated with B-27, such as ankylosing spondylitis, are the most common systemic immune disorders associated with anterior uveitis.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Conjunctivitis is inflammation of the conjunctiva, which is the transparent layer covering the sclera. Conjunctivitis may cause redness of the eye, pruritis, or discharge. Most cases are infections causedbyvirusesorbacteria.Conjunctivitisalonedoesnotleadtoleukocytesintheanteriorchamber,as described inthequestion.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Episcleritis is inflammation of the episclera, the outermost layer of the sclera found immediately beneath the conjunctiva. Clinical features include focal redness and irritation. Episcleritis alone does not lead to leukocytes in the anterior chamber, as described in the question.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Scleritis is inflammation of the sclera, the white portion of the eye. The sclera is a fibrous, protective layer made of collagen and elastic fibers. Clinical features of scleritis include redness and pain.Thepain mayworsen with eye movementbecause the extraocularmusclesinsertintothe sclera.

Answers E (incorrect answers): Inflammation of the choroid occurs in posterior uveitis because this structure is part of the posterior portion of the uvea. In contrast to anterior uveitis, posterior uveitis is more likely to be painless. Patients with posterior uveitis develop visual changes such as floaters and decreased vision, although these can sometimes occur in anterior uveitis as well. The normal examination of the vitreous humor, retina, and posterior chamber in this case makes posterior uveitis unlikely.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman from a remote village is evaluated for bilateral eye pain. Examination of the eyes shows white spots with scarring in the conjunctiva beneath the eyelids. The left eyelid is contracted and turned inward with eyelashes pressing into the conjunctiva. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this woman's presentation?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This woman has trachoma, an eye condition caused by infection with chlamydia trachomatis. Trachoma is among the leading causes of blindness worldwide. Trachoma is endemic (endemic : commonly found in the population) to remote, resource-limited areas of the world where poor hygiene is common. Infection with C. trachomatis occurs through exposure to eye and nasal secretions from infected individuals. Active infection with C. trachomatis causes conjunctivitis. The organism classically affects the palpebral conjunctiva, which is the conjunctival lining of the eyelids. Active infection may cause formation of follicles, which are collections of inflammatory cells that form white bumps on the inner lining of the eyelids. Many patients with active infection are asymptomatic but some develop redness and discharge. Screening programs often inspect the inner surface of the upper eyelid for follicles as a sign of early disease. to roll inward (called "entropion"). Repeated infection may also cause eyelashes to press into the globe of the eye (called "trichiasis"). Eventually, the cornea can become clouded, leading to blindness.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Vitamin A deficiency can cause blindness in malnourished patients. Vitamin A deficiency also leads to drying of the eyes. The classic finding is the presence of Bitot spots, which are keratin accumulations in the conjunctiva. This woman's scarring of the tarsal conjunctiva suggests trachoma, not vitaminAdeficiency.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Adenovirus causes acute conjunctivitis with symptoms of redness and watery discharge. Scarring of the tarsal conjunctiva, entropion, and trichiasis do not typically occur. conjunctivitis. Typical symptoms are redness and purulent discharge. IIH

questions.question: A 20-year-old woman presents for evaluation of red, itchy eyes. Two days ago, she developed the abrupt onset of bilateral, red, intensely pruritic eyes with watery discharge. On examination, there is bilateral conjunctival hyperemia and chemosis. The redness is most pronounced in the bulbar and tarsal conjunctiva. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this woman's presentation?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (incorrect answer): Adenovirus causes viral conjunctivitis. This condition usually begins with unilateral eye involvement, although it can spread from one eye to the other to become bilateral. The abrupt onset of bilateral redness and itching in this case is most consistent with allergic conjunctivitis. Itching is a hallmark of can occur in viral conjunctivitis, viral infection more commonly causes burning or "grittiness" of the eyes. conjunctivitis. This condition is often unilateral and causes a purulent (contains pus) exudate.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Chlamydia trachomatis can cause trachoma, a form of conjunctivitis that predominately occurs in resource-limited locations with poor hygiene. Trachoma is among the leading causesof blindness worldwide. Infants born by vaginal delivery to mothers with C. trachomatis can develop neonatal conjunctivitis or neonatal pneumonia. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 10-day old baby boy is evaluated for irritability. He was born by vaginal delivery to a mother who received no prenatal care. The baby has been crying and is difficult to console. On examination, there is mucopurulent discharge from both eyes. Conjunctival hyperemia is present bilaterally. The eyelids are swollen with red, thickened conjunctiva. Cardiac and pulmonary examinations are normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this baby's condition?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This baby has neonatal conjunctivitis caused by Chlamydia trachomatis. Neonatal born vaginally to mothers with an untreated infection may develop conjunctivitis or pneumonia from these bacteria. The incubation period for C. trachomatis is 5 to 14 days, and most cases of neonatal chlamydia conjunctivitis occur in this period. In contrast, conjunctivitis caused by N. gonorrhoeae can occur earlier, usually between two and five days after birth. Gonococcal conjunctivitis is rare because babies are routinely administered prophylactic erythromycin ointment to the eyes after birth. C. trachomatisis the most common cause of neonatal conjunctivitis. Babies present with mucopurulent conjunctiva beneath the eyelids may be swollen (chemosis).

Answer B (incorrect answer): Airborne allergens cause allergic conjunctivitis. This condition is usually bilateral and associated with itching. Allergic conjunctivitis is very uncommon in the neonatal period as the immune system has not become sensitized to allergens.

Answers C and D (incorrect answers): Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pneumoniae cause bacterial unilateral and causes a purulent exudate.

questions.question: A 40-year-old man presents with complaints of difficulty reading fine print and seeing objects up close. The patient notes After an eye examination, the diagnosis of hyperopia is made. What type of corrective lens is most appropriate for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (incorrect answer): Bifocal lenses are designed for individuals who have both hyperopia and vision and one for distance vision. This patient has only hyperopia, which can be addressed with positive lenses alone.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Cylindrical lenses are used to correct astigmatism, which occurs when the cornea has an uneven curvature, causing blurry or distorted vision.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Multifocal lenses are similar to bifocals but have more than two prescription areas, typically used for patients with presbyopia. These lenses correct both near and far vision. This patient has only hyperopia, which can be addressed withpositive lenses alone.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Negative lenses (concave lenses) are used to correct myopia (nearsightedness), where light focuses in front of the retina. These lenses diverge light rays, moving the focal point further back to allow clear vision for distant objects. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 4-year-old child is brought to the pediatrician for an eye exam due to complaints of blurry vision. The child has been having difficulty seeing clearly, especially at night. Upon examination, the pediatrician notes cloudy corneas. There is a family history of metabolic disorders. A disorder involving which of the following is most likely to explain this condition?

Marfan syndrome is not associated with the development of cataracts at a young age.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Sorbitol is a sugar alcohol that can accumulate in tissues when excess glucose is present. In the lens, sorbitol accumulation can lead to cataracts, particularly in individuals with poorly associated with diabetes-related cataracts in adults. Mc

questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder caused by mutations in the fibrillin-1 gene, affecting the integrity of the extracellular matrix in various connective tissue beds. One of the classic ocular findings in patients with Marfan syndrome is lens displacement (i.e., dislocation). The lens typically dislocates upward and outward due to weakened zonules that cannot properly hold the lens in place. This is the most common ocular abnormality in Marfan syndrome occurring in up to 80% of patients.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Cataracts are characterized by clouding of the lens and can cause blurry vision. dislocation is the most common ocular abnormality in these individuals, especially in younger patients.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Hyperopia (farsightedness) is a refractive error where near objects are blurry, but distant objects are clearer. Hyperopia can occur in individuals with Marfan syndrome, but it is not the most common ocular manifestation of the disease.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Myopia (nearsightedness) is a refractive error where distant objects appear blurry, but near vision is clear. Although refractive errors like myopia can occur in some patients with Marfan syndrome, lensdislocationis morecommon.

Mc Graw

questions.question: A 2-day-old infant is brought to the pediatrician by her parents. The baby was delivered at home, and the mother received a purplish rash on the trunk and extremities. Which of the following additional findings is most likely to be present in this infant?

Answer C (incorrect answer): Although rubella can cause a variety of complications, it is not commonly associated with liver failure. Liver failure would present with jaundice and abnormal liver function tests, which are not noted here.

Answer D (incorrect answer): A Marfanoid body habitus refers to the physical features seen in Marfan syndrome, a genetic disorder often marked by a tall stature, long limbs, and hypermobile joints. These features are typically not seen in newborns as they develop later in life, and this baby lacks evidence of Marfanoid body habitus.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Myopia (nearsightedness) is a refractive error in which distant objects appear blurry, but near vision remains clear. Myopia is not a common finding in newborns and does not cause the cloudiness seen in this infant's eyes (which is due to cataracts). Mc

questions.question: A 65-year-old woman presents with complaints of difficulty reading small print, especially in low light conditions. She has been holding reading materials farther away to focus over the past year. She has no other visual disturbances and has no history of eye trauma or systemic conditions. Her father had diabetes complicated by retinopathy, and she has a maternal uncle with Marfan's syndrome. Her ocular examination reveals no significant abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): Presbyopia is the age-related loss of accommodation (changing in shape of lens), where the lens becomes less flexible, leading to difficulty focusing on near objects. This typically occurs in individuals over the age of 40 and progressively worsens with age. This patient's complaints of difficulty reading

Answer A (incorrect answer): Astigmatism is a refractive error caused by an irregular curvature of the cornea or objects, it would not be expected to only cause difficulty with near vision, as seen in this patient. Astigmatism is also generally present earlier in life, not primarily as an age-related condition.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Ectopia lentis refers to the dislocation of the lens, which can be caused by genetic conditions such as Marfan syndrome or homocystinuria. This condition is easily identified on eye examination, and this patient has no lens abnormalities on ocular exam.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Hyperopia, or farsightedness, is a refractive error where distant vision is clear, but near vision is blurry. questions.question: A 65-year-old man is evaluated for poor vision. Over the past year, he has developed cloudy vision. He has difficulty seeing at night, especially while driving. Eye examination is shown below: Which of the following is a modifiable risk factor for this man's condition?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This man has cataracts, an opacification of the lens of the eye that obscures vision. The pupil should be black, but in the image, it appears white due to clouding of the lens from cataracts. Patients with cataracts develop cloudy vision. They often have problems seeing at night. Important risk factors for cataracts include older age, smoking, excess alcohol consumption, diabetes, obesity, and chronic treatment with corticosteroids. Chronic sunlight exposure is a modifiable risk factor for cataracts. Ultraviolet (Uv) light from the sun can cause oxidative stress in the lens, leading to cataracts. Wearing sunglasses reduces the risk of cataracts byblocking Uv light rays. cataract development. In these cases, cataracts occur in infancy and may be present at birth. Classic galactosemia and galactokinase deficiency are inborn errors of metabolism. These are considered non- modifiableriskfactors.

Answer C(incorrectanswer):Corticosteroid useisa riskfactorfor cataracts,butnot the use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

Answer E (incorrect answer): A high sodium diet is not associated with the development of cataracts. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 19-year-old man is evaluated for blurry vision. He is a college student, and finds it hard to read words projected onto a screen in the lecture hall. He has no trouble reading books or computer screens. Which of the following conditions best explains this man's presentation?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This man has symptoms consistent with myopia, also known as nearsightedness. Myopia occurs when the focal point of the cornea and lens occurs in front of the retina. This can occur if the eye is too long or the refractive power of the cornea and lens is too great. The greater the refractive power of the lens, the closer the focal point of light will be to the front of the eye. Too much refractive power focuses light to a point in front of the retina, causing myopia. Patients with myopia can focus on objects close to the eyes (hence the name nearsighted), but objects far from the eyes appear blurry.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Presbyopia is a loss of lens elasticity that occurs with aging. This causes problems with accommodation, leading to an inability to focus on near objects. Presbyopia does not cause problems with far vision and is unlikely in a 19-year-old.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Hyperopia is also known as farsightedness. This is the opposite of myopia and occurs when the focal point of the cornea and lens occurs behind the retina. In hyperopia, far objects can be seen clearly, but near objects appear blurry.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Astigmatism (Greek for "lack of a pinpoint") is an uneven curvature of the cornea that may cause multiple focal points. Blurry vision occurs at all distances in this condition.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Cataracts are opacities of the lens of the eye. Patients with cataracts develop nearsightedness. Cataracts are common among older patients. Cataracts at a young age are rare outside of special circumstances like classic galactosemia. II!H

questions.question: A 25-year-old woman is evaluated for blurry vision. She has to squint to read books or computer screens because the image is blurry. This has caused her to develop headaches at work, where she uses a computer. She reports no trouble reading words at the movie theater or reading billboards while driving. Which of the following will most likely correct this woman's vision problem?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This woman has symptoms consistent with hyperopia, also known as farsightedness. Hyperopia occurs when the focal point of the cornea and lens occurs behind the retina. This happens if the eye is too short or the refractive power of the cornea and lens is too low. The lower the refractive power of the cornea and lens, the further the focal point of light will be from the front of the eye. Low refractive power can focus eyes (hence the name farsighted), but objects close to the eyes appear blurry. Hyperopia is treated with a converging lens (i.e., eyeglasses or contact lenses). Converging lenses are positive lenses, meaning a lens that is thickest at the center compared to the edges. These lenses have a convex shape, g lenses are essentially magnifying glasses which move the focal point closer to the lens. Converging

Answers A, B, C, and E (incorrect answers): Myopia (nearsightedness) is treated with diverging lenses. Diverging lenses are negative lenses which are thicker at the edges and thin at the center. They have a concave shape, the focal point further from the lens. This is helpful in cases of myopia, where the focal point lies in front of the retina. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 65-year-old male presents for a routine eye examination. He reports difficulty seeing objects in the periphery of his vision. His vision seems to be getting worse over the past several months. He reports no eye pain or discomfort. options.A: Blocks ciliary epithelium from releasing aqueous humor

Answer A (incorrect answer): Beta-blockers (such as timolol) and alpha-2 agonists (such as apraclonidine) block the ciliary epitheliumfrom releasing aqueous humor.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Muscarinic agonists (such as pilocarpine) contract the ciliary muscle to improve aqueoushumordrainage.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (such as acetazolamide) decrease aqueous humor synthesis.

questions.question: A 72-year-old man presents to the emergency department with the sudden onset of severe eye pain, blurred vision, and headache. He reports that his vision has been progressively worsening over the last few hours. On examination, his right eye appears red, and his pupil is fixed and mid-dilated, unresponsive to light. which of the following drugs is contraindicated in this patient at this time?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This patient presents with symptoms of acute angle-closure glaucoma including severe eye pain, blurred vision, fixed mid-dilated pupil, , and headache. Epinephrine is contraindicated in these patients as it activates β2 receptors, causing pupillary dilation (mydriasis). This can narrow the already constricted drainage angle, worsening the condition by blocking aqueous humor drainage and increasing intraocular pressure (IOP).

Answer A (incorrect answer): Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic used to reduce intraocular pressure by drawing fluid out of the eye. It can be safely used in this man's condition.

Answer B(incorrect answer): Acetazolamide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that reduces aqueous humor production. It is not contraindicated in angle-closure glaucoma.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Timolol is a beta-blocker that decreases aqueous humor production. It can be used safely to treat this patient. aqueous humor drainage. It is not contraindicated in angle-closure glaucoma. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 62-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with the severe eye pain and blurred vision that began suddenly two hours ago when she entered a dark room. On examination, her right eye is red, with a fixed, mid-dilated pupil. The patient also reports seeing halos around lights. Which of the following changes contributed to the development of this patient's condition?

options.B: Increased aqueous humor flow through pupil
options.D: Increased distance between iris and cornea

questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): This patient presents with acute eye pain, blurred vision, a fixed mid-dilated pupil, and halos around lights, which are all classic signs of acute angle-closure glaucoma. The condition is caused by anterior displacement of the lens, which blocks the normal flow of aqueous humor through the pupil. This can be triggered by pupillary dilation on entering a dark room as seen in this case. Lens displacement causes the iris to press against the cornea. This obstructs aqueous humor drainage and increases intraocular pressure (IoP).

Answer B (incorrect answer): Increased aqueous humor flow through the pupil is not the cause of acute angle- not the primary cause of acute angle-closure glaucoma. The condition is primarily due to anatomic changes that blockthedrainagepathways.

Answer D (incorrect answer):A decreased distance between the iris and cornea, not an increased distance,leads to the narrowing or closure of the drainage angle.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Miosis (pupillary constriction) does not cause acute angle-closure glaucoma. The condition results from anterior displacement of the lens, which blocks the drainage of aqueous humor. Mc Graw

The physician prescribes a new medication that activates muscarinic acetylcholine receptors to help manage his condition. Which of the following effects would this medication have on the ciliary muscle and aqueous humor drainage?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This patient presents with gradual peripheral vision loss and difficulty seeing in dim light, symptoms consistent with open-angle glaucoma. This condition is caused by increased intraocular pressure (IoP) in the anterior chamber and can be treated with drugs that increase aqueous humor outflow. Muscarinic acetylcholine receptor activation causes constriction of the ciliary muscle, which increases aqueous humor drainage by opening the trabecular meshwork. This improves outflow through the Canal of Schlemm, reducing IOP.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Muscarinic agonists contract (not relax) the ciliary muscle. Relaxation would reduce aqueous humor drainage. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 70-year-old woman is referred for ophthalmologic screening. She smokes one half pack of cigarettes per day, and consumes one to two beers each evening. Her body mass index is 32 kg/m2. Intraocular pressure is increased, and slightly higher than one year ago. questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This woman has open-angle glaucoma, a condition associated with increased intraocular pressure (IOP). Open-angle glaucoma is usually asymptomatic until vision loss occurs. The diagnosis is usually made through routine screening. Glaucoma is diagnosed in patients with increased IOP and either optic nerve damage on fundoscopy or visual loss. The fundoscopy image in the question shows optic nerve to the larger optic nerve disc. In patients with glaucoma, the cup becomes larger (i.e., the cup to disc ratio increases). questions.question: A 70-year-old woman is referred for ophthalmologic screening. Intraocular pressure is increased. Fundoscopic exam shows optic nerve cupping. This woman's condition is caused by an excessive amount of a substance produced in which of the following locations?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This woman has open-angle glaucoma, a condition associated with increased intraocular pressure (IOP). Open-angle glaucoma is usually asymptomatic until vison loss occurs. questions.question: A 75-year-old man is referred for ophthalmologic screening. Intraocular pressure is increased. Fundoscopic examination shows an increased cup to disc ratio. A drug with which of the following mechanisms of action may be beneficial for this man's eye condition?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (incorrect answer): Alpha-2 receptors are found on peripheral sympathetic neurons. Activation of agonists like apraclonidine and brimonidine decrease production of aqueous humor from the ciliary epithelium by inhibiting the release of norepinephrine onto beta receptors. Alpha receptor antagonists have no role in treating glaucoma.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Prostaglandins are lipid-signaling molecules that are necessary to maintain outflow of aqueous humor from the anterior chamber. Prostaglandin analogues like latanoprost can be used to glaucoma. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 78-year-old man is referred for ophthalmologic screening. Intraocular pressure is increased. Fundoscopic exam shows optic nerve cupping. He is treated with pilocarpine. Which of the following adverse effects may occur with this drug?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (incorrect answer): Darkening of the iris (hyperpigmentation) and eyelash growth can occur in patients treated with prostaglandin analogues like latanoprost or bimatoprost.

Answers Cand D (incorrectanswers): Mydriasis s (pupillary dilation) and dry mouth are responses to muscarinic antagonist drugs. Drugs in this class include atropine and scopolamine. These drugs are generally not used for treatment of glaucoma.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Alpha-2 receptor agonists like apraclonidine cause ocular hyperemia (i.e., red eyes) in over 10% of patients. Alpha-2 receptors are found on peripheral sympathetic neurons, where they provide release of norepinephrine, which decreases production of aqueous humor from the ciliary epithelium. By blocking the release of norepinephrine (which is a vasoconstrictor), these drugs significantly increase blood flow, which can cause redness of the eyes. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 65-year-old woman is evaluated for sudden-onset left eye pain and vision loss. Her symptoms began one hour ago when she entered a dark room in her home. She developed throbbing eye pain, saw halos of light, and then lost vision in the eye. Examination of the eye shows diffuse conjunctival hyperemia and clouding of the cornea. The pupil is mid-dilated and does not react to light. This woman's problem is caused by an abnormality in which of the locations below?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This woman has acute angle-closure glaucoma, a condition caused by a sudden increase in intraocular pressure (IoP). Elevated IOP occurs when there is too much aqueous humor in the anterior chamber of the eye (the image in the question is of the anterior chamber as seen by optical coherence tomography). Aqueous humor drains into the trabecular meshwork located at the angle of the anterior chamber (also called the iridocorneal angle or simply "the angle"). This angle is formed by the junction of the iris and the cornea. The most common form of glaucoma is open-angle glaucoma, a painless, slow-onset condition of elevated IOp question. Acute angle-closure glaucoma develops when outflow of aqueous humor through the angle into the trabecular meshwork abruptly decreases. This classically occurs when a patient enters a dark room, since low light causes the pupil to dilate, which can constrict flow through the angle. Another common trigger is a cold medicine with anticholinergic properties that causes pupillary dilation. Special note: Because mydriasis (pupillary dilation) can worsen outflow through the angle, drugs which cause mydriasis are contraindicated in angle-closure glaucoma. This includes drugs historically used in open-angle glaucoma like epinephrine and apraclonidine. This is not an issue in modern practice because these two medicines have not been used regularly to treat glaucoma for decades. In addition, the anti-cholinergic blocker atropine causes mydriasis and may trigger angle-closure glaucoma. This drug essentially has the same effect on the pupil as entering a dark room. Acute, angle-closure glaucoma is an ophthalmologic emergency since eye sight can be lost without rapid intervention. Symptoms include eye pain, halos of light, and vision loss. On examination, the eye is red with clouding of the cornea. The eye may feel "rock hard" from elevated pressure in the anterior chamber.

Answers A, C, and D (incorrect answers): Angle-closure glaucoma is associated with closure of the angle, as the Mc Graw

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman presents with progressive, painless vision loss in her left eye over the past several days. She reports no flashes of light or floaters. Her medical history is significant for uncontrolled hypertension and systemic lupus erythematosus. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This patient is experiencing an exudative, or serous, retinal detachment, which is a type of non-rhegmatogenous detachment. It occurs when fluid accumulates between the neurosensory retina and the retinal pigment epithelium without the presence of a retinal tear. The patient's gradual, painless vision characteristic of this type of detachment. Her underlying conditions of systemic lupus erythematosus and uncontrolled hypertension are known risk factors that can lead to inflammation or choroidal vascular leakage the underlying pigment epithelium further support this diagnosis.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) presents as sudden, painless loss of vision in one eye, usually due to an embolic or thrombotic event affecting the central retinal artery. This patient's gradual vision loss and dome-shaped retinal detachment are not consistent with CRAO. occurs when fluid from the vitreous cavity enters through a tear and lifts the retina. This patient's vision loss accompanied by findings of retinal elevation are not characteristic of macular degeneration.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Posterior vitreous detachment occurs when the vitreous gel separates from the retina, often causing flashes of light and floaters. It is common with aging and can sometimes lead to a retinal tear, but by itself, it does not cause retinal detachment. This patient's absence of flashes or floaters and the presence of retinal elevation without a tear make this diagnosis less likely. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 74-year-old man presents with sudden-onset vision loss in his left eye. The symptoms began a few hours ago and have gradually worsened. He describes seeing flashes of light, followed by the sensation of a curtain descending over his visual field. He has a history of posterior vitreous detachment which occurred a few months ago. The patient is otherwise healthy. with no history of trauma or systemic disease. Which of the following is the direct cause of this patient's condition?

options.A: Autoimmune-mediated inflammation of the uvea leading to retinal ischemia
options.B: membrane leading to photoreceptor Deposition of drusen within Bruch's atrophy
options.D: Increased intraocular pressure causing compression of the optic nerve
options.E: Retinal tear leading to separation of retina from underlying epithelium

questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This patient is presenting with symptoms of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, which is characterized by flashes of light (photopsia) followed by the sensation of a curtain or shadow descending over the visual field. These symptoms are often due to a retinal tear, which allows vitreous fluid to enter the subretinal space, leading to separation of the retina from the underlying retinal pigment epithelium. A prior posterior vitreous detachment (PvD) increases the risk of retinal tears by causing vitreous traction on the retina. AnswerA(incorrectanswer):Autoimmune-mediated inflammation of the uvea,suchas uveitis,can lead to retinal ischemia or scarring, but does not directly result in rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.

Answer B (incorrect answer): The deposition of drusen in Bruch's membrane is associated with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and can lead to photoreceptor atrophy and central vision loss. AMD does not cause rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Fluid accumulation beneath the retina occurs in rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, but it is a result of a retinal tear, not a direct cause. In rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, a tear in the retina allows vitreous fluid to leak into the subretinal space, causing the retina to detach from the retinal pigment epithelium.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Increased intraocular pressure is a hallmark of glaucoma, which causes optic nerve damage and vision loss over time. Glaucoma does not directly cause rhegmatogenous retinal detachment. This patient's symptoms are more consistent with retinal detachment, which is typically related to mechanical causes,suchasretinaltears. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 68-year-old woman presents with complaints of black spots and flashes of light in her vision over the past few weeks. questions.explanation:

Blockage in this artery can lead to vision changes, but typically causes sudden, painless vision loss rather than the floaters and flashes of light seen in this case. Additionally, there would likely be signs of retinal ischemia or infarction, which are not present in this patient.

Answer B(incorrect answer):The choroid is the vascular layer of the eye that provides blood supply to the outer layers of the retina. Although disorders of the choroid, such as choroidal neovascularization, can cause vision changes, they do not typically present with floaters and flashes of light.

questions.question: A 67-year-old woman is evaluated for sudden-onset vision loss in her right eye. For the past several days, she has noticed flashing lights and spots. Funduscopic examination is shown below: Which of the following is a major risk factor for development of this woman's condition?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This woman has a retinal detachment. The retina contains photoreceptors (rods and cones) that convert light into neural impulses. Retinal cells are metabolically active, requiring significant blood flow from the underlying choroid. If the retina detaches from the choroid, the retinal blood supply is lost and retinal cells can die, leading to vision loss. The most common type of retinal detachment is a "rhegmatogenous" detachment. In this condition, a tear or hole develops in the retina. Fluid then leaks through the hole or tear, causing the retina to detach. Beneath the retina is a layer of tissue called the retinal pigmented epithelium which sits on top of the choroid. When the retina pulls away from the underlying pigmented epithelium and choroid, there is loss of blood supply. Retinal detachment is often preceded by posterior vitreous detachment. Vitreous humor is a gelatinous substance that fills the back of the eye. It is surrounded by a membrane called the vitreous membrane (also called the hyaloid membrane), which is in contact with the retina and other structures. With aging, the vitreous shrinks, and the vitreous membrane can detach from the retina. When this occurs, patients may notice flashes of light or "floaters", meaning dark spots in the vision. In some cases, when the posterior vitreous detaches, it causes a tear or hole in the retina, leading to retinal detachment. The symptoms of retinal detachment are the abrupt onset of vision loss, sometimes described as a curtain shade membrane detachment. Fundoscopy shows a crinkling of retinal tissue (top left portion of image). Retinal detachment is an ophthalmologic emergency with urgent intervention required to preserve vision. Myopia (nearsightedness) is a major risk factor for retinal detachment. Myopic patients have rates of detachment four times higher than patients with non-myopic eyes. Patients with myopia have eyes that are relatively long with thin retinas. Other risk factors for retinal detachment include eye trauma, prior cataract surgery, and proliferative diabetic retinopathy.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Hyperopia (farsightedness) is a refractive disorder like myopia but is not associated withretinal detachment.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Astigmatism occurs when the cornea has an irregular curvature, leading to blurry vision. This is not associated with retinal detachment.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Scleritis is inflammation of the sclera. This causes redness of the eye and eye pain. Scleritis is not associated with retinal detachment.

questions.question: A 65-year-old woman with type II diabetes mellitus presents for ophthalmologic examination. Her physician recommends treatment with ranibizumab. The primary goal of this therapy is to prevent which of the following complications?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): The question describes a woman with proliferative diabetic retinopathy. In this condition, ischemia associated with diabetes causes new blood vessel growth on the optic nerve or retina. This occurs because ischemia causes production of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), which leads to new blood vessel formation. New blood vessels are weak and prone to hemorrhage. Bevacizumab is a recombinant monoclonal antibody that blocks blood vessel growth by inhibiting VEGF. The two major complications of untreated proliferative retinopathy are vitreous hemorrhage and retinal detachment. In vitreous hemorrhage, new blood vessels grow out from the retina into the vitreous humor, the gelatinous material found in the back of the eye. Blood in the vitreous humor obscures transmission of light to the retina, leading to vision loss. disorders are not major complications of proliferative diabetic retinopathy. among patients with multiple sclerosis. Chronic hyperglycemia leads to changes in the retinal blood vessels that cause retinopathy. These vessels become prone to both leakiness and occlusion. On fundoscopy, findings of diabetic retinopathy include microaneurysms, which can rupture and lead to hemorrhage. Areas of ischemia may develop wool spots. Diabetic retinopathy is associated with changes in small blood vessels of the retina that have been well- characterized in the basic science literature.Basement membranes thicken and endothelial cell tightjunctions are lost. In addition, there is a decrease in the number of pericytes, which are contractile cells that derive from the mesoderm. In retinal capillaries, pericytes regulate perfusion pressure, similar to smooth muscle cells of peripheral arterioles. In diabetic retinopathy, pericytes undergo apoptosis leading to loss of control over capillary perfusion. This can lead to formation of microaneurysm and hemorrhage.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man presents with sudden, painless vision loss in the right eye. He noticed blurred vision over the past few days, with the vision loss becoming more pronounced in the last 24 hours. Fundoscopy findings are shown below. On examination of the anterior segment of the eye, which of the following findings is most likely to be observed in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This man has a branch retinal vein occlusion (BRvo), a retinal vascular disorder characterized by blockage of a branch of the central retinal vein. This leads to sudden, painless vision loss and a retina located in the back of the eye, and does not directly involve components of the anterior segment of the eye such as the cornea, iris, pupil, and lens.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Corneal opacification is usually associated with infections, trauma, or inflammatory conditions affecting the cornea, such as keratitis or corneal scarring. It is not an expected finding in patients with branch retinal vein occlusion (BRvO), which is a retinal problem.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Iris discoloration is typically caused by inflammatory conditions, such as iritis or uveitis, or by certain medications (e.g., prostaglandin analogs used in glaucoma treatment). In branch retinal vein occlusion (BRvO), there is no involvement of the iris, and no iris discoloration would be expected.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Lens distortion or cataracts typically result from aging, trauma, diabetes, or long- term corticosteroid use, and primarily affect the structure of the lens. Branch retinal vein occlusion (BRvO) does not involve the lens, and there is no direct impact on the anteriorsegment structures.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Pupillary irregularity is usually a sign of trauma, neurogenic conditions (e.g., Horner syndrome), or inflammatory eye diseases (e.g., iritis, uveitis). Branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO) does not affect the anterior segment or the pupillary reflexes. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 65-year-old woman presents with sudden, painless vision loss in one eye. On examination, the visual acuity in the affected symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Answer A (correct answer): The patient has clinical features of a retinal artery occlusion (RAO), which is characterized by sudden, painless vision loss due to blockage of a retinal artery. A cherry-red spot is a classic sign of central retinal artery occlusion (cRAo), where ischemia causes retinal pallor, but the macula retains its red appearance due to its rich blood supply. Atherosclerosis is the most common cause of CRAO. In this condition, atherosclerotic plaques from the carotid arteries or aortic arch may embolize, blocking the central retinal artery or its branches. These emboli lead to retinal ischemia and the characteristic findings on fundoscopy.

Answer B (incorrect answer): Cardiac thrombi may also embolize to the retinal artery resulting in a retinal artery occlusion, but this is less common than atherosclerosis. Cardiac emboli are more likely in patients with atrial fibrillation, valvular heart disease, or heart failure. cause a cherry-red spot in the macula due to the accumulation of metabolic products in retinal cells. Inflammation of blood vessels in the retina can occur in conditions like giant cell arteritis or systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), but these conditions usually present with additional systemic symptoms, such as fever, weight loss, and headache. questions.question: A 58-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus presents for a routine eye exam. He has experienced mild visual blurriness and difficulty with near vision over the past few months. On fundoscopy, the finding indicated by the white arrow below is identified. which of the following best describes this finding?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This man has clinical features of nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR), a common complication of long-standing diabetes. The image shows hard exudates which are yellowish, lipid-rich deposits in the retina due to leakage of lipids from damaged retinal blood vessels. They are commonly associated with macular edema. On fundoscopy, hard exudates are often seen as bright, yellow, well-defined deposits in the macula or around the optic disc.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Cotton-wool spots appear as white, fluffy, or cotton-ball-like lesions on the retina. These spots indicate nerve fiber infarctions from microvascular occlusion and are typically seen in diabetic retinopathy, they are distinct from hard exudates.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Retinal hemorrhages in diabetic retinopathy usually appear as red, dot-shaped, or blotchy lesions on the retina. They result from the rupture of small retinal capillaries, which is common in the early stages of diabetic retinopathy. Hemorrhages can also occur in more advanced stages, particularly in proliferative diabetic retinopathy, but they do not appear as yellow lipid deposits like hard exudates.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Microaneurysms are small, round, red dots that represent localized areas of capillary dilatation. They are one of the earliest signs of diabetic retinopathy and are caused by the weakening do not have the yellow, lipid-rich appearance seen in hard exudates.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Neovascularization refers to the growth of new, abnormal blood vessels on the surface of the retina, a key feature of proliferative diabetic retinopathy. These vessels are fragile, prone to rupture, and can lead to vitreous hemorrhage or retinal detachment. Neovascularization does not appear as yellow exudates and is not seen in nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy unless the disease progresses to more severestages. Mc MeiS

questions.question: A 15-year-old boy is evaluated for vision loss. Over the past three years, his vision has declined significantly. He also finds it difficult to see in dim light. Answer C (correct answer): This boy has retinitis pigmentosa, a genetic condition associated with loss of photoreceptors (rods and cone) in the retina. From a genetics standpoint, retinitis pigmentosa is famous for them x-linked, some autosomal dominant, and some autosomal recessive. In retinitis pigmentosa, rods and cones undergo apoptosis. Poor night vision is one of the earliest signs. Patients may find it difficult to see in dark light, such as at dusk or in movie theaters. Vision loss occurs slowly and may go unnoticed for many years. Eventually, legal blindness may occur. questions.question: A 65-year-old man is evaluated for vision loss. Findings on funduscopic examination are shown below: Which of the following is most appropriate for this man?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This man has the dry form of age-related macular degeneration (AMD), a degenerative disease of the macula that results in central vision loss. Patients with dry AMD present with slowly- progressive central vision loss. The classic finding on fundoscopy in dry AMD is the presence of drusen, which are yellow deposits localized in the macula. In dry AMD, drusen accumulate between Bruch's membrane and the retinal pigment epithelium. Approximately 90% of patients with AMD have the dry form (the other 10% have wet macular degeneration). Two interventions are recommended in patients with dry AMD: smoking cessation and supplementation with antioxidant vitamins and zinc. Dry AMD progression is associated with smoking, and all patients with this condition who smoke should be advised to stop. In clinical trials, supplementation with antioxidant vitamins asa 'a p o ossod o u ' o ( s)s patients with significant drusen.

Answers A, C, and E (incorrect answers): Bevacizumab is a monoclonal antibody that targets vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) to limit abnormal blood vessel growth. Photodynamic therapy involves injection of a dye that is activated with a laser to limit blood vessel growth. Macular translocation surgery is an experimental technique that moves the macula to a healthier area of the eye. All of these are treatments for wet AMD. Wet AMD has a different appearance on fundoscopy compared with dry AMD. Wet AMD occurs when new blood vessels form ("neovascularization") from the choroid and penetrate Bruch's membrane. These vessels may leak or develop hemorrhage.In contrast to the slowly progressive vision loss of dry AMD, wet AMDcan cause rapidly progressivevisionloss. Wet AMD is less common than dry AMD. All patients with wet AMD have dry AMD first, with progression to the wet form. For this reason, regular screening of patients with dry AMD is important so that wet AMD can be treated early. Key point: The presence of neovascularization distinguishes wet AMD from dry AMD. Management of dry AMD is aimed at preventing disease progression and early identification of wet AMD. questions.question: A 72-year-old man is evaluated for abnormal vision. Two years ago, he underwent renal transplantation. Prior to treated with cyclosporine, azathioprine, and prednisone. For the past three days, he has noticed floaters and blurry vision in This man's condition is caused by a virus that reactivated from which of the following locations?

Answer D (correct answer): This man has retinitis caused by cytomegalovirus (CMv). CMV is a member of the herpes virus family and is a DNA virus. It can cause disease in patients with immunosuppression, such as occurs via hematogenous spread of the virus to the eye. CMV can be transmitted in many ways, including via sexual contact, from blood or tissue exposure, from close after initial exposure. Primary CMV infection (i.e., infection after first exposure) is often asymptomatic, but can cause a mononucleosis-like illness in some cases. Following initial infection, CMV always establishes latency, life if cellular immunity becomes depressed, such as from immunosuppressive drugs, as in this case. of anti-CMV IgG antibodies and negative anti-CMV IgM antibodies indicates prior exposure and latent infection. There are currently no therapies to eradicate CMV in patients with latent disease. Besides retinitis, CMV can cause other disorders in immunosuppressed patients, including pneumonitis and gastroenteritis. On fundoscopy, the classic findings of CMV retinitis are yellow-white, fluffy lesions in the retina close to the retinal vessels with associated hemorrhage (see image). This is sometimes described as having has the appearance of a"pizza pie."

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman is evaluated for headache. She reports a constant, throbbing bilateral headache for the past two weeks. She also reports occasional scotoma. To make the diagnosis of IIH, a lumbar puncture is performed to measure the opening pressure. An elevated Mc opening pressure on lumbar puncture is a diagnostic criterion for IIH. Elevated intracranial pressure causes a downward displacement of the brainstem. This presses the sixth cranial nerve as it crosses the petrous ridge of the temporal bone, which can lead to nerve dysfunction. The abducens nerve innervates a single eye muscle: the lateral rectus. Abducens nerve palsy leads to medial deviation of the eye on the affected side. This causes a form of strabismus (misalignment of the eyes) called esotropia. In esotropia, one or both eyes are turned inward. Other forms of strabismus include exotropia (eye turned outward) and hypertropia (vertical misalignment of eyes with one eye higher than the other).

questions.question: A 26-year-old woman presents with daily headaches that have been progressively worsening over the past month. She describes them as pulsatile and worse when lying down. questions.question: A 22-year-old man presents with painless, progressive vision loss in his right eye. One month later, he develops similar symptoms in his left eye. He reports difficulty reading and recognizing faces. Fundoscopic exam shows optic disc hyperemia and vascular telangiectasias. His maternal uncle experienced similar vision loss in early adulthood. Answer C (correct answer): Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHoN), also known as Leber Optic Neuropathy, is a mitochondrial disorder that causes subacute, painless, central vision loss, typically beginning in one eye and then affecting the other within weeks. It primarily affects young adult males and is often associated with optic disc hyperemia and vascular telangiectasias on fundoscopic exam. The reason for the higher incidence in males compared to females is poorly understood. LHON is caused by mutations in mitochondrial DNA, which is inherited exclusively from the mother. This is only mothers pass it on because fathers do not transmit mitochondrial DNA to their offspring. As a result, the condition may appear in multiple relatives connected through the maternal line, such as maternal uncles, brothers, and sons. In this case, the presence of an affected maternal uncle supports the diagnosis.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) typically occurs in older patients with vascular risk factors such as diabetes or hypertension. Answer E (incorrect answer): Optic neuritis is a demyelinating condition that causes acute, painful vision loss and is frequently associated with multiple sclerosisIt is not maternally inherited and does not involve mitochondrial mutations.

questions.question: An 82-year-old man is seen in follow-up after a stroke. On neurologic examination, there is right facial droop. Strength is decreased in the right arm and leg. Clinical features of MCA stroke include contralateral weakness of the facial muscles and the extremities with the arms affected more than the legs. MCA strokes can affect Broca's area in the frontal lobe, which leads to an expressive aphasia. The presence of aphasia with hemiparesis indicates a cerebral location for the stroke. Neglect, visual field loss, and aphasia are called "cortical" signs that indicate the stroke involves the cortex. Horizontal conjugate gaze is initiated by the frontal eye fields (FEFs) of the frontal lobes. Neurons in this the FEF cause deviation of the eyes toward the affected side. questions.question: An 82-year-old man is seen in follow-up after a stroke. On gaze testing, he is unable to look to the left. Answer E (correct answer): This man has one and a half syndrome caused by a stroke. This syndrome is caused bylesionsinvolving theparamedianpontinereticularformation(PpRF)andmedial longitudinalfasciculus (MLF). Lesions of the PPRF cause inability to gaze laterally toward the affected side (left in the case of this man). When asked to look right, the left eye does not move past midline, consistent with an MLF lesion. The two lesions together are called one and a half syndrome.

Answer A (incorrect answer): This man has a lesion of the left PPRF causing inability to gaze toward the left. He also has a lesion of the MLF causing inability of the left eye to move medially (toward the nose) on rightward conjugategaze.

questions.question: An 82-year-old man is seen in follow-up after a stroke. On neurologic examination, his pupils are midline at rest when looking forward. He is unable to look to the left. Horizontal gaze to the right is normal. Convergence testing is normal. A lesion involving which of the following areas of the brain is most likely in this man?

Answer C (correct answer): This man has a horizontal conjugate gaze palsy caused by a lesion of the paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF) on the left side. Conjugate gaze refers to the ability of the right(i.e.,horizontally). Horizontal conjugate gaze is initiated by the frontal eye fields (FEFs) of the frontal lobes. Neurons in this location project to the PPRF in the pons. The PPRF activates muscles of both eyes to enable conjugate gaze.In the eye that moves medially on conjugate gaze (i.e., toward the nose), the PPRF sends signals via the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) to activate the contralateral oculomotor nerve, which innervates the medial rectus muscle. In the eye that moves laterally (i.e., away from the nose), the PPRF activates the nucleus of cranial nerve VI to trigger contraction of the lateral rectus muscle. Simultaneous contraction of the medial rectus on one side and the lateral rectus on the other allows for conjugate gaze. Lesions involving any of the conjugate look left, meaning the left eye does not move laterally and the right eye does not move medially. These movements are coordinated by the PPRF. Answer D (incorrect answer): Lesions of the medulla are not associated with conjugate gaze palsies.

questions.question: A 78-year-old man is evaluated for diplopia. He has a history of diabetes and carotid artery stenosis. On eye examination, the left eye is depressed and abducted, and there is mild ptosis on the left. The patient is unable to adduct or elevate the left eye. His pupils are equal and reactive to light bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this man's presentation?
questions.explanation:
Answer D (correct answer): This man has oculomotor (cranial nerve III) nerve palsy, (sometimes called a diabetic third nerve palsy) caused by ischemia. The oculomotor nerve innervates the levator palpebrae muscle of the eyelid along with several ocular muscles, including the medial rectus, superior rectus, inferior rectus, and inferior oblique muscles. Patients with oculomotor nerve lesions present with ptosis and an eye that is abducted and depressed ("down and out") on the affected side. Paralysis will be present to adduction and elevation. In patients with diabetes, microvascular dysfunction can impair blood flow to the third cranial nerve, leading to third cranial nerve to control the pupil. For this reason, pupillary size and reactivity are normal.

Answers A and B (incorrect answers): Oculomotor nerve palsy may also develop if the third cranial nerve is compressed by an aneurysm, tumor, or AV malformation. These masses compress the third cranial nerve, and also parasympathetic fibers that travel with the third cranial nerve. For this reason, compression of the oculomotor nerve leads to abnormalities of pupillary function, in addition to an eye that is down and out. The parasympathetic system constricts the pupil. With loss of parasympathetic innervation, the pupil becomes dilated and non-reactive to light. nerve. In contrast, a normal pupil seen with third nerve palsy suggests microvascular ischemia (i.e., not compression of the nerve) is the cause. This is sometimes called the "rule of the pupil" for cranial nerve III palsies. Key point: Presence or absence of pupillary abnormalities in third nerve lesions carries clinical significance. Patients with oculomotor nerve palsies and normal pupillary function almost always have microvascular ischemia pupil is abnormal in the setting of a third nerve palsy, neuroimaging is imperative to evaluate for an aneurysm or mass.

Answer C (incorrect answer): Pseudotumor cerebri refers to intracranial hypertension. This condition leads to headaches and papilledema. The classic cranial nerve defect in pseudotumor cerebri is a sixth cranial nerve palsy (abducens nerve). Lesions of this nerve cause the eye to turn inward. Depression with ptosis does not occur.

Answer E (incorrect answer): Lung tumors located at the lung apex on the left (Pancoast tumors) may disrupt sympathetic innervation to the face on the affected side. This can lead to Horner syndrome, with clinical features of ptosis, pupillary constriction (miosis), and anhidrosis (lack of sweat). Oculomotor deficits do not occur inHorner syndrome. Mc MU

questions.question: A 72-year-old man presents with sudden loss of vision on the right side of his visual fields. He has a history of hypertension and atrial fibrillation. questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This man has a right homonymous hemianopsia, which refers to loss of the right visual field in both eyes. This type of visual field defect is caused by a lesion beyond the optic chiasm, often due to ischemic stroke, particularly those involving the posterior cerebral artery. This man's history of hypertension and atrial fibrillation place him at increased risk for stroke. The left optic tract carries visual information from the right visual fields of both eyes. A lesion in this location results in right homonymous hemianopsia consistent with this patient's symptoms.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Meyer's loop is located in the temporal lobe and is part of the optic radiations upper quadrantanopia, not a complete right homonymous hemianopsia.

questions.question: A 64-year-old woman presents to the emergency department after experiencing a sudden loss of vision in her left eye while reading. She describes the vision loss as a "curtain shade" falling over her eye that resolved within a few minutes. She has a describes the type of visual disturbance this patient experienced?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (incorrect answer): Hemianopsia refers to the loss of half of the visual field in one or both eyes. It is associated with lesions in the optic tract, optic radiations, or occipital cortex. This is not consistent typically with this patient's description of transient, monocular vision loss.

Answer D (incorrect answer): Quadrantanopia is the loss of one quadrant of the visual field and is typically caused by lesions in specific parts of the optic radiations, such as Meyer's loop or the parietal lobe. It does not describe the transient, monocular vision loss in this case.

Answer E (incorrect answer): A scotoma is an area of partial or complete loss of vision surrounded by a field of normal vision, commonly due to retinal or optic nerve pathology. It usually presents as a persistent blind spot not a transient, complete loss in one eye. Mc Graw

questions.question: A 41-year-old woman presents for an annual medical evaluation. Her physician performs a visual field test by asking the patient to fix her gaze on his nose while he slowly moves his finger laterally into her left visual field. The patient reports that she can see his finger. This ability is due to direct projections to which of the following structures from this woman's retina?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (incorrect answer): The parietal lobe contains part of the optic radiations that carry information about the lower visual fields. Like Meyer's loop, it does not receive direct input from the retina.

Answer D (incorrect answer): The optic radiations are pathways that transmit visual information from the lateral geniculate nucleus to the visual cortex. They do not receive direct input from the retina and are therefore not the first central relay in the visual pathway.

Answer E (incorrect answer): The visual cortex is the final destination for visual signals, where conscious visual perception occurs. It does not receive direct input from the retina. Instead, retinal signals first pass through the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus before being relayed to the visual cortex. Mc Graw

questions.question: An 87-year-old man is evaluated after a stroke. He has a visual field defect involving the lower right quadrant of both eyes. This defect can be explained by damage to fibers found in which of the following locations?
questions.explanation:
Answers A (incorrect answer): Lesions of the frontal lobes do not cause homonymous quadrantanopia. In terms of visual processing, the frontal eye fields are located in the frontal lobe. Lesions in this region cause the eyes to deviate toward the side of the lesion ("Look at the lesion").

Answer B and C (incorrect answers): The temporal lobe carries information from the superior quadrant of the visual field in each eye. Damage to these fibers produces the "pie in the sky" lesion.

Answer D (incorrect answer): A lesion of the right parietal lobe would cause a left homonymous quadrantanopia, not a right homonymous quadrantanopia as described in this patient.

questions.question: A 56-year-old man presents with fatigue, erectile dysfunction, breast enlargement, and loss of vision. Visual field testing identifies the abnormality shown below. questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This man has classic clinical features of a pituitary adenoma, a benign tumor that Mc arises from the pituitary gland. Headaches may develop from expansion of the tumor. Symptoms may also occur due to hormone release from the tumor. Adenomas may secrete prolactin, growth hormone, adrenocorticotropic hormone, or gonadotrophic hormones. Hormone-producing adenomas most commonly secrete prolactin Prolactin also suppresses the synthesis of sex hormones. In men, this may lead to symptoms of low testosterone, including fatigue, decreased energy, reduced libido, and erectile dysfunction. Bitemporal hemianopsia (loss of vision in the lateral half of the visual fields) occurs in rare circumstances when very large pituitary tumors compress the optic chiasm located next to the pituitary gland. Answers E and G(incorrect answers): Lesions of the optic tract or occipital lobe cause homonymous hemianopia. This defect involves loss of the right or left half of the visual field in each eye.

questions.question: An 80-year-old woman is evaluated following a stroke. Visual field testing identifies the abnormality shown below. This patient's stroke most likely affected which of the following structures?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): This patient has homonymous hemianopsia, a visual field defect involving one-half of the visual field in each eye. This occurs with damage to the optic tract or occipital lobe on one side of the body. Sensory information from half of the visual field of each eye is transmitted to the occipital lobe on the contralateral side. This means that the right half of the visual field in each eye is transmitted to the left occipital lobe and vice versa. Strokes that involve the occipital lobe can lead to homonymous hemianopia.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Lesions of the optic nerve lead to anopia, meaning complete loss of all visual information from one eye. This woman does not have complete visual loss in either eye.

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman is evaluated for abdominal pain. She reports the sudden onset of throbbing abdominal pain in the right upper quadrant that began three hours ago. Since then she has vomited twice. Ultrasound imaging shows gallbladder wall thickening with a dilated common bile duct. Serum levels of amylase and lipase are increased. which of the following findings is most likely in this woman's retroperitoneum?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This woman has acute pancreatitis from a gallstone obstructing pancreatic duct flow ("gallstone pancreatitis"). Gallstones may enter the common bile duct and block the flow of pancreatic enzymes into the duodenum. This leads to accumulation of pancreatic enzymes within the interstitium of the pancreas. Most pancreatic enzymes are secreted in an inactive form called a zymogen but pancreatic lipase is an exception secreted in an active form. This enzyme breaks down fat, triggers inflammation, and leads to fat necrosis. Mild cases of acute pancreatitis may involve only acute inflammatory changes and mild fat necrosis. Severe cases may include vascular inflammatory injury and hemorrhage. Fat necrosis may occur within the pancreas and elsewhere in the retroperitoneum including omentum, bowel mesentery, and subcutaneous fat.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Coagulative necrosis is the most common form of necrosis but does not occur in acute pancreatitis. This type of necrosis is common in ischemia of organs like the heart, spleen, and kidney.

Answers B and E (incorrect answers): Chronic inflammation is not expected in this woman with acute pancreatitis. This is seen in chronic pancreatitis which may lead to fibrosis of the pancreas. Mc GraW

questions.question: A 42-year-old man is evaluated for fever and cough. Two days ago, he developed a sore throat. For the past 24 hours, he has had a severe cough with yellow sputum production. He has also felt feverish with shaking chills. Temperature is 101.5°F, pulse is 112/min and blood pressure is 114/72 mmHg. Physical exam reveals crackles in the right lower lobe. Chest x-ray shows a right lower lobe infiltrate. He is admitted to the hospital for treatment with antibiotics. Which of the following is an important mediator of this man's fever?
questions.explanation:
Answer B (correct answer): This man has right lower lobe pneumonia with a systemic response to infection In the setting of infection and inflammation, cytokines are released into the systemic circulation by inflammatory cells. The major cytokines of acute inflammation are IL-1, TNF-alpha, and IL-6. All of these are "endogenous pyrogens" meaning substances produced by the body that lead to fever. These also lead to many other features that occur with infection or sepsis including muscle wasting (cachexia), elevated white blood cell count, and hypotension. To remember these cytokines, just remember the radio call signal for acute inflammation: "one-alpha-six". In response to these pyrogens, prostaglandin E2 is produced in the hypothalamus. This works locally within the hypothalamus to alter the temperature set point and cause fever. Key point: The mechanism of fever involves pyrogens like IL-1 or TNF-alpha that circulate systemically leading to increased production of PGE2 which works locally in the hypothalamus.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Histamine is important for mediating effects of inflammation such as vasodilation, but it does not play a major role in causing fever.

Answers C and D (incorrect answers): In contrast to acute inflammation, chronic inflammation involves the cytokines IFN-gamma and IL-12. The radio call signal for chronic inflammation is "gamma-twelve."

questions.question: A 72-year-old man is evaluated for abdominal pain. He reports constant left lower quadrant abdominal pain for the past twelve hours. He is nauseated and has vomited twice. Temperature is 100.1°F. Pulse is 95/min and blood pressure thickening in the sigmoid colon. questions.explanation: Answer D (correct answer): This man has acute diverticulitis, an inflammatory process in a diverticulum of the colon. IL-6 is one of the acute inflammation cytokines (the others are IL-1 and TNF-alpha). Its level rises with acute inflammation. IL-6 stimulates the liver synthesis of acute-phase reactants—proteins whose serum concentrations rise in the setting of inflammation. These include ferritin, fibrinogen, serum amyloid A, C reactive protein, and hepcidin. Albumin is a negative acute-phase reactant. Its level will fall in this man with acute inflammation of the colon.

Many cell types including epithelial cells contain proteins called "NoD-like receptors"(NLRs) within the cytoplasm. These receptors are similar to toll-like receptors which are found on the cell membrane surface. NLRs bind numerous components of necrotic or dying cells including uric acid, excess ATP, or free DNA (collectively called damage-associated molecular patterns or DAMPs). They have also been shown to bind some components of bacteria (called environment and bound to cytoplasmic NLRs. Once activated, many NLRs assemble into a multi-protein complex called the inflammasome. This structure activates the enzyme caspase-1 that generates IL-1 to initiate an inflammatory response. This is sometimes called the "NLR-inflammasome pathway" of initiating inflammation. It may play a role in some autoimmune diseases. Key point: Toll-like receptors are found on cell membranes and within endosomes. NLRs perform a similar function but are intracellular.

questions.question: An 83-year-old woman is evaluated by echocardiography for mild dyspnea on exertion. She has no history of chronic medical disease. Images show evidence of calcification at the annulus of the mitral valve. Her echocardiogram is otherwise normal. Which of the following most likely contributed to this finding?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This woman has mitral annular calcification (MAC), a common incidental finding on echocardiography or other cardiac imaging among older patients. MAC results from endothelial dysfunction and chronic inflammation, leading to dystrophic calcification. It shares many similarities with atherosclerosis, including a higher prevalence with aging. It is almost always asymptomatic, but in rare, severe cases it can impair mitral valve function. This can lead to mitral regurgitation, mitral stenosis, or heart failure.

questions.question: A 54-year-old man is referred for a positron emission tomography (PET) scan. He has a 30-pack-year history of smoking. is administered radio-labeled glucose. PET scanning demonstrates significant glucose uptake in the right upper lobe. Subsequent biopsy of the nodule identified squamous cell carcinoma. Which of the following explains the glucose uptake of this tumor?
questions.explanation:
Answer E (correct answer): In a positron emission tomography (PET) scan, radiolabeled glucose is administered with the patient placed in a scanner to detect radiation emission. One of the most commonly used radiolabeled forms of glucose is 18-fluoro-2-deoxyglucose (FDG). Like all forms of glucose, FDG is taken up in excess by cancer cells. The FDG radiation is detected by the camera and indicates areas of possible malignancy. This technique can be used to distinguish benign from malignant lung lesions since benign lesions will not take up excess glucose. Malignant cells such as those in squamous cell carcinoma metabolize glucose via aerobic glycolysis. Despite the presence of oxygen (i.e., an aerobic environment), cancer cells preferentially metabolize glucose into lactate via glycolysis rather than into pyruvate for the TCA cycle. This is called the Warburg effect and generates less ATP under anaerobic conditions in normal cells. As a result, tumor cells must take up significantly more glucose than normal cells to meet their ATP needs. For this reason, more glucose transporters are found on the surface of cancer cells. Also, more hexokinase is present within cancer cells to trap glucose inside the cell. The overall result is significantly increased glucose uptake, which may be detected by a PET scan.

Answer A (incorrect answer): Most cancer cells do not produce glycogen, and excess glycogen does not explain increased glucose uptake in malignancy.

Answers B and c (incorrect answers): Because cancer cells utilize excess glucose, they are often unable to sustain growth on glucose alone. As a result, they are capable of metabolizing fructose and galactose when glucose supplybecomeslimited. oxidative phosphorylation. Mc M

Answer E (correct answer): Telomerase is found in the vast majority (>9o%) of breast carcinomas. This enzyme stabilizes the ends of chromosomes in replicating cells. The presence of the telomerase enzyme allows malignant cells to divide indefinitely (i.e., to become immortal). Normally, telomerase is only found within fetal cells and germ cells with little or no activity in somatic cells like those of the breast.

Answers C and D (incorrect answers): Many breast cancers express the progesterone receptor and the estrogen receptor. Overall, about 75 to 80% of invasive breast carcinomas are positive for one of these hormone receptors. questions.question: A 55-year-old man is referred for a screening chest x-ray due to a 20-pack-year history of smoking. A 2-centimeter pulmonary nodule is identified in the left lower lobe. Surgical excision is performed. Grossly, the lesion is tan-colored, well- encapsulated, and firm. Microscopic examination reveals a heterogeneous collection hyaline cartilage, fat, respiratory epithelial cells, and smooth muscle. Which of the following would most likely have occurred if this lesion had not been removed?
questions.explanation:
Answer C (correct answer): This man has a pulmonary hamartoma, a benign lesion that is responsible for about 10%of pulmonary nodules. They are the most common benign tumor of the lung. Hamartomas contain disorganized but normal tissue from the organ in which they are found. In the case of lung hamartomas, these lesions typically contain fat, epithelial cells, fibrous tissue, and cartilage. In some cases, calcification is present which helps with identification by x-ray or CT scan. Hamartomas grow slowly over years and carry an excellent prognosis which is why they are classified as benign.

Answer D (correct answer): Ovarian serous cystadenocarcinoma is a malignant form of epithelial cell ovarian tumor. The management of ovarian cancer is complex and depends on the staging of the cancer. Generally, the initial treatment of ovarian epithelial cell cancer is total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo- remove both ovaries and the uterus. If the tumor has spread beyond the ovaries and reproductive system, cytoreductive surgery, also known as "tumor debulking," is often performed. This involves removal of tumor from the peritoneal cavity and adjacent structures. Adjuvant chemotherapy is then administered, which may include a platinum-based regimen, commonly paclitaxel plus carboplatin or cisplatin. and bilateral oophorectomy are the first step in treatment.
