questions.explanation: Explanation Emergency Medicine > Trauma > Chest Trauma Flail Chest • Multiple rib fractures from massive chest trauma · Segment of rib cage detaches ("floats") ▪ Two fractures in each broken rib Blunt Force · At least three ribs with two fractures · Decreased or absent breath sounds ·Paradoxical motion of flail segment • Flail segment willsink with inspiration · Budge with exhalation RECT ESUS 1111 Case courtesyof Drlan Bickle,Radiopaedia.org,rl D 37961 Answer A (correct answer): This patient has flail chest,which is a paradoxical movement of the chest wall when in the setting of massive chest trauma when multiple adjacent ribs each have at least two fractures. Patients present with decreased or absent breath sounds on the affected side and abnormal movement of the damaged ribs. Because the flail segment moves independently from the rest of the rib cage, it sinks in with inspiration and is pushed out with expiration. Patients usually also have an associated pulmonary contusion. Treatment includes oxygen administration, pain control with intravenous opiates or a nerve block, and hospital admission to monitor the patient's respiratory status. Pulmonary contusion can cause delayed onset of hypoxia, sometimes requiring noninvasive positive pressure ventilation or intubation and mechanical ventilation. Pneumothorax is the presence of air in the pleural space, which is trauma. Smoking is a risk factor and it is more common in tall, thin males. Treatment of a large pneumothorax, in which greater than 20% of the lung is collapsed, is tube thoracostomy where a tube is placed into the pleural space to evacuate the air collection. The tube is placed in the fourth or fifth intercostal space at the midaxillary line, and it is inserted over the rib. When a thoracostomy tube is successfully placed, there may be an audible rush of air through the tube. The tube is attached to a suction system, and a postprocedural chest x-ray is obtained to confirm placement. questions.explanation: Explanation Emergency Medicine>Trauma>Fractures Stress Fractures ·Tiny cracksinbones ·Causedbyrepetitiveforce andoveruse ·Jumping up and down ·Running long distances ·Commonlocations: ·Tibia ·Metatarsals (foot) .Ankle .Femur Answer E(correct answer): This patient has a stress fracture of her second metatarsal. Stress fractures are caused by repetitive stress and overuse; classically this injury affects endurance athletes and military recruits, but it can occur in anyone who suddenly increases their activity level or is engaged in repetitive exercise. Stress fractures are common in the metatarsals of the foot but can also occur in other weight-bearing bones, including the ankle, tibia and femur. This injury is typically a nondisplaced, tiny hairline fracture. It can sometimes be identified by x-ray, but a negative x-ray does not rule out a stress fracture and the diagnosis can be made clinically. If a stress fracture is suspected but the x-ray is negative, a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan may identify an occult fracture; however, advanced imaging is often unnecessary when the clinical presentation is highly suggestive of stress fracture. Treatment is reduced weightbearing, use of a splint or boot and other supportive care measures including rest, ice and analgesia with over-the-counter pain medications. Obesity increases resistance to insulin-mediated peripheral glucose uptake, and central/abdominal obesity appears to be a more significant risk factor than subcutaneous fat. Patients with T 2 DM may be asymptomatic or present with the slow onset of classic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss). This patient has acanthosis nigricans, which are hyperpigmented plaques found on the neck, axillae and intertriginous sites and they are associated with insulin resistance and T 2 DM. This leads to glycosuria and an osmotic diuresis causing volume depletion.Patients present with polyuria, polydipsia(increased thirst), polyphagia (increased hunger), nocturia or nocturnal enuresis and weight loss. T 1 DM is the most common cause of diabetes in children, but it can also occur in young adult patients like this woman.Type 1 diabetescanbe distinguished from type 2 diabetesbased ontheacuteonsetof symptoms,body mass index under 25 kg/m², a personal or family history of autoimmune disease and positive antibodies (including islet cell, insulin, glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) and zinc transporter 8 (Zn T 8) antibodies). Given this patient's acute onset of symptoms, BMI of 23 kg/m²,family history of type 1 diabetes and positive islet cell and insulin antibodies, she is most likely to have type 1 diabetes. The risk of developing T 1 DM is only 0.4% in patients with no family history. Answer C (incorrect answer): Obesity is also not a risk factor for developing type 1 diabetes mellitus. Her fundal height is 28 cm and there is a most appropriate diabetes screening test in this patient?
questions.explanation: Explanation Endocrinology>Diabetes>Diabetes Mellitus Glucose Tolerance Test ·Oralglucoseload administered ·Plasmaglucosemeasured 1-3 hourslater ·Highglucose indicates diabetes ·Oftenusedtoscreenforgestationaldiabetes ·Some insulin resistance normal in pregnancy ·Fasting glucose and A 1 c not reliable ·Need tostudyresponsetoglucoseload fordiagnosis Answer E (correct answer): Universal screening of women in pregnancy for gestational diabetes is performed at hyperosmolar glucose solution, and have serum glucose levels drawn 1, 2 or 3 hours after ingestion. Gestational diabetes is defined as serum glucose ≥ 2 o 0 mg/d L after oral glucose challenge. Pregnancy is associated with increased insulin resistance and gestational diabetes mellitus develops in women whose pancreatic function is insufficient to overcome the insulin resistance. Approximately 6% of women in the United States develop gestational diabetes, and the prevalence has increased over time. Risk factors for gestational diabetes include a family history of diabetes mellitus, previous birth of an infant weighing over 4 kg, multiple gestation and BMI greater than 30 kg/m². Answer A (incorrect answer): Urinalysis is not used to screen for gestational diabetes. A positive urine dipstick not rule out gestational diabetes mellitus. In addition, glycosuria with a normal blood glucose level is common in pregnant women because of reduced reabsorption of glucose, which results in higher rates of urinary excretion. Answer B (incorrect answer): Hemoglobin A 1 C is not used to screen for gestational diabetes as there is no clear threshold for A 1 C in the second and third trimester of pregnancy.

The disease has an insidious onset with an average duration of symptoms of 12 years before diagnosis. Patients present with coarsened facial features, enlarged resistance, visceral organ enlargement (e.g., enlarged thyroid as is seen in this patient), joint pain and cardiovascular disease such as hypertension and left ventricular hypertrophy. In normal patients, a glucose load suppresses GH, but in patients with acromegaly, the serum GH level remains elevated after a glucose load. Transsphenoidal surgical resection is the treatment of choice for patients with growth hormone secreting adenomas. The surgical cure rate approaches 7 o%. The most common complications are recurrent disease and pituitary hormone deficiencies. Surgical resection generally resolves the metabolic abnormalities of acromegaly, butit does not reduce joint pain or bony abnormalities. Premenopausal women with hyperprolactinemia present with infertility, abnormal menses, decreased bone mineral density and, rarely, galactorrhea. Diagnosis of prolactinoma is made based on an elevated serum prolactin level and a pituitarymassonmagneticresonanceimagingofthebrain. Patientswhoaresymptomaticfromprolactinomasmaybe treatedwithadopamineagonistsuchas cabergoline or bromocriptine. These medications mimic the effects of dopamine. This mass effect can cause headaches and visual field deficits like bitemporal hemianopsia due to compression of the optic chiasm. In addition, ACTH is derived from the precursor proopiomelanocortin (POMC), which also gives rise to melanocyte-stimulating hormone (Ms H). questions.question: A 64-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) presents with decreased appetite, cough with rust- colored sputum, shortness of breath, and muscle weakness. After a thirty-year history of daily cigarette smoking and alcohol consumption, he quit both within the last year. His current medications include an inhaled beta agonist and a bronchodilator. He is on day 3 of a 7-day course of prednisone for an acute exacerbation. His weight has decreased 10 Ibs in the last three months. Physical examination reveals dark skin on his face, round cheeks, a fat pad on the back of his neck, multiple bruises, and a barrel chest. Further investigations reveal elevated serum cortisol levels. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this man's condition?
questions.explanation: Explanation Cushing's Syndrome Causes ·ACTH-independent (↓ACTH) .Glucocorticoid therapy ·Adrenaladenoma ACTH-dependent(TACTH) ·Cushing'sdisease(pituitary ACTHsecretingtumor) ·Ectopic ACTH (small cell lung cancer) 。↑ACTH → adrenal hyperplasia → ↑cortisol Answer D (correct answer): This man has small cell lung cancer (SCLC), a highly malignant neuroendocrine lung cancer.The most important risk factor for development of SCLC is cigarette smoking. This man also has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), a lung disease that results in limited airflow and alveolar damage. COPD is a risk factor for lung cancer. Patients with lung cancer present with cough, hemoptysis (blood in sputum or rust-colored sputum), and shortness of breath. Upto 20%of SCLCtumorssecreteadrenocorticotropichormone(Ac TH),whichstimulatesadrenalproductionof cortisol.Increased cortisol levels canlead to Cushing's syndrome.Clinical features of Cushing's syndrome include fat deposition on the cheeks, the base of the neck, and the abdomen, easy bruising, and thin skin. High levels of ACTH lead to increased melanin production, which results in skin hyperpigmentation (most obvious in the palms, soles, and gums). Patients with s CLC who develop Cushing's syndrome present with weight loss, muscle weakness, and metabolic disturbances such as hyperglycemia. At the time of diagnosis of SCLC, most patients have evidence of cancer spread throughout the body (metastasis). The mainstay of treatment is chemotherapy and radiation.Prognosis depends on the extent of local invasion and metastasis atthe time of diagnosis. Answer A (incorrectanswer):While this man is taking the glucocorticoid prednisone,a 3-day course is not sufficient to cause Cushing's syndrome. The clinical features of Cushing's syndrome require months to develop. In addition, this patient has alarm features for lung cancer, including weight loss and hemoptysis. Answers B (incorrect answer): Patients with adrenal adenomas do not present with hemoptysis and respiratory syndrome. They will, however, typically have hypertension and hyperglycemia as a result of elevated cortisol levels.

questions.question: A 39-year-old woman presents with depression, fatigue, and irregular menstrual cycles. Physical examination reveals a blood pressure of 156/92 mmHg, a weight gain of 15 Ibs in 3 months, bruises on her arms and legs, and hair loss. She does not take glucocorticoids and denies any other use of endogenous steroids. Two separate 24-hour urinary cortisol levels are 91 mcg/day
questions.explanation: Explanation Endocrinology(NEW)>Adrenals>Cushing Syndrome Cushing's Syndrome Diagnosis ·Step 1:Establish Cushing's syndrome ·Step 2:Establish cause ·Key test is serum ACTH level ACTH-Dependent Causes ACTH-Independent Causes (High ACTH) (Low ACTH) Steroid therapy Cushing's disease Ectopic ACTH Adrenal adenoma Answer E (correct answer): This woman has Cushing's syndrome, a state of elevated cortisol that has distinct symptoms and signs along with biochemical abnormalities. Common clinical features include fat deposition in the cheeks (moon cheeks) and neck (buffalo hump), supraclavicular fat pads, weight gain, menstrual irregularities, hypertension, bruising, and hyperglycemia. Establishing the diagnosis of Cushing's syndrome requires elevated cortisol levels. She has evidence of elevated cortisol levels based on her elevated urinary cortisol results. This confirms the diagnosis of Cushing's syndrome. The next step is to determine the cause of Cushing's syndrome. The best test is a serum adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). This test distinguishes elevated cortisol levels due to high ACTH secretion (ACTH dependent) from those not due to high ACTH (ACTH independent). High ACTH levels point toward ACTH-secreting tumors, which may occur in the pituitary gland or lungs. Low ACTH levels point toward exogenous steroids (e.g.. prednisonetherapy)oradrenaltumors. Answers A,C,D(incorrectanswers):Late-nightsalivary cortisoltesting,low-dose dexamethasone suppression testing, and early-morning serum cortisol testing are used to establish the diagnosis of Cushing's syndrome. This woman alreadyhasanestablisheddiagnosisbasedonherurinarycortisolresults,sothesetests arenot necessary.

questions.question: A 45-year-old obese woman presents with fractures after a fall. She lost her balance while standing and sustained bilateral forearm fractures. A bone density test reveals a T score of -2.7 (normal between -1 and +1). She is administered 1 mg of dexamethasone at night, followed by a measurement of serum cortisol in the morning. Results show a morning serum cortisol level of 6.2 mcg/dL (normal <1.8 mcg/dL). Serum adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) level is 74 pg/ml (normal 10 to 50 pg/ml). she is administered 8 mg of dexamethasone followed by a measurement of serum cortisol in the morning. Serum cortisol level the morning after administration of dexamethasone is 3.9 mcg/dL (normal <5mcg/dL). which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Explanation Answer C (correct answer): This woman has Cushing's disease, a condition caused by a pituitary tumor that secretes adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). In Cushing's disease, excess ACTH stimulates adrenal release of excess cortisol, resulting in clinical features of Cushing's syndrome. No TE:Signs and symptomsofexcesscortisol =Cushing'ssyndrome;pituitary ACTH-secreting tumor causing Cushing's syndrome = Cushing's disease. Cushing's syndrome affects multiple body systems, including reproductive (abnormal menses), skin (thin skin, bruising, striae), metabolic (hyperglycemia, obesity), cardiovascular (hypertension), neuropsychiatric (depression, mood swings), and musculoskeletal (muscle weakness, osteoporosis). A fall from a standing height that causes bilateral forearm fractures is unusual in a healthy 45-year-old woman. Fractures that occur after minor trauma often indicate underlying bone pathology ("pathologic fractures"). This can occur among patients with diseases affecting the bone matrix, such as cancer, osteoporosis, inherited bone disorders, and infection. Osteoporosis is a common feature of Cushing's syndrome that often presents as a pathological fracture. Cortisol has a catabolic (breakdown) effect on bone. With high cortisol levels, bone breakdown is increased, bone formationis decreased, and less calcium is absorbed from the intestines. Dexamethasone is a glucocorticoid that acts like cortisol in the body. The low-dose dexamethasone suppression test involves administration of 1 mg of dexamethasone at night and measurement of serum cortisol the next morning. In normal patients, morning cortisol levels will be low due to dexamethasone suppression of pituitary ACTH release. This woman's low-dose dexamethasone suppression test shows elevated morning cortisol, indicating that she has Cushing's syndrome. Her ACTH levels are also elevated, indicating that the cause of her Cushing's syndrome is due to overproduction of ACTH (an "ACTH-dependent" cause). The high-dose dexamethasone suppression test involves 8 mg of dexamethasone at night and measurement of serum cortisol the next morning.This test distinguishes pituitary ACTH-secreting tumors from ectopic(usually pulmonary) ACTH-secreting tumors. A pituitary tumor will respond to the high-dose test with suppression of ACTH release,while anectopic ACTH-secreting tumor will not.This patient's high-dose dexamethasone serum cortisol was no longer elevated after high-dose dexamethasone). This result suggests a pituitary tumor. Answer A (incorrect answer): Pseudo-Cushing's syndrome (also called physiologic Cushing's syndrome) is a condition of elevated cortisol levels due to a systemic disease and is not related to the hypothalamic-pituitary- adrenal (HPA) axis. Systemic conditions, including pregnancy, severe obesity, and poorly controlled diabetes, canleadtoelevatedcortisoldespiteanormal HPAaxis.Patientsmayhavesomefeaturesof Cushing's syndrome, such as the weight gain and fat deposits, but rarely have skin problems(easy bruising, thin, friable skin) or muscle disorders (weakness, atrophy). This woman has pathologic fractures due to osteoporosis at a young age, which suggests a true underlying endocrine disorder, not pseudo-Cushing's syndrome. Answers B and E (incorrect answers): Adrenal hyperplasia and adrenal adenomas are ACTH-independent causes

questions.question: A 29-year-old man presents with weight gain, new-onset hypertension, and new-onset hyperglycemia. Further investigation demonstrates a right-sided adrenal mass. He is given ketoconazole for medical therapy and develops bilateral breast enlargement. This man's breast changes are due to inhibition of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Explanation Endocrinology(NEw)>Adrenals>Cushing Syndrome Ketoconazole ·Antifungal ·Blocks ergosterol synthesis in fungi ·Alsoblocks 1 st step in cortisol synthesis ·Desmolase(side chain cleavage) Can be used to treat Cushing's syndrome Also potent inhibitor androgen synthesis · Key side effect: gynecomastia Desmolase Ho Pregnenolone Cholesterol Cortisol Answer D (correct answer): This man has Cushing's syndrome due to an adrenal adenoma, a cortisol-producing adrenal tumor. Approximately 1 o% of patients with Cushing's syndrome will have adrenal adenomas as a cause. Patients with adrenal adenomas commonly present with cardiovascular and metabolic disturbances of Cushing's syndrome, such as hypertension and diabetes mellitus. Ketoconazole is an antifungal agent that is used to treat Cushing's syndrome. This drug blocks the conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone by inhibiting the enzyme desmolase. This reduces production of adrenal cortisol. Ketoconazole also inhibits the synthesis of testosterone. With ketoconazole therapy, a decrease in androgens leads to a relative excess in estrogen effects. (Estrogens are present in males, but normally androgen effects dominate.) This can cause breast enlargement (gynecomastia), decreased libido, and impotence. Answer A (incorrect answer): Inhibition of androgen breakdown results in increased circulating androgen levels.

In addition, they should have a hemoglobin A 1 C level measured every 6 to 12 months and a dilated eye examination, dental examination and comprehensive foot examination annually. questions.question: A 38-year-old male presents for a follow-up visit. He was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus one year ago after presenting with polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss and a hemoglobin A1C of 8.2%. He was treated with lifestyle modification along with metformin and glyburide. His BMI is 27 kg/m?. He is afebrile with a heart rate of 70 beats/min and a blood 6.4%. This patient's reduction in hemoglobin A1C is most likely to reduce the risk of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Explanation Endocrinology>Diabetes>Diabetes Complications Diabetes Mellitus Benefitsofloweringbloodglucose ·Severallarge,randomizedtrialsofintensiveglycemiccontrol ·Comparisonsof lowerversushigher A 1 ctargets Type 2 diabetes ·Lowerriskofmicrovascularcomplications ·Mostly retinopathy and nephropathy ·Little impact onmacrovascular disease(MI,stroke) ·ACCORD trial:A 1 c 6.0 to 6.5%→increased mortality ·Type 1 diabetes ·Lowerriskofmostcomplications ·Microvascularand macrovascular Answer C (correct answer): This patient has type 2 diabetes mellitus (T 2 DM), which is characterized by hyperglycemia, insulin resistance and impaired insulin secretion. The complications of T 2 DM are divided into macrovascular (cardiovascular, cerebrovascular and peripheral arterial disease) and microvascular (retinopathy, nephropathy and neuropathy). In patients with T 2 DM, antidiabetic drugs are used to lower blood glucose levels with the goal of preventing diabetes complications. Of note, tight glycemic control reduces the risk of microvascularbutnotmacrovasculardisease. In terms of microvascular disease, several clinical trials including the United Kingdom Prospective Diabetes Study (UKPDS), the Action in Diabetes and Vascular Disease (ADVANCE) study and the Action to Control Cardiovascular Risk in Diabetes (ACCORD) study found reduced rates of microvascular complications with intensive glycemic control, especially retinopathy and nephropathy. This patient would expect a reduced risk of retinopathy as his blood sugar control improves. Answers A, B, D and E (incorrect answers): Several studies of macrovascular complications in type 2 diabetes mellitus failed to show reduced rates of complications with intensive glycemic control. questions.question: A 61-year-old male with type 2 diabetes presents for a semi-annual endocrinology follow-up. He was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes ten years ago when he was hospitalized for hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state. Other medical history includes tobacco or alcohol use. His father had a stroke at age 78. His medications include metformin, glyburide, amlodipine and atorvastatin. His BMI is 27 kg/m2. He is afebrile with a heart rate of 70 beats/min and a blood pressure of 127/79 mmHg. and sensation in his feet. Laboratory evaluation reveals a hemoglobin A1C of 7.3%, an albumin/creatinine ratio of 22 mg/g creatinine and an LDL cholesterol of 98 mg/dL. which of the following will be the most likely cause of death for this patient?

Complications of diabetes mellitus include coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular disease, kidney disease, neuropathy and ocular disease. The most common cause of death in patients with type 2 diabetes (T 2 DM) is coronary artery disease (CAD), including myocardial infarction. Like smoking, hyperlipidemia and hypertension, diabetes is an independent risk factor for CAD. The risk of CAD is significantly increased in patients with diabetes compared to patients without diabetes. Answer A (incorrect answer): Hypoglycemia may occur in T 2 DM but is less common compared to type 1 diabetes and is not a leading cause of death. Hypoglycemia in T 2 DM is often related to use of hypoglycemic in patients with T 2 DM. complication of T 2 DM caused by markedly elevated serum glucose. questions.question: A 52-year-old woman with a history of bipolar disorder and sarcoidosis presents with complaints of increased thirst and institution and is on lithium for mood stabilization. On examination, she has a flat affect and is poorly responsive to questions. Laboratory results show serum glucose of 105 mg/dL, plasma sodium 136 mEq/L, plasma osmolality 270 mOsm/kg (normal: 275-295 mOsm/kg), and urine specific gravity 1.003. After an 8-hour water deprivation test, the urine specific gravity is 1.015. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation: Explanation Renal (NEW)> Electrolytes > Diabetes Insipidus Answer C (correct answer): This patient has primary polydipsia, also known as psychogenic polydipsia, which is characterized by excessive water intake, usually due to psychiatric causes. The maximum amount of water the kidneys can excrete in a day is approximately 15 liters. Water intake above this amount leads to a water overload state, diluting plasma sodium and reducing plasma osmolality. In response, the kidneys excrete dilute urine (mostly water) in an attempt to restore normal plasma osmolality. Her lab results show low plasma sodium and low plasma osmolality, consistent with dilution from excessive water intake. The low urine specific gravity indicates a normal response to the low plasma osmolality, as the kidneys are trying to excrete excess water. After water deprivation (which stimulates ADH release), the urine osmolality increases, indicating that the kidneys are capable of concentrating urine. This finding rules out diabetes insipidus (DI) and confirms the diagnosis of primary polydipsia. The most appropriate treatment for primary polydipsia is fluid restriction, which eliminates excessive water intake and reduces polyuria and polydipsia. Answer A (incorrect answer): Amiloride is used for lithium-induced nephrogenic DI by inhibiting the entry of lithium into renal cells. This patient does not have lithium-induced nephrogenic DI. Answer B (incorrect answer): Desmopressin is used to treat central diabetes insipidus, where there is a deficiency of ADH. In primary polydipsia, the problem is not a lack of ADH but excessive water intake. Desmopressin would not be helpful in this patient. In central DI, patients present with polyuria, polydipsia, normal or increased plasma osmolality, and low urinary osmolality (less than 300 m Osm/kg). Administration of the ADH analog, desmopressin, increases urinary osmolality significantly in central DI as seen in this case. questions.explanation: Explanation Endocrinology>Diabetes>Diabetic Ketoacidosis Diabetic Ketoacidosis Treatmentmonitoring ·Closemonitoringofserumglucoseandelectrolytes ·Whenglucose approaches 200 mg/d Ladd 5%dextrosetosalineinfusion ·Allows continued insulin infusion to suppressketones ·Avoidshypoglycemia ·Can also decrease insulin infusionrate ·DKA resolves when: ·Anion gap normalizes(less than 12 mEq/L) ·Beta-hydroxybutyrate absent(if available) ·Patient can eat Resolved Answer E (correct answer): This patient has diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) in the setting of known type 1 diabetes mellitus. DKA results from insulin deficiency. Without insulin the body is unable to use glucose for energy, so it begins to break down adipose tissue to meet its energy needs. The resulting free fatty acids are broken down to ketones, which results in ketosis and metabolic acidosis. There are three major ketone bodies in the circulation and beta-hydroxybutyrate, which can be measured in serum, is the dominant acid in patients with DKA. Glycogen and proteins are catabolized to glucose, and the resulting hyperglycemia leads to osmotic diuresis and dehydration.DKA is characterized by a serum glucose over 250 mg/d L,a pH of less than 7.3, a serum bicarbonate level less than 18 mEq/L, elevated serum ketones and dehydration. The initial treatment of DKA includes intravenous (IV) fluids, IV insulin and potassium. Patients with DKA are generally profoundly potassium depleted, yet the serum potassium is often elevated initially. This is because hyperosmolality and insulin deficiency cause a shift of potassium out of cells and into the extracellular fluid. Insulin drives potassium back into cells which uncovers the true hypokalemia. When the serum glucose approaches 250 mg/d L, dextrose should be added to the IV fluids. This prevents hypoglycemia and allows continued infusion of insulin to suppress ketone production. In general, resolution of hyperglycemia, normalization of bicarbonate level and closure of the anion gap is sufficient to stop insulin infusion. questions.question: An 18-month-old male presents for a well visit. His parents are concerned that he is a very picky eater. He eats mostly fruit and consistently refuses meat, eggs, milk, vegetables and cereal. He was exclusively breast-fed until 10 months of age. He takes no medications. His family history is significant for a father with hypertension and a mother with celiac disease. His length and weight are at the 3rd percentile for age and his head circumference is at the 3Oth percentile. He is afebrile with a open anterior fontanelle, frontal bossing, thickened wrists and bilateral bowing of the legs. Bilateral wrist x-rays reveal fraying and cupping of the distal radius bilaterally with decreased bone mineralization. which of the following are expected in this patient for alkaline phosphatase, serum PTH and 25-OH vitamin D?
questions.explanation: Explanation Endocrinology>Other Topics>Hypoparathyroidism and Vitamin D Vitamin D Deficiency Rickets Bone disorders .Osteomalacia ·Softening of bones ·↓vitamin D→low calcium→↑PTH→↓bone mineralization ·Bone pain or tenderness .Fractures ·Rickets ·Occurs in children Deficientmineralization of growth plate ·Bone pain ·Distal forearm/kneemost affected(rapidgrowth) ·Bowing of femur/tibia(classic X-rayfinding) Answer B(correctanswer):Thischildlikelyhasnutritionalricketscausedbyinadequateintakeofcalciumand vitamin D. His risk factors include a restricted diet that is low in vitamin D, a history of exclusive breastfeeding and the possibility, given his family history, of undiagnosed celiac disease. Risk factors for nutritional rickets include maternal vitamin D deficiency during pregnancy, exclusive breastfeeding, low sun exposure and malabsorption from conditions such as such as celiac disease or cystic fibrosis. Patients with rickets present with failure to thrive, delayed closure of the anterior fontanelle, frontal bossing, craniotabes (soft skull bones), swelling of the wrists and bowed legs. X-rays reveal widening of the epiphyseal plates, fraying and cupping of the growth plates and decreased bone mineralization.

She is afebrile with a heart rate of 125 beats/min (normal). Physical
questions.explanation: Explanation Endocrinology>Other Topics>Hypoparathyroidismand Vitamin D Vitamin D Breast feeding ·Breastmilklowinvitamin D ·Evenifmotherhassufficientlevels ·Mostinfantsgetlittlesun exposure ·Exclusivelybreastfedinfants→supplementation ·400 international units (drops) ·Beginning a few days afterbirth Answer D (correct answer): This exclusively breastfed infant should receive 4 oo international units daily of vitamin D supplementation beginning within a few days after birth. Vitamin D supplementation is required in newborns because of the low vitamin D content of breast milk, lack of cutaneous vitamin D synthesis from sun exposure and the risk of rickets among exclusively breastfed infants. Supplementation should be continued until the infant drinks at least 33 ounces of vitamin D-fortified formula or vitamin D-fortified cow's milk, and the child is older than 12 months of age. Infants should receive either vitamin D 2 (ergocalciferol) or vitamin D 3 (cholecalciferol). Most infants receive ergocalciferol because it is available in a liquid formulation that can be mixed with a small amount of breast milk. Answer A (incorrect answer): Iron supplementation with ferrous sulfate is recommended beginning at 4 months of age in exclusively breastfed infants. This should be continued until infants are eating two or more servings of iron-fortified infant cereal daily. Answer B (incorrect answer): Fluoride supplementation with sodium fluoride is recommended beginning at 6 months of age for infants who consume ready-to-feed formula as the sole source of nutrients and fluid intake or who are exclusively breastfed. Once teeth are present, topical fluoride can be applied to all children every three to six months to promote mineralization of the dental enamel. Answer C (incorrect answer): Calcium supplementation with calcium carbonate is not necessary in exclusively breastfed infants.

Other risk factors for vitamin D deficiency include decreased vitamin D intake (e.g.. metabolism (e.g., phenytoin) and decreased vitamin D synthesis. Vitamin D deficiency may be defined as a serum 25-OH vitamin D level less than 20 ng/m L, although some guidelinesrecommendthatvitamin Dlevelsbekeptabove 30 ng/m L.25-OHvitamin Disthestorageformof vitamin D, and the levels reflect a combination of dietary intake and sun exposure. Adult patients with vitamin D deficiency are at increased risk of hypocalcemia, osteoporosis, fractures and, in severe deficiency, osteomalacia.Pediatricpatientsarealsoatriskofhypocalcemia andosteomalaciaandmaydeveloprickets. Vitamin Ddeficiencyresultsindecreasedintestinalabsorptionofcalciumandphosphateanddecreased resorption of calcium and phosphate from bone. In addition, chronic vitamin D deficiency is also associated with an increase in the serum parathyroid hormone (PTH) level which exacerbates bone loss. Patients who do nothavesevereliver orkidneydiseasearetreated withsupplemental vitamin D 2(ergocalciferol)orvitamin D 3 (cholecalciferol)plus oral calcium supplementationfor several months. questions.question: A 45-year-old female presents for a post-operative follow-up visit after a thyroidectomy for localized thyroid cancer. She reports intermittent numbness around the mouth, but denies muscle cramps or twitching, tingling, mood changes, abdominal pain or diarrhea. She is otherwise healthy and not taking any medications. She is afebrile with a heart rate of 70 beats/min decreased sensation of her face. Laboratory evaluation demonstrates a serum calcium of 7.8 mg/dL. which of the following is the most appropriate management of this patient's symptoms?
questions.explanation: Explanation Hypoparathyroidism Managementofhypocalcemia ·Goal:lownormal serumcalcium ·Normalrangefortotalcalcium:8.5 to 10.0 mEq/L ·Acuteorhighly symptomatic Tetanyzuresrolonged Qtinrvl ·Often post-op after thyroidectomy or other surgery ·Intravenous calcium(calcium gluconate) ·Chronicorminimalsymptoms ·Oral calcium and vitamin D supplementation ·Rare cases: recombinant human PTH (teriparatide) Answer D (correct answer): This patient has hypocalcemia caused by accidental surgical excision of the parathyroid glands which may happen during total thyroidectomy. Hypoparathyroidism occurs in up to 20% of patients following surgery for thyroid cancer. Patients with mild hypocalcemia present with paresthesia around the lips, mouth, hands and feet. Patients with more severe hypocalcemia may develop muscle twitching, muscle cramps,tetanyorseizures. When hypoparathyroidism is the cause of hypocalcemia, patients require treatment with both calcium and vitamin D. Hypoparathyroidism leads to low serum calcium and decreased activation of vitamin D to its active form, calcitriol, which is also called 1,25 OH vitamin D. Patients with hypoparathyroidism require calcium to resolve symptoms of hypocalcemia and calcitriol to replenish vitamin D activity. Patients with mild symptoms of hypocalcemia, such as this patient with perioral numbness, can be treated with oralcalciumcarbonateorcalciumcitratepluscalcitriol. Answer A (incorrect answer): Intravenous calcium gluconate is indicated for the acute management of severe, symptomatic hypocalcemia. These patients present with muscle twitching, muscle cramps, tetany or seizures. This patient has only mild hypocalcemia, so oral replacement with calcium carbonate and calcitriol are appropriate. Answer B (incorrect answer): Calcitriol alone would not improve this patient's symptoms of hypocalcemia. She shouldbetreatedwithbothcalciumandvitamin D. Answer C (incorrect answer):Oral calcium supplementation is only transiently effective in patients with hypoparathyroidism, unless combined with vitamin D. Active vitamin D (calcitriol) allows for normal absorption of oral calcium. Answer E and F (incorrect answers): Ergocalciferol is the inactive form of vitamin D 2, and cholecalciferol is the inactive form of vitamin D 3. The active form of vitamin D, calcitriol, should be used for the treatment of this limited.For thisreason,repletionwith theactiveformofvitamin D,calcitriol,is preferred.Supplementation

questions.question: A 50-year-old man is seen for his annual physical. He denies headaches, difficulty breathing, chest pain, constipation or joint pain. He was diagnosed with Hodgkin's lymphoma at 19 years of age and treated with chemotherapy and radiation. He smokes 1 pack of cigarettes per day and denies alcohol or drug use. He has Hashimoto's thyroiditis that is treated with Fine needle aspiration reveals large, empty-appearing nuclei with central clearing and psammoma bodies consistent with papillary thyroid carcinoma. which of the following is the most significant risk factor for this patient's condition?
questions.explanation: Explanation Endocrinology>Thyroid Gland>Thyroid Nodules Papillary Carcinoma ·Mostcommonformthyroidcancer(~80%) ·Increasedriskwithpriorradiationexposure ·Childhood chest radiation formediastinal malignancy Papillary Carcinoma ·Survivors ofatomicbomb detonation Japan) ·Nuclear power plant accidents(Chernobyl) ·Median age at diagnosis is 51 years ·Presents asthyroidnodule ·Sometimes identified on imaging(CT/MRI) ·Diagnosismadeafterfineneedle aspiration(FNA) Answer A (correct answer): This patient has papillary thyroid cancer, the most common form of thyroid cancer in the United States. The most significant risk factors are a history of radiation exposure (either from childhood cancer treatment or environmental exposure) and a family history of thyroid cancer.Patients are most commonly asymptomatic and present with a palpable thyroid nodule or are diagnosed incidentally following a findings that are concerning for thyroid cancer include irregular margins, microcalcifications and hypoechoic (dark) nodules with central vascularity. Surgical resection (lobectomy or total thyroidectomy) is the primary treatment for patients with papillary thyroid cancer. Postoperatively, patients may also need radioactive iodine and thyroid hormone suppression. Answer B (incorrect answer): Hashimoto's thyroiditis is not a risk factor for papillary thyroid cancer, but it is associated with an increased risk of primary thyroid lymphoma. Answer C (incorrect answer): Male sex is not associated with an increased risk of papillary thyroid cancer. The usual female-to-male ratio of papillary thyroid cancer is 2.5:1, with most of the female preponderance occurring duringthefourthandfifthdecadesoflife.

Risk factors include previous cholecystectomy and terminal ileum resection, both of which are associated with decreased bile acid absorption in the small intestine.The presence of excessbile acids in the colon leads to increasing mucosal permeability,colonic water secretion and decreased colon transit time. Treatment is with the bile acid sequestrant cholestyramine. This drug binds bile acids in the intestine to form an insoluble complex that is excreted in the stool. questions.explanation: Explanation Gastroenterology>Other Topics>Diarrhea Clostridioidesdifficile Colitis Treatment ·Non-severe:ORALvancomycinorfidaxomicin ·Severe orrecurrentdisease: ·Oralvancomycin orfidaxomicin ·Stool transplant(oral orrectal) ·Fulminant disease ·Oralvancomycin plusmetronidazole ·Surgery (colectomy) Answer B (correct answer): This patient has fulminant Clostridioides difficile colitis (also known as severe, complicated C. difficile infection). Risk factors include recent antibiotic use, advanced age, hospitalization and chronic proton pump inhibitor use. Patients with C. diff present with watery diarrhea, abdominal pain and also have fever and leukocytosis. Fulminant C. difficile is characterized by a white blood cell count greater than 15,0 o 0 cells/m L, a serum creatinine of at least 1.5 mg/d L, elevated serum lactate, shock and hypotension. Diagnosis is made with a stool antigen test which detects C.difficile toxin.The treatment of fulminant C.diff includes oral vancomycin and IV metronidazole. Complications of fulminant disease include toxic megacolon, which is characterized by loss of colon contractility,intestinal dilation and distension,bloody diarrhea and persistent shock. If ileus is present fecal microbiota transplant (rectally administered) may be considered. Patients with toxic megacolon require nasogastric decompression and may require surgery. Answer A(incorrect answer):Ten days of oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin are the treatment of choice for patients with mild C. difficile infections. Mild infections are characterized by a white blood cell count less than 15,0 o 0 cells/m L and a serum creatinine less than 1.5 mg/d L.This patient has a severe infection and needs more aggressive treatment. Answer C (incorrect answer): Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) refers to instillation of processed stool collected from a healthy donor into the intestinal tract of a patient with Clostridioides difficile. FMT is generally safe;mild to moderate adverse events (such as abdominal discomfort) are usually self-limited.There is a risk of typically used in patients with recurrent C. difficile infections, usually after the third recurrence. It can also be considered in a patient with fulminant C. difficile with the presence of ileus. This patient has not had recurrent C. difficile infections and he had a normal abdominal x-ray so FMT would not be appropriate. Answer D(incorrect answer):Oral budesonideis a steroid that is used as anadjunctive agent inpatients with ulcerative colitis. It depresses the activity of inflammatory mediators (such as prostaglandins). Side effects are uncommon but include decreased bone mineral density and suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis.

Patients with bacterial gastroenteritis present with high fever, abdominal pain and gross blood or mucus in the stool. Laboratory evaluation includes stool culture, fecal leukocytes and Escherichia Coli 0157:H 7 and Shiga toxin testing. Empiric antibiotics are indicated in cases of acute diarrhea that have clinical features suggestive of a possible bacterial cause. This includes patients with severe symptoms (fever, more than six stools per day, hypovolemia, bloody or mucoid stools) and in patients at increased risk of complications (immunocompromised). This patient is considered immunocompromised given her methotrexate treatment. Treatment options for acute diarrhea in these select patients with severe symptoms, or with risk for more severe disease, include azithromycin or fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin). Empiric therapy for community-acquired acute diarrhea may reduce the duration of symptoms by one to two days. Patients with more severe infections present with profuse diarrhea, dehydration, elevated white blood cell counts and may have an elevated creatinine. Risk factors include recent antibiotic use, hospitalization and chronic proton pump inhibitor use. questions.explanation: Explanation Gastroenterology>Intestines> Colorectal Disease Sigmoid Volvulus Management ·Immediate surgery if signs of peritonitis ·Mostpatientstreatedwithendoscopicdetorsion ·Sigmoidoscopy to untwist colon ·Restores bowel flow ·Protects blood supply Large bowel (colon) Sigmoidoscope Answer B(correct answer):This patienthas a sigmoid volvulus caused by an air-filled loop of the sigmoid colon twisting around its mesentery. It is a common cause of large bowel obstruction and occurs most commonly in male patients older than 70 years of age. Patients present with slowly progressing abdominal pain, abdominal distension and constipation and frequently have symptoms for three to five days before presentation. Diagnosis is made with abdominal x-ray or computed tomography (CT). X-ray findings include a U-shaped distended colon (known as the "coffee bean sign"), which is present in 60% of cases. CT scan is more sensitive and findings include a whirl pattern, caused by the dilated sigmoid colon around its mesocolon and vessels, and a bird-beak appearance of the afferent and efferent colonic segments. Treatment, if there is no evidence of peritonitis, is with endoscopic detorsion, which uses sigmoidoscopy to untwist the colon, restore bowel flow and protect the blood supply to the colon. Surgical resection of the affected portion of bowel should be performed, evenif endoscopic detorsion is successful,to avoidrecurrence. Answer A (incorrect answer): Immediate surgical repair is indicated in patients with intestinal perforation and peritonitis. These patients present with fever, tachycardia, hypotension, abdominal guarding, rigidity and rebound tenderness. This patient's presentation is not suggestive of perforation. patients with Ogilvie's syndrome (acute colonic pseudo-obstruction). Neostigmine works by increasing colonic motility. Side effects include bradycardia, hypotension, seizures, restlessness, tremor, bronchoconstriction, nausea,vomiting, salivation, diarrhea, sweating and abdominal cramps.Neostigmine is contraindicated in patients with a mechanical intestinal obstruction. He reports weight loss of 4 pounds in the past month. He denies fever or dyspnea. Vital signs include temperature of 98.6°F, pulse of 68/min, respiratory rate of 12/min and blood pressure of 140/82 biopsy shows squamous cell carcinoma. This malignancy affects the proximal esophagus. In addition to smoking and alcohol, dietary factors are the major risk factors, particularly consumption of foods containing N-nitroso compounds, such as cured meats. Esophageal adenocarcinoma, on the other hand, occurs in the distal esophagus, and arises from metaplasia (Barrett's esophagus) related to long standing gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). longstanding GERD. This is a known risk factor for esophageal adenocarcinoma but is not associated with squamous cell carcinoma. Answer C (incorrect answer): GERD is a risk factor for esophageal adenocarcinoma, which affects the distal esophagus, but is not associated with squamous cell carcinoma, which arises proximally. She denies fever, but does complain of nausea, vomiting and decreased appetite. She is otherwise healthy, and her only medication is an oral contraceptive. She has two dogs and a turtle at home. She is afebrile with a heart rate of 85 beats/min and a blood no abdominal distension, rebound tenderness or guarding. Laboratory evaluation is shown below. Abdominal ultrasound reveals a 10-cm anechoic, smooth, round cyst in the right lobe of the liver with central necrosis and wall calcifications.
questions.explanation: Explanation Gastroenterology> Liver >Liver Masses Hydatid Liver Cyst ·Echinococcusgranulosus ·Eggs shed in dog stool (dogs are hosts) Echinococcus ·Fecal-oral ingestion of eggs ·Large cysts:hepatomegaly,RUQpain ·Canrupture ·Usuallyidentified byultrasound features ·Treatment:albendazole ·Drainage requiredfor large cysts Answer C (correct answer): This patient has a hydatid liver cyst caused by infection with the tapeworm Echinococcus granulosus. The initial phase of primary infection is always asymptomatic, and the clinical presentation depends on the site and size of the cysts. In patients with liver involvement, the right lobe is involved in 85% of cases, and symptoms develop when the cyst is greater than 10 cm in diameter. Symptomatic patients present with hepatomegaly along with right upper quadrant pain, nausea and vomiting. Laboratory evaluation is frequently normal, but may also demonstrate leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and eosinophilia. Abdominal ultrasound reveals an anechoic, smooth, round cyst in the right lobe of the liver with central necrosis and wall calcifications. Definitive diagnosis is made with cyst sampling and either serologic or antigen testing. Treatment is with a combination of surgical or percutaneous drainage and albendazole. Answer A(incorrectanswer):Chemoembolizationisnotusedinthetreatmentof Echinococcusgranulosus infections. It is used in patients with metastatic or locally advanced hepatocellular carcinoma to decrease pain and obstructive symptoms. Answer B (incorrect answer): Oral contraceptives are not a risk factor for Echinococcus granulosus infections.

questions.question: A 60-year-old female is evaluated for abdominal pain and decreased appetite. She reports occasional dizziness that resolves after drinking orange juice. She has lost 10 Ibs in the last three months. She lived and worked in Southeast Asia from age 25 to 55 and had an acute hepatitis A infection six years ago. She has hyperlipidemia treated with atorvastatin and has taken low- dose aspirin daily for 10 years because she read that it could prevent heart attacks. Family history is significant for her father dying of an MI at age 49. She is afebrile with a heart rate of 80 beats/min and a blood pressure of 131/77 mmHg. Physical ng/mL. Abdominal computed tomography with contrast reveals a 4-cm mass in the liver and liver biopsy confirms the diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma. Patients frequently present with metastatic disease and Hc C has a five-year survival rate of 18 percent. It is usually associated with chronic liver disease, including cirrhosis of any etiology, hepatitis B and C, hemochromatosis and a-1 antitrypsin deficiency. Other risk factorsfor Hc Cincludealcoholuse,tobaccouse,obesity,nonalcoholicliverdiseaseandcertainenvironmental toxins. Exposure is uncommon in the United States, because of agricultural screening programs, but it may occur in some non-industrialized regions such as Southeast Asia where testing is less commonly performed. Dietary consumptionof aflatoxinsis anestablished riskfactorfor Hc C. Patients with Hc C present with upper abdominal pain, weight loss, early satiety or a palpable mass in the upper abdomen. Other symptoms include hypoglycemia (caused by the tumor's increased metabolic demands), erythrocytosis and hypercalcemia. Laboratory abnormalities include non-specific elevations in AST and ALT and elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein(AFP). Diagnosis is confirmed by liver biopsy.Treatment may include surgical resection, radiofrequency ablation, radiation therapy, systemic therapy and chemoembolization; although even with treatment, prognosis is poor. Patients with cirrhosis are at significantly increased risk of HCC and should be screened every six months with a liver ultrasound and serum AFP level. develop Hc C secondary to increased rates of chronic hepatitis, more frequent exposure to environmental toxins and the protective effects of estrogen. questions.explanation: Explanation Gastroenterology>Intestines>Small Bowel Disease Appendicitis Diagnosis ·Diagnosedbyhistory/exam,CTscanorultrasound ·Children withclassicfindings: directlyto surgery ·Ultrasonographyused in other cases ·Adultswithclassicfindings:CTscan ·Pregnant women:ultrasound ·Supportive evidence Most patients havemild ↑WBC ·Appendicitisunlikelywith normal WBC encountered during pregnancy. The incidence is highest in the 2 nd trimester and the diagnosis is frequently missed in pregnant women because of the high prevalence of abdominal discomfort, anatomic changes related quadrant pain (frequently dull pain), nausea and vomiting. Non-classic symptoms include diarrhea, heartburn, flatulence and irregular bowel movements. Physical examination findings include rebound tenderness, abdominal guarding and rectal tenderness. The most appropriate initial imaging in pregnant women with suspected appendicitis is abdominal ultrasound (US). Advantages include ease of performance and lack of ionizing radiation or IV contrast. Disadvantages include the gravid uterus altering the location of the appendix, poor visualization of the appendix and compression of the appendix, particularly in the third trimester. Us findings may include a non-compressible blind-ended tubular structure in the right lower quadrant with a maximal diameter greater than 6 mm. The treatment of pregnant patients with appendicitis is appendectomy. Answer A (incorrect answer): Abdominal MRI is used in pregnant women whose Us is inconclusive and in older children who can cooperate with the procedure. Advantages include lack of ionizing radiation or IV contrast, but theappendixis notidentifiedinupto 40%ofcasesand theremaybeadelayinobtaining MRI. He reports that the pain started yesterday and is present in the right lower quadrant. He also reports two episodes of vomiting, but no diarrhea. He is overweight with a BMI of 29 and is not taking any medications. His temperature is 100.8°F, heart rate is 95 involuntary guarding. questions.explanation: Explanation Gastroenterology>Intestines>Small Bowel Disease Appendicitis Diagnosis ·Diagnosed by history/exam,CTscan orultrasound ·Childrenwithclassicfindings:directlytosurgery ·Ultrasonography used in other cases ·Adultswith classicfindings:CT scan ·Pregnantwomen:ultrasound ·Supportive evidence Most patients havemild↑WBC ·Appendicitis unlikely with normal WBC Answer A (correct answer): This patient has appendicitis, which is an acute inflammation of the appendix caused by nonspecific obstruction of the appendiceal lumen. It occurs most commonly in males in the second and third decade of life. Patients present with anorexia, periumbilical pain that migrates to the right lower quadrant, nausea and vomiting. Physical examination findings include right lower quadrant tenderness, a positive Rovsing sign (pain in the RLQ with palpation of the left side of the abdomen), the iliopsoas sign (RLQ pain with passive right hip extension) and the obturator sign (RLQ pain with flexion and internal rotation of right hip). The most appropriate initial imaging in adults with suspected appendicitis is abdominal CT scan with IV contrast. CT scan is more accurate than MRI or ultrasound. CT scan findings include enlarged appendiceal double-wall thickness, appendiceal wall thickening, peri-appendiceal fat stranding and appendiceal wall enhancement. The treatment of patients with appendicitis is appendectomy. women and is recommended over CT in these populations because it does not expose the patient to radiation. While Us does not require ionizing radiation or IV contrast, it does not identify the appendix in 50% of cases. US findings may include: noncompressible appendix with double-wall thickness diameter of greater than 6 mm, focal pain over appendix with compression, appendicolith, increased echogenicity of inflamed peri-appendiceal fat and fluid in the right lower quadrant. Answer C (incorrect answer): While surgical resection is the treatment of choice in adults with appendicitis, definitive diagnosis with CT scan is necessary prior to surgery. Children with classic features of appendicitis may be referred for surgery without abdominal imaging, but adults should have imaging first to exclude other diagnoses (e.g., diverticulitis, malignancy).

questions.explanation: Explanation Hematology and Oncology >Red Cells >Normocytic Anemias Normocytic Anemia Chronic Kidney Disease ·Decreasedproductionoferythropoietin ·Erythropoiesis-stimulatingagents ·Recombinanthuman EPO ·Epoetin ordarbepoetin(longer-acting) ·Usedwhen Hgb<10 g/dL ·Goal Hgb:10 to 11.5 g/dL Renal papilla ·Higher Hgb:↑mortality andmyocardial infarction Renal ·May cause orworsen hypertension ·Good response requires iron ·Iron deficiency→poorresponse Renal Fibrous Major calyx Minor calyx Kidney Anatomy Answer E (correct answer): This patient has end-stage renal disease (Es RD), requiring dialysis. Patients on dialysis should have their hemoglobin checked every three months because anemia is common. The anemia generally occurs because of inadequate erythropoietin production and decreased red blood cell survival time. Patients with a hemoglobin of less than 10 g/dL should be started on an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent (ESA). Epoetin is the initial ESA used in most patients and is administered three times per week with a goal of maintaining a hemoglobin level between 10 and 11.5 g/dL. The most common side effect is hypertension. The most common cause of inadequate response to Es As is iron deficiency. Iron is required to form hemoglobin, and iron deficiency prevents an adequate bone marrow response to Es As. This patient should have iron studies, including serum ferritin and transferrin saturation. Patients with low iron will be unable to respond to ESAs until their iron stores have been replenished. Answer A (incorrect answer): Increasing the dose of epoetin is not appropriate until iron deficiency has been ruledout.Allpatientson ESAsshouldhavehemoglobinmeasuredmonthlyand transferrinsaturationandserum ferritin measured every three months. questions.explanation: Explanation Hematology and Oncology>Red Cells>Normocytic Anemias Reticulocyte Count ·Usedinanemia todetermineif bonemarrowresponseis adequate ·Reticulocyte count should rise if bone marrowresponding normally ·Must be correctedfordegreeofanemia ·If<2%→inadequatebonemarrowresponse Het 45(normal) Het 11 Retic 1% (normal) Retic 8% Answer D(correct answer):Thispatienthas severenormocytic anemia,possiblycaused byhydroxychloroquine- induced aplastic anemia. Patients with severe anemia present with fatigue, dyspnea, pallor, tachycardia and tachypnea. when patients with normal bone marrow function develop anemia, their bone marrow will increase production of red blood cells. This causes a rise in the number of reticulocytes, which are immature red blood cells. Therefore, in the setting of anemia, the reticulocyte count will be elevated if the bone marrow is healthy and capable of producing more red blood cells. If the bone marrow is unable to mount an appropriate reticulocyte response, the reticulocyte count will be low or normal. Sometimes, in severe anemia, the reticulocyte count will be somewhat elevated but not appropriately elevated for the level of anemia. A corrected reticulocyte countcanbecalculated todetermine if thebonemarrowresponse to anemia is appropriate.To determine the corrected reticulocyte count,the measuredreticulocyte countis multiplied by the hematocrit divided by 45. For this patient, the corrected reticulocyte count is: 2% X (22/45) = 0.97% lead to a normocytic anemia, with a normal mean corpuscular volume (Mc V). Of the answer choices, only bone marrow failure is associated with a low reticulocyte count and a normal Mcv. The cause of this patient's bone marrow failure cannot be conclusively determined based on the information given; however, hydroxychloroquine is a potential cause of aplastic anemia. Other potential causes of impaired bone marrow response to anemia include lack of an essential red cell nutrient (e.g., vitamin B 12, folate or iron), myelodysplastic syndrome or bone marrow invasion by malignant cells (e.g., leukemia). Further workup, such as a bone marrow biopsy, may be indicated. Key point: Even though this patient's reticulocyte count is increased above the normal range, it is too low for the degree of anemia. Answer A (incorrect answer): Hemolytic anemia is associated with a normocytic anemia and a corrected reticulocyte count greater than 2%. Although hemolytic anemia results from premature destruction of red blood cells (RBCs), the bone marrow in patients with hemolytic anemia should be able to make new RBCs. Answer B (incorrect answer): Chronic blood loss leads to iron deficiency and a microcytic anemia,with a low MCV. This patient has a normal ferritin, which indicates normal iron stores, and a normal Mcv.

Most patients with Vw D have normal platelet counts and normal prothrombin time, although some may have a slightly increased partial thromboplastin time (PTT). Vw D screening tests include the Vw F antigen tests and thevw F activity test. The antigen test measures the quantity of Vw F protein in the plasma, which will be low in patients with Vw D. questions.explanation: Explanation Hematology(NEW)>Red Blood Cells>Sickle Cell Disease Sickle Cell Trait ·One mutated beta globin gene · Usually no sickling ·Normal beta gene more effective→>50%beta globins ·Need >50% Hb S for sickling ·One exception:Renal medulla ·Mayseelossofconcentrating ability ·↑ risk of renal medullary carcinoma (>than sickle disease) Hb S (α2 S 2) Sickle Cell Trait Hb A (α2β2) MHE Answer D (correct answer): This fetus has sickle cell trait due to a heterozygous p.Glu 6 Val mutation in the β- globin gene (HBB).The p.Glu 6 Val mutation is the most common cause of sickle cell disease worldwide.It is a missense mutation in which glutamic acid (Glu) at position 6 of the β-globin chain is replaced by valine (Val). This amino acid substitution creates hemoglobin S (Hbs), which polymerizes under low-oxygen conditions. In the heterozygous state (sickle cell trait), patients are usually asymptomatic but have increased risk of renal complications. Sickling in the hypoxic renal medulla damages the vasa recta, leading to hyposthenuria, or an inability to concentrate the urine. This results in polyuria and nocturia. Frequent urination is often the only clinical problem in patients with sickle cell trait. These patients also develop dehydration more easily in settings of water deprivation. They generally do not develop more serious sickle cell disease complications like hemolysis, pain crises, or asplenia. questions.explanation: Explanation Hematology(NEW)>Red Blood Cells>Sickle Cell Disease Sickle Cell Disease Renal Dysfunction · Papillary necrosis ·Severeocclusionofvasarecta ·Sloughingofrenalpapilladuetorenalvaso-occlusion ·Usually painless, gross hematuria Source: Kemp WL, Bums DK, Brown TG: Pathology: The Big Picture the renal papillae leads to gross hematuria with flank pain. This region is vulnerable to necrosis in sickle cell disease because the renal medulla has low oxygen tension which promotes sickling of red blood cells. The vasa recta are thin, straight capillaries that run alongside the loop of Henle and are responsible for maintaining the medullary osmotic gradient. Because they have sluggish blood flow and are in a hypoxic environment, they are particularly prone to occlusion by sickled cells. Occlusion of the vasa recta cuts off the blood supply to the papillae, leading to ischemia, microinfarction, and necrosis. This explains the patient's flank pain and red urine without significant proteinuria or casts, along with the CT findings of irregular papillary hypodensities. questions.question: A 4-year-old boy with sickle cell disease is brought to the pediatric emergency department due to lethargy. His parents state that he was well until this morning when he was difficult to arouse for preschool. The boy has been sleepy and has complained of abdominal pain. There has been no nausea or vomiting. Medical history is significant for two episodes of otitis media. Vital signs include blood pressure of 66/30 mmHg, pulse of 146/min, respiratory rate of 28/min, and temperature 99.3 F. On exam, the boy appears lethargic and is difficult to arouse. He has dry mucous membranes. He grimaces on abdominal palpation and a mass is noted in the left upper quadrant. Laboratory testing shows hemoglobin of 5.2 g/dL (normal 13.5- 17.5). Which of the following best accounts for this boy's presentation?
questions.explanation: Explanation Hematology(NEW)>Red Blood Cells>Sickle Cell Disease Answer C (correct answer): This child is presenting with signs of shock including hypotension and tachycardia. His physical examination demonstrates a left upper quadrant mass consistent with splenomegaly. Laboratory testing shows severe anemia. This presentation is consistent with splenic sequestration crisis which can be the initial presentation of sickle cell disease in about 20% of patients. The pathophysiology of splenic crisis is believed to involve vaso-occlusion of the splenic microvasculature which results in obstruction and pooling of blood in the spleen. This leads to severe anemia and hypovolemic shock. The spleen rapidly enlarges causing abdominal pain and splenomegaly on exam. Mortality is high and rapid transfusion of blood products is required. After the acute episode is over, splenectomy is indicated due to the high risk of recurrence. Note that older sickle cell patients (e.g., over 5-years-old) have splenic fibrosis and cannot develop this complication. It is seen only in the early stages of sickle cell disease. Answer A (incorrect answer): Aplastic crisis occurs when the bone marrow is unable to adequately produce erythrocytes. Infection with parvovirus B 19 may cause aplastic crisis in sickle cell disease but hypovolemic shock would not be present. Answer B (incorrect answer): Hemolytic crises are exacerbations of anemia due to increased hemolysis in patients with sickle cell disease. Hypovolemic shock and massive splenomegaly would not be present. Answer D (incorrect answer): Vaso-occlusive pain crises are a common initial presentation of sickle cell disease in children. Dactylitis, which is swelling and pain in the hands and feet, is often the chief complaint.

questions.explanation: Explanation Hematology (NEW) > Red Blood Cells > Sickle Cell Disease Answer E (correct answer): In patients with sickle cell disease, hemoglobin S forms due to the replacement of the amino acid glutamic acid by valine in the beta-globin chain. The substituted valine molecule is nonpolar residues on other beta-chains. This causes altered protein structure that forms polymers. dimensional) structure of the protein. The primary structure of a protein is the amino acid sequence. This is abnormal in sickle disease due to amino acid substitution. The secondary structure is formed by hydrogen bonds and includes shapes like alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets. The tertiary (3 D) structure is determined by interactions of the R-groups in amino acid residues. Abnormalities of this structure result in the conformational changes seen in hemoglobin S among sickle cell patients. When deoxygenated, the abnormal hemoglobin S gains polymerizes (i.e., links together) with other molecules of hemoglobin S forming large protein fibrils. These fibril polymers distort red cells into the classic sickle shape. They also decrease the cell's ability to "deform" (i.e., to adapt its shape) to squeeze through tight areas in the vasculature. This leads to vaso-occlusion. It is also believed that hemoglobin S fibrils cause membrane damage and increased adherence of sickled cells to endothelium. Answer A (incorrect answer): Hydrophilic protein interactions are more likely to occur with polar amino acids. Answer B (incorrect answer): The secondary structure is the local conformation of a protein such as alpha- helices or beta-pleated sheets. The secondary structure of the hemoglobin beta chain is not significantly altered by the sickle cell mutation. Answer C (incorrect answer): Tetramers of beta-chains form in patients with alpha-thalassemia major but are not seen in sickle cell patients.

questions.question: A 25-year-old female is evaluated for urinary frequency. She has a history of sickle cell disease for which she takes hydroxyurea. She complains of waking three to four times per night to urinate. This has interrupted her sleep and she is tired at work. She denies fever or dysuria. She has no history of renal disease. Serum BUN and creatinine are normal. Urinalysis shows no white cells, casts, protein, or glucose. A defect in which of the following may explain this woman's presentation?
questions.explanation: Explanation Hematology(NEW)>Red Blood Cells>Sickle Cell Disease Answer C (correct answer): Patients with sickle cell disease commonly develop impairment in urinary concentration which can lead to polyuria and nocturia.Concentrated urine contains relatively little water.When the nephron is unable to concentrate urine normally, excess water is excreted. This leads to a high urine volume and symptoms of frequent urination. The defect in urinary concentration among sickle cell patients is caused by sickling in the vasa recta of the renal medulla. The vasa recta are renal capillaries responsible for maintaining high osmolarity in the medulla. This osmolarity draws water out of the urine. Damage to the vasa recta in sickle cell disease impairs urinary concentration. Normally, the kidneys can maximally concentrate urine to about 12 o 0 mosm/kg. Among sickle cell patients, the maximum urinary osmolarity is about 450 msom/kg. This makes it difficult to conserve free water and causes excessfreewater excretion. Answer B (incorrect answer): Urinary dilution is normal in patients with sickle cell disease.Urinary dilution does not require high gradients in the medulla. In the absence of ADH, sodium resorption is intact and the kidneys can produce a maximally dilute urine (e.g., urinary osmolarity 5 omosm/kg). Answer A (incorrect answer): Glomerular filtration should be normal in this woman with no history of kidney disease.

Generally, all children receive the Pc V 13 as part of routine childhood vaccinations, and all adults aged 65 or greater receive the Pps V 23 vaccine; however, adults at risk for severe pneumococcal infection should receive both PCV 13 and Pps V 23. High-risk groups for severe pneumococcal infection include patients with immunocompromise, splenic removal or dysfunction, cochlear implant, cerebrospinal fluid leak or prior pneumococcal meningitis. Patients are typically given PCV 13 first and then given Pps V 23 at least eight weeks later. This method of vaccine administration, called the "prime boost" strategy, is supported by randomized clinical trial data showing showed improved immune response in patients who received Pc V followed by Pps V. Low back pain accounts for 1% of all health care visits and most patients, particularly those without underlying health conditions, are diagnosed with"nonspecific back pain." Ms is an autoimmune disease in which T-lymphocytes react to myelin antigens, causing demyelination of nerves. Tests that may be able to confirm a diagnosis of Ms include a lumbar puncture showing oligoclonal bands and magnetic resonance imaging showing scattered, enhancing lesions within the white matter. This man's ocular findings are consistent with internuclear ophthalmoplegia. His right eye is unable to adduct instructed to look to the left. There are no deficits when he is asked to look to the right. Internuclear ophthalmoplegia occurs due to abnormalities of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF), which is a highly myelinated structure that coordinates the activities of the cranial nerve VI and cranial nerve III. Unilateral damage to the right MLF would cause the impaired right eye adduction seen in this case. Internuclear ophthalmoplegia is a classic neurologic finding in Ms due to the highly myelinated fibers found in the MLF. Answer A (incorrect answer): The pathophysiology of Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) involves immune cross reactivity between bacterial antigens and proteins of peripheral nerves. This phenomenon is called "molecular mimicry." Antibodies formed to bacterial proteins may cross-react with neuronal proteins, such as gangliosides on peripheral nerves. This leads to demyelination and weakness. Answer B (incorrect answer): Patients with metachromatic leukodystrophy have an arylsulfatase A deficiency. questions.question: A 27-year-old woman with a history of optic neuritis presents with weakness for the past two weeks. She says her legs feel heavy and slow. She has tripped three times while walking on flat surfaces. She also feels a shock-like sensation that shoots down the back of her legs. A lumbar puncture is done which shows oligoclonal bands. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain shows scattered, enhancing white matter lesions. Injury to which of the following cells may explain this woman's condition?
questions.explanation: Explanation Neurology(NEW)> Other Neurology Topics > Multiple Sclerosis Answer D (correct answer): This woman has multiple sclerosis (Ms), an autoimmune demyelinating disorder that commonly affects young woman. The clinical course of Ms often includes relapsing and remitting symptoms, which means varying neurologic deficits that come and go over time. Clinical features can include motor weakness and sensory changes. This woman has a prior episode of optic neuritis, which is a classic symptom of MS. Gel electrophoresis performed on the cerebrospinal fluid (Cs F) of patients with MS may reveal "oligoclonal bands", which are collections of immunoglobulins. These are found in the Cs F in cases of Ms and other inflammatory neurologic conditions. Magnetic resonance imaging of patients with Ms can show multiple white matter lesions. The pathologic hallmarks for MS are demyelination and loss of oligodendrocytes. Oligodendrocytes are glial cells of the central nervous system. Glial cells are non-neuronal cells in the nervous system which support and conduction of action potentials along axons. With myelin loss in Ms, neuronal conduction is impaired. Answer A (incorrect answer): Astrocytes are also glial cells that support neurons within the central nervous system through structural and nutritional support. Astrocytic processes, which are projections that stem from the cell body, may develop at synapses (allowing the astrocytes to affect neuronal signaling) or overlying blood vessels (allowing the astrocytes to release cytokines or other inflammatory mediators into the bloodstream). Astrocytes grow larger in the setting of brain injury, a process called reactive astrocytosis. Abnormalities of these cells are not known to play a role in the development of Ms. Answer B (incorrect answer): Microglia are the resident macrophages of the central nervous system. Like other macrophages, microglia are activated by pathologic conditions including injury, neurodegeneration, and infection. Injury to microglia is not known to play a role in the pathogenesis of MS. Answer C (incorrect answer): Ependymal cells secrete cerebrospinal fluid within the nervous system. They line the ventricles and the central canal of the spinal cord. In addition to creating the cerebrospinal fluid, they help to circulate this fluid through movement of cilia.

It reflects demyelination of the cervical spinal cord and is a form of neuropathic pain. Pregabalin, a calcium channel blocker, is used to treat neuropathic pain by inhibiting excitatory neurotransmitter release in overactive pain pathways. It is an appropriate treatment for Lhermitte sign in MS. Answer A (incorrect answer): Baclofen is used to treat spasticity in MS by acting as a GABA-B receptor agonist in the limbs or bladder. PML is an inflammatory central demyelinating disorder that occurs due to reactivation of latent JC virus in patients who are immunocompromised due to malignancy, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) or treatment with immunosuppressant drugs such as natalizumab. It is administered for a number of different conditions, including Guillain-Barre syndrome, immune thrombocytopenia and primary hypogammaglobulinemia. It is not used to treat PML.
