High-dose folic acid therapy should be continued at least through the first trimester. After that, the dose can be reduced to O.4 mg daily. Although guidelines vary regarding the appropriate dose of folic acid supplementation for women on many antiepileptic drugs, there is a consensus that women on carbamazepine or valproic acid (which bothpose a high risk of congenital malformations) should take 4 mg of folic acid daily.Some guidelines recommend thatwomen onother antiepileptic medications should take 4 mg of folic acid daily,whereas other guidelines advise that O.4 mg of folic acid is sufficient. Women who arerequired to take high-dosefolic acid should either be given a prescriptionfor folicacid or given specific information on how to use over-the-counter folic acid. It may be dangerous if a woman takes multiple daily doses of a multivitamin dailyin ordertofulfill the 4 mg offolic acidrequirementbecausetoxicitiesfrom other vitamins may occur. Answer A(incorrectanswer):All womenofchildbearingpotential should take O.4 mgoffolicacid dailyin order to lower their risk of neural tube defects. This should be started at least one month prior to conception and continue throughout pregnancy.Women taking carbamazepine need a higher dose. Answer B (incorrect answer): Women at a moderate risk for having an infant with a neural tube defect may be advised to take 1 mg of folic daily. For example, women with diabetes mellitus, gastrointestinal malabsorption, end-stage renal disease, alcohol overuse or advanced liver disease should take this intermediate dose of folic acid in order toprevent neural tube defects.Women taking carbamazepine need a higher dose. Answer D (incorrect answer): Discontinuation of carbamazepine in this woman will put her at risk for developing seizures. A fetus may be adversely affected by maternal seizures. Tonic-clonic seizures in particular may lead to hypoxia and lactic acidosis, which may harm the fetus. Other risks of maternal seizures may include fetal injury and placental abruption.

questions.question: A 41-year-old woman with a history of epilepsy presents to the emergency room reporting nausea and vomiting. She also reports slurred speech and double vision. The symptoms started approximately 3 days ago. Her home medications include phenytoin, ciprofloxacin and acetaminophen. She denies recent changes in her dose of phenytoin and has been taking this medication as prescribed. She started ciprofloxacin and acetaminophen five days ago after she was bitten by her dog. She reports drinking four 12-ounce beers per day and smoking one pack of cigarettes per day. Vital signs show a temperature of 98.5°F, pulse of 105 beats/min, respiratory rate of 18 breaths/min and blood pressure of 122/72 mmHg. On examination, she has slurred speech. Examination of her eyes shows that her she has rhythmic rapid downward eye motions that are worse when she looks laterally or inferiorly. Her biceps and patellar reflexes are 3+ bilaterally. She is unable to walk heel-to-toe mg/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, total protein 7.5 g/dL and albumin 4.1 g/dL. Urinalysis is normal and urine drug screen is negative. A serum phenytoin level is 35 mg/L. which of the following factors most likely led to this patient's current condition?
questions.explanation: Explanation Neurology>Seizures>Seizure Treatment Phenytoin Acute Toxicity/Overdose ·Altered mental status ·Nystagmus ·Ataxia ·Abnormalreflexes ·Oftenduetoconcomitantdrug ·P 450 metabolism (e.g,TMP-SMX) ·Heavily albuminbound(e.g,valproicacid) ·Ofteninpatientswithliver/kidneydisease Pixabay/Public Domain Answer B (correct answer): This woman has phenytoin toxicity due to the recent initiation of ciprofloxacin. Phenytoin is a sodium-channel inactivating antiepileptic medication that has many drug-drug interactions. It is metabolized by the cytochrome P-450 system. Ciprofloxacin is an inhibitor of the cytochrome P-450 enzymes; therefore, administration of this medication can reduce the metabolism of phenytoin, leading to high serum levels of the drug. Symptoms of phenytoin toxicity may include vertical nystagmus, diplopia, ataxia, slurred speech, tremor, hyperreflexia, nausea and vomiting. If serum levels increase to 40 to 50 mg/L, patients may develop lethargy, confusion or disorientation. At serum levels greater than 50 mg/L, patients may develop coma or seizures. Phenytoin toxicity is relatively common, but typically not life-threatening. The mainstay of airway if needed, cardiac monitoring for detection of arrhythmias and treatment of seizure activity with benzodiazepines. Answer A (incorrect answer): The majority of phenytoin is excreted in the bile, which is not affected by kidney (e.g., nephrotic syndrome), the free fraction of phenytoin increases and toxicity may occur. This woman has a normal serum creatinine, normal blood urea nitrogen and normal urinalysis indicating no evidence of renal disease. Answer C(incorrect answer):Theuse of acetaminophendoesnot affectserumphenytoinlevels.Acetaminophen is not a major substrate of the cytochrome P-450 system. It does not typically bind to serum proteins such as albumin, and therefore does not increase free levels of phenytoin by this mechanism.

questions.question: A 36-year-old woman with a history of epilepsy presents to the emergency room with fever and rash. She developed sweats, chills, malaise and achiness three days ago. She then started to notice red splotches with purple centers on her face; these lesions then spread to her upper chest. Other symptoms include pain with eating and swallowing. Current medications include carbamazepine, which was started seven days ago. Vital signs include a temperature of 102.1°F, pulse of 111 beats/min, respiratory rate of 22 breaths/min and blood pressure of 107/62 mmHg. On examination, she has conjunctival injection bilaterally with purulent discharge. Evaluation of the oral cavity shows hemorrhagic erosions involving the lips and vermillion border; ulceration of the tongue is also noted (see photo below). There are erythematous lesions on the face that are associated with sloughing of the skin. In addition, she has erythematous macules, vesicles and bullae present on the upper chest, upper back and bilateral arms. The presence of which of the following HLA genes may have put this woman at increased risk for developing this syndrome?
questions.explanation: Explanation Neurology>Seizures>Seizure Treatment Answer D (correct answer): This woman has Stevens-Johnson syndrome (Sjs) caused by the recent initiation of carbamazepine.The HLA allele HLA-B*1502 may put individuals at increased risk for developing this complication. Because of the strong association between SJS and this HLA allele, some patients are referred for HLA-B*1502 screeningprior tostartingcarbamazepine. Stevens-Johnson syndrome is a life-threatening condition which may be triggered by antiepileptic medications including carbamazepine, lamotrigine and phenytoin. Symptoms typically start from 4 to 21 days after initiation of the medication, often preceded by a prodrome of symptoms including fever and flu-like symptoms. Patients then develop erythematous, coalescing macules on the face and then the body. These lesions may result in necrosis and sloughing of the skin. Unlike other drug eruptions such as AGEP (acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis) there is typically involvement of the mucosal surfaces. Ocular involvement is also prominent with SJS. SJS is considered to exist along a spectrum with toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN). TEN is the more severe condition and involves skin detachment of over 30% of the body surface area. Treatment of SJS involves prompt cessation of the offending drug and aggressive supportive care. Patients may require treatment inaburnunitduetoextensivesloughingofskin. Answer A (incorrect answer): HLA-DR 4 is classically associated with the development of rheumatoid arthritis; however, it may also be associated with the development of type 1 diabetes mellitus. It is not associated with drug hypersensitivity reactions. Answer B (incorrect answer): The HLA-B 27 gene is associated with the development of ankylosing spondylitis. This allele is found in 80 to 95% of patients with ankylosing spondylitis, compared to 6% of the general population in the United States. Ankylosing spondylitis is an inflammatory arthritis of the spine. People with this gene may also be at risk for inflammatory bowel disease and psoriasis. Answer C (incorrect answer): The HLA-DQ 2 gene is associated with the development of celiac disease, which is a gluten-sensitive enteropathy. HLA-DQ 8 is also associated with celiac disease. Patients with celiac disease who have HLDA-DQ 8 or HLA-DQ 2 are predisposed to develop dermatitis herpetiformis, which is a rash associated with gluten sensitivity.Patients with dermatitis herpetiformis have pruriticpapules and vesicles on various parts

questions.question: A three-month-old baby girl is brought to the pediatrician for a follow-up visit by her mother. The mother is noted to have hair growth along her upper lip, chin and dorsal surfaces of her hands. Family history is significant for seizure disorder in the baby's mother. The baby's vital signs include a temperature of 98.5°F and pulse of 120 beats/min. Weight is at the 10th percentile, height is at the 10th percentile and head circumference is at the 2nd percentile. Examination shows a cleft lip, cleft palate, broad nose and wide-spaced eyes (see photo below). Auscultation of the heart shows a regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2 and no murmurs. There are equal breath sounds bilaterally with no wheezes. The extremities show ten fingers, ten toes and normal movement in the arms and legs. Examination of the back shows an intact spine with no this child's abnormalities?
questions.explanation: Explanation Neurology>Seizures>Seizure Treatment Fetal Hydantoin Syndrome NEWS ·Associatedwithphenytoinuseinpregnancy ·Growthdeficiency ·Abnormal facial features ·Broad, short nose ·Wide-spaced eyes ·Malformed ears Microcephaly Classically cleft lip and cleft palate Answer C(correct answer):Phenytoin use in pregnancy may lead to thefetalhydantoin syndrome.Infants affected by this syndrome may have cleft lip, cleft palate, microcephaly, growth deficiency, widely spaced eyes, malformedears and abroad, shortnose. Phenytoin works by inactivating sodium channels, and requires close monitoring. Side effects of phenytoin use and reduced bone density. Overdose with phenytoin may cause altered mental status, nystagmus, ataxia and abnormal reflexes. Management of a patient who becomes pregnant while on phenytoin is challenging. In making decisions about changing antiepileptic medications, the risk of teratogenicity must be weighed against the risk to the mother/fetus from maternal seizures. In some cases, phenytoin may be continued, particularly if the time in which structural birth defects may occur (the first 8 weeks after conception)has passed when the patient changes in hepatic metabolism and renal clearance during pregnancy. All pregnant women should take folic acid supplementation to decrease the risk of neural tube defects, but women on seizure medications should take a higher dose of folic acid. Answer A (incorrect answer): Lamotrigine is a sodium-channel blocking antiepileptic medication that is considered to be relatively safe in pregnancy; however, like many other antiepileptic medications, it may cause Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Other potential side effects include aseptic meningitis, neutropenia, pancytopenia and agranulocytosis. The drug level of lamotrigine should be monitored, and pregnant women should be given the lowest effective dose. Women who need to take anti-seizure medications during pregnancy should take high doses of folic acid supplementation in order to reduce the risk of neural tube defect in the fetus. Answer B (incorrect answer): Diazepam is a benzodiazepine medication that may be administered to stop seizure activity. It is not administered chronically to prevent the development of seizures. Diazepam may cross the placenta and have teratogenic effects.Limb malformations,rectal-anal stenosis/atresia and cardiovascular abnormalities have been described.

questions.question: A seven-year-old boy with a history of gastroesophageal reflux disease and febrile seizures presents to the clinic with episodes of inattention at school. During these episodes, he stares straight ahead, does not respond to his name and does not move. They last for approximately 10 seconds and occur several times a day. After an episode he doesn't have any confusion or lethargy. His home medications include cimetidine and a multivitamin. He lives with his brother, mother and stepfather. He is in the first grade and has met all appropriate developmental milestones. An electroencephalogram done during an episode shows 3 Hertz spike-and-wave activity. What is the treatment of choice for this condition?
questions.explanation: Explanation Neurology > Seizures > Seizure Treatment Ethosuximide ·Blocksthalamic T-type Cachannels ·Drugofchoice:childhoodabsenceseizures ·Mostcommonsideeffect:upsetstomach(nausea/vomiting) ·Rare sideeffects:drowsiness Answer C (correct answer): This boy has childhood absence epilepsy, a condition of absence seizures. Absence seizures involve a suddenimpairment of consciousness with no change in motor tone.They typically last a few seconds in duration. The treatment of choice for this condition is ethosuximide. This medication blocks thalamic T-type calcium channels and prevents the occurrence of absence seizures.Common side effects mayinclude nausea or vomiting and, more rarely,drowsiness.Unlike many other antiepileptic medications,ethosuximide does not have many drug-drug interactions, but serum levels can be followed to assure adequate dosing. In contrast, medications such as carbamazepine, phenobarbital and phenytoin may induce CYP 450 enzymes which can impact metabolism of other medications. This child is on cimetidine, which tends to inhibit CYP 450 enzymes, and could make therapy with these antiepileptic medications more challenging. include gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, megaloblastic anemia and reduced bone marrow density. It has multiple absence seizures. Answer B(incorrectanswer):Carbamazepineisasodiumchannelblockingantiepilepticmedication.Side effects may include Stevens-Johnson syndrome, bone marrow suppression, liver toxicity and hyponatremia. This medication should be avoided in childhood absence epilepsy because it may increase the frequency of absence seizures. Answer D(incorrectanswer): Levetiracetamis a commonly-used antiepilepticmedication thatworksbyan unclear mechanism of action. Benefits of this medication include its efficacy for many seizure types, lack of significant side effects and minimal drug-drug interactions. The use of levetiracetam has been studied in childhood absence epilepsy, but it has shown mixed effectiveness. Answer E(incorrectanswer):Patientswithchildhood absenceepilepsyshouldbetreated,soobservation withouttreatment is not appropriate.Absenceseizures mayinterferewith learning at school and social

questions.question: A 23-year-old woman with a history of epilepsy presents to the emergency department with seizures. She takes levetiracetam, which normally controls her seizures, but she has had multiple tonic-clonic seizures over the past two days. Three days ago, she noticed pain with urination, urinary frequency and low-grade fevers. Vital signs include a temperature of 100.5°F, pulse 108 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min and blood pressure 127/62 mmHg. In the emergency department, she suddenly develops stiffness in her muscles followed by jerking movements in her arms and legs. The nurse positions her on her side. The jerking is still continuing after five minutes. Which of the following should be administered at this time?
questions.explanation: Explanation Neurology> Seizures>Seizure Treatment Status Epilepticus ·Check airway,breathing, and circulation (ABCs) ·First-linetreatment:IVlorazepam ·Alternative: diazepam · Multiple doses may be used ·Loading of intravenous antiseizure drug: ·Fosphenytoin, valproate, and levetiracetam 10 ml LORAZEPAM ·Prevent recurrent seizures jection USP · If still seizing: phenobarbital 2 mg/ml ·Often requires general anesthesia and intubation Answer A (correct answer):This womanhasseizure activity that has been ongoing for five minutes,which is considered status epilepticus.The treatment of choice tobreakseizures is intravenouslorazepam,a seizures, including status epilepticus, and multiple doses may be needed to abort seizure activity. If unsuccessful, other antiepileptic medications such as fosphenytoin, phenytoin, valproate or levetiracetam may be used. This woman has dysuria, urinary frequency and fever, which suggest a urinary tract infection. Infections lower the seizure threshold and in patients with epilepsy infection maylead to breakthrough seizures (i.e., seizures risk for having seizures include sleep deprivation, exposure to flashing lights, fever, illicit drug use, withdrawal from drugs, lack of adherence to maintenance antiepileptic medications or initiation of a new medication that mayaffecttheserumlevelofanantiepilepticmedication. Answer B (incorrect answer):Phenytoin is an antiepilepticmedicationthat works by inactivating sodium channels.It maybe given if benzodiazepine medications fail to stop the seizure activity.Often a loading dose of 20 mg/kg is given intravenously for patients in status epilepticus. Possible side effects of phenytoin administration include hypotension and cardiac arrhythmia therefore it should be infused slowly. Intravenous phenytoin may also cause the "purple glove syndrome", in which skin distal to the infusion site turns blue or reducedincidenceofthepurpleglovesyndrome. Answer C(incorrect answer):Ethosuximideis an antiepilepticmedication that blocks thalamic T-type calcium receptors.Thisresults in an increase in the seizure threshold and reduces neuronal transmission in the cerebral cortex, making seizuresless likely to occur.This medication is typically given to patients with childhood absence epilepsy.It is not givenfor status epilepticus. Answer D (incorrect answer): Valproate is an antiepileptic medication that has effects on GABA and sodium channels.It maybe given as a second-line agent for status epilepticus if benzodiazepinesfail to stop seizure

questions.question: A 37-year-old woman presents with a headache that developed gradually over the last few days. Other symptoms include blurred vision and nausea. Her past medical history includes diabetes mellitus, prior miscarriage and childhood asthma. Her home medications include oral contraceptive pills and metformin. Vital signs include a temperature of 98.3°F, pulse of pain. She is alert and oriented to person, place, date, and situation. Cranial nerves two through twelve are intact. No motor deficits are noted, and sensation is intact bilaterally. Laboratory results show a prothrombin time (PT) of 14 seconds, international normalized ratio (INR) of 1.1, partial thromboplastin time (PTT) of 30 seconds, hemoglobin 14.5 g/dL and platelet count 240,0o0/mm3. Computed tomography imaging of the brain reveals a thrombosis in the superior sagittal sinus.
questions.explanation: Explanation Neurology>Stroke and Hemorrhage>Stroke II Venous Sinus Thrombosis ·Head CT may show edema ·Often normal ornonspecific ·Diagnosis:CTor MRvenography ·Dye in venous system “Filling defects"from thrombus ·Treatment:heparin ONFLUEN 9 L TRANG. Answer B(correctanswer):Thiswomanhascerebralvenoussinusthrombosis.Cerebralvenoussinus thrombosis occurs when a blood clot develops within the dural venous sinus, which normally drain blood from the brain. Thrombosisleads toincreased intracranialpressurebecauseit obstructs this normal drainage ofblood.Patients with this condition present with symptoms of increased intracranial pressure including the gradual onset of headache,nausea andblurredvision.A riskfactorfor the development ofthisconditioninhercasemaybe her use of an oral contraceptive which is associated with increased risk of blood clots. The diagnosis is confirmed by computed tomography venography imaging which shows a lack of blood flow in a cerebral vein. The mainstay of treatment of this condition is anticoagulation with heparin. After her symptoms improve, the heparin can be transitionedtoanoraldruglikewarfarinordabigatran.Dabigatranisadirectthrombininhibitor,and ithas similar efficacy and risk of bleeding when compared to warfarin. Many patients may prefer the use of dabigatran over warfarin because it does not require serial monitoring of the INR. Anticoagulation should be continued for at least three months in patients with venous sinus thrombosis. Answer A (incorrect answer): Intracranial stenting is not used to treat cerebral venous thrombosis; however, intracranial stenting is used in some cases of cerebral aneurysm. Answer C(incorrect answer):Thedirectfactor Xainhibitor apixaban reduces factor Xa activity and is treatment of cerebral venous thrombosis. Additionally, in the acute phase, patients with cerebral venous thrombosis are typically treated with either heparin or low-molecular-weight heparin and then transitioned to oral anticoagulation. increased intracranial pressure. This drug may be given if she continues to have increased intracranial pressure despite treatment with heparin; however, it is not indicated as an initial therapy for cerebral venous thrombosis.

questions.question: A 63-year-old woman with a history of antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, hypertension, chronic migraines, diabetes mellitus and hyperlipidemia presents with a loss of sensation on the right side of her body. she also complains of a throbbing headache which she rates as a 6/10 in severity. These symptoms have been present for 24 hours. Vital signs include in the upper and lower extremities bilaterally. Sensation to pinprick and light touch is impaired on the right arm and right leg, but intact on the left arm and left leg. Reflexes are 2+ bilaterally at the biceps and patella. No other neurologic deficits cause of her symptoms?
questions.explanation: Explanation Neurology>Strokeand Hemorrhage>Stroke II Lacunar Strokes Subtype Other Details Symptoms Paralysisofface,arm Posteriorlimb Pure Motor andlegonone side internalcapsule Completesensoryloss Pure Sensory Thalamus one side of body: Face,arm,andl Internal capsule Ataxic Hemiparesis Weakness/ataxia Basepons Dysarthria and Internal capsule Dysarthria-Clumsy Hand clumsiness(weakness) Base pons Syndrome of the hand *Over 20 subtypes described Answer A(correct answer):This woman has had a pure sensorylacunar stroke.These strokes are small,non- cortical infarctions caused by occlusion of branches of large cerebral arteries. This patient's stroke involves the thalamus, which has led to sensory loss on one side of the body; thus, she has a pure sensory subtype of lacunar stroke. Other subtypes are shown in the table above. These strokes are strongly associated with hypertension. tomography imaging. In particular, the use of MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging may be able to identify early ischemic strokes. The headache this patient describes has only been present for a few hours. Also, although neurologicdeficits suchasweakness or cranial nervepalsies can occur with cerebralvenoussinus that allows for visualization of the cerebral venous system. This study may be helpful in identifying cerebral venoussinus thrombosis,whichwould cause afillingdefect. Answer C (incorrect answer):Migraine headaches are episodicheadaches that are classically unilateral, throbbing and associated with nausea, vomiting, phonophobia or photophobia. Headache may be preceded by an aura of non-headache symptoms such as visual loss, weakness or numbness. The aura typically lasts for less than onehour.This woman has had a loss of sensationforover a day,making this less likely tobe an aura associatedwithmigraine. Answer D (incorrect answer): A middle cerebral artery (Mc A) stroke can cause motor and sensory loss as seen in hemianopsia) and facial droop may also occur. Imaging with CT scan is usually abnormal.

questions.question: A 67-year-old woman with a history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus presents with sudden loss of vision in the pattern depicted below. Vital signs include temperature of 98.99F, pulse of 84/min, respiratory rate of 18/min and a blood pressure of 162/86 mmHg. Physical examination shows a well-appearing woman in no acute distress. Her pupils are equally round and reactive to light. Extraocular movements are intact. Motor strength is 5/5 bilaterally in her upper and lower extremities. Reflexes are 2+ bilaterally at the biceps and patella. Sensation is intact bilaterally to pain and light touch. which of the following anatomic structures is most likely affected in this patient?
questions.explanation: Explanation Neurology>Strokeand Hemorrhage>Stroke II Posterior Cerebral Artery Stroke ·Posteriorportion of brain ·Occipitallobe,themedialtemporallobeorthethalamus ·Visualcortex ·Contralateral homonymoushemianopsia ·Thalamicinfarct:contralateralsensoryloss Answer E (correct answer):This womanhas the sudden onset of neurologic deficit,whichsuggests shemaybe havinga stroke.Shedescribesa visualfield defectcalled homonymoushemianopsia.A lackofblood flowtothe temporal and occipital lobe, as may be caused by a posterior cerebral artery stroke, results in a loss of the contralateral (opposite) side of the visual field (refer to diagram above). Although visual loss is the most common finding in posterior cerebral artery strokes, other deficits may also result from this type of stroke, such as contralateral sensory loss from a lack of blood flow to the thalamus.A right posterior cerebral artery stroke may cause an inability to recognize faces (prosopagnosia). A left posterior cerebral artery stroke may cause an inability to read (alexia) or difficulties in word-finding (anomic aphasia). Answer A(incorrect answer):A stroke involving the anteriorinferior cerebellar artery (AICA) causesreduced blood flow to the brainstem and cerebellum. This may result in ipsilateral facial weakness, deafness, dizziness and uncoordinated eye movement. AICA stroke does not typically cause vision loss. Answer B (incorrect answer): A stroke involving the anterior spinal artery (As A) causes a loss of motor function below the level of the occlusion. The defects may be bilateral.As A strokes do not affect visual function.

questions.question: A 74-year-old woman with a history of diabetes mellitus presents with pain behind her right eye. She notes that a few weeks ago she started to have pain and redness near her right nostril but had not sought care for this complaint. She also complains of double vision that is worse when she looks to the right. On examination, this woman has a cranial nerve six(abducens nerve) palsy on the right due to impairmentofthisnerveasittraverses thecavernoussinus.Theabducensnerveinnervatesthelateralrectus muscle, which is responsible for abduction (lateral movement) of the eye. Without the function of the muscle, the affected eye cannot move laterally.Patients with abducens nerve lesions often have double vision which may worsen when trying to look towards the affected side. questions.question: A 75-year-old man with a history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus presents three hours after the onset of a right-sided facial droop. He denies any history of intracranial hemorrhage, prior stroke, head trauma or internal bleeding. On examination, he speaks one word at a time and has difficulty forming complete sentences. The right side of his mouth is lower than the left, and he is unable to smile on that side. He can wrinkle his forehead bilaterally. Motor examination shows strength 5/5 for flexion and extension of the left knee, 4/5 strength of flexion and extension of the right knee, 5/5 strength for flexion and extension of the left elbow and 2/5 for flexion and extension of the elbow on the right. Sensation to light touch is 85/min, respiratory rate of 16/min and blood pressure of 180/100 mmHg. Labs show a prothrombin time of 18 seconds, international normalized ratio of 1.3, partial thromboplastin time of 35 seconds, hemoglobin of 14.0 g/dL, platelet count of 149,000/mm3 and blood glucose of 315 mg/dL. Non-contrast computed tomography imaging of the brain is normal. Tissue plasminogen activator is administered urgently. This man's examination is consistent with a stroke involving which anatomic area?
questions.explanation: Explanation Neurology>Stroke and Hemorrhage>Stroke II Middle Cerebral Artery Stroke ·Mostcommonterritoryofstroke ·Frontal,parietaland temporallobes ·Contralateralmotor/sensorydeficit ·Arm and face>leg ·Spastic(UMN) paralysis ·Ifleft(dominant) sided ·Aphasia ·Ifright(nondominant) side ·Hemineglect Answer C (correct answer): This man has had a middle cerebral artery stroke, resulting in his facial droop. Clinical features of MCA stroke include contralateral hemiparesis and hemisensory loss of the face, upper and signs such as aphasia and neglect maybe present.Early in the course of an ischemic stroke, the ischemic lesion administered to a patient without evidence of ischemic stroke on head CT as long as the clinical presentation is highly suggestive of stroke, cerebral hemorrhage is ruled out and the patient has no contraindications to TPA administration. This patient has no contraindications to the administration of TPA.Contraindications to TPA include active internal bleeding, any history of intracranial hemorrhage, ischemic stroke within the past three months, blood pressure over 185/110 mmHg, platelet count less than 100,000, INR over 1.7 and PTT over 40 s.He presented three hours after symptom onset, which is within the three-hour window of benefit for this medication (selected patients may receive TPA up to 4.5 hours after the onset of symptoms). Common complications of TPA may include intracerebral hemorrhage, systemic bleeding and angioedema. Answer A (incorrect answer): Strokes affecting the posterior cerebral artery territory can impact the occipital lobe, medial temporal lobe and the thalamus. This can cause deficits in vision (including contralateral homonymoushemianopsia)andcontralateral sensoryloss,butitwill notcauseaphasia,impairedsensationor facial weakness (which are typical with MCA strokes). Answer B (incorrect answer): An ischemic stroke affecting the anterior cerebral artery territory may cause contralateral weakness of the leg or, to a lesser extent, the arm.Cognitive defects or confusion may occur. Facial weakness does not typically occur.

questions.explanation: Explanation Neurology> Other Topics>Neuromuscular Disease LEMS Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome ·Also a disorder of NMj (less common) ·Paraneoplastic syndrome (small cell lung cancer) ·Antibodies against pre-synaptic Ca channels ·Prevent ACh release ·Diagnosis:VGCC antibodies ·Antibodies to voltage-gated calcium channel (VGCC) ·Key test: imaging for lung mass ACh Choline ACh Acetate ACh E Nicotinic Receptor Answer D(correct answer):This manhas Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome(LEMs)based onhis proximal muscle weakness and positive antibodies to voltage-gated calcium channels (VGc C). LEMS is a paraneoplastic syndrome often associated with small cell lung cancer. This, in addition to the patient's smoking history and weight loss, makes a diagnosis of lung cancer likely. He should undergo computed tomography imaging of the chest to evaluate for an underlying lung mass. Patients with LEMs develop slowly progressive, symmetric, proximal muscle weakness without an elevation in serum creatine kinase (as occurs in myositis). Clinical features of LEMS can resemble myasthenia gravis (MG), but the weakness of LEMs improves with muscle use whereas it worsens in MG. Patients can have decreased reflexes in LEMS while reflexes are normal in MG. Ptosis and diplopia occurs less commonly in LEMS compared to MG. Patients with LEMs often have autonomic symptoms, whereas patients with MG do not. Answer A (incorrect answer): Motor nerve conduction studies may provide supportive evidence for a diagnosis of LEMS and may help differentiate this diagnosis from MG; however, this testing is not critical given his clinical history and the positive VGCC antibodies, both of which support a diagnosis of LEMS. It is more important to assess for a lung malignancy.

MG is a disease of the neuromuscular junction that causes muscle fatigability, diplopia and ptosis. It has a bimodal age distribution and tends to affect women aged 20 to 30 and men aged 60 to 80. It is characterized by increasing muscle weakness with increased muscle use that is seen both clinically and on motor nerve conduction studies. It is a first-line treatment for myasthenia gravis. On evaluation, he is well appearing and is in no acute distress. Pupils are equally round and reactive to light, extraocular movements are intact and his tongue and palate are midline. His heart and lung exam are normal. Motor strength with shoulder abduction/adduction is 4/5 bilaterally and elbow extension/flexion is 5/5 bilaterally. and a waddling gait. questions.explanation: Explanation Neurology>Other Topics>Neuromuscular Disease DMD Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy ·Diagnosis:genetic testing ·Usually with polymerase chain reaction ·Identifiesmostcommon DMDgeneabnormalities ·Muscle biopsy(rarely done) ·Treatment:glucocorticoids NDC 0591-5052-01 Prednisone Improvemotorfunction Tablets USP Delaylossofambulation ·Multidisciplinary care 5 mg .Physical therapy ·Monitoringrespiratory function Answer B (correct answer): This boy has clinical features of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), an X-linked recessive disorder caused by mutations in the DMD gene. Affected patients develop weakness in early childhood and may initially present with difficulty running, jumping or climbing up stairs. Proximal muscles are typically affected before distal limb muscles. Diagnosis may be confirmed by genetic testing. Becker muscular dystrophy is also caused by mutations in the DMD gene, but symptoms typically do not start until age 5 or later and they are generally less severe. Duchenne muscular dystrophy should be treated with glucocorticoids such as prednisone as steroids are the mainstay of disease-modifying drug therapy in DMD. Glucocorticoids have been shown to improve motor function and delay the loss of ambulation. Answer A (incorrect answer): Amifampridine, also known as 3,4-diaminopyridine or 3,4-DAP, is used in the treatment of Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMs). LEMS causes symmetric proximal muscle weakness and autonomic dysfunction and typically occurs in adults who have an underlying malignancy, such as small cell lung cancer. It is not used in patients with DMD. autoimmune conditions including myasthenia gravis, but it is not used for DMD.

The ECG shows an irregularly irregular rhythm with wide QRS complexes, consistent with atrial fibrillation conducting through an accessory pathway. In Wpw, AV nodal blocking agents (e.g., beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, adenosine) are contraindicated because they can promote preferential conduction through the accessory pathway, potentially resulting in ventricular fibrillation. The most appropriate treatment is intravenous procainamide, a sodium channel blocking antiarrhythmic drug. It slows conduction in both the atria and the accessory pathway and can restore sinus rhythm or safely lower the ventricular rate. Answer A (incorrect answer): Intravenous adenosine is an AV nodal blocker and is contraindicated in WPw with atrial fibrillation. By blocking the AV node, adenosine may force conduction down the accessory pathway, leading to extremely rapid ventricular rates and increasing the risk of ventricular fibrillation. Answer B (incorrect answer): Oral diltiazem, a calcium channel blocker, is too slow-acting for acute arrhythmia management and is also contraindicated in WPw with atrial fibrillation. The episodes begin and end abruptly and are not associated with chest pain or syncope. He has no past medical history and takes no medications. His physical examination is normal. This pathway bypasses the AV node, allowing electrical impulses to activate the ventricles earlier than normal. The result is a shortened PR interval and a slurred upstroke of the QRS complex called a delta wave. The delta wave reflects early (pre-excited) depolarization of ventricular myocytes via the accessory pathway, rather than through the normal AV node-His-Purkinje system. Answer A (incorrect answer): Atrial myocytes are normally activated by impulses from the SA node and are not the target of the abnormal conduction in WPW syndrome. The delta wave is a result of abnormal conduction to the ventricles, not the atria. Answer B (incorrect answer): The AV node is bypassed in WPW syndrome. The accessory pathway directly connects the atria to the ventricles, allowing impulses to reach the ventricular myocardium without traveling through the AV node. Answer C (incorrect answer): The bundle of His lies within the normal conduction system downstream of the AV node. Selective dorsal rhizotomy (SDR) involves cutting specific sensory nerve rootlets of the lower extremities in the lumbosacral spine that contribute to spasticity. By reducing this abnormal reflex arc, the procedure improves lower limb tone and mobility, directly targeting symptoms of spasticity like leg stiffness and scissoring. Answer A (incorrect): Delayed speech is common in cerebral palsy in children with bulbar involvement or global developmental delay. Selective dorsal rhizotomy does not affect cranial nerves or speech centers, and would not improve language development. questions.question: A 19-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a high-speed motor vehicle collision. He was unrestrained and ejected from the vehicle. On arrival, he is unconscious and does not respond to painful stimuli. CT scan of the head shows remains in a coma and dies one week later. which of the following is most likely to be seen at autopsy on examination of brain tissue?
questions.explanation: Explanation Traumatic Brain Injury TBI ·Avulsionolfactorynerverootlets · May severe CN 1 → loss of smell ·Diffuse axonal injury (DAI) ·Shearing of white matter tracts ·Widespread axonal swelling ·Axonal transport impaired ·Accumulation of substances ·Amyloid precursor ·Alpha-synuclein · Seen on path examination in TBI Answer B (correct): This 19-year-old man suffered high-velocity head trauma with persistent coma. He has abnormal MRI findings in the corpus callosum and brainstem, both white matter regions made up of neuronal axons. These are classic regions affected by diffuse axonal injury (DAI). the most characteristic histologic findings is accumulation of amyloid precursor protein (Ap P) within damaged axons due to impaired axoplasmic transport. APp is often used as a marker for axonal injury in both research supports the diagnosis of DAI. Answer A (incorrect): Red neurons appear 12-24 hours after ischemic injury. This man had traumatic brain injury, not ischemic injury. Furthermore, at one week post-injury, red neurons would no longer be the predominant histologic feature. Answer C (incorrect): Bilateral retinal hemorrhages are typical of shaken baby syndrome and are not found in adult traumatic brain injury from a motor vehicle crash. Answer D (correct): While CT imaging may be normal in diffuse axonal injury, microscopic changes are not. Autopsy will show abnormalities such as axonal swelling and APP accumulation in damaged white matter.

questions.explanation: Explanation Neurology (NEW) >Introduction to Neurology >Brain Injury Lower Motor Neuron Damage ·Injury along the path: ·Cell bodies in the spinal cord or brainstem ·Axons in the peripheral nerve Neuromuscular junction ·Reduced muscle tone (hypotonia) ·Flaccid muscles ·Hyporeflexia orareflexia ·Muscle atrophy ·Fasciculationsandfibrillations Answer B (correct answer): This man has a shoulder dislocation with injury to spinal nerve roots C 6, C 7, and C 8. Of the answer choices, a diminished biceps relfex is the only example of a lower motor neuron finding in this man's right arm. The biceps reflex is mediated primarily by the musculocutaneous nerve, which receives contributions from the C 5 reflex. Answer A (incorrect): Biceps clonus is a repetitive, rhythmic contraction that results from upper motor neuron damage. Clonus is not seen with lower motor neuron lesions such as nerve root injuries. questions.question: A 6-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his caregiver for evaluation of excessive sleepiness and vomiting. The child has no known medical problems. On examination, the infant is lethargic and has bruising over the upper arms and chest. CT of the head shows subdural hemorrhages of varying ages. The physician is concerned for shaken baby syndrome. If this diagnosis is correct, abnormalities are most likely to be seen in which of the following examinations?
questions.explanation: Explanation Neurology (NEW) >Introduction to Neurology >Brain Injury Abusive Head Trauma ·From shaking motion ·Shearing of bridgingcorticalveins ·Shearingforces onvitreous and retinal vessels ·Bilateralretinalhemorrhages ·Bulging fontanelles ·Subduralhematomas Answer B (correct answer): This infant has clinical features concerning for shaken baby syndrome, a form of abusive head trauma caused by repetitive acceleration-deceleration forces. This leads to tearing of cerebral bridging veins causing subdural hemorrhage. It may also cause retinal hemorrhages from traction on retinal vessels. Fundoscopy is the most likely examination to reveal abnormalities in these cases and is critical in the evaluation of suspected shaken baby syndrome. Retinal hemorrhages visualized by fundoscopy are highly specific for abusive head trauma in infants. Answer A (incorrect answer): Anorectal examination may reveal findings in cases of sexual abuse but is not associated with shaken baby syndrome. Bruising or trauma in this region would suggest other forms of abuse, not repetitive acceleration-deceleration injury. Answer C (incorrect answer): Laryngoscopy is not typically abnormal in shaken baby syndrome. It may be used in airway evaluation or suspected foreign body aspiration, but it is not relevant for intracranial or retinal injury from abusive head trauma. Answer D (incorrect answer): Otoscopy may reveal signs of ear trauma or otitis media but is not useful in the diagnosis of shaken baby syndrome, which involves intracranial and retinal injury.

A lesion in the internal capsule disrupts upper motor neuron pathways and would not cause fasciculations. questions.question: A 68-year-old man is brought into the emergency department after being found unresponsive on a park bench. His initial Glasgow Coma Scale score is 4 and he is intubated for airway protection. Computed tomography scan of the brain without contrast shows no acute abnormalities. He is admitted to the neurologic intensive care unit for additional evaluation. Vital signs show a temperature of 97.2°F, pulse of 95 beats/min and blood pressure of 135/70 mmHg. His respiratory rate exceeds the rate set by the ventilator. Pupils are equally round and reactive to light. He is able to look up and down, but not from side to side. Corneal reflexes are intact bilaterally. when told that one blink means "no" and two blinks mean "yes," the patient is able to appropriately and accurately respond to yes/no questions. There is no movement of his arms or legs in response to painful stimuli. Reflexes are 2+ bilaterally at the biceps and patella. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

They typically retain awareness and the ability to blink and move their eyes vertically. Answer A (incorrect answer): A middle cerebral artery stroke typically causes a contralateral motor and sensory deficit.Itdoesnotcausebilateralweakness. Patients may have hyperactive delirium which presents with increased motor activity and restlessness, orhypoactive delirium which presents with decreased motor activity, lethargy and drowsiness. Patients with delirium do not develop quadriplegia. Even with hypoactive delirium patients will withdraw from painful stimuli. questions.question: An 81-year-old man presents to the hospital and is diagnosed with diverticulitis. His past medical history includes hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. His home medications of amlodipine, aspirin and insulin are continued upon admission to the hospital. He is calm and oriented on admission but develops agitation and confusion overnight. Vital signs include a temperature of 100.5°F, pulse of 105 beats/min, blood pressure of 151/71 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min -uou shal pup swun s!y buiow s! pup snoixuo puo Kbams sinaddo ay 'uononisa uo 'io woou uo %se jo Kunawixo asind pun purposefully. He is oriented to self but not to date or location. During the examination he tries repeatedly to get out of bed and leave the room despite attempts to redirect his behavior. The nurses report that he has been trying to pull out his peripheral venous catheter. A one-to-one sitter is arranged but the patient's agitation escalates and the sitter is unable to keep him calm. questions.explanation: Explanation Neurology >Other Topics>Altered Mental Status Delirium Treatment ·Treatunderlyingcause Electrolyte abnormalities ·Hypo/hyperglycemia Thiamine deficiency ·Hypercarbia ·Hypoxemia ·Haloperidol Injection,USP ·Other antipsychotics (Fptlimediate Release) Injection,USP 5 mg/m L (5 mg/m L) FORINTRAMUSCULAR USEONLY Answer B (correct answer): This man has delirium which is an acute decline in attention and cognition that may be associated with disturbances in sleep, mood and behavior. Delirium symptoms usually arise over hours to days and some patients may have hallucinations. Symptoms may fluctuate during the day and tend to be worse at night which is referred to as "sundowning." Delirium is commonly the result of an acute medical disorder, substance use or withdrawal or a medication side effect. Unlike dementia, which has a slow onset and is irreversible, delirium is usually acute and reversible. Delirium may be hyperactive, hypoactive or mixed, and patients may develop delirium superimposed upon dementia. This man has hyperactive delirium which presents lethargy and drowsiness. The management of delirium involves identifying and addressing the underlying cause, if possible, such as hypoglycemia, infection, electrolyte disturbance or renal insufficiency. This man has delirium due to symptomatic hypoglycemia. His serum glucose is low likely due to decreased oral intake, increased metabolism from infection and insulin therapy. Hypoglycemia may cause sweating, tachycardia and confusion as seen in this case. Left untreated, his hypoglycemia may worsen leading to seizures. The best next step in management is administration of dextrose to resolve the hypoglycemia. Answer A(incorrect answer): Lorazepam is a benzodiazepine that can be used totreat agitation or anxiety in some situations, such as alcohol withdrawal. However, in elderly patients benzodiazepines may cause or worsen deliriumandshouldbeavoided. Answer C (incorrect answer): Antipsychotic medications such as haloperidol may be used for agitated delirium if nonpharmacologic approaches, such as using a one-to-one sitter and reorienting the patient, are unsuccessful. However, there is some controversy about their use and this use is "off label." Haloperidol is a first-generation antipsychotic. questions.question: A 92-year-old woman with a history of hypertension, hypothyroidism and osteoarthritis presents to the hospital with a urinary tract infection and acute kidney injury. Her home medication of lisinopril is held due to reduced renal function. She does not smoke, use alcohol or use illicit drugs. She lives alone with the support of a home health aide who assists her with showering three times a week. She cooks her own meals and manages her own finances. She has groceries delivered because joint pain prevents her from shopping. On evaluation, she is awake, alert and oriented to place, situation, date, name and time. The Canadian CT Head Injury Rule is a clinical decision-making tool to help determine if a head CT is needed in a patient with a minor head injury. It is appropriate for patients who have a GCs of 13 to 15 and at least one of the following: ·Loss of consciousness · Amnesia to the injury · Disorientation after the injury The Canadian CT Head Injury Rule has high-risk and low-risk criteria. The high-risk criteria are: · GCS score of less than 15 two hours after injury ·Open, depressed or basilar skull fracture ·Age of 65 years or older ·2 or more episodes of vomiting The medium-risk criteria are: ·Retrograde amnesia of 30 minutes or moreto the injury · A dangerous mechanism of injury (e.g., car accident, fall from a high height) If the patient meets one high-risk criterion, a head CT is indicated. If she meets only medium-risk criteria a head CT canbe considered but is optional. This patient has a GCS score of 15 and is amnestic to 20 minutes prior to the injury. She does not meet any medium- or high-risk criteria so a head CT is not required, and she canbe observed at home.

questions.question: imaging shows a calcified, cystic mass at the sella turcica (see image below). Which of the following conditions is most likely to be present in this patient?
questions.explanation: Explanation Neurology>Other Topics）CNSMalignancy Craniopharyngioma Bitemporal Hemianopsia ·Benign ·Symptoms fromcompression Visual field defects ▪ Can compress optic chiasm • Bitemporal hemianopsia ·Behavioral change (frontal lobe) ·Pituitary dysfunction Hyperprolactinemia · Diabetes insipidus · Panhypopituitarism Answer A (correct answer): This patient presents with bitemporal hemianopsia and a calcified, cystic mass in the sella turcica, which is suggestive of a craniopharyngioma. These rare tumors are non-malignant tumors (i.e., they rarely metastasize) that can compress the pituitary gland, pituitary stalk or nerve fibers in the optic chiasm. Compression of the optic chiasm leads to visual field defects, including bitemporal hemianopsia (loss of the outer half of the visual fields). Compression of the pituitary gland can also cause loss of pituitary hormones. This can lead to diabetes insipidus (from loss of ADH) or deficiency of other hormones such as growth hormone the pituitary gland. This will lead to elevated prolactin levels since dopamine normally inhibits prolactin release by the pituitary gland. Craniopharyngiomas derive from Rathke's pouch, an invagination of the ectoderm that protrudes from the roof of the mouth. They have a bimodal age distribution, occurring in children ages 5 to 14 and adults ages 50 to 75 years. Treatment options include surgery, often endoscopic with a transsphenoidal approach, and radiation. Answer B (incorrect answer): Craniopharyngioma may result in diabetes insipidus, not diabetes mellitus. Compression of the hypothalamus or pituitary gland can reduce antidiuretic hormone (i.e., vasopressin) release.

questions.question: An 18-year-old man presents for evaluation of a headache when coughing. The intensity of headaches has worsened over the past three months. He has no other neurologic symptoms, head trauma, bruising, fever or other unusual symptoms. He has no significant family history. On examination, he is alert and fully oriented, but his gait is somewhat unsteady. He has normal strength in all extremities. MRI shows posterior displacement of the cerebellar tonsils. which of the following is most likely to be present in this patient?
questions.explanation: Explanation Neurology > Other Topics > Congenital Neurology Chiari IMalformation ·Abnormalshapeofcerebellartonsils ·Tonsils=smallroundedstructure atbottomofcerebellum ·Tonsilsdisplacedbelowforamenmagnum ·Associatedwithsyringomyelia Chiari I Syringomyelia Public Domain Answer E (correct answer): This patient has a Chiari I malformation which may be associated with syringomyelia. The Chiari I malformation is characterized by downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils below the foramen magnum. Symptoms usually do not present until adulthood, with a mean onset at age 18 years. Headaches occur due to meningeal irritation, which is worsened by coughing. Ataxia may be present due to cerebellar dysfunction. Patients may also have cranial nerve dysfunction secondary to brainstem compression. Answer A (incorrect answer): Dandy-Walker malformation involves cerebellar hypoplasia and dilation of the 4 th ventricle. It is not associated with Chiari I malformation. Patients with Dandy-Walker malformation may have hydrocephalus, developmental delay, impaired hearing, vision deficits, poor coordination and ataxia. Answer B (incorrect answer): Encephalocele is herniation of the meninges or brain through a skull defect. Signs and symptoms may include hydrocephalus, hypotonia and seizures. This condition is not associated with a Chiari I malformation. Treatment involves surgical repair. Answer C (incorrect answer): Meningocele is not associated with Chiari I malformation. Meningocele results from herniation of the meninges through a defect in the vertebral bodies. The hernia sac does not contain spinal cord so neurologic symptoms are usually mild or absent with this form of spina bifida.

In meningomyelocele (also called myelomeningocele), both meninges and spinal cord herniate through a spinal defect in the lumbosacral region. Babies born with this condition may develop multiple related conditions including partial or complete paralysis below the lesion and urinary or bowel dysfunction. Affected patients may also have co-existing hydrocephalus and associated Chiari II malformation. In Chiari II malformation, the cerebellar vermis and tonsils are displaced downward through the foramen magnum. Affected children will often have hydrocephalus, developmental delay, hypotonia, spasticity (later finding), poor coordination and ataxia. Patients with Dandy-Walker malformation may develop enlarged head circumference due to hydrocephalus, vision and hearing deficits and other abnormalities. Answer B (incorrect answer): Anencephaly occurs when the rostral neuropore does not close anteriorly. This results in the absence of major portions of the skull and brain. Babies born with anencephaly may be stillborn or survive briefly after birth. Answer C (incorrect answer): Encephalocele is a neural tube defect that results in the meninges or brain herniating through a skull defect. Signs and symptoms vary according to the size, location, and amount of brain tissue herniating through the defect. Hydrocephalus, hypotonia, seizures and progression to spastic paralysis may occur. Treatment is surgical reduction of the hernia and repair of the skull defect. This condition may require multiple surgical interventions. Answer D (incorrect answer): Holoprosencephaly results from failure of the forebrain to fuse. This condition may result in facial abnormalities such as cleft lip, cleft palate and cyclopia. It is also associated with fetal alcohol syndrome, trisomy 13 and trisomy 18. Severe defects are not compatible with life.

On exam, he demonstrates mild bradykinesia and increased muscle tone in the right arm. His gait is slow, with reduced arm swing on the right side. The physician suspects Parkinson disease. If this is correct, which of the following maneuvers is most likely to increase this man's tremor?

options.A: Holding his hand out from his chest

questions.explanation: Explanation Neurology(NEW)>Other Neurology Topics>Parkinson Disease Tremor ·Occurs atrest ·Improveswithmovement ·Most common in hand ·"Pill-rolling"tremor ·Thumb and fingers come together ·Often presenting feature Graw Hill Answer C (correct answer): This man has clinical features of Parkinson disease, a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by a resting tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity, and gait disturbances. The tremor in Parkinson disease is usually most pronounced when the affected limb is at rest and supported against gravity. Resting the hand on a knee places the limb in a relaxed position, making the resting tremor more noticeable. This helps distinguish Parkinson disease from other forms of tremor that appear during voluntary movement. Answer A (incorrect answer): Holding the hand out from the chest engages postural muscles and suppresses a resting tremor. This maneuver may bring out a postural tremor, such as seen in essential tremor, but it does not enhance a resting tremor associated with Parkinson disease. Answer B (incorrect answer): Making a fist involves voluntary movement and usually reduces the visibility of a resting tremor. In Parkinson disease, tremor often disappears with purposeful activity.

questions.explanation: Explanation Obstetrics and Gynecology>Breast>Breast Masses Atypical Hyperplasia ·Coreneedlebiopsyfollowedbysurgicalexcisionalbiopsy ·Exclude possibility of associated higher-gradelesion ·Up to 30%of caseswillbe“upgraded" There are two subtypes of AH identified on breast biopsy: atypical ductal hyperplasia and atypical lobular hyperplasia. Although considered a benign lesion, AH is associated with a substantially increased risk of developing a future breast cancer. Management of AH often includes risk reduction strategies such as annual mammograms, twice yearly breast exams, discontinuing hormonal therapies or oral contraceptives and considering usage of a selective estrogen receptor modulator or an aromatase inhibitor. After AH is identified on core needle biopsy, it is usually followed by a surgical excisional biopsy to remove the abnormal tissue and exclude an adjacent higher-grade lesion. In up to 30% of cases, subsequent excisional biopsy of a larger area of tissue will show a higher-grade lesion than was identified on core needle biopsy. Answer A (incorrect answer): Management of AH typically includes risk reduction strategies including annual mammograms. While breast cancer screening guidelines vary by organization, current guidelines typically recommend mammography every 1 to 2 years starting at age 40. Patients with AH are recommended to undergo annual mammogram regardless of age. Answer B (incorrect answer): Management of AH typically includes risk reduction strategies including discontinuation of hormonal therapy and oral contraceptives. Therefore, starting hormonal contraceptives would not be appropriate in this patient with AH.

This is thought to occur from suppression of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (Gn RH) and luteinizing hormone (LH), thereby reducing ovarian activity, although the exact mechanism remains unknown; however, breastfeeding is not a reliable form of contraception. Because the immediate postpartum period is considered a hypercoagulable state, estrogen-containing forms of contraception are typically avoided. Therefore, it must be taken at the same time every day. questions.question: A 42-year-old male is seen in the clinic after having a vasectomy four weeks ago. The patient has recovered from the procedure and is feeling well overall. He is interested in having sexual intercourse with his wife and asks if they may restart having sex without fear of her getting pregnant. What counseling should be provided to this patient? "It is safe to restart sexual intercourse O (A) 2.54% now."

options.B: 'Use other contraception until a semen analysis is done in eight weeks."
options.C: "You should avoid ejaculation until two months after surgery."
options.D: "You should have a serum testosterone level measured."

questions.explanation: Explanation Vasectomy ·Ligationofbilateralvasdeferens ·Usually outpatient under local anesthesia ·Semenanalysisthreemonthspostoperativelytoconfirmsterility ·Ifsperm at 3 months→follow-uptest 1 to 2 monthslater ·Failureif spermatfollow-up after>20 ejaculations and>3 months ·Usealternatemethodofcontraceptionuntilsemenanalysis .Usuallypermanent ·Rare cases of recanalization(~0.2%of patients) ·Reversalpossibleinsomecases Answer B (correct answer): A vasectomy is a surgical ligation of the bilateral vas deferens, typically performed as an outpatient under local anesthesia. Vasectomy is considered a permanent form of male sterilization. While reversal may be possible, it has only been reported to be successful in 50 to 7 o% of men.After a vasectomy, the patient must follow up for a semen analysis three months postoperatively to confirm sterility. Until sterility is confirmed, patients should use alternate forms of contraception. Because sperm is stored throughout the vas deferens and seminal vesicles, multiple ejaculations are required to fully evacuate all viable sperm. Answer A (incorrect answer): It is important for patients to use an alternate form of contraception prior to following up for a semen analysis postoperatively to confirm sterility. Answer C (incorrect answer): Patients are actually encouraged to ejaculate after surgery to ensure that any viable sperm are evacuated. It is recommended that patients should have at least 20 ejaculations since the time of vasectomy prior to follow up for semen analysis. Vasectomy is considered a failure if viable sperm are present after greater than 20 ejaculations and greater than three months have elapsed since the procedure.

questions.explanation: Explanation Obstetrics and Gynecology>Obstetrics>Aneuploidy Screening AFP Alpha-fetoprotein ·Variesduringpregnancy ·Reportsasmultipleofmedianforgestationalage(Mo M) Reduced AFP(<0.5 Mo M) Increased AFP(>2.5 Mo M) Neural tubedefects Trisomy 21 or 18 Abdominalwalldefects(e.g,gastroschisis) Fetaldemise Incorrectgestational dating Multiplegestation Incorrectgestational dating Answer D (correct answer): This patient has an isolated increase in maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (Ms AFP) level (i.e., MSAFP more than 2.5 multiples of the median or Mo M). One potential cause of increased AFP levels is a neural tube defect such as meningocele. This patient is taking carbamazepine which, if taken in pregnancy, increases the risk of neural tube defects.Other causes of increased Ms AFP levels are abdominal wall defects such as gastroschisis and omphalocele, multiple gestation pregnancy and incorrect gestational dating. Answer A (incorrect answer): Fetal demise is associated with decreased rather than increased levels of AFP. Answers B and C (incorrect answers): Trisomy 21 (i.e., Down syndrome) and trisomy 18 (i.e., Edwards syndrome) are associated with decreased rather than increased levels of AFP. Additionally, Down syndrome is associated with increased beta-hc G, inhibin A and decreased unconjugated estriol levels while Edwards syndrome is characterized by decreased beta-hc G, unconjugated estriol, and decreased or normal inhibin A.

questions.explanation: Explanation Obstetrics and Gynecology>Obstetrics>Aneuploidy Screening Cell Free DNA cf DNA ·Somefetal DNAdetectableinmaternal circulation ·Canbeusedtoscreenforaneuploidy ·Maternal plasmamusthave adequatefetal cf DNA ·Testmyfind“noresult”ininadequatecases ·Notused before 10 weeksgestation(cf DNAlevelslow) ·Lowfetalcf DNAinobesewomen DNA Answer C (correct answer): Cell free DNA (cf DNA) is DNA found in the maternal plasma outside of cells. Some cf DNA comes from the fetus (the "fetal fraction") and can be used to screen for fetal aneuploidy. The fetal fraction can be identified after 10 weeks' gestational age but, in some women, the fetal fraction may remain low, leading to an indeterminate test result. Women with higher body weight have lower fetal fractions. For this reason, an indeterminate result may occur when cf DNA testing is performed in obese women. Answer A (incorrect answer): Although this patient has type 2 diabetes mellitus, this condition is not known to cause indeterminate cf DNA results in pregnant women. Answer B (incorrect answer): Although this woman has a past medical history of hypertension, this condition is not known to cause indeterminate cf DNA results in pregnant women. Answer D (incorrect answer): Although this patient smokes one pack of cigarettes per day, smoking is not known tocauseindeterminatecf DNAresultsinpregnantwomen.

questions.explanation: Explanation Obstetrics and Gynecology>Gynecology>Dysmenorrhea Gn RH Agonists Leuprolide,Nafarelin ·Second-linetherapyforendometriosis ·Binds to Gn RHreceptorsin pituitary ·Down-regulation of receptors Pituitarydesensitization→↓LH/FSH Gonadotropin Releasing Hormone (Gn RH) ·Leadsto amenorrhea andendometrial atrophy ·Maybegivenwithestrogen/progestins ·Minimizeshotflashesandmenopausalsymptoms Answer B (correct answer): Leuprolide is considered a second-line treatment for endometriosis. This patient with symptomatic endometriosis has not improved despite an adequate trial of a nonsteroidal anti- inflammatory medication and a combination oral contraceptive (Coc). Therefore, it is appropriate to use a second-line medication. Leuprolide is a gonadotropin-releasing hormone(Gn RH)agonist and actsbybinding Gn RH receptorsin the pituitary. Hyperstimulation of Gn RH receptors leads to pituitary desensitization and subsequent downregulation of Gn RH receptors, ultimately causing a drop in luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle- stimulating hormone (FSH) levels. Low levels of LH and FSH lead to a state of hypoestrogenism, causing amenorrhea and endometrial atrophy, which decrease the symptoms of endometriosis. Gn RH agonists (and Gn RH antagonists) may have side effects including hot flashes, fatigue, weight gain and decreased libido, so they are not commonly used as first-line agents. The use of combination oral contraceptives (Co Cs) or progesteroneadd-backtherapy alongside Gn RHagonists canmodulate thesesideeffects. Answer C (incorrect answer): Progestin-only medications can be used in the treatment of endometriosis to inhibit endometrial growth. Their mechanism of action is similar to COCs. Physical examination reveals multiple large clots and active bleeding from the cervix. She also demonstrates pallor, hypotension and tachycardia. Therefore, it is appropriate to forgo further workup and initially treat her heavy menses with COCs. Further workup may include thyroid-stimulating hormone, prolactin, follicle-stimulating hormone, estradiol, luteinizing hormone or coagulation studies. If symptoms do not improve after treatment with Co Cs, a pelvic ultrasound is recommended to assess for structural causes of Au B such as endometrial polyps, adenomyosis, leiomyomas or malignancies. Answer A (incorrect answer): The patient tried a course of ibuprofen which did not resolve her symptoms, therefore it is more appropriate to try another treatment modality, such as a Co C, rather than choosing another nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medication. Answer C (incorrect answer): A hysteroscopy can be performed in select cases of abnormal uterine bleeding. It allows for direct visualization of the endometrial cavity, can detect polyps, small fibroids and other lesions and indicate a need for hysteroscopy at this time. This may be reconsidered if she does not respond to initial treatment and pelvic ultrasound is suspicious for intrauterine pathology. Answer D (incorrect answer): Patients with thyroid dysfunction, both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism, may have abnormal uterine bleeding. This patient has no other clinical features of thyroid dysfunction so thyroid function studies are not the next best step. Symptoms of hypothyroidism include weight gain, cold intolerance and fatigue. Symptoms of hyperthyroidism include weight loss, heat intolerance and anxiety. Thyroid function

questions.question: A 25-year-old female returns to the clinic for follow up of recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis. She has been seen three times in the last six months for treatment of candida vaginitis and has been treated with oral fluconazole and topical clotrimazole with minimal effect. During her last visit to the clinic, a vaginal culture was taken which grew candida glabrata. Which of the following would be the best course of treatment in this patient?
questions.explanation: Explanation Obstetricsand Gynecology>Gynecology>Vaginitis Candida Glabrata Candida Glabrata ·Rarecauseofsymptomaticinfection ·Identifiedbycultureincomplexcases ·Poorlyresponsivetoazoles ·Treatment:intravaginalboric acid Answer E (correct answer): This patient has resistant vulvovaginal candidiasis caused by candida glabrata (rather than the more common candida albicans) based on a vaginal culture. Candida glabrata is a rare cause of symptomatic vaginitis. It is typically diagnosed by vaginal culture after complicated cases of candidiasis that do not respond to treatment with azoles. The optimal treatment for candida glabrata remains unknown, however, treatment options include topical boric acid and, if boric acid is ineffective, topical amphotericin B. Answers A and B (incorrect answer): This patient has already failed treatment with oral and topical azoles for presumed candida albicans. Now that she has been diagnosed with candida glabrata, topical boric acid is indicated. Answer C (incorrect answer): Amphotericin B is an antifungal used in refractory cases of fungal infection. First- line treatment for candida glabrata is topical boric acid. If the patient does not respond to intravaginal boric acid, vaginal amphotericin B suppositories can be considered.

questions.question: A 42-year-old female is seen in the clinic for vaginal itching that has been increasing over the past two weeks. She is otherwise feeling well and does not have abnormal vaginal discharge, painful urination, abdominal pain, nausea or vomiting. She had strep throat approximately one month ago that was successfully treated with amoxicillin. She takes ibuprofen as needed for mild headaches. She is in a monogamous relationship with her husband and takes combination oral contraceptives for birth control. She has never been pregnant. She is otherwise healthy and takes no other medications. She was recently seen by her primary care doctor who sent screening blood tests with the following results: HgbA1c 5.7%, total cholesterol of 195 mg/dL, triglycerides 75 mg/dL, LDL 100 mg/dL and HDL 60 mg/dL. Family history is significant for rheumatoid arthritis in her mother. The patient does not smoke or drink alcohol. Her BMI is 26.4 kg/m?. questions.explanation: Explanation Obstetrics and Gynecology>Gynecology>Vaginitis Vuvlovaginal Candidiasis Risk Factors ·Antibioticuse:depletionofnormalbacterialflora ·Diabetes(consider A 1 ctesting!) ·Immunosuppression Answer E (correct answer): In vulvovaginal candidiasis, commonly referred to as a "yeast infection", there is overgrowth of candida species of fungiin the vagina.Candida species are part of the normal vaginal flora in approximately 10 to 20% of women, and if allowed to grow excessively, these fungi can cause vaginitis. Risk factors include antibiotic use, (which depletes normal vaginal flora that keep candida levels low),diabetes, overgrowth of candida species. Clinically, vulvovaginal candidiasis predominately presents with vaginal itching, sometimes associated with burning or dysuria. Vaginal discharge may be minimal or absent. On physical exam, there is classically a thick, white, clumpy discharge in the vagina. It may be described as "cottage cheese" or "curd-like." There can also be erythema of the vulva and vaginal mucosa. There is typically minimal odor associated with candidal infections. Diagnosis may be confirmed by potassium hydroxide wet mount which shows budding yeast and pseudohyphae. First-line treatment for candida infections is oral or topical azoles. Answer A (incorrect answer): Diabetes with poor glycemic control is a risk factor for vulvovaginal candidiasis, but this woman does not have diabetes. Her recent screening showed a hemoglobin A 1 c of 5.7%, which is below the diagnostic cutoff of 6.5% for diabetes. It is important to note that candidiasis can be a presenting symptom Answer B (incorrect answer): Multiparity, not nulliparity, is associated with an increased risk for vaginal candidiasis.

questions.question: A 23-year-old female presents with painful urination and new yellowish vaginal discharge. She also reports vaginal itching and discomfort. She is sexually active with a new partner and she uses combination oral contraceptives for birth control. She has never been pregnant and does not use barrier protection. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation: Explanation Obstetrics and Gynecology>Obstetrics〉Abortion Complete Spontaneous Abortion ·Documentedintrauterinepregnancy ·Bleedingand cramping ·Closed cervicalo S ·Noproductsofconception(Po C)evident ·Noevidenceofectopicpregnancy ·Management: supportive ·Antibiotics insome cases Methylergonovinemaybe used:↓retained tissue and infectionrisk Answer A (correct answer): This patient with previously documented intrauterine pregnancy presents with vaginal bleeding, abdominal cramping and a decreased fundal height relative to the gestational age. questions.question: A 25-year-old G1P0 woman comes to the physician at 13-weeks' gestation for an initial prenatal visit. She has no concerns. She does not drink alcohol or smoke cigarettes. Her vital signs include a temperature of 96.8°F, a blood pressure of 110/80 mmHg, a heart rate of 85 beats/min and a respiratory rate of 16 breaths/min. The physical examination reveals the uterine fundus at the level of the pubic symphysis. A transabdominal ultrasound shows two embryos surrounded by one chorion and two amnions. On which day after conception did the zygote cleavage most likely occur?
questions.explanation: Explanation Obstetrics and Gynecology>Obstetrics>Multiple Gestation DICHORIONIC DIAMNIOTIC Monozygotic Twins ·Dichorionic,diamniotic ·Days 1-3 ·Mayhave twoplacentas ·Monochorionicdiamniotic SEPARATEPLACENTAE 2 CHORIONS ·Days 4-8 2 AMONS ·Chorionalreadyunderdevelopment ·Monochorionicmonoamniotic MONOCHORIONIC DIAMNIOTIC MONOCHORIONICMONOAMNIOTIC ·Days 9-12 ·Chorionandamnionalreadyunderdevelopment ·Conjoined twins ·Day 13+ ·Alsomonochorionicmonoamniotic SINGLEPLACENTAE SINGLEPLACENTAE 1 CHORION 1 CHORION 2 AMNIONS 1 AMNON Answer C (correct answer): Two embryos surrounded by one chorion and two amnions are monochorionic diamniotic twins. Twins can be either dizygotic or monozygotic. Dizygotic twins are conceived by simultaneous fertilization of two eggs by two sperm cells. In contrast, monozygotic twins are conceived by fertilization of one egg by one sperm cell followed by zygote cleavage, which creates two embryos with identical genetics. Dizygotic twins will always be dichorionic and diamniotic. For monozygotic twins, the characteristics of the chorion and amnion will depend on the days after fertilization that the zygote cleaves. Both the amnion and chorion line the amniotic cavity. The amnion is the inner membrane of the uterine cavity and the chorion is the outer membrane. Pregnancies may be mono- or di- chorionic and mono- or di- amniotic. If zygote cleavage occurs within the first four days after conception dichorionic diamniotic twins develop, similar to the development of dizygotic twins with each twin having its own chorionic and amniotic membrane. Ifcleavageoccursfrom 4 to 8 daysafterfertilization,monochorionicdiamniotictwinswilldevelop.Duringthis time period, the chorionic sac has already formed and will be shared by both twins, although each will develop its own amniotic sac. If cleavage occurs from 8 to 12 days, monochorionic monoamniotic twins develop where the twins share a single chorion and amnion. Finally, if zygote cleavage happens after 13 days, there is a significant risk of incomplete cleavage which results in conjoined twins. This patient has monochorionic diamniotic twins, therefore zygote cleavage likely occurred between 4 and 8 days after fertilization. Answers A and B (incorrect answers): Zygote cleavage which occurs between days 1 and 3 leads to the development of dichorionic diamniotic twins.

questions.question: A 24-year-old G2P1 woman comes to the physician at 36-weeks' gestation for a routine prenatal visit. She has a past medical history of cesarean section with her first pregnancy due to breech presentation. Her vital signs include a temperature of 97°F, a blood pressure of 120/75 mmHg and a heart rate of 93 beats/min. The physical examination reveals the uterine fundus 27 cm from the pubic symphysis. Transabdominal ultrasound reveals that the fetal long axis is perpendicular to the maternal long axis. Which of the following terms best describes the fetal lie in this pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Explanation Obstetricsand Gynecology>Obstetrics>Laborand Delivery I Fetal Lie and Presentation ·Fetallie:longaxisoffetuscomparedtolongaxisofmother ·Longitudinal,transverseoroblique ·Fetalpresentation:partoffetusoverlyingpelvicinlet ·Mostcommonpresentation:longitudinal,cephalic ·Breech presentation:longitudinal,buttockspresenting OBLIQUETRANSVERSE CEPHALIC BREECH Answer B (correct answer): The fetal lie indicates the position of the fetal long axis relative to the maternal long axis. Since the fetal long axis is perpendicular to the maternal long axis in this pregnancy, the fetal lie is transverse. Vaginal delivery of a baby with a transverse lie is associated with an increased risk of maternal and perinatal complications. In 85% of pregnancies, the fetus spontaneously converts to a longitudinal lie before delivery. The safest fetal position for vaginal delivery is a longitudinal lie with a cephalic presentation. If spontaneous conversion from a transverse lie does not occur, external cephalic version (Ec V) can be performed. Ec V is the manual conversion of the fetus from non-longitudinal to longitudinal lie by the obstetrician using a specific technique of sequential pressure on the abdomen. If Ec V is unsuccessful, a fetus with a transverse lie generally requires a cesarean delivery. Answer A (incorrect answer): The longitudinal fetal lie is present when the fetal long axis is parallel to the maternal long axis. Answer C (incorrect answer): The oblique fetal lie occurs when the angle between fetal and maternal long axis is between 0 and 90 degrees.

questions.question: A 27-year-old G2P1 woman presents to the emergency department in active labor and delivers a female infant via spontaneous vaginal delivery. The mother had no prenatal care. Her first child was born at home. Immediately after delivery, the baby appears in respiratory distress. She is pale with generalized edema. Apgar scores are 5 and 6. The baby is warmed and stimulated, and her oropharynx is suctioned. Due to ongoing respiratory distress, she is intubated and placed on mechanical ventilation. On transfer to the NICU, vital signs show a temperature of 98.6°F, heart rate of 170 beats per minute obtained: Lab results Hemoglobin:11.7mg/dL Hematocrit:35% Peripheralbloodsmear:anisocytosisandpolychromasia Totalbilirubin:44mg/dL DirectCoombs'test:stronglypositive A diagnosis of hemolytic disease of the newborn is made. which of the following most likely represents the blood type of the mother and baby?
