This can occur when an Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive baby. If a Rh-negative mothercarries an Rh-positive fetus, she can develop antibodies against the Dantigen on Rh- positive fetal red blood cells. This is called Rh D alloimmunization. In subsequent pregnancies with an Rh- negative baby, these antibodies can lead to hemolysis of fetal red blood cells. Rho GAM is given to Rh-negative mothers in each pregnancy to prevent the development of antibodies against the baby's Rh-positive blood cells. In mothers who do not have access to adequate prenatal care, however, Rh D alloimmunization may occur. This Rh-negative mother has antibodies against the D antigen on her baby's Rh-positive blood cells. The ABO blood type of themother and fetus is not relevant.If an Rh-negative mothercarries an Rh-positive fetus,and maternal and fetal blood cells mix, the mother's immune system can form antibodies that will attack the fetus' Rh-positive blood cells in subsequent pregnancies. This mother is likely to be Rh-negative and her baby is likely to be Rh-positive.

questions.question: A 35-year-old G2P1 woman at 38-weeks' gestation is found to have a persistent breech presentation at a routine prenatal visit. Her first baby was born by spontaneous vaginal delivery with no complications. On examination, the cervix is 1 cm dilated with 20% effacement, and the fetal station is -3. questions.explanation: Explanation Obstetrics and Gynecology>Obstetrics>Labor and Delivery Complications Breech Presentation Managementwith Cephalic Version ·External cephalicversion ·Performed afterweek 37 ·Abdominal pressure toturnfetal position ·Successfulabout 50%ofcases ·More often successful inparouswomen ·Selection criteria: ·Normal fetal heart tracing ·Adequateamnioticfluid-absenceof Ro M ·Presenting part not descended tobirth canal ·No placental abruption or previa Answer B (correct answer): This patient with breech presentation at 38-weeks' gestation is a candidate for external cephalic version, a procedure in which external pressure is applied to the abdomen in an attempt to convert a fetus from breech presentation to vertex presentation. Breech presentation refers to fetal positioning in the uterus with the buttocks or the feet closest to the cervix, rather than a head-down (vertex) position. This patient is an appropriate candidate for external cephalic version because she has a breech presentation at term with a normal fetal heart tracing and adequate amniotic fluid.In addition,the fetusis not engaged in the birth canal, she is not in labor and there is no evidence of placental abruption or placenta previa. In deliveries complicated by shoulder dystocia, the head is delivered but the fetus' anterior shoulder gets stuck against the mother's pubic bone. Standardized maneuver such as the Mc Roberts maneuver (lifting the mother's legs to her abdomen) and suprapubic pressure may be used to facilitate delivery. Most babies with shoulder dystocia have no complications; however, excessive stretching of the baby's head or neck may occur during delivery, which can injure nerves of the brachial plexus. These Erb's palsy presents with unilateral upper extremity weakness with internal rotation of the arm and flexion at the wrist, sometimes called a "waiter's tip" deformity. Stretching nerve injuries usually resolve over time, but tearing injuries may result in permanent weakness and sensory impairment. questions.question: A 31-year-old G2P1 woman is brought to the emergency department at 38-weeks' gestation due to regular uterine contractions and leakage of clear fluid from the vagina. She has a past medical history of intermittent asthma treated with albuterol, and hypertension treated with labetalol. Cervix is 80% effaced and dilated to 8 cm. Thirty minutes later, she delivers a baby girl via vaginal delivery in the emergency department. Apgar scores are 8 and 9 at one and five minutes. The placenta is delivered and is intact on visual inspection. After delivery of the placenta, she has profuse vaginal bleeding that does not resolve with uterine massage. Her vital signs include a temperature of 96.8°F, blood pressure of 95/80 mmHg and cervical or vaginal lacerations. Laboratory tests at the time of presentation were normal. which of the following interventions is indicated in this patient?
questions.explanation: Explanation Obstetrics and Gynecology>Obstetrics>Postpartum Uterine Atony ·First-line treatments:oxytocin anduterinemassage ·Additional“uterotonic”therapiesmayberequired ·Methylergonovine ·Mayraisebloodpressure ·Contraindicatedwithhistoryofhypertension ·Carboprost ·Prostaglandin analog ·Contraindicatedinasthma ·Misoprostol ·Severecases:balloontamponade,embolizationorhysterectomy Answer D (correct answer): This patient with significant and persistent postpartum vaginal bleeding, hypotension, tachycardia and a boggy uterus most likely has uterine atony. Uterine atony is the lack of uterine smooth muscle contraction after delivery of the fetus. The myometrium normally contracts after delivery to constrict uterine blood vessels which prevents hemorrhage. If contraction is absent or insufficient, severe postpartum bleeding can result. Thebestinitialstepsinthemanagementofuterineatonyareuterinemassageandoxytocin,bothofwhich stimulate uterine contractions. If uterine massage and oxytocin are ineffective at controlling postpartum hemorrhage, then uterotonic medications such as methylergonovine, carboprost and misoprostol may be used. If uterotonic medications are also ineffective, procedures such as intrauterine balloon tamponade, uterine artery embolization or hysterectomy may be required. Answer A (incorrect answer): Methylergonovine can be used in patients with uterine atony if uterine massage and oxytocin are ineffective for controlling postpartumhemorrhage;however,it is contraindicated inpatients with hypertension. Answer B (incorrect answer): Carboprost can be used in patients with uterine atony if uterine massage and asthmatic patient due to its bronchoconstrictive properties.

questions.question: A 29-year-old G1P1 woman comes to her physician six days after delivering a baby girl at 39-weeks' gestation, reporting delivery. The patient has no dysuria or urinary frequency. Her vital signs include a option for this patient?
questions.explanation: Explanation Obstetrics and Gynecology>Obstetrics >Postpartum Septic Pelvic Thrombophlebitis Diagnosis ·Suspectedinpatientswithpersistentfeverdespite antibiotics ·Oftenadiagnosisofexclusion,provenbyresponsetoanticoagulant ·Diagnosis:CT or MRI ·Bestforidentificationofovarianveinthrombophlebitis ·Negative study does not exclude SPT ·Small,deeppelvicbranchesnotwellvisualized Pelvic CTScan ·Empiric treatment whenimaging negative with ongoingfevers ·Treatment:antibioticsplusanticoagulation ·Broad-spectrum antibiotics(gentamicin+clindamycin) ·Intravenous heparin or LMWH Answer E (correct answer): This patient with lower abdominal pain, a fever unresponsive to antibiotics and a rope-like mass extending from uterus to the lateral pelvis likely has septic pelvic thrombophlebitis. Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis is an infection and thrombosis of ovarian or deep pelvic veins. Ovarian septic pelvic thrombophlebitis presents with fever and lower abdominal pain within one week after delivery. Physical and thrombosed ovarian vein. Deep septic pelvic thrombophlebitis (another subtype of septic pelvic thrombophlebitis) has a more subtle presentation. These patients present with fever but are not acutely ill-appearing and abdominal or pelvic tenderness may be absent. Pelvic imaging may be normal or may show enlargement of an involved vein, sharp enhancement of the vessel wall or a filling defect from a thrombus. Sincesepticpelvic thrombophlebitisinvolvesbothinfectionand thrombosis ofpelvicveins,the treatment includes antibiotics and an anticoagulant. The preferred antibiotics are gentamicin and clindamycin. These are Typically,eitherintravenousheparinorlowmolecularweightheparin(enoxaparin)ispreferred. not cover the gram-negative bacteria that may cause septic pelvic thrombophlebitis.

questions.question: A 24-year-old G1p0 woman is evaluated for respiratory distress after delivering a healthy, male infant by spontaneous vaginal delivery. Her pregnancy, labor and delivery were uncomplicated. During physical examination, the patient develops generalized tonic-clonic seizures that resolve with intravenous diazepam. Her vital signs include a temperature of 97oF, blood for a hemoglobin of 8 mg/dL and platelet count of 90,000 cells/mm3. PT is 20 seconds, INR is 2 and PTT is 50 seconds. An amniotic fluid embolism may occur when amniotic fluid or fetal cells enter the maternal circulation. A generalized inflammatory reaction occurs against the amniotic fluid and fetal debris, which results in the clinical syndrome associated with amniotic fluid embolism.There are two phases of amniotic fluid embolism.In phase I, the patient presents with respiratory distress, hypoxemia and hypotension. Phase II is characterized by complications suchas disseminated intravascularcoagulation(DIC)andseizures.Patientsin DICmayhave thrombocytopenia, prolonged PT/INR and PTT as well as hemolytic anemia. Treatment for amniotic fluid embolism is primarily supportive and may include mechanical ventilation and fluid resuscitation.Amniotic fluid embolism is a rare but catastrophic condition that may be fatal despite supportive care. Answer A (incorrect answer): Sheehan syndrome is a pituitary gland infarction caused by significant postpartum hemorrhage. This patient did not have postpartum hemorrhage, and she has normal TSH and total T 4 levels, making Sheehan syndrome unlikely. questions.question: A 26-year-old G1P0 woman is admitted to the labor and delivery suite at 37-weeks' gestation with regular uterine contractions and leakage of clear fluid from the vagina. Her prenatal ultrasound at 12-weeks' gestation revealed a twin pregnancy. She has no significant past medical history. The patient undergoes vaginal delivery of vertex/vertex twins. The placenta is intact on visual inspection. Her vital signs 20 minutes after delivery include a temperature of 98.6°F, blood oxytocin. The physical examination reveals a boggy, minimally tender uterus with a normal postpartum cervix, vagina and vulva. The abdomen is otherwise soft and nontender. Coagulation studies are pending. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's postpartum bleeding?
questions.explanation: Explanation Obstetrics and Gynecology>Obstetrics>Postpartum Postpartum Hemorrhage Causes ·Uterine atony (most common) ·GU trauma(cervical lacerations) ·Coagulopathy ·Retainedplacentaormembranes Answer A (correct answer): This patient has significant postpartum bleeding and vital signs suggesting hypovolemic shock. Postpartum hemorrhage is the loss of 500 m L of blood after vaginal delivery or 10 o 0 m L of blood during cesarean delivery. The main causes of postpartum hemorrhage can be remembered by the 4 T's: Tone (uterine atony), Trauma (cervical or vaginal lacerations), Tissue (retained placenta) and Thrombin (coagulopathy). The most common cause of postpartum hemorrhage is uterine atony. Risk factors for uterine atony include uterine distension from multiple gestation pregnancy, macrosomia, prolonged labor, uterine fibroids, excessive oxytocin use and magnesium sulfate administration. A boggy uterus on postpartum physical examination, as is found in this patient, is suggestive of uterine atony. Answer B (incorrect answer): Disseminated intravascular coagulation can cause postpartum hemorrhage, but uterine atony is a more common cause. This patient with twin pregnancy has an increased risk for uterine atony. Answer C (incorrect answer): Although cervical laceration can cause postpartum hemorrhage, uterine atony is a more common cause. This patient has a normal cervical exam.

questions.question: A 36-hour-old full-term infant is transferred to the NICU for poor feeding. The infant's temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), heart rate is 130/min and respiratory rate is 45 breaths/min. Laboratory evaluation reveals a serum glucose of 38 mg/dL and a venous hematocrit of 67%. Which of the following is the most likely etiology for this infant's current symptoms?
questions.explanation: Explanation Pediatrics>Newborns>Delivery Room Care Polycythemia of the Newborn ·Newbornsnormallyhaveincreasedredcellmass ·Fetus in a relatively hypoxic environment in utero ·Usual hematocrit healthy infants: 61% ·Splenomegaly normal in newborns ·Polycythemia:hematocrit>65% ·Occurs in 1 to 5% of newborns ·Most common cause: delayed cord clamping ·Delayed cord clamping (T cord RBCs) ·More likely with IUGR/placental insufficiency ·Preeclampsia, SGA, post-term babies Answer B (correct answer): This infant has polycythemia, which is defined as peripheral venous hematocrit concentration greater than 2 standard deviations above the normal value for gestational and postnatal age clamping. This leads to the transfer of maternal red blood cells into the newborn circulation. Less commonly, polycythemia results from increased erythropoiesis in the newborn. This may be seen when the baby is exposed to hypoxia in utero, such as with placental insufficiency caused by maternal hypertension, maternal smoking and high altitude. Infants are usually asymptomatic but can present with hypoglycemia (secondary to increased red blood cell glucose utilization), hyperbilirubinemia (secondary to increased breakdown of red blood cells), vomiting, and poor feeding. Diagnosis is made by elevated hematocrit, and patients should also be monitored for hypoglycemia and hyperbilirubinemia. Treatment options in symptomatic patients include IV hydration and partial exchange transfusion. Answer A (incorrect answer): Prolonged rupture of membranes is associated with an increased risk of neonatal sepsis. Patients with sepsis can present with fever, hypothermia, irritability, hypoglycemia and poor feeding. score of less than 6. Neonatal sepsis is not associated with polycythemia. Answer C (incorrect answer): Maternal diabetes is associated with an increased risk of neonatal hypoglycemia. Patients are most commonly symptomatic, but can also present with lethargy, irritability and seizures. Neonatal hypoglycemia can also occur in the setting of polycythemia secondary to excessive red blood cell glucose utilization. While maternal diabetes can lead to polycythemia, delayed cord clamping is the most common causeofanelevatedhematocrit Answer D (incorrect answer): Rh incompatibility is associated with the development of erythroblastosis fetalis, also known as hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN). Infants present in the first 24 hours of life with jaundice (caused by increased bilirubin production), tachycardia, lethargy and poor feeding. Laboratory abnormalities include indirect hyperbilirubinemia and anemia, along with increased reticulocyte count and a positive direct or indirect antibody test.

questions.question: A full-term newborn infant is evaluated at 1 hour of life. The mother is concerned because the infant is breathing fast and grunting. Delivery was complicated by meconium stained amniotic fluid. The infant is afebrile with a heart rate of 130 beats/min, respiratory rate of 55 breaths/min and an oxygen saturation of 88% on room air. Physical examination is heart sound and the lungs are clear. Which of the following is most likely to provide a definitive diagnosis in this infant?
questions.explanation: Explanation Pediatrics>Newborns>Delivery Room Care PPHN Persistent Pulmonary Hypertensionofthe Newborn ·Pulmonaryvascularresistanceshouldfall atbirth ·Oxygen to lungs → PVR falls ·Persistenthigh PVR→shunting→hypoxemia ·Fetal shunts persist (foramen ovale, ductus arteriosus) ·Apparentduringfirst 24 hoursof life ·Respiratory distress and cyanosis ·Low Apgar scores ·Often co-occurs with meconium-stained amniotic fluid · Usually occurs in term infants bymeconiumaspirationsyndrome.PPHNprimarilyoccursinterminfantsandisassociatedwithpersistent elevation in pulmonary vascular resistance, which leads to right-to-left shunting through the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus, leading to hypoxemia. Other risk factors include both large and small for gestational age babies, maternal Ss RI use, maternal diabetes and advanced maternal age (over 35 years). Patients with PPHN present with respiratory distress (hypoxemia, tachypnea, retractions and grunting) within the first 24 hours of life. Other signs include cyanosis, meconium staining, a prominent second heart sound (an indicator of high pulmonary arterial pressure) and a harsh systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border (caused by tricuspid insufficiency). Chest x-ray is normal and definitive diagnosis is made based on echocardiogram findings (right-to-left shunting and a displaced ventricular septum). Treatment includes 100% oxygen (which functions as a pulmonary vasodilator), inhaled nitric oxide (relaxes pulmonary vascular smooth Answer A (incorrect answer): Chest x-ray findings are most commonly normal in patients with PPHN. Abnormal findings are associated with the underlying cause, such as congenital diaphragmatic hernia or meconium aspiration. Patients with PPHN caused by meconium aspiration can have abnormal chest x-ray findings, including hyperinflation, flattened diaphragms and diffuse patchy densities. questions.explanation: Explanation Pediatrics>Newborns>Delivery Room Care Neonatal Resuscitation Apnea/gaspingandheartrate<1 oobpm ·First step: positive pressure ventilation ·Intubation ·Chest compressions ·Epinephrine via umbilical vein ·Laboredbreathingorcyanosiswithheartrate≥1 oobpm · Clear airway ·Use pulse oximetry to monitor O 2 ·Administer supplemental oxygen Answer B (correct answer): This infant has bradycardia which is most likely caused by neonatal hypoxia. The most appropriate first step in infants who are apneic AND have a heart rate below 1 oo beats/min is at least 15 seconds of positive pressure ventilation (Pp V) with a self-inflating bag at a rate of 40 to 60 breaths/min. In addition to Pp V, infants should have pulse oximetry and electrocardiographic monitoring within 1 minute of delivery. If the heart rate does not improve with Pp V, the next steps include repositioning (infants should be placed on their back with the neck slightly extended), suctioning of the nose and mouth, and adjusting the mask to ensure an airtight seal. Answer A(incorrectanswer):Chestcompressionsareindicatedinnewbornswithaheartratelessthan 60 beats/min despite adequate Pp V for 30 seconds. questions.question: A newborn infant is assessed at 1 minute of life. The infant has a heart rate of 110 beats/min, a weak cry, and coughs and Which of the following is this infant's 1-minute APGAR score?
questions.explanation: Explanation Pediatrics>Newborns>Delivery Room Care Apgar Scores Sign All pink All blue Blue extremities Appearance >100 bpm Pulse <100 bpm Absent Absence Weak grimace Cough/cry Grimace Limp Activity Some flexion Fully active Weak cry Absent Good cry Respiratory Answer C (correct answer): This infant has a 1-minute APGAR score of 7. The APGAR score is assigned to children at 1 and 5 minutes of life and is used to assess the status of a newborn infant immediately after birth. Infants are assigned a score of O, 1, or 2 in five categories: appearance, pulse, grimace, activity, and respiratory status. Approximately 90% of infants have an APGAR score of 7 to 10. Infants with an APGAR score below 7 require further evaluation and may require interventions (including resuscitation).

questions.question: An 18-month-old female presents for a well-child visit. Her mother is concerned because she frequently loses her balance while walking. The mother has noted repetitive hand movements such as clapping and wringing and reports that the child is no longer speaking in two-word phrases. The patient is afebrile with normal vital signs. Her length is at the 30th percentile for age, her weight is at the 25th percentile for age and her head circumference is at the 15th percentile for age. Of note, her for a broad-based gait with mild ataxia. which of the following is the inheritance pattern for the most likely cause of this child's symptoms?
questions.explanation: Explanation Pediatrics>General Pediatrics>Developmental Milestones Rett Syndrome Genetics ·X-linked disorder ·X-linked dominant:1 abnormal gene→disease ·99%cases:sporadicgenemutation ·Girls ·Two Xchromosomes ·Random Xinactivation>somecellswithnormalgene ·Males ·One Xchromosome:all abnormal genes ·Lethal Answer D (correct answer): This patient has Rett syndrome, an X-linked dominant neurodevelopmental disorder that primarily occurs in females. The most common cause is a mutation in the MECP 2 gene on the X chromosome and 99% of cases result from a sporadic (de novo) mutation. Patients develop normally in the first year of life and then begin to lose developmental milestones. Patients present with stereotypic hand movements, gait abnormalities and deceleration of head growth. Abnormalities include hand clapping and wringing, ataxia, loss of speech and cognitive decline. Diagnosis is made based on a combination of clinical presentation and the identification of a mutation in the MECP 2 gene. There is no cure for Rett syndrome and treatment is multidisciplinary, including aggressive nutrition and symptomatic management.

Answer B (incorrect answer): 2-year-olds can run well, kick a ball, climb two steps, undress but not dress themselves, speak in two-word sentences, follow two-step commands, stack six blocks, copy a line and have a 50- to 200-word vocabulary. Red flags at 2 years of age include a vocabulary of less than 50 words, an inability to climb the stairs and an inability to feed and undress themselves. The child can sit up without support but does not walk. The child responds to his name, smiles and babbles, but does not wave bye-bye. Red flags at 6 months of age include lack of smile (4-month milestone), not rolling over and a lack of head control. Answer A (incorrect answer): A 2-month-old child can begin to smile at people, make gurgling and cooing sounds, turn their head towards sounds, begin to follow things with eyes and recognize people at a distance and lift their head up when prone. Diagnosis is based on clinical history and improvement within hours after withdrawal of the affected protein. The gold standard for diagnosis is an oral food challenge, but this is not necessary in patients with a history of vomiting and diarrhea that resolves after stopping a cow's milk or soy-based formula. Infants with FPIES should be transitioned to a casein hydrolysate-based (hypoallergenic) formula. This leads to villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia of the small intestine. Infants present with vomiting, diarrhea and failure to thrive, but can also have bloody stools. There is a history of phenylketonuria in a paternal aunt. She is interested in breastfeeding her child. which of the following would be an absolute contraindication to breastfeeding this infant?

Women with HIV infection in developing countries may breastfeed if there are no other safe or affordable options for breast milk replacement. questions.explanation: Explanation Pediatrics>Other Topics>Pediatric Orthopedics Legg-Calvé-Perthes Disease Diagnosis and Treatment Legg-Calve-Perthes Disease ·Insensitive · May be normal in early disease ·MRI: very sensitive ·Treatment: ·Avoid weight bearing ·Splinting ·Rarely requires surgery (controversial) · Often resolves (bone heals) ·Can lead to early osteoarthritis Answer A(correctanswer):Thispatienthas Legg-Calve-Perthes(Lc P)disease,asyndromeofidiopathic avascular necrosis of the hip that occurs most commonly in children aged 4 to 8. Risk factors include male gender (4:1 male to female ratio), a family history of LCP and underlying conditions (renal failure, HIV and systemic lupus erythematosus). Patients most commonly present with a painless limp that does not improve with rest or Ns AID therapy, along with decreased internal rotation and abduction of the hip. Hip x-rays may miss LCP disease. Definitive diagnosis is made with hip MRI, which reveals bone marrow changes consistent with avascular necrosis of the femoral head. Initial management includes non-weight bearing and splinting with a goal of containing the femoral head within the acetabulum. Over time, the femoral head will heal in most cases, particularly in children diagnosed before 6 years of age. Answer B (incorrect answer): Glucocorticoid injections are not useful in the management of children with LCP. Glucocorticoid injections in children are primarily used as initial management in patients with oligoarticular and polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA). Answer C (incorrect answer): Surgical stabilization is not necessary in most patients with LCP and there are no initial treatment of choice in patients with LCP. Surgical stabilization is the treatment of choice for patients with SCFE.

SCFE is the most common hip disorder in adolescents and occurs most commonly in overweight children aged 12 to 14.Patients with SCFEpresent with pain (hip, groin, thigh or knee) that is worse with physical activity, altered gait and usually no history of trauma. LCP occurs in younger children(most commonly age 4 to 8), most commonly presents with a painless limp. X-rays are frequently normal early in the course of the disease; MRI is more sensitive and is ordered in cases of high clinical suspicion with a negative x-ray. questions.explanation: Explanation Pediatrics>Other Topics>Pediatric Orthopedics Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip Diagnosis ·Often runs in families ·Clinicaldiagnosiswithimagingconfirmation Hip Ultrasound ·Less than 4 months:ultrasound ofhip ·X-rays have limited value ·Bones are cartilaginous and not ossified ·More than 4 months:X-ray Answer C (correct answer): This patient has developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) caused by abnormal development of the acetabulum and proximal femur. Risk factors include female gender, breech position in the 3 rd trimester (the most significant risk factor) and a family history of DDH. Patients present with hip instability, include a palpable clunk while pushing the trochanter anteriorly during hip abduction (the Ortolani maneuver - reduces a dislocated hip) and palpable clunk with hip adduction (the Barlow maneuver - induces dislocation of the hip). The most appropriate first step in evaluating infants under 4 months of age is a hip ultrasound. Treatment options include abduction splint and surgical reduction; long-term complications include avascular necrosis and earlyonsetofosteoarthritis. Answer A (incorrect answer): A hip x-ray is appropriate in patients with DDH who are older than 4 months of age. X-rays under 4 months of age are not useful because the femoral head and acetabulum are cartilaginous and unossified. X-ray findings in older infants include lateral and superior positioning of the ossified portion of the femoral head and neck as well as delayed ossification. Answer B (incorrect answer): An abduction splint (e.g., Pavlik harness) is the most appropriate initial treatment of DDH in children under 6 months of age. The Pavlik harness prevents hip extension and limits adduction (which can lead to dislocation)butpermits flexion and abduction.It is generally required for two to three months.The most common complications of the Pavlik harness are osteonecrosis and skin breakdown. This child needs a firm diagnosis prior to the use of an abduction splint.

questions.question: An 8-year-old male presents with facial tics. His mother noticed the onset of facial grimacing and frequent eye blinking twelve months ago, and the symptoms are getting worse. She also noticed grunting noises that occur frequently throughout the day. The patient is in the 3rd grade and gets As and Bs in school. His weight is at the 4Oth percentile for age and his minute, and intermittent facial grimaces. Which of the following is the most appropriate drug to treat this child's current symptoms?
questions.explanation: Explanation Pediatrics > Other Topics > Child Psychiatry Tourette Syndrome Treatment ·Behavioral therapy(especially if OCD,ADHD) ·Antipsychotics VMAT ·Haloperidol, pimozide, and aripiprazole ·Fluphenazine,Risperidone ·May cause tardive dyskinesia ·Tetrabenazine("dopamine depletion") ·Inhibits VMAT-2(vesicularmonoamine transporter type 2) ·Blocks uptake of dopamine synaptic vesicles (pre-synapse) D 2 ·Less dopamine storage/release Answer D (correct answer): This patient has new onset Tourette syndrome, a neurologic disorder characterized by motor and phonic tics. Patients present during childhood with motor tics (eye blinking, facial grimacing, shoulder shrugging, and head jerking) and phonic tics (grunting, barking, moaning, throat clearing, sniffing and hollering) that have been present for at least one year. Treatment options include habit reversal training, alpha- 2 agonists and antidopaminergic drugs. Habit reversal training focuses on tic awareness and voluntary movements that are incompatible with the motor or phonic tic. Medication is more effective in most children and antidopaminergic drugs are first-line therapy. Tetrabenazine inhibits vesicular monoamine transporter type 2 (VMAT), leading to dopamine depletion. Side effects include sedation, depressed mood and Parkinson-like symptoms, although the side effects are less common with Tetrabenazine than with typical and atypical antipsychotic drugs, such as haloperidol and aripipazole. Answer A (incorrect answer): Fluoxetine is first-line treatment for obsessive compulsive disorder, which is found depression.Fluoxetine is not effective in treating motor or phonictics. Answer B (incorrect answer): Methylphenidate is first-line treatment for ADHD, which is found in up to 60% of patients with Tourette syndrome. Stimulant drugs, such as methylphenidate, are associated with new onset of tics and worsening symptoms in children with tic disorders. Children with Tourette syndrome and ADHD benefit from alpha-2 agonists, including clonidine and guanfacine.

Other comorbid conditions include mood disorders, disruptive behavior and learning disability. Treatment options include behavioral therapy, alpha-2 agonists and antidopaminergic drugs.

questions.question: α current obstetric ultrasound showing oligohydramnios, she is scheduled for a cesarean section the following day. Which of the following is most likely to occur if this pregnancy were allowed to progress beyond 42 weeks?

The low rate of post-term pregnancies is because most women are induced or have a cesarean section before 42 weeks of gestation. The most important risk factor is a previous post-term pregnancy, but other risk factors include obesity, male fetus and advanced maternal age. macrosomia. questions.explanation: Explanation Pediatrics>Newborns>Pretermand Postterm Infants Large for Gestational Age Complications Shoulder Dystocia ·Macrosomia associatedwithbirthinjuries ·Maternal complications ·Vaginal lacerations ·Severepostpartum hemorrhage ·Increased likelihood of cesarean delivery ·Infant complications ·Shoulder dystocia ·Brachial plexus injury ·Clavicularfracture Answer B (correct answer): This infant is large for gestational age (LGA), which is defined as a birth weight greater than 4000 grams or above the 90 th percentile for gestational age. Risk factors include maternal diabetes, excess maternal weight gain during pregnancy and females who are overweight prior to pregnancy. Complications of LGA infants include hypoglycemia, polycythemia and birth injuries, including shoulder dystocia, clavicle fractures and brachial plexus injury. Following initial evaluation in the delivery room, the most appropriate next step in this infant with a 5-minute APGAR of 9, normal vital signs and a normal physical examination is skin-to-skin contact and immediate initiation of breastfeeding because of the increased risk of hypoglycemia. Up to 20% of LGA infants develop hypoglycemia in the first 24 hours of life. Answer A (incorrect answer): LGA infants should have a serum glucose performed immediately after the first feeding and every three to six hours for the first 48 hours of life because of the increased risk of hypoglycemia. There is no need to wait for the first serum glucose to initiate breastfeeding. Answer C (incorrect answer): Polycythemia occurs more frequently in LGA infants of both diabetic and nondiabetic mothers. Although LGA infants should have a venous hematocrit performed within the first 24 hours of life to rule out polycythemia, immediate initiation of feeding is a higher priority because of the increased risk of immediate hypoglycemia in LGA infants.

A midgut volvulus is characterized by twisting of the small intestine around the superior mesenteric artery, which leads to small bowel obstruction and ischemia. Patients present between three and seven days of life with bilious vomiting, mild abdominal distension, blood in the stool and may have signs of sepsis (fever, tachycardia and hypotension). Approximately 30% of patients with duodenal atresia have a chromosome anomaly(most commonly Trisomy 21).Other associationswith duodenal atresia include prenatal polyhydramnios (develops late in the 2 nd trimester), maternal smoking and maternal pseudoephedrine use. Polyhydramnios develops in pregnancies associated with duodenal atresia due to decreased fetal swallowing of amniotic fluid (any obstruction of intestinal flow can lead to decreased fetal swallowing and polyhydramnios). Patients with duodenal atresia present in the first one to two days of life with bilious vomiting and increasing abdominal distension. Abdominal x-ray classically reveals a "double-bubble" sign (distension of the duodenal stump and stomach) with no distal gas. Initial treatment includes making infants Np O (nothing by mouth), correcting electrolyte abnormalities and placing a nasogastric (NG) tube to decompress the stomach. Risk factors include recent viral infections (especially adenovirus), bacterial enteritis androtavirusvaccine.Patientspresentwithintermittent,severe andprogressive episodes of abdominal pain accompanied by periods of crying (the episodes last 15 to 20 minutes) along with streaks of blood in the stool and vomiting. questions.explanation: Explanation Pediatrics> Other Topics >Congenital Gastroenterology II Meckel's Diverticulum Diagnosisand Treatment Meckel's Diverticulum (technetium scan) .Technetiumscan ·Also called a“Meckel’s scan"” ·Tracertakenupbygastriccellsindiverticulum ·Treatment(symptomatic):surgery Answer D (correct answer): This patient has Meckel's diverticulum, the most common congenital GI tract anomaly. It is a true diverticulum (contains all three layers of the small intestinal wall) and frequently contains ectopic gastric tissue. Although most patients are asymptomatic, the most common presenting symptom in young children is painless rectal bleeding. The bleeding occurs as a result of ulceration of the small intestine caused by gastric acid secretion from ectopic gastric tissue. The rule of twos is a classic description of the features of Meckel's diverticulum: it occurs in approximately 2 percent of the population with a male-to-female ratio of 2:1, is located within two feet from the ileocecal valve and is two inches in length. The most appropriate diagnostic test in hemodynamically stable children is a technetium scan (or Meckel's scan). It is a nuclear medicine study used to identify ectopic gastric tissue with a sensitivity of 97% in pediatric patients. Treatment is surgical resection in symptomatic patients. Answer A(incorrectanswer):Abdominalultrasound isnotthediagnostictestofchoiceinpatientswith suspected Meckel's diverticulum or painless rectal bleeding. The infant is exclusively breastfed and had 1 wet diaper s o u s t s o h i i ss u p · Chloride: 95 mmol/L · Potassium: 2.7 mmol/L · Bicarbonate: 31 mmol/L Abdominal ultrasound demonstrates a pyloric muscle thickness of 9 mm (normal 3 to 4 mm). which of the following is the
questions.explanation: Explanation Pediatrics >Other Topics >Congenital Gastroenterology II Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis Target or Donut Sign String Sign ·Diagnosis:ultrasound (contrast X-ray) (ultrasound) “Target sign”or"Donut sign” ·Hypertrophied hypoechoicmuscle ·Surroundsmucosa ·Upper GI contrast X-ray ·Done if US equivocal ·String sign ·Elongated pyloric canal ·Treatment: .Volume resuscitation .Surgery Answer D (correct answer): This patient has moderate dehydration caused by infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (IHps), a form of gastric outlet obstruction caused by hypertrophy of the pylorus. Patents present between three and six weeks of life with non-bilious projectile vomiting but are hungry immediately after post- prandial vomiting. Other findings include a palpable mass in the right upper quadrant ("olive sign") and a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis on laboratory evaluation. While definitive management of IHPs is surgery, the initial treatment of infants is fluid and electrolyte management. Infants with moderate or severe dehydration require fluid resuscitation with a 20 cc/kg bolus of least 3.5 mmol/L,a serum chlorideof at least 100 mmol/L and a serum bicarbonate of less than 26 mmol/L. apnea. Answer A (incorrect answer): An upper GI contrast study is not appropriate in the initial evaluation or management of patients with IHPS; the first study for suspected IHPS is abdominal ultrasound. An upper GI series is most appropriate in patients with a nondiagnostic ultrasound and demonstrates an elongated pyloric canal (known as the "string sign"). They are not used to treat volume depletion as seen in this case. Maintenance fluids are appropriate in patients with normal electrolytevalues and no evidence of dehydration.Maintenance IVfluids should include 5%dextrose with one-half normal saline (0.45% Na Cl) and 10 to 20 m Eq KCl per L.

Otitis externa (OE) is defined as infection and inflammation of the external auditory canal and it occurs in all age groups. Risk factors for OE include swimming, trauma to the ear canal, hearing aids and contact dermatitis. Patients present with ear pain, pruritis, ear discharge and hearing loss. Physical examination reveals pain with ear manipulation, swelling and edema of the ear canal and white or gray debris coating the ear canal. Complications of OE are rare, and treatment is with ear drops. Mild disease is treated with a combination of acetic acid and hydrocortisone while moderate to severe infections are additionally treated with antibiotics such as ciprofloxacin or ofloxacin. Delayedcapillaryrefill(morethan 2 seconds) o Pallor o Cyanosis Ill-appearing infants require stabilization (including immediate fluid resuscitation), early empiric antibiotics (within one hour of presentation to the emergency department) for presumed bacterial infection, a complete laboratory evaluation that includes blood, urine and cerebrospinal fluid cultures and hospitalization. questions.question: A 75-day-old female presents to the emergency department with fever. She does not have upper respiratory symptoms or a rash. She was born at term and is feeding well. Her temperature is 101.4°F, heart rate is elevated at 140 beats/minute and management of this infant?
questions.explanation: Explanation Pediatrics>General Pediatrics>Ear Infections and Fevers FWS FWSin Infants Up to 90 Days of Age Infants 7 to 90 Days •High risk of sepsis orseptic shock • Work-up based on age • Many possible underlying infections · Youngcr infants [< 60 days] • Bacteremia • Hospitalization often necessary • Meningitis • Older infants [60 to 90 days) • Pneumonia • Septic arthritis · Approach varies by specific age group Boards Beyond Answer B (correct answer):Thisinfant hasfever withoutsource(Fws)at 75 days of age.Febrile infantsless than 90 days of age should receive treatment based upon their age and the level of concern for an invasive infection on examination and no recognizable viral infection such as bronchiolitis or influenza should have urine culture and either urine dipstick or microscopic urinalysis.Evaluation of the urine is indicated in infants of this age with Fws because infection of the urinary system often produces no symptoms other than fever. Patients with normal preliminary urine testing (negative dipstick for leukocytes and nitrites, less than 5 WBCs/hpf on spun urine, or less than 1 o WBCs/mm? and negative Gram stain) can be observed as an outpatient with close follow-up and no antibiotic therapy. Patients with abnormal findings on urinalysis should be started on oral antibiotics with close follow-up. Answer A (incorrect answer): Reassurance is not appropriate in febrile infants who are less than 90 days of age. At a minimum, all infants should have a urinalysis and urine culture. As explained above, urinary infection in infants can present as FWs with no localizing clinical signs. Answer C (incorrect answer): Hospitalization is indicated in all febrile infants under 29 days of age, in infants between 29 and 60 days of age who have abnormal urinalysis, complete blood count or lumbar puncture or temperature at or above 101.5°F or all sick-appearing infants under 90 days of age. There is no indication for hospitalization in this infant who is well appearing with no evidence of dehydration. Answer D (incorrect answer): A single dose of IM ceftriaxone (50 mg/kg) with close follow-up in 24 hours for a urinalysis, complete blood count and lumbar puncture and a temperature between 100.4°F and 101.4°F.

questions.question: A 16-year-old male is evaluated for an itchy skin rash. The rash started on his arms but has spread to his chest and thighs. He is sexually active, and his girlfriend developed cough and congestion two days ago. He also recently returned from a weekend hiking trip with his father and younger brother. He is in the 10th grade and plays football and basketball. His vital signs are normal. Physical exam reveals multiple dome-shaped, flesh-colored papules with central umbilication (see below image). His temperature is 100.7°F, his heart rate is elevated 1- to 2-mm gray spots on the buccal mucosa. Vitamin-A supplementation has been shown to improve outcomes in patients with measles. Primary prevention is with the MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine. Answer A(incorrectanswer):Pneumonia is the most common cause of death in childrenwith measles,but it occurs less frequently than diarrhea. Other pulmonary complications of measles include bronchiolitis and croup. Answer B (incorrect answer): Coronary artery aneurysms are not a complication of measles. Risk factors for cardiac complications in Kawaskai disease includelate diagnosis, delayed treatment with intravenous immune globulin (IVIG), male gender and age less than 6 months. questions.explanation: Explanation Psychiatry> Substance Abuse >Alcohol Use Disorder Alcohol Use Disorder Wernicke-Korsakoff ·Wernicke Encephalopathy ·Visual disturbances/nystagmus ·Gait ataxia · Confusion • Often reversible with thiamine ·Korsakoff Amnesia · Recent memory affected more than remote · Can't form new memories · Confabulation: Can't remember so makes things up · Lack of interest or concern (apathy) · Usually permanent Answer B (correct answer): This patient is presenting with short-term memory loss, confabulation and apathy, which is consistent with Korsakoff syndrome (Ks). KS is a manifestation of Wernicke encephalopathy, which is characterized by severe anterograde amnesia. The syndrome is most commonly seen in patients with alcohol use disorder after multiple episodes of Wernicke's encephalopathy, which is caused by thiamine deficiency. Clinically, KS presents with deficits in memory, especially in short-term memory and anterograde memory. Patients often demonstrate confabulation (fabricated speech) and apathy (lack of interest or concern). Attention and socialization are typically preserved. The diagnosis is made based on the clinical history. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain can demonstrate disproportionate atrophy of the mammillary bodies and medial thalamus. These MRI findings are specific for Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome and are different from thefindings seen in other dementia syndromes such as Alzheimer's disease.While Wernicke's encephalopathy can be reversed with thiamine treatment, Ks is irreversible, resulting in persistent cognitive dysfunction. In addition to his risk factors for Ks, this patient has normal blood counts, electrolytes, renal function, thyroid Answer A(incorrect answer):Ksis associated with alcohol use,but Ksis not reversible with abstinence from alcohol.

He drinks 12 beers a day and has done so for the last 10 years. He has been admitted for alcohol detoxification three times in the last year but has not had seizures. His home medications, which are continued during this hospitalization, include hydrochlorothiazide, diphenhydramine at bedtime and lorazepam 0.5 mg as needed for insomnia. Seventy-two hours after admission, the patient becomes agitated. He states, "I just have to get out of here, I don't know what the government is doing to me here." These findings are consistent with delirium tremens (DT). DT is a severe complication of alcohol withdrawal that occurs 48 to 96 hours after the intake of alcohol. Characteristic clinical featuresincludehallucinations, disorientation,agitation and autonomichyperactivity.Patients are at riskfor hypovolemia and electrolyte abnormalities, due to fluid loss from sweating and hyperthermia. Hyperventilation iscommonleadingtoarespiratoryalkalosiswhichdecreasescerebralbloodflow. Management of DT is primarily supportive. Benzodiazepines are used for psychomotor agitation and withdrawal signs areimportant components of the supportive treatment.DT generallylasts one tofive days. Answer A(incorrectanswer):Alcoholichallucinosispresentswithhallucinations thatdevelopwithin 24 hoursof the last alcoholic beverage and typically resolve within 24 to 48 hours. Patients remain oriented and are often ablerecognizethehallucinations,whichcausesdistress. Answer B (incorrect answer): Benadryl has anticholinergic properties. Anticholinergic toxicity presents with ("blind as a bat"), delirium ("mad as a hatter") and urinary retention ("full as a flask"). Delirium tremens and anticholinergic toxicity can be differentiated by the presence of diaphoresis which is absent in anticholinergic poisoning. Although this patient received the antihistamine diphenhydramine (which has anticholinergic side effects),chronic dailybedtime useis unlikelytocause an anticholinergictoxidrome.

questions.question: A 42-year-old man is brought to the hospital for acute alcohol intoxication. He was transferred by emergency medical services after being found outside of a local bar yelling at other patrons. The patient has a medical history of alcohol use disorder and alcoholic liver disease. He does not take any medications. He is admitted to the hospital where he is treated for alcohol withdrawal symptoms. At discharge he states "I know that I need to stop drinking." Over the years he has spoken to multiple doctors about abstinence support programs, but he doesn't want to pursue one now. He believes it will be too difficult to abstain and he doesn't think he has the willpower to stop drinking. This man is in which of the following stages of change for his alcohol use disorder?
questions.explanation: Explanation Psychiatry>Substance Abuse>Alcohol Use Disorder Stages of Change PROGRESS recontemplation Contemplation Preparation Action Maintenance Toddatkins Answer B (correct answer): Patients with substance use disorder go through several stages of change in making progress towards abstinence. This man is currently in the stage of change known as contemplation. During this Patients in this phase are often focused on the obstacles (e.g., lack of willpower) that make abstinence difficult. The stages of change model applies to any significant lifestyle change; it is not specific to substance use patient who has already prepared can be encouraged to begin taking action, and a patient who has achieved a goal can be encouraged to create a maintenance plan. opposed to contemplating or planning. Actions could include taking a medication shown to reduce alcohol Answer C (incorrect answer): By generating a strategic plan (preparation) and taking action on this plan (action), meaningful change can be accomplished. Once change has been successfully accomplished patients enter the maintenance phase. During the maintenance phase, the patient may modify the original plan, but will continue tomaintain the changesthatwere successfully achieved. Answer D (incorrect answer): During the precontemplation stage, the patient is not aware of the problem, is not interested in changing the behavior or may viewthe problem as having an external source.Thesepatients are notyetinterestedinconsideringmakingachange.

questions.question: A 61-year-old male presents for an annual wellness examination. He has hyperlipidemia that is treated with atorvastatin but is otherwise healthy and he has no concerns. Review of systems is negative for weight loss, fatigue, shortness of breath, headache, difficulty urinating and weakness. He does not use tobacco or illicit drugs but drinks 8-12 beers per day. He has had two driving while intoxicated citations in the past year. He is afebrile with a heart rate of 70 beats/min and a blood gynecomastia or other skin abnormalities. He has mild hepatomegaly. Laboratory evaluation reveals an AST of 1020 U/L and an ALT of 375 U/L. Which of the following findings are most likely in this patient?
questions.explanation: Explanation Psychiatry>Substance Abuse>Alcohol Use Disorder Alcohol Use Disorder ·Recurrent drinkingcausingimpairedsocialfunctioning ·Manymedical complications Chronic Pancreatitis ·Gastrointestinal ·Gastritis, hepatitis, cirrhosis, pancreatitis ·Cardiac ·Dilated cardiomyopathy, refractory hypertension ·Malignancy ·Esophageal and oropharyngeal cancers Answer C (correct answer): This patient has chronic alcohol use disorder (Au D), which is defined as a recurrent pattern of alcohol use that leads to significant functional impairment or distress (e.g., impaired work performance, home stress or legal difficulties associated with alcohol use). Risk factors include male gender, other substance use disorders and mood or personality disorders. Alcohol use disorder is associated with excess morbidity and mortality and is the 3 rd leading preventable cause of death in the United States. Laboratory findings in patients with AUD include elevated alkaline phosphatase, total bilirubin, gamma- glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT), alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST). In patients with AUD, AST is generally significantly more elevated than ALT. Other findings include elevated mean corpuscular volume (Mc V) secondary to folate and vitamin B 12 deficiency, elevated prothrombin time (PT), elevated partial thromboplastin time (PTT) and hypoalbuminemia. Impaired liver function results in impaired synthesis of clotting factors and albumin, resulting in elevated PT/PTT and reduced serum albumin. Medical complications of alcohol use disorder include resistant hypertension, cirrhosis, pancreatitis, hepatitis cancer. Answers A and B (incorrect answers): Patients with alcohol use disorder are at increased risk of hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia and hypophosphatemia. This is caused by a combination of decreased intake, malabsorption and increased renal losses. Answer D (incorrect answer): Patients with alcohol use disorder have elevated levels of GGT. questions.question: A 52-year-old woman presents for an annual evaluation. She reports intermittent abdominal pain, but has no headache, vomiting, diarrhea, shortness of breath or fatigue. She has lost five pounds in the last six months. She smokes one pack of cigarettes per day and drinks three to four beers and one bottle of wine per day. She reports that she has been using this amount of alcohol on and off since she was a teenager. She has a history of major depression and was hospitalized with a seizure two years ago after she stopped using alcohol. She is afebrile with a pulse of 75 beats/min and a blood pressure of 145/84 mmHg. Physical examination reveals bilateral erythematous macules and purpura of the legs and erythema of the thenar eminence. There is no jaundice. Her abdominal examination reveals abdominal distension and hepatomegaly. Laboratory evaluation reveals an aspartate aminotransferase (AsT) of 710 U/L and an alanine aminotransferase (ALT) of 215 U/L. Which of the following is the most likely complication in this patient?
questions.explanation: Explanation Psychiatry>Substance Abuse>Alcohol Use Disorder Alcohol Use Disorder ·Recurrent drinkingcausingimpairedsocialfunctioning ·Many medical complications Chronic Pancreatitis ·Gastrointestinal ·Gastritis, hepatitis, cirrhosis, pancreatitis ·Cardiac ·Dilated cardiomyopathy,refractory hypertension · Malignancy ·Esophageal and oropharyngeal cancers Answer B (correct answer): This patient has chronic alcohol use disorder (Au D), which is present in up to 15% of adults in the United States. Patients can be asymptomatic or present with features of advanced liver disease, angiomata,whichare telangiectasias on the face,trunk and upper extremities.Laboratoryfindingsinclude elevated alkalinephosphatase(oftentwotothree timesnormal),aswell aselevatedaspartate aminotransferase (As T), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), total bilirubin and gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT). In patients with AUD, AST is often elevated significantly more than ALT. Long term complications of AUD include cirrhosis, resistant hypertension, gastritis and dilated cardiomyopathy. Dilated cardiomyopathy is directly related to the amount and the duration of alcohol use. Most patients with alcohol-related cardiomyopathy have a history of at least 15 years of alcohol abuse with a daily intake of 80-90 g of ethanol (one liter of wine, eight standard-sized beers or one-half pint of hard liquor per day). Patients may present with shortness of breath, chest pain and jugular venous distension. Definitive diagnosis is made by blockers, ACE inhibitors and a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists. Answer A(incorrect answer): Restrictive cardiomyopathy is not associated with chronic alcohol abuse. Answer C (incorrect answer):Choreoathetosis,irregular contractions accompanied by slower twisting and writhing movements of the mouth, tongue, face and limbs, do not generally occur in the setting of Au D. This movement disorder may occur in patients with chronic use of dopamine antagonists, such as first-generation antipsychotic drugs.

questions.question: A 66-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with confusion and difficulty walking. Her husband reports that she has had trouble walking for the last 3 days. She reports blurry vision and has lost seven pounds in the last year. She has no fever, headache, chest pain, shortness of breath, difficulty urinating or weakness. She drinks approximately % pint of vodka per day and does not use tobacco or illicit drugs. Pathologic findings include atrophy of mammillary bodies in the medial thalamic nuclei. Diagnosisismadeclinicallyas thiamine testing is notreadilyavailableinmostclinicalsettings.Wernicke encephalopathy may be precipitated in patients with alcohol use disorder (AUD) by administration of intravenous (Iv) glucose without thiamine. Thiamine is a co-factor in glucose metabolism, so administering high doses of glucose in a thiamine deficient patient can acutely worsen thiamine deficiency. Because Wernicke encephalopathy may lead to coma and death if untreated, affected patients should receive IV thiamine for seven days. Oral thiamine is not sufficient because of poor gastrointestinal absorption. For example, playing contact sports is a socially acceptable way to express aggression. Answer C, D and E (incorrect answers): Repression, denial and undoing are unconscious defense mechanisms. questions.question: A 69-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital after a pathologic fracture of her right femur. She is informed that pathologic examination of her bone reveals malignant disease that is likely of gastrointestinal origin. A positron emission diagnosis and prognosis and recommends the chemotherapeutic drug capecitabine. The patient has a past medical history significant for asthma and generalized anxiety disorder. She works full-time as an engineer. On examination, the patient is appointment with the oncologist, but the patient responds "No thank you. I don't need that. I just have a broken leg." which of the following defense mechanisms is this patient using to manage her anxiety?
questions.explanation: Explanation Psychiatry>Abnormal Psychology>Defense Mechanisms Denial ·Refusingtoacceptunpleasantreality ·Examples: ·Patient thinks doctor is wrong about diagnosis ·Heavy drinker believes she drinks socially Peter/Flikr Answer D (correct answer): This patient was recently told that she has stage IV cancer which is likely to induce significant anxiety. In an effort to reduce her anxiety she is using the defense mechanism of denial, by stating that her only problem is a broken leg despite being told that she has advanced cancer. Denial is the refusal to admit, to oneself or others, an obvious truth that is supported by facts. Other examples include a patient who has multiple citations fordriving under the influence of alcoholyetrefuses toself-identify as analcoholic,or a parent who refuses to consider a speech delay in their child who is non-verbal at age four. Answer A (incorrect answer): Regression is a defense mechanism in which people revert to coping patterns or behaviors associated with earlier stages of development. If this patient were demonstrating regression she might rock back and forth, cuddle a stuffed animal or cry out for her mother in an effort to reduce her anxiety about having cancer. Answer B (incorrect answer): Reaction formation is a defense mechanism that reduces anxiety by adopting the feeling or behavior that is opposite to the feared feeling or reality. For example, a person afraid of failure may become obsessed with presenting signs of success or a father who feels disconnected from his child may shower them with gifts. He reports that he has a scheduled court appearance tomorrow. The patient has no other past medical history and takes no medications. He denies use of tobacco or illicit drugs. He works as a waiter. questions.explanation: Explanation Psychiatry>Psychiatric Disorders>Somatic Disorders Malingering ·Consciously falsified medical symptoms ·Doneforsecondary(external)gain ·Allows patient to miss work but get paid ·Obtain workman's compensation ·Self-limited ·Endswhen secondarygain achieved ·Nota DSM-V psychiatric disorder Answer E (correct answer): This patient's presentation is concerning for malingering. Malingering is not a for external motivation or secondary gain. External motives could include avoiding work or school, obtaining medications or housing and avoiding jail or military service.In this example, there is a clear discrepancy between the patient's complaint of hand pain and the objective physical examination and radiologic findings. Note that it would be unusual for a patient to developbruised knuckles from a fall on an extended hand. It is In contrast, primary gain occurs when patients benefit from illness by resolving an internal conflict. Some examples of primary gain include avoiding intimacy with a spouse, relieving guilt over infidelity or avoiding tasks atwork due tofear of inadequacy.A determination that a patient is malingering should be made cautiously. Answer A (incorrect answer): Antisocial personality disorder is characterized by a long record of reckless and deceitful behavior, aggression and a lack of remorse for behaviors that begins in childhood. This patient's remorse about the recent assault is not typical of antisocial personality disorder. Answer B(incorrectanswer):Conductdisorderisdefinedbyrecurrentactsthatviolatetherightsofothersor societal norms, including aggression to humans or animals, property destruction or theft. This patient has not beenarrestedbeforeand thereis noevidenceofrecurrentviolence. Answer C (incorrect answer):Factitious disorder(previously called Munchausen Syndrome)is theintentional falsification or exaggeration of physical or psychiatric symptoms in the absence of secondary gain. Individuals with factitious disorder are motivated by obtaining sympathy for being ill and, sometimes, these patients will induce physical symptoms or illness by injecting themselves with substances such as insulin or fecal material.

Typical presenting symptoms for PE include specific findings such as pleural effusion or atelectasis. Bedside echocardiography can be helpful in the evaluation of pulmonary embolism. Large pulmonary embolisms cause markedly elevated pulmonary arterial pressure. This leads to right ventricular dysfunction which can be seen with echocardiography. This sign is highly specific for acute pulmonary embolism. Other echocardiographic signs of pulmonary embolism include a dilated right ventricular cavity and tricuspid regurgitation (TR). Tricuspid regurgitation occurs for two reasons. The dilated right ventricular cavity pulls apart the tricuspid valve annulus allowing for leakage. Also, the elevated pulmonary pressure increases right ventricular pressure, which forces blood backward through the tricuspid valve into the right atrium. The massive DVT obstructs venous drainage of the entire lower extremity, leading to severe pain, swelling, and cyanosis. Arterial blood supply to the lower extremity is impaired, which causes distal cyanosis and ischemia Definitivemanagement of PCDis emergent medical thrombolysisand/orthrombectomy.While awaiting definitive therapy with thrombolysis or thrombectomy, it is important to start anticoagulation with intravenous unfractionated heparin. Answer A (incorrect answer): This patient does not have any symptoms that suggest pulmonary embolism (PE). thrombosisinhospitalizedpatients.Theydonothavearoleintheacutemanag gementof Dv T.

questions.question: A 76-year-old woman presents to the hospital for severe dyspnea. Emergency department evaluation reveals a submassive pulmonary embolism and right femoral deep venous thrombosis. She is treated with intravenous heparin and admitted to the hospital. Three days later, the heparin is stopped, and she is transitioned to oral rivaroxaban in preparation for

options.B: Discontinue rivaroxaban and monitor pulmonary status
options.C: Discontinue rivaroxaban and perform pulmonary thrombectomy
options.D: Discontinue rivaroxaban and place inferior vena cava filter
options.E: Discontinue rivaroxaban and start intravenous heparin

questions.explanation: Explanation Pulmonary Critical Care>Other Topics>DVTand Pulmonary Embolism IVC Filter ·Used in high-risk DVT patients ·Alsopatients with contraindication to anticoagulation ·Placed to prevent pulmonary embolism 25 mm Answer D (correct answer): This patient initially presented with pulmonary embolism and deep venous thrombosis (PE/Dv T) and was appropriately treated with intravenous anticoagulation. Patients that are initially administered intravenous or subcutaneous anticoagulation are typically transitioned to oral anticoagulants prior to discharge. Unfortunately, this patient developed a complication of anticoagulation and suffered an upper gastrointestinal bleed. Patientswithaseverebleedingcomplicationofanticoagulationshouldhaveanticoagulantmedications stopped. In addition, this patient should have placement of an inferior vena cava (Ivc) filter. IVC filters are placed if patients who have complications on anticoagulation, or those who have a contraindication to starting anticoagulation. Answer A (incorrect answer): This patient has a significant gastrointestinal bleed; therefore, anticoagulation needs to be stopped. additional PEfromher DVT. questions.question: A 31-year-old man is admitted to the intensive care unit for altered mental status. He was found unconscious in a local park, surrounded by needles and drug paraphernalia. Per report from emergency medical service providers, he temporarily awoke after naloxone administration, but then became comatose again within minutes. He was intubated on arrival to the emergency department. Toxicology screen was positive for benzodiazepines and opiates. His past medical, social, and family mode, with tidal volume set to 550 mL, positive end-expiratory pressure of 5 cm H2O, respiratory rate of 16/min, and Fi02 of
questions.explanation: Explanation Pulmonary Critical Care>Critical Care>Respiratory Failure Endof endotracheal tube Carina Answer A (correct answer): This patient has a malpositioned endotracheal tube, which has been advanced too far.The tip should be above the carina but is located in his right mainstem bronchus.Endotracheal tubes advanced past the carina into a mainstem bronchus will aerate only one lung. Malposition is often detected early after intubation by pulmonary auscultation which reveals absent breath sounds in one lung. If the endotracheal tube remains in an abnormal position, hypoxemia can develop. Chest x-ray confirms the diagnosis by showing the tip of the endotracheal tube past the carina. Other imaging findings of right mainstem bronchus intubation can include leftward mediastinal shifting and elevated hemidiaphragm on the left, which both suggest under-inflation of the left lung. Answer B (incorrect answer): Mechanically ventilated patients that are hypoxemic should have either the Fi O 2 important to confirm that the endotracheal tube is properly positioned. Answer C(incorrect answer): Chest tubes are placed for treatment of pneumothorax or pleural effusion. Although this decreased breath sounds can occur with pneumothorax, this man's chest x-ray shows a right mainstem intubation.

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman is brought by ambulance to the emergency room due to altered mental status. The patient is lethargic and unable to provide reliable history. Temperature is 99.59F, pulse is 48/min, blood pressure is 104/70 mmHg, respiratory rate is 8/min, and oxygen saturation is 97% on nasal cannula oxygen. The patient is arousable only with sternal rub. Lungs are clear to auscultation. Heart sounds are regular but bradycardic without murmurs or gallops. Arterial blood gas is obtained with results displayed below. This patient's respiratory failure is due to which of the following mechanisms?
questions.explanation: Explanation Pulmonary Critical Care>Critical Care>Respiratory Failure Acute Respiratory Failure ·Inadequateoxygenationofblood ·Low Pa 02 or 02 sat % ·V/Q mismatch ·Shunting ·Diffusion impairment ·Inadequateexcretionof Co 2 ·Elevated Pa CO 2 ·Always indicates hypoventilation ·Increased dead space Answer A (correct answer): This patient is presenting with acute hypercapnic respiratory failure, as indicated by theelevated CO 2 level.Hypercapniaisalways associatedwithalveolarhypoventilation.The alveolarminute V(A) = RR x (TV - DS) Where RR is respiratory rate, TV is tidal volume, and Ds is dead space. When respiratory rate or tidal volume increase,alveolarventilationincreases,andviceversa.Paco 2 is inverselycorrelatedwiththealveolar ventilation (i.e.,moreventilation leads tolower Pa CO 2 and vice versa). This patient is suffering from an opiate overdose, as suggested by hypopnea (slow breathing), bradycardia, and altered mental status. Pinpoint pupils are also a common finding. Opiate overdose typically leads to alveolar hypoventilation from low respiratory rate and tidal volume, which leads to elevated Pa CO 2. Note that this patient has a normal Pa O 2. While hypoventilation can cause hypoxemia, this patient has been given supplemental oxygen to maintain a normal oxygen level. In cases of alveolar hypoventilation, supplemental oxygen often normalizes the Pa O 2, but has no effect on Pa CO 2. To improve Pa CO 2, the minute ventilation must increase, either through higher respiratory rate or higher tidal volume. Answers B,D,and E (incorrect answers):Diffusion impairment, shunting,and ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatcharemechanismsofhypoxemicrespiratoryfailure.Theycancausehypoxemiabutnotelevated Paco 2.

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman is brought by ambulance to the emergency room due to altered mental status. The patient is lethargic and unable to provide a history. She is intubated and admitted to the intensive care unit. She is placed on volume control mechanical ventilation, with tidal volume set to 800 mL, positive end-expiratory pressure of 5 cm H20, respiratory rate of 12/min, and Fio2 of 50%. The patient's weight is 60 kg. Her current arterial blood gas results are displayed below. Chest x-ray step in management?

When initiating volume-control, typical settings include tidal volume of 6 to 8 m L/kg, respiratory rate of 12 to 16, and positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) of 5 cm H 2 O. This patient's tidal volume is set at 800 m L which is too high. Her tidal volume should be between 360 to 480 m L based on her weight of 60 kg. Reducing the tidal volume will improve her respiratory alkalosis. Answer A (incorrect answer): Endotracheal tubes should be 2 to 5 cm above the carina. This patient has proper positioning. Answer B(incorrectanswer):Althoughdecreasingrespiratoryratewouldalsoimproverespiratoryalkalosis,this

questions.question: A 53-year-old man is admitted to the intensive care unit with community-acquired pneumonia and acute respiratory distress syndrome. The patient is on volume control mechanical ventilation, with tidal volume set to 5o0 ml, positive end-expiratory pressure of 5 cm H2O, respiratory rate of 20/min, and Fi02 of 100%. The patient weighs 90 kg. His most recent arterial blood gas is displayed below. A chest x-ray is obtained showing the endotracheal tube at 3.5 cm above the carina, with diffuse
questions.explanation: Explanation Pulmonary Critical Care>Critical Care>Respiratory Failure Mechanical Ventilation(Management Basics) Afterintubation,check for proper placement (2-5 cm above carina) and ABG Situation Adjustment pa CO, is high + respiratory acidosis Increase RR/VTtoincreaseventilation pacoislow+respiratory alkalosis Decrease RR/VTtodecreaseventilation FIO and PEEP in steps to achieve pa O 2 >60 mmHg pa 0, is low pa 0, is high Decrease FI 0 in stepsto 50% and then slowly reduce PEEP in 3-5 mmHg increments, maintaining pa 0 >60 Refractory Hypoxemia Pressure control mode,proneventilation,or Ec Mo ↑Peak Pressure Can be elevated with low lung compliance, but also ↑ airway resistance (mucus plugging, obstructed ET tube) ↑ Plateau Pressure Elevated with lowlung compliance Answer D (correct answer): This patient is admitted to the intensive care unit due to pneumonia complicated by bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, as seen in this case. This patient is currently hypoxemic on his current ventilator settings, as his Pa O 2 is 50 mmHg, while his goal should be greater than 60 mmHg. In order to increase oxygenation, either Fi O 2 or positive end expiratory pressure (PEEP) should be increased. This patient is on the maximum Fi O 2 currently at 100%. His current PEEP should be increased in order to improve oxygenation. Patientswith ARDSareventilatedwithlowtidalvolumesandhigh PEEP.Studieshaveshownlowermortality and more ventilator-free days in patients managed with this ventilator strategy. Answer A (incorrect answer): This patient is hypoxemic and has a goal Pa O 2 of greater than 60 mmHg. Leaving him on the current settings may deprive vital organs of oxygen. Answer B (incorrect answer): This patient is hypoxemic and decreasing Fi O 2 will further worsen the hypoxemia. patient tolerates higher levels of PEEP, the Fi O 2 should be weaned down.

questions.question: A 75-year-old man is admitted to the intensive care unit with severe community acquired pneumonia that has caused acute s u s tracing is displayed below (normal pressure is less than 30 cm H2O). which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's elevated pulmonary pressure?
questions.explanation: Explanation Pulmonary Critical Care>Critical Care>Respiratory Failure Inspiratory Hold ·Ventilator technique to evaluatehighpressures Peak pressure Plateau pressure ·Set tidal volume delivered ·Airflow stopped ·Eliminates flow resistance ·Peak pressure measured ·“Plateau pressure”measured Pressure ·Elastic pressure plus PEEP Time Significance Peak Pressure Plateau Pressure High Low compliance High High Airway Resistance Normal Answer D (correct answer):This patient is presenting with elevated pulmonary pressures while undergoing mechanicalventilation.Whileonvolumecontrol ventilation,thepatientreceivesa setvolume ofair ata set respiratory rate. Airway pressure rises until the machine delivers the set tidal volume. In some cases, airway pressures canbecome excessive causing theventilatorto alarm. When elevated inspiratory pulmonary pressure occurs, the first diagnostic step is to perform an inspiratory hold in which the full tidal volume is delivered, then held momentarily in the lungs without allowing exhalation. This maneuver will generate a graph of pressure over time with two peaks as shown in the graph in the question. The first peak is the peak pressure, the highest pressure that occurs while the breath is being delivered. This pressure is influenced by compliance of the lungs and airway flow resistance (because air is moving and meeting resistance). The second peak pressure is the plateau pressure (named because it forms a plateau in the graph) and is not affected by airway resistance since flow in or out of the system is zero. The plateau pressure is thereforeonlyaffectedbylungcompliance. Normal airway pressures should not exceed 25 cm H 2 o. In the question, the peak pressure is elevated at ~40 cm resistance.Airway resistance can be elevated if there is blockage of the endotracheal tube (e.g., biting the tube) or blockage of the airways (e.g., bronchoconstriction or mucus plugging). Mucous plugging is common in intubated patients and leads to elevated airway pressures. The treatment is ingn redse

questions.question: A 95-year-old man presents to the emergency department for dyspnea. The patient reports 24 hours of fever, chills, productive cough and dyspnea. His past medical history is notable for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, and he is on 4 L/min of 134/84 mmHg, respiratory rate is 18/min, and oxygen saturation is 88% on 6 L/min nasal cannula. The patient is resting regular without murmurs or gallops. Lung sounds reveal diffuse fine rales in the mid and lower lung fields bilaterally. A chest x- ray demonstrates evidence of right lower lobe pneumonia superimposed on his baseline pulmonary fibrosis. Arterial blood management?

options.A: Intubate patient and start mechanical ventilation
options.C: Place patient on 8 L/min of oxygen via venti face mask

questions.explanation: Explanation Pulmonary Critical Care>Critical Care>Respiratory Failure Acute Respiratory Failure Treatments 02 Delivery Method Nasal cannula 2-6 L/min (Fi 02 24-40%) Face mask 5-8 L/min (Fi 02 30-50%) Venti mask 6-10 L/min (Fi 02 24-50%) Non-rebreather 8-10 L/min (Fi 02 60-80%) 10-60 L/min (Fi 02 up to 100%) High flow nasal cannula Noninvasive Ventilation Fi 02 up to 100% Mechanical Ventilation Fi 02 up to 100% Answer C(correct answer):This patient is presenting with acute on chronichypoxemic respiratoryfailure.He flowrateachievablevianasalcannula. The patient is not in acute respiratory distress and is not tachypneic or using accessory muscles. In addition, his arterial blood gas shows that he is appropriately exchanging CO 2, with near normal pH and Pa CO 2. Therefore, thenextbeststepin managementwouldbe toincreasethe amountofoxygen delivered to thepatient. Providing oxygen therapy via a venti mask can deliver up to 10 L/min of oxygen (up to Fi 02 ~ 50%). A venti mask is a normal face mask that uses a venti valve, which is a type of valve that can strictly regulate the amountofoxygendeliveredtothemask. Answer A(incorrectanswer):Intubationandmechanicalventilationisrequired inpatientswithacute respiratory distress or impending respiratory failure. If this patient were to worsen clinically (i.e., become more tachypneic, develop increased work of breathing, worsening hypercapnia or hypoxemia), then mechanical ventilation may be necessary. Answer B (incorrect answer): This patient is currently hypoxemic, so maintaining current oxygen therapy would risk ischemia of vital organs.
